When strategy meets action, there's a slim chance for success. FTL doesn't know what a no-win situation is, and smashes through the gaming barrier of the two genres with pinpoint accuracy. This game belongs in your library. Here's why:
Space. The final frontier. These are the voyages of you in a tiny little vessel struggling to stay ahead of a fleet that is gunning for you with big, nasty battle-cruisers capable of vaporizing your ship and your crew with it.
...but not if you're clever.
FTL puts you in the seat of the captain, granting you the freedom to wage war, (or not) at your discretion. You place people at the con, promote others to chief engineer, or grant them control over the weapon systems. It's up to you, and their lives are riding on your ability to think on your feet. If you've ever seen an episode of Star Trek, you know that things don't ever go the way you plan them to. The same applies here.
Should you grant sanctuary to a rogue mantis? Will you risk the lives of your crew to stop a fire spreading on a colony? Dare you grant mercy to the crew of the warships trying to kill you?
The choices are real, and the consequences can come back to haunt you on your next jump. So many times have I been stuck staring at the screen, with the grim understanding that I've just backed myself into a corner. However improbable though, your split-second decisions can turn the tide of war in your favor, yielding great riches or rare devices for your ship.
The soundtrack is stimulating. With a score by Ben Prunty that not only keeps you pumped, but grants that delightful sense of immersion through ambience, you'll be wanting the OST by the end of your first playthrough. Invest in the soundtrack bundle.
The dialogue is believable, and well-crafted. You'll never meet a situation that you're bored by, as you meet not only malicious bounty hunters, but obscure traders who sell black-market goods in the dark corners of the galaxy. With the ability to name and customize your crew, the chance to lose yourself in the cast of your very own sci-fi thriller is quite likely.
You'll get attached to ships. You'll invest great time and effort into crafting the perfect frigate or cruiser, stealth bomber or invasion drop-ship as you find new and creative ways to travel the universe. You'll regret losing crew-mates, and you'll feel genuine rage at the overwhelmingly intelligent AI as they access the weaknesses of your vessel and turn your ship into a bucket of holes.
Most of all though; you'll never look back and question that this game was money well-spent. FTL is a must-have for any person who wants to get infinite-replay value on the bridge of a starship. Don't take my word for it though...

The game is alright.. I got it for 3 dollars, so my opinion is mildly biased.
Pros
---------
- Cool graphics.
- Cool creation system.
- Enemies are cool enough for what the game tries to be.
- Very unique compared to the usual 8-bit games.
- Clever use of randomly found objects like 'nailboxes' and 'tubes' to create and do certain things.
- Sound effects feel professionally done and very, very immersive.
Cons
---------
- Is done through a level system, not an open world, which this type of game SHOULD be.
- Items are super, super tough to see and pick up. You track back through areas a few times just trying to find them.
- Highlighted objectives are poorly highlighted. Makes seeing them difficult.
- Menu and HUB feels super amateur and poorly done.
- Game is very annoying to try to get in to at first. I died to a wall that was just waving colors and had 0 idea it was somehow supposed to be an enemy. Everything else isn't insta-death, but the wall was.
- Some sounds are VERY, VERY annoying to the point where you hate being in certain areas. There's 'factory-like' settings with huge machinery, and while the sound effects are really good, some are just scratching noises or VERY loud machine-like noises that actually make it sound really, really unpleasant and loud. Too much of a good thing becomes a bad thing.
- The graphics lose their appeal after a little bit and make the game feel kind of annoying when 90% of your screen is actually just black all the time. It makes environments more immersive but makes it feel cluttered and claustrophobic almost for the player. Again, too much of a good thing becomes a bad thing.
- Little variety with graphics and/or settings.
- NOT a $13.99 game whatsoever.
Overall the game is good. Is it great? No. Does it have its problems? Many, maybe even more so than positives, but overall there will be people that will find it good. If you're a "sensitive" gamer like I am who gets irritated by unordinary things like super bright weird colors shooting across your screen randomly, weird sound effects that just sound really unpleasant, a poorly done minimalist HUD, etc etc, then sit this one out. If you're more casual and can handle a bit of annoyance, go for it, but buy it when it's on sale.

Takes Portal type puzzle solving up exponentially.  In Antichamber you don't just have to solve the puzzle based on the standard mechanics of objects around you, but you have to discover what those mechanics are, from their abilities to their limitations, and usually entirely on your own.  The world itself has its own set of rules (or extreme bending of rules, like an Escher-scape) that you have to discover, remember, and exploit.  The artstyle is simple and colorful, the world has a consistent aura of mystery about it, and while some puzzles can be frustrating at first it's all the more rewarding when you figure things out.  If you enjoy solving very challenging puzzles and mind-bending maze running in non-euclidean space, I absolutely recommend.

When I first got this game I was undecided, I thought that it was sometimes a little slow and sometimes frantic and in this, I thought that the game pacing was off. It was not until I got further into the story that I realised why I loved the story, the progression, the fights, the dialogue options and most of all the customisation. I love this game because it takes me back to a time where games kicked you down and tried everything to keep you down. I cannot tell you how many times I lost most of my team because my spacing was either too tight or too loose (you need to keep to the Goldylocks method in this game ie - just right).
In my experience, this game, while brutal if you do not know the basics in either of the lore or the mechanics is at the same time extremely easy to pick up and play. The recorded time played (17 hours) is actually all from about 5 days where I played nothing else but this game. I created different characters and different classes and I (again with the Goldylocks) found the perfect middle ground of tactically punishing if you slip up, but oh so pleasing when you walk into a mission 4 strong and you walk out the same way. I grew attached to my team after a while and I really did care about them if they were taking too much damage or if they were kept in the back without tasting the action of the fight.
Overall, I really believe that this is one of, if not the best, team based strategy games where you also have a dash of RPG and a hint (really bit hint) of just one more turn/mission.
Overall opinion, brilliant and looking forward to playing through as a really bad guy next time (they really do have more fun it seems ;) )

As far as Minimum Requirements go I run Windows 7-64-bit and I had 40GB of HDD space. Everything else I fail. DDR3 RAM, I still run DDR2. i5 3.3GHz CPU, I still run a Q6600 2.4GHz. NVidia GTX560, still running a GTX460 SE. But it still runs perfectly fine.
As for the game itself,  were you to remove almost all the clunkiness from Dead Island and introduce some of the working elements of Far Cry 3/4 and Skyrim and you'd basically arive at something resembling the finished product here.
At just over 20 hours in I can honestly say the only 2 elements that bother me are the rate of decay on weapons and the wonky SAVE system. Weapon breakage, while nowhere near as bad as it was in Dead Island, can still be frustrating when you get a weapon modded out the way you want only to lose it to breakage a few hours later. This is, of course, simply me nitpicking just to find something I am not enjoying. The SAVE system seems a little wonky as well when switching between COOP and SP in that you'll get to Point C with the friends you were playing with and then load into your single player and instead of saving at Point C where you all clearly got to it will set those who weren't hosting back at Point A in their stories. Can be tedious repeating quests to keep single player games concurrent with COOP, BUT the extra XP from repeating can be a boon. So, that's more a wash than an actual negative.
tl:dr = Buy it. Play it. Enjoy it.

It is not often that I buy games as soon as they come out, but me and a few other friends decided to take the plunge and get the game. I didn't expect much at first, I have played my fair share of zombie games and they all seem pretty similar. That is where Dying Light surprised me. I was so pleasantly surprised to find out how fun this game is. The weapons are really neat and the upgrades add a good depth of customizability and uniqueness to every weapon. The guns leave a bit to be desired but I don’t mind. The upgrade system for weapons is actually very good. I'm not normally an advocate for weapons that degrade from use, but dying light handles this quite well, with various upgrades you can modify the durability, damage, or handling of the weapon by finding weapon mods which are scattered throughout the city. I played a few hours solo but almost exclusively played it with a friend, let me say this now, playing with a friend, or better yet four, makes the game immensely more fun. The game is pretty demanding and you will need a pretty decent PC to run it, the settings and FPS range are very strict, between max settings and min setting at 1440p I was only see about a 10 fps difference. Another problem I ran into was certain areas ran butter smooth and some just wrecked my FPS, could be the game, could be my system but it is something to note.
The story was somewhat predictable and I didn’t get very attached to the characters, which is what the game wants you to do, but I did have some good variety and was quite long. My friend and I played the game for about 2 1/2 to 3 weeks before finishing it, but we played Extremely thorough and stopped at every police car and van we saw. We also did a large amount of side quests and missions, while doing some zombie killing on the way. The day and night cycle is very well done and is really fun. Normally in games it is not a big deal to go out at night, but the very first night, I was sweating bullets. The night time play really does make that game that much more immersive and dare I say, terrifying, the monsters that are out at night are scary and quick, a deadly combo, later in the game this is less of an issue but early on being out at night is very difficult.
Depending on how thorough you are and how often you play will change your experience quite a bit, My friend and I played exclusively together and I only played a few hours solo. Doing most side quests and stopping at any spot to help someone, do an air drop, or loot a police car while doing the story gave us about 30 hours of play time. We are still doing side quests and awaiting DLC, which leaves MUCH to be desired, only a couple short, and I mean short missions for the first drop. The weapons and upgrade system leaves you always checking shops, looting vans for upgrades, and grinding out levels to get better gear, the blueprint system is ok but I found myself sticking to toxic and bleed, the fire and shock seem cool on paper but are not so fun in reality, killing a zombie sets them on fire then they fall at your feet, setting you on fire, not good, same with electricity.
What really makes this game unique in its own way is the parkour, its like assassins creed meets left for dead, with a hint of borderlands. It adds a whole new way to explore the environment, you can play stealthy, running on rooftops, or go through the streets killing everything in site. You will also be in for a real treat when you hit level 13 on your survivor rank, one of the three skill trees, and it completely changes the game. Speaking of skill trees, there are three in total, survivor, agility, and power. Towards the beginning the skills are very good and change the way you play, as you progress they get less and less unique and really usable, and are just fillers. The skill trees add yet another form of replayability and dynamics to the game that leaves you grinding for more XP to get that new ability or the next weapon in the shop.
Overall I am extremely happy with my purchase and so are my friends, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a very good game for COOP play and if you love looting games and upgrading your gear, that makes it even better. I would but it again in a heartbeat and love to go back and play. It is a very fun game that is probably the best zombie game I have played in a long time.

As the Silver Surfer, Herald of Galactus and bestowed with the Power Cosmic, approaches planet Earth, he is subdued by Dr. Doom and his surfboard broken into several cosmic bricks. The supervillain then plans to use these to conquer the world with a little help from Abomination, Loki, Venom, and of course, his invention: Dr. Doom’s Doomray of Doom.
LEGO MARVEL Super Heroes (October 2013) is not only LEGO’s and Traveller’s Tales second sandbox game (the first being LEGO City Undercover, March 2013), no, it is also whole lot of fun play while not straying from the LEGO formula. In the fashion of previous titles, players go through 15 different levels where they take on the roll of various Marvel Comics superheroes to try to save the day. Sadly, as with its predecessors, players are required to know the characters as well as the lore behind them beforehand to understand their motivations. In this particular case, it might therefore be advisable to have either read the comics or watched several of the Marvel-based superhero motion pictures starting with X-Men (2000) down to Marvel’s The Avengers (2012), as this production references a lot of them, be they by Sony, 20th Century Fox, or Marvel Studios themselves.
Of course, as this is by LEGO, family friendliness is at its core. Any violent scenes from the movies has been toned down and MARVEL Super Heroes even features two save slots, so that siblings can share one copy. Furthermore, a second player can join or leave a session at any point, given that they are in the same room as the first player. This title only supports local but not online multiplayer. With that in mind, even though it is possible to use a keyboard, the game heavily relies on the usage of an analog stick to maneuver and should definitely be played with a controller, preferably an Xbox 360 one.
Speaking of controls, they can be a bit of a hassle. Like other sandbox games, this production includes a slurry of activities alongside the main story. Players can engage in car or flying races, obstacle courses, or simple fetch quests, giving the game around 35-40 hours of content. Unfortunately, while most of the stuff is a lot of fun, the controls get in the way of some of the side activities. The remote controlled car challenge on a rooftop in the Lower East Side, for example, can take up to an hour to complete and is very frustrating to get through. There, the camera will assume a top-down position and the vehicle will be controlled like a real RC, which means that going left or right are dependant on where the car is facing, which gets confusing quickly. Another downside is this game’s inconsistent sign posting. For example, when players want to find the gold brick hidden around the Empire State University campus, they are initially given a trail of gold coins to follow, which then mysteriously ends with no other obvious clues given. Hadn’t it been for a YouTube video, I might not have figured out how to find the brick.
Finishing these side quests or replaying previously visited stages, of course, rewards one with new playable characters. And there are a lot of big names to choose from with 132 Marvel Comics heroes, villains, as well as side characters in the base game, and an additional 16 DLC characters spread out over two packs. So, it’s highly likely that one’s favorite is hiding amongst them somewhere. Sadly, not all of them are equally well-designed, with some, like Gwen Stacey or Aunt May, left without any special abilities at all. It would’ve been nice if the developers had given them unique side missions, or abilities like lock picking, or anything, really to justify picking them up. Even something as outlandish as Lex Luthor’s Warsuit (yeah, I know that that’s DC) would have been fine.
By and large the game should run pretty smoothly on older computers, like the 32-bit Windows Vista Home Premium desktop PC with an Intel Core 2 CPU, 3070 MB RAM, DirectX 11, and a GeForce 9500 GT graphics card that I used. There, it fluctuates between 20-30 fps (frames per second) with everything set to high, so parents shouldn’t be worried about that. However, a couple of minor bugs might pop up here and there.
Occasionally, when swapping out heroes, the game would get stuck in the switch animation and then transform every playable character into a random citizen, while at other times, I had Jean Grey get stuck between two floors while free roaming through New York. The truly disturbing bugs though, popped up during boss battles:
During the boss fight in stage 6: Red Head Detention, Captain America is expected to use his shield to approach the bad guy, but when he did do so during the freeplay of the level, nothing happened. At that point, I had unlocked the classic outfit for Captain America, but the game wouldn’t let me progress unless I used the default costume. Then, during the story playthrough of stage 14: A Doom With a View, The Thing stood in the top left corner of the arena when a Doombot (V-Series) ran towards it. The bot got stuck and The Thing was too large to walk past it, so the boss fight could not continue. When these bugs showed up, the only way to continue was to turn the game off and on again in order to continue playing.
Overall, even though it still carries over some of the bad controls from previous titles, LEGO MARVEL Super Heroes is one of the best LEGO games out there. The story is filled with comedy and everything simply looks adorable. However, like its predecessors, the game sometimes has a hard time communicating what it wants players to do, or just straight up forgets to tell them. Despite that, the amount of fun that’s to be had easily makes up for that and the unlockable content is also a nice addition.

I've wanted to get this game ever since it came out. Bit of a history lesson, not only do I love Marvel Comics
, but I also love Lego, especially their video games. If anyone remembers the Lego Harry Potter Creator game on PC that came out in the late 90s, I loved playing that. I had a PlayStation 2 growing up, and I had pretty much every Lego game that was released on it. The Star Wars games, the Indiana Jones games, you name it. So, when I heard that a Lego game was finally going to be made with Marvel characters, you can bet I was excited. Problem was..I didn't have a console to play the game on. So, when I saw that the game was on sale during the Steam Summer Sale, along with pretty much every other Lego game, I knew I had to pick it up.
I honestly don't have any issues with how the game looks, plays, or runs on my HP laptop. It's 2 years old or so, has Windows 10, and this game has run perfectly fine. I don't know what frame rate it's usually at, but I've never experienced any major frame drops.
The world of Lego Marvel is a strange blend of the comics universe, with elements of the Cinematic Universe mixed in. You have a classic looking Captain America, Wolverine, and Hulk, with an African American Nick Fury, Phil Coulson (voiced by Clark Gregg), and an Iron Man obviously inspired by Robert Downey Jr. And while I love the Marvel movies, I would have liked to see more comic-accurate versions of some of these characters.
One thing I have to point out quickly is that the writing....it's incredibly cheesy. Sometimes, I really don't like it. But then other times, I find myself laughing at just
cheesy they make it, and I know it's intentional.
The game plays like what I assume most Lego games play like on PC, which isn't bad, not at all. I actually like the controls. And giving the player the option to remap controls is nice, in case there is a button that doesn't make sense, or is awkward to press. Like, maybe someone's running around and wants to press ` to attack, or q because it's near w.
After a good 7 hours with the game, I can conclude that
, I have enjoyed Lego Marvel Super Heroes. Whether it's exploring New York City, or just running over Captain America with the Britmobile, this game has made me cringe, and laugh in pure enjoyment in a single session. That's impressive. If you have $6 to spare, and are looking for a puzzle/action/exploration game, and just happen to like Lego or Marvel, I'd say pick this up.

Okay, let's be real honest for a moment. South Park is arguably one of the most offensive shows on TV. It's also arguably one of the funniest. So, I expect that people are going to be pretty polarized about a game featuring the same humor as the show. For that reason, I'll seperate this review into two parts, first covering the game mechanics, sound, etc., and then covering the content.
Mechanics: 4/5
The mechanics of the game, i.e. input notification and intuity, are actually very good. Combat is turn-based and thus is not hard to learn. Some bosses seem to be fairly hard to beat, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Attacking and defending is based on a "Quick Time" prompt where you press a button when you see a flash of some kind. Not hard to learn, but some people may have problems with poor quality controllers.
It should be obvious to most that a Port-to-PC is going to work better with a controller, but it was still very easy to play with M-n-K.
Controls: 5/5
The game has some pretty snappy, dead on target controls as long as you are using a controller like the Logitech F510 or the Microsoft controller. Sometimes when using the M-n-K there was a missed response or a failed timing, and a few embarassing wrong key presses, but overall it was still quite playable without a controller.
To be honest, the game played much better than I had expected and very similar to any top dollar game. As I said, I had a few issues with using computer keyboard and mouse, but when I switched to using my Logitech F510 controller, they all went away. If you're using the Microsft console controller you shouldn't have any problems, as I tested that as well. No gaurantees on how other controllers will perform.
The only issue I had, was with learning some of the "dragon shouts" as they didn't seem to convey the steps input moment needed quite accurately.
Sound: 5/5
The sound is actually very impressive, filling my headphones perfectly with directional audio. Given that the game primarily focuses on 1 axis of movement, I would have been very disappointed if the developers couldn't get left and right audio cues correct.
Music: 5/5
The music is really good, parodying "recent" RPGs like Skyrim with the main BGM and portraying a good feeling of immersion overall in the various locations. In addition, many places had radios that would play the various songs from the show, which was funny as heck.
Graphics: 5/5
Uh... It's a South Park game so, the characters look like paper-cutouts filmed with some sort of stop motion to show speech, motion, and facial changes. It looks very much like the show, so if that doesn't bother you the game won't either. I never bothered to check FPS or anything like that since the system requirements are so low, but there's been no lag whatsoever on my rig, even while it's not running to spec due to ram speed issues.
If you've got a "modern" PC with a dual-core running @2GHz, a video card that's come out in the last 5 years  and 4 GB of ram then you should have no problems.
Now I'll cover the content of the game. These won't be rated as it's entirely subjective to the individual.
Humor:
South Park's humor tends to be crass, disgusting and politically incorrect, not unlike a number of other popular TV shows like The Simpsons, Scrubs, Just Shoot Me, or Married With Children, and this game follows that theme reliably. From the Unplanned Parenthood Clinic, to Chef singing on the radio, to Aliens probing you rectally the humor is in your face and unapologetic. Parents, this is not a game I would let young children play, just as I wouldn't let them watch the show, but teens would probably be fine.
Characters:
You have all the usual South Park charactors, from Cartman to Kenny, Token to Tweek. In addition, you have many "Guest" characters as well, such as Mr. Hanky and Al Gore. If you're familiar with the show, you'll be happy.
Overall, I'd recommend this game if you like the show and like RPGs.

Like the first game, Syberia II uses its slow pace and dreamlike atmosphere to immerse the player in its wonderful world of clockwork machinery and snowy landscapes. As an adventure game, it also turned up the puzzle difficulty, sometimes significantly.
Syberia II is, from beginning to end, one large journey, continuing straight from the ending scene of the previous game. Once again, we participate in a long trip of the returning protagonist, Kate Walker and the mysterious heir she chased all the way through the first game, Hans Voralberg.
Syberia II is a sentimental tale, where the theme of the first game has matured into such questions as how long would someone go to fulfil their old dreams before their days run out, and how one can re-evaluate their purpose in life when they find a cause worthy enough to leave everything behind.
As with most stories full of allegories, it is very slow and very dreamlike. The scenery reflects how our protagonists gradually leave the edge of civilisation as the last post of humanity, a small post-Soviet barter town fades into the distance of the vast Russian tundra, where the end of the tracks may hold the answer in their search of the last resting place of the remaining mammoths, the mythical island called Syberia.
The game uses another tool to let the players immerse themselves in its world and atmosphere besides the slow pacing: the puzzles. They don’t use the warped point ‘n’ click logic that ruined many great games, but many of them rely on trial and error or constantly travelling from one end of a large gameplay area to another. The last third of the plot is especially notorious, where the difficulty quickly rises to almost legendary levels.
But all that hardship will be worth it. Worth it for one of the most bittersweet, wonderful endings we can witness in an adventure game.

Conceptually, Fairy Fencer F would seem to be a return to the roots of the JRPG genre: a traditionally-styled game with a distinctly Japanese story and aesthetic. Consider the alliteration in Fairy Fencer F’s title, which calls Final Fantasy to mind, or the game’s development team, which includes composer Nobuo Uematsu and artist Yoshitaka Amano, both of Final Fantasy fame. How unfortunate, then, that Fairy Fencer F is no glorious return to the heyday of the JRPG, but rather a strange, distorted effort, terrifically fun in bursts but plagued by unfortunate technical issues.
Fairy Fencer F is the story of young warrior Fang and his fairy partner, Eryn. Fang's excessively cynical and derogatory attitude is likely to grate within mere minutes of starting the game, in which he constantly complains about his new path in life. You see, as the game begins, Fang is told by a shopkeeper that if he is capable of pulling out a strange sword embedded in a rock, he will be granted any wish he desires. All he wants is tasty food (a running obsession that becomes unfunny almost instantly), but, upon yanking out the sword, he is greeted by semi-amnesiac Eryn, told he is a legendary fencer, and asked to free the world's Goddess from her stasis by finding and using Furies, fairies trapped in mythical weapons. Fang’s annoyance at having such a burden suddenly dropped on him is understandable, but his continued whininess and apathy is exceptionally irksome. Eryn is more likeable, though the moment another female appears on the scene she goes into (similarly unfunny) jealous-possessive-angry mode.
Fairy Fencer F's least irritating character.
I soon met Tiara, a stuck-up, bratty fencer who harbors a genre-standard terrible secret. She also doubles as an exposition machine, teaching you about the plane beyond reality where the Goddess and evil deity are sealed and giving you a free inn to recover at--when she's not being bossy and condescending. Notice a theme here? The majority of Fairy Fencer F's cast was ripped straight from the pages of Anime Character Tropes You Can Implement Easily. Suffice to say, it takes a fair amount of time before a truly likeable character joins the troupe. Certain party members become more tolerable as time goes on, but it's hard to shake those awful first impressions.
Layers of Fear Announcement Trailer
Check out this new psychedelic horror game from the Polish developer Bloober Team.
Saddled with a party of people I would have liked to punch in the face given the opportunity, I ventured out into the exploration portion of Fairy Fencer F. Much to my relief, exploration and combat are a fair bit more energizing than watching barely-animated character cutouts complain to each other. Combat is turn-based with positioning elements: You and your enemies move around a small field and trade blows with each other, launching area-of-effect spells and utilizing strategic positioning to your advantage. The basics aren't tough to grasp, and as you earn more weapon points in battle, you can customize your stat boosts and add multi-hitting combo capabilities to your characters' strikes.
This kind of cringe-worthy dialogue is par for the course.
The majority of Fairy Fencer F's cast was ripped straight from the pages of Anime Character Tropes You Can Implement Easily.
A neat addition to the formula is the tension gauge: as characters attack and use skills, their tension increases and multiplies the damage they deal. Once tension reaches a certain point, characters can "fairize," transforming into quasi-robot-armored fighters with access to special, super-damaging techniques. However, playing overly defensively--using lots of healing items and spells, retreating from enemies, running away from battle--reduces the tension, and if it dips below a certain point, your combat efficacy will suffer. It's a neat system that makes the combat considerably more engaging. It's quite fast-paced, as well--the handy L2 button allows you to skip a lot of long-winded combat animations.
You can find new dungeons to explore at set points in the story, where you'll find some Furies to collect (along with the fairies that inhabit them and/or possibly another fencer). Once you've got a Fury/fairy combo, you can summon the pair to remove one of the binding blades sealing the Goddess and the Vile God. Doing so upgrades the abilities of the fairy, who can then either be assigned to one of your party members or to a dungeon via a process called "world shaping." While the stat bonuses fairies can provide to party members are nothing to be sneezed at (and they also level up through combat), world shaping is particularly cool: by assigning a fairy to a dungeon, you also get persistent effects throughout that dungeon, i.e. an experience boost when defeating enemies. This helps make sub-questing less of an out-and-out grind, as it helps tailor some dungeon settings to your liking. The dungeon romping itself is also more engaging than developer Compile Heart's previous endeavors, with multi-level layouts and traps.
This still frame is only a little slower than the game's average frame rate.
As much as I enjoyed the fundamental combat and dungeon-crawling, it was sometimes difficult for me to enjoy them. In many of the dungeons, Fairy Fencer F suffers from an atrocious and varying framerate, frequently dipping into the sub-20 frames-per-second range. Compile Heart games tend to suffer from this problem, even though the visuals aren't terribly complex, but Fairy Fencer F is particularly awful, to the point where dungeon crawls can lead to motion sickness and headaches.
The irritating cast and miserable framerate dips aside, you must also contend with sudden difficulty spikes, recycled environments, and an inconsistent art style. Even the much-touted Yoshitaka Amano and Nobuo Uematsu’s contributions are disappointing. Amano's contributions are a handful of art concepts, while Uematsu's--or more specifically, Uematsu's team of musicians, the Earthbound Papas’--music is uneven; some tracks are absolutely fantastic, while others are entirely unmemorable. Yet there are glimpses of a game that could have been consistently entertaining: combat, when it's not running like a slideshow, is satisfying; there's a lot of customization available to the player; and that butt-rock theme that plays during fairizing is rousing in much the same way Uematsu's Blue Dragon boss music was.
Fairy Fencer F has its bright spots, but it's not a game I can heartily recommend--there's too much detritus to dig through in order to get to the fun bits. Compile Heart has announced a sequel, so here's to hoping the move to more recent hardware will solve their games’ lingering technical problems--and here's to hoping the resulting games will be better as a result.

You just cannot keep up with those who would pay for crystals to get the Shadowverse daily deal for card pack.And then what happens is that you are restricted in the number of deck types you can field. And then those who are in this position will go around grumbling about this and that card/s, deck/s that they don't have being overpowered.
As for aggro, Shadowverse is quite "anti aggro". Instead Shadowverse is orientated towards combo decks and wins are accomplished by steady reduction of hitpoints OR a surprise burst of damage. If you don't like combo generated burst of damage, DON'T start playing Shadowverse where you have only 20 health points and when a combo kicks in, it usually though not necessarily means game over. Its a east vs west culture thing.
Games are thus designed by intention to be short, anything above turn 10 is pretty epic and both are probably playing control.

As for going for face, aggro decks well lets put it this way, you drop 2 or 3 warded minions before turn 4 and typically, aggro Sword or aggo Bat will concede. And there is ample early board clear available. You want to see aggro being supreme, play Faeria as Yellow. You don't even need to harvest mana from the well.
Play a go for face, face is the place type of deck, prepare to be conceding a lot of times.
I used to harvest on ladder/rank the much gripped about Blood Spawn deck (pre nerf) until they nerfed it and my cheese got moved. Now I harvest aggo. :) If you cannot find the gap in the meta, well, go reddit and call for nerfs and say you want to go back to Hearthstone. I dropped Hearthstone because I found that in Shadowverse, it is much cheaper to maintain my status and infinitely more fun. When I get combo-ed/meme, it actually brings a smile on face while swearing... and I promptly go about trying to recreate that deck if it is new to me.
I strongly suggest that if you are going to play Shadowverse, you be prepared to buy a 1200 crystal set each month. USD29.98. This 1200 crystal will allow you to buy 24 packs over a month using the daily offer. Then save the gold you get  from daily task, enough to buy a pack typically, for buying packs from the quarter expansion. Yes there is a new expansion set every 3 months. The extra cards you can from the daily deal, you liquify for vials (crafting resource) and save them for the new expansion. I am typically able to open 150+ new expansion card packs at the start each expansion this way.
Using this strategy, you will have more than enough resources to get all the cards each expansion. And right now there is offer to for newbies to get 7500 crystals are a discounted price and you can get the discounted price for up to 3 purchases.
Also note that Shadowverse ladder system is newbie friendly. Its operates on a leagues model. There 5 ranks/leagues before Master rank. You don't lose you rank each month but you can stop yourself from ranking up to a more competitive rank if you don't have a competitive card collection. And at Master rank, you compete to be in the top 10000 players for vials and 10 free card packs each month.
Card expansion rotation is expected in 2018 so that should limit the initial financial outlay if you are starting now and decide to be serious about the game. Basic card set and maybe 4 expansions will in play each time. Maybe more than 4. And remember, you don't have to decide so soon, there are tonnes for free packs to get just starting the game and from story mode and you will be insulated from a cut throat competitive because of the league/rank laddering system.
I am pretty sure it will be fun assuming you are not going to be F2P, the meta will change each expansion, people will grip about this and that, there will be nerfs, the meta changes again BUT all the while, there will be plenty of opportunities to harvest the "sheep" decks by using the correct techs against the sheep decks or by using one that specifically targets it.
Your ability to analyze and arrive at a solution against "sheep" decks (aka netdecks) will be be rewarded in Shadowverse. Intelligence gets used and gets you the wins.
Still has some jank in the performance, but goddamm if this isnt a fun thrill of a game.

If you want the short version of a review for Shadowverse, it's less expensive than MTG online, it's more well balanced than Hearthstone, and it has a larger card selection than Gwent. It is, simply put, the most affordable, and next to MTGO, the most well balanced CCG on the market right now.
With that out of the way, we can move to a more detailed review.
Pros:
-Pricing: Shadowverse is, hands down, the cheapest card game to play on the market. The game is incredibly generous with new players, giving players access to nearly 1,600 cards in game start giveaways and easily completed challenges. Once a player has run out of free cards at the start, the game still provides a player with approximately two packs of cards each day, ensuring that even players who play totally for free can remain competitive. The only real reason to pay anything for Shadowverse is if you'd like to play multiple tournament decks in rapid succession, as the free cards can only really maintain one to three competitive decks at a time. As I see it, the biggest appeal of Shadowverse is that the game truly is the only remaining free to play card game on the market, with the exception of CD Projekt's Gwent.
-Balance: Shadowverse stands next to MTGonline as the most well balanced CCG on the market right now. Each of the game's seven classes offer several major routes for deckbuilding, so the ladder is filled with close to a dozen viable archetypes for each class (except Runecraft) at any given time. Shadowverse generally avoids the rock-paper-scissors matchups which plague online CCGs like Shadow Era or Hearthstone by providing so many disparate paths to victory that few decks can be built that completely shut down other strategies.
-'Collectable' Cards: One of the draws of CCGs has always been collecting cards for the variety in gameplay, and in seeing all the pieces of art the game has to offer. Shadowverse certainly delivers in that regard. Card artworks are full of character and life, and offer quite a few good pieces so long as the anime inspired art style appeals to you.
-Evolve System: Shadowverse's evolve mechanic adds a layer of tactical depth and bluffing to the game that makes the game play quite a bit differently from other CCGs. It's difficult to adequately describe the depth that the evolve system grants without experiencing it for oneself, but the system adds quite abit for how simple the concept would seem.
Cons:
-Game Ending Cards: Though veterans of games like MTG or Hearthstone are accustomed to the idea of a finisher card (a monster or spell powerful enough to kill an opponent basically on its own,) new players to the CCG genre should be warned of these cards. Many new players feel cheated as victory can be taken from them by a single card in their opponent's hand, and until new players learn to anticipate and prepare for enemy finishers, dying to an enemy demon or combo finisher can be a very frustrating experience for players just getting started. If you find 'instant win' cards frustrating, Shadowverse might not be the game for you, as many games come down to single finishing blows out of nowhere.
-Voice Acting: as with many games brought over from the land of the rising sun, Shadowverse's voice acting can often feel like listening to two lobotomy patients talk trash over their game of checkers while on horse tranquilizers. If bad voice acting gets under your skin and you like to play games with sound on, Shadowverse will irritate very quickly. (I swear to god, the next time I hear 'Mother, Father, COME ON' I'm never playing Shadowcraft again)
-Net decks: a phenomenon common to all CCGs is that of netdecking (the use of tournament or professionally edited deck lists downloaded from the internet, instead of player generated decks.) While I personally have no issue with net decks, I would be remiss not to warn prospective players that Shadowverse has its fair share of net decks on the ladder.
Conclusion:
Shadowverse, just like any CCG, has its own fair share of problems that can wear on certain players. However, its combination of true free to play collecting, well balanced class system, and surprising tactical depth (and all the anime boobs) allow me to recommend the game wholeheartedly.

Look, I really wish I could just give this a mixed review, so take my thumbs up give a grain of salt.  This is absolutely a game you can have fun with... as long as you don't care about ever beating it.  As long as you're playing it blind, just trying to last a bit longer, it's a very tense and fun and scary experience.
But once you get over that and settle in to trying to actually complete the challenge in front of you, the game loses all its charm.  For starters, you basically have to use your knife to get through the first few levels, and the knife mechanics are awful.  Rather than slashing where you aim, you slash way off to the right of your aim, forcing you to emply bizarre super-gamey strafing to stand a chance.  But even then, the hit detection is awful; I've lost count of how many times my knife clearly clips right through a monster who then proceeds to smack me 3 times in half a second.  But unless you can manage to pull off perfect knife-only runs on levels 1-3, you might as well not even bother continuing the game because you won't have enough life or ammo for later levels.  I hate this so much; the game's gunplay is loads of fun but you're forced to play in a much less entertaining and more frustrating way if you want to succeed.
I'm also very disappointed in the roguelike elements of this game.  You pretty much always get the same items on every level, barring a couple secret room items that are probably useless canguns anyway, meaning that you will always use the exact same strategies in every run.  In fairness, the randomized maps are pretty great and make for some entertaining battlegrounds... you know, assuming that your fights aren't 5 minutes of circling an enemy waving your knife around.
Still, this game was fun when it was fun.  I recommend you get it on sale, have a blast for a few hours, and put it away.

When strategy meets action, there's a slim chance for success. FTL doesn't know what a no-win situation is, and smashes through the gaming barrier of the two genres with pinpoint accuracy. This game belongs in your library. Here's why:
Space. The final frontier. These are the voyages of you in a tiny little vessel struggling to stay ahead of a fleet that is gunning for you with big, nasty battle-cruisers capable of vaporizing your ship and your crew with it.
...but not if you're clever.
FTL puts you in the seat of the captain, granting you the freedom to wage war, (or not) at your discretion. You place people at the con, promote others to chief engineer, or grant them control over the weapon systems. It's up to you, and their lives are riding on your ability to think on your feet. If you've ever seen an episode of Star Trek, you know that things don't ever go the way you plan them to. The same applies here.
Should you grant sanctuary to a rogue mantis? Will you risk the lives of your crew to stop a fire spreading on a colony? Dare you grant mercy to the crew of the warships trying to kill you?
The choices are real, and the consequences can come back to haunt you on your next jump. So many times have I been stuck staring at the screen, with the grim understanding that I've just backed myself into a corner. However improbable though, your split-second decisions can turn the tide of war in your favor, yielding great riches or rare devices for your ship.
The soundtrack is stimulating. With a score by Ben Prunty that not only keeps you pumped, but grants that delightful sense of immersion through ambience, you'll be wanting the OST by the end of your first playthrough. Invest in the soundtrack bundle.
The dialogue is believable, and well-crafted. You'll never meet a situation that you're bored by, as you meet not only malicious bounty hunters, but obscure traders who sell black-market goods in the dark corners of the galaxy. With the ability to name and customize your crew, the chance to lose yourself in the cast of your very own sci-fi thriller is quite likely.
You'll get attached to ships. You'll invest great time and effort into crafting the perfect frigate or cruiser, stealth bomber or invasion drop-ship as you find new and creative ways to travel the universe. You'll regret losing crew-mates, and you'll feel genuine rage at the overwhelmingly intelligent AI as they access the weaknesses of your vessel and turn your ship into a bucket of holes.
Most of all though; you'll never look back and question that this game was money well-spent. FTL is a must-have for any person who wants to get infinite-replay value on the bridge of a starship. Don't take my word for it though...

This game is hard. I mean holy Jesus almighty on a pogo stick, this game is really hard. I've played this game alot, and still haven't made it though Level 6 out of 10. It is also utterly brilliant. It is a roguelike that gives the reward of experience and knowledge for your defeats, rather than new bonuses to help you on your next run. The best you can get is a checkpoint start at a later floor, and you are purposely underpowered if you choose to use this option. From when you start in the cold broom closet on Level 1 to when you are facing down the AI Core on Level 10, you are on your own. A bullet will kill you just as easily. The atmosphere of tension and fear that this creates is palpaple. Peeking around corners for huge minigun wielding zombies, running chased by swarms of taser armed robot drones, or locked in a room with hulking warwalkers, terror will be your primary emotion. The second will be the mixture of relief and sadness as your latest run comes to an end. If you like winning games, then maybe this isn't your cup of tea, most people will never complete this game. If you want a wild ride, and the pleasure of inching closer to your goal, learning how to survive in a brutal enviroment, this is your game. Get it right now.

This may be a nit picky but neither the engine nor the gameplay really warrants that change from 3 to a 4. Given the original plan of releasing Enter the Dominatrix as a DLC instead of an entity of its own, it's understandable the game feels like more of an expansion than a sequel. Still, the naming convention raises expectations more than it should.
With that said, SR4 is a fantastic love letter to the entire series as well as geeky culture in general. References pertaining tv shows, movies, internet culture, and video games are littered everywhere. And some of the mechanics SR4 tries to mimick from other games they actually did better in SR4 than the original source.
Gunplay is improved and the progression of gun power and upgradable skills is far smoother than before. Now the scale is completely different as superpowers bump up all the bars. However, relative to crazy, the scaling is much smoother than in SR3 where you go from zero to invincible in a blink even on the highest difficulty.
Writing is still brilliant, hell more brilliant than before. Stupidly fun.
Vehicles are still in and they are still very customizable as well as fun to pilot/drive. They are however highly overshadowed by the fantastic super powers. Some will find this a bit of an odd design decision while others will find it as adding more options on top of the existing.
It's not all rainbows and unicorns however. As of writing this (September, 6 2013), coop is buggy as bananas on a panda. Constant crashes, disconnects, and weird glitches stuck in animation or stuck in a menu transition are pretty commonplace. Patches are happening and things are getting ironed out so hopefully it'll relatively bug free.
All in this expansion (nope not calling you a sequel) is a fantastic send off for the series. It addresses one of the major complaints of SR3 as well as ramp up the humor to wtf?!?! If you love the Saints Row series, give this a try, even if you skipped 3 because of the drastic direction change to more humor less serious, SR4 pays proper homage to the series as a whole and sends it off guns/super punches-a-blazin', This is how a series should end, before it is milked of all dignity and left a drained sack of poopy on the sidewalk shunned for what it has become and with its glory days lost in the poop.

Great character development, story, and interesting combat (see the Neptunia games for gameplay, they're almost practically the same in that regard). About a 20-25 hour playthrough. Lots of touching moments, plot twists, and other stuff that will keep you on the edge of your seat. Worth the 8.99 I spent on it, and wouldn't mind paying $30 for it. I'll be picking up Advent Dark Force for PS4 at full price when it releases. I doubt it will get one, but I really hope this game gets a (true) sequel, ADF is just a remake with some added content and endings, similar to how Neptunia has the the Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth remakes. Also, its much more well optimized compared to Re;Birth 1, whereas that game I get a framerate all over the place (on my laptop, haven't tried either of these on my desktop, due to some issues that will hopefully be resolved soon) FFF I usually get a constant 30 FPS. Controller support is great, played the entire game with a Steam Controller.
+Overall story
+Characters you'll love and get attatched to
+Well optimized port, as well as controller support
+Fantastic Dub, never switched to JP voices
-Some moments in the story are a little silly, or should be explained better in my opinion
-Certain area in the game where I had to grind for awhile, this could be the fact that I was underleveled prior to a boss, or the game just had a weird difficulty spike
-Don't like to complain about the length, but I really wish this game was longer. 20-25 hours is a pretty decent amount of time for a game, especially today, but the devs should take this complaint as a compliment being that I loved every moment so much I wish it could just be a little longer.
Overall, I would give this game 8.75/10. I'm sure I'll be doing another playthrough before I know it, somewhere in the near future. Thank you IFI for releasing this on PC, don't think I would have picked it up on my PS3. Again, I bought this game on sale, but I would easily pay full price for it, on PC or PS3. I'll pay $60 for Advent Dark Force on PS4 when that comes out too. I'm glad I played this game, just goes to show what masterpieces JRPGs can be. Even if this game doesn't have as much of a budget as your Final Fantasy, Persona, whatever you like, its such a different experience from other games I've played and I might even put it up there as one of my Top 20 games. This review was all over the place due to me forcing myself to write it at 4 AM, right after completing the game, but thanks for reading. Hope I convinced you to purchase it, because this game certainly deserves all the money it can get.

I played this game when I was really young, so for me this game is straight nostalgia.  This game and Halo, both coming out on the Xbox pretty much made Microsoft into the console giant it is now. Luckily this game came out on the pc too. The game is ruled by a totalitarian state, known as combine who move people around in camps basically doing whatever they want (killing, torturing, and experiments.) There are also a variety of zombies that can scare the crap out of you when you least expect it. Just wait till you get to Ravenhold. I would pick up garry's mod while your at it. I didn't want to give out to many spoilers in my description. The game goes back and forth between a fast paced, action packed, first person shooter with a lot of enemies coming for you and  puzzles that can leave the best FPS players stumped.

Note:Played the game through to the Ending, except for the Riddler Sidequest. Some gameplay was done in offline mode hence the low hours.
Graphics were pretty good on my 1060 6gb with a i5-3550p. This was sufficient for all settings nearly maxed out save anisotropic filtering turned to to trilinear and I found it neccesary to turn off several of the nvidia bonus features. The game was silky smooth with no stutterings at any point. I experienced not a single crash during the entirety of gameplay.
Controls were absymal, with many awkward key combinations required in combat. I found it very hard to pull off any combos correctly and after purchasing certain upgrades only prompts for those appeared limited variety. Switching between items was a nightmare right up to the finale, as I struggled to get the hacking device out or use a timely batarang. Often the game forced you into using a smoke pellet as the right click function. The vehicle controls were unbelievably difficult, with controls changing depending on mission;left control to fire immobilizers when left\fire clicking was disabled anyway. The control scheme lacks cohesive unity, entirely bizarre and borderline unplayable. At about 65% total completion I had to switch to Easy just to be able to make progress.
The game presents a massive open world with tons of quests, but it is an inch-deep ocean. Side quests get wrapped up way to easily with little story and repetivive controntations. I did all of them except for Riddler, who sees you needing to get 250 trophies simply scattered across Gotham. The last mission to unlock was particularly dissapointing, ending with a simple beatdown of dozens of weak grunts. My favourite was the APC chase scenes, played with a CO-OP parter who fired the immobilizor for me. The towers and checkpoints were pathetic, forcing the player to engage swarms of enemies with no tactics available. Landmine clearing was fun but a bit repetitive with dozens and dozens of tanks flooding at you;later on they dont even try to pretend they are driving in, and simply spawn in from the sky right in front of you. I insta-killed one turret because it landed on my car and its feet couldnt be set on the ground correctly. The car combat wasnt that bad for me. Some of the car races were absurdly frustrating however.
The storyline was dissapointing. Events played out in cliched, over the top scenes that often made me burst out laughing at the absurdity of it all, even when some essential character was being murdered it simply couldnt be taken seriously. The world of Gotham was especially disapointing, a dystopian world that is impossible to believe anyone could or would choose to live here. Its a living hell which should simply recieve a nuclear bomb to its face. Characters kept prattling on about protecting Gotham, but the population only consisted of thugs and the few policemen foolish enough to remain on the Islands.
The most enjoyable part of the game is finally just being done with it, and uninstalling this frustrating waste of time from my hard drive. I got the game for less than 10$ on the steam summer sale, but its largely the time wasted I would rather have back. In the future, never again. Any game that is said to have "batman style combat" will be a game ill steer clear of.

I've only played this game for maybe 15 minutes or so so far, but I can already tell that it's just not my kind of game. I honestly have no idea when and how I got this game (probably as a download code at PAX Prime last year), but it's been sitting in my library for a really long time and I thought I may as well try it out.
I don't think I'll be touching this game a whole lot anymore.
First of all,
Unlike the demographic this game was probably aimed for, I lack any kind of controllers compatible with Steam or even a mouse (laptop player here), so the game is really awkward and clunky as a result; which strongly contrasts with the "intense, fast, Dark Souls hard" gameplay. Navigating the menu is a disaster, shooting and aiming a gun is a nightmare, and melee attacks will usually leave you aimlessly punching while your health slowly depleats.
It's also worth noting that the camera moves like a drunk version of The Sims. It has a top down perspective and the camera moves with you as you move, but it swerves around and never stays in a fixed location and will black out areas from your sight depending on where you are. I can only imagine that this will greatly increase the difficulty of the game later on.
On top of all that, the game just feels dead. The graphics, while intentionally undetailed, make it difficult to distinguish things from one another, so there isn't a strong vision of what's going on. Not to mention that there's no music at all. You could say that this is done to create a feeling of isolation and helplessness ala Metroid, but even that game from 1986 was able to drive home those feelings
If there's one good thing I can say about this game it's that it only has five total trading cards, meaning that you can level it up pretty quickly, but if you feel like you may have the same opinion as me, then look for other games that can help you achieve that with the bonus of being fun. Like I said in the begining, just because I don't like it doesn't necessarily mean that you won't, but I just couldn't get into it.

Not a ton of playtime thus far, but I can still firmly recommend this game. Weapons feel good to use (except the god awful starting revolvers for the gunslinger, but that's just like, my opinion man), the music is good, the art is good, but different from the first game, and gore that sticks around just feels really nice if your squad can hold a single point for multiple rounds and watch the limbs pile up.
Pros
-Best "paint the town red" simulator I've ever found
-Guns sound/feel good to use
-Most maps have a good balance of open space and narrow passages, giving a nice sense of risk to most kiting paths
-You basically never feel safe, for survival horror this is a good thing, I never notice those dang floor grates man
-The characters are actually unique this time, yay!
-I don't have to spend $80 for the sake of character model changes unlike KF1
-Scrakes do this weird spinning attack that is really funny until you realize that their arm is a revved chainsaw
-Fleshpounds feel like they don't take 3 years to kill with field medic weapons and swat SMGs
-Sirens aren't just magical, they're now partially cybernetic, hence why they can scream and literally disarm mid-flight RPG rockets
Cons
-Collectible searches on some maps actually require you to find less items than are on the map, looking at you Zed Landing
-I seriously hate the freakin twin revolvers in this game, this is personal bias
-Sometimes in KF1 you had those "Oh sh*t" moments when a Fleshpound snuck up on you, I raise you 2 Fleshpounds, 2 Scrakes, a Bloat, and 3 Sirens, because that actually happened in one of my games today on round 10
-Sometimes you can sprint face first into a pile of clots and not get grabbed, but the one time you're getting chased by a raging Scrake I guarantee you one will grab you from 8 feet away
-The healing darts on medic weapons literally home in on allies, I've had ZED time pop and shot a healing dart into someone who had 1 arm partway on the edge of my screen instead of the guy at 5 HP dead center of my screen, and I constantly watch my healing darts change trajectory mid-flight to hit my allies, I mained Field Medic in KF1, this feels like a cheap replacement for skill at landing darts for the sake of getting a warm fuzzy feeling when you press M3 literally every time
-I literally cannot tell the different between clots/cysts or gorefasts/gorefiends apart from model differences
Tl;Dr, The game feels food to play, if you liked the first game or something akin to Left for Dead then you will like this game, particularly worth it if you get it on sale.

This is a game unlike an other I've played before, a game that only make you allow the best. As you progress further and further it pushes you to the limits, there are no gimics or cheese in the game only combo based gameplay. It is and can be challenging to only allow the best however the payoff is like a surge of immense dopamine. As a player who has achieved 100% of the trophies and 240% the story it was time well spent.
The game only stuters in some moments in the batmobile so after the dust has settled it is now a fully functional and succesfully ported game and this is comming from a guy plays on a laptop. I played with keyboard and mouse due to not having a controller and the controls are very comfortable on keyboard. Theres no pausing in movement to input a combo while fighting due moving your hand awkardly.
The city and level design are extremely detailed and full of life and colour even though its Gotham city, a city notorious for its crimes in the DC Universe. The city is extremeling appealing to the eyes and the rain, sea, and vegitation are very detailed more so than Arkham City which felt like only 1 theme of being a depressed borough in Gotham where as Arkham Knight has mutiple themes on Miagani, Bleake and Founders island. Bleake island a borough that focuses on horizontal zonation being day to day work life and housing for the Gothamites such as China town. Miagami island a city that takes influences from many captial cities around the the world that includes a monorail station, a grand avenue like street that that is surrounded by the tall skyscrapes. Founders island; a redevelopement project that focuse on coprate skyscrapers like Wayne International, a Gotham Lexcorp building (A nod to Lex Luthor) and Gotham Cental Bank. All in all the greatest city world game to date.
The combat is very similar to its predecessor Arkham Origins who focused more so on he combat than all other aspects of an Arkham Game. However Arkham Origins and City had beter boss fights than Arkham Knight, something Arkham Knight lacked in. The game takes more focus on the people of Gotham and the Arkham Knight's army rather than the villans of Batman. Expect complex levels with varing classses of mobs to enter combat with. The "Predator" amd Stealth of the game is extremeling satisfuying in which it makes the enemies adapt to counter the Batman, you can't do the same stealth takedown more than twice. If you are looking for more of a challenge; play the AR challenges they are unique and challenge you to peform the best and only accept the best.
The Batmobile combat gameplay is very straight foward and easy to play, not much of a challenge. It most feels clunky if you are dong the racing AR challenges and can be frustrating at times. The times where the Batmobile shined was the Riddler challenges and the Campaign for Disarment those were extremely enjoyable and complex. I highly recommend buying the 60's Batmobile racing challenges the racing courses are extremely detailed and full of refrences to the TV show. The game really forces you to use the Batmobile to get to A to B in story missions which it could of toned down a higlight being the Deathstroke/Slade Boss Fight which was a rehashed version of a story mission batmobile boss fight. I wanted to face Slade in hand to hand combat like in Arkham Origins.
The DLC of the game I would recommend being the Seasons of Infamy. The Mr Freeze and Ra's Al Ghul side story lines were extremly fleshed out and provided a variety of gameplay and re shaped Gotham such as making Gotham encased in snow. The Matter of Family of DLC would only be recommended for fans of Batman Universe and want more of Mark Hamil Joker. The DLC gives more characterisation on Joker's stance on the Bat-Family and Tim and Barbras compatibility with each other. Overall the DLC is slightly above average compared to most City.
Like all Stories a conclusion has to made and Arkham Knight accomplshes that surpurbly. The ending is extremely satisfying for a game trilogy and that for Batman's career. The story is extremly engaging and brings much shock value espically for those who are new to the Batman Universe, however if you have read stories such as Knightfall, The Killing Joke, Under the Redhood and even Batman the Animated series you can see plot points and conflcts from a mile away. The story respects source material extremely well but that is to be expected of an Arkham game. However what really engaged me was the characterisation of Bruce and Batman persona. It really brings forth ideas and reflections of what would happen if Batman was to put away the cowl and why he shoulders Gothams safety on his shoulders. The Voice acting by Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamil is amazing they always have to work together if they want to make Batman on media an amazing, marvelous and memorabile story.
So should you buy Arkham Knight? Yes you are definetly getting your moneys worth for only $20. Rocksteady made a ground breaking conclusion to a game series that outshines others like Final Fantasy: Lightning returns, Mass Effect 3, Call of Duty Modern Warfare, Metal Gear Solid 5 (Story Wise and though its a presequel). If this game was released like it was after the PC Port was fixed it would have been game of year hands down. Thank-you for reading this review it was my first and one that was definetlt deserved for Rocksteady's equal Magnun Opus Arkham City.

Teleglitch is an anomaly. That's a play on words, based on the ever-present black goo that engulfs every corner of this game. But seriously folks, I have put in quite a bit of undocumented hours into Teleglitch: Die More Edition and have yet to beat it. So my perspective is from someone who hasn't beat level 6 yet.
I say it's an anomaly, because so many reviews describe it as repetitive, esoteric, self-indulgent, and impossible, and yet so many describe it as more horrifying and entertaining than any other game they've played. From my point of view-- it's a little of both. But, in the end I side with the latter.
Set in a science facility on an uninhabitable planet, placed on the outer reaches of known space. A black gyrating void has breached the compound and corrupted the facilities AI, using the armed robotic soldiers, necrotic tissue specimens, and multi limbed plankton monsters to purge the planet of any human life. Except they missed one... you. As an engineer, living off of canned food for weeks in a broom closet, you leave your haven to find the master teleporter to send you back to Earth. There is only one problem. You have to navigate 10 randomly generated levels of monster and robot infested hallways and courtyards, teleporter by teleporter, until you reach Earth. When you die-- you die. Fortunately, there are chests, hidden caches, and monster dropped equipment to help you along the way. And being an engineer has its perks, like being able to improve your weapons and make devices to warn you of any impending dangers, or shell any impending dangers, or set exploding meat traps for any impending dangers. Did I mention this game has IMPENDING DANGERS?
Sometimes, I just want to end my life after some impending dangers end my hard work, over and over again. It's gets grating after awhile, like the devs designed it to never be beaten by anything that can competently operate a keyboard and mouse. Yet, many have done it... there is hope.
Bottom line is, buy this game. Play through that "This game is too ♥♥♥♥ing hard!!!!!" phase that all of us go through, and learn how to invest time and thought into making your next move, as if you were really stuck on a planet full of impending dangers.
UPDATED REVIEW..................
Since my review I have reached level 9. I stepped away from the game for a week and returned with the passion of a thousand fires and slowly worked my way up. Defeating the Heavy Destroyer Snake is almost muscle memory now, and the Blue Walker even easier. How did I achieve success and guaranteed advantage to eventually beat the game?
Arena.
The weapon combinations in Arena help prioritize which builds you want for certain enemies with each passing level. Plus, it gives incentive to use explosives like the nailbomb, which is the Deus Ex Machina of ammo conservation, otherwise a very overlooked piece of arsenal.
I could go on, but the most important thing I learned during this last bout is that this game is not for casual gamers. It's a game of passion, that separates those who enjoy building twitch skills through negative reinforcement, and those who would rather... I'm not sure how to end that actually. Who wouldn't want to build up their skills?
In an interview, test3 developed the game with testing and building their gaming skills in mind. Roguelike games, and "grind like" games like the Souls series are what keep me interested in gaming, and these kinds of projects draw the line between people who want to game, and those who want to run their thumbs over their phone screens like they're rubbing one out.

I will buy and play basically any local co-op game, especially ones that have more than two players.  Boss Defiance looked like an interesting twist on the game Crawl, where one player is the hero and the others control dungeon traps and monsters.  In Boss Defiance, one player is the boss and the other players are heroes.  You race through the stages trying to kill the boss or destroy the dungeon crystal before the other side wins.  Boss Defiance owes a huge debt to Crawl (to the point of feeling like a knockoff), which is not a perfect game but is leagues ahead in fun and polish.
This feels like an early alpha.  The bosses and characters are unbalanced, some being completely useless; the hit detection and gameplay are off; and there's little sense of motion or feedback.  There's a kernel of a good idea at the core of this game, but it doesn't get close to being fun.

The steam showcase videos appear to stress heavily on combat but this is misleading, as there is a lot of text to be read, and no voice acting; very disappointing after hearing the trailer.
Despite being excellently written, with interesting location descriptions (if a little verbose,) and crafty dialogue, the campaign was short and uninspired - your standard murder mystery with a sci-fi twist. ONCE AGAIN, so, so many grammatical errors! In a text-heavy game, this is unacceptable, whether developed under a small budget or one of millions, I can not fully appreciate nor take a game seriously when such simple errors are so obviously overlooked.
Note that Shadowrun Returns is 100% linear, which I believe is the biggest flaw, with few slim chances to deviate from the main storyline, and very few side quests - certainly not what I consider to be a 'proper' RPG. Only toward end game did the stagnant plot become mildly interesting, and the combat more frequent, which is a shame as enemy encounters are really fun!
Combat offers turn-based tactical play with plenty of scattered objects to hide behind and utilise as cover - similar to the XCOM format. AI is intelligent, so making the best use of your surroundings is important and the consideration of placement and enemy flanking should be taken into account.
Character skills are first-rate, and the UI is intuitive. Never falling short of different tactical styles, you can combine the best of both to singe and slaughter, or take the direct approach and pepper your foes with bullets. A 'jack of all trades, master of none' approach will do you no favours here though, and the game appears to encourage specialisation in only a few fields. This may initially seem unappealing, but you will constantly hire temporary runners from all walks of life and skillset. This
dismantle the feeling of a team structure, though allows easy access for playing around with other builds to your tactical advantage - if you have the dough to pay for their services.
(Runner work doesn't come cheap ya know!)
Wonderful art and design style with beautifully detailed character portraits and a 2D, seemingly hand-painted backdrop does this game justice, but is marred by awful, janky character models, which leave a lot to be desired. The soundtracks perfectly compliment the art style, capturing the industrialised futuristic theme, and psyching you to get down and dirty.
Replayability is pretty much nonexistent in the main campaign unless you wish to test yourself with varying degrees of difficulty. I personally am in no way compelled to revisit this particular story again, and yes, it is relatively short. However, with workshop support, there is DREK-LOADS of user-generated content available, expanding the universe and adhering to the D&D theme of its successor.
As a Kickstarter crowdfunded game and a remake of the original tabletop Shadowrun Role-Playing game, I can understand the hype but can't say that this is anything special.
I did have a small measure of fun, but perhaps my high expectations of the game had a negative impact on my experience, perhaps even, the clue in the title (Returns) alluded to potential differences from its predecessor.
Still, it scraped the bar in terms of enjoyment for me but is ultimately interesting enough to entice me toward the other titles in the series. 'Only just' a positive review, definitely worth a play for previous Shadowrun title fans if bought on sale, but don't expect a triple-A game.

Before Enemy Unkown I had not even heard of the franchise. When I saw early videos and screen shots I thought this would be just another boring turn-base game, but boy was I wrong. The plot is simple, you are the commander of the newly initiated XCOM military group and the objective is to fight off the alien scum trying to take over the Earth. What makes this game so excellent is that even though most of the combat is seen from a bird's-eye-view; whenever you score a critical hit or something awesome just happens the camera switches to a hollywood-movie-esque camera view allowing some truly epic moments. It's important to note that while you can easily be sucked in for hours on end, it's also a great game if you don't have a lot of time since you can play a mission or two when you have time and still feel like you acomplished something. Even on the lower difficulties this game will be brutal thanks to perma-death (which can be deactivated but that wouldn't be any fun would it ;} ), because in one mission you can send in a squad of your most hardened veteran, and it will take only one turn of bad luck and you may only return with a couple, if any. The soldiers may be fairly generic no matter how you customize, but when your favorite dies, you will feel it in your gut when you have to start from scratch. The last part I will touch base on is the customization options. I don't mean helmet, hair, facial, and armor choices, I mean the variety of weapons, abilites, and classes, allow for a massive selection. So check out one of the best strategy gams I have ever played (and did I mention it was designed by the Civilization V team?)

the game opens up once you get the third gun, but that means half the game is a frustrating bog of backtracking, randomly throwing solutions at a wall, and continuously hitting ESC to see if maybe you should just try another puzzle. if you have a lot of patience, the design of this game is enough to make it worth it, and there aren't many games like this at all. but i could see a lot of gamers getting turned off from this game in the first hour.

As a game goes, it stands up well enough.  The turn based combat doesn't take away from the action at all.  I understand this was a crowd funded effort and there's a lot of love out there for the Shadowrun universe, including the table top game, the novels and the first video games on the SNES and Genesys systems.   I played the original Shadowrun on SNES many years ago.
That said, this is a different game from the original series.  The original series wasn't linear.  You could roam around a HUGE city at will, and collect clues and talk to a huge variety of people.  The combat wasn't turn based, and required some decent reflexes, but wasn't insane hard.  It was an awesome RPG experience, and at least gave the impression that it was a very open world.
This game is just a linear play through.  There's not even options about who or what you need to do or speak to in order to advance to the next story line.  The next "story line" almost always involves stepping out of the room you're in and being whisked to another room, usually with a team of people, and have a big fight.  Then returning afterward to a large bar where you advance the story line further.   The story isn't bad, but it just doesn't feel like I'm exploring the world to uncover that there is a story here.  It is just thrust upon me and I have to go do it.
I also miss being able to recruit, outfit and keep around my favorite merc friends.  Building relationships with those in your party is a big part of the immersion experience, and it's just lacking in this game.
I'm a huge fan of the universe, and am super happy that someone is attempting to keep it alive, and I realize that there is fan content that adds further "missions", but those again appear to be strictly linear short fire fights.
This is a good game but it makes me yearn for the SNES experience.
