This was an amazing follow-up to Saints Row: the Third. When I first started playing the Third, I immediately got submerged in the story. The over-the-top gameplay and dark comedy of the Third kept me hooked to the end, and then some. Yet, even with the Season Pass and extra DLC campaigns that expanded upon the endeavors of the Third Street Saints, after I beat the game, I still felt kind of empty. I got that all too common feeling of "Okay, now what?" Then, a few months after I had already beaten the unholy hell out of everything that had to do with this game, along came "Saints Row: the Third; Enter the Dominatrix." I was so overly happy that we'd finally get more additions to the action-packed story, I actually saved up for it. Little did the world know that Volition saw the opportunity to turn what would've been Saints Row's "ODST" into its own game.
Saints Row IV takes everything in Saints Row: the Third and multiplies it by about 3.1637%. There's more vehicles, customization, weapons, all that jazz. It was really the follow-up that I was hoping for, and I couldn't stop playing it until the end.
Although, with all of its pluses, every good game has its downs. Volition knew what they were doing when they were turning a DLC into a standalone title, but they could've spent a little more time thinking like that. The powers and the difficulty of the game is a bit less difficult than that of its predecessor. Plus the game is buggier than an anthill covered in syrup.

Following its namesake, Syberia II features the American lawyer Kate Walker on her voyage alongside Hans Voralberg, an stunded genius and Oscar, their automaton train operator. Like its predecessor, the game is set in a post-Soviet backdrop of unspecified geography and features various locations ranging from a Russian mining town, a Monastery, and Subarctic forests, to Youkol settlements and even a dream-trance state of Valadilène (the town from the first game) through all of  which the player guides Walker throguh many difficulties of their journey.
The plot, straightforward as it appears, features many details regarding Hans' obsessions, as well as Kate's former life, flesh out the storyline. There is an underlining theme of the Hans' quest comes across as one of almost prophetic proportions, which lends the game an odd mixture of magical realism tinged by the Art Nouveau-themes steampunk of many locations.
The user interface is slightly cluncky and direction arrows may get slightly confusing at times. The same applies for the interface on puzzles: the game features only one icon for interaction (a magnifying lens) regardless of the nature or the direction of the said interaction. While this doesn't prevent puzzles from being solved (as they're not impossibly difficult anyway), it does nonetheless lack intutivity.
Overall, Syberia II provides a fitting conclusion to Benoît Sokal's great duology (soon to be a trilogy, apparently). Its simple combination of a beautiful plot with elegant artwork makes Syberia II a necessary addition to adventure game collections even after more than a decade of its release.

This is one of those games where you wish you could forget, just so you can experience it first-hand again.
I've ever rarely played J-RPGs, but when I played this game, I was truly in love with it. If you're a fan of J-RPGs and romance anime, you'll surely love this game. TL;DR down below.
Throughout the entire game, you are given a good amount of characters to choose from with more in the later parts of the game. As you progress further into the story, a bit of farming may be needed as enemies become more and more tough to deal with, but as a J-RPG it was already expected. The mechanics of the game maybe a bit tacky and confusing at first, but eventually it becomes easier as you continue to play.
Now, the story was probably one of the best stories I've ever experienced in video games. Each part of the dialogue does its job well, when you need to be happy or laugh, you are met with corny jokes and ridiculous events, but when you need to feel for the characters in the game, you will without a doubt feel the sadness they show. Honestly, as you continue playing the story, you will become immersed and will develop a love for each and every character you play as. Hell, maybe you'll love some characters who you don't even play as.
Next, the replayability potential is high as there are four different routes you may choose from and because there is also a new game+ type system where your stats from your previous run will be brought over to your next run and don't worry, the enemies won't get easy because of this.
Finally, if you actually read all the way here, I give my thanks for doing so and for considering to buy this beautiful, funny and amazing game. I was truly surprised by how much I loved playing this game and regretted for not getting it sooner. As a gamer, I know that some people are out here to buy only one game and that there are many games to choose from. Believe me, I had high doubts when I first bought it since I was entirely new to the J-RPG genre in general. But, this game has been a blast to play through and I wish more people could experience it. Idea Factory truly have outdone themselves with this game.
As it stands, I have finished this game and no longer have a purpose to play it once more. Not having a reason to see my favorite characters again, truly made me sad. But, their sequel is coming and I hope it will live up to its predecessor.
I, as an avid gamer, am looking forward to the next sequel Idea Factory is releasing and hope to see my favorite characters once more.
tl;dr: Beautiful, amazing and funny. What more could you ask for?

I'm rewriting this review even though no one cares because I feel so strongly about my non-recommendation that it deserves a stronger defense than I'd given in the prior rant.
I own Syberia II because I got the bundle for cheap. If I'd bought them individually, I wouldn't have bothered with part 2, as part 1 put me to sleep. Even after I gave up and watched a Let's Play instead, THAT put me to sleep. To be fair, 2 is a little less narcolepsy-inducing, but not enough for me to keep going beyond ALMOST getting out of the first area.
It's rather discouraging, because the reviews are overwhelmingly positive otherwise. Why do so many other people enjoy what feels like a very pretty but dull exploration game? Because that's what it feels like--the "puzzles" are a bit obtuse (having spent far too long trying to figure out the basic controls during part 1), and much of the solutions are just find SOMETHING to interact with and try everything. It's not even enjoyable watching Kate Walker... walk... and walk... and walk... and walk BACK... etc. I can think of so many games that have a world that FEELS larger in fewer screens, just because the amount of interactive content per "room" is so much higher, and the attention to details that convey character in and of themselves. Syberia overall has a lot of empty content for really no reason other than I guess the art department planned out a map and the programmers worked around that. At least in part 2 there are fewer doors for Kate to declare she won't even bother trying to open.
Furthermore, I realized that what I don't like about this style of point-and-click game is the "distant" feel of the characters. Every dialogue is from at least twenty feet away, perspective-wise, so it's more like eavesdropping than actual interaction. There are no close-ups (other than the shadowy cutscenes in part 2), so I get no feel for the characters' emotions except through the (kinda bad) translated voice-acting, because they're as stiffly animated as puppets. The closest it got to providing any depth or emotion was how part 1 kept interrupting what little gameplay there was with random phone calls that only served to show how much nobody really respected Kate, while part 2 took a different tack and put in sorely-needed cinematics (that seemed to inflate Kate's importance far above and beyond her original "buy a toy factory" job... but then I fell asleep through half the story to fully appreciate the drama).
It's not like 3D can't accommodate the kind of character animation that 2D can provide easily--just look at any Telltale Games game (Sam & Max, The Wolf Among Us) or even a game like Ankh or the Gabriel Knight 20th Anniversary remake... though the GK remake admittedly feels as clunky as Syberia, the interview sections and cutscenes still draw the player out of "watch from a distance like a creepy stalker" mode enough to convey a real sense of who the characters are.
Yes, I get that they were going for this realistic world to explore, and they've done a good job of that. Once I've seen a room once, though, it gets boring seeing it about fifty more times in trying to progress the story.
tl;dr: Just watch a walkthrough on Youtube, it's a lot less clicking.

This is a game unlike an other I've played before, a game that only make you allow the best. As you progress further and further it pushes you to the limits, there are no gimics or cheese in the game only combo based gameplay. It is and can be challenging to only allow the best however the payoff is like a surge of immense dopamine. As a player who has achieved 100% of the trophies and 240% the story it was time well spent.
The game only stuters in some moments in the batmobile so after the dust has settled it is now a fully functional and succesfully ported game and this is comming from a guy plays on a laptop. I played with keyboard and mouse due to not having a controller and the controls are very comfortable on keyboard. Theres no pausing in movement to input a combo while fighting due moving your hand awkardly.
The city and level design are extremely detailed and full of life and colour even though its Gotham city, a city notorious for its crimes in the DC Universe. The city is extremeling appealing to the eyes and the rain, sea, and vegitation are very detailed more so than Arkham City which felt like only 1 theme of being a depressed borough in Gotham where as Arkham Knight has mutiple themes on Miagani, Bleake and Founders island. Bleake island a borough that focuses on horizontal zonation being day to day work life and housing for the Gothamites such as China town. Miagami island a city that takes influences from many captial cities around the the world that includes a monorail station, a grand avenue like street that that is surrounded by the tall skyscrapes. Founders island; a redevelopement project that focuse on coprate skyscrapers like Wayne International, a Gotham Lexcorp building (A nod to Lex Luthor) and Gotham Cental Bank. All in all the greatest city world game to date.
The combat is very similar to its predecessor Arkham Origins who focused more so on he combat than all other aspects of an Arkham Game. However Arkham Origins and City had beter boss fights than Arkham Knight, something Arkham Knight lacked in. The game takes more focus on the people of Gotham and the Arkham Knight's army rather than the villans of Batman. Expect complex levels with varing classses of mobs to enter combat with. The "Predator" amd Stealth of the game is extremeling satisfuying in which it makes the enemies adapt to counter the Batman, you can't do the same stealth takedown more than twice. If you are looking for more of a challenge; play the AR challenges they are unique and challenge you to peform the best and only accept the best.
The Batmobile combat gameplay is very straight foward and easy to play, not much of a challenge. It most feels clunky if you are dong the racing AR challenges and can be frustrating at times. The times where the Batmobile shined was the Riddler challenges and the Campaign for Disarment those were extremely enjoyable and complex. I highly recommend buying the 60's Batmobile racing challenges the racing courses are extremely detailed and full of refrences to the TV show. The game really forces you to use the Batmobile to get to A to B in story missions which it could of toned down a higlight being the Deathstroke/Slade Boss Fight which was a rehashed version of a story mission batmobile boss fight. I wanted to face Slade in hand to hand combat like in Arkham Origins.
The DLC of the game I would recommend being the Seasons of Infamy. The Mr Freeze and Ra's Al Ghul side story lines were extremly fleshed out and provided a variety of gameplay and re shaped Gotham such as making Gotham encased in snow. The Matter of Family of DLC would only be recommended for fans of Batman Universe and want more of Mark Hamil Joker. The DLC gives more characterisation on Joker's stance on the Bat-Family and Tim and Barbras compatibility with each other. Overall the DLC is slightly above average compared to most City.
Like all Stories a conclusion has to made and Arkham Knight accomplshes that surpurbly. The ending is extremely satisfying for a game trilogy and that for Batman's career. The story is extremly engaging and brings much shock value espically for those who are new to the Batman Universe, however if you have read stories such as Knightfall, The Killing Joke, Under the Redhood and even Batman the Animated series you can see plot points and conflcts from a mile away. The story respects source material extremely well but that is to be expected of an Arkham game. However what really engaged me was the characterisation of Bruce and Batman persona. It really brings forth ideas and reflections of what would happen if Batman was to put away the cowl and why he shoulders Gothams safety on his shoulders. The Voice acting by Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamil is amazing they always have to work together if they want to make Batman on media an amazing, marvelous and memorabile story.
So should you buy Arkham Knight? Yes you are definetly getting your moneys worth for only $20. Rocksteady made a ground breaking conclusion to a game series that outshines others like Final Fantasy: Lightning returns, Mass Effect 3, Call of Duty Modern Warfare, Metal Gear Solid 5 (Story Wise and though its a presequel). If this game was released like it was after the PC Port was fixed it would have been game of year hands down. Thank-you for reading this review it was my first and one that was definetlt deserved for Rocksteady's equal Magnun Opus Arkham City.

Another Edit: I really do enjoy the game. I'm getting good at it. It's fun. I can, apart from glitches in some map areas and some balancing stuff simply not say I don't like the gameplay. It is amazing, at least with friends.
The review still stands, though.
There is a lack of connectivity information when joining servers.
Matchmaking sometimes just stops working altogether.
So many essential software basics are missing, such as a coherent chat window. Instead of every section of the game (lobby, pre-game, game, post-game) having its own chat. The interface is glitchy, options sometimes reset, plenty of smaller but obvious flaws like health bars obstructing view on enemies until you reduce UI size so much you can't read the names anymore. Shooting zombies is great when latency is low but the game "envelope" never really got into polishing phase. In that regard, it reminds me a lot of ArmA II. Great content but buggy as ♥♥♥♥.

Batman: Arkham Knight is definitely a good game and a great way to end the Arkham series. While it falls short in some ways when compared to it's predecessors (story, boss battles etc) it also improves in many things that affect the gameplay, especially the combat. They've added lots of new things that make it feel very different and that's a good thing, but it often feels like it relies on these new pieces of content a bit too much, a good example would be the Batmobile. While it is well done and it can be very enjoyable to drive around the Gotham with it, you have to use it a bit too much for my liking. About the story though, while I do think that it's worse than Arkham City's, it's not bad at all itself but actually pretty good as well. You can definitely see that the developers tried their best to make this game the best they could as it's full of all sorts of nice details and things that you might not notice at first, not to mention that if you pay attention to your surroundings, you will find lots of DC related easter eggs everywhere.
Overall I'd say that it's a solid Arkham game and definitely worth playing, but just don't expect it to be better than Arkham City as City had better story and better boss battles (though this one barely has any). Though ofcourse these things are also very subjective and I know that there are quite a lot of people who do prefer Knight over City. Whatever the case, if you played the previous instalments and enjoyed them or even if you're just a fan of Batman/DC Comics, I see no reason not to recommend this to you.
Also, despite having lots of issues during launch, Arkham Knight's PC port works close to perfectly these days, so you don't have to worry about the infamous issues the game used to have.

as a non-euclidian journey into game design and making players trip out just by going from stage to stage, antichamber succeeds. as a first-person puzzle game, it leaves a lot to be desired. the near absolute lack of feedback certainly adds to the atmosphere of the game -- almost quasi-portal, where you feel like you are journeying through a research lab -- but the cryptic hints sometimes aren't enough to progress to the next area on your own. there are "eureka" moments where you realize a cute solution on your own, but more often than not, i found myself googling the room name to figure out where the eff i was supposed to put blocks.
the game opens up once you get the third gun, but that means half the game is a frustrating bog of backtracking, randomly throwing solutions at a wall, and continuously hitting ESC to see if maybe you should just try another puzzle. if you have a lot of patience, the design of this game is enough to make it worth it, and there aren't many games like this at all. but i could see a lot of gamers getting turned off from this game in the first hour.

So far, KF2 seems to be a fun, mostly mindless co-op Horde Mode Survival game.
The enemy variety is good (so far, I've encountered about 8 different enemy types on Normal difficulty) and weapons seem to perform quite differently. I've really enjoyed playing the Sharpshooter so far (gotten him to lvl 10) as I'm best a clicking on heads.

My most recent lobby had me stationed in the middle with the autosniper (that's what it's called in CSGO, anyway), crouched and pumping bullets into the heads of zombie hordes rushing at us, while our two Berserkers hacked away at those who made it through to our squad. Our Medic was busy healing the Berserkers and our Support kept us from running dry on ammo. The Gunslinger in our group would float, helping out whoever was being overrun with his high-DMG, but slower revolvers. This was by far the best lobby I joined, with everyone using mics and coordinating tactics. It was a beautiful gaming experience.
If you have friends who own the game (or who you can convince to get the game), certainly give KF2 a try if you're looking for a fun night of zombie slaying. The music is awesome, too, as you mow down the hordes of undead to blaring metal tracks. It feels kind of like Doom back in the day - just pure awesomeness, killing zombie after zombie to heavy guitar riffs.

Graphically the game got much better than the first game. It looks decent, with proper lighting but pretty low-res textures. Of course it is nowhere near to any really great looking title. If you had the chance to play any other Tripwire game then you can pretty much expect not-so-great performance. And you pretty much get it. Effects like blood and explosions are a constant threat for your PC. I get 60 fps constant out of fight but it often drops below 30 when things happen. The game is no longer in early access but it seems like optimization is still quite lackluster and it is likely that this will not change.
Monster design is good however most of them are just better looking versions of the originals from the previous game. Still, it is good to see these creatures with higher poly count. Level design is quite inconsistent with better and worse maps in the list. As I see later additions tend to be worse with smaller size and mostly tight and mindless layout. Collision geometry is also pretty weird and overall pretty distracting. In games developers can pretty much do this two ways. Either you can do the collision based on the displayed mesh or use primitive boxes. In KF2 boxes were used but it mostly so simplified that I often collide with thin air.
Last time I played the game on a free weekend more than a year ago the whole experience felt quite half-baked. Movement and overall feel was quite sluggish with too much camera movement and recoil. Now that I finally decided to buy in, I am surprised that the game might got worse. In the old game it was easy to get headshots with sharpshooter without aiming, here the whole thing feels out of place and I rarely know where I am aiming at. Weapons might became more realistic perhaps. In a horde game this feels simply too convoluted that it stops being fun when I cannot hit anything because the camera keeps moving in a freakish way. Other aspect that I am not satisfied with is the matchmaking and the overall bugginess. The game often hangs at session start, hud elements like health does not refresh, control bindings get fkd up, etc. Speaking of matchmaking this morning I just had 3 matches (2 normal and 1 hard) and I encountered a staggering amount of 2(!) players. Steam says that more than 4 thousand people play KF2 at the moment, still I am not able to play a single game properly in EU. Somehow based on the popularity of the first KF I thought it is going to be better.
The music included in KF2 is good. Nothing that I would listen to outside of the game but a soundtrack does not have to be anything more than an addition to the action on-screen. Sounds and effects are quite similar to those heard in the first game. When the horde comes you will not going to hear much anything than screams and the noise of weapons. Some more ambience would have been good. One thing that is good is that I can distinguish various bigger zeds based on their sound before I am able to see them. This is quite useful and supports the lack of extra sounds.
I enjoyed the original Killing Floor. I mostly needed more refined mechanics and some extra progression from the game. KF2 has some of the extra depth. There are 25 levels instead of 5 per class. More appearance options and collectibles. I am still not sure whether the copy-paste skin system from CS:GO is a bad thing or not with the purchasable keys and other stuff. Number of levels and 'classes' are good. They definitely grant quite a few hours of play.
Based on a few hours of play I am surprised that KF2 is not early access still and that Tripwire released something like this as a final product. Mechanics did not get much better since the first game, I would say quite the opposite. With the rather expensive store items I have the feeling that this is just a half-effort money-grab for them. This is why it is so disappointing to see that one of the better co-op games and one of the better studios from the last 10 years seem to become another poor example of anti-user business practices.
Update: New weekly challenges showcase even more how broken the mechanics are. Level collision and stupidly innacurate melee weapons spoil the fun on higher difficulties. I am not even getting started on the various issues with rewards not showing up properly...

HL2 shows that a game does not need to be open world for it to be amazing. Fairly open level design gives freedom but subtley directs the player in the correct direction. The locations are varied, but the transitions from one area to another make sense. The story is deep and interesting. Graphics still hold up over a decade later and sound design and music are fantastic, and the supporting characters are actually helpful, interesting and memorable. Most of all, the game stresses the falseness of safety and comfort in its world and shows you how alone you as the protagonist are. (One of the best examples of this is the sequence leading into the Raveholm chapter.)
HL2 is an amazing experience, unique and fun. There are frustrating/difficult moments and some of the areas are rather long, but they don't overly detract from the experience. HL2 does not hold your hand, and that is one of its best attributes, as it lets the player feel a sense of accomplishment when they figure out a puzzle or get through a tough sequence. HL2 is definitely one of the greatest games ever made and I highly recommend it for everyone.

Antichamber is a masterpiece of psychological trickery that systematically deconstructs and plays with every single unspoken assumption you have about the way FPS environments and 3D puzzle games work.
Assume you're operating in Euclidean space?  Think again.  Assume a corridor will still take you to the same place if you walk down it facing backwards?  Think again.  Assume if you walk around a corner and then walk back around the same corner that you'll end up in the same place you started from?  Think again.
Every time you get stuck in Antichamber it's either because you have an unspoken assumption about the way 3D games work.  Inspect your assumptions and work out which assumption to discard, and suddenly the whole game opens up again as what seemed like an intractable problem is solved by an action that - in retrospect - now seems as simple as "turn left" or "walk backwards"... but which you were never even aware was an option before.
If you like your assumptions unchallenged, this is not the game for you.  If you want your intuitions about 3D spatial navigation violently rearranged in the same way as Portal did your understanding of physics and mechanics, this might be the game for you.  It's only short, but you'll be thinking about it for months afterwards.

"Dying is part of the fun.... No, seriously". FTL is a game where you go through randomized playthroughs attempting to get to your destination. Explore, guess, think, evolve and try again, that's what will keep you on the edge of your seat for hours straight with FTL.

This feels like a game that really encourages specialization, where you can end up with some useless skills if you haven't got a clear idea of which playstyle you want to go with and how to achieve it. I didn't have any previous experience with the Shadowrun franchise in any way (it's originally a tabletop RPG), but I had played Deus Ex and similar games before which proved helpful. I chose to be a conversational elf mage specializing in rifles and was able to almost max out all the skills associated with that. It led to a very enjoyable gameplay experience.
Unlike Deus Ex, this is a turn based game, which means you can only move a few steps at a time while in combat. Combat worked really well and, like all turn based games I've played, there are many tactical options. In the later stages of the game, you sometimes start a level in combat mode and remain there the whole time, needing to go through several turns before you even spot an enemy. This is one of the few things that annoyed me with the game. Luckily, most of the game is in exploration mode, where you can move freely and run quite quickly from A to B
Another minor issue is that the story went on a bit longer than I thought, but this isn't a long game, something others have criticized. I felt like I had been through many interesting levels/encounters and the ending did give me closure, so all is well that ends well. Being a kickstarter project and/or through intentional design, there is no voice acting or facial expressions/body language, which felt a bit poor compared to Deus Ex and similar games, but I got used to it and the writing is pretty good (better in the sequels, people say).
This being a cyberpunk game, you get to hack computers and go inside cyberspace to get data and fight countermeasure programs. I never did this unless the story required it, because I've heard some bad things about it and that this game, unlike the sequels, didn't provide much for "deckers" (i.e. hackers). The hacking went fine, but I never thought I missed out by not hacking more frequently.
Overall, I had a really good time, mainly because there are so many options, not to mention the way you can roleplay your character by choosing different dialogue options. You get to hire different team mates with various talents (can try out different people on different missions), there are several vendors you can buy interesting gear from and some missions can be done in different ways.

Saint Row IV
I was really excited to play this game! I had huge expectation about it, cause I really liked SR2 and SR3, SR3 was for me a non-stop fun!
so, after I got this game, I launched it... and right at the get-go, I was in tears!
Story
The story is just crazy-funny-weird-unrealistic as you would imagine Saints Row,  You have been elected to be the President of the United States,
After a few years of ruling with swag on you lovely nation, you've been attacked by Aliens, which abducted you friends and you, but, the Boss alien isn't satisfied with just abducting you,
He placed you in a virtual prison\world which is SteelWater city, and from here, you try to hack the system and get out of the 'program' (Matrix anyone?).
Graphics
Graphics is good! it's almost like SR3 but obviously they added some more features and it's a bit more nicer.
now, I can't say it looks amazing like Metro: LL, they weren't trying to make a game looking like that, and TBH, you would need a Monster system to run something like that since it's an open-world.
anyways, for me, the graphics works.
Gameplay
And now for the Pièce de résistance!
I think someone in the Backlog Attack! chat said that this game is a game that meant to be a parody about games, at first, I didn't know what he meant, but after playing the game, it's so true!

The game features many types of mini-games just like SR3, some different and some are same like Insurance Fraud.
now, they've added the super powers feature and it's just pure awesomeness, if you've played Prototype, it's just like that, and it's really fun!!
Conclusion
Some say that SR4 is just a huge DLC for SR3, but IMO it's not, and if it is, then it's worth the money!
The game is just 100% fun, you can do whatever you want, how ever you want, the dialogs and cutscenes are just hilarious!
the game got tons of references to other games and movies which I found really funny and fun to find.
bottom line, this game is worth the money! it's really really fun!

This was an amazing follow-up to Saints Row: the Third. When I first started playing the Third, I immediately got submerged in the story. The over-the-top gameplay and dark comedy of the Third kept me hooked to the end, and then some. Yet, even with the Season Pass and extra DLC campaigns that expanded upon the endeavors of the Third Street Saints, after I beat the game, I still felt kind of empty. I got that all too common feeling of "Okay, now what?" Then, a few months after I had already beaten the unholy hell out of everything that had to do with this game, along came "Saints Row: the Third; Enter the Dominatrix." I was so overly happy that we'd finally get more additions to the action-packed story, I actually saved up for it. Little did the world know that Volition saw the opportunity to turn what would've been Saints Row's "ODST" into its own game.
Saints Row IV takes everything in Saints Row: the Third and multiplies it by about 3.1637%. There's more vehicles, customization, weapons, all that jazz. It was really the follow-up that I was hoping for, and I couldn't stop playing it until the end.
Although, with all of its pluses, every good game has its downs. Volition knew what they were doing when they were turning a DLC into a standalone title, but they could've spent a little more time thinking like that. The powers and the difficulty of the game is a bit less difficult than that of its predecessor. Plus the game is buggier than an anthill covered in syrup.

This game is painful right from the start, enemies spawn in a tiny trickle meaning you will find more containers than you can afford to open. When you can open them, you get given random power-ups chosen from ranks of rarity. There is a relic item that allows you to choose which item you get, but you still have to rely on rarity and being fast enough to choose before you get killed.
After the first few minutes in the round, you should be getting a regular stream of enemies now, which you need to loot to open as many chests as you can. As time moves on, enemies increase in spawn rate and difficulty, elite mobs become more frequent.
So you've succeeded in completing your first zone. You've got yourself some nice items, even a couple green ones. Then you hear the bell. Enemies spawn in larger waves, yellow d0uchb#gs are teleporting to you, red guys are setting the ground on fire and those orange b#st#rds are firing half a dozen homing missiles at you. You're shooting like a madman, but it's doing barely anything against the tide of elite mobs. Then you hear the roar of a Magma Worm. You look but you can't see the indicating arrow in the sea of hostiles. Your health dropping like hail, you see the worm... a second too late as it fires up out of the ground, instantly wiping out the rest of your life. You're left a broken mess among the horde of creatures, the game taunting you for being such a wimp. And all that's left, is to start all over again.
What can I say about Risk of Rain? Will you die? Yes. Often? Yes. This is one of those Dark Souls type of games where only the stubburn will keep trying and trying and dying until they finally succeed and graduate to the next level, where they are immediately crushed again.
If you do manage to survive long enough and are lucky enough to get a number of good drops, you begin to feel the confidence of being a demi-god. At the late game when you have a couple hundred items, you feel like you're invincible.
Risk of Rain is very good at seperating out the masochists and the clinically insane, and putting them through high intensity combat requiring strategy, fast reflexes and an iron will.
WARNING: This game will likely make you want to throw your monitor out the nearest window.

Mirror's Edge, when it came out, met with mixed reviews, but remains a fan-favorite with the gaming community. I am happy to say that I am one of the many people who loved this game.
You play as Faith, a runner, whose job it is to carry messages and info between targets in a city where that kind of knowledge is banned. However, when a popular candidate for pope (who promised change within the city) and Faith's sister, Kate (a cop), is wrongly accused of committing it, Faith must come to the rescue. Too be honest, the story was the weakest part of this game. It felt tacked on, like it was just written as a way to tie together levels. This leads me to the writing: GOD, is it cheesy. Everything is very "dramatic" and jokes (thankfully far and few in-between) feel unneccesary. You won't have to deal with it for very long, though; the game's length (and arguably the biggest complaint of the game) is extremely short, with my first playthrough lasting about 5 hours spread out over a 10 chapters (including the prologue). Hopefully the second game handles it's story and length issues much better than this first installment to the series.
Now, the strongest part of this game, is of course, the gameplay. Mirror's Edge is a first-person platformer that centers around the movements of parkour. You run, jump, roll, and run some more, all from Faith's perspective (this is actually the first game I've seen in a while that allows you full vision of the character's legs in first person). The gameplay really shines when there is space to run and build up momentum, as speed is one of the biggest factors in the game. However, Mirror's Edge loves to throw tight spaces, buildings, vents and more at the player, grinding all of that speed to a halt. There are also a few jumping puzzles, which makes you have to stop and think where to run to and jump next. It completely halts the gameplay and happpens far too much. Also the combat is very weak, involving punches and kicks that take a different effect when adding movements like jumping or sliding to them. The gunplay, oh the gunplay. It is extremely clunky and limited. There are only a handful of them to choose from, and most of them also kill your speed, so avoiding battles when possible or guns in general is reccommended. I have yet to realize how DICE, the development team, could have messed this up, considering their back-catalog of games include the Battlefield series, a SHOOTER. Still, even with it's flaws, Mirror's Edge finds a way to engross the players in the world and enjoy the plusses of the gameplay, including it's unique parkour movements and varied enviroments.
The game looks absolutely gorgeous for 2008. The art style is poppy; white everywhere, with splashes of red, orange, blue, or green for good measure. It really adds to the totalitarian-society-from-the-future setting the game throws you into. There aren't as many options as I had hoped for in this PC port, but the game still looks beautiful for what it gives you.
The music isn't especially memorable, but lends to the setting with it's techno-style beats. The game's theme song, Still Alive (no, not Portal) by Swedish singer Lisa Miskovsky is great and is sure to leave a lasting impression as the game's final credits roll.
Now, this game, while great for what it gives you, is not perfect by any means. It's short, the combat is clunky at best, and the story feels like something thrown together sloppily to meet the release date of the game. The biggest offense, however, is the port. There aren't many options, and the worst part: for a first-person game on PC, there is a locked FOV (field of view). This may not be a huge problem for console players, as the TV is usually further away from the face, but with a PC, the moniters are usually very close. This becomes a problem for those who suffer easily from motion sickness, and I was forced to install a mod that increased the FOV. This should be a requirement on PC for all first-person games. So those who suffer from motion sickness easily, avoid this game.
If not, then I highly reccomend you take the chance and play the game. It's not for everyone, that's for sure. But despite all of its shortcomings, the game completely engrosses you in its inventive gameplay and atmosphere.

7/10. Good but has a lot of problems.
2017-11-12 edit:
HOW TO GET PAST THE FREEZING PART:
When doing the mission with the bugs, your entire crew needs to be in the same room as Marie-Louise. If you are within visible range of Jessica Watts, Jessica will taunt you, and the game will freeze. If Jessica cannot see you, this event does not occur.
Contrary to my original review, the game does radically change based on your character build. The problem is that you will have no idea what changes because the changes are incredible subtle. For example, the mission about rescuing Coyote has a part where you get zebra meat from a vendor. As far as I know, this vendor does not appear if your charisma is lower than 2. There's another NPC in the same zone who will ask you to fetch the dead woman's necklace if your charisma is higher than a certain level. If your charisma is too low, he just tells you to screw off. I have also read that data jacks will not appear unless you are a decker and you have a deck equipped as an item. This means a person playing through the game as another class will assume the game has no data points, so one would never think to play the game a second time as a decker.
Original Review:
Game is completely broken. I am unable to complete it because the game freezes at the exact same part every single time. It's a fight near the end of the game where the villain stops the fight to taunt me, and the UI stops responding after the dialog ends. A quick google search shows that many others have experienced the same problem, and it has never been fixed.
I was having fun until this freezing BS. I would give the game a 7/10 up to this point.
The good:
The combat is infrequent and simple, so the game is more of a visual story than anything else. I really like the story so far. A friend is murdered, and I'm hunting down the killer or killers. I meet people along the way, the plot has a few twists and turns, and I really want to see how the story ends. It's such a shame the developers phoned in the last part of the game so it can't be completed.
The bad:
I bought this game because I hoped it would be like Shadowrun for the Sega Genesis. The Sega version of Shadowrun was very open and nonlinear. It was almost like playing Fallout 3 or STALKER. There was an entire world to explore. There were tons of people to meet. There were lots of different Mr Johnsons who gave different types of missions. There were numerous ways to solve any problem (open locks with a magkey, hack a terminal, or use a frag grenade). I would say 90% of that game was totally unrelated to the main story. If you wanted to roam around Seattle and shoot random civilians, you could do that in the Sega version.
Shadowrun Returns is nothing like that Sega game. This game is extremely linear. There are no side quests. There is no free travel. There are no respawning enemies. It's basically like playing Call of Duty where the whole thing is on rails and there's no going back. Even if I had the ability to finish the game, I would say this game has little or no replay value because it's completely linear. My current character is a samurai, but I'm sure the game would be exactly the same if I played as a decker or shaman.
Another problem is that it seems like none of my dialog choices matter. I have 3 different ways of saying yes or I have 3 different ways of saying no. I would like to see something more like Fallout New Vegas. The dialog could range from agreeing to work with someone to immediately attacking the person without warning. It should feel like my choices have some impact in the game.

Game itself is fun. Repetitive, glitchy, but simple zombie slayer fun. When it works.
It's the uncertainty and the circumstance of me not being able to play the game I purchased license for that make me not recommend this game. Behind all these bugs and technical issues, there is a fun zombie shooter that, despite its limitations, really feels enjoyable, alone or with friends. It's a shame they don't seem to be able to maintain their product's availability on the Steam platform.
I personally care more about the product working than about which company is to blame.
-----
Another Edit: I really do enjoy the game. I'm getting good at it. It's fun. I can, apart from glitches in some map areas and some balancing stuff simply not say I don't like the gameplay. It is amazing, at least with friends.
The review still stands, though.
There is a lack of connectivity information when joining servers.
Matchmaking sometimes just stops working altogether.
So many essential software basics are missing, such as a coherent chat window. Instead of every section of the game (lobby, pre-game, game, post-game) having its own chat. The interface is glitchy, options sometimes reset, plenty of smaller but obvious flaws like health bars obstructing view on enemies until you reduce UI size so much you can't read the names anymore. On any supported and maintained game, that sort of issue would have been fixed in days for how obvious and easy to solve it is.
Overall, it feels a bit like a very well-made tech demo without much effort on turning it into a customer experience. It lacks the bug-fixing of nerdier studios such as the guys behind Factorio. Shooting zombies is great when latency is low but the game "envelope" never really got into polishing phase. In that regard, it reminds me a lot of ArmA II. Great content but buggy as ♥♥♥♥.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes is a Lego-themed action-adventure video game developed by Traveller's Tales and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Wii U, PlayStation 4, Xbox One and Microsoft Windows, and published by Feral Interactive for OS X. The game features gameplay similar to other Lego titles, such as Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga and Lego Batman 2: DC Super Heroes, alternating between various action-adventure sequences and puzzle-solving scenarios. The handheld version of the game by TT Fusion was released under the title Lego Marvel Super Heroes: Universe in Peril for iOS, Android, Nintendo DS, Nintendo 3DS and PlayStation Vita. Characters include Iron Man, Captain America, Hulk, Spider-Man, Black Widow, Hawkeye, Thor, the X-Men, the Fantastic Four, Silver Surfer and Nick Fury. A spin-off to the Lego Marvel series titled Lego Marvel's Avengers was released on 26 January 2016. A sequel, Lego Marvel Super Heroes 2, was announced to be in development on 15 May 2017, is set to release for Microsoft Windows, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One on 14 November 2017.
It starts with the characters. Where LEGO Batman 2 offers a sizable roster of heroes and villains, the campaign in LEGO Marvel delivers more playable heroes in a much more coherent story about collecting cosmic bricks around the world before villains do. The first mission starts with Iron Man and Hulk, but the selection of playable characters soon grows to include the rest of the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, loads of X-Men, and even Spider-Man. You'll even switch heroes mid-way through many of the missions, with Cyclops and Jean Grey rescuing Storm and Iceman during an assault on the X-Mansion, or the Human Torch flying in to assist Black Widow and Hawkeye as they infiltrate a Hydra base. The entrances and exits are all handled as part of the story, which gives you a chance to play several characters who all feel like they're part of a single narrative.
I finished the main campaign in under 12 hours, but I've been coming back to collect extra characters and bricks for days after. In between missions, there's a massive open-world map of Manhattan to explore, from the Statue of Liberty and Battery Park to the X-Mansion up past Harlem. There's also the massive SHIELD Helicarrier floating over the East River. The city has loads of attractions, complete with characters to collect and challenges to beat. Over the course of the side missions, you'll help Heimdall take out frost giants on the docks, battle Sentinels in the streets, or take control of a neglectful boyfriend's mind and make him climb the Empire State Building to apologize to his girlfriend.
Overall, I would give this game a 9/10. Great game, fun levels and a good speed to get trough the whole game and archieve 100%, all deadpool jokes also fit nicely and all extra missions are fun.

Civ V - Definitely worth a look
Civilization V is a very well rounded game for the strategy genre. While it isn't quite as encompassing as Civ IV in terms of tactical knowledge, strategy experiences, etc. It's still a decently solid game. The controls are easy and familiar, as with many of the Sid Meier games. Civ V graphics are also completely beautiful. I love that they have really created an immersive world for strategy.
I do love the perks and advantages of all of the Civilizations to choose from. I often find myself going back to this game to go through all of the leaders and trying to win different scenarios with each one. I do think that some leaders are extremely better equipt and have massive advantages over others. But, I do realize that this helps balance gameplay.
As for customizing your gameplay experience. I was quite pleased with what Civ V had to offer. If you find yourself rolling your eyes at the pitiful attemps of barbarians around you. You can always change the setting in the gameplay beforehand and make barbarians harder. I also like the random personalities feature for each leader. This helps add some unpredictability to the game.
Overall, as much as I truly love strategy games, I think Civ V is definitely up there in the ranks of the top. I always enjoy my experience in it. While it is lacking in some areas of warfare tactics, it is still a completely enjoyable game to play.

I loved the LEGO Star Wars game (the one which the 6 Lucas movies). I enjoyed the LEGO Jurassic Park game. This one... I'm a bit ambivalent on. I haven't done a 100% on it yet, but I have run through the story and played a few side-missions.
As with all of the LEGO games, Marvel Super Heroes is a "smash blocks and collect tokens while running through a stage" platformer. It's set in the Marvel Universe, but not in any particular version or movie. It does borrow a lot from the recent movies (up to Iron Man 3 and Guardians of the Galaxy, I think), but also contains the Fantastic Four and the X-Men (though not from their respective movies).
The hub for the game is the SHIELD Helicarrier and the city of Manhattan. Not the entire thing, but the hub is not only broad, but also very vertical. It's a good job then, that there are a number of characters who can float or fly. There are a number of activities to unlock various blocks and characters, in addition to the usual story-mode/free play collect-a-thon.
The story is nothing very special. I think I liked the story for Ultimate Alliance better. But it's the typical "villains teaming up so good guys need to team-up" story. Every stage has a big old boss fight in it, sort of a gimmick as opposed to a straight-up knock-about. The voice-acting carries the game more than the story, though the humour sometimes falls a little flat.
Voices and sound are both top-notch. They got great voice-actors for Iron Man, Wolverine, Deadpool, Spider-Man, Hulk, Thor, Loki and Nick Fury... and the others aren't too bad. The music is thematically appropriate, though the hub-music tends to grate a bit.
The graphics are pretty nice. I love the designs of the characters and Manhattan. The characters look too glossy and shiney in some of the cutscenes and that bothers me a bit. But aside from that, it looks pretty okay.
There's a very good variety of heroes and villains in the game. The major Avengers are here, as are the Fantastic Four. There's a good selection of X-Men. Spider-Man, Deadpool and SHIELD are in there. From the other side, we have Dr. Doom, the Sinister Six, Galactus, the Brotherhood of Mutants, and various minions from Doom, AIM and Hydra. I think the main reason I got this game is because of all of the characters it has.
I didn't enjoy playing the campaign quite as much as I enjoyed the other LEGO games, however, There have been way too many times that I couldn't figure out what I had to do or where I had to go to progress, because there was too much going on. All of the fights are puzzle fights, and so many of them would be full of "You can't fight back until this guy tosses something at you".
There have also been various times in which my character would get stuck on geometry, usually because it seemed that the designers didn't realize I would wind up there when I flying, swinging, or being knocked about by an invulnerable enemy in a chaotic arena.
Regarding the boss fights, it's also somewhat annoying when you're attempting to show the bad guy what-for, and you get swarmed by infinite minions. Fighting them isn't hard (even the ones who have powers or guns), but if you have to build something, and keep getting interrupted, it's very annoying.
I know it sounds like I'm being very negative about LEGO Marvel Super Heroes, but it is a game that I'd hoped would be better than it is. As it stands, I'm still going to recommend it for having such a great, big sandbox with so much going on, but it's still not as good as the other LEGO games that I've played.

Overall, Syberia II was a fantastic game and a great sequal to the original.
As a sequel, it's very similar to the first game in terms of gameplay, so a lot of my opinions are the same in that regard.
The pros:
-I usually prefer point-and-click in the first person, but the movement was pretty smooth, not awkward, not too slow to the point of it being an annoyance (double-click to run, people!), so this ended up not being a problem; in fact, it worked a lot better with the type of story this tells
-Graphics were appropriate for the game style and the settings were beautiful and unique
-Puzzles were challenging enough for an adult to enjoy, and maybe even get stumped on; this is a good game to graduate to if you got started on similar games targeted at a younger audience - like Nancy Drew - and are starting to find them too easy
-Characters were fun, unique, and real; they did not seem boring or single-faceted; you see variety and development over the course of the game
-The storyline was one-of-a-kind and not quite the same as any other game you've playing in this genre
The cons were minimal:
-The only thing that really bugged me was that the dialogue box often said things that weren't exactly the same as what was actually being said. It was either phrased in a different way, it missed a few words, added a few words... nothing that was important for understanding the story, but it was odd, and I don't see how they couldn't find someone to accurately transcribe the dialogue. It doesn't matter if you are listening to it with volume, like I did, but I found it weird.
-Running a round was a liiiiittle bit slow when I was backtracking for no reason or running around trying to figure out what to do, but not enough to be annoying.
-The game as a whole is not extremely fast-paced, but it really depends on what kind of person you are + what you want out of a game. It kind of works with the type of game and the story, but some (the impatient?) might find it too slow and thus boring.
As a sequal, it gets points for staying true to the original and continuing on with its story without a hitch. It feels identical in almost every way, albiet is even more exciting because you're reaching the end of your journey and seeing even more interesting people and places.
All-around, it was a great game for me. Whether it's the right game for you I can't say, but if you have a history of point-and-click, mystery games, and adventure games, it's generally so cheap to get these games (they might even show up in a cheap pack -- that's how I got them), that if you think you might be into it, you aren't losing much by giving it a shot. Some games I also have enjoyed that I think have some similarities, though none are exactly the same:
Nancy Drew
The Hardy Boys
And Then There Were None - Agatha Christie
Mysterious Island
Myst
Riven

I loved Syberia 1, but I have to say Syberia 2 was a bit of a let-down.  Whereas Syberia 1 felt like an inspired game with a very unique sense of mood, mystery, depth-of-characters, and interesting settings, Syberia 2 felt bland and boring by comparison.
Syberia 2 Pros:
+If you like Syberia 1, you'll get the same basic engine, style, characters, etc.
+I didn't find anything to be overly frustrating, or any of the puzzles to be very poorly constructed.
Syberia 2 Cons:
-Settings were a bit disappointing.  Maybe my hopes were too high after some of the great level designs in Syberia 1, but these levels felt uninspired.
-Puzzles were not as satisfying as Syberia 1.  I found the puzzles in this one to be more tedious than enjoyable.
-The sense of mystery from Syberia 1 is gone.  You already know a lot from what you discovered in Syberia 1, and there's really no mystery added.  This game is pretty much just about getting from point A to point B.  It kind of feels like filler.
-The new characters were mostly bland, and the game's antagonist is just annoying.
-No spoilers, but I was not completely happy with the plot.
-As with Syberia 1, the game just ends with no real ending or sense of resolution.  (And as of this writing, Syberia 3 has not been released, which is leaving me even more unsatisfied.)

Ultra-mega short review of the game: It is both a card game and an online competitive game. This may be all that needs to be said about it, because the pros and cons of this game are typical of those kinds of games...
The pros: Like you would expect from a good card game: the deckbuilding is nice, experimenting wacky stuff is fun, there is a lot to learn, collecting cards is a joy(its both cool to watch your collection grow and it feels good when you have it completed), the art on some cards is quite gorgeous, winning over an opponent that packs a deck full of gold/legs with a deck of almost only bronze and silvers is a magical awesome moment, other awesome moments: you pull a comeback, win with a very clever play(rare moments, but the rarity is what makes them so good)
Like most online games: The game keeps evolving, you will always have oponents to play against with all levels of skill, if you take the ranking seriously, you will always have something to fight for, another higher objective to reach or fight to keep at the top if you are in grandmasters, the comunity is quite active and new interesting ideas pops quite often, and beating oponents using top tier decks using niche decks feels awesome(super awesome if you build the deck yourself from scratch)
The cons: Happens in all cards games(that i play-magic, yugioh and hearthstone anyway...): Powercreep in the newer sets of cards that render old sets useless, busted staples cards that are almost not optional for a particular type of deck, win condictions cards that forces specific cards into your deck just to counter their game-ending effects, bad luck in the draw can be frustrating(especially if happens across multiple matches is a row)
Online games always fuffer from: When the meta stabilizes, it is in a state where the is a large gap between "B" and "S" tiers decks, the "S" and "A" tier variety is usually very thin and deviating from that often results in frustrating losing streaks. Toxic players, after "A" rank, you always expect the salty ragequit that leaves you with a loading screen, muting oponents emotes is a must, foruns always have the obligatory oblivious jerk on every topic
Specific about this game: It is, for good or bad, very anime-esque: Manga style of art, overcrowded with females with oversized breasts, some historical characters turned females for some reason, have its share of cat-women... If that kind of thing triggers you, dont even bother...
Comparing to other cards games, this one heavily favors the attacker: if its not your turn, you are in spectator mode, there is no way to interfere in the oponent's turn AND the agressor gets to choose how the battles will occur. The only defense mechanic is ward, basic skill that forces the oponent to remove that creature before he can deal direct damage. There is no traps to be afraid of and the turn dont have a specific battle phase, so the agressor can, for example, summon or play spells between attacks.
There is also no deck or hand destruction, you only have to worry about losing a card if you put it in the field. This combos with the lack of defenses to favor a very snipey meta. The vast majority of people will either play agro or go for some OTK, and often you will see it coming but still lose because the options to protect yourself are so lackluster.
AS a final comparison to other card games: it is inferior to the physical games, but it is much cheaper than magic and yugioh just cant make a decent game(there is a large number of games out there, the sayng goes that when u have many things to fill the same role is because they all suck). I also consider this game much better than hearthstone, they share many problems and hearthstone also suffers from things like overly random cards(really the amount of rng there is getting out of control)
The general opinion is that game is golden in unranked, against a friend, in take 2 or until your rank is high to the point where you will be put against nothing but "S" and "A" tier decks. Well, i have to agree. Do i recommend it? I wish steam allowed me to make a neutral review, but i have to say yes or no, so i gess its Yes, it is a good game, if you like both card and online games this game features some of the best of both, just know that it also packs the worst of both.
I only beat it once (Normal Ending) but it was fun to play :D

Starforged Legends: Another new meta ruined by non-interactive deck archetypes because of obviously broken cards that should never have been printed in their current form. Despite claiming that they would not design cards like this anymore, Cygames continues to do so. Rune, Forest, Dragon, and Sword are all now fielding decks that either go straight for the face with turn 6 storm lethal or they play severely undercosted cards that simultaneously clear the opponent's board and generate face damage. Cards that have been design space problems since their release (i.e. roach, Sibyl) continue to be the backbone of degenerate decktypes because Cygames refuses to nerf them. While Cygames claims that the game is becoming more balanced due to equalizing win/loss ratios, the reality is that this is only happening because games are increasingly decided by the luck of the draw: with cards like this, every game simply snowballs out of control. Almost all decision-making skill elements are gone from the game.

Not sure how to describe it, but I'd say this is more of a brain teaser then puzzle game. If you are a fan of Portal this game brings that whole idea to the next level.
The hand-drawn/cell animation style is really cool, it's like a trippy dream.
One of the things that I liked about the level design is that the puzzles made sense. Without giving anything away, it felt like the levels all followed the same set of rules.  There wasn't any infuriating puzzles that made you curse the developer, when you figured something out, it was like "oh of course, that makes sense". It really shows the developer's design skills when you can make an environmental puzzle challenging without resorting to stupid tricks.
The story: It leaves a lot open to interpretation, I don't want to ruin it, but there is something going on. It's creepy but not scary. Like you are waiting for something to jump out and attack you at some point. It keeps you on your toes and pushing you toward your ultimate goal.
I highly recommend this game, I have yet to play anything like it and doubt I ever will again.

Antichamber is a 2013 fps puzzle game that came seemingly out of nowhere for me. Having been a fan of puzzle games such as the Portal series, which ventured in a similar genre, Antichamber seemed like a game I'd really enjoy. Having played through it in it's entirety, it is certainly a challenge, and an enjoyable one at that. Where games like portal usually have straight-forward solutions that are tricky to figure out and understand, Antichamber tends to think outside the box. Sometimes literally. Having little memos along the way to serve as hints, Antichamber brings brand new aspects to the puzzle genre that I've not seen before. Sometimes you'll get stuck on a certain puzzle only to find the answer was right under your nose the whole time, and the feeling of satisfaction is immense when the puzzle is finally finished. All in all, I'd recommend Antichamber to anyone who's a fan of the puzzle genre. It's quite a new and interesting experience.

Space. The final frontier. These are the voyages of the starship (insert name here) it's immediate mission to outrun the rebellion, deliver a message, to get as far away from here as possible!

The Review:
Antichamber is created with a very unique somewhat 'minimalistic' style and appearance, focusing mainly on the white's for it's puzzle area's, Black's in the hub and the proverbial drawings. Followed by Blue, Green, Yellow's and Red's for blocks and some lighting in specific puzzles or corridors. As a visual appeal I found it to be a little different and unique but after a while really came to appreciate it's approach and use.
The puzzles are quite interesting and pretty varied. Certain puzzles or paths require specific upgrades to the tool you have which adds a kind of 'metroidvania' feel to it in a way, Except you can teleport to any previously visited puzzle instead of having to wander back. Some puzzles do require you to do a chain of puzzles beforehand in order to progress and that can be a puzzle in itself in working out where you need to go first to get to the right puzzle to then progress.
The story I would say would probably be best left unspoken. It tries to be more of a journey of life than anything else with drawings that when inspected will give you a little proverbial message that act as a hint at the puzzle and maybe some aspects of life and such. But really it comes out leaving a more pretentious feeling if anything rather than anything truly gripping or thought provoking.
Overall I would definitely recommend it to any puzzle enthusiast but I wouldn't rate it very high on a difficulty scale, More relaxing and tricky than a serious, difficult puzzler. It has a nice art style that for me, I really grew to appreciate and enjoy. Just don't hold out on it's gripping story to keep you enthralled in the game.

So far, KF2 seems to be a fun, mostly mindless co-op Horde Mode Survival game.
The enemy variety is good (so far, I've encountered about 8 different enemy types on Normal difficulty) and weapons seem to perform quite differently. I've really enjoyed playing the Sharpshooter so far (gotten him to lvl 10) as I'm best a clicking on heads.
With a decent team, you can synergize your defenses around your characters' own strengths. My two perks give me +20% damage while standing still and an additional 30% damage and 20% movement speed while crouched. My most recent lobby had me stationed in the middle with the autosniper (that's what it's called in CSGO, anyway), crouched and pumping bullets into the heads of zombie hordes rushing at us, while our two Berserkers hacked away at those who made it through to our squad. Our Medic was busy healing the Berserkers and our Support kept us from running dry on ammo. The Gunslinger in our group would float, helping out whoever was being overrun with his high-DMG, but slower revolvers. This was by far the best lobby I joined, with everyone using mics and coordinating tactics. It was a beautiful gaming experience.
If you have friends who own the game (or who you can convince to get the game), certainly give KF2 a try if you're looking for a fun night of zombie slaying. The music is awesome, too, as you mow down the hordes of undead to blaring metal tracks. It feels kind of like Doom back in the day - just pure awesomeness, killing zombie after zombie to heavy guitar riffs.
8/10. The game gets more fun as you level your characters and unlock perks. This is where the real strategy and variety comes into play.

Graphically the game got much better than the first game. It looks decent, with proper lighting but pretty low-res textures. Of course it is nowhere near to any really great looking title. If you had the chance to play any other Tripwire game then you can pretty much expect not-so-great performance. And you pretty much get it. Effects like blood and explosions are a constant threat for your PC. I get 60 fps constant out of fight but it often drops below 30 when things happen. The game is no longer in early access but it seems like optimization is still quite lackluster and it is likely that this will not change.
Monster design is good however most of them are just better looking versions of the originals from the previous game. Still, it is good to see these creatures with higher poly count. Level design is quite inconsistent with better and worse maps in the list. As I see later additions tend to be worse with smaller size and mostly tight and mindless layout. Collision geometry is also pretty weird and overall pretty distracting. In games developers can pretty much do this two ways. Either you can do the collision based on the displayed mesh or use primitive boxes. In KF2 boxes were used but it mostly so simplified that I often collide with thin air.
Last time I played the game on a free weekend more than a year ago the whole experience felt quite half-baked. Movement and overall feel was quite sluggish with too much camera movement and recoil. Now that I finally decided to buy in, I am surprised that the game might got worse. In the old game it was easy to get headshots with sharpshooter without aiming, here the whole thing feels out of place and I rarely know where I am aiming at. Weapons might became more realistic perhaps. In a horde game this feels simply too convoluted that it stops being fun when I cannot hit anything because the camera keeps moving in a freakish way. Other aspect that I am not satisfied with is the matchmaking and the overall bugginess. The game often hangs at session start, hud elements like health does not refresh, control bindings get fkd up, etc. Speaking of matchmaking this morning I just had 3 matches (2 normal and 1 hard) and I encountered a staggering amount of 2(!) players. Steam says that more than 4 thousand people play KF2 at the moment, still I am not able to play a single game properly in EU. Somehow based on the popularity of the first KF I thought it is going to be better.
The music included in KF2 is good. Nothing that I would listen to outside of the game but a soundtrack does not have to be anything more than an addition to the action on-screen. Sounds and effects are quite similar to those heard in the first game. When the horde comes you will not going to hear much anything than screams and the noise of weapons. Some more ambience would have been good. One thing that is good is that I can distinguish various bigger zeds based on their sound before I am able to see them. This is quite useful and supports the lack of extra sounds.
I enjoyed the original Killing Floor. I mostly needed more refined mechanics and some extra progression from the game. KF2 has some of the extra depth. There are 25 levels instead of 5 per class. More appearance options and collectibles. I am still not sure whether the copy-paste skin system from CS:GO is a bad thing or not with the purchasable keys and other stuff. Number of levels and 'classes' are good. They definitely grant quite a few hours of play.
Based on a few hours of play I am surprised that KF2 is not early access still and that Tripwire released something like this as a final product. Mechanics did not get much better since the first game, I would say quite the opposite. With the rather expensive store items I have the feeling that this is just a half-effort money-grab for them. This is why it is so disappointing to see that one of the better co-op games and one of the better studios from the last 10 years seem to become another poor example of anti-user business practices.
Update: New weekly challenges showcase even more how broken the mechanics are. Level collision and stupidly innacurate melee weapons spoil the fun on higher difficulties. I am not even getting started on the various issues with rewards not showing up properly...

This is THE Batman game. Having Gotham as an open city plus the Batmobile makes such a big difference. I liked the first Arkham game, but wasn't crazy about the second one. It was an open world but felt so claustrophobic. This game fixes all of that. You're running around as Batman, driving the Batmobile. It's dope.
My favorite part of this game is the fact that so many of his suits and Batmobiles from throughout the decades are not only playable, but lovingly rendered. From the 60s show, to the 70s comic, to the Burton movies to the Nolan movies, this game has everything. The one thing I wish I knew going in is that you can't play with the alternate Batmobiles until you beat the main storyline. I would have spent less time on the side quests and saved them for later when I could have "dressed up" more.
The weakest part of the game is all the tank gameplay. This game takes the Batmobile design excesses of the 21st-century Batman movies to their logical conclusion and makes the Batmobile a straight-up tank. For a game that does such a good job making the player feel like Batman, having you do Batman things, tank battle gameplay feels really out of place. I guess they probably felt like they needed to make the Batmobile segments more gamey instead of just throwing it in there to get from point A to point B. IMO they could have scrapped all of the tank gameplay and the game would have been stronger for it, though also shorter, which I'm sure was the point.
I love the segments where you're fighting with a sidekick. I wish you could also ride around in the Batmobile with your sidekick of choice (Robin, Nightwing, Catwoman) and fight crime together, but I guess that would have raised too many technical difficulties. It felt to me like the game was leading up to that but never followed through.
Still, it's incredible how much work was put into this game, and how beautiful it looks. All around an impressive piece of work. And of course the voice acting for Batman and the Joker are just great.

The Review:
Antichamber is created with a very unique somewhat 'minimalistic' style and appearance, focusing mainly on the white's for it's puzzle area's, Black's in the hub and the proverbial drawings. Followed by Blue, Green, Yellow's and Red's for blocks and some lighting in specific puzzles or corridors. As a visual appeal I found it to be a little different and unique but after a while really came to appreciate it's approach and use.
The puzzles are quite interesting and pretty varied. Certain puzzles or paths require specific upgrades to the tool you have which adds a kind of 'metroidvania' feel to it in a way, Except you can teleport to any previously visited puzzle instead of having to wander back. Some puzzles do require you to do a chain of puzzles beforehand in order to progress and that can be a puzzle in itself in working out where you need to go first to get to the right puzzle to then progress.
The story I would say would probably be best left unspoken. It tries to be more of a journey of life than anything else with drawings that when inspected will give you a little proverbial message that act as a hint at the puzzle and maybe some aspects of life and such. But really it comes out leaving a more pretentious feeling if anything rather than anything truly gripping or thought provoking.
Overall I would definitely recommend it to any puzzle enthusiast but I wouldn't rate it very high on a difficulty scale, More relaxing and tricky than a serious, difficult puzzler. It has a nice art style that for me, I really grew to appreciate and enjoy. Just don't hold out on it's gripping story to keep you enthralled in the game.

A solid, but often frustrating, end to the Syberia saga.
The two Syberia games form a coherent, long-winded, beautiful journey, and they should be played together.
This game brings the Voralberg storyline to a pretty satisfying, if a little underwhelming, conclusion. I really grew fond of these characters, environments and Benoit Sokal's style of epic storytelling, and I was saddened to see it end. These games have some of the most memorable moments in adventure gaming history, even if the world feels a bit sterile.
The animation and the graphics are slightly improved over the first game. The gameplay is pretty much identical, however. My biggest gripes remain with the UI and the puzzles: 1) Finding "hot spots" is often like trying to find a needle in a haystack. Oftentimes you get stuck because you missed a doorway or a box of crates in some remote corner. Ugh. I really recommend keeping an FAQ at hand... 2) Especially because the puzzles can be really opaque and strange. Some of the puzzles are very logical and satisfaying. On the upside, the game is not trying to hold your hand. Everything is abstract and solvable. But unfortunately, on the downside, some of the solutions require a bit of psychotic tinkering.
(As far as a good FAQ is concerned, I highly recommend the spoiler-free (!) UHS hint system:
Those who have invested time into the first game should definitely see the story to its conclusion. If the disappointing aspects of the gameplay - frustrating UI and obtuse puzzles - had been mitigated, this would have been a masterpiece.
Overall: 7/10

An homage to old-school cRPGs, as well as a re-launching of the Shadowrun brand in PC gaming.  The story for the primary campaign ("Dead Man's Switch") is very linear, but suitable to the cyberpunk genre, and the Shadowrun setting in particular.
For me, the best part was the atmosphere.  Not the story, mind you, but the
in which it takes place.  So many "cyberpunk" games these days get wrapped up in the "cyber" (ie: fancy tech and bio-implants) and forget about the "punk" (you're a poor♥♥♥♥♥misfit living on the wrong side of the tracks.)  Cyberpunk is supposed to be about how the disenfranchised and the unfortunate survive in a technologically advanced world that doesn't care about whether they live or die.  This game nails the Shadowrun atmosphere, although the actual plot can be a bit thin at times.
Other than choosing how much lip you give back to NPCs, you can't do too much to influence the story (and being sassy rarely seems to alter the course of events.)
Also, there are a surprising number of typos in the last stretch of the game.  Missing letters, repeated words, completely wrong words ("wish" instead of "which").  It's like whoever was in charge of proof-reading stopped 2/3rds of the way through the game.  It's just typos as opposed to poor translations (it's not hard to figure out what they meant), but it's still annoying and the sort of thing that shouldn't be in a finished product, IMHO.
If you enjoy cyberpunk as a genre (and don't mind the addition of literal magic, elves, orcs, etc) then you'll probably enjoy this game for the ambiance.  However, if you're looking for an original, thought-provoking story or a game where your choices can really influence the outcome, you might be more interested in something else.
You like Shadowrun as a P&P RPG, or you fondly recall the old SNES Shadowrun game.  (I'm not saying it's
the older SNES game, but it's in a similar vein and it does the setting justice.)  Or if you just like cyberpunk done right, and don't mind a popcorn story experience.
