Disclaimer. As with any review, this is my personal opinion of the game, so feel free to disagree. If you want a shorter, more focused review, then scroll to the bottom, as I have a more direct one there.
ANTICHAMBER
Antichamber was released on January 31, 2013 by indie game designer Alexander Bruce. The game is a first person puzzle game based around optical illusions, impossible shapes, and colorful movable blocks. The end goal is to escape the chamber you find yourself in, and along the way perhaps learn something about life from the assorted pictures that are scattered around the area. In my opinion the game was one of the best games of 2013, and remains one of my favorite games of all time.
But why do I think Antichamber is so good? Well, as far as the gameplay goes, it’s a very well done game. The puzzles aren’t so hard that they make you want to just give up, but not easy enough so that you can breeze through, at least on your first try. The controls are simple enough, and are more or less what you’d expect. Space is jump, WASD are the directions, Shift is walk, and you use the mouse to move around and interact with certain objects. The game itself has a wide enough range of resolution settings, up to 1920x1200 down to 1024x768, so you can reliably run it without lag on most computers, but the most interesting part of the settings menu is where it is located. When you start up the game, you don’t get a menu screen, instead it just puts you in a small room, and on one of the walls is the settings menu. This makes it so you change your settings by looking at a wall, instead of in a menu like most games have you do.
However, the wall with the settings on it isn’t the most interesting one, in my opinion that would be the wall to the left of the settings menu wall. This wall is blank when you start up the game, but as you progress through it slowly fills up with the pictures I mentioned previously. You find these picture on the walls as you travel through the chamber. Many of them are hints, others are insights into life. Some people might find them distracting, but I enjoy them, especially the artwork on each one. Each picture has a beautiful hand drawn image, as well as a sentence or two about something, depending on what it is.
And this takes us to the next point. How good are the graphics in the game? Well, I’ve already said that I think that the drawings look amazing, but the rest of the game looks good as well. Not to the same degree, but it is fitting for the game. You will spend a decent amount of your time wandering down solid white corridors, but almost all of the puzzles themselves are a splendid blend of bright colors. And there is no shortage of challenging puzzles to be found. A perfect example is one of my favorite rooms, a room filled with boxes, each different face containing a different optical illusion, or impossible geometric shape, and each different shape or illusion is a beautiful blend of colors, some contain many brilliant shades of red, others hold lively blues and greens. And many of the faces change when you look away. One moment it can be bright red, but if you look away, it will quickly change to a dull yellow. The colors contrast wonderfully on the white backgrounds that permeates the games, which is most likely one of the reasons for it.
Now comes the trickiest part. The plot. I think the plot is well done, but it’s hard to say why, because that would ruin the game. And that is one of the biggest problems with the game. The replay value is quite lacking, as it is with all puzzle games, and when you’ve solved it once, it becomes a walk in the park to replicate that feat. Another issue some have with the game, though it doesn’t bother me, is the fact that you can’t make multiple saves. For some, this is aggravating, but most have no problem with it. Just keep this in mind if you want to play separately, from say, a family member who uses the same computer, as you will have the save the files manually by going into the save data in the assets. Another issue is the lack of support for color deficient users. If you are color deficient I highly suggest that you do NOT pick this game up, as you will not get near as good an experience, and some of the puzzles may be rendered next to impossible, as with the movable colored blocks I mentioned much earlier. There is also an inability to rebind keys, which may detract from your enjoyment, though not immensely.
Even so, despite the issues Antichamber has, if you are a fan of puzzle games, optical trickery, handcrafted artwork, or art in general, I highly suggest that you pick this game up and give it a try. You can find it on Steam for twenty dollars, and I think it is well worth the price.
My name has been Allen Fierte, I thank you for reading this, and hope you have a nice day.
Rating
Controls: (9/10) - A competent control scheme, but no key rebinding.
Plot: (7/10) - A well done plot, but suffers from the same thing that many puzzle games do, a lack of replay value.
Graphics: (8.5/10) - Personally I love the color scheme, but it’s not for everyone, and the graphics aren't the highest quality as the game was made by a small number of people.
Audio: (7.5/10) - Not much to say about the audio, as there isn’t much to say. The music is nice, but it doesn’t really stand out, and there’s really no voice acting to speak of.
Price: (6/10) [$20] - I love this game, and would pay twenty dollars no problem, but for some that may be a little pricey, for a game with so little replay value.
Overall: (7.6/10) - I highly recommend this game, at least to play through once, as I think even that is worth it, but if you don’t have twenty dollars to spare, or don’t care much for philosophical art, then consider passing this game up.

This game is a must-have for anyone who's a fan of turn-based strategy.  The game combines turn-based squad skirmishes, roguelike mission generation elements, and squad/gear leveling and progression into a neat package.  The tactical gameplay makes up the meat of the game; but your missions are randomly generated as part of an over-arching campaign where you're leveling up, learning new techs, and managing your resources to get better in-game bonuses.
It's fantastically addictive.  The game has a number of levels that it tries to turn around in different ways, with various monster spawns and objective types.  It steadily introduces new alien types to throw curveballs at you, some of which you'll learn to fear.  Some of it can get kind of samey, especially after multiple playthroughs, and the formula becomes apparent.  I'd advise that you don't worry too much about it, just enjoy the ride.
The game is technically quite sound.  The graphics aren't fantastic, but they have a variety of settings and their art style is distinct for each tileset.  I've had a few crashes, and most notably obnoxious is that autosave is turned OFF by default...so you'll definitely want to get that turned on ASAP.
The biggest gripe I have is that the multiplayer is pretty lackluster.  Being able to run a squad coop and play online would be an absolute blast; I haven't dabbled in the PvP XCOM/aliens stuff because it doeesn't strike me as fun.

Shadowrun Returns is the first of three games set in the Shadowrun universe, made by Harebrained Schemes, part of which are responsible for the IP in the first place. This the first game of three, is sadly a trope-filled, buggy and generic sorta mess, and not at all on the same narrative level as the two follow up games. In part however the reasons for why this is deserve some sympathy. I will try to explain why, from a slighty unorthodox angle.
I'm a student of social psychology, and as such believe that nothing a human does is ever without its reasons. Our actions are affected on a deep level both by things we actively think about, as well as shadows of issues or formative positives that never surface, but are equally -if not more- significant for explaining why we act or make the decisions we do.
Role playing games are therefore of interest to me (and bloody well should be for the scientific community), as the idea of players constructing a character to play as, very likely mirror something about that person. They might have insecurities to exorcise, or ideas about themselves or even the social situation such a game entails that define or direct the characters they play and how.
It is therefore in my opinion imperative that the DM of any roleplaying game takes the role of stage manager extremely seriously, for the group is for all intents and purposes not just playing around with elves or dwarves, but with aspects of their personalities, vulnerabilities, or even more undefined deep seated parts of themselves they could not put their finger on if you could ask them. The cathartic possibilities of roleplaying are real, but so are the risks of insensitive harm made to players by DM or PC. I am almost reluctant to type this down as the responsibility I feel a DM made aware of this has, is almost so huge that neither they nor the players should actually have to be made aware of it. I might have runied roleplaying for you. I know I have for myself.
Hobby-downer-existential ponderings aside, what about the DM's shadow? Where does the similar mental depths of players project themselves for the game-custodian? The perhaps obvious answer is the world they play in of course, and nowhere is this so apparent to me than in Shadowrun Returns.
The game, viewed from a psychological angle is extremely iterative on the trials and tribulations of what it means to be a DM, to a point where the game's actual story becomes comically generic. Every element of it can be viewed as deeply associated with an aspect of DMing from the notion of the role they play/perceive themselves to play, to their relationship to the players and idea of what makes a good rpg romp.
I would argue many of the elements that seem tropey and generic in this game -and possibly others- are so vey common specifically because they correspond with the mental perception of the self as a DM in conjunction with the social situation an rpg session entails. As a result, a game such as this where part of the context surrounding it comes down to the developers (that also originally developed Shadowrun even) trying to reawaken an entire franchise, these mental flashpoints become noticeable because the pressure to be a good DM (or game story creator) forced itself onto the creative process, giving us for all intents and purposes, a window into what the cognitive perception of DMing is like, when the DM don't dare add personal flare to the base experience from fear of making something nobody likes.
This serves to explain why there are so many generic tropes in this game compared to the ones that followed.
For the team, nervous to succeed they might well have been subliminal shorthands, rather than an actual lack of creative effort. I will go through them briefly below. Why you ask? Because I feel the need to defend Harebrained schemes from criticism, when so much of the game seem seeped in this genuine need to make a great experience.
Please take these with a grain of salt as i have hardly conducted studies as much as made qualified guesses/musings based on what I know and have observed within the gaming and roleplaying scenes respectively. Spoilers are sadly unavoidable. TLDR buy the other two shadowrun games.
The game like many others starts off with solving a murder. I can tell you as a former DM that all of us dream of creating a functioning honest to goodness whodunit and pit our players against it. Investigations, linear or no, are a great place to roleplay, as it gives the PCs a lot of agency and free room to muck about, and is as such a very safe bet for the DM to put one in, as it is almost guaranteed to be engaging. (Hell, the current ruleset for DnD fifth editions have a specific skill specifically called "investigate"). The backside of it however is specifically how common they are, and given the niche nature of the game, most of its seasoned audience had already investigated their fair share.
The gruesome murders is of course committed by a crazy psychopath holed up in an old mental institution. Psychos and old buildings are both old tropes (Bloodmire manor anyone?), and arguably spawned from the very real DM fear of being overly controlling. The psychopath, always one step ahead of the players, and often with more initial agency over the world, is on the one hand a cathartic villain to thwart to players, who get to take back control in the process. But the trope also serves as a very real mirror image of the DM as they might end up in relation to the players if they try to controll their actions too much. The fear of faliure, here as with the murder mystery, might have dictated Harebrained's use of the psychopath as a plot hook.
Another more positive iteration on the DM's relation to the players is the common occurence of the clown or jester character. In Shadowrun Returns, we are greeted with the tropey and utterly unneccesary Harlequin (yea yea, i know he is old guard fan-service, shut up :P), servant of totally-not-Lofwyr and who comes along for the big schabang at the end. As with the psychopath the jester can arguably be traced to the relationship to the players again, but rather than as the personification of what you risk becomming, as a personification of what you hope to be. All DM hope to entertain, dazzle and generally make their PCs enjoy themselves, and as such tropes such as Harlequin are common. The archetype is so embedded in the idea of a person being able to make people have fun that they may well almost be comforting to write.
I scrapped mine before litterally and figuratively making a fool out of myself, but all the same I, as many other DM before, still wrote one, tropey as he was.
There are probably more examples that are not as obvious, and as a result might require more effort to look for, but you get the idea. One could argue that the precence of so much fan service and source material is partially there to help alleviate writer worry as well. Especially since the game in general contain so many tropes that seem to be there because of the preassure the "DM" felt. But then again, maybe sometimes a shadowrun game with a story based on shadowrun source material is what it is specifically because that was the plan all along. No matter, I hope that perhaps in the face of some of the critique the game has recieved, the reasons for falling short might perhaps be more clear to you :)
(At least if you buy my bullcrap, and you don't have to if you don't want to).
In the end though, contextualized or not, Shadowrun Returns's story elements is still very much as generic as they come, and it is mechanically blunt compared to the second and third games in the series. I do recommend it as it holds a special place in my analytically interested intestines, but I strongly advice playing it before the other two if you want them all, as they will spoil you on everything from the story to the gameplay.
If you can only get one however, get Dragonfall. It runs laps around Returns.

I beat this game in one sitting. I referenced a guide one time for a puzzle I was unable to complete.
Abandoned is a very short, point n' click, escape the room style puzzle game. When I say short I mean for most people it'll take an hour tops. There's a simple plot about looking for your missing brother which, spoiler alert, has nothing to spoil. The story is hardly brought up and has little relevancy to anything you do or see. Basically he found another dimension and you are following his trail to try and find him.
The puzzles are simple and mostly what you'd expect from one of these games. None of them gave me any trouble save for one. It is probably the hardest puzzle in the game and its a shame that I was challenged for all the wrong reasons. There's a cube made up of 8 rooms where you can change the color of each. Outside of the cube is a rotating hologram of the cube with the color combination you need for each section of the cube. The problem is, the hologram is rotating and flickering at the same time. The 'puzzle' here is you have to figure out which room is the room you enter from so that you know where the other colors go in relation. This isn't too hard but the big issue with this puzzle is this: I'm colorblind. Not to the degree that some people are but just enough that it makes it hard to differentiate between similar colors, like the four shades of blue in this puzzle. It wouldn't even be that bad if it wasn't for the flickering and rotating. I realize that this won't affect everyone but it did annoy me. Without that issue I'm sure the puzzle's pretty easy actually.
Beyond that every puzzle was straight forward. Too easy in fact which made me feel like I was wasting my time. And there's no real reward for solving the puzzles. You aren't really given any substantial info about why the world you're in works the way it does or why lightbulbs are so damned important. The art is actually quite good but it does nothing to tell you about this alien world, its importance, history or why the hell you should care about it other than your brother was there at some point. This game could take place in a normal city setting and it would work just as well in terms of story.
So the puzzles are easy and the story is pointless. I just don't see what you are meant to get out of this game. If one was decent than it could justify the other's shortcomings. But as it is, apart from the art it has very little to offer and is less appealing than most of the free games of similar style on newgrounds.

So here's the thing about Fairy Fencer F. Its one of many modern Jrpgs that focuses more on style than substance. The two minute long video on the store page is testament to this. Its not a game for everybody, but those who like this sort of thing will probably enjoy Fairy Fencer F.
Here's a pro/con list of some things I noticed while playing the game.
Pro:
-The battle system can be very flashy and exciting
-There is lots in the way of equipment, items to keep you scouring the game
-The female characters are pretty hot (Yes its a video game but the characters adequetly represent the image of beauty by which they were designed)
Con:
-The dialogue is terrible. Its just bad. I suppose you might enjoy it if you're a diehard anime fan or teenager. But as someone who prefers dialgue that is both well-written and engaging I found this to be unbearable.
-The main character is on-par with the most annoying characters in Jrpg history (right up there with Squall and Tidus)
-There is little in the way of exploration or engaging interaction with the world. You pick an area, go into a dungeon, deal with random cutscenes filled with nonsequitor dialogue then head back to the hub screen. There are no towns, no npcs living in the world, no depth or quirkiness to establish the world as anything more than the 2D backdrop for all the fluff and nonsense this game calls a story.
I'd keep playing this game if I had nothing else to play ONLY because the combat can be mildly enjoyable in short bursts. It is ABSOLUTELY not worth the retail price. Even at 70% off (8.99) I'm hesitant to recomment a purchase. I'd say get this ONLY if you're a wild fan of the waifu anime girls, 14 years old, and struggle getting into games with deep and engaging plotlines.

What starts out as a fun, difficult platformer, slowly gets worse and worse. The platforming is fun, I had a few issues with clipping through the spinning gears at the start, but overall, a fun platformer. However, the bosses slowly stop being about surviving fast, difficult fights using skill and pattern recognition, to fight after fight of "repeat a single pattern for 10 minutes without screwing up while avoiding randomly falling objects". The level design aslo feels like it slowly degrades from planned out difficult to just "lol this'll kill a bunch of people". There's a shift from rooms of enemies whose placements complement each other to make every approche a do-able challange, to just putting falling insta-kill spikes outside of view.
I donno. I want to like it, I love games filled with secret areas and bosses and all that metroidvania sweetness, and the game clearly has some love put into it, but I didn't really like it the first time I played it, and 2 years later, I still don't. I don't want to just give a flat "no", because it does deserve better, but Steam doesn't really have a good spectrum for voting and I can't honestly say I would recommend it, so I guess that's that.

I really enjoyed the first three Batman games but the first thing that went through my head when I completed the main story for this one was 'thank feck that's over'.
The game looks stunning and traversing the environment, whether it be by gliding or with the Batmobile is excellent. On my previous machine (win7, 2600k, 16Gb ram, gtx970) the game ran fine, although on my new machine (win 10, ryzen 5 1600x, 16Gb ram, gtx1070) I experienced several crashes until I switched off some of the specific nvidia fancy bits, been running well since then with everything maxed out (except nvidia bits).
The story was interesting enough to pull me through the game, but having the Riddler in it was just plain annoying, not the riddles themselves, some of them were quite enjoyable (not that I did anywhere near the required 300?) and the use of the Batmobile in them, whilst a bit silly, certainly made them interesting. But the Riddler himself was just an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, made me wish Batman didn't have the no killing rule. Equally dissappointing was the use of the Joker. I personally am done with that particular character and was genuinely pleased to see the bugger burning at the start of the game. It's kinda sad that they keep dragging him into the games, he's just not needed here, especially when a character like Scarecrow could be equally as interesting.
It's been mentioned in many places about the Batmobile combat, so I'll not go on too much about that, suffice to say that I enjoyed first battle, but all the rest were a bit pants, and certainly not fun.
Now my main gripe. I really, really enjoyed the combat from the first three Batman games. It took me a while to get into it but with a lot of swearing, rage quitting and practice I sussed it and enjoyed racking up big combos and twatting goons left, right and center. The designers of the combat in this game seem to have decided that big combos are a thing of the past and that putting enemys that break your combo were a good thing, so they put loads in, e.g. mobs that electrify other mobs or revive downed goons (don't mind that tbh), the fights also seem to be much tighter in than before, Batman feels much more crowded in this game.
For me, they have removed the enjoyment, the sheer joy from fighting off loads of baddies. There was a relaxing almost zen like flow to the combat in the previous games, which is missing here. Although the mechanic where you fight with a partner is great. Admittedly I've only recently started replaying the game again and I'm a bit rusty, but playing this time is reminding me why I didn't in enjoy it so much before.
I will no doubt keep playing for a bit longer, because the game looks superb and being Batman is just plain cool, but this game can be very frustrating and ultimately is just not as much actual, honest to goodness fun as any of the previous games.

I've noticed this happens a lot when there are extensive areas without a save point, so you have to play through the same areas again, get just a bit further and BAM!! Another instant death. The creator of this game LOVES his falling spikes and they have contributed to most of my deaths. I get it. The game is hard, but the difficulty curve goes way up before you are even comfortable in a new area. I'm still going through it and I want to beat it. I enjoy it, but I feel like I am getting slapped in the face with each new area I find and it's not usually with a new, interesting layout. You can pretty much copy and paste the map anywhere and just make it look like a cave, or a castle, or a forest. It is usually met with an instant death and it's all *Shrug* Sorry, ya messed up! I'll be honest: I'm an impatient gamer. I don't have as much time as I like to play games nowadays and when I do, I'd rather spend it on games that I find fun. So in the first 30 minutes of the game, I will make a call on whether to proceed forward or give up. Rarely do I ever sit around longer to see if it picks up.
I'll be honest some more: this game would not be in my library had it not been packaged with one of the humble bundles I purchased in the past.
I found Teleglitch's minimalistic pixel graphics unappealing and distasteful. It is a mish mash of colors where elements like enemies and items are hard to pick out from the background. I started off with the storyline and the pixelated text immediately made me feel sleepy. I know there's a story to immerse in but ugh, do I have to strain my eyes to read it?
So ten minutes into the story mode I stopped. I decided to check out arena which surprisingly was pretty fun. You choose a level, a loadout, and then its mindless pixel monster killing from there (I don't know what they are supposed to be). I expect it'll be fun for another 2 hours before I uninstall the game.
Overall, I am not a fan of top down shooters or pixel/minialist graphics/games. This appears to be one of them and it nearly put me to sleep. $13 is a VERY steep asking price for a game like this even though I understand Indie devs need to eat, I'd rather pay $5 for that mindless grind of a game full of microtransaction and money hungry devs called PAYDAY 2. I do like one thing: the sound design of the guns is rad. I hope someone doesn't come along to humiliate me by saying that they were pulled from a royalty free library from the internetz.

Shadowrun: Returns is nothing short of a return to the glory days of classic computer RPGs, dressed in the unparalleled fantasy-cyberpunk cult setting of Shadowrun - and created by none else than Jordan Weisman, author of not only the Shadowrun itself but also other landmark tabletop games such as BattleTech and Mage Knight. If you have felt let down by the video-game industry since the 90s and have been waiting 30 years for anything that could even be compared to Black Isle titles like Fallout 2 or Planescape: Torment, then you've come to the right place!
No - even though I make the comparisons, SR is not as big in scope as those games of yore. It's a smaller game and the sheer complexity isn't nearly on the level of Fallout 2 and the story isn't anywhere near the heights of P:T. However, what it does it does well: to translate the tabletop RPG experience into a computer video game in a faithful manner. At that, it succeeds perfectly as much as those older games that tried to do the same, even if smaller in scope.
This is definitely and by far my favorite game from the crowd-funded, so-called "cRPG revival". Other games such as Divinity: Original Sin and Wasteland 2 tried to make the jump to 3D engines and, in my experience, failed at it (feel free to look at my reviews for them). Shadowrun Returns keeps it simple and thrives on it. The combat is simple but never shallow, the interactions with NPCs are limited but yet puts any Fallout 4 or The Witcher 3  to shame and back again laughing all the way meanwhile. There are a few things that could be improved regarding the UI (which I hear have been fixed in the following 2 games in the series) and the couple final areas feel a wee bit less polished than the rest of the game but not enough to detract from the experience.
[EDIT I actually didn't found any mods to be worth my time. Shadowrun Unlimited seems especially interesting but won't launch with the latest version and they just migrated it to the Shadowrun: Dragonfall workshop instead]
I have gotten the entire series at 80% discount from Humble Bundle but if you don't want to wait the game is absolutely worth the full asking price! Good luck in the shadows, chummer and remember to never, ever cut a deal with a dragon.

X-COM Enemy Within is a throwback to expansion packs, before the days of DLC. Nowadays a few new maps or a couple of new story missions is all a company needs to put out to rinse you of your hard earned cash. But back in the old days, before a sweet internet connection in every home was as commonplace as it is now, developers had to release extra content as an expansion pack. These retail releases cost less than a regular game sure, but they still had to turn up with a damn sight more than a couple of maps if they expected to part you of your hard earned cash. X-COM Enemy Within brought more…a lot more.
Where to start? Well you can now convert your soldiers into either a genetic super soldier or mechanical warrior using two new laboratories: the Genetics Lab and the Cybernetics Lab. The genetic modifications include muscle upgrades that allow your operatives to leap tall buildings in a single bound, or even go Doctor Who Style with a second heart which causes your soldier to be critically wounded rather than killed the first time they go down in a fight.
Not into that GM nonsense? Always wanted to get a pair of robot arms and sunglasses implanted directly into your face? Well then X-COM has you covered too with the addition of MEC soldiers. The soldier’s entire body is replaced by a mechanical version, turning him into a massive hulk of metal and death. MEC soldiers are incredibly powerful; armed with miniguns as standard, they can be upgraded with fusion cannons, grenade launchers and even rocket powered fists. Yes you heard me…rocket powered fists. The downside to being built like an Autobot is that your guy becomes somewhat more conspicuous on the battlefield, so he’ll be attracting a lot of enemy firepower.XCOM Enemy Within MEC
If you want to make yourself some super-human soldiers though, you’re going to need the new resource that Enemy Within adds, a mysterious substance called MELD. MELD is found scattered throughout the map during alien encounters, but here’s the twist. Each canister has a countdown clock tied to it, and if you don’t snag the canister in time it explodes. This forces you out of your comfort zone as you have balance the risks between advancing too quickly and losing the MELD. This extra nuance to the gameplay really spices things up. Finally, Firaxis have rebalanced a lot of the squad promotions to make them more competitive.
Not a big fan of transhumanism? Do you remember the days when wars were won with soldiers and determination, not gene mods and robots? Well then X-COM caters to you too, allowing you to upgrade your soldiers by awarding them service medals. Each medal has one of two perks attached to it, though once you choose one all medals of that type must offer that same perk. There are six medals to be unlocked, all of which can also thankfully be renamed, hence why my Colonel is currently wearing the Medal of Awesome. Medals are unlocked during missions and can be assigned to any soldier you like, creating the interesting dilemma; Do you pile them onto a few super soldiers but risk losing them all, or spread them out amongst the troops to soften the blow of being a man down?
The X-COM chaps don’t get all the new toys with this expansion though, as the aliens have themselves a few new units to throw into the fray. Firstly there is the Seeker. Essentially a floating mechanical squid, the Seeker’s job is to pick off isolated X-COM agents and hit their weak spot for massive damage. They have a few tricks up their sleeves to this end. For one thing, they can turn invisible, allowing them to sneak up on unsuspecting opponents. Once they’re within striking distance they can use a special strangle attack, which damages and incapacitates the targeted soldier. Much like the Smoker in Left 4 Dead, your entangled agent will require a team mate to damage the Seeker before it will let go. The other new enemy is the Mechtoid, a little Sectoid dude strapped into a big old mech walker. Pretty dangerous on its own, the Mechtoid becomes a real beast when another Sectoid psychically links with it to project a force field around it. The new enemies are both welcome additions, but it would have been nice to see one or two more new faces in the extra-terrestrial line up.
XCOM Enemy Within Mechtoid
Bored of shooting aliens? Want to bring some high-tech weaponry down on your fellow man instead? Well then you’re in luck, because Enemy Within is all about the enemy within, a human faction called EXALT. Think Cerberus from Mass Effect but without Martin Sheen running the show (sadly) and with a similar level of technology to X-COM. EXALT are up to no good trying to secure alien technology for their own nefarious purposes, whilst simultaneously throwing spanners into X-COM’s works so you’d do well not to ignore them. To track down EXALT and put an end to their interference, you need to send an agent on a covert operation to steal intel. Once they’ve stolen the intel, you’ll then need to perform a special extraction mission to safely pull them out, fighting off waves of EXALT agents whilst your operative secures the intel before pulling out. These missions give you clues as to the location of EXALT’s main base. Once you’ve figured out where they are hiding, you can launch an assault and give them what for. This new factor adds more depth to the experience, as you have to balance resources between the fight with EXALT and the alien menace.
A lot of new toys then, but what’s the point in having an arsenal to shame the Galactic Empire if you have nowhere cool to show it off? Enemy Within adds 47 new maps as well as offering tweaked versions of older maps with new spawn points which drastically alter how you can tackle a mission. There are also a host of new missions including some which connect together to form a sub-plot, much like the Slingshot DLC missions. There are a couple of standout missions, one of which takes place in an abandoned fishing town which provided some of the most tense X-COM gameplay I’ve experienced to date. Another mission, set a little closer to home, crops up later in the game which I won’t spoil for you, but trust me, you’ll love it.
XCOM Enemy Within Chrysalid
Enemy Within adds a metric ton of new content and it should be congratulated for that, but it’s not without its issues sadly. X-COM has been given some seriously dangerous new toys to play with, but the aliens and EXALT haven’t stepped up their game accordingly. This means that by the time you get Plasma weapons, it’s pretty much game, set and match. This can be countered by cranking up the difficulty or sticking the game on Ironman Mode, but it would have been nice to see our enemies pulling out a few more surprises to keep themselves competitive in the late game.
Overall though X-COM Enemy Within is an absolutely stellar expansion to the already acclaimed Enemy Unknown and should not be missed. Adding a ton of new content and really mixing up the standard X-COM formula, a game of Enemy Within feels like a totally different beast to Enemy Unknown, building on the already great foundation and then adding in a huge variety of new options to keep things fresh.

Teleglitch: It’s like Doom’s Rouge-like cousin
Teleglitch is an interesting game in that it has a really cool sci-fi premise, a beautiful ‘retro-esque’ appearance that harkens back to the PS1, and is a combination of horrifyingly hard and incredibly rewarding.
The problem is it’s really slow and takes way too long to complete. Infact, I’ve never gotten past level five. There are ten levels, by the way. On top of that, I’ve only made it to level five… once!
Now by themselves, these are not bad things nor are they deal breakers. I happen to love hard games and Rogue-likes. And while I do like Teleglitch… I just don’t want to have to have to wade through it.
let me explain:
The game has very large, sprawling, randomly generated levels. Filled to the brim with mutants, zombies, and micro-chipped soldiers that are very literally waiting to rip you limb from limb on sight. Sounds pretty standard, so far. But, the thing that’s tough is that if you want to do well you have to traverse the entirety of the level to find hidden health and weapons. Otherwise you’re going to have to fight hundreds of zombies and mutants with nothing but a knife and a few explosives. Did I mention that the levels are really freakin’ huge? Cause they’re huge.
It takes me probably ten to fifteen minutes to fully explore the first level being careful not to die and being sure to try and find everything I need before moving on. That’s if I don’t die.
‘Cause I die a lot in this game. There are so many damn mutants roaming this decrepit facility that every encounter is you versus about five or more at a time. And these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are fast. They’re also really damn strong too. One hit takes away about two hp, which admittedly doesn’t seem like much, except they can hit you about ten times before you can kill them if you don’t know what you’re doing. It takes two or three hits with a knife to kill one mutant, and you will definitely get hurt while slicing them to death, I guarantee it.
Sadly the guns you find in the first few areas don’t help much either. It still takes two shots from the 9mm pistol to kill just one enemy. Hopefully you don’t miss either, cause the guns aren’t all that accurate... Also the ammo for said guns is pretty scarce. Irritatingly so. Encounters can go from, “I got this!” to “The contents of my veins are smeared all over the floor!” incredibly fast. 0 to dead in four seconds flat…
That is not to say that Teleglitch isn’t fun. It very much can be fun. But, most of the time it feels like a slow march to my grave. I bitterly fight to get to level 4 and then get jumped by dudes who have guns as they murder me off screen.
There’s nothing worse than trying to sort through my inventory, minding my own business, while unbeknownst to me a death squad as silently rolled up behind me and begins gunning me down from the edge of the screen. I was doing so well too...
I love a challenge… I just don’t find that Teleglitch plays fair.
There are so many ways for everything to go wrong, and very, very few ways for things to go right. Maybe I’m just bad.
This game, at its best, is thrilling, action packed, dark, oppressive, and fun. It’s not afraid to make you work for your victory, or to let you sit in the quiet desperately checking every corner.
At its worst, it’s a long walk to your own death. Slowly marching through long hallways and being whittled down into a greasy puddle.
I will mention that once you reach certain levels-- I believe 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9-- you have the option of starting there, instead of climbing your way to the top. However, in my experience the gear that you start with is not as good as if you had started from scratch and made sure to collect everything yourself.
I find it harder to start from the checkpoints than to start from the beginning…
Teleglitch is a really interesting game. It has an amazing premise, a great world, and is genuinely scary. I just think that it is too difficult for it’s own good.  Perhaps it’s just a perception on my part, but slowly making my way through four levels only to die in a three seconds encounter hurts. It’s worse when you realize it took your close to forty-five minutes. My main complaint with Teleglitch is that it just takes too long…
If you really like Rogue-likes, I would recommend it! However, this game is REALLY niche in my opinion. Unless this game speaks to you at a fundamental level, I would pick it up on sale.
Perhaps I’m just bad! Give it a shot if you’re interested. But be warned, this game is a jerk.

I feel like this game is overly pretentious and utterly underachieving. Bear with me, I will explain why.
Let us start with the bugs. Sometimes (fairly rarely) you'll find yourself locked in an area because the randomization algorithm screwed it up. Tough luck bro, start again. Much worse is the randomization of the enemies, which ***relatively often*** unbalance the game. For instance,an unjustifiable large number of enemies waiting you right by the first room of a new map. Nowhere to run, no pillar to hide behind, no means of defence - it often means "death in 2s" or "good bye all ammo and medkits".
That wouldn't be all that hateable if only you would be allowed to save at the end of each map. The game "checkpoints" allowing you to start at lvl 3,5,7 or 9 once you finish lvl 5,7,9 and 10 respectively. That is mostly a trap, however, since you start with a much inferior gear in a game where ammo is already scarce.
I like a difficult game more than most (check my profile) and I have completed all the achievements (took me quite long), but this game just doesn't deserve permadeath in my opinion. If anything, there should be a "permadeath mode", for those who like a challenge - like me. Having to put up with the flaws of the randomization system while trying to learn how to play, learn which ammo is more useful against each enemy, all of this just makes this game sound overly pretentious, achieving very little or nothing and giving absolutely no satisfaction. It feels like the only reason the permadeath is there, is to make the game hard. The devs should tune down their tone.
Other remarks
- "It has Quake aesthetics!" did you mean "the colourpallete and nothing else"?
- "Wow, this is a nice horror game!!": I feel zero sympathy for my 8 pixels protagonist, and not scared or tense whatsoever.
- "But it has so many nice reviews!" I've seen an awesome explanation to this phenomena, too bad I can't find it. Teleglitch was given "for free" in a bundle, many people got it for the free cards. Those people reviewed with "good game" and "cool" and have around 3~5h gameplay. Think twice before trusting that Steam Rating up there.
At least the achievements are well developed.

is a wave based shooter. They say a polished turd is still a turd; I have no evidence to refute that claim.
This is a very strait forward, run of the mill wave based shooter. It has your assault, recon and support classes. Your rifle, sniper, and shotgun with some variations in armor sort of base differences. You shoot robots on various maps while collecting currency to refill health/ammo as well as buy upgrades and different weapons.
There is no limb damage, aside from head shots doing slightly more damage. The basic enemies as well as even most of the “higher” tier enemies just sort of stoically proceed in your general direction and swipe at you. (Some have guns.) I thought at one point I had done some limb damage to one of the enemy robots as it had a broken arm; I later discovered this was just a different marker for a suicide robot. Having a limb damage system I realize would have taken time to implement and possibly too much to ask for a small studio; however having it a game wherein enemies are constantly “at” you, mitigating or impeding their monotonousness onslaught might have lent
additional strategy other than “shooting all the things”.
The enemies will occasionally spawn behind you in the proverbial “monster cave”. A section of map designed to obfuscate from the player that enemies are being spawned into the environment. There is no environmental damage aside from bullets decals and the occasional red explosive barrel.
The guns feel weak, the enemies unresponsive to not only your presence but your attacks. Getting trapped in a corner with little or no ammo is certain death.
At times, the screen shakes while firing your weapon that seems ostensibly an effect to obfuscate the fact the weapons are ill-contrived for the task at hand. This effect was so violent and accosting to my eyes it truly fooled me into thinking my weapon was an effective means of dispatching these mini terminators.

Super Hexagon was originally designed as a mobile game, but I got it on Steam to spare my phone's battery.
It is more akin to a mechanical bull than it is a video game.  It's fast paced, with lots of spinning and dizziness, and also has a great chiptune soundtrack.  It could be a great party game with the right group of friends, as it has an arcade mode you can enable so you and your friends can easily compare your best times.  It also has online leaderboards so you can compare your time to everyone else in the world, if you want.
This game has a reputation for being maddeningly difficult, but I use this game to clear my mind, because there's no time to think.  It's very Zen, in that way.

Similar to Nr.2, but infuriating enough to deserve it's own point: who makes a game with two core mechanics (clicking or using items on something) and then expects the player to realise at one of the last puzzles that you need slide a freaking door out of the way? Not click, slide. Wanna have a drag item mechanic? Sure, why not, but then introduce it early and/or in such a way that the player realises this is even an option.
4. I finished it, but I can't say I enjoyed it much. The beginning was okay and it mostly looks nice, but the atmosphere and the satisfaction of solving puzzles was not there.

Risk of Rain review:
Gameplay: This is one of my favorite Steam games when it comes to gameplay. It's essentially a survival game, but has a very perfectlty balanced combat system. each charater you play as has 4 abilities, and another space in your hotbar for upgrades. This is great because during battle, an oppertunity for one of these moves will come up, and it's incredibly satisfying to tackle enimies strategically. But the controls work perfectly with this, and for a 2D Platformer. There are certain places in the environment where you can easily platform without enimies attacking you. This works flawlessly, especially with a gamepad. The combat is fast, the platforming is great, so the gameplay is a 10 for sure.
Graphics/Design: The graphics in this game are simple, but have more to it than you may think. The games graphics work so well with the world, becasue everything is so clear. Sure the pixel graphics are overdone, but in this game, it really helps define the game. And the character design is amazing, each character feels so alive and real. The level design is also great. It helps the player, and kills the player at the same time. Sometime you'll be exploring and out of nowhere, you fall in a pit. This may make you panic but luckily there are always nice ropes or maybe a bounce pad to help you out. It feels like the style of this game complements any gameplay aspects it has. For it awesome look and great desin, the Graphics/Design gets a 8/10.
Story: As far as I can tell, this game doesn't really have too much of a story. But this will get a pass because other survival games such as Minecraft and Don't Starve, are'nt too big on story either. But it appears that we crashland on a random planet, and must find a teleporter to repair and use to warp away. The story doesn't change for each character, but there is always a clear goal. As i said though, not much survival games have too much story, so this will get a 7/10
Sound: The sound in Risk of Rain is amazing. The music, first of all, is very mysterious sounding, and really captures the environment. When shots are placed a stisfying blow sound will be delivered. I love all the mixes that go with the music, and overall there isn't anything to complain about here. So sound, will get a 8/10
Extras: The upgrades and other characters in this game are fantastic. This adds so much replay value when everytime you play you can switch character. When you get into the game, multiple chests are randomly placed. Theses cost gold, but are worth it because these give your characters even more variety. When playing, there is always a completely different feeling of combat that works so well. Also, there are over 200 items, and your character can hold infinite amounts of items. There is also Co-op and online multiplayer. The online has sadly never worked for me, so there isn't much I can say there, but local is a blast. There is also a log that fills up when you find new things in the game. It's fun to keep and upgrade, so Extras gets a 9/10
Risk of Rain is an amazing game with tons of great music, characters, extras, and replayability. Risk of Rain gets a score of 9/10.

A solid JRPG that's a nice way to unwind after a hard day at work/school/being a rich bastage and swimming in a vault of good coins.
It's kinda hard to describe what makes this game such a joy because it's really just a matter of a polished gestalt. Every bit of design - art, music, animation, game designs - is INTELLIGENT and comes together sensibly. To give an easy example, you know how in some JRPGs, the animation times for your most powerful attacks can sometimes get tiresome because it just makes the battle TAKE SO LONG!? Well in Fairy Fencer, nearly all of them feel quick and snappy. With some notable exceptions, the game treats your time with respect. Dungeons never overstay their welcome and fights are quick and to the point, perhaps even too easy. Additionally, the voice acting is surprisingly solid, the dialogue is rather witty, and visuals are colorful and eye-catching. The characters may be heavily based on anime & RPG tropes, but they're all likeable in their own way (and the ones who aren't turn out to be villains har de har).
So I do thoroughly recommend this game, but with a couple pieces of advice. There's some "quests" that require rather onerous item grinding and there's a character that can only be unlocked if you're a certain level which requires some more grinding. I'm a bit of a reluctant completionist and so ended up doing these. In hindsight, I wish I hadn't. They don't appreciably advance the story and, in fact, make the game too easy. The result was that I finished with less excitement and joy than I otherwise would have. Unless you plan on beating the game 2x, I'd avoid the grinding. But then if you're gonna beat it 2x anyway, why worry about the grind the first time?

A New World: Kingdoms is a 4X game that has some gamebreaking issues.
*Updated for patch 1.2
You can find a about 13 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

The story of this game is a bit thin, the information on the steam page is basically the whole game story. You control a Kingdom, with the goal to wipe out the opposing Kingdom. You can do this by either destroying the AI's main city, or by purchasing it for large amount of resources. This gives you the choice of concentrating on building your empire to gain resources quickly or raising an army... at least that appears to have been the idea.
To start with the good - I like the graphic style. The low poly environment is nice and appears to be based on the same design of the last game this developer created. The game music sits nicely in the background, as does the ambient sounds. The units have a limited range of things to say and you will hear the same line over and over, but it was a good addition if the alternative was nothing.
That's where it ends. I ran into repeated bugs which stopped the game turns from progressing. I would start a game, take my first turn and that was it. Quitting and restarting the game resulted in the same issue. After 5 restarts where the game wouldn't move past the 1st turn, I had to quit the program and restart it before it would move onto turn 2. Even then, the same thing occurred at about turn 5. As I type this the game is downloading an update that should resolve this issue.
The blur option in the graphics that blurs out the map screen when you are in a menu is problematic. I found that if I started a game with this option enabled, everything would be blurred - always. I had to go into the options, disable and re-enable it to get the game running correctly. Eventually I just disabled the option, as on game restarts it would return.
The AI itself is a potato. In the few games that would keep going, the AI did nothing. It produced no units and didn't defend when I attacked. In the game I have linked above, it produced 1 unit in 19 turns - enough to delay the destruction of its city for 1 turn. I found no way to increase the difficulty of the game, so I have to assume that's as good as the AI gets.
As someone who has not played 4X games in years, a tutorial would have been a good addition. The first dev video on steam appears to have a tutorial message, but I did not see an option to launch it in the game. I bought the game based on the graphics and because it had been so long since I played a 4X style of game. Unfortunately I was frustrated from the start as I had no idea what I was supposed to do, so it took me a few minutes of clicking to figure things out. It didn't help that I hit the turn bug which made me wonder what I had missed.
At the time of posting this, I cant recommend this game. Thankfully the turn bug has been resolved, and I expect the blur issue will be sorted quickly as well. But until the AI is improved, the game just offers no challenge. Hopefully the Devs can sort this out as well.

Mirror's Edge is my favorite game of all time. Its graphics, art design, and gameplay are unique and nearly perfect. I had it on the 360 before I got it on Steam, and have tons of hours logged on both the time trial and countless campaign replays. The thing this game absolutely NAILS is the sense of momentum and speed. It really does feel like you are controlling a person, not a floating camera. The campaign, while short, offers a lot of unique levels and environments with tons of ways through them. Level design is phenomenal; just the other day I picked up ME again and found a new, faster route through a section of the first level. It's a complex maneuver to climb up a section with some boxes into a vent that saves me maybe two seconds. Yeah, maybe it doesn't sound like much, but it's complex and actually difficult to do each time and it feels great to have figured it out on my own. Finding a new route or way to tackle an obstacle is an awesome feeling once you string it all together and make a perfect run. The replay value is huge, as the time trials are addicting (Especially the expansion pack) and challenging. In summary, ME has a short but sweet campaign, lots of replay value because it is so unique, excellent visuals, and a wonderful sense of speed and momentum that is unmatched by any other first-person game.

I'll add a summary at the end for who wants to jump all my thoughts.
Let's start with the pros:
First of all longevity: I took around 30 hours to complete the main story quest and all side quests plus some challenge, witch for nowdays standards I found to be very impressive. The graphic is pretty good too, and, while in the first month/s of release it had some frame rate issues, i did not found any problem of such kind even in most crowded areas. Now the most important thing: gameplay, it could be a bit repetitive sometimes but I'll explain this in depth later in the cons.
The game has and RPG leveling up skills The Elder Scrolls style (the more you do something regarding that field, the more you got points to level up in it) with 2 branches of abilityes and 1 of "perks", you have Agility skills tree, Strenght skills tree and the Survivor one, You will HARDLY find any ability completely useless as any of them open some interesting options. The Agility tree offers you abilityes that allow you to move faster and avoid contact with zombies better, the Strenght gives you better chaces to deal with them faster and the Survivor one gives you the possibility to create interesting buffs and elemental throwing weapons and shields.
We can say that the main core of the game is running and exploration, and the game does this particularly well, expecially the runnig part: you will often find around ramps and various hints that you can use to climb over obstacles faster and in a more spectacular way. I had fun even just running around finding the fastest way to reach point B from point A.
How zombies reacts to your hits is really satisfying: their physics is pretty good and you really have the feeling of hitting something.
Some side quests are surprisingly well developed and interesting and the day/night cicle changes a lot of things gameplay wise (only at the beginning) since very powerful and agile zombies come out at night.
The cons:
The thing that really set me off is difficulty. The game is hard at the beginnig the first couple of hours, but once you start to leveling up and obtaining better weapons it becomes really TOO EASY: I was around 56% story completition and i had a weapond that could deal 753 damage points, what does that mean? That means that i could one-hit kill normal zombies and 2-3 hit max bigger zombies reaching 5 hits to kill a night monster. I could, being cautious enought, single handedly kill a horde of zombies, don't get me wrong, it's very satisfying the first couple of times, but the you realize you have no match and inmersion goes off. Not talking about how I ended up with TONS of materials, I could create whatever I need at any time, not very "survival" in my point of view.
You can add elemental damage to any weapons such as: bleed damage, poison, fire, electricity, impact and such but unfortunately these effects are applyed to enemies only once every 10-15 hits, not very useful, and, more importantly, why should I apply those effects if I can slice a zombie in half with a single hit? Those are more for aesthetics purposes than something else. It would have made more sense if Techland had put some type of zombies vulnerable to some effect.
Difficulty speaking, as mentioned above all the abilities you unlock are useful, but not exactly NECESSARY, explaining better: yes, they unlocks some interesting option to wide up your game style but eventually you'll become so powerful you will not need specifically any of those, you'll never come to the point that you'll need a specific ability to deal with a certain type of zombie, just sayin'. As above, drop kicking a zombie off a roof is funny, but not necessary, just for aesthetics than anything else.
As I said before, during nightime powerful zombies comes off, and you have to change your approach to a stealthy tipe or else you'll be aggroed by a lot of this kind of enemies leading to almost certain death, but these zombies have a VERY limited field of view, and even in you enter in the "cone of view" of some of this monsters they'll not spot you immediatly, giving you enought time to get away anyway. Why creating night monsters that cannot see well in the dark? We'll never know.
At last but not least, the story is a "already seen" one, but that doesn't bother me much
***********************SUMMARY*****************************************
Pros:
+ Longevity
+ Enemies physics and how they react to your hits is satisfying
+ Interesting and well developed side quests
+ Running around and exploring is done very well
+ Graphic and audio
+ Useful abilities, you will hardly find any of those compleately useless
Cons:
- Difficulty going downhill instead of uphill
- Not exacly absolutely necessary abilities
- "Already seen" main story
- Night time seems a bit too easy and could have been more difficult
- Weapon modifications are pretty much just for aesthetics
***************************************************************************
As final thoughts I had fun with and enjoyed Dying Light, that's what games suppose to do so fine with me but what really pisses me off is that this could have been a FANTASTIC zombie game if some attentions were payed during development. Techland however is releasing a patch that will add "Hard mode" to the game and i'll definetly replay this game in that mode and surely modify this review according to it

I could write a long review, but I'll try to keep this kind of short. Besides, I'm biased.
I will try to keep this spoiler-free. Put simply, Fairy Fencer F might not be for everyone, but if you like turn-based JRPGs, lots of customization, or VN-styled cutscenes, it's perfect. Plus there are waifus. And husbandos, if you like that.
+ Runs very smoothly, even on my toaster computer (you can change resolutions too)
+ Tons of customization with World Shaping/Furies and the WP system
+ Cute art, cool designs, and likable characters, with character development!
+ Not your typical battle system - action yet turn-based, tension gauge which you use to 'Fairize' aka power up
+ Cool skills, and you can also skip them and make battles go much faster by holding down the Next button
+ Fully voiced in Japanese! Even the fairies are voiced!!
+ Multiple endings and subevents in a kinetic visual novel style; multiple playthroughs available/needed
+ Harley and Ethel
* Very easy without any way to change the difficulty
* Difficulty also doesn't change on next playthrough, though makes the playthrough much faster
* Synthesizing/alchemy and quest system, but don't have any real impact or incentives
* Some of the OST is memorable, but others are just typical RPG fare (I like the second Fairize song best)
* Dungeons and 3D look alright, but are reused and are fairly short
* Plot twist is only somewhat predictable, but a little frustrating
- Pretty bland setup with some stereotypes and a cliche JRPG backstory (two deities fought, good vs. evil, wish-granting)
- Characters might seem annoying at first (Fang was awful at the beginning, but even he matures by the end)
- No Harley or Ethel route [Edit: Looks like this was improved in Advent Dark Force, so get that!]
- Godly Revival has no effect on actual story (you'll see what I mean)
Basically, get it because Tiara is best girl.

Before we start, keep in mind that I will make a lot of comparisons with Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth 2, that I will call from now on R2. I've made a review of that game too, so if you're curious go to my profile and read it.
Fairy Fencer F was a game that I bought shortly after R2, and paid full price. At first, I thought it was just a simplified copy of R2 and I left the game on the side for months. A week ago, I chose to give a chance to the game, and I'm really glad that I did, because it was a unexpected awesome journey.
Let's talk about the combat first: It's a turn-based JRPG, but you can move in your turn. Each character has a different attack range, and you move in your turn to reach the enemies to attack.  You can attack normally, use skills, magics, itens, escape, activate each characters special condition or Fairize. This last command can be activated when your tension gauge is full and it lets your character make a fusion with your fairy, making you temporally stronger and activating some special skills.
The normal attacks, unlike R2, only hit one enemy, despite the range of the weapon. Speaking of weapon, since your fairy is your weapon, you can boost the atributes and unlock skills, magics and normal attacks. For example, you can raise the amount of normal attacks you can perform in your turn, unlike R2 where all characters can attack 4 times and there is no ''skill tree'' to unlock.
You will collect more than 20 fairies in the game, and you can equip them to each character to make a resonance effect, and create some new abilities or boost some attributes in the equipped character. Since the story of the game talks about the battle of the Evil God vs the Godless, you can go to a certain shrine where both are pierced by many swords of different ranks, and you can use fairies of the matching rank to take away that sword in a battle and create a shaping effect on your fairy. This shapping effect will buff or debuff certain attributes or skills in the dungeons and some even change the enemies of those dungeons.
Each character has some kind of achievement to complete, like ''Walk 1000m as the leader'' or ''Win 10 battles without taking damage''. Those achievements will raise stats like Agi, Str, HP, SP, etc. It's something that it's not present on R2 but it's now present on R3.
Leaving the combat mechanics behind, let's talk a little about the story and character development. Since Fairy Fencer F it's from the same creator as Hyperdimension Neptunia, and Neptunia it's a game with a lot of jokes, without taking itself too seriously (except if you take a specific route in R2 that it's dark as ♥♥♥♥), I was expecting the same here, and when the main character first appeared, I thought this game would be a bad copy of Neptunia. At first, Fang is basically an idiot and I wasn't liking the character in the first hours.
But the game managed to surprise me with one thing: character development. Soon, Fang starts to get more mature and the events around him force him to change. This is another crucial difference from R2: the story is way more serious. There will be blood, deaths and regrets. As the story progresses, even the way Fang talks change, reflecting his own change. There are three endings: the Normal End and two endings, one for each girl. I will not tell who they are. I've only got ''A girl ending'' but the romance felt convincing and I really cared if they would manage to stay together in the end, which is a surprise, giving that most games have bad developed character interactions and romances. Unfortunately, not all characters are developed and I didn't care about some of them in the end. There's one in specific that I think it's very stupid (Pippin), and ironically you can use him as a weapon in R2.
Oh, there is another surprise too: the OST. The songs are awesome. Check them out on youtube.
But there are a few bad things, for example. there's just little world customization compared to R2, and less endings too compared to R2. The enemies are repetitive, only changing colors as they grow stronger, and some dungeons are repetitive too. Those are the same problems of R2, but I felt that there's only a few original enemies in Fairy Fencer F compared to R2. I missed some events and characters, but I don't feel like playing it again to complete what I missed, unlike R2 where I beat the game 3 times.
That said, with it's great story, character development, combat mechanics and progression and an awesome OST, Fairy Fancer F is worth full price, and it's a game that I will always remember with care. If you like this genre, go ahead and buy it. You will not regret it.

Excellent storyline defines this game's playability. Although the theme of the story doesn't seem special at all, the developer must be complimented for building a haunting gameplay upon it. Elements of longing, mysticism, fantasy, and mystery are well-blended, and will make you want to play further and further. Dialogues are well-written and entertaining. Visuals are dated and nothing special. While playing it on a 24" 1080p monitor wasn't a great experience – the blurry edges around all objects were quite visible – my enjoyment of the game wasn't impeded in any sense. Puzzles are quite straight-forward, and don't require any critical thinking skills; just be alert to your surroundings at all times, and pay special attention to all objects that your character can interact with, for be assured, such objects will have some use in the game.
The only irritant – a big one – in the game is its tedious gameplay. Your character will need to walk around a lot in order to solve puzzles and find things and NPCs. All that could've easily been bypassed by making the character appear at the location of interest with a single click. But no! The sadistic game designers make you watch as the character meanders her way to the desired location, which will make you terribly impatient and peeved, and you might even turn-off the game in anger...only to return a few hours later :).
SCORE: 7/10 (3 points deducted for tedious gameplay, average visuals, and unintelligent game design)
PS: To play the complete story, you will need to play this game

I've had this game for a while now and I thought this game should get the attention it deserves. This game to me is the best in it's genre. I highly recommend anyone who enjoys puzzle games to check out this game. The best way you can describe this game is portal in combination with Stanley's Parable on crack. This game makes you have to think outside the box to complete certain puzzles and by the end you probably wouldn't have seen even a quarter of the game. There's so much to see and do in this game, the first time you play through it it will take you a couple of hours if not days, if you know the map which you probably will once you reached the end it will only take you minutes to complete this game a second time if you know all the shortcuts, that's what I enjoy about this game, there's so much pointless in it that would keep you busy in a normal play through, it will eventually lead you along paths that progress the game to the finish, but you wouldn't know this until you finished the game. This game is just all around odd and the music just adds so much to the atmosphere, normally when I play video games I have the music on for a couple minutes and than switch to my music, but with this game I recommend you just leave the music on at all times. To me this is one of the best games I played on Steam and if I had to give it a rating I'd give it a perfect 10.

This game is infinitely frustrating. Having deaths as an achievement already made me question if this game was worth the effort. So many times the developer thought it was a good idea to not only make the spikes kill you instantly but put them right on the edge of the screen as you enter the next area. It's not fun gameplay, it's stupid.
They are very limiting on items. Even the vendors are frustrating. You think you are doing a good job of collecting money and saving up, getting 2 or 3 coins from each enemy you kill here and there. Then, suddenly, you run into someone asking for 20,000 gold to buy something that will give you one less tick of damage. It's not rewarding to have to backtrack to buy items. You will end up farming for gold just so you don't have to trek through some stupid area again just to get one item.
The monsters are equally frustrating. You end up running into the same types of monsters a lot but with different twists. You think you are fighting another shambling zombie but it ends up spitting out maggots after it dies. You have no control over the damage you take other than to die and "be more cautious."
Bosses are more a battle of hitboxes than fun gameplay. You have a small area you can hit some of them. One slip up and you lose half your health.
This game probably isn't for me but when I see the term Metroidvania, to me, it doesn't mean aggrivating and difficult.

I wasn't entirely sure which way to rate this one, but I think a thumbs-up is the fairer. Antichamber is fresh and different, challenging and thought-provoking, and offers a variety of inventive problems to solve, all presented in a unique but generally effective "whiteout" style of visuals. Channelling the spirit of Portal into an artsier indie package, it's a welcome experience for adventure/puzzle fans. On the other hand, it's prone to induce as much frustration as fun, especially when the labyrinthine environments and abstract progression conditions cause you to start running in circles. When combined with the surreal imagery, this can make it feel like some kind of bizarre purgatory which your starving soul will never escape. But then, given some trial-and-error and perhaps the odd hint from the community pages, you'll break out of these loops soon enough. So if you enjoy this kind of game, it's worth a try.

Having beat the game recently, I figured I'd write a review of it. Here we go!
First, this game is very difficult. However, its difficulty is steeped in the old "definition" of difficult. What might that be? Well, I'll tell you! It's a single word, and that word is "memorization." This game is a game that derrives its difficulty from placing enemies and traps at every turn. Expect to see A LOT of death spikes line the floors, walls, and ceilings. Some of the ceiling spikes will even fall on you! There are even some "Gotcha!" traps strewn about here and there, though some can be glaringly obvious. All of that said, the game's difficulty goes down in a sense when you've gone through a room a few dozen times and know which enemies are where and what traps are in the room. You know that those blocks will crumble, you know which ceiling spikes are gonna fall... Like I said. Memorization. This is the old "Nintendo hard" of way back in the NES era, and some of the way into the SNES era. Also, go into this game expecting to die A LOT when you're learning the rooms. If this kind of difficulty isn't for you, I already suggest giving this game a pass; you won't like the game, you'll get mad, and you'll write a review that will show it (and be unfair in the process). This game, for the most part, teaches you the kinds of traps you'll find through the game pretty early on, at which point you simply have to watch your surroundings. After the first area, if you find a trap "unfair" then it's very likely on you for not watching the environment. Very rarely are you presented with a hazard that is well and fully a bullcrap move (off the top of my head of writing this, about three come to mind). Either you were moving too fast, too slow, you didn't jump when you should have, you jumped when you shouldn't have, or weren't observant.
Next is the gameplay. The controls are rather tight and responsive in most cases. Most errors you might blame on poor controls are, in fact, most likely player error. The only time I would fault the controls are your ground movement. You move at a pretty brisk pace, and releasing a direction doesn't stop you on the dime. You seem drift forward a pixel or two, which is enough to sometimes be the difference between life and death. If you have a nitpick about that, you won't like a few sections, especially one that leads to a "key" to one of the most powerful magic spells in the game. Combat is very touch and go initially; you start with about 4 HP (might be 5) and you move up from there. This means you are most certainly are not a tank. As someone who has 100%-ed this game, I can say that even with 50 HP and the best armor in the game, you will NEVER be a tank except against the lowest and some of the middle mooks. Face rolling in this game will lead to frustration of your own creation. The other side of combat player side is your weapon. At first you start with the shortest, and weakest sword in the game. This makes fighting somewhat dangerous, though as you go you will get stronger and longer swords. Some weapons aren't even swords; one is a throwable axe ala Castlevania, another is a boomerang, and yet another is a bow and arrow. Alongside your weapon upgrades you will also be rewarded with HP hearts from each boss you defeat, with a few exceptions. There are also specific one-time items that give more than +1 to your max hp, so you have that too. Also as a fair warning, this game lacks a proper in-game map system. This means you will have to either memorize where things are, draft your own map, or look for a map someone else made. Movement between areas is a thing for a while until you pick up a certain relic that allows you to use special teleportation statues. With these, you can access a nexus of statues that you unlock as you find them. The area also has a save point within it, which makes said area VERY handy. Save statues are frequent through the game, and act more or less as checkpoints in areas (as long as you hit save at them) as well as healing stations. I will say that at times, the game seems poorly checkpointed, but thankfully this isn't a constant issue. It's also worth noting that some bosses have gimmicks to them. I should also mention that the right weapon and magic combinations can trivialize bosses.
Third would be the music. It's good in my opinion, and I enjoy it a lot. Some areas have better tracks than others, but that's how it goes. Not much to write out here.
Story is very cut and dry, not much to expound upon here. There are two different endings depending upon your item completion, but that's all I'll say.
I seriously doubt I need to write about the graphics, because they're right up there at the top of the page. Those shots are pretty dang true to the game.
All in all, I advise fans of older games to give this a buy and beat it. It can be a fun game once you get into the groove. Deaths usually don't set you back too far, except in a very few instances where it feels like things are checkpointed poorly. Combat makes you consider your weapon, magic, enemies, and environment a bit before you engage, and the bosses are varried. Those who simply dislike the old generation of games, give this a pass. This game is NOT for you, and I kindly advise you move along.

The game is enjoyable. I am glad to have access to a Shadowrun system simulator even if it is somewhat watered down.
My only major complaint is the discontinuity of stories and story modules. The main campaign has you going after the big payday, but once you get it, you can't spend it on anything and it disappears with the end of the main story, so the big score is practically meaningless.
The story modules are not really setup in a way that is friendly to running a single character across multiple campaigns, and the whole thing is obviously not setup to facilitate open worlds though some of the modders manage.
One of the great joys of video games and role playing games is the social aspect of inhabiting characters in parties. The fact that this is a strictly single player system ultimately is to its detriment. This is especially acute because of Shadownrun's Matrix/internet which is intrinsically social and basically absent.
I played through with a Decker Troll to start--which I know to be a relatively suboptimal character type--but I found the game and main story module practically necessitated that I drop any pretense of being a decker in favor of going max-min'ed street samurai just to survive the escalation of lethality and extensive combat. While there are certainly opportunities to make use of Decker skills and tech, the practical conditions of the design of modules and the main story necessitate that the primary character be nothing short of a combat monster. Decking in large part is rare and usually provided for by a hired specialist or story character.
It is good for what it is, but it lacks the general spirit of the Shadowrun setting. Overall solid proof of concept and first rough draft.
