This was my first game of the Civilization series and I absolutely love it.  The game has eight difficulty levels, making it very approachable for newbies.  It's the ultimate "easy to learn, difficult to master" game.  The best part is that it has virtually infinite replay value because each game plays out very differently based on several factors, including: which civ you're playing as, what resources you start near, which other civs you start near, which other civs are in the game (some you might not meet until halfway through the game), what the map is like (most maps are randomly generated each game based on scripts), and more.
Further extending replay value, there are several different options you can choose when setting up a game (size of map, map type, number of civs, game speed, difficulty, number of city states, barbarian behavior, and more)
Each AI-controlled civ has it's own "personality" that determines its behavior, and it's fun getting to know each civ over different playthroughs.  There are four main victory types (domination, science, cultural, and diplomatic) as well as a fifth "Time Victory" that triggers on turn 500 if no civs have reached victory (this victory condition can be disabled and I play with it turned off).  So there are a variety of strategies that can lead you to victory.
I've won many games without going to war once, just as I've war mongered my way to victory in other games.  The fun in the game is in learning to adapt to each situation the game puts you in as no two games play out exactly the same way.  The only real negative about the game is you can easily lose track of time as you become so engrossed in the game, and end up playing into the wee hours thinking "just one more turn" over and over.
Definitely buy the complete edition or at the very least the two expansions (Gods and Kings and Brave New World).  The extra map packs are pretty optional, but you pretty much need the expansions and you'll definitely want to have all of the available extra civs at your (or the AI's) disposal. I don't know if the devs gave up on it, or they just reached a point at which most people didn't have it, or what.
So, assuming you don't get the hang-up, the game is pretty awesome and there is a fair amount of workshop modding done for it, including lots of story content.  You could have hours and hours of entertainment doing the mod campaigns, even if you have the bug.

Overall, Final Rush is not a bad game and you could have some fun if you buy the game together with some friends. The game is quite steep and there are better games that offer the same kind of gameplay. One game that comes to mind is "Interstellar Marines", which also has a mode in which you destroy robots, just not in waves.

So I bought this rather than Lego Marvel's Avengers on the advice of a friend who said this had more content. He wasn't kidding! It's packed full of tidbits and Easter Eggs, nods both heavy-handed and subtle.
Same basic gameplay you get in every Lego game - if you've played any before, there's very little new offered here. The hub world is a mini Manhatten, and it's impressively sized. Hundreds of side quests, races, hidden gold bricks, and characters are dotted around, and hunting them out can be quite the challenge! There's an impressive array of heroes, mutants, monsters etc. available, though apart from Iron Man very few people get even one alternative version - mostly just palette-swaps, although in some cases (Iron Man, Green Goblin and Jean Grey are the foremost) the alternative can be radically different. There are also vehicles available to collect and buy in a similar fashion, although since you unlock Iron Man as the very first character, as soon as you're free to explore the hub world you can fly anyway, so vehicles feel a little superfluous except for some of the racing side-quests.
Levels are linear, and for the most part quite simple - though there is the occasional part that may leave you completely stumped! These games are aimed at a generally younger audience, so don't assume there'll be a great deal of challenge. There is a nice variety of challenges though, even if quick-time button-mashing gets a little stale.
Overall, a bright and witty package that, while not difficult, still has enough content to entertain most people for some time. I've 100%ed it in just under 50 hours, which is a fair amount of playtime. One for fans of Marvel, or younger gamers.

This is a short point and click adventure with some unique and novel concepts added. It's similar in some fashion to a masterpiece called 'Rhem' in that the puzzles themselves hold the atmosphere of the game as well as help tell a story. The developer is from the Ukraine and can be found here...
The biggest disappointment here is that English is not his native tongue and that is particularly evident when you compare the grammar and literacy of the various notes hidden around the place which tell a hodge podge story thrown together from all sorts of various inspirations starting from the movie 'Cube' to the game 'Metro 2033'. Having said that you can also tell that the developer is really trying to produce something which gives you a sense of wanting to explore and solve the mystery of an alien landscape.
Here lies the gem of the game. The map layout is actually really well designed and the puzzles compliment the whole entire journey without it being that hard at all. In fact even though an ingame connection to a walk through is kindly provided by the developer it's hard to imagine that you will need one as there are plenty of clues to the observant eye. Just as you begin to get immersed in this out of world experience the story finishes with a question mark and another door which leads to his sequel of this game 'Abandoned 2'.
Also there is four magical letters you can find and hilight which will present you with four additional diary entries by your brother as a special ending if you care to go that extra mile.
In final I really did appreciate this short adventure and will be looking at his next. I do suggest that the developer seriously thinks about hiring or gaining the confidence of a volunteer writer which could help enhance this story. As for map and puzzle layout, you seem to have nailed it by presenting a worthy enjoyable experience. The cartoon or animation could do with some slight tweaking by adding in a more detailed artwork and beautiful backgrounds. Having said that it was still quite justifiable though it seemed cheaply drawn because of its numerous unique settings it constantly presented to you.
You seem to be on a good thing here, hopefully with further improvements in both art and story this game will never truly be abandoned.

Atmospheric, top-down roguelike that uses lighting for tense effect. Roam around dark corridors, trying to catch slivers of light to see approaching monstrous threats, finding plenty of loot on the way, should you survive.

(As others have said, the game is available for free elsewhere on the internet, but I believe the graphics are a slightly better resolution in this version.)
Production values:
I really enjoy the hand-drawn art style, and the music does a good job of creating an otherworldly atmosphere. Also, unlike other commenters, I had no problems installing or running the game on my laptop. It was a smooth, glitch-free experience.
Gameplay:
The puzzles are fairly intuitive, and if you are willing to think creatively and pay attention to details, you will not need to resort to a walkthrough. I personally liked the challenge level, it was a brainteaser without being frustrating.
The tone of the game is supernatural in nature, so don't expect everything you see to make sense; however, there is a solid adventure-gaming logic behind each of the puzzle solutions. (Ex. Why does hitting a gong have the effect it does? Who knows? But you don't need it to make sense to understand the simple item-combination puzzle behind it: You know you need to hit the gong, therefore you know you need something to hit the gong with. You can easily suss that out on your own.)
My only complaint is there were one or two hotspots that could have been implemented better (I'm looking at you, Secret #3).
Story:
This was where the game started to fall apart for me. The plot is a rough outline at best, and is mainly a hodge-podge of vague sci-fi and adventure tropes. It doesn't feel like it has any real substance, and there wasn't enough of a payoff at the end for finding all the hidden clues. It just left the game on a hollow and abrupt note. I understand this is the first in a planned series of games, but I am still left with a lingering sense of "is that all?" I think if the game had been a bit longer, with a more substantially developed plot, it would have been more satisfying.
As is, this is a decent point-and-click puzzler that will give you 45-90 minutes of brain-teasing fun. The graphics and music are great, and the story is not-so-great, but overall the gameplay is solid.
I would give it a 7/10. If you are unsure about it, play it online for free. If you like it and want to own a copy, it's worth paying a dollar or two to support the creator.

Replay value is massive. There are multiple characters, some of which are well hidden. They all play differently, using melee, ranged weapons, or a combination of the two. Dozens of items buff your stats, or give you new passive or active abilities. There are even modifiers in the game, called artifacts, which can alter every run. One makes enemies explode into a bundle of bombs, if you feel like making your life harder.
Wholeheartedly recommend this game.

You want a hard as balls platformer with genuinely fun gameplay, as well as Binding of Issac style pickups and unlockables?  Buy this game.
It has thoroughly beaten me up and taken my lunch money on more than one occasion.  It will punish you, and you will enjoy it. Because you will restart, determined to do better than the previous attempt.  It is extremely addicting, and as such, is fun as hell.
Every class has a unique style to them. Each has a TOTALLY different method of traversing maps, taking advantage of terrain features, and destroying enemies in your path. I love it. A LOT of unrecognized love was clearly put into this game, and a lot of love has already been recognized.
Get bored of the game for a bit? Burn out?  Read the enemy and item descriptions as you unlock them.
Graphics: 2D. 9/10 for the little details, love'm.
Sound: 8/10.  Some sounds are piddly, most are pretty great.
Music: 10/10.  The music in this game will pull you INTO this game. It's repetitive game music, but it still has made some games intense as all hell.
Story: Uh... there is a story... right. 2/10, I forgot about it, but it is relatively unimportant to the gameplay to be honest, which is never something I thought I'd say.
Gameplay: 10/10. Your mistakes are your fault.  If you die, it is because you have not yet reached the appropriate level of 'git gud'. Your mistimed jumps, misfired shots, and hestitation can and frequently DO get you killed. This is quite a skillful game, and is a lot of effort to actually stay alive.
Learn the characters, find out which one you like, then forget about it because you need to use all the characters to unlock all the things.  I fell in love with this game very quickly, and it is a great way to spend either five minutes, or an hour, depending on how lucky you are that time.
Pro Tip:  The Engineer is the best class. ;)

I thoroughly enjoyed Fairy Fencer F as is apparent by my play time. The game play is very similar to Hyper-dimension Neptunia and take the role of a third person turn based RPG. The level grinding in the game never got to tedious and each battle did require some strategy and the characters equipment and move customisation took quite a lot of thinking, you could also put certain effects on the dungeons which put even more thought into what to do. The story is overall very engaging a throws some unexpected curve balls that even I, an avid anime fan and RPG player didn't see coming, which should be commended. The humour in Fairy Fencer F should also be praised, it had me laughing quite a few times. The characters are one of the best parts of the game, the main character, Fang's character development was really incredible as he retains his attitude but at the same time turns into an empathetic character who genuinely cares about his friends. The other characters such as Tiara and Eryn get little to no character development (excluding Ethel, best girl) but are still funny, admirable and relatable, you really do come to care about these characters. The music was also overall good though some tracks did start to lose some appeal after a while they still remained decent to listen to. There is also a fair amount of stuff to do after you finish the game and is impossible to do everything in one play through. Okay I've talked this game up enough time to delve into it's flaws.
First of all the difficulty, in my first play through I completed the game in about 32 hours during that time I died twice. For clarification one of those times was because I wasn't paying attention to the game and did one battle too many while EXP grinding. As long as you aren't a complete idiot and pay attention this games difficulty isn't that high and overall isn't the most challenging though I'm an RPG veteran. Secondly, there was a point where they say you have to pull all the swords out of goddess to unseal them and then they completely forget about it and it has no impact on the ending. Thirdly, the ridiculous hidden characters/fairies, as an RPG I understand secret characters are going to be difficult to unlock but Lola's requirements are really unforgiving as you need to complete all of her side quests, which are really easy to miss. For the two S-rank fairies I have no issue but one particular A-rank fairy, Dohn, is completely asinine much worse than Lola. To unlock him you need to do a  pub request that only appears when you haven't completed a certain dungeon and you have to complete it immediately and you get it after you complete the dungeon. Now you might think that's not so bad but allow me to provide some context, you get given no signs that you get this fairy after completing this request, the quest is only available for a short while when you haven't completed a dungeon so you are viable to miss it. Adding onto the chance of missing it is the fact that pub requests barely offer any good rewards for completing them and most of the time you won't have requests high up on your priorities. All of this culminates in a fairy that even harder to get than the S-ranks.
I think that this game is for casual gamers who haven't got all the time in the world but can spare a couple hours a week to play this game. It's funny, engaging and entertaining.
Overall, a good game.

This game isn't fun.   It feels like it's going to be a TON of fun in the early stages.  You start getting hearts, armor and weapons to increase your power, making combat feel much better and more rewarding.   However, the further you get into the game, the more you start encountering not just some areas with spike traps that you have to memorize, but entire sections where you have to make every jump perfectly, despite mediocre controls.  You have to go through these long sections to pick up an item that is absolutely required to progress forward, so you cannot skip over it.  This will mean you're stuck in this spot trying this challenge repeatedly until the game decides it's going to agree with your button presses and lets you move forward.   So, the majority of the gameplay here is watching the same 3-6 screens while you are pulling your hair out wondering if you're doing something wrong for 10-20 minutes, only to finally get it perfectly, doing the exact thing you've been doing the whole time...
I really want to like this game... The progression feels really nice, but the constant 1 hit kills ruin it all.  What difference does it make if you have 50 hp or 5 if all of the traps are instant death?   The combat quickly becomes more pointless than the platforming because you vastly outpower every enemy in the game.  Even the bosses are a joke with the right weapon/magic combo.   But, when you've downed that boss, you'll run into the next screen, and die instantly because you forgot there was a spike pit 1 square away from the starting tile, and the game didn't remove your momentum when you jumped through the screen, causing you to have to redo the entire section again... Not because it's hard, but because fk you...
There is an achievement to die 500 times.  This is not because the game wants you to sit in one spot farming deaths, but because the developer thinks that you dying 500 times over the course of a playthrough is good game design.  Despite giving you tons of tools to avoid death from enemies in combat, you'll never get a tool that will help the game register a half jump 6 times in a row because the game decided that's the challenge you need in order to get a specific item to keep going.
Couple this with random freezing and crashing, which can cause your success of these traps to be an instant failure anyway, I just cannot recommend this title if you value your time...  I plan on getting 100% complete on it, but only because I've already gotten so far, I may as well finish it off, however, I can see them ramping these perfect trap "challenges" up to the point of forcing me to quit before that happens.   And to be clear, I don't mind twitch gaming if the controls are on point.  But that is just not the case here, plenty of times you'll have to double jump across 2 screens, and while it's switching screens, it just won't pick up the second jump, but a perfectly timed jump is required, leaving you jumping between the screens a few times in order to properly even change locations.  They also have no qualms putting spikes under these jumps, so you can redo an entire section 10 times all because the game refuses to let you get that perfectly timed double jump.   The buttons are just too floaty for this level of precision required.
When you reach the Windy Ruins, you'll find out just how bad it all gets.   Suddenly you have jumps that you have to make across multiple screens on almost every map, despite double jump only working about 3/4ths the time during this event.  On top of this, you are only allowed to stand on a single block, because otherwise it's spikes for you (1 hit death despite all of your leveling to this point because fk you.)  To make it even more "fun" the terrible developer decides to make this ground constantly push you toward the spikes.... Hey, it's WINDY right, and as we all know, wind pushes people in armor around like they are leaves.  Not enemies though, because again, fk you.   It's really a shame the developer couldn't develop some proper controls, because this MIGHT almost be fun then.   Though, terrible level design that just keeps getting worse in the most unfun ways possible as you progress makes this seem very unlikely.
If you get this game, get ready to die unfairly often.  Spikes often blend into the ground, and they have no issues with putting a single one on a slope so that you don't notice it, but so it'll get you if you touch it on the way up, AND when you come back down, since it's naturally right in the path your character falls, but you'll forget it's there, since it blends almost perfectly with the environment.  I'm a huge fan of the Dark Souls series.... This game is the opposite in almost every way.  Dark Souls rewards exlporation with engaging combat and interesting item placement.  This game sticks everything in a 'hidden' wall, and punishes you for not moving across every screen at a snails crawl.   The combat should have been the focus here, but it quickly becomes the side dish, as you get annoyed having to fight the same guy over and over because of the shoddy platforming.

At first, I was loving the game until the logical puzzles were introduced with the block gun because I felt the game was set up do some really unique things that could only be done from a first person perspective and logical puzzles like those made it seem like a waste of such a build up. I still felt that way after the green upgrade but, upon getting the yellow upgrade, I was glad to find the puzzles that try one's lateral thinking were back and better than before. It was definitely worth giving the game a second chance because it is one of the better games of the genre and a uniquely worthwhile experience.

This second part of Syberia has improved on many levels, not only the graphics are more beautiful and more dynamic, but also the gameplay is a lot smoother and finally the circle that you use to move Kate has an arrow pointing the direction, in the first part it was sometimes annoying not knowning the direction where Kate is going. The puzzles are also a bit harder, but not very difficult, even though some of them require a lot of observation and attention to details. Castle in the Darkness is a challenging retro platformer that starts off very enjoyable, but ends up becoming a frustrating experience of instant death traps everywhere and save points few and far between.
So what's good about the game?
- The soundtrack is awesome, even weeks after playing it's still stuck in my head.  If you're into chiptune music, you won't be disappointed.
- Exploring and backtracking is encouraged and rewarding.  There are secrets everywhere, and most of them require a good eye or an upgrade you'll acquire later in the game.  There are plenty of optional bosses, upgrades, and money to be found.  Weapons and armor that are sold are generally affordable if you've been exploring everything.
- Most bosses are balanced.  While some of them seem brutally difficult at first, after you learn their attack patterns, you'll be kicking yourself for not beating them sooner.
- Magic is fun and intuitive to use.  Casting magic requires it to be charged similar to Megaman's charged shots, but it has unlimited uses, making it great for tearing up normal monsters as well as bosses that have limited windows of vulnerability.
- Bonus content for completionists!  I won't spoil anything, but getting 100% ties up a few loose ends in the story.
Sounds fun!  So what's wrong with the game?
- Instant death traps.  Not a big issue early on, but by the second half there's so many instant death spikes, you begin to wonder why the game even gave you a health bar.  There are several instances of spikes dropping from the ceiling that are near impossible to avoid without knowing about them ahead of time.  This kind of platforming can be enjoyable, but it was poorly implemented here, mostly due to the next issue:
- Save points.  The game is balanced enough for the first half of the game that save points aren't an issue, but as the platforming becomes more difficult, the save points feel further and further apart.  Not only that, but the placement of save points are poorly done as well.  There are a few boss fights where save points are several screens away in either direction, leaving you at risk of instant death before you can even reach them.  Nothing more frustrating than beating a boss and dying before you can even save.
- Warp points.  For a game that prides itself on exploration and backtracking, there aren't nearly enough warp points.  This game is massive, and even getting to a warp point can take a while.
- Broken/glitched bosses.  In a single playthrough, I encountered 2 bosses that stopped attacking and moving completely in the middle of the fight, making it an easy win but an empty victory.  Another boss was shifted from its usual movement pattern when it was hit with my magic attack, making the fight nearly impossible to win.
- Lack of equipment swapping on the fly.  When you first find new weapons/armor/magic, you have about 2 seconds to decide if you want to equip or not.  After that, you can only change your loadout at save points.  When some bosses are very hard to beat without a particular type of magic, you are practically forced to die over and over while you test each type of magic to see what works.
- Some secrets are too well hidden.  While most secrets can be found with a good eye (cracks in the wall, etc.), some are just flat out too hard to find.  We're talking illusory walls with absolutely no hints.  Spending hours jumping into every wall in hopes of a secret is not fun.
- No map.  I don't know what they were thinking with this one.  A Metroidvania platformer of this size with no map is just ridiculous, especially with the amount of secrets that are in the game.
So would I recommend this game?  It's tough to say.  I loved the music and almost all of the boss fights, but my mind keeps going back to the frustration of cheap instant death traps and having to repeat those areas over and over.  I imagine anyone just doing a casual playthrough would have a pretty good time, but if you plan to go for 100% completion, well, don't say I didn't warn you.

I just completed the game. And I've decided to give it some rankings, from 1-10.
The story is beautifully engineered as a thrilling, scary, exciting and a mindblowing stage, where you get so pent up, you can't play the game for long at a time (at least that's how I feel about it). This game is everything the other freeroaming zombie games should have been like, for example Dead Island. The last time I experienced such a feeling was when I was 9 years old, playing Zelda: Ocarina of Time. From the moment I started the game, I was excited. When the game ended, I felt so relieved, because I managed to go through that earthly hell, and make it. Therefore, I have to thank you guys for reviving that feeling within me. Just because of that, the game was definitely worth the money, and beyond that. Not to mention, when you have ended the main story, you are free to do exploring, kill zombies out of pleasure, do some awesome parkouring, do the sidequests, or simply all of them.
The mechanics as a whole in the game is very well made, whereas to the parkouring. It offers a lot of free mobility when you travel across the map within the game, it gave me a "superman" feeling without being overly exaggerated. You have to be precise and plan your route carefully and dynamically every second, all from dodging zombies, to jumping from one building to another. This concept is really exciting, and has never been utilized within games like this, Spiderman is an example of such a game, but minus all the zombies that are chasing you, adding another exciting factor to this feature of the game. My hats off to you.
While not having a powerful enough GPU to run the game at it's maximum settings, I must say that despite that, the graphics was pure, clean, and beautiful. There were massive details in human/zombie models, the building, when you see the rest of the city in distance, birds or flying debris in the air, which was really well made. I hope to get a more powerful GPU in the future, for I am dying to see how it feels like to play the game with everything run to the max. But overall, besides all that, the graphics is well, and more than enough to put in a feeling of realism into the game, making it very enjoyable.
I recommend this game to anyone who loves exciting and mindblowing stories, zombies, or simply parkouring. After I played this game I wanted to do some parkouring, but I highly doubt I'll be able to hoist my fat butt up walls anyday soon.

EDIT: Starforged Expansion came out. Game is still absolutely miserable because of power creep, with multiple problematic cards created through multiple expansions. Still don't recommend it. For 4 expansions in a row now going first is a huge advantage (roughly 10%-20% winrate difference depending on your deck) for nearly every deck in the game. Old problematic cards continue to be untouched. Basically same old problems new expansion.
If you're a competitive card game player stay far, far away. Power creep through 4 expansions, soon to be 5, has made the game into two people trying to out solitaire each other. The devs have recently started nerfing problematic cards, but honestly it's far too little far too late. All of the meta factions have extremely uninteractive decks and playstyles, the game isn't about outplaying your opponents in any degree, you're only outdrawing them.
If you're looking to play casually the game is fun in low ranks when nobody has the expensive cards necessary to play meta decks. So if you don't plan on playing seriously you can probably have fun.

Shadowverse is a card battle game thingamajigs.
And of course, being a dumb person myself, I hate things with strategy in it.
Shadowverse has that a lot.
but you know what. I like it.
You build decks, use the deck to battle with another deck.
However, what makes it interesting is the mechanics on the characters.
Each characters has these trait on which cards they could use.
There are Forestcraft, Swordscraft, Havencraft, etc. and to me, that's what makes me really like the game.
The tactics and playstyle within each crafts are so vastly different.
Use Forestcraft if you like spamming low points cards in your field.
Use Havencraft to slowly gain the control as you spawn cards in a timely manner.
Or play by risking your leader health to get damage boosts on your card.
What I also like with this game is, they're not forcing you to grind.
Yes, you can grind, but it's really easy to get cards.
Play several times, login one time, there you go, a pack of cards.
And despite having microtransactions, I never took notice as they never shove it up your face.
It's a good game, with good people backing it.
It's a solid consistent game of fun.
Despite hating strategy game, Shadowverse made it fun for me.
Which I would rate as a success for a game.

Killing Floor with robots is how this was sold to me.  I can see it potentially getting to that point, but it's not there yet.
Missing are a wider variety of robot behaviors, weapon impact, and interesting environments.
The robots tend to plod in your general direction in predictable "robotic" waves.  Maybe that's by design, but it is so basic that it gets boring quickly.
Weapons lack punch, which is probably due a combination of muted visuals and sound design.  The customization and weapon variety look like they could be fun, but right now there's just no impact from your shots.  A shotgun should FEEL like a shotgun.
It's a sci-fi setting, but the metal corridors and rooms are just too clean and symmetrical to create varied encounters...especially combined with robotic waves.
Needs some more spit and polish, but there's potential for the setting/concept.

Great indie RPG series with a classic PC vibe.
The old Shadowrun tabletop RPG is such a great intellectual property that I find it hard to believe it hasn't been capitalized on to a larger degree (Microsoft's shooter doesn't count, as it failed to either capture the essence of Shadowrun or stand out among an oversatured genre).  If that oversight allows weird little indie RPGs like this one to get published, I'm fine with it.
If you aren't familiar with the lore, it's cyberpunk meets fantasy; and it's every bit as ridiculous and awesome as it should be.  If you want to be a shotgun-toting orc with a pink mohawk, bionic legs, and a cyberjack implant for hacking the matrix, Shadowrun welcomes you.
The Shadowrun Returns series in particular are narrative-oriented tactial RPGs.  This first installment has some technical issues, but is well worth playing regardless - there's a pleasant surprise in store for fans of the SNES game as well.  The second installment Dragonfall is even better than the first - a criminally overlooked game.
All three Shadowrun Returns games include editors for creating your own campaign.  I believe Dragonfall and Hong Kong are the favored platforms for the community.

Killing Floor 2 has finally released. I was really hyped for Killing Floor 2 as launch was coming up. I liked the first one, but I didn't play too much of it. Killing Floor 2 had a lot of really nice improvements (better gunplay, the gore system makes shooting feel like it has a lot of impact). I bought it as soon as it was available on Steam. The updates were a bit slow but I was having fun.
Let's just say early access for this game was a ride. As the game went through development I became less and less interested. The introduction of the patriarch was nice, but the maps it brought along were terrible. Farmhouse in particular is awful. I decided to take a break from the game. Then I heard that they added zed resistances and other stupid changes. I continued to ignore it until just before release. I booted up the game and... it was exactly the same. It feels like no feedback was taken from the community at all.
Farmhouse is
the same as when it launched. Other maps have changed very little and the last official map we got was Prison... which was back in April. What the ♥♥♥♥? We have 3 community maps but they are not nearly as refined as Biotics or Burning Paris. It felt like the game was designed to be interesting for early access/press and then they just shoehorned in everything else.
I'm not going to bother to talk about the comestics other than to say they're insulting. The drops you get on a daily basis are ♥♥♥♥ing useless too. Wow a flat cap or another useless encrypted USB that I'm not going to buy a key for.
The classes are nice but there are too few weapons. So the weapons become "tiers" and some weapons are too weak for their cost that most people just end up skipping them.
I don't know how many times I need to be burned before I realize that Early Access only serves to harm me but Killing Floor 2 is an excellent example of a game going downhill as it got "finished".
Oh and ♥♥♥♥ you Tripwire for putting KF2 on sale mere weeks after its release on Early Access. :styx3:

Castle in the Darkness is one of the best purchases I've made on Steam. The game has a lot more depth than I expected it to have; there is actually a LOT of stuff to explore, and the game is full of hilarious easter eggs and references to classic video games that clearly inspired it.
This should be an obvious point, but this kind of a game needs to be played with a controller or joystick to be enjoyed properly. People who choose to play CITD on a keyboard are just setting themselves up to be disappointed.
The graphics, sound, and gameplay are all top-notch. Clearly, COTD's developer was going for an 8-bit retro vibe, and succeeded tremendously in terms of having this game play and feel like one of the best titles from the NES.
One complaint you are likely to encounter a lot in reviews of CITD is its difficulty. Although there are plenty of insta-kill traps, they often had me laughing because they are clearly parodies of tropes from classic video games. I don't feel that they spoil the game because screens where you can save your progress are ubiquitous, so there weren't many occasions when I had to spend a lot of time replaying a section of the game whose insta-kill trap(s) kept getting me. After dying, I'd usually respawn only a few screens away from the death trap if I had been humble enough to save when the opportunity presented itself.
I will attest that one-hit kills from spikes can get frustrating toward the end of the game, but in the vast majority of cases, I died because I failed to jump with enough precision. (I can only think of one part in the game in I repeatedly died because I found it very difficult to notice a spike that kept falling on me every time I walked underneath it.) That having been said, the game is refreshingly hardcore and does not hold your hand like modern games tend to. It's tough but fair - just the way I like it!
CITD doesn't have much of a story, but it wasn't meant to, so I can't really fault the game for that fact. Besides, when it comes to a game like this, I'd rather spend my time enjoying the action than waste it trying to skip over tediously superfluous dialog or text boxes.
I bought this game expecting to get some retro-themed hardcore action and maybe a few funny references to classic video games. What I got was a surprisingly polished and well-made homage to classic gaming that's one of the best Metroidvania-style games I've ever played, and is quite funny to boot. This game gets a solid recommendation from me, but it will induce frustration at times unless you are incredibly humble and patient. Despite (or perhaps because of) that point, I am very happy with my consumer investment in this game.

Disclaimer: i'm a sucker for zombie games so i might be biased in the review for this game since i just love games which include zombies and they instantly gain at least +1 point in grading.
There are plenty of zombie games on the market and thematic is rather washed out, but for me the game is pure fun. If one played Dead Island than this is similar to what one can expect from the game, but with much improved weapons, handling, physics and fine-tuned elements.
Some people and reviews complain about the story. I don't want to spoil it, but for me the story is far from bad one. It isn't great as in Mass Effect, but this game has a completely different concept one should take in account. The story is good and IMO decent enough to keep you going. Plus, the side quests add to diversity of the game and give you extra reason to further explore the city.
The game is rather well balanced and it will go easy on you at start and become increasingly difficult as you progress through the game. Also, skill tree (BTW, there are three different skill trees), weapons and environment options really add up to the diversity of gameplay and playing style.
Technically the game is decently optimized for PC. Yes, there were some problems with some GPU's and CPU's (mostly AMD) but most of the issues have been fixed and they're actively working on fixing the rest.
From audio point of view if one has a decent headset or surround sound system audio really adds to the immersion in the zombie infected city. Screams in the background and soft music adds to the great game atmosphere. Combine that with well-designed environment (good graphics) and day-night cycle which cycles between rather dull and slow zombies to aggressive ones which are supported by extra powerful zombies which appear only during the night, and you get a great zombie game.
Some reviews point out that the missions are repetitive and most of them are based on the same concept which is go-to-location-X-and-fetch-object-Y. While i agree that missions are mostly of that type, they have enough variety to keep player interested for the game and further explore the game. Secondly, just think of it for a second. If one would really find him/her-self in a zombie infected city there would be rather high demand for brave people who would risk their lives to get necessary supplies from dangerous locations infected with zombies. For me this makes 100% sense. And third, if one pays close attention to detail one can hear irritation in Kyle's (main protagonist aka YOU) voice when he needs to do a go-and-fetch mission again.
All i have written so far is for single player and on top of that the game offers a nice CO-OP mode which one can play with his/her friends or random players. Plus, there is a multiplayer addition to the game too which is a mixture of Left 4 Dead and Evolve game. In the multiplayer one can choose to be one of the four survivors or be super powerful zombie. CO-OP and multiplayer are highly dependent on people one plays with, as any other multiplayer experience. If one is playing with friends or good players fun is guaranteed and if you play with trolls or bad players who don't respect CO-OP/MP one will have bad time and a free test of his/her tolerance.
The game has some amazing extra value which comes in form of weapon dockets (ie. gold keys if you played Borderlands) which will give player top tier weapons when reclaimed in the game (1 docket = 1 weapon). And the game has a companion app for Android and iOS where one can play Dying Light in a form of Facebook Mafia Wars where one sends scouts on missions. Great thing is that loot from the missions can be transferred to the original game one is playing on the PC or console!
To sum things up, i would highly recommend the game to any player and it would be a must to those who love zombie games. To be completely hones, i haven't played such a great zombie game for quite a while. For those looking for numbers, here is my game review roundup:
Video: 9/10
Audio: 8/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Fun factor: 10/10
Extra value: 8/10
At the end, one is killing zombies in many creative ways, and if you don't have fun with it and all you have is frustration from the game - you must be doing something wrong.
Very addicting, fun, and worth the price.

Awesome game. Valve makes the great games, and Half-Life 2 is the epitome of all their games. Only Halo and Gears of War can contest with HL2 for best sci-fi shooter, and I personnaly think it is better than both. My favorite parts are the intense and heart-pounding moments of action, interactive "cutscenes" that you can just mess around in, and amazing facial detail (keep in mind this was released in 2004, and the details, textures, and facial movements are so good that someone who doesn't know about it might think it was made in 2010 or later).

I'm uncertain about how well this matches up to the tabletop RPG in terms of gameplay, but in terms of setting, characters, overall feel, this is a great introduction to the system, and certainly makes me want to play the p+p version. The story is engaging, I'm a fan of murder mysteries and this is a great one to go through as a slow-burn play. The music direction is cool and atmospheric. Sound design in general is very well managed. The perspective greatly benefits the feel that they're going for. Art design is really nice, striking the careful balance between looking ugly but still looking easy on the eye. Combat could do with some tweaking as it unfortunately suffers from XCom percentages syndrome, but this is a minor complaint compared to everything else that can be praised. It would also have been nice to have voice acting, but again, a minor gripe.
It's especially good at addressing the problem of the matrix that I am familiar with due to playing Cyberpunk 2020, in that instead of having characters sit there twiddling their thumbs for God knows how many rounds, it nicely alternates. Sadly this is a fix that is only provided when in combat, and it would be nice to be able to do the same outside of it, but it's a nice fix that can certainly be expanded upon in later games.
Finally, and I can't believe I have to give it praise for this, but it actually gives a satisfying ending, instead of finding some really irritating way to pull a fast one on you, whether it's making it so your decisions don't matter, having one of the NPC's perform the supreme sacrifice, ultimately rendering your character's involvement superfluous, or any other manner of rubbish ending that takes all agency away from the player.

A faithful adaptation of an old classic with a modern, experimental, twist.  The combination of turn based tactics and real time strategy overworld is always engaging.  Having beaten the game three times (on normal, classic, and normal ironman) I can say that it is definitively worth your time if you like any sort of turn based combat games, and is worth a look if you like RTS.  An engaging storyline mixed with solid mechanics adds up to a game that will give you an amazing ROI for the money you put into it.
I am a fan of most of the games of the series, and this is a worthy successor.  While I will admit I prefer the more iterative approach of TFTD (which I spent hundreds of hours on and bought another copy on steam just because), this game is a very faithful follow up to the original series.  The turn based combat feels like the original, and it mirrors the tried and true strategy of move with reserving time units (or not, if you're dangerous like that).
If you're new to the series, this is probably the best place to start:  It is a faithful recreation of one of the best games of the last thirty years, and has a good learning curve on the lower difficulty levels.

The first thing I did before even starting to write this review was to give the "thumbs up".
Before I started this amazing adventure, I had little to no experience with "zombie" games, and to be quite frankly, I am now a zombie killing machine. I am a zombie grinder, I am the zombie terminator. I am Legend.
All of that said, and despite all the QQ around the AMD systems (which is my case), I've had absolutely no problem whatsoever with FPS, quite the opposite. The graphics are close to the best I've seen.
The soundtrack will keep you wondering if death is upon you, or just around the corner.
The gameplay is incredibly good, as you can "visit" most of the buildings, and you can parkour your way around Harran.
Obviously, not everything is perfect, and to me, the biggest disappointment is the story itself. It's amazing until near the end, where it just feels it's being wrapped up quickly, leaving some loose ends, and wondering you what the heck just happened.
Unless their plan is to continue the story with Dying Light 2 or some DLC, the ending is quite meh, whereas the rest of the story is quite good, making you shed a tear once or twice. Them feelings...
The crafting part of the game is quite regular, and you've plenty of options to make your killing weapon of choice even more deadly, and prettier. From bats, to axes, to hammers, you can use anything to kill a zombie. The combat system is nice, and the guns feel a bit awkward, which just leaves you more excited to melee everything down, and feel the blood and guts hitting you as you hack and slash your way to the top. Top of something, that is.
If you are looking for a "survival" game, there's not much survival to do here, as you can pretty much skip sleeping the entire game, eating only helps regening some health, and there's no drinking or anything similar. It's, however, a scavenger heaven, since you can find loot pretty much anywhere.
I'd easily recommend this game to anyone, as it's quickly climbing to the top of my all time favourite games.

This game reminds me of Lord of the Rings the Third Age for gamboy advance. You Control a certain amount of units against an enemy in a dynamic chess game that changes the rules on every mission. This rule change is sometimes welcome others not so much. The game can catch you completely off guard with tactics it has pounded into your head from previous missions. The ONE MAJOR PROBLEM I have with this game is the AI cheats. Especialy on harder difficulties the AI breaks its own rules to get the edge. The same shot that you have a 45% chance of making(and miss 90% of the time) they seem to have a certain 100% chance of making, and that is only on the classic difficulty. This game is best played on normal simply because the mechanics dont feel like the game is cheating you. It is tough but fair. The higher difficulties are not fair. The second problem I have is the shooting through walls and buildings because the animations dont line up right. I wish this game had a line of sight system because It would have fixed the AI's cheating and made the cover system easily understood. For instance if my character is standing around a corner of a fast food building all of a sudden somone inside the building steps out shoots through the corner and kills my man, but the corner remains intact. This is a problem because there is a TON of destructability in the game, but its inconsistent.
Overall Phenomenal I pointed out 2, and the only 2 problems I had, and ran out of time to tell all the incredible things about this game.

Quick summary: A nifty small game worth a few dollars and a few hours. Never have I yelled "Don't tase me bro" with such sincerity and volume. As of 12/1/2014 what you pay is what you get, no microtransactions or DLC.
No proper tutorial to point out the games features. Especially the UI.For example: Health is of course located at the top along with a "shield" however health is segmented, and as you take damage your health regens only a segment. In order to fully regen your health you need to either sprint to the health station or purchase an upgrade at the store via the somewhat hidden upgrade tab. I found the upgrade tab after maybe 3 failed games.
Levels are rather ho-hum. Little bits of moving machinery here or there to give some 'life" but theres no awe. Which helps in a a way, no real distractions while fighting. Levels feel legit like factories/storage units in which there would be plenty of robots. However they feel like legit factories and storage units, rather dull but serviceable.
Currently there are 8 enemy types each having their own range of somewhat charming taunts,Of which only one you will learn fear from. The taser-bot. You will feel the dread of Sarah Connor meeting the terminator in the 2nd movie as you are approached by its blue tinted fury.  As far as the rest of the cast goes, they lack any real intimidation or "character". Which yea I get "robots, what character?" but it does leave ya wanting when games like Leaft 4 Dead and all of its Boomers, spitters, Tanks and whatnot exist.
You can have a total of 3 weapons by the end of a "Rush", your side arm, your main, and an "alternative weapon". Weapons feel about as good as they can when shooting against wire and metal, though a rather lacking selection of guns may put you off. 3 upgradeable weapons (standard shotgun, rifle, and sniper-esqu rifle) and 1 upgradeable side arm are what you choose between entering a match. As you play each match you accumulate points to spend at the shop which allows you purchase a standard/all around upgraded version of the starting selectable weapons (main), two preference weapons (alt), and two "experimental weapons" (alt). The experimental weapons provide a sort of "reward play" as they become accessable after so many rounds of accumulated points, you may destroy hordes of robots with dangerous lobs of lightning or incinerate them with essentially a laser cannon.
Your 4 upgradeable weapons are manageable in the combat profile screen, there you can view and customize your weapons and character though only somewhat. Armor is purely for looks, mix and match as you unlock, some weapons have alternative firing modes however scopes give "recoil reduction bonuses" which should be a pure cosmetic choice not a somewhat forceful upgrade. Aside from firing modes, the upgrade paths of weapons are linear. Your character also has a skill tree, after obtaining the trainee perks your able to choose 3 of 6 (plus 1 required) perks from each branch of Assault, Ranger and Support. While respec-ing is easy enough, its a shame they don't let you have multiple pre-sets of perks. The perks in question generally give damage or accuracy buffs or give a grenade or ammo clip ever 2 minutes. Nothing too amazing but the choices are decent choices as opposed to a blantantly better perk to choose from that its been paired with.

I would totally recommend this game on both mac and pc for anyone who's looking to get into the strategy genre or anyone who is already familiar with it, or even experienced players of the genre who need a simpler game. Also note that this review is written by someone who played with ALL dlc.
Pros:
-nice artstyle
-many unique civs who each have a unique ability and unique building or unit (or in some cases tile improvement)
-a lot of roads to victory
-simple mechanics
-great music
-simpler, smoother gameplay and a friendly UI
-steam workshop allows for a lot of mods that add hours and hours to the base game (scenarios, civs and maps)
-big, friendly community which constantly spews out more mods and also guides for beginners.
Cons:
-little to no variation in best possible strategy with most civs
-social policies are unbalanced (most people pick liberty because free worker & settler, or tradition, honor or piety are useless in comparison)
-some civs are unbalanced (america for example is underpowered, yet babylon is incredibly OP)
-you can infinitely spam out wonders
-less depth than civilization 4
-advisors ar really annoying if you haven't figured out how to disable them
-multiplayer is kind of buggy (especially with cross-platform play)
If I had to describe civilization V in three words it would probably be like: risk, on steriods.
Because it can be like risk if you're planning to go for the domination victory, only your warmongering will have consequences on your happiness. This feature of happiness and unhappiness might seem like it balances the warmongering out, and it does... until the late game comes.... (or when you have a few tenets in the order ideology)
The game has four roads to victory; science, domination, culture and diplomacy (or economic victory, as you will need to bribe a lot of city states to get this victory, or play as greece, complete a quest and instantly become allies).
Science involves you discovering every little secret of the universe and launching a rocket to outer space.
Domination is the most straight forward victory, just burn every other city on the map and you'll be set.
Culture is the most confusing and imo the hardest to get victory, as you will need to acquire tourism, once your civilization has generated more tourism than another civ in a lifetime, you win. Unfortunately tourism comes later and in smaller forms than your first batches of culture, so you'll have quite a bit of catching up to do.
Diplomatic basically has you bribe every city state on the map (if there are no city states just build the forbidden palace and make sure you're the host of the world congress.). A victory by diplomacy is quite easy to acquire, provided you stay alive long enough for the elections.
Managing cities in this game might be the easiest in any 4x strategy game I've played to date, as it's as simple as this:
there are a few resources your city gets out of tiles in its borders (these are worked by your citizens, which you don't even have to assign manually).
-food: helps your city to grow and work more tiles
-production: the higher production you have, the more you can build.
-science: your ability to advance in the tech tree to boost the other stuff.
-culture: makes sure your border grows so none of your citizens go unemployed.
-faith: your ability to create your own religion
Yes, you can create your own religion and (violently) spread it to every city on the map, because nobody expects the babylonian inquisition to spread hinduism to their neigbours; the aztec empire. Religions basically have traits (which you can choose) that improve your cities (e.g +1 gold per turn per 4 citizens following this religion).
Combat is also pretty straight forward: try to be ahead in science, numbers and promotions and try not to kill your entire army. because once you have the numbers you can just charge at everything the enemy has.
So short story, if you want to continue the legacy of alexander the great, immortal dictator of the greek empire, the founder of islam, conquerer of america, russia and china with death robots, I'd recommend you buy this game on sale!

Teleglitch is like a procedurally generated classic DOOM with a top-down view. Lots of weapons, a map that reminds me of the good old Doom one, the color palette, the choice of mutants and monsters... yet it's different, and adds more to it.
It really takes some effort to get through the first levels when you're new to the game, but when you get a hang of it, you can even slay the most atrocious enemies the game throws at you! Collect and manage your inventory, craft enhancements, weapons, even drugs! Find your way to the core to destroy it once and for all!
I haven't found the core yet but I'm inching my way forward bit by bit. Permadeath prevents ma from using savegames, but you get the chance to pick up a game with a randomized inventory two stages below the one you just entered. Say I get to stage 7, which triggers my ability to start a game in stage 5. Getting through every level in one go is favorable though, because you might get a better inventory than what the game generates for you! Too many times I failed at the end of stage 8 because I ran out of ammo on that huge robot killing machine... until I finally beat it, barely!
The story is interesting, with little snippets to discover along the way. Hidden areas give you a little headway if you can find them, and you should invest in some advanced scanners or mutant hordes will devour you alive when you make the wrong step!
This game runs well on lower end machines, and it builds a very dense horror atmosphere, now even with an arena mode to practice all those weapons before you head on out to use them for real.
A defeinite recommendation!

I hate this game so much.
It's a cool concept, but It's a concept that's been done better by almost every other game of it's type. The thrill in these games comes from barreling through obstacle after obstacle while the stakes are raised with each passing second. In this game, you aren't playing to beat the obstacles. You're playing to beat the effects. Before anyone criticizes me of only hating this game because i'm bad at it, I've played plenty of harder games. That isn't why i hate this game.
Nothing is consistent. Sometimes levels will start off with just a gentle spin, while others chuck you into the deep end with the screen spinning like jet engine, pulsating as if about to burst. The player has no control over this. It wouldn't be so much of a problem if it was only aesthetic, but it's the only challenging factor about the game. Take it away, and the game is easy. Ramp it up to the same levels this game does, and it becomes unplayable. Walls will lunge towards you at inconsistent rates due to the pulsing, inputs will be missed due to the untimely rotation switches and walls will appear much closer to you due to the screen tilting.
But of course, that is to be expected from ultrahard games like this. On their own, none of these elements are out of place. It's how random they are that ruins this game for me. You can't control the difficulty of this game. Even if these effects were optional, or only part of harder levels, this game would be greatly improved.
Anyway, that's the concept out of the way. Now onto the controls!
The controls are sensitive to the point of frustration. Accuracy isn't possible in this game. The slightest touch of whatever controls you use is enough to ruin a run. This game (for the most part) takes place on six lanes. Why not have it so you switch lanes at the touch of a button? There's no reason for all the middle ground here. So many times Iv'e messed up, simply because I wasn't sure if I'd gone where I wanted to go. All the crazy effects going on in the background make it even harder to see your character, Especially while also focusing on the oncoming walls.
So, yeah. the most enjoyment I got out of this game is writing this review. Go play 140 if you want a better (if easier) example on how to make a game like this satisfying and interesting.

Final Rush is a very bad copy of Killing Floor's gameplay. The goal is to survive through timed waves that spawn robots and getting points to spend in a shop that appears between two waves. There you can buy weapons and upgrades only.To buy ammo or health, go find the two automated distributors that are elsewhere on the map so you have to choose what to go for, because despite the futuristic environment, you can't carry stuff to heal you on the way...
The story is set in a highly advanced technological future, and robots got corrupted. That's all we know, seems a bit lacking of context here.
Maps are small, only 4 of them, and so many choke points you can't use for yourself because you'll get swarmed with robots in no time. No welder to seal doors and taking a stand, absolutely no strategy here. Only way to survive is to continuously run around the (small) map and gather a horde behind you until the clock goes zero, then shoot them all. But beware of the map itself : you can jump, but can't jump above a tiny obstacle to flee the horde, which will bash you to death.
There is only 3 weapons to begin with, and an infinite ammo pistol (and bashing that merely damage bots or push them away...). Aim is tedious because of a very high recoil that screw your aim after each shot. Weapons don't feel powerfull as it can't one-shot a basic bot in the head. Oh, there is grenades too, but they'll bounce a weird way and blast radius is so ridiculous (maybe 1-2 meters), unless they badly bounce back at your face and kill you. It's safer to throw rocks and it might do more harm to those bots.
Tried the online game too, no server below 130 ping, all empty...
It seems there is an xp counter, but no profile page yet to see if there is perks to unlock, so there's no point to grind highly difficult waves of uninteresting robots for peanuts.
So it's an early access game, but it is still very unpolished in the current state. Even at 10€, get Killing Floor instead, or wait for KF2.

Short and sweet Point-and-Click adventure game.
Your brother went adventuring in the mountains of Tibet and found something mysterious and exciting.  But he disappeared, leaving only journal entries giving you tantilizing hints.  Follow in your brother's footsteps and discover the mystery!
The game consists of a sequence of screens that you can click left, right, up, and down to move (if possible depending on location) from screen to screen.  There are items you can pick up and use.  Unlike some other point-and-click games, this one does not hold your hand and show you possible moves.  Click everywhere until you figure it out.  Usable items will show up at the bottom of the screen in your inventory.  There are also journal entries your brother left behind that you can gather and read for clues.  Use the items by clicking on them in your inventory and dragging them where you want them used.
The puzzles are mostly logical and mechanical.  Though once or twice there were times when it didn't make sense because I could have done something in real life but the game wouldn't let me do it.  But overall they were good puzzles.  Some of these point-and-click games and hidden object games have crazy uses for items.  I'm happy to say that this is not one of them.
The graphics are a huge plus for me.  I love the cartoon look.  Or hand-drawn, or whatever it's called.  It just looks so cool to me.  But that's personal preference, and you can decide for yourself if you like the screenshots.
The music is just kind of spooky ambience background sounds.  Nothing special.  But it definitely fits the theme of the game.
Time to Finish: 1 hour or less.  Depends on how quickly you figure out the puzzles.  Also there are optional bonus items to find that reveal some more of the story.  You can find them along the way or return to the game after you finish.
Oh, and I guess there's a free version online somewhere.  Just so you know.

SO MUCH FUN.  It's pretty much like NES games, where it seems tough at first but slowly you learn the level layouts, you get a good feel of how your character and the enemies move and then you just breeze through it. You will die a lot but it's not bad and most bosses have an easy pattern or a way to easily beat them. I wasn't sure I would like it but I got hooked.  The music's neat, the art is fun to run through, and the level layouts are not just fillers.
Many people complaining about this game point out how it's lacking modern features like maps or mutliple spawn points : the point though is to recreates the feel of older games and a HUGE part of the game is about memorizing map layouts, which you can only do if you go through areas multiple times. There ARE generous health-restoring save points before bosses that are long to beat, and those that take shorter time by exploiting a weakness have more distant save points.  You can also eventually teleport to move through the levels faster when backtracking. Plus I'd say It's actually easier than other similar genre of game like say Megaman 9.
Of course, if you're one who has no grit, gives up easily and just wants to prance through the nice graphics without anything resembling a challenge laid across your path, and if you have absolutely no capacity of learning from your mistakes, there are plenty of recent games available for you on Steam but it is not this one.

Played: Feb 2014
PROS:
+ More cinematics
+ Voice acting better than episode I
+ Does not have the graphics problem episode I had with switching to windowed mode in-game
CONS:
- Story STILL does not go anywhere
- Voice acting (English) still a bit silly
REVIEW: Let’s be honest: if I hadn’t purchased Syberia II along with Syberia I as a super-cheap combo pack, I wouldn’t have bothered at all. Everything that is “good” about Syberia II is only relatively good when compared with the terrible Syberia I; there is nothing superlative about any facet of this game.
A good thing about this game is that it has more cinematics than its predecessor. A game that sells itself on story should have many movies, and there are some here. For a game released in 2004 the visuals are not bad, but they haven’t aged well at all and alone they shouldn’t induce you to buy this game. Furthermore, the voice acting won’t make you wince as often; as when intonation is way of or a word is mispronounced, but you will definitely notice strange moments in the dialogue.
The main draw of this game is supposed to be the “amazing story” but here is the problem: it never develops beyond the premise that your protagonist wants to help an old guy reach Syberia (and still features the intelligence-insulting idea that he couldn't have gotten there when he built the rails the first time).
In general, stories depend on the quality of conflict for their weight, and the weak opposition and half-sketched puzzles (either extremely easy or nonsensical due to total lack of clues) simply don’t contribute any to a satisfying conclusion. It’s more like you progress through a series of trivial events and the game stops. Even in its most pretentious moments trying to induce pathos, the characters never manage to be any more impactful than a mildly annoying fly at the dinner table.
So what should induce you to buy this game? I can only imagine it must be the inflated ratings it seems to be getting elsewhere (why I tried when both games together were $3). Don’t bother unless you have time to waste and the patience of Job for flimsy characters (slightly less) annoyingly voiced.
SPOILER PLOT COMPLAINT: One more thing I could leave off here-I couldn't believe it but the developers actually show you going so far north that you see Antarctic Emperor Penguins. Come on, were they complete idiots, or did they just think I'm one?

The core concept of FTL was so intriguing that I purchased this game as soon as it was released. Navigating through space in a spaceship I could customize - from weapons to interior deck-plans - anyway I wanted, whilst taking random missions and hiring and controlling my crewmates individually; it sounded a dream come true. Unfortunately, the hype for this game far oversold its capabilities; the customization - though satisfactory - is not quite as extensive as I could hope for, and while the game does feature random missions, the overall quest never changes.
Worse, the main quest forces a time-limit (of sorts) on you, which means you can't just wander the galaxy endlessly but are relentless forced towards and end-game battle. The game is intentionally Rogue-like in that you can't reload a save to correct any mistakes, but when combined with the aforementioned time-limit and the random missions it makes the game frustratingly hard. FTL has its moments but - barring the addition of a proper "sand-box" mode - is hard to recommend even at Indie-game prices.

This was my first game of the Civilization series and I absolutely love it.  The game has eight difficulty levels, making it very approachable for newbies.  It's the ultimate "easy to learn, difficult to master" game.  The best part is that it has virtually infinite replay value because each game plays out very differently based on several factors, including: which civ you're playing as, what resources you start near, which other civs you start near, which other civs are in the game (some you might not meet until halfway through the game), what the map is like (most maps are randomly generated each game based on scripts), and more.
Further extending replay value, there are several different options you can choose when setting up a game (size of map, map type, number of civs, game speed, difficulty, number of city states, barbarian behavior, and more)
Each AI-controlled civ has it's own "personality" that determines its behavior, and it's fun getting to know each civ over different playthroughs.  There are four main victory types (domination, science, cultural, and diplomatic) as well as a fifth "Time Victory" that triggers on turn 500 if no civs have reached victory (this victory condition can be disabled and I play with it turned off).  So there are a variety of strategies that can lead you to victory.
I've won many games without going to war once, just as I've war mongered my way to victory in other games.  The fun in the game is in learning to adapt to each situation the game puts you in as no two games play out exactly the same way.  The only real negative about the game is you can easily lose track of time as you become so engrossed in the game, and end up playing into the wee hours thinking "just one more turn" over and over.
Definitely buy the complete edition or at the very least the two expansions (Gods and Kings and Brave New World).  The extra map packs are pretty optional, but you pretty much need the expansions and you'll definitely want to have all of the available extra civs at your (or the AI's) disposal.  The game goes on sale often enough so if you can't afford full price, add it to your wishlist and wait for a sale.

The gameplay isn't anything revolutionary. It's really just an isometric turn based combat system, and that's fine. I didn't mind the combat at all. It was fluid, and I had zero issues with doing exactly what I wanted. My problem was staying in combat even after the combat was over, which yeah, extends to another fight scene but the enemies were sometimes 4 rooms ahead.
The visuals were lovely. I loved the scenery and the atmosphere the game created and the cyberpunk thematic can be heavily felt throughout the entire game. The characters weren't exactly a sight to behold, but being an isometric game, it wasn't really an issue. Besides, the interaction with the NPCs goes through text boxes and portraits that depict them, and they were very well drawn so, nothing to whine about there.
I absolutely loved the music on this one. Working together with the visuals, it paints an astonishingly gritty, dark, vampire the masquerade meets transmetropolitan, post apocalyptic atmosphere, with all the hookers, beggars, smart drugs and what not in the slums.Amazing!
The controls weren't any trouble, it's pretty much all point and click so there's not much to say about it.
The story wasn't unique, and the bugs did kinda make it quirky but it was still enjoyable, though if I felt like replaying it would be to try different builds rather than the story.
The characters on the other hand were amazingly fleshed out and unlike many AAA "story driven" games, they really felt like they were a part of the story and adding up to it, rather than simply being there out of sheer necessity to fill out the blank spots.
All in all, I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys the cyberpunk/gothic thematic.

Saints Row 4 is the fourth installment in the Saints Row series, and is a direct sequel to Saints Row: The Third which was released in 2011. As in previous titles in the series, the player controls the leader of the Third Street Saints, who has now become the president of the United States.
Graphics wise, SR4 uses the same graphics engine as its predecessor and while this may make it feel like a glorified DLC (which it originally was, until it was made into a standalone game), the gameplay in SR4 is just pure fun.
The most important addition is the use of Super-Powers where you can sprint faster then any cars, leap to unimaginable heights with just a single jump, and basically obliterate any and everything that stands in your way. Its abit like giving you God-Mode and letting you go crazy in the open world sandbox city of Steelport. It is an absolute joy just to fly around and wreck havoc everywhere.
Music selection is very good with artistes like Haddaway, Stan Bush and many other pop culture favourites. Listening to Stan Bush's "The Touch" while gliding around the city is definitely something that everyone should try at least once. Excellent selection of tunes, and fantastic voice-work with some great talents. You can feel the enthusiasm and can definitely tell that the voice actors really enjoyed themselves.
Downsides, i felt that the superpowers were way over-powered and while they are extremely fun to use, they trivialize alot of the open world mechanics. Why would anyone still drive a car and take the time to upgrade them, when you can run faster then even the fastest car? It would have been better I think, if super-powers were introduced a little later in the game, so you can at least appreciate driving around in the open world more.
Also, while the main campaign story is meaty and full of laughs, the side missions are time wasting filler repeats of each other, and can be rather tedious to play through them. They have to be played thru though, if you want to unlock some of the special weapons and powerups available.
Graphical and co-op glitches are abundant, and there was a part at the final mission where me and my co-op partner simply got stuck at a loading screen, and unable to proceed further. Turns out that I had to load my game and play thru my progression before we both can co-op together to finish up the last mission.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
While SR4 is definitely a fun and crazy game, I felt SR3 had a funnier story. Nevertheless, whether you are a fan of the Saints Row series or not, definitely pick this up if you like wrecking havoc on an open world city with super powers. This game is stupidly gloriously fun.

There's a couple things that will determine whether you like the latest saints row game or not. Did you like the last one? If yes, you'll like this one. Did you like Prototype 1 or 2, crackdown, infamous, city of heroes or champions online? If yes, this is for you.
Saints Row is like the scary movie of the gaming world, incoherent stories, nonsensical jokes and pointless cameo's. But, it works in a game. If you can sit back and accept the pure stupidity and absurdity being burped into your face while you play, you'll have a great time.

Why does banging a gong make handholds appear in a cliff face? Why does pulling a lever make an unpowered mine cart move itself? Why does changing the colors of 8 rooms make a cube turn into a lightbulb? Why is a gear with 12 teeth called a hexagon? Why do I need binoculars to look at a cube less than 2 feet away? Why does another cube turn into a lightbulb when you pull a lever? Why is the combination to the dimension door hidden in windows that need to have light shone through them, with lightbulb fixtures on the opposite side?
This game is not for people who like puzzles that make any sense at all. The art is pretty good, though.

A game that looks like just another basic indie 2D rogue shooter from steam. And that's exactly what it feels like the first few times you try it. Chnces are, many will put it aside after the first 5 minutes, unable to see what's so great about it. But for those who are willing to hold just for a little longer (1 hour should be enough) will quickly understand it's systems and how they conect and work. What looks like an impossibly hard game in the first five minutes, will feel very much playble, and based on skill. Almost said "fair", but come to think of it, It's not fair. If you re loomking for fair, look somewhere else. It's not fair, and it's not meant to be fair. It's meant to be random. An organized chaos.
You will be droped in a hostile 2D platform world, with a character of your choosing (initially, there's only 1 available-the commando) and your only single objective is to find the teleporter. Or so the game tells you. Tutorial is minimalist, and the game doesn't hold your hand explaining everything, rather expects you to find things on your own. And it was a good choice for the type of game.
So, off you go, looking for "the teleporter". As you go about, in the first 60 seconds you will realize enemies are hard and deadly. And the more you kill and the longer you take the harder things get. Each of them drops coins and health when they die.
You will also discover the teleporter is not that hard to find, but the first time you find one... oh boy! what a joy! The temptation to press the button and activate it as soon as you find it!(as the game urges you to).
And when you do press it, a countdown of 90 seconds begins until the teleporter actually fires.  And the level Boss shows up to wipe you out from the face of the planet, bringing a ton of his f(r)iends with him.
That's when you realize that the game forgot to tell you you should make sure you are prepared to survive the Boss and his minions for 90 seconds. And the way to do that, is by using the coins you find to open crates and buy items that spwn all around the world, items that in turn will offer different skills, buffs, weapons.
All in all, it's very adictive, and a mighty fun game.

I can't play it for more than a few minutes, because the sound effect that plays when you get multipliers (such as for getting headshots) is so much louder than the rest of the game that it gives me a headache. I tried to communicate this problem to the developer before writing a review, and he quickly released a patch to 'fix' it, but it's still awful. How awful? I recorded some of the gameplay audio to check it out, the BAMNFFF sound effect is a full TEN DECIBELS louder than anything else in the game (if you aren't knowledgable about audio editing, 10 decibels is a huge difference in volume).
Other than that, the only enemy type that appears for the first couple waves is a generic looking robot with animations that look like they were done by a child. They have a huge amount of health compared to first-wave enemies in typical wave-based shooters, which I guess makes the game unique, but I just find them silly and annoying.
