The three starting weapons all feel very lackluster; if you like memorable gunplay, this probably isn't the game for you, although it's possible some of the purchasable weapons have a better feel.
The graphics are nice for an indie game, nothing mindblowing, but far better than, say, Killing Floor. If only anything else in the game could hold a candle to games like Killing Floor.
I probably have less than an hour logged but that was more than enough time to tell this is by far the worst wave shooter I've ever played. Take my opinion how you will, but I will say based on my experience that this game is a joke, the developer doesn't seem to have good taste or know what he's doing (and doesn't understand why professional gaming news sources won't give him the time of day), and you can get far better co-op gameplay for a lower price elsewhere. Nice short (~1 hour) room-escape puzzle/adventure.
I have to explain the genre a bit: "room escape" is a genre of small games (typically free flash games) that originally had you puzzle your way out of a locked room by searching the room and using objects and contraptions found within to ultimately find the key. There's no storyline (or not much of one), often no hints or help (except for the obligatory Youtube video walkthrough), and the door you need to open to escape is usually readily visible but locked. The genre then expanded to allow for multi-room scenes, and one of the most famous representatives is Mateusz Skutnik's "Submachine" series of games. Abandoned is so well done that many people (including
) found the parallels striking. It's a very good room escape game.
You can find
on the usual sites on the net. You can play it there for free, but if you buy it on Steam, you get slightly better graphics (the images were scaled down for free online publication), and of course you're supporting the developer. I did play it on Kongregate (it was in my "to do" playlist, actually) and then bought it here for 50% off (release promo).
After downloading, instead of being ready to play, a game installer starts which actually installs a DRM-free copy of AbandonedHD on your computer. There's a bit of a glitch as the game is showing screens to the right and left (and on a bigger screen presumably also top and bottom), but you can probably ignore that. After that, it's all point&click and brains.
Hints that I would have needed:
1. If you are exploring extra well, you can find up to 4 secret symbols that will allow you access to as many bonus story pages at the end of the game.
2. The puzzle at the very top with the cube and the two switches can be solved right there, it doesn't need anything that is elsewhere.
The playthrough took me about an hour (of course the walkthrough is only 9 minutes, but that's ok). The production values are cheap: it's a flash game with hand-drawn graphics; but the soundtrack is effective, the puzzles are very well designed, and the game works well.
It's short, it's cheap, it's recommended - and if you have doubts, look for the free version (search for "Abandoned" and "Krutovig") and check it out before you buy. Or get a refund.

The game is basically dialogue and combat. There is no exploration really. You unlock different areas of the map as you progress, but they are stand-alone dungeons. It's turn-based inside an "encounter" arena that lets you move around to position before attacking or performing some other action. The dungeons were very bland and generic, but the cutscenes and character art were awesome.

A few major issues really kept me from genuinely enjoying most of my time playing the game.
The controls are pretty good for what it's worth, and the music is generally stellar. The pixel-art style is decently solid, though sometimes it varies or loses focus a bit in what they're going for, but it's ultimately pretty good.
The "humor" and constant lame references are every bit as present as you'd expect from most indie games that rely on pop culture rather than good writing, genuine humor, or subtlety. Also, it has no true fullscreen mode and you always are stuck with your taskbar.
Framerates were solid and good in the 55-60 range, so no complaints there.
So what's my beef? It feels amateurish in a lot of ways, mostly code and mechanics. A lot of the level design is cheap - not challenging, but cheap. "Gotcha!" style. There's no way to predict or react, you just die.. and the problem with this is that the save points are rigid and often annoying super close, or super far apart, for no apparent reason.
There's no saving automatically or checkpoints, even right after a boss, and often no saves after bosses either, forcing you to backtrack numerous rooms to reach a save and if you make one wrong step.. redo the boss!
You can't check or change your equipment except at save points, which is just clunky. There's no real pause I could find besides leaving focus from the game, which to their credit does seem to pause it, but it's awkward.
Back to the gameplay and code aspect - enemies can hit you before and after you leave the screen. If you move from one screen to another while sliding you will retain momentum and shoot right off edges or cliffs with no way to know, predict, or react. Another example is the boomerang - if you throw it and jump it tracks with you up and down at all steps of your movement.. but doesn't do so on the back and forth axis, making it useless when running forwards and stupidly awkward to jump and through because it goes right back down at you rather than gracefully going out down and back to where you end up at. Again, really bad/sloppy code.
It's got some decent aspects but it's also pulled down by what feels like some sloppy code and sloppy design, which could perhaps be something of an engine if it was game maker, which I suspect it was somethin' like that, but that's still no excuse. People have made stellar, tight games on those platforms and more, it just takes more time and effort.
No ability to customize controls or change any of that and minimal options - my controller didn't work at all out of the box using DS4 Windows so I had to use xpadder to get it working.. pretty lazy but for some reason this seems standard with indie devs lately. No control customization, shoddy support for controllers, no ability to choose inputs, etc. Also the game launched with music and SFX at 0 initially.. minor, but weird and kinda dumb.
But really it's the level design that bugs me most - far too many "you die instantly" spikes and such just randomly thrown in your way, and often they're near indistinguishable from background colors or simply don't stand out enoughor aren't prominant enough and then, suddenly, you're twenty screens back at a save because there haven't been any in a while for no real reason. Blocks which break when you stand on are not always distinct from regular blocks which are not distinct from blocks which you can jump on once before they crack and again before they break. Just this same awful, lazy terrible design. Anyone can entirely hide something from a player so that the plaer falls victim to it, that's not good game design and, despite what people seem to think and their ego these days, it's not "challenging" either. It's memorization, it's muscle memory, it's trial and error. Any idiot can bumble their way through it sooner or later with enough time - it discourages skill and reaction and encourages repetition.
I also have to mention that the game actively punishes you for exploring - more often than not I'd go through a stretch of screens past a secret wall or in an out of the way area and just end up at a dead end where I clearly need something to pass - double jump and such. But for some reason the secret wall is accessible without double jump, therefore wasting time and providing no reward for noticing secrets nor exploration. Again, bad game design.
It ain't bad but it has more than enough shortcomings to keep it from being genuinely good.

When I got gifted this game, I had about 0 expectations for it. I expected it to be some anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that I might find amusing and I was curious about the combat. What it actually ended up being was possibly my GOTY 2015 and that’s not even a joke.
Initially, Fairy Fencer F seems like it’s pretty much stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that gets by on being moderately amusing and has really anime jokes that are tired and obnoxious- a refined woman who’s slightly masochistic, a busty blond who’s too casual about nudity, the same♥♥♥♥♥♥you’ve rolled your eyes at a thousand times if you like anime. And at the start of the game, the combat’s nothing special either, as like most RPGs it has the terrible habit of not giving you many tools other than “press attack, maybe cast a spell if you’re feeling saucy” for the first hour of the game.
What made me keep playing was the UTTER goofiness of Fairize (a sort of super mode you get) and the music that comes with it. Full Contact starts with the lines METAPHORPHOSIZE YOUR HEART, UNLEASH THE HELL INSIDE and doesn’t get any less ridiculous from there, and every time you Fairize there’s a (skippable, something I was grateful for by hour 20) magical girl transformation cutscene where you impale yourself with your weapon. The other thing was the ridiculousness of the protagonist Fang, who starts off as a lazy hedonist who’s only glimmer of a better nature is agreeing to help his fairy partner when she reveals that she’s lost her memory. The writing is genuinely enjoyable too, although early on is marred by the previously mentioned anime staple “jokes”.
However, it only gets better. The battle system opens up, and while disappointingly I never felt challenged to prove my mastery of the combat system, it was still interesting and engaging to learn and improve at. The game’s one real flaw to me (aside from fanservice, especially with Harley) is it’s just too easy- a flaw that’s only noticeable because the battle system is so good you can feel that there’s room for real challenge outside of “my numbers are higher”. The story and characters meanwhile, skyrocket in quality, with everyone quickly becoming likeable, the main character having a real and noticeable character arc, and the tone seamlessly and naturally escalating in scope and gravity without ever having a jarring “when did the comedy end” moment. Even some of the tired jokes get used in actually funny ways, and the rest fade into the background or simply vanish.
Fairy Fencer F is legitimately a great game, which is the absolute last thing I expected it to be. I highly advise anyone who has any interest in RPGs or anime-y games to pick it up.
Also, it has accessories like in a Tales game, and that’s awesome. They’re also reflected in the transformation cutscene, as are alternate costumes (of which there are very few)
Buy this game, seriously, it’s good.

Castle in The Darkness is an RPG platformer with a very vast world. Sadly, it is truly unforgiving.
I'll start this review right away by mentioning that the game is filled with insta-death spikes, traps and cheap mechanics. There are many instances in which you will kill a boss or complete a very hard platforming session only to be welcomed by a death-trap. There are even a few rooms in the game where you die as you enter the room/press a switch...
Now, if you're still here after this, well congratulations, you might have just found your new game! Onto the good aspects of this game... First of all, the awesome, awesome soundtrack! It's a huge chiptune OST with very memorable songs and it is easy to see that the composer has spent a lot of time spent composing those! The graphics are very nicely done in a pixelart style.
There's a bunch of items and weapons and armors to collect, most of them have special abilities and there's tons of secret rooms with game references and/or very powerful rewards. No one's playthrough will be the same for their first times. Speaking of this, one small piece of advice, without spoiling anything at all... When you get the double-jump powerup, please, be aware that you are able to reach a lot of new places in the old/new zones you will discover! I have personally almost reached the final boss with minimal gear as I was not finding new upgrades because I did not go back after getting the double-jump powerup!
What more to say... well the game is very hard for once. There are many checkpoints, but rarely are they after boss-rooms! You can and will die a few times after beating bosses by going through difficult zones in order to find a checkpoint. They are quite sparce in the later parts of the game.
Now, back to a bit of... displeasing things about the game. There are no mini-maps. Some secrets (which are required in order to 100% the game) are very, very hard to get as they require very specific methods. You need a lot of wit and puzzle-solving abilities and a good sense of observation and being good at deciphering text in order to get some of the best items.
So overall, it is a very good game, albeit being rage-inducing due to cheap death mechanics... I would recommend this game to platformer adepts and people who enjoy a good retro challenge.
As for the game length, obviously very dependant on skills, it takes a good 5 hours to complete the game. Around 10 hours if you want to complete the game with 100% achievements/items. More if you want to replay NG+ or the secrets levels that you unlock during the game.
In my Opinion the game is just great to kill some time. Great Fun and Great Game!

The Good:
1) Parkour: This is what makes the game so damn fun. DICE put a lot of work making it feel real and fun at the same time, and it pays off really well. The fact that its first person makes you feel like you're actually doing it. Despite the combat not being up to par, the parkour works so well that you almost forget about it
2) Graphics: For a game that came out in 2008, this still looks great. Not only does the world feel real, but the art style is just so memorable. It makes me wish a city like this was real
3) Soundtrack: For an electronic soundtrack, it creates a relaxing feeling. It fits the tone and world perfectly
4) Level design: While the game is very linear, it makes up for it with well thought out levels that give you multiple paths to get to your destination.
The Bad:
1) Length: It's only 5-6 hours. Should've been at least 8-10 hours
2) Combat: I wish you could chain your parkour with your fighting skills to take down enemies while still moving fast, instead of having to come to a complete stop every time you want to do a takedown. Also, the punching and kicking animations feel stiff. Using guns is even worse; I wish they would have improved the hand-to-hand combat and removed guns completely.
Despite its flaws, this is my favourite game of all time. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a unique action-adventure game.

Disclaimer: i'm a sucker for zombie games so i might be biased in the review for this game since i just love games which include zombies and they instantly gain at least +1 point in grading.
There are plenty of zombie games on the market and thematic is rather washed out, but for me the game is pure fun. If one played Dead Island than this is similar to what one can expect from the game, but with much improved weapons, handling, physics and fine-tuned elements.
Some people and reviews complain about the story. I don't want to spoil it, but for me the story is far from bad one. It isn't great as in Mass Effect, but this game has a completely different concept one should take in account. The story is good and IMO decent enough to keep you going. Plus, the side quests add to diversity of the game and give you extra reason to further explore the city.
The game is rather well balanced and it will go easy on you at start and become increasingly difficult as you progress through the game. Also, skill tree (BTW, there are three different skill trees), weapons and environment options really add up to the diversity of gameplay and playing style.
Technically the game is decently optimized for PC. Yes, there were some problems with some GPU's and CPU's (mostly AMD) but most of the issues have been fixed and they're actively working on fixing the rest.
From audio point of view if one has a decent headset or surround sound system audio really adds to the immersion in the zombie infected city. Screams in the background and soft music adds to the great game atmosphere. Combine that with well-designed environment (good graphics) and day-night cycle which cycles between rather dull and slow zombies to aggressive ones which are supported by extra powerful zombies which appear only during the night, and you get a great zombie game.
Some reviews point out that the missions are repetitive and most of them are based on the same concept which is go-to-location-X-and-fetch-object-Y. While i agree that missions are mostly of that type, they have enough variety to keep player interested for the game and further explore the game. Secondly, just think of it for a second. If one would really find him/her-self in a zombie infected city there would be rather high demand for brave people who would risk their lives to get necessary supplies from dangerous locations infected with zombies. For me this makes 100% sense. And third, if one pays close attention to detail one can hear irritation in Kyle's (main protagonist aka YOU) voice when he needs to do a go-and-fetch mission again.
All i have written so far is for single player and on top of that the game offers a nice CO-OP mode which one can play with his/her friends or random players. Plus, there is a multiplayer addition to the game too which is a mixture of Left 4 Dead and Evolve game. In the multiplayer one can choose to be one of the four survivors or be super powerful zombie. CO-OP and multiplayer are highly dependent on people one plays with, as any other multiplayer experience. If one is playing with friends or good players fun is guaranteed and if you play with trolls or bad players who don't respect CO-OP/MP one will have bad time and a free test of his/her tolerance.
The game has some amazing extra value which comes in form of weapon dockets (ie. gold keys if you played Borderlands) which will give player top tier weapons when reclaimed in the game (1 docket = 1 weapon). And the game has a companion app for Android and iOS where one can play Dying Light in a form of Facebook Mafia Wars where one sends scouts on missions. Great thing is that loot from the missions can be transferred to the original game one is playing on the PC or console!
To sum things up, i would highly recommend the game to any player and it would be a must to those who love zombie games. To be completely hones, i haven't played such a great zombie game for quite a while. For those looking for numbers, here is my game review roundup:
Video: 9/10
Audio: 8/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Fun factor: 10/10
Extra value: 8/10
At the end, one is killing zombies in many creative ways, and if you don't have fun with it and all you have is frustration from the game - you must be doing something wrong.

The first thing I did before even starting to write this review was to give the "thumbs up".
Before I started this amazing adventure, I had little to no experience with "zombie" games, and to be quite frankly, I am now a zombie killing machine. I am a zombie grinder, I am the zombie terminator. I am Legend.
All of that said, and despite all the QQ around the AMD systems (which is my case), I've had absolutely no problem whatsoever with FPS, quite the opposite. The graphics are close to the best I've seen.
The soundtrack will keep you wondering if death is upon you, or just around the corner.
The gameplay is incredibly good, as you can "visit" most of the buildings, and you can parkour your way around Harran.
Obviously, not everything is perfect, and to me, the biggest disappointment is the story itself. It's amazing until near the end, where it just feels it's being wrapped up quickly, leaving some loose ends, and wondering you what the heck just happened.
Unless their plan is to continue the story with Dying Light 2 or some DLC, the ending is quite meh, whereas the rest of the story is quite good, making you shed a tear once or twice. Them feelings...
The crafting part of the game is quite regular, and you've plenty of options to make your killing weapon of choice even more deadly, and prettier. From bats, to axes, to hammers, you can use anything to kill a zombie. The combat system is nice, and the guns feel a bit awkward, which just leaves you more excited to melee everything down, and feel the blood and guts hitting you as you hack and slash your way to the top. Top of something, that is.
If you are looking for a "survival" game, there's not much survival to do here, as you can pretty much skip sleeping the entire game, eating only helps regening some health, and there's no drinking or anything similar. It's, however, a scavenger heaven, since you can find loot pretty much anywhere.
I'd easily recommend this game to anyone, as it's quickly climbing to the top of my all time favourite games.

While the premise and store page suggest an adventure game with a heavy emphasis on Jewish philosophy, The Shivah is closer to being a great and short point ‘n’ click that happens to have a rabbi as protagonist.
The Shivah is one of the early games of Dave Gilbert, founder of Wadjet Eye games, where we can already see some of his trademark design elements in work.
The story follows a bitter rabbi of a poor and empty synagogue, who suddenly ends up with a large sum of money and as the prime suspect of an investigation. From this setup, we get a largely conventional but realistic murder mystery, where gameplay takes a secondary role behind the characters, situations, and dialogue. In other words, do not expect too much resistance from the adventure game parts.
However, The Shivah struggles to follow up on its own premise. The entire Jewish aspect is mostly downplayed, the story could just as easily follow a pious person of any religion. This means it is more accessible to anyone, but also feels like something that never achieved its own goals.
Great game if you put yourself into the mindset of an investigator. The game is more linear because of this, but a very enjoyable story with good characters. 8/10

It's hard to express my feelings about this game.  I've been playing the Shadowrun pen and paper RPG with friends for about 20 years now.  I was hoping for a bit of that experience in this game... and I got almost none of it.
The story is absolutely Shadowrun 101 level stuff.  No real surprises here.  No new ground being tilled story wise or lore wise. The only way this story would work is if you've never heard of SR before, much less played it.  The dialogue is so cliche and out of character, much less contradictory with actual human nature, that I was pushed out of immersion time and time again.
The combat is INFURIATING.  I have a character with a shotgun.  I'm standing many squares away and my chance to hit is 40%... ok, that's fair.  I spend 1 of my precious action points moving moving to stand almost directly next to the enemy character.  My chance to hit is now 80%?  I mean, at that range I could put the shotgun barrel up their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and blow their last meal into their skull pan, but instead miss with my next two shots. I lost count of the amount of times that a "sure thing" was a miss and I sat there with my hands up in the air and a "what the ♥♥♥♥ was thaaaat?" look on my face.
The best thing you can bring to every single run are characters with assault rifles.  All other weapons are sub par and have very little utility.  Simply put the highest damage on a target at a time until it dies and the highest damage is always assault rifles since they apply their damage at any range.
The gearing in this game is terrible.  Gearing your own character is boring and tedius instead of exciting like most RPG's.  The variation in gear yawn worthy.  This  goes for cyberware also, which has vastly different essence costs than in the books.  Missing entirely from the game is bioware, which I always preferred for my characters over metal.
Physads are trash.  All of the good physad abilities from the books are missing or poorly represented in game.  My last several characters in the P&P game were physads, they are hands-down my favorite thing to play, but here they are just boring and terrible.

A mixed bag of a game. Playing as a rabbi is novel and interesting, and having to type in search terms and passwords to discover clues and continue the plot is an excellent concept, though nothing you have to type in is remotely difficult to find, so it hardly feels like detective work. That theme is continued with the inventory and clue system. The game is just too short to utilise them fully, I suppose. As a result, it's hard to categorise this game as either a point-and-click adventure or a detective game, since it borrows elements from both but doesn't go deep enough with either.
Simple as it was, I quite enjoyed the plot, but it felt like it should have just been the opening act to a longer story. My biggest criticism, however, is of the game's combat scenes, particularly the last one, where you'll likely resort to guesswork and have to replay the entire scene multiple times as you choose the wrong options.
Graphically, the game looks dated, even though it's been remastered. Pro tip: use the "winsetup.exe" file (or the Mac/Linux equivalent, I guess) and select a 4x graphics filter to increase the resolution. I'm not sure why those settings aren't available from the game itself or from a pre-launch menu. The music is good, while the voice acting is a bit shaky, but acceptably so for an indie game like this. It's not enough to be a distraction in any case.
Despite its flaws, I had fun with The Shivah, and it was dirt cheap, so I'll give it the thumbs up. Recommended.

If puns really get tiresome for you after a while, don't play this game.  It's rife with horrible puns and doesn't care to stop to make real jokes.
Other than that, the game is pretty solid, and if you run into a few bugs where the level doesn't load some key features properly, it's a problem with the archaic way this game loads stuff for the player to interact with, and I've struggled with it for pretty much a few years since I've started playing these games.  Their quality assurance leaves something to be desired in a few places, but at least the gameplay works just fine.  You get to play as over a hundred Marvel characters, unlock more if you buy the DLC, and nearly all of them are vital tools for going after those Gold Bricks.
Word of advice for 100%-ers out there.  Use a guide.  In fact, don't stop at using a guide.  Use videos when the guide fails you.  I was stuck on the level Red Head Detention (for the love of Christ, these puns), and I thought it was some kind of bug or I just wasn't doing something correctly when I came up with a puzzle where, using a character who has hacking abilities, I had to solve a puzzle where you twist the pannels into their proper place.  What the game and the guide I use don't tell you is the exact pattern of said puzzle, which by the way, lights up whenever it thinks a piece is in proper place.  So, pretty much how puzzles work in video games, right?  WRONG.  This puzzle is absolutely unsolvable without a video of someone else's playthrough.  I'm sure they've gotten better with their puzzles since then, but this was just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  Then again, it can be a bit hard to describe what you have to do, but it can't be THAT hard.  Look, I'll do it for all the FAQ writers out there:
Make the panels look like two wide verticle curves.  Like a giant S on it side.  If it doesn't work one way, try the other and see if it lights up.
There, was that so hard?  Oh, and that's a free protip to everybody struggling with that BS.  The rest of the game isn't -too- terribly difficult.
tl;dr, I hate the loading bugs, I hate the puns even more, I love the gameplay, I love the character selection, and please don't make puzzles like the one on Red Head Detention anymore.

Saints Row 4 is the fourth installment in the Saints Row series, and is a direct sequel to Saints Row: The Third which was released in 2011. As in previous titles in the series, the player controls the leader of the Third Street Saints, who has now become the president of the United States.
Graphics wise, SR4 uses the same graphics engine as its predecessor and while this may make it feel like a glorified DLC (which it originally was, until it was made into a standalone game), the gameplay in SR4 is just pure fun.
The most important addition is the use of Super-Powers where you can sprint faster then any cars, leap to unimaginable heights with just a single jump, and basically obliterate any and everything that stands in your way. Its abit like giving you God-Mode and letting you go crazy in the open world sandbox city of Steelport. It is an absolute joy just to fly around and wreck havoc everywhere.
Music selection is very good with artistes like Haddaway, Stan Bush and many other pop culture favourites. Listening to Stan Bush's "The Touch" while gliding around the city is definitely something that everyone should try at least once. Excellent selection of tunes, and fantastic voice-work with some great talents. You can feel the enthusiasm and can definitely tell that the voice actors really enjoyed themselves.
Downsides, i felt that the superpowers were way over-powered and while they are extremely fun to use, they trivialize alot of the open world mechanics. Why would anyone still drive a car and take the time to upgrade them, when you can run faster then even the fastest car? It would have been better I think, if super-powers were introduced a little later in the game, so you can at least appreciate driving around in the open world more.
Also, while the main campaign story is meaty and full of laughs, the side missions are time wasting filler repeats of each other, and can be rather tedious to play through them. They have to be played thru though, if you want to unlock some of the special weapons and powerups available.
Graphical and co-op glitches are abundant, and there was a part at the final mission where me and my co-op partner simply got stuck at a loading screen, and unable to proceed further. Turns out that I had to load my game and play thru my progression before we both can co-op together to finish up the last mission.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
While SR4 is definitely a fun and crazy game, I felt SR3 had a funnier story. Nevertheless, whether you are a fan of the Saints Row series or not, definitely pick this up if you like wrecking havoc on an open world city with super powers. This game is stupidly gloriously fun.

Shadowverse is an online collectable card game available on Steam, iOS and Android.
The game follows a number of characters as they go about pursuing various objectives, from a woman trying to resurrect her dead fiance to a young girl just going on an adventure for the first time and attempting murder as she does. The idea of having a variety of characters all pursuing different goals and encountering each other as they do so is certainly an interesting one, but none of them feel terribly interesting or unique to me. The whole game has this problem, to a certain extent - it all feels simply like a generic fantasy world without any real distinguishing features. Additionally, there is very little context for what the different cards represent in the game world, assuming they represent anything, and for how the card battling represents conflict in the game.
On the gameplay side, things aren’t a whole lot better. The game is very similar to Hearthstone in its play, the biggest difference I’ve seen so far being the card evolution mechanic, which allows you to power up two or three creatures, depending on whether you went first or last, after a certain number of turns has passed. While I can’t say I’ve seen that specific mechanic before, it alone isn’t enough to make the game feel unique.
One thing I can praise, however, is the art design. The cards, the characters, and even the backgrounds are quite detailed and nice to look at. The voice acting is also much better than I expected from a free-to-play card game, though that isn’t saying a whole lot. The music is also pretty good, though not exceptional.
Pros:
There is a wide variety of playable characters, each with different mechanics, storylines, and personalities.
It is interesting to see how different characters’ storylines intersect and to see those interactions from both sides.
The art design is overall pretty good.
The voice acting and music is also pretty good.
Cons:
The gameplay borrows very heavily from Hearthstone without adding much other than the card evolution mechanic.
The setting feels generic, without any unique touches or twists.
Little context for what, if anything, the cards represent in-universe.
TL;DR
A competent card game, though one that doesn’t stand out as anything special. All in all, I would suggest that more effort be paid to giving the game a more unique feel and mechanics.

Arkham Knight has various side quests called Most Wanted where you hunt down some of Gotham's most notorious criminals. As an avid Batman fan (all media formats) I can safely say Arkham games have always been at the top of my list of most anticipated games. Having played all the former games I was pretty excited for Rocksteady to make their return to this title. (To clarify, I enjoyed playing Origins a lot. By atmosphere and structure it was a lot different than City but offered a solid Arkham-experience nevertheless.)
The hype for this game was off the roof. From the first teaser to the last trailer, I was pumped to get it as soon as it got out. And I'm glad I didn't - as we all well know the launchtime drama AK ended up having. I kind of anticipated it too, I had decided not to pre-order stuff anymore after some disappointments in the past. It's an unfortunate side-effect of modern games.
Somehow, I managed to go spoiler-free for the whole 8 months I waited to purchase this game. It took a lot of self-discipline. But it was definitely worth it to wait. I was able to have a clean, bugless gaming experience (that should have been available at start but-)
ANYWAYS. AK completely blew my mind. It felt like a complete upgrade of City. It was beautiful, it was wonderful. The map is enormous, Gotham's design really rang close to my heart. To be able to visit those places familiar from the comics, man, it really made my nerdy heart flutter.
Driving around the street with awesome TANK-BATMOBILE, having true chaseups with bad guys, really cool stuff (if lag didn't ruin it). Flying around the highest most detailed rooftops, amazing. Doing some old-school detective work and murder-solving. Very interesting and vivid stories (new [but oldschool] Batman villains!).
Batman's stuggle with Joker's death is the main event of this game, but it branches out to pretty interesting lengths...
The main story is what got me big time. Like I previously said I had been able to avoid the spoilers, so it was the purest way I could have experienced it and I was so happy! Y'all got me!!
Before the game got out, there were months and months of the speculation about the Knight's identity.
I had just given up on trying to guess and had lost all my hope of it being the person we all wanted him to be.
...And they gosh dangly did it!!! It was exactly him. All flesh and blood.... and in some other media than comics! (He is my favorite DC character of all time, so you can imagine my tears and all the whale noises I produced during his parts)
All these reasons considered, it's not hard to raise AK as my top Arkham game. Because for all of it's flaws, Rocksteady still came through to give one last big bang. Probably not one of the best games out there, but definitely the best Batman game!
I highly recommend this gaming experience for any Batman fan, new or old, it won't be a disappointment.

You can buy these using the points you earn from beating games and leveling up. There are about 4 options for each armor piece, including head, bodym shoulders, legs, and boots. This game could use more content and workshop support, but it has enough to earn a quite a few fun hours. What they need is more gamemodes and levels. WARNING: Do not play this game, it is thinly veiled Devil worship.
What first attracted me to this game, I can't remember, and after seeing it for what it really is, I dare not look back to find out.
The game consists of a single screen in which you play a triangle connected to a hexagon. Your goal as the triangle is to avoid the incoming shapes as they approach the hexagon and are absorbed into it. If they touch you, the game ends. While this may seem an innocent setup, the hexagon's six sides, six stages within each game mode, and six game modes within the game are anything but an innocent coincidence. In reality, the player as the triangle is caught in a nightmare realm, where the Devil, whose mouth is the hexagon, feeds on the lesser shapes and lines that approach It, which the player must avoid for as long as they can, for if the player is hit by one, they are pushed by it right into the six-sided mouth of the Devil.
Like Tetris, this game is unwinnable and only allows you to hold off your inevitable defeat, implying that the Devil is an all-powerful figure who will inevitably "eat" us all. This is not truthful by any stretch of the imagination, but unfortunately those who do not see the game for what it is may gradually come to believe it.
The only redeeming aspect of this game is its music, and even that is purposed to lure the untrained mind into a trance so that it remains blind to the evil scheme in front of it. Please avoid this game at all costs and spread the word in your youth groups so nobody else falls victim to this manifestation of the Devil's handiwork.

I love hard games, I love castlevania, and I love metroid.
But god damn do I hate, absolutely hate platformers, especially "hard" platformers. You know the kind where spike traps are every where and they are one hit death, yeah ♥♥♥♥ those.
Modern updates to the metroid and castlvania games are usually welcome, but sprinkle in cancerous platforming and you have a deal breaker.
I love the enemies and magic is a nice touch, the animation for attacking cancels out far to quickly, leaving you with a very short range attack that can be spammed but must be very precise because you can't buffer your attack. Damage can be piled on as you're only invincible for a nano-second after taking dmg, so bosses can deal 80% dmg in a very small amount of time. You get power ups and health, but enemies generally scale so it never feels like your getting stronger.
The boss fights are the best part about this game, hands down. And there are a good amount of them.
I threw in the towel, not that I wanted to, but after getting spiked traped to death I said ♥♥♥♥ it, I hate platformers. I like the ones that are fun, not the frustrating ones. Theres also some really trolly platforming and falling spike sections in this game, like the creator thought he was funny making those level designs. Reminds me of those super mario bros mods that are hidden blocks everywhere so you just die all the time.
Everything else is solid, though it lacks the polish and general pacing of better metroidvania games.
Also be forewarned its more castlvania NES era than metroid.
There are a litany of better options within this genre, that plus the terrible platforming and trolly insta-death spikes, I can't recommend it. However there is enjoyment to be had in this game, and I would have rather given it a mediocre review, but steam doesn't let me do this.
I can see some people really enjoying it, and I really did appreciate the boss fights and enemy designs.  But once again, spike traps and falling spikes that insta kill in every single level and in large portions of the game, ♥♥♥♥ that.

Teleglitch: Die More Edition - AKA Hotline Miami's abusive father is definitely a most-have for masochists and those just looking for a great survival horror experience.
The graphics are terrible, but if you play the game in a fast-paced, brave way, you can get the survival horror experience that the self-proclaimed "survival horrors" of today fail to produce - that is, the moment when you're being pursued, you're absolutely loaded on weaponry, and yet you're smashing things together and thinking about the future rather than now. You're going to need the ammo later - it's not like the "I gotta save this for later" philosophy used in RPGs that results in a resource never being used. Everything will be used. You have to use it all wisely, quickly, and think your way out of an onslaught in less than a few seconds. There will be moments that you use all of your resources in a sticky situation, get out alive, and realize that you have nothing left.
Those moments you escape a hopeless situation only to realize you're being watched.
Those moments that you just have a blink of an eye to reload before that guy pulls out his gun.
And that's okay.
You just have to die, die, and die again.

It's boring. It's incredibly boring.
This is generally true of all Lego games. You run from level to level mashing the attack button constantly to destroy the environment and the enemies that pose absolutely no threat whatsoever. Scattered throughout the levels are various gates that can only be bypassed with certain abilities. Most people would call these "puzzles," but I don't think it qualifies as a puzzle when you run up to it and the game tells you exactly what you need to do. It's just a hoop thrown out by the developers to make players jump through it before they can move on to the next section and continue destroying everything in sight to collect studs. After doing this for what feels like seven eternities back to back, there will be a boss fight where the boss spends 99% of the fight utterly invulnerable to your attacks until a certain amount of time has passed or until you've killed enough of the enemies that spawn to remind you how terrible the combat is. Want to master the combat? Press the attack button. That's all there is to it.
This is the last time I'm going to try to get into one of these games. Since the original trilogy's Star Wars game on PS2, I've been trying, and I'd guess that I've played at least seven different Lego games, including Dimensions, which my sister poured nearly $700 into. They are all exactly the same: run around, smash everything, collect studs, press the attack button until enemies are dead, use the character the game tells you to use to solve one of its "puzzles," and then move on to the next area to repeat.
It's almost like a psychological experiment to determine the bare amount of "gameplay" people can put up with, or an experiment to determine how many times the same exact game can be re-released with different character sets. This game sucks, and Telltale needs to stop re-releasing it. I'm ashamed of myself for buying it, because I knew exactly what I would find--the same thing found in literally every other Lego video game.
So the experiment is clearly a success.
Now please, Telltale Games, call it off.

The core concept of FTL was so intriguing that I purchased this game as soon as it was released. Navigating through space in a spaceship I could customize - from weapons to interior deck-plans - anyway I wanted, whilst taking random missions and hiring and controlling my crewmates individually; it sounded a dream come true. Unfortunately, the hype for this game far oversold its capabilities; the customization - though satisfactory - is not quite as extensive as I could hope for, and while the game does feature random missions, the overall quest never changes.
Worse, the main quest forces a time-limit (of sorts) on you, which means you can't just wander the galaxy endlessly but are relentless forced towards and end-game battle. The game is intentionally Rogue-like in that you can't reload a save to correct any mistakes, but when combined with the aforementioned time-limit and the random missions it makes the game frustratingly hard. FTL has its moments but - barring the addition of a proper "sand-box" mode - is hard to recommend even at Indie-game prices.

My lets play for the series:

I enjoyed the game because of the atmosphere. You don't really know what's ahead or what happens next. You also happen to command a small ship with small crew through several events. The very first gameplay is worth the money but the experience degrares fast and new content doesn't unlock in timely manner to compensate that. The user interface is simple enough to grasp in few minutes. There are lot of text to read, although you eventually get to skip things because you've already read it once, except that you end up skipping also the stuff you didn't read yet.
The quality of stories and graphics are good. I didn't spot any of the worst scifi cliches in this game. But there could have been more to provide.
FTL forces you to proceed into the end with a deadzone. This sucks because it stops being space exploration game at this point. You have multiple ships to choose from, but they need to be unlocked first. It's by random chance, not by difficulty whether you manage to unlock a ship. It's also by random chance whether you stumble upon something that obliterates your crew or hull. It could use some more determinism. Not to remove the feeling of constant crisis but to give more stuff to crash upon.
I would have also wanted more customization choices and more weapons to the game. I find that this game could have easily packed more content and be more interesting. Also there were quite too few ways to totally mess up, there should be more of it. This game starts getting boring at the approximate point of 100 gameplay hours.
The game has achievements. I'm bored to the achievements structure. Some game could finally acknowledge that it's a fad and get rid of it.
This review looks grim but the reality is that I am really picky person and I remember these things about the game best. I hope someone else concentrates on the virtues of this game. It's mostly a small game so it can't get lots of everything. We'll see how the update next year changes the game.

Cyberpunk meets fantasy. Nice combination. Think Blade Runner with elves and dwarves.
The graphics are great. Even the slightly dated 3D characters are ok. But the backgrounds are the best. They really take you into the mood of a cyberpunk world. And the music helps, definitely. It's got that Johnny Mnemonic-vibe to it. All the blips and blops.
As for gameplay... It's really straightforward. Just like in any RPG, you have to save a lot. If you do that, you can change choices that might have some impact upon the progress, and you won't have to run through an entire level again. The main drawback with the gameplay is the camera. It is fixed. Even very old Playstation1-TRPGs had rotable cameras. The most you can do here, is zoom in and out, and that doesn't help at all. This makes it difficult to aim, and might make you click the incorrect square. But, it's not a dealbreaker. Even on Normal difficulty level, it is a quite easy game to finish.
So if you want 10hrs of nice cyberpunk-crime story, get this game. You won't regret it.

After nearly 100 percenting this game, with over 30 hours, I can say this is probably the most over-the-top game I have ever played. From the Aliens to the crazy weapons and super-powers, this game is absolutely crazy. If you just really want to have fun, blowing stuff up and running really fast, I would recommend this game. These super-powers are also not overpowered, as the enemies are also very strong, especially as you progress in the story. This game is also full of great humor, and I find very few problems with it.
One thing I found that was recurrent was that vehicles are merely not as fun as before, because being able to jump over even the largest buildings and sprinting much faster than any car makes vehicles mostly obsolete.
If you are looking for a more realistic game with more in-depth story, you should probably try Grand Theft Auto. But if you are looking for super crazy over-the-top fun, you should pick up Saints Row IV.
Another thing I found was that after I finished the story, there was not very much for me to do. Granted, I finished all of the activities and collected all of the collectibles, so all I really had left to do was to complete challenges, which can become monotonous.
Bottom Line: This is a ton of fun and is hilarious, but if you really want realism and a well-crafted story, stick with GTA.

After getting 100% achievement completion, I still feel like I suck at this game.
This game is hard for all the right reasons; you may feel limited at first (given how everything in this game is in-game achievement locked), but the game starts you out with the easiest-to-use character and a basic set of simple items that help ease you into how things work.
The game says that it won't save your scores on the easy difficulty, but what it doesn't tell you is that
. Use this to your advantage and play on easy until you think you've gotten a feel for how the game handles (as well as unlocking a few things in the process), then put the game back on its regular difficulty setting and proceed to get obliterated in a brutal fashion.
For extremely skilled players (or masochists), there's even a hard difficulty setting, as well as collectible 'artifacts' that can be toggled to make the game even harder (or easier in a few cases).
This game is completely playable without a guide. However, should one feel inclined to seek advice (which is very likely), there are
helpful guides written by other players that go in detail about combat strategies, how to unlock things, and even just general advice for beginners and veteran players alike.
In conclusion, Risk of Rain is a 2D platformer where you're constantly fighting for your life while scavenging the land for items that passively improve your combat abilities in every way, ultimately reaching the end where the final boss is the only thing standing in your way between you and freedom. Good luck.

Loathsome on a first playthrough, but a joy to play (if occasionally frustrating) on future runs. Also prone to performance issues-- Playing normally I experienced a 2-3 second hang on most screen transitions, including transitions to and from the death screen. In a game like Castle in the Darkness, where you die often, that adds up. I switched to compatibilty mode and managed to avoid hangs, but the trade-off was occasional lag... which actually helped out a bit in some of the late-game boss battles... but I digress.
The first half of the game is an absolute blast. The play control is nearly flawless-- comfortable speed, jump height control feels natural, you can swing most weapons as fast as you can mash the attack button... not to mention when the going gets tough, you can always bust out your magic spells (though the high-pitched squealing of the magic charging grates on the nerves after the 1000th time) to really put down some pain.
Then you get about halfway in, and suddenly the game shifts from a metroidvania/platformer/action game to platform hell, and instant-death spikes might as well be the local currency because you CAN'T GET AWAY FROM THEM. Fighting enemies is never a problem-- you always have options, places to go, things to do in previous areas to buff yourself up for a strong encounter. But those instant-death spikes... there's nothing you can do to make those parts easier except to simply... git gud. And that sucks.
There's also the issue of a lot of those "places to go" and "things to do in previous areas" being, well, secrets. I.e. things you're not gonna know about on a first playthrough. If you're one of those people who's just GOTTA play their games blind and fresh, then buckle up, because by buying this game you'll be buying yourself a one-way ticket to the PAIN TRAIN. Or... a one-way ticket FOR the pain train? I dunno.
Also, the sound that plays when you die is really loud. And sharp. Dying all of a sudden by accidentally falling onto some omnipresent instant-death spikes is only made more frustrating when you're simultaneously having your eardrums blown out. It ain't fun. And some of the hardest platforming sections in the game are necessary to truly beat it! Makes you wanna bring the level designers somewhere where THEY gotta do precise jumps through a 3 block high hallway with spikes... all up in it. You know what I'm sayin'?
That second playthrough is where it's at. Knowing where everything is allows you to play the game without hitting nearly as many roadblocks, which means the whole thing flows a lot better.
...Except for the water dragon boss. That guy can go suck a squash.

Imagine a game that is a cross between the game design of Castlevania 2: Simon's Quest and the difficulty of Zelda II: The Adventure of Link.  If you can imagine that, you're imagining Castle in the Darkness.  It is mostly a Metroid-style game, but with a fantasy setting and RPG elements.  It contains a truckload of references to old 8-bit games and maybe other things from the 1980s, some of which I don't even get, but it's fun to find them all and very funny when you know what something references.  But I'm going to warn you early, this is the most difficult 2-D Metroid-style game I have ever played.  The worst of it is confined to 2 areas (
), but this game is still borderline controller-throwing hard.  That said, let's move on to the breakdown.
Graphics:  8/10  Pretty faithful to the 8-bit generation, but in places I could pick out things that were a little bit more smooth than what the NES could really do.
Controls:  7.5/10  Actually controlling the character worked perfectly well for me with an XBox One controller, but I have to dock the devs serious points on this one because there is absolutely no way to pause the game unless you change the active window on your PC.  After that, you do have to press a key to unpause, but the only way to pause in the first place without the game disappearing is to just find a safe area, clear out the enemies and then put the controller down.  That's literally all you can do.  I have never seen a game without a pause button my whole life, except this one.  Shameful.
Game Design:  7/10  Other than my opening paragraph, you can see the basic game design by looking at the video on the game's Steam Store page.  On the surface, it seems like Mr. Kap focused a little too hard on all the references in the game and didn't do enough to make the game stand on its own apart from the old games it pays homage to, but if his primary goal was just to create a game that plays like a love letter to the whole 8-bit generation, I guess he succeeded as well as anyone could.  Honestly, the biggest problem I found was that they put the Wing Boots item so far into the game after you passed so many areas where you needed it, it was hard to remember all the areas you needed to revisit without an in-game map.  I know the lack of a map is another homage to the 80s, but I never would have found everything in this game without a guide.  Luckily, there is a very good one here on Steam which uses a PDF file, so look for it if you want it.
Music:  8/10  The synthesized chiptune sounds are very authentic to the NES.  As far as composition goes, at the beginning of the game, I didn't think much of it.  But the further I got, the more I realized that even though it's not the caliber of Koji Kondo, and not really good enough to listen to outside the game, most of the tracks are very well-suited to their areas and every time I quit playing the game, I had one of the tunes in my head for hours afterward.
Replay Value:  6/10  After you 100% the game, there is a very fun New Game+ that you can do to push the game further and fill out the extras menu, but after you complete all of those things once, you won't immediately feel the need to do it again just for enjoyment.
Overall Score:  7/10
In summary, I cannot really say that Mr. Kap made a great game here, but he did make a good game, and certainly an excellent nostalgia trip.  If you are a person who lived through the days of the NES, considering the relatively cheap price of this game, I think it would be worth playing it at least once, as long as the difficulty doesn't put you off.  I would have been very skeptical at first, and might have even decided not to buy the game, were it not for a glowing review I read on
, but I'm glad I didn't miss out on it after all.

I made a review of this game a while back and at the end of that i said something on the lines of "the game in its current state is 6/10, 8/10 if patched properly."
And take a quess what i would give right now. 5/10, but numbering is subjective to the reviewers own personal scale, lets try something i know everyone remembers. The dreaded school-grade system.
Before plastering the grade all over your faces, i might as well recap some of the main problems in this game.
On the GAMEPLAY side, it is simplified greatly. Mostly for the console ports, this means little-to-no modification of squads inventory. Unless you count changing the off-hand items and body-armour, which i dont mind you..
Movement and actions, are done by spending two (2) Action-Points. Now this sounded questionable to me the first time i played the game, but afterwards i came to the conclusion, that it is actually a good decision. It makes combat and strategic planning more questinable, knowing whether moving a soldier in that certain piece of cover (Il get to that point later), Protects him from any enemies that might appear behind the corner. And some of mote frantic combat bits are also made more tense with the finite number of actions you can do. Although, the game has a terrible tendency to CHEAT. Yes the AI cheats like a Free-to-player on mobile devices who got his hands on his moms credit-card.
Multiple times, the AI takes an impossibly accurate shot. Through several walls and straight into the face of soldier who was in heavy cover and while in the tactical screen before going to combat, the AI decides to introduce three squads of baddies out of the blue, after you move one soldier just 5 meters (or the blue movement-indicator). This caused me a great pain when i decided to do the obligatory Ironman run. My poor assault specialist moved to a piece of cover i thought was safe at the time and suddenly 3 squads of Mutons appeared and pretty much circled the poor fellow. And as they circled the guy, the Mutons kept looking at eachother as asking "Who brought the lube ?"
And the vaguely-referencing to-intimacy situations didn't stop there, there were multiple other similiar happenings all the way throught. Argh.. i cannot talk about it, it gave me PTS.
What else?... Graphics.
Graphical quality is console-level. And by that i mean early Xbox360. Bland and boring, low-resolution and just overall... Meh.
And while on the subject of graphics, i need to bring up the Unreal Engine. It does this game no favours. I'm trying to think game that came out at the same time as XCOM and used Unreal as its engine. But my brain draws blank. Unreal Engine has its quirks, and for some reason i always see glitches when playing XCOM, even today as i Rage-Quitted another Ironman session due to the AIs cheating ways.... The camera goes spaztic randomly, pointing in random directions getiing stuck in some places and generally being broken.
And there is whole another bag of delightfull glitches always hiding somewhere. in case you didnt know im playing the base game, since Enemy Within cost a bit too much on release and when it actually was on sale i had no money. So im not entirely sure whether the bug-fixes were in the expansion, following the CapCom way of balancing with its fighting games, or do i just have an obsolete version or do i need to re-install the game again, for the umpthteenth time... Nope its up-to-date.
Oh and another minor nitpick. The randomly forgets its set Graphics options. Out of the blue, just like that. b*llocks to that.
Writing this is making me angry, not because of the game per-se. (Kinda funny that last word, it means A*SE [*R] in Finnish)
Im angry because the game is just.... Just.... ADEQUATE.

If I had to describe civilization V in three words it would probably be like: risk, on steriods.
Because it can be like risk if you're planning to go for the domination victory, only your warmongering will have consequences on your happiness. This feature of happiness and unhappiness might seem like it balances the warmongering out, and it does... until the late game comes.... (or when you have a few tenets in the order ideology)
The game has four roads to victory; science, domination, culture and diplomacy (or economic victory, as you will need to bribe a lot of city states to get this victory, or play as greece, complete a quest and instantly become allies).
Science involves you discovering every little secret of the universe and launching a rocket to outer space.
Domination is the most straight forward victory, just burn every other city on the map and you'll be set.
Culture is the most confusing and imo the hardest to get victory, as you will need to acquire tourism, once your civilization has generated more tourism than another civ in a lifetime, you win. Unfortunately tourism comes later and in smaller forms than your first batches of culture, so you'll have quite a bit of catching up to do.
Diplomatic basically has you bribe every city state on the map (if there are no city states just build the forbidden palace and make sure you're the host of the world congress.). A victory by diplomacy is quite easy to acquire, provided you stay alive long enough for the elections.
Managing cities in this game might be the easiest in any 4x strategy game I've played to date, as it's as simple as this:
there are a few resources your city gets out of tiles in its borders (these are worked by your citizens, which you don't even have to assign manually).
-food: helps your city to grow and work more tiles
-production: the higher production you have, the more you can build.
-science: your ability to advance in the tech tree to boost the other stuff.
-culture: makes sure your border grows so none of your citizens go unemployed.
-faith: your ability to create your own religion
Yes, you can create your own religion and (violently) spread it to every city on the map, because nobody expects the babylonian inquisition to spread hinduism to their neigbours; the aztec empire. Religions basically have traits (which you can choose) that improve your cities (e.g +1 gold per turn per 4 citizens following this religion).
Combat is also pretty straight forward: try to be ahead in science, numbers and promotions and try not to kill your entire army. because once you have the numbers you can just charge at everything the enemy has.
So short story, if you want to continue the legacy of alexander the great, immortal dictator of the greek empire, the founder of islam, conquerer of america, russia and china with death robots, I'd recommend you buy this game on sale!

+ Great writing
+ Solid plot progression
+ Puzzles all make logical sense
+ Multiple endings
+ Unintrusive crossover with the Blackwell series
- Not enough guidance sometimes
- Abrupt endings
- Climax of the story is trial-and-error. Just use a walkthrough to get through the hard part.
- Nobody calls the police even when they should really, really call the police
The Shivah is a short experience. It took me two hours, including the time it took to exhaust all dialogue options and click on every object to read their (often witty) descriptions. Rabbi Stone is a fine protagonist, who manages to be bitter without becoming entirely unlikeable.  Dialogue branches will generally take you to the same conclusion, but the option to respond in different ways personalizes the experience enough that I didn't miss having more meaningful choices most of the time.
That said, there
a few choices to be had, which will affect what ending you get. Refreshingly, the changes are all logical consequences of your actions, rather than the game simply giving you better endings as a reward for good behaviour. (Although needless to say, being the best person you can be never hurts.) Unfortunately, very ending cuts off a bit too abruptly, but there's enough sense of satisfaction from the climax of the story that I didn't feel too cheated. Overall, the game makes for a good short story.
One additional note: I didn't realize before picking up The Shivah that it was a crossover with the Blackwell series. Luckily I love those games, and the character cameos here were subtle enough not to detract from the plot. I recommend fans of The Shivah try the Blackwell games if they haven't already; Blackwell fans might also enjoy this game, with the caveat that it's an earlier and therefore less polished work.

I bought this one in a bundle a while back and it's taken me a while to dig it out of my backlog. ;)

What I like about this game is how unique it is.  I'm not Jewish but the Rabbi makes for a brilliantly kooky PI, and you can almost imagine a TV series about him.  In my first playthrough I tried to take the mick a bit and use the Rabbi's question-for-a-question response for every bit of dialogue... my character quickly ended up in jail!  I had to laugh!!  (Later that's the very tactic I needed...)
So: this is a cautious recommendation.  Judge the game on its own low-budget terms and you should enjoy it.  Just remember to make (physical) notes of names because sometimes they're only mentioned in passing and you need them to progress - and the game doesn't always remind you. ;)

Everyone has to start somewhere, and Wadjet Eye Games started with The Shivah. Originally created as part of a game jam, The Shivah was improved and expanded and eventually released as a retail product. However, even a high-effort start can be a rough one and it really shows here. Lacking the scope or detail or steady pacing of more established games, The Shivah still feels very much like a first effort, one that's best skipped to get right on to its aforementioned peers.
You play as Russell Stone, a Rabbi in a run-down synagogue that's on its last legs. The bills are piling up, the congregation is leaving, and Stone just doesn't have the heart to carry on. Then in an instant all that changes, in such dramatic fashion that Stone can't just accept his windfall without digging deeper. That digging proves to be a dangerous choice, leading him into the shadows of Manhattan and its Jewish community.
The religious angle is certainly unique among adventure games, which is a colossal shame because the elements of Jewish culture and history are far and away the best parts here. At the core of the conflict is a question of faith and orthodoxy, one with significant repercussions and no easy answer. Exploring the impact of this conflict puts Stone in all sorts of uncomfortable situations, both with his people and those connected to them. This framework holds up a tale of doubt and redemption that not many games can match for how grounded it is emotionally. However, it's pretty much ONLY grounded emotionally because by the end, matters will have spiraled far from the calm conversations and investigations of reality.
I wasn't sure what I expected from the actual gameplay of The Shivah but it wasn't the wafer-thin clicking exercises I got. Most of your time in the game is either going to be spent listening to people talk, or breaking into their computers via their hilariously insecure passwords. Dialogues are lengthy and emotional but break occasionally to give player input in the form of three vague approaches like "confrontational response" and "Rabbinical response". These as you might expect have the old Mass Effect problem of not properly expressing to the player what they're going to do, especially the "Rabbinical response" which came off as some sort of insipid rhetorical questioning.
No matter what opaque choices you make the dialogues are still going to end up in roughly the same places anyway because there's only one path of progression through the game. The info you get from people opens up new scenes to explore around Manhattan, and also new names and leads to search the online Jewish community for. This is the best example of a puzzle the game has, because taking half-remembered names and business cards and doing clever searches to work out addresses and email access is at least more realistic than constructing makeshift tools out of brooms and coat hangers. It's also the best example because it's pretty much the only example... you're only going to have three inventory items the whole game (and you start with two of them), and the game's Clue system that keeps track of useful notes as conceptual items is barely used at all.
There's not a lot to the game in either challenge or depth, which isn't great but wouldn't really sink a title with me on its own. What killed The Shivah for me was the ending, which I won't spoil but pretty much trips over every hurdle an ending needs to clear. It comes mostly out of nowhere, it escalates the stakes beyond reason, no one involved does anything that makes sense, it requires an infuriatingly exact string of decisions to get through, and it doesn't wrap the game up in a very satisfying way considering what it reveals. It's the sort of ending that would have worked with a longer, deeper game that gave time to develop the characters and build up to a wild crescendo, but hitting it after an hour or so of mostly empty rooms was a real sucker-punch.
The Shivah is far from a bad idea for a game, and honestly more adventures should be made that are similarly rooted in real-world ethos. But it ends up being a bad game for not giving its story room to breathe, not giving the player enough to do, and not wrapping things up in a sensical or tolerable way. There are other little irritations too, like the inconsistent audio quality of the voice acting and the lack of feedback when you learn key information to progress. Really though, the core problem is that this one needed more time and more effort for what it became. The Shivah may be an important part of Wadjet Eye's history, but it's better off being left as a footnote in favor of more polished games.

I honestly love seeing people complaining about the meta and the expansions. I've been playing Shadowverse since one of the earlier expansions, and I've been climbing steadily, and I still find this game rather chill and laid back, fun to both win and lose. In my opinion (I STRESS THAT OUT) there is less RNG and luck in Shadowverse than in Hearthstone, and getting packs is a hell of a lot easier. However, seeing all the negative reviews on this game, I'd like to point out that half of it is not true, with the only true part being that the Cygames team do come a bit late with the nerfs (but they still come and don't wipe away half our beloved cards *ahem*blizzard*ahem*). The false part is how the gameplay is centred around certain decks, it's too aggro in the past few expansions, as well as how it's a pain in the backside to climb. If  you know your matchups and invest a tiny bit of your time into the game, you can realise that every deck has a weakness, for example 'Aggro Bloodcraft' runs out of cards really quickly in the early game, and falls low on health. This in turn means as soon as you gain board control (if your health isn't too low) you win. And honestly, all the cards in the game is playable, as long as you have a deck built around it, so people saying how the game is only "one deck because every other deck is trash" or "too aggro" or "expansion based as old cards are now getting retired" they are completely wrong (IMO) and all they need is to invest some time in learning and understanding the game.

I tried this game out about a year ago. I initially wrote it off because I'd just come hot out of Hearthstone and was looking for something different. I saw this game let you include 3 copies of a legendary in your deck and had a larger deck size, and had made incorrect assumptions about how this would affect the price of the game. I stopped playing CCG for awhile, and eventually came across Eternal, one of this games competitors. I enjoyed my time with it, but at the end of the day, it had similar deck value problems to HS - neutral cards are not particularly powerful in Eternal, and thus, each deck requires its own set of legendaries, making each deck very expensive. Due to the deck size being what it is, you also need a full set of them in order to actually have a chance at drawing them. They're appropriately generous with their reward structure to compensate for this, but it also sits in a unique position where spending money provides little value compared to most other CCG, and the drip-feed reward structure requires two or three months of active play before it really starts paying off.
Eventually, I was fed up with the decidedly western-style fantasy art. Between Hearthstone and Eternal, I'd been staring at very similar characters and cards for years, and wanted something different. Thus, even though I'd written off Shadowverse initially, I heard some buzz about an upcoming expansion and decided to look into it with a little more detail.
The starting value of a new account is insane. You are gifted enough packs for completing the tutorial to craft at least one meta-ready deck, and if you happen to actually open any cards that are required for the deck of your choice, you'll have some change left-over to start building towards another meta-ready deck. There are also a series of easy to complete (albeit slightly time consuming) one-time achievements that will award you roughly 50 more packs worth of rupies, which can certainly afford you another meta-ready deck, or bring you very close to it. The daily and monthly reward structure settles in to something more akin to Hearthstone from there (though it's still more generous) - you get enough quests per day, to, on average, buy about 1.2 packs. The daily login bonuses will give you about 14 packs of value just for logging in every day (spread out over a 30 day period), so a month of active play will net you approximately 50 more packs. Again, assuming that this entire time you haven't pulled a single card you need for a meta deck, this still crushes down to enough resources to build yet another meta-ready deck. 30 days in and you've opened 140-160 packs without even spending a dime. No other game is this generous with its rewards.
Should you decide to drop some cash on this game, it's even been mathematically proven that buying a card pack at full price (100 gems) provides more value in terms of cards / resources acquired than any other game out there. Not content with that, Cygames provides a daily card pack discount that allows you to buy a single pack per day for 50 gems. While there isn't an easy way to buy 1500 gems, this amount (worth roughly $30) will get you an extra card pack per day for an entire month, provided you're patient enough to wait for the daily discount.
I am reasonably certain that the only audience for Shadowverse, at least in English speaking regions, is players that are fed up with one of this games competitors, such as Hearthstone or Eternal. As I have experience with both of these games, here's a bit of a comparison to help you judge whether or not you'd like this game.
Compared to Hearthstone;
-Different art style, which may be more appealing or off-putting, depending upon personal taste
-40 card decks instead of 30 card decks.
-You can put 3 copies of a card per deck (including legendaries) instead of 2 for common/rare/epic and 1 for legendaries
-Combos are similar, most of them are simple (play two cards back to back for an added benefit, or based strictly on the number of cards played in a turn)
-Less powercreep
-Significantly less RNG
-Neutral cards aren't quite as powerful overall. Some of them are good and function as important parts of certain meta decks, but you won't see mandatory pack-ins for every deck like Sylvanas and Dr. Boom were with Hearthstone.
-Ladders NEVER reset. You will never have to fight against a legendary-level player when you're just starting out. Once you achieve a certain ranking tier, you're stuck in that rank until you can play well enough to advance to the next one.
-Significantly reduced time-cost for free to play gamers. You're gifted enough resources as a new player to actually make a meta-ready deck immediately, instead of being forced to slum it up for a year or more if you can't pay
-Significantly reduced money cost for people that want to buy in to the game and start playing with more good decks immediately
-You can play the "Draft" (arena) mode against your friends for free. No rewards for doing this, but it's a great way to play against your friends, especially if their collection of cards isn't as good as yours
Compared to Eternal;
-Different art style, which may be more appealing or off-putting, depending upon personal taste
-Fixed deck size of 40,  instead of (minimum)75 card decks.
-You can only put 3 copies of a card per deck instead of 4
-Combos are possible!
-Absence of influence / power cards as a mechanic means "flood" and "screw" are never problems you have to deal with.
-roughly equal powercreep per set / expansion
-Story isn't gated behind a paywall; entire campaign is a free to play experience with rewards attached to its completion
-Slightly more RNG
-Neutral cards are significantly more powerful, there are reasons to put them in your decks
-Ladders NEVER reset. You will never have to fight against a master-level player when you're just starting out. Once you achieve a certain ranking tier, you're stuck in that rank until you can play well enough to achieve the next one.
-"draft" mode doesn't allow you to keep your cards, however, the cost of the draft mode is significantly cheaper, and you never have to worry about the opportunity cost of "rare drafting" compared to drafting to win
-Roughly equal time-cost for free to play gamers. However, Shadowverse's reward structure is very front-loaded, which means it takes less time to get started
-Less expensive to buy into the game
-You can play the "Draft" (arena) mode against your friends for free. No rewards for doing this, but it's a great way to play against your friends, especially if their collection of cards isn't as good as yours
