Back when the game was released on Steam it used to be an interesting concept with nice looking art and lots of free packs to keep the player entertained without having to pay anything and remain competitive which made the game popular in certain circles. As time went on it became duller and duller since there wasn't much strategy other than drawing the right cards or playing aggressively and preying on the opponents bad luck. But we accepted it and expected the game to expand and fix itself. (God, how innocent we were)
Time went on and contrary to everyone's expectations they didn't fix the core problem of the game and just added more powercreeps just to nerf them (or at least part of it) after a couple of months later leaving the terrible aftertaste of what is this game about anymore or what can we expect from the future. Of course it just got worse with the time until everyone that had a slight chance of interest on it gave up and went away.
To summarize the game it's basically a heavily luck based, go first, curve it out and dominate sort of play with a few exceptions that are barely playable these days. The comeback factor is very flimsy as you probably can count in your hand the times you really felt like you actually used a smart strategy to fool your opponent and get the best of it. No opponent hand destruction, no traps, no control mechanics at all. Drop followers (minions, creatures etc) and do your worst that's the game. Also plenty of spells can deal damage to the player health so you can exploit that too.
The absurd amount of cheap kills and highly annoying cards that can snowball your game or just dumb stuff that can simply autowin when played (ahem, Eachtar) only makes Shadowverse a terrible and stressful experience either when you win or when you lose. No balance allowed! must be their motto. Most of the time you simply get a better hand go face (player health) and the opponent concedes. The card game feel is completely nonexistent and it feels like a grinder, a cute anime girl parade grinder. Exactly like, you know, those puzzle block games you meddle around with your smartphone for quick time killing brainless fun... which is exactly what the devs always wanted this game to be from the very beginning if you read their interviews. Guess we just had the wrong expectations from this (?) who knows.
Anyway, let it rot. All the time I wasted on this wasn't worth at all and surely the same will be true for you. Go play something else, really. You've been advised.

Have you ever hungered for a roguelike with a mix of careful planning and fast paced action peppered about? Then maybe Teleglitch is for you. From the very start, you’ll go about the usual roguelike style of killing and progression (no leveling here) and collect various materials which can be crafted into useful items, weapons, and even armor to help you progress through the game.
Combat is a quick and dirty endeavor and typically will be resolved within a few seconds depending on various factors. I found using choke points and blind spots to be the best path to victory, as being able to fully unload on an enemy at point blank range (before they are able to retaliate) is a great recipe for success. I would also highly recommend that you get the detector and EM detector upgrade ASAP as being able to know where enemy swarms come from, as well as the location of entrenched opponents, is absolutely vital to your survival.
Once you get the hang of the overall combat and crafting systems, Teleglitch is a fairly straightforward game that rewards careful planning and precise execution (and punishes recklessness and haste!) It will definitely take you 10 or so deaths before you finally get the hang of the game. But, if you hang in there, you’ll be glad that you did.

8 bit games are tough and have that razor sharp challenge to them that make you want to re-arrange your organs and throw them out a jagged broken window. this is not for any casual gamer whatsoever and if you have never played an old school title before (either in cart or an emulated format) i highly suggest you think hard before buying. Castle in the darkness is an amazing game with graphics and music that scream "put me in a cartridge and lets play!". the game as a whole is a complete homage to the games of yesterday which includes many secrets and easter eggs for you to find. the controls are responsive and flow with moderate grace but you may take a "FALL" or two (you'll see). the pixel art and the color pallet remind me of a cross between a good data east and capcom game from back in the day and its beautiful.the story is simple and sweet, saving the princess and the kingdom, standard fantasy stuff but simply well done. now that all of the good has been shared, let me tell you why its hard.
- enemies can be cheap
- falling is too easy
- your death will not be your fault (well, maybe)
- where am i?
- just use the map!
- what map?!?!?!? (Metroidvania without a map is not good)
- armor does work but towards the end it is like your wearing nothing
- bosses can just be unfair
in closing the game is amazing for what is good about it but at the end of the day i have to be honest and tell you what i really think. i think hard is great and challenge is always welcome, but in this case artifical difficulty is no friend to anyone. sometimes a game can just be Broken and it still be a worthy title to be in your library. if you feel brave, like ghosts and goblins brave, then please buy this awesome game.

After getting 100% achievement completion, I still feel like I suck at this game.
This game is hard for all the right reasons; you may feel limited at first (given how everything in this game is in-game achievement locked), but the game starts you out with the easiest-to-use character and a basic set of simple items that help ease you into how things work.
The game says that it won't save your scores on the easy difficulty, but what it doesn't tell you is that
. Use this to your advantage and play on easy until you think you've gotten a feel for how the game handles (as well as unlocking a few things in the process), then put the game back on its regular difficulty setting and proceed to get obliterated in a brutal fashion.
For extremely skilled players (or masochists), there's even a hard difficulty setting, as well as collectible 'artifacts' that can be toggled to make the game even harder (or easier in a few cases).
This game is completely playable without a guide. However, should one feel inclined to seek advice (which is very likely), there are
helpful guides written by other players that go in detail about combat strategies, how to unlock things, and even just general advice for beginners and veteran players alike.
In conclusion, Risk of Rain is a 2D platformer where you're constantly fighting for your life while scavenging the land for items that passively improve your combat abilities in every way, ultimately reaching the end where the final boss is the only thing standing in your way between you and freedom. I was an original backer of the Kickstarter campaign back then and have to admit that my review might be mildly biased due to having very fond memories of playing the pen&paper ruleset of Shadowrun in various editions.
Shadowrun Returns isn't a triple A game, but it basically boils down to XCOM battles in the Shadowrun universe with an actual story, dialogues, multiple options to solve maps as well as a ginormous amount of playable user generated content, many of which is surprisingly well made and often allows character import from the main campaign, therefore enabling the player to continue their player character's legacy many times over.
I personally spent three time the amount of playtime within user generated content than it took me to complete the campaign.
The art design hits home, the cyberpunk feeling is successfully conveyed every single step and at every corner and the soundtrack is very fitting without sounding too invasive.
There's nothing bad I can say about Shadowrun Returns except for the fact that it does lack polish in the UI  department (which is most likely a result of it being optimized to allow usage on mobile and tablet systems) and regarding visual effects as well as character animations.
I recommend this title to any person that enjoys turn based tactical battles based on a RPG ruleset, likes cyberpunk or even the Shadowrun franchise itself, as they will have many hours of joy with this title.
Again, I cannot stress enough how much content there is available in the steam workshop, there's a few golden campaigns in there that even put the main campaign Dead Man's Switch to shame.

Having not known anything about Shadowrun settings beforehand I went in blindly into the unique fantasy-cyberpunk world in this game. Now I love it, and I love it very much. I've already played through the main campaign three times, and I'm planning on playing some more with different characters.
Graphics, although I don't consider them very important, give the game a nice style with its semi 3D isometric setting. It gives off the vibe of classic cRPGs while at the same time not feeling outdated. The character portraits are also oftentimes a wonder to look at, so in general I am very much satisfied with the visuals. Character animations are ok, even if not outstanding, but that's to be expected in a turn-based strategy game, I guess. Character models are a bit limited in their appearance, though (the troll is always ugly in-game regardless of how handsome Mr. Kluwe is on his portrait) my guess is that it's the game's perspective and camera distance from the character that made it less of a priority for detailed in-game models. There isn't much going for it in terms of special effects, but environments are still nice to look at, very detailed at times, give you a nice sense of ruthlessness and crudeness of the setting.
Gameplay-wise, I enjoy the system this game has. I'd hate to compare it to XCOM because I haven't played it, and I'm very reluctant to do so because every single turn-based or strategy game review I've read is compared to it like no other games exist. That being said, I've played turn-based tactical RPGs before (Think Pool of Radiance, Gorky 17, Commando series and MASSIVE CHALICE from the top of my head that rely on turns fully in comparison to semi-action system of Neverwinter Nights or Dragon Age) and, while in general there is not much going for it in terms of its complexity, it definitely works and gets the job done. There's really not much to say about it, reliance on range to hit and on cover to reduce damage with limited action pool. Nothing outstanding, but nonetheless satisfying.
The game has a ton of variety with multiple classes (or archetypes, as "there are technically no classes in Shadowrun" apparently) that let the player adapt to a different playstyle and experience the game differently, so far, having played a StreetSam, Shaman/Decker, a Mage (Returns), Rigger, some Physical Adept (Dragonfall) and Mage/Shaman (Hong Kong) I can definitely say that the way these classes are played feel different depending on your choices.
Skill trees are vast, even if very straightforward. Apart from my Physical Adept I never really had a problem of deciding where to put my skill points, because the system is very self-explanatory. It still branches out for different paths, so that's a plus in my book.
Variety of choices you can make in-game regarding your build are mostly class dependant. Equipment choices are more defined at character creation and skill spending where you decide which gun to use, Street Sams and Riggers have a steady progression of better equipment coming their way, but have little in regards of choosing a different path than other representatives of their classes. It's a similar situation for other classes, Mages, Shamans, Deckers and Physical Adepts, where you have a limited spellbook with maximum of 6 slots (except for Deckers and their ESPs), but where you can choose specific spells/abilities from a bit more significant amount of choices in your available pool. If you have no prior knowledge of the game or Shadowrun setting, for your first playthrough I suggest playing one of the two former classes just because you won't get confused in your possible ability choices. I definitely needed some prior knowledge before playing the latter classes to their maximum efficiency.
Difficulty is mostly based on your luck with RNGeesus, who decides whether or not you actually have a chance to hit that 95%-chance-to-hit-enemy. The higher the difficulty goes, the less to-hit chance you have, and the more to-hit chance your enemies have. Still, the difficulty did not spike up to particularly formidable levels until the last two or three missions, with the exclusion of the 1st mission (where I'm never specced up for the predetermined equipment) the solo bit at early stages of the game (1v1 as a shaman/decker vs a hellhound is not fun on very hard difficulty) and MAYBE the mission half-way through after which you get an additional action point (but I'm saying it just because I didn't manage to save one of my crewmates). Overall, it does not feel overwhelming even on the highest difficulties if you know what you're doing, but having started a Dragonfall playthrough on highest difficulty as PhysAd I can't say I'm very much dissatisfied with the level of the challenge.
The game has a couple of small puzzles and mini-games, usually involving password recoveries or opening secret doors, but it also includes class-specific games, like using drones, finding, summonning and controlling shaman spirits, or getting on the ley-line spot as fast as possible. The biggest mini-game of all being obviously decking, gives you a very nice sense of hacking, while at the same time granting nice leverage in the meat-world. There are a few non-lethal encounters during the runs where you have to talk your way through to progression, and one mission in particular gives you a variety of options to go about it, either by stealing, or forging a card to get through the level via front door, or using a backway entrance. Overall, they are very well built-in sequences into the whole story, and are nice as moments of relief from combat. One thing I have to say that I feel torn by, though, is that there are marker icons on the screen on every single object of importance. While it is useful to go around outside of runs, it kind of breaks the in-game satisfaction of discovering the secret if it is marked on your map from the get-go, which makes one question why bother with other options of progression if there's a secret back entrance available ( after 3 playthroughs of the main campaign I still kept using the same entrance, so I still didn't find that out).
The sense of in-game action is felt less through the intensity of combat (obviously, it's a turn-based game), but you can steel feel the tension in relation to how important your fight is by means of a well-written story. The amazing soundtrack also does its part, but it may feel a bit repetitive at times, and especially out of place in some parts of the game where you are still registered in a turn-based movement system, but where there is nobody around you to fight against.
As far as replayability goes, the game definitely does have its perks that may tempt you to try it again, as multiple dialogue options, etiqquetes and class/stat specific actions unlocking even more ways to go about the game, different class choices for different feel of combat, and different equipment specifications for certain classes. I have to say, the third time around I don't even play through the game for the story but rather trying out different builds, and it may be that unless I get a break from DMS I'll get bored easily, so replayability only goes as far as it does. Luckily, there is some user-generated content for different story missions, and I'll definitely give them a try at some point. I'd say replayability value of the game comes from the quality of UGC in this case, but hey, regardless of it, if you've played the game once, you might definitely want to get back to it at some point and try a different path.

The Shivah is 1980's-style pixelated point-and-click adventure starring a depressed, grieving rabbi passing time in a indebted, poorly-attended synagogue.  When a former congregant is murdered, the rabbi decides to throw a metaphorical deerstalker hat over his yarmulka and go sleuthing.
The game is short, with only handful of sparsely decorated locations.  There are no inventory-use puzzles.  Items can be picked up and examined for clues, but they can't be combined or applied to the environment.  As there's so little in each location, pixel hunting isn't much of an issue.  Gameplay is typical of the genre, with a couple of potentially frustrating puzzles that become quite easy once you realize that you solve them by acting like a rabbi.  How does one do that?  Don't worry, the game will tell you.  Repeatedly.
The two things that make this game recommendable are: 1) The humour is excellent throughout, from jokes on the rabbi's computer, to his reactions to certain items and people in the environment, and voice-acting bloopers accessible once you've finished the game.  2) The heavy Jewish ambiance and symbolism.  I don't think there's another game like this, at least none that I've seen this side of the Israeli border.  The cursor is a chai (Jewish symbol of life), and the music always feels like it's three notes from shifting into Sunrise, Sunset.
My only complaint about the game is length.  I would have liked it to have been about three times longer, and three times bigger, so the mystery could take it's time unfolding.
If you've been looking to scratch that broken-hearted-rabbi-hunts-for-a-killer itch, this is the game for you.
If you actually have that itch?  Either you've read all of Harry Kemelman's Rabbi Small books, or it's been too long since you called your mother.

This game on its own is fun for the first couple hours, but after a while it gets tedious.  The graphics are great, but thats all I have to compliment this game on.  The game itself eventually becomes nothing more than a glorified board game.  The sheer amount of time it takes to even acheive victory in one of these games can be awful.  It becomes nothing more than waiting for next turn to pop up.
One of my main disappointments with this game is its lack of diplomacy and trade.  Its been to simplified and leaves me disappointed with lack of things to do.  This game eventually becomes a matter of waiting however many turns for the next thing for some mild action.  The trade deals are unique to say the least.  For one more strategic resource the other nation will propose a completely unfair deal of you giving up a large lump sum of cash with other strategic or luxury resources to boot.  This has ruined my faith in the trading mechanics of this game.
The AI is also very odd in this game.  At times they will do seemingly irrational and straight up idiotic things.  In all the games I've played the only real threat they have ever possesed was having more troops and better technology than me.  Needless to say this results in a less than interesting game that becomes "Who has the more military power".  This AI problem is fine at lower levels of difficulty, but in higher difficulties they still maintain the same irrational behavior only with more of everything.  This really bothers me.  The AI never changes, but at higher levels the game simply gives them military superiority and spam you with troops.  The already irrational AI is given so many bonuses instead of having their own itelligence boosted.  This is what has sincerely bothered me the most.

The Shivah has some really big flaws that got in my way of fully appreciating it:
- There was one puzzle about a third of the way into the game that I felt had no obvious clue of how to solve it. I ended up using a walkthrough to find out the solution and it was not at all clear how you were ever supposed to know that information.
- The final segment of the game is tedous. You can't save during it, and if you fail you have to watch the opening scene animation all over again, then hit space bar a million times after you've loaded the most recent game to skip through dialogue you've already read. I think I had to do that 5-6 times before I was able to beat the game properly.
Having said all that, the subject matter of the game was very unique, and even though I'm not Jewish I found it refreshing and interesting. I'd love to play more games with such unique atmosphere.

The Shiva is a charming and overall enjoyable game, that has a lot of problems though.
The Story of Rabbi Stone trying to solve a murder mystery of former congregation member is a good setup for an interesting story that tackles questions of faith, and the few characters you meet are interesting and well written and vioced. But ... it's about that.
The game Rushes to it's conclusion so fast, that you can finish it in half an hour when you know the puzzle's solutions, only 3 (!) NPCs are important to the murder mystery, the mystery itself is found out through a quite clever puzzle idea, but that idea is overused and about the only thing you can do to advance the Plot. A certain way of talking is used as a joke, but while funny initially (and again at the end) it soon loses it's comedic value.
The end fight itself is done in a unique and clever way, and fun once you figured out what to do, but the leadup to that fight is a series of more or less random dialoge choices that will lead to game overs over and over again unless you find the right path via trial and error. A puzzle shouldn't be done like this. This wasn't a puzzle. It was a chore.
So what could have easily been a 9/10, ends up a short 6/10, or perhaps a 7/10 if you like the music and the setting.
I can recommend the game wholehardetly if you can get the Key cheaply in a bundle or on Ebay, but don't expect too much from it. It is good to waste a rainy hour, but not for much more.

This game is extremely clever. The first part lets you explore the environment to understand the rules of its non-Euclidian geometries and weird ways to interact with various objects - which also introduces the recurrent notion that this game will challenge your assumptions. Eventually, it becomes more about logical puzzle-solving with mechanics that are more or less clear.
If you like puzzle games, this is a great one. It really lets you gradually learn methods of exploration and problem-solving all by yourself. However, if you're more into exploration and novelty than pure puzzle-solving, the former things wear off about halfway through.
The visual style is both minimalistic and bold - though the same features that make it unique and interesting are what makes it hard for me to play, as it tends to give me pretty intense simulator sickness.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the first hour or so, then the game gradually lost me to mechanics that interest me a lot less. However, that's very personal, and I believe that the high praise this game received is entirely deserved.

Since I grew up with 8-bit NES, I am a big fan of retro 2D platforms.
However, I'm starting to leave negative reviews for the games that fail to properly emulate the old style masterpieces.
One of such games is "Castle In The Darkness". There is simply one reason why I'm leaving a negative review; the game would be perfectly done except for one thing: the threshold between "challenging" and "frustrating".
In few words (and IMHO) a good game ceases to be challenging when it becomes repetitive; it's ok to die several times and having to get back and repeat the stage from some checkpoint, but games like this are made to accumulate a dozen hours of gameplay in expense of the fun. I've played 2-hours worth of gameplay titles who gave me so much enjoyment and satisfaction thus had no need to be any longer to beat.
My advice: add some more freaking save points for once. Then take better care of the commands response, to not have to repeat half a stage and die on a stupid spikes jump.

Quick review: super fun modern day, turn based strategy game with some strong RPG elements. Highly recommend.
Long review: This game is awesome. Just about every day for 3 months now, I have been opening my steam library and saying, “I’m going to play something new today” and then I start up X-Com again. I just can’t stop playing. Planning ambushes and assaulting Alien mother ships has just never been so satisfying.
X-Com is essentially a turn based RPG set in modern day warfare. It utilizes a top down view to control a squad of customizable soldiers. Your team, equipped with the fanciest new gear, is tasked with meeting the alien invasion on the battlefield and pushing them back.  It goes beyond combat though. You have to manage your resources to keep the countries funding you happy and at the same time construct your own facility and research new technology so you can construct new equipment.  As with most games, there are scaling difficulties; in the case of X-com these settings truly range from very forgiving to extremely harsh, including an optional “ironman” mode in which you cannot revert to previous saves, making all decisions permanent when that mode is selected.
I have to be honest, there are some definite low points for this game:  it has a boring and overly generic story with some downright bad voice acting to go along with it. The graphics were nothing impressive, and sometimes the animations glitch out and you end up shooting backwards, completely not facing your target.  Without the expansion, it was at times annoying to target aoe moves, as the ground target would bounce you screen around erratically.  However, for me, none of that was enough to detract from the pure enjoyment of the gameplay. I have logged like 100 hours at this point and I can’t bring myself to stop playing this game. The replay value is insanely high. There are tons of customizable options for subsequent play throughs, but even if you left all the options the same your game experience would be completely different. Not to mention all the additions the expansion brings to the table.
I can understand that this type of game may not be for everyone, but if you have any interest in strategy gaming, this would be at the top of my list of recommendations. Also I won’t be writing a full review of the expansion, but if you enjoy the game, do not hesitate to get the expansion. It makes the game even more awesomer..er.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown achieves a perfect balance between resources and choices.  At almost every level you have a difficult decision to make.  You want it all, but have to prioritize.  Offensive or Defensive technologies?  Research doesn't do any good without Engineering, but how do you balance which type of facility to spend your money on?  You get more requests to help than you can respond to - which countries support (in the form of money, research and/or engineering) can you afford to lose?  Do you build a well-balanced squad comprised of one of each type and manage their unique benefits in the fight or build smaller fire teams that can break up and bring more direct pressure on the enemy?  Don't forget about air force.  You need satellites to know what is going on in a country, but that doesn't do much good without the interceptors to bring down the enemy aircraft.
No time to cope with the buyer's remorse from whatever decision(s) you just made because it's another alien attack.  Loading out your squad, again, is a delicious balancing act - your options a direct result of your earlier decisions.  The turn-based squad warfare is the core of the game and where you really feel the weight of your decisions.   You can tell the environments are hand-crafted and a work of beauty to dissect for the best opportunities to get position on the enemy.   The destructible environments, somewhat randomized enemy spawns and the occasional soldier with low willpower panicking and losing control keeps the combat experience fresh.  The "action cam", music and voiced soldier responses are implemented well and keep you immersed.
Really enjoy the promotion of soldiers and the consequence of them getting wounded in battle, or even permanently killed.  As they experience combat they increase in ability and have more options for you to augment their capabilities.  It is a sad moment when a character you brought up from rookie, and over the course of 7 or 10 missions, promoted to Captain is killed in action (especially when you have customized the names of your soldiers to match you friends).
It is probably the greatest compliment to a game when the only critic is that you want more.  As is with this game.  On one hand, I wouldn't mind a deeper tech tree, more facilities to construct, more countries to protect, more varied weapons, an extra soldier or two in my squad, larger maps, more soldier customization, etc.  On the other hand, I don't want any of that because I don't want to risk the perfect balance they have achieved.
The most satisfying aspect of the game is the ultimate result of being so well-crafted.  I really feel all my decisions have weight and consequences.  From being on the ground ordering a veteran Assault soldier to move to a flanking position - hopefully safely drawing enemy fire so other units can move up, but possibly getting wounded and being unavailable for the next fight - to making the high-level decision on which country to favor over another.
In my opinion, one of the greatest games ever made.

I'll never understand how to enjoy DOTA or any MOBA. I think they are pretty dull, tedious games in general, and are filled with some of the most vile, immature punks I've ever encountered online. Free2Play games are a magnet to racist and homophobic 12 year olds. I can't change any of that. Every time I've tried to play a round of DOTA 2 I've been met with insults and rage within 60 seconds of the round start.
I am also not competitive by nature. I never visited arcades growing up. I play games for the immersion and escapism; to visit a new world and be someone else after a day of work. I also like coopertive stuff. The closest I've come to competing is being the best at Super Smash Bros Melee out of a dozen players I knew locally. I never trash talk.
Having said all that, this was a pretty good documentary. Excellent editing and visual quality. They put a lot of effort into it, which is perhaps the reason why the footage is almost 3 years old. It explores a lot of the social stigma of videogames that I'm sure we all grew up with in our families; parents who just don't get it. The most depressing part for me was the reaffirming of how anyone over the age of about 26 just doesn't have the reflexes anymore to compete, and I find that personally very true. I've loved Counter Strike for 14 years, not for the competition, but for the game itself, but these days I find that no matter how much I practice, I am just holding my team back. I may be strong and healthy in real life, but as far as gaming is concerned, I haven't had that feeling of being "in the zone" for almost a decade.
I say props to all these kids who can actually make a living playing professionally, but there is something else to be said for having a backup plan in life. I feel no sympathy for those who go home with little to no prize money. You need to have a source of income to fall back on. Never forget the astronomical odds weighing against you.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes is an action-adventure game themed and designed around the world of Lego and the Marvel universe. Played as either single-player or split screen co-op, you’re tasked with stopping Dr. Doom and his cohort of super villains from yet another scheme to destroy New York and more importantly,  the world.
When you start the game, you’ll be granted a bit of backstory and your first few superheroes to work with. Starting the game will throw you into one of fifteen main story-line missions with an additional twelves side missions you’ll need to unlock as you progress. During the first rendition of each level, you’ll be limited to a very specific few characters that it [the level] was designed around. After completing the level, you’ll unlock “free play” which allows you to use any character you’ve sense unlocked. You’ll also unlock “free roam” which puts gives you a sizable amount of New York to explore for side quests, missions and general mischief and mayhem.
Speaking of characters, the game goes all out on character design and implements well over a hundred different characters to choose from. The main characters are all voiced, albeit not from the well-known voice actors of the movies except Agent Coulson who is in fact voiced by the one, Clark Gregg. While the difference in voices is noticeable, I never found them to be off-putting or felt they detracted from the character’s overall appeal. To substitute for this, the characters in-game were modeled by their real life counterparts.
Depending on the character you play, they each have specialized abilities that you'll need to use to complete levels and collect items during your adventures. For example, larger characters like the Hulk can lift heavy objects, while Iron Man can destroy silver and gold bricks with his weaponry. Characters like Beast can dig, Mr. Fantastic can stretch into various shapes and sizes and Captain America can deflect lasers with his shield. There is a long list of abilities that keep the characters somewhat unique and refreshing. Granted, there is obvious ability overlap, but that is to be expected.
The meat and strongest aspect of the game comes down to the content it supplies. As mentioned above you have 27 total missions to complete, but there are a slew of secrets, mini games, time trials and collectibles to find for those willing to put in the time and effort to find them. Even if you’re not an achievement hunter or a “completionist”, you may find it beneficial to find these items to unlock some of your favorite characters or alternate costumes. Having completed everything in the game, I thoroughly enjoyed it from start to finish. The game isn’t by any means perfect and it does have some issues that would have taken it from a good game to a great one. Collecting everything in the game doesn’t come off as a chore and there never felt like there was an excess of side quests as a facade for a lack of available content. All that said, there are some key issues I wish the game addressed.
Marvel Super Heroes is just one of the Lego games that offer split-screen co-op, but no global co-op ability. Having played the game entirely in co-op split screen, the game felt fluid and responsive to jumping in and out of sessions at will in terms of frames, but did trip over itself while doing so when it comes to the mechanics. We ran into several issues during our time playing co-op.
Sometimes the mini map or markers would fail to show for player two, or markers wouldn’t show for side quests unless you talked to the NPC twice, such as in the Spiderman photo quests. The more prevalent and obnoxious issue was when you’re playing co-op and one player is doing one side quest, and the second player starts theirs. Often the quest of the first player will glitch and many or all of the components will seemingly disappear. The only one to fix this is by either fast traveling to a new area or reloading the game. It was prevalent enough to the point that we rotated quests so we didn’t ruin the other’s progress; it was a real issue.
Lastly, the camera was problematic for us while we played. Playing split-screen would cause the camera to occasionally have difficulties panning far off screen to targets at the edge of the map, forcing us to frantically move the control stick to get the camera to pan properly, or temporarily dropping in and out to give one player the full screen. There is an option for a more dynamic camera that will change based on your location from one another, but we found that caused more harm than good and chose to leave it off in favor of the fixed view.
On a final note, for those wondering about controller support, the game works fine with a controller and I recommended playing it with one instead of a mouse and keyboard, as the game felt cumbersome with a keyboard.


Overall and despite the drawbacks, the game as a whole is still enjoyable, but you’ll find yourself fighting some of the above issues we had more than once during your playtime. While they can be frustrating, I still feel the game offers some fun, but it’s limited by camera issues and buggy co-op play that may turn off some potential buyers.

This will contain NO spoilers (except those seen in the SR4 videos/screenshots here on Steam, aka aliens and superpowers).
"Haters gonna hate" and all that. Despite the harsh, and mostly unjust criticism (SR4 is not a DLC), this game brings a lot to the Saints Row table. If you at all enjoyed SR2/SR3 for either the story or the gameplay (ignoring how poorly the third-party contractor that ported SR2 to the PC did), you will definitely be in for a treat with this game.
Saints Row 4 is NOT a DLC-sized game, in any sense of the word, the DLC SR3 was supposed to have (called Enter the Dominatrix (ETD)) is becoming a DLC for SR4, not SR4 itself. ETD is scheduled as being part of the Season Pass for SR4. It simply makes more sense that it is put into SR4 rather than SR3 as well, because the story of it all fits much better. The only sense of simulation seen in SR3 was seen at the nuke plant.. And  I would make more comparisons as to why, but that would be spoiling either SR3 or SR4 story.
The story adds a great, although admittably odd, turn of events in the Saints' story - An alien invasion, and the Boss' newfound superpowers (realism went out the door in SR3 anyway, do not deny it). Despite how farfetched this sounds, the story does have all the classic Saints Row moments with either vulgar or downright crude humor, it offers the same back and forth between the characters as previously seen in the series. You are still fighting gangs in Steelport, but also quite often aliens, of course. The story has been met with very hesitant views and closed eyes, but I would like to be one to say that I enjoyed the story. I do not know if I am just more open to an alien invasion as part of the Saints' story, or if I do not know what makes a good story, but I had a lot of fun with it. Additionally, it wraps up a lot of loose ends in the Saints Row continuum, ranging from SR1 to SR3's stories, and  it opens up a lot of possibility for future DLC.
Of course, there is also the usual mayhem that follows the Saints; Genki has got some new plans, there are new tools of mass destruction, heck, even new vehicles of mass destruction, some activities make a return in SR4, with some new ones as well. Oh, and on top of that, can you imagine what kind of carnage you can bring to Steelport with superpowers?
The biggest downside to the game, in my point of view, is that its set in the same old Steelport, with some changes. The game does use alternate areas quite a lot (for missions), which brings you around to old places (think SR1 or SR2) or new places that are outside of Steelport, but you always return to Steelport after your mission is done, which does get a bit lackluster if you played over a hundred hours of SR3 as well.
After finishing the game, I was not at all disappointed at all, and can with certainty say that most reviews are done by bandwagon people clinging on to the whole "SR4 is a DLC thing". I am very excited to see what they can come up with in regards to DLC missions/stories. There are so many hilarious and interesting possibilities to be put into the series, especially with how the story played out in the end (no spoilers)!

This is so far the only multiplayer card game to grab my attention, and one of the few multiplayer oriented games I enjoy period.
Shadowverse does an amazing job of creating a card game that both has a lot of strategy to it and is easy to learn and to play. The basic rules are simple; you are given cards of varying degrees of value with offense and defense number stats where the higher the offense the higher the opponents' defense cards you're able to destroy. Just as well, the higher a card's defense, the more damage said card is able to take from an offense. Or, to put things more simply, a card with an offense of 3 will be able to destroy any enemy card with a defense of 3 or less, generally speaking. Cards with higher defense can handle higher leveled offensive attacks. In addition, the higher the value the card, the later in the game you're allowed to play it, as starting with turn one, you are only able to play cards of value 1 (and this increases by one each turn that passes to a maxiumum of 9). And then of course many cards have special effects and so on to add a bit of variety, and the kinds of cards and playstyles available depend upon the initial class you pick. Its an interesting and easy to learn/easy to pick-up game with a large amount of strategy and variety with regards to what sort of decks can be made and how you can use them to counter other opponents' decks.
In addition, while Shadowverse's multiplayer PVP is the main draw of the game, the game also features a singleplayer campaign with short yet interesting stories regarding the characters and their classes with regards to who they are within the game's lore. Each individual character campaign is fairly short and mostly exists to introduce the player to their particular playstyle, but the plot and character interaction add a bit more depth to the game's world and universe.
Finally, beyond gameplay, the game features gorgeous card art of many different styles by large quantities of highly skilled artists and fast, well orchestrated, exciting music to accompany duels so as to make them feel more adventurous and like more than just a card game.
And the best part of all this? Its free! And you might be worried that its pay to win since the developers have to make money some way, but in reality, the game gives you so many free card packs that you can make good decks without paying a cent and without spending a lot of time on this game.
All in all, Shadowverse is a fantastic free card game that avoids the pay-to-win problem that so many other free-to-play games have whilst offering players a fun strategy filled fun fest with excellent music and art to boot.

I really can't say I know of any games quite like this one. It may be short, but it leaves one heck of an impact, and will easily draw you in for more. Having previously played it on the Xbox 360, I can attest that while you can finish the whole story in one sitting with relative ease, you'll likely be playing the bits you liked over and over again.
The story is where the game really shines. You quickly learn that the primarily trigger-based controls are, while unique, pretty intuitive after a while. Everything in the game feels natural pretty quickly. Finding a path, stringing together acrobatic moves, and generally making your way around. Only the combat really feels stilted, with a same few punch animations. You're mostly encouraged simply to disarm opponents by tapping the Y button when their weapon is highlighted, which gives you their gun and instantly knocks them out. This can get tedious, but pacifist runs are possible.
The cutscenes have an animated comic sort of look to them. This is decent enough for getting the point across. The plot exists, primarily to get you between things to run around. It does a well enough job, and has quite a few surprises for only ten levels. The actual story levels themselves are like a combined puzzle platformer, as you mull over how to get where you're going and pull off some intensely satisfying parkour once you get the hang of it. The color scheme and lighting keeps the areas distinct from each other and easy on the eyes. It's a very particular, stylized look that benefits the game well.
As for replay value, as the main story is short and sweet (it does not overstay its welcome by any stretch, but you may be expecting a bit more at the end), the game banks on you enjoying time trials. Really, really enjoying time trials. Because that's all there is. No other challenges in any way, shape, or form, just be the fastest. To be fair, it's quite clear the game is designed for this exact purpose when you start shaving valuable seconds off and learning how to keep momentum going throughout your run, but if you don't like them, already got the three runner bags hidden in each level, and, for whatever reason, don't feel a little thrill at pulling an awesome time off, you've pretty much finished the game as soon as the credits roll.
The music is excellently fitting. The game overall can put a fantastic feeling of adrenaline into you, and a feeling of success when you figure out a new way through a level. There's no faster way to give someone a fear of heights than having them fall to their death in this game. The loading times are almost gone in the PC version (only three "Loading Level" screens still appeared for me), but the lengthy elevator rides and various delays meant to mask them are still perfectly intact, leading to some rather pointless waiting in the middle of a good run. Finally, the time trial scores are not registered through Steam. They are tracked through an EA Online account, which basically means you will not be finding your friend's times and racing your ghosts without a lot of undue effort.
In the end, though, this is quite the amazing game, and I must still recommend it, if only because it leaves an amazing impression and stands alone as an experience. There's just nothing quite like it.

If you are looking for BALANCE PvP game, this is not for you.
While I am neutral about the "new gameplay style" it introduces on every new expansion, I heavily dislike how they ignores obsolete cards.  No, there's no extremely OP cards, but there's a  lot of obsolete cards exist in this game.
"Alice, Wonderland Explorer vs Goliath":
Both provide the same basic stat, except one of them is will have "Fanfare to boost your other allied Neutral Follwers in your hands."
Guess which one is it?  Late release or early release one?  Harder to obtain one or easier to obtain one?
It's late release one AND also harder to obtain (card rarity).  This is just one example...
That's why I decide to give up on this game -- they ignore obsolete cards and never buff them.  They only nerf OP cards and call it a day.
If you play any other PvP (ex: Moba) game, will such imbalance allow to happen?  Are you required to have the latest champion/item to play?  Is it okay for the latest champion/items to be stronger than earlier one?
No, it's just not okay.
If your argument is: "there's no true balance in PvP," my arugment is "at least they TRY and this game doesn't even try."
If your argument is: "That slight better stat cards is more difficult to obtain," my argument is: "It's called P2W."
If your argument is: "Other card games also did the same," my argument is: "No other modern PvP genre will do this, time to change."
Until then, stay out of this game if you want balance card game experience.  I will wait for another Game Developer to try this genre.

Having watched mostly Marvel films growing up over the years, the only Batman film I have seen is the 2008 film, The Dark Knight. I can now say that even though I have only played Arkham Knight for 3.3 hours (so far) I now really want to dive into the universe of Batman, it's characters, story lines and even Graphic Novels (something I don't usually read).
Comparing what I have seen in the Marvel universe, Batman's darker settings and tones is drawing me in to getting lost in its rich lore and world. When I got to the Evidence Room in the GCPD (Gotham City Police Department) I walked around and listened to every audio log for each entry for extra snippets of information, which for a newcomer to the Batman universe felt very enriching. Having only played this game so far in the series it was a warm welcome to be given backstory and context to the event's both previous and current to Arkham Knight. Every cut scene I have seen so far feels like you are watching a Batman film, they are so well done and really pull you in to the story and characters, making you actually care for what happens to them. At times I feel like I am watching a film Noir.
I got lost exploring old film sets in the Panessa Studios and jumping into grates to find hidden passageways, all the while the Soundtrack really sets the tone, atmosphere and mood of Gotham City, it feels straight out of the films.
Also, I will never get tired of how kickass Batman looks whenever you call on the Batmobile as he jumps and backflips like a badass into the Batmobile, just pure awesomeness.
Speaking of the Batmobile, it’s so FLIPPIN’ WICKED! Spinning doughnuts around and doing The Riddler's underground race that I found (I hope there are more of these later) was so damn good! When I realised there was a 1st person mode for the race I went and re did the challenge a further 3 times or so to try and beat my best times. The way the Batmobile changes shape in the assault/firing mode is so fluid and smooth. Also, smashing up the environment is so satisfying with chucks of rubble flying everywhere, who doesn’t want to own a real life Batmobile!?
I opted to play with a mouse and keyboard, despite having an XBox 360 Controller as for me personally I found the controls more comfortable as this is the setup I am used to. Although I will try the controller for the driving sections in the future. Combat feels punchy (pun intended) responsive and solid and the takedown sequences look so badass every time.
As an extra that I found in the pause menu, I really like the addition of the "Photo Mode" I have taken some sweet screenshots with this which I will be using as Desktop Wallpapers for sure.
On the Performance side of things I noticed 0 framerate drops or performance issues. I am also running the game with every setting on max and all the NVIDIA special settings turned on. This game plays like a dream on my PC. I am running on Windows 10 Pro with an NVIDIA GTX Founders Edition 1060 6GB, Intel i7-7700k @ 4.20 GHz, 16 GBs DDR4 RAM and the game is installed and running on an SSD.
I recommend this amazing masterpiece, at full price it is worth every penny for the amount of passion, detail and love that went into crafting this fantastic game.

Antichamber is a beautiful game that explores the manifestation of human will and determination when faced with the impossible task of surviving in a world that was not made for them. The developer's artful use of deep and thoughtful puzzles opened my eyes to the human condition.
I'm joking. Antichamber is only one of the things I mentioned, and that is a puzzle game. Like some people have mentioned, it's easy to look at it and say "oh, a portal knockoff", but the truth of the matter is that it's a bit more complex than that, and by a bit, I mean much. Instead of exploring the "what if" of making a tunnel between anywhere, Antichamber explores the "what if" of walking through a door and not being where you came in from if you walk back out of it.
The puzzles are rarely ever given to you straightforward. The game relies on the player paying attention to their surroundings on a completely different level. It isn't too dificult to figure out the right answer, and you feel really rewarded when you maange it. My one gripe is that after every puzzle, the game gives you a sort of cryptic hint, but typically, this hint is for the puzzle you just figured out on your own.
Overall, if you're the kind of person who loved fooling around in Portal/Portal 2 trying to break the tests to see if you could sneak into somewhere you don't think you were intended to be, or tried to drag a cube into another test chamber, you'll be pleasantly surprised to know that Antichamber encourages that sort of thinking, and in fact, the game outright requires you to "break" its puzzles. It isn't really breaking the rules if the rules weren't there, is it?

IGNORE WHAT THE OTHER REVIEWERS SAY

It is easy to misjudge this as "some sort of Portal clone" from the trailer. It is NOT.
In summary, you draw cubes from rooms and you can lay them in another point of the room to solve a puzzle e.g. building a stair climb up a ledge or placing it in a socket to close/open a door. Doesn't sound much interesting, but the chambers take place in some sort of mind-bending reality, playing with your perspective: rooms look like something else depending from where you are looking... Its hard to explain without spoiling the exploration feeling, I'm doing my best here! Expect many WTH moments.
Puzzles are usually not trivial, some are even quite challenging, and the mind-bending mechanic is rarely used to impose "fake" difficulty (that is, the puzzles follow a logic that you can as well follow). Some chambers require some dexterity.
I have two critiques about the game:
- No achievements... c'mon...
This game is fantastic, and even though the price tag sounds a bit too high, it is more than worthy.

It's like every other roguelike but 300% harder and 300% more enjoyable. You will get your butt handed to you on a silver platter many times. Sounds fun, right?
The story is that you are a person who works on Medusa-1C, a hostile planet with a single research facility that was experimenting on unlimited teleportation. Until everything went wrong. Something came through from the other side. The AI goes rogue, the mutant soldiers started rampaging, and everyone died. Except you. You barricaded yourself in a supply cabinet to wait for rescue, but nobody has come. You have run out of food, and your only hope is to escape Medusa-1C using the experimental unlimited-distance teleporter to teleport back to Earth. How? By killing everything in your way to the teleporter with guns and bombs and stuff. It's like a sci-fi action movie, but the protaganist has the potential to die. In fact, he dies 95% of the time.
On to the gameplay. It's a top down shoot em' up where risk can be equal to reward. Or death. There are plenty of guns, and even more modifications you can make to them! 1 single-shot grenade launcher + 2 tubes = 1 triple-shot grenade launcher. Or you can modify a 9mm pistol to hold more ammo and be fully automatic. The crafting system makes every item you get useful for killing stuff.
Overall, this game is hard enough to be super challenging, but is fun enough to keep you coming back. And if you're not sure if you want it, you can play the demo! Teleglitch: Die More Edition gets a thumbs up from me.

So, this game. Oh, this game. For the thoughtful gamer, this game isnt really your place. The narrative is rather weak, with the story filled to the BRIM with cliches, and NONE of the characters are really memorable or worthy enough of your ♥♥♥♥s. In fact, I had to write this review very early just so I wouldnt forget what little the game had in story. Its basically, (And im NOT spoiling anything, you will see these plot points from a mile away.) "Go to city. Get bit m8. Go stop bombers from blowing up harran. Go kill villian." Amazing plot, amirite? I played dead Isl on the console, and one of my FAVORITE parts was the weapon modding. Here, it... it isnt as creative. Just poison, impact, fire, and electricity. (Correct me if i missed a mod.) And it sorta keeps true to the dead isl formula, with suicide zombies, spitters, big guys, and bigger guys, virals are new, if Im correct. Virals were the worst out of the bunch, as they will do parkour almost as well as you do. But get on top of a van, and keep kicking them off. It works. At night, a new type of zombie comes out, known as "Volitiles". These guys will crowd you, and with their combined strength, reduce you to nothing but zombie food.
Dying light is BEAUTIFUL in the graphics section, (Most of the time) you will require a pretty decent computer to run it at max. The side missions arent TOO interesting, with most of them introducing a character with 3 different lines, most of which you will forget immediatly, and then eventually the character in and of itself. I know im just dissing the game here, but I love this game for its main gameplay mechanics, like PARKOUR. Holy crap, the parkour here is THE BEST ive played in a long time, beating the little bit of validity out of assassins creeds system, with this one actually tiring for the main protagonist to climb all the time. And its challenging. If you miss pressing the spacebar button, or are not intelligent enough to solve its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t climbing puzzles, youre screwed, dude.
The skill mechanic is very detailed, with it going along with skyrims system, (In my opinion, its just skyrims system with less skills.) There are three skill "Trees". Survivor, which will help you, guess what, survive. Agility, which levels your, you guessed it, agility. THE POWER LEVEL. ITS OVER 9!!! The power level (Heh) helps you level up your fighting skills, how long you can fight, the durability of your weapons, and how many "Repairs" a weapon has.
The repair system works like this: You can only repair your stuff so many times, so youll have to ditch it eventually. This mechanic sorta ruins later gameplay, after the ending, it lets you continue. But, in my opinion, ALWAYS do not play after the ending, and just bring your stuff into a friends coop session and help em' out. Overall, a good 8/10. A good continuation of Dead isl- I mean a good start out for techlands new series. Hopefully we will see more in the future.

XCOM reminds me a lot of games like Fire Emblem, Advance Wars, or Tactics Orge, but it sprinkles some western elements into it as well as some sci-fi giving it a unique identity of its own. Overall, this game ends up culminating into a big pile of difficult, stratigec, rewarding fun. And honestly? I wouldn't have it any other way.

Now that we've gotten that out of the way, I usually try my hardest to beat a game before I review it, but I've given it try after try after try, and still my labor has yielded nothing. I still only have 3 of the 9 available cruisers and have yet to actually beat the boss (The Rebel Flagship). This game is brutally unforgiving and plays on your emotions, for example. You see a ship that is vastly superior to your own attacking a civilian transport ship. Your only options are to let the civilians die, or fight the ship and odds are, get yourself killed.
The scrap (currency for the stores) may not seem of much use at first, as you don't need that much to beat the first few sectors, but it becomes incredibly crucial the later you get in the game. If your ship is not up to par for that sector, then there is a very, very, very slim chance of you getting out, but it'll be by the skin of your teeth and with your ship in tatters.
Do I like this game? Yes, I do love incredibly difficult games, they provide near endless playtime as they are hard to beat and can't simply be beaten in a few hours, but this game cuts it really close. It is incredibly difficult and I enjoyed this for the time that I played it, but eventually, the game gets repetitive, and since there really is no feeling of progression because you simply die and get sent back to the start as if nothing ever happened, the game can get tedious and cause you to leave before experiencing the full game, which is what I feel happened to me, I will continue playing this game, because it is an overall amazing game, and I may update this review later on after I've gotten better at the game itself, but until then,
I recommend this game,
TL;DR This is a great game, though it may be a tad excessively difficult for little reward.

Shadowrun Returns is set in mid-21st century Seattle. You play a shadowrunner, a mercenary hired to perform shady work in a world full of shady characters. The game’s campaign, “The Dead Man’s Switch,” opens with you receiving a recorded message from a recently-deceased friend, Sam Watts, who charges you with solving his murder. Throughout the next 10-12 hours, you’ll unravel a mystery that involves an organ-harvesting serial killer, a religious cult, a giant corporate conglomerate, and poison-spewing spectral insects. In other words, pretty standard stuff.
From the start, Shadowrun Returns was billed as a storytelling engine—not only an RPG adventure in and of itself, but a system for creating your own adventures. The truly exciting feature of Shadowrun Returns, and why it will probably deserve another review a year from now, is the included campaign editor tools. Given Jordan Weisman’s experience as creator of the pen-and-paper Shadowrun, it makes sense that he’d want Shadowrun Returns to also serve as a mechanism for players to tell their own stories.

This will contain NO spoilers (except those seen in the SR4 videos/screenshots here on Steam, aka aliens and superpowers).
"Haters gonna hate" and all that. Despite the harsh, and mostly unjust criticism (SR4 is not a DLC), this game brings a lot to the Saints Row table. If you at all enjoyed SR2/SR3 for either the story or the gameplay (ignoring how poorly the third-party contractor that ported SR2 to the PC did), you will definitely be in for a treat with this game.
Saints Row 4 is NOT a DLC-sized game, in any sense of the word, the DLC SR3 was supposed to have (called Enter the Dominatrix (ETD)) is becoming a DLC for SR4, not SR4 itself. ETD is scheduled as being part of the Season Pass for SR4. It simply makes more sense that it is put into SR4 rather than SR3 as well, because the story of it all fits much better. The only sense of simulation seen in SR3 was seen at the nuke plant.. And  I would make more comparisons as to why, but that would be spoiling either SR3 or SR4 story.
The story adds a great, although admittably odd, turn of events in the Saints' story - An alien invasion, and the Boss' newfound superpowers (realism went out the door in SR3 anyway, do not deny it). Despite how farfetched this sounds, the story does have all the classic Saints Row moments with either vulgar or downright crude humor, it offers the same back and forth between the characters as previously seen in the series. You are still fighting gangs in Steelport, but also quite often aliens, of course. The story has been met with very hesitant views and closed eyes, but I would like to be one to say that I enjoyed the story. I do not know if I am just more open to an alien invasion as part of the Saints' story, or if I do not know what makes a good story, but I had a lot of fun with it. Additionally, it wraps up a lot of loose ends in the Saints Row continuum, ranging from SR1 to SR3's stories, and  it opens up a lot of possibility for future DLC.
Of course, there is also the usual mayhem that follows the Saints; Genki has got some new plans, there are new tools of mass destruction, heck, even new vehicles of mass destruction, some activities make a return in SR4, with some new ones as well. Oh, and on top of that, can you imagine what kind of carnage you can bring to Steelport with superpowers?
The biggest downside to the game, in my point of view, is that its set in the same old Steelport, with some changes. The game does use alternate areas quite a lot (for missions), which brings you around to old places (think SR1 or SR2) or new places that are outside of Steelport, but you always return to Steelport after your mission is done, which does get a bit lackluster if you played over a hundred hours of SR3 as well.
After finishing the game, I was not at all disappointed at all, and can with certainty say that most reviews are done by bandwagon people clinging on to the whole "SR4 is a DLC thing". I am very excited to see what they can come up with in regards to DLC missions/stories. There are so many hilarious and interesting possibilities to be put into the series, especially with how the story played out in the end (no spoilers)!

Back on release in August (October for PC) of last year I would not hesitate to recommend Shadowverse to new players.  In fact I would've said it was the best CCG on the market with a balanced and competitive meta, beautiful card design, and fun gameplay.  But as the months have went by things slowly started to change bit by bit for the worse...
Basically the developers have the mindset that matches should be short and end around turns 7-8.  This poses a unique problem for game design where cards are extremely powerful and legendaries can often swing all tempo to end a game.  Predictably as more expansions are released powercreep sets in which causes a wildly imbalanced, yet stale metagame as everything plays mindlessly on curve with little to no decision making or skill checks involved.  It's just gotten worse and worse every expansion and the nerfs the developers have patched instill little confidence in me as they are either too soft or completely target the wrong problematic cards.  Just for a little bit of reference a user-submitted data stat tracker site for the game at one point reported that a deck had over 60% winrate going first and 48% playrate on ladder...
So what's the bottom line?  I'd still say Shadowverse is a decently fun CCG if you're a newbie to the genre or want to take a break from Hearthstone considering the developers give you free packs like candy meaning anyone can have a functional T1 deck starting out!  But as a competitive game it holds no real value and makes a mockery of the genre.  Thanks to the design philosphy it tends to get stale very quickly as you find yourself losing more to the coinflip than a lack of skill.
Maybe if I was a Japanese Salaryman looking for something to kill the time on his short train commute to a soul-crushing office job I would find this game more fun...

I want to say, I was really intrigued by the premise. A previous altercation with a member of his congregation gives him a second chance, and the investigation reveals his long history of stubbornness and insular thinking. Antichamber is a beautiful game that explores the manifestation of human will and determination when faced with the impossible task of surviving in a world that was not made for them. The developer's artful use of deep and thoughtful puzzles opened my eyes to the human condition.
I'm joking. Antichamber is only one of the things I mentioned, and that is a puzzle game. Like some people have mentioned, it's easy to look at it and say "oh, a portal knockoff", but the truth of the matter is that it's a bit more complex than that, and by a bit, I mean much. Instead of exploring the "what if" of making a tunnel between anywhere, Antichamber explores the "what if" of walking through a door and not being where you came in from if you walk back out of it.
The puzzles are rarely ever given to you straightforward. The game relies on the player paying attention to their surroundings on a completely different level. It isn't too dificult to figure out the right answer, and you feel really rewarded when you maange it. My one gripe is that after every puzzle, the game gives you a sort of cryptic hint, but typically, this hint is for the puzzle you just figured out on your own.
Overall, if you're the kind of person who loved fooling around in Portal/Portal 2 trying to break the tests to see if you could sneak into somewhere you don't think you were intended to be, or tried to drag a cube into another test chamber, you'll be pleasantly surprised to know that Antichamber encourages that sort of thinking, and in fact, the game outright requires you to "break" its puzzles. It isn't really breaking the rules if the rules weren't there, is it?

- No achievements... c'mon...

I'm going to tell you a story,
Killing Floor 2, was a fantastic game. I say was because my enjoyment of the game has gone down. When I first purchased the game in January of 2016 I was amazed. The perks were balanced and the game was good. It was a game where you kill stuff nothing more nothing less. Then ZEDconomy came out. I thought it was pretty sweet. I've always been a fan of ingame collecting so I was pretty hyped. New maps were added, new characters, and then Gunslinger came out. I was pretty stoked. So I played Gunslinger and it was broken. No dispute when Slinger first came out it was broken. But the game was still balanced. The game never felt too easy even with the Gunslinger being able to knockdown everything and the .500 Mangums murdering everything. Then after a while a very dramatic shift happened. Berserker, my favorite perk next to Support was nerfed. Now I'm always one for nerfing and buffing in games, but this 'overhaul' I feel was too much. Essentially it removed the tankiness of the Bersker and made the Berserker a very weird and awkward perk to play as.
After a while more perk overhauls were added. I wasn't used to these changes and I was not a fan either. I began to miss the days were each perk was so unique and niche, but then they slowly began to overlap. A lot of game mechanics were changed and rewritten. The one that made me quit was the rewrite for Hell on Earth. With more ammo drops, more Dosh, and Zed spawn changes; Hell on Earth became as easy as Normal to me. I quit because the game lost the sense of urgency and challenge.
When Sharpshooter was released I came back and decided to give it a whirl. It was fun. I got roped back into the game for some time and decided I'd be here to stay for a little longer. More changes were made and then SWAT was released. SWAT destroyed the game. It was this point I began to question Tripwire as a developer. I remember telling my friend that I wanted to work for Tripwire so that I could smoke what they were smoking.
Then Survivalist came out and I was done. It felt like such a copout. A perk that was good at nothing. Survivalist was and still is awful. It offers nothing to the game. If you want melee go Bersker. If you want Shotguns go Support. If you want Healing go Medic. Why bother going a perk with half the capabilities as the others.
Killing Floor 2 is game that was one of the best PvE games on the market, but through odd changes and questionable choices became easier and easier. Not to mention the 0-25 level grind is mind numbing. In a PvE game I look for an easy base and a near impossible ceiling. The game was easy to pick up and easy to understand. It was hard to master and understand the mechanics. After a while the game became trivial.
TL;DR: Killing Floor 2 was a good game to me. It is not a bad game. New players will enjoy it, but for Veterans such as myself; wthe changes were a bit too much. I would reccommend it to others for sure. I just hate a lot of the changes. It's not the same game and not as good as it used to be.

If you want a rock hard 2D rogue-lite game with satisfying combat and a dizzying amount of combat styles and builds, Risk of Rain does not dissapoint.  The game does not start off easy, and will kill you very quickly if you're not careful.  And as a mechanic, it will only get harder the longer your session goes.  With a timer, when it hits certain intervals the difficulty jumps, it becomes a balancing act of staying around and grinding enemies or tracking down items or moving on to the next stage as quickly as possible to try and beat it while it is a bit easier.  This balance can be a little tipped on the grinding side depending on RNG, however, as you might get lucky enough to obtain an absurdly powerful combination of items (drones are your friends) can quickly make the increase in difficultly negligible.  Conversely, if you have a run with bad luck in your item drops, especially ones without some form of crowd control, prepare to run up against an almost unbeatable brick wall as you get swarmed by horders of enemies with very high hp and damage.  This balance can again be tilted depending on the character you're playing as, with characters that have movement based abilites and temporary immunities having a much easier time. With enough perserverance and a little luck, however, you can push through, and it can be immensely satisfying when you do finally beat it.  If you've already burned your way through Isaac or Rogue Legacy, and you are okay with RNG being a bit of a heavier deciding factor, then Risk of Rain is something I'd highly recommend.  Also, the soundtrack is AMAZING.

So, I definitely enjoyed Shadowrun Returns, and as my first experience with a Shadowrun game, I'm going to be judging this without any knowledge of past games and playstyles.
That being said, Shadowrun Returns is a great game! I had a good time with it. However, I did feel like it had a few issues you may want to be aware of before going into it.
Pros:
+Well-written and engaging story
+Actual impactful skill trees
+Fantastically designed environments
+Interesting and very real NPC's
Cons:
-Pretty short main story
-A bit cheesy at times (Not a con if you like that sort of thing)
-Combat system can be a little tedious (Mostly Quality of Life stuff, see below)
Realistically there isn't much I would say is wrong with this game, but there were parts of the combat system that I found annoying (For example, not allowing you to end a character's actions for that turn. If you aren't doing anything with one character that turn but they are first or second in your party, it will jump back to them repeatedly which can be rather frustrating).
The main story was also pretty short, I probably beat it in well under 30 hours. HOWEVER, Shadowrun does have an extensive steam workshop listing, which (although I haven't tried any of the stories in there yet) I am sure makes up for this. Integration for steam workshop stories is built directly into the game.
Most of the cheesiness is minimal and for the most part, Shadowrun really does feel almost as if you are playing a tabletop rpg, with a DM dictating all the dialogue to you. The narration of scenery and facial/body motions really adds to that effect.
Overall, probably an 8.5/10. Definitely would recommend if you enjoy tabletop games and/or turn-based strategy.

Long story short:
Risk Of Rain
-Surviving rogue-like game
-A lot different gear and items, as well 12 playable characters with different stats and abilities.
-Jump n' shoot (or slice) (or blow up)
-Pretty sweet soundtrack
-The randon generator system works well
-Characters are well made in my opinion. Some of them might seem really ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but it could be that it doesn't fit your style or it takes time to practise.
-The local co-op should have some fixes. Especially a split screen instead of shared screen.
-Single player is fun, multiplayer not as fun.
Risk of Rain is a surviving game. You build your character into a god of war by opening chests and picking items from different type of holders by gold, which you get from killing enemies or opening small containers.
Your character level ups as you kill enemies and open containers. The goal in the game is to get out from the planet alive by proceeding through teleports to the final stage. The longer you play, the harder it gets, as the enemies' level and spawn rate gets higher.
One mechanic that changes each playthrough a bit is the random generator on items, bosses and teleporter's position. The stages differ as well, but only the 4 first ones between two stages.
The game is pretty fun time killer. Getting new gear and growing your guy into a terminator is satisfying. All the items are useful in my opinion, so despite what you get, its always bonus. You can also unlock new characters with different abilities and stats. There are artifacts that can change your game as well, which is a sweet addition.
Moving in this game might share opinions, though. Jumping takes some time to get used to, since its short compared to the gaps you need to get over between platforms. The characters have different moving speed, and some of em have a mobility ability, which makes moving faster. But luckily there are items to improve both jumping and moving.
Now, it all comes down to which purpose you want to get the game: single player or multiplayer.
Single player is okay as long as you like games like Binding of Isaac. Although after few playthroughs the game might get boring due seeing the same maps and enemies over and over again.
The multiplayer however needs some fixes in my opinion. The local co-op was one reason I wanted to buy the game in the first place, and I actually enjoy it. But the problem comes when you notice that you share the same screen with your partner. Despite how big your screen is, its annoying when you need to wait for your friend. Also, platforming between platforms and long drops becomes really risky, since if your pal misses the jump, the camera goes between you two, forcing the other to come closer. This game should have a split screen for local co-op, which shouldn't be so hard to do.
Also in local co-op, you need to share your gear. This can be either a good mechanic or bad one. Depends on the player. I like the idea personally. Though, the increased enemy spawn rate makes things harder. When there is♥♥♥♥♥♥loads of enemies in the screen, you can barely see your character (since your guy is really small compared to everything else) nor survive, since there isn't any invulnerability after getting a hit. Of course this highly depends on which character you have and which items you've got so far. Also, you can lower the difficulty, but that would be too much for my pride to handle as a gamer.
Coming back to the artstyle, I love pixel art, but on co-op it gets hard to see your guy. There should be a big arrow or something to point out which one of the guys is yours, or where it goes when there are 100 enemies around you. It should also show your health, since its hard to focus on your character and watch how much you have health time by time.
My apologies for such long rant about the co-op only. I haven't played the online multiplayer, since I've never had the chance. I just wanted to point out some of my opinions about the local co-op, since it was one key feature to me.
If you buy the game, I hope you enjoy it.
