FTL: Faster Than Light is the charming indie game you’ve never heard about. Or if you have heard about it, count your lucky stars. FTL has the feel of an instant classic and brings back everything you love about old games: humble yet lovely graphics, whimsical music, satisfying gameplay, and a dash of storytelling.
In FTL, you play a sole ship escaping to the safety of the Federation. Since the game is a space strategy game (see roguelike), you will be using your wits to survive lest you be blasted into animated space debris. If you like strategy games, or even open-ended RPGs, you cannot go wrong with FTL. As long as you can appreciate the retro graphics, the game will reward you with surprising depth and atmosphere. Space. It’s awesome.
Gameplay is where FTL delivers and micromanaging your ship is just as fluid as piloting a Nesasio Stealth Cruiser. You can open and close doors to prevent intruders or fire, send your crew to repair vital systems (or face certain death), toggle the power to your shields, and so on. A variety of ship upgrades and crew selection create choices that actually matter to the player. Outfitting your ship is complex and can be the difference between making it to the next solar system or not. Ship battles are extremely satisfying. At first, I would fire my weapons as soon as they became available. It wasn’t until my fourth run that I learned to time my lasers to break through defenses. That’s how FTL is — learning the layers of gameplay. It might seem a bit daunting at first, but the charming atmosphere will lure you in and you will be pleasantly surprised as you learn more and more.
I doubt I’m the only one to have Malcolm Reynolds pilot my ship and Tali’Zorah as my trusty engineer. It’s easy to become attached to your crew, made up of certain species with their own advantages and disadvantages. Which makes it that much harder when you accidentally send them into room with the airlock open (sorry!). The playable races range from quick-repairing Engi, vicious Mantis, to well-rounded, of course, Humans. While the actual story of the game is light, the lack never detracts from the feel of the adventure. Since the solar map is randomly generated, your crew will face different dangers each play through. Still, the scenarios will eventually be familiar and may even become monotonous. But by then, you’ve already had too much fun to care.
As for the music, it is nothing short of a retro masterpiece. The soundtrack is even sold on Steam. Bleeps and bloops bring out the charming space atmosphere and will play in your head even when you’re not playing the game. Rarely has a soundtrack fitted a game as perfectly as in FTL.
Unlockables provide substantial replay value. New ships are the main rewards and each ship has a different playstyle. The Slug Cruiser relies on taking out the enemy crew and the Zoltan Cruiser has the protection of a unique shield. A slight drawback to the game is a lack of DLC, which is weird to say since many games suffer from too much DLC.
You will die. You will die a lot. The “Normal” mode should really be called Death. Yet even when losing FTL is satisfying and not many games can pull that off. You have a sense of “maybe if I did this next time, things will go smoother” and space runs are quick enough that you won’t regret starting over. Do you have a hipster friend who tells you games are too easy these days? Yeah, right. FTL, enough said.
So like most strategy games, the most satisfying part is using a mix of brains and luck to overcome a particularly difficult situation. FTL is a master of creating those scenarios. Your ship will be on its last leg, limping just ahead of the Rebels with your crew fighting Rockmen while slowly suffocating from lack of oxygen. Oh, and your ship is on fire. What will you do? Whatever you have to do to survive.
Tip: Never fight alien spiders. Never!

FTL is a turn-based roguelike with real-time ship-to-ship combat.  Your mission is to escape the Rebels into Federation space, surviving strange alien races, electrical storms, meteor showers, and every slaver's and pirate's attempts to destroy you and take your stuff.  It can be played casually or with some degree of challenge, based on the difficulty, the ship & layout selected, and the routes taken to best navigate through the areas.  Risk the blind mask of a nebula to buy yourself a little more time, or book it through hostile territory in the hopes that you might gain some extra scrap (credits $$), a new crew member or perhaps some additional equipment for your ship...the choice is yours and that choice can mean everything!
This is easily one of the best games on Steam.  Purchasing it at full price is certainly worth the money, but it goes on sale very regularly so look for discounts!  You will not regret it :)

8/10:
When you can kill other players as the dreaded night hunter zombie, what's not to love? (That mode disconnects half the time though).
REVIEW:
This game is like L4D mixed with Dead Island and Mirror's Edge and, with Skyrim / Far Cry 3-4 tossed in too.
Very stable, almost bug-free, performs well on most rigs (when patched); a crowning technical achievement for Techland.
Pros:
- beautiful graphic fidelity and performance
- superb first-person parkour system
- improves on Dead Island melee combat mechanics and co-op in every way (co-op now has random challenges which yield great rewards)
- great weapon crafting system and skill trees for added depth
- night time is terrifying: avoid the volatiles at ALL COSTS! (Even the regular zombies step up their game a little)
- excellent world levels & Skyrim-like / Rockstar game-like random events
- as mentioned before: "Be The Zombie" mode (especially with the fantastic co-op) is the other reason to buy this game (the "parkour combat + loot" loop against zombies & bandits being the other)
Cons:
- Be the Zombie mode disconnects half the time on average! Actually, it doesnt even forge a connection to begin with sometimes. Do the XBO and PS4 players have this problem?
- story is run-of-the-mill (so far: but from what I hear of the endgame the whole thing is uninspired), but the game doesn't fail to hook you in from the beginning

Very very generous and fun game, i've not had this much fun on a F2P game in... well ever? usually you start to feel the f2p grind in f2p games, or the walls, but in this one its refreshing as hell.
I've noticed a lot of complaints about the higher amount of neutral cards in some recent negative reviews, which is strange as the whole theme of the current expansion is neutral synergy, just go look through all the wonderland cards and you will see what i mean, clearly they aren't using their heads otherwise they'd see this obvious theme.
Balance wise, the game is good, ccg's always suffer balance issues so what people need to watch isn't what is strong but how the developers work with that information, in this case monthly balance patches.
recent one did really good, unfortunatly it has a lot of backlash from some people, some people were very reliant on a certain card to get them wins and when it got nerfed well you see them complaining while most are happy about it.
And the beauty of it is that these cards are still usable, they are just salty from the loss of their advantage because their deck was one of the more harder ones to make vial wise (stuff you get from destroying duplicates which allows you to make other cards).
it is annoying because this is clearly a great game, i don't like the hearthstone system personally yet here i am playing it and having a blast because the balance is good, and the f2p model is more than generous to the point i can't play anything else because i've been spoilt by this and that is not a bad thing at all but...
The community while often times wonderful, sometimes is the weak point of this game, they in their salt are currently giving negative reviews in a pathetic hope to get something out of it yet that can only harm the game not help it and the balancing won't be undone because the balancing is the right thing, it is already showing improvements to the meta and is very exciting to see.
but of course no matter how good a dev does things, no matter how generous they are if you take something away that was an easy source of dopamine for them they'll react in a visceral need to latch onto it which leads to what we are seeing now.
how a game can go from very positive to below 50% just after a single expansion that has solved issues from before is literally mind boggling and it is safe to say not a very good indicator of the quality of the game, its just plain and simple salt.
is the game buggy? no
is the game fair? yes
is the game generous to free players? hell yes
is the game monetisation method fair? very much so
does the developer support their game well post release? very much so
is the community friendly and/or active? yes
is there a strong competitive scene? yes
is there a strong casual scene? yes (meme decks using ideas that aren't competitive are very popular amongst communities)
is there a strong youtube scene? yes
Con's :
Balance isn't perfect, some things are a bit too strong like eachtar, or some things aren't so much strong but rather unhealthy to the creative side of meta like bahamut (shouldn't be neutral card but dragoncraft imo).
to any new players out there, there are a ton of guides online for you guys, do elite and elite 2 ai battles, beating each for each leader is 200 each so 200 x2 = 400    400 x 7 =  2800 gold, that is 28 booster packs.  (100 each).
The game also gives from the get go 10 boosters of each expansion and i think more from the core (i can't remember), at the start of each new expansion every 3 months you get 10 more boosters from that expansion.
logging in every day gives you 20 gold (30 on 2nd week, 40 on third), exception is end of the week where you get a booster pack except third week which gives you a take two ticket (arena which even if you lose all 5 battles you get a booster).
meanwhile events like the football one on right now are throwing a card back and emblem at you as well as a booster from every set, one for each day you log in and some other stuff.
if you look up online you'll find threads for people looking for private matches, this is because of an achievement that gives 100 gold per unique person faught up to 20, match has to be finished till the end, no conceding basically, you don't need to win either. that's 2k gold aka 20 packets.
For me that took 3 hours lol
See what i mean by the game being god damn generous?
You can't earn gold in from just playing tho (for me i like it, ranked is about points not grind)
however there is a monthly score thing that is refreshed each month where the more points you get you unlock stuff like boosters, gold, vials, tickets, card backs, emblems etc     essentially every time you earn points in ranked you get progress on the achievs, you can't lose points from losing in ranked either so thats great :)
this to me makes ranked feel less of a chore and more fun but that is 100% bias from my side as i think its just psychological difference.

if anything, you've got nothing to fear from just going in and having a try, join the discord for shadowverse to join the community and last but not least just have fun and enjoy opening a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of packs at the start haha

Before the Blackwell series, before Technobabylon, before Gemini Rue, a man named Dave Gilbert got together with a few artists and voice actors and made a short little entry for an adventure game competition, about a jaded Rabbi trying to unravel the reasons behind an unexpected inheritance.  The entry was so well received that Mr. Gilbert formed a company called Wadjet Eye Games, expanded the contest entry to be longer, and released it as his new company's first game: The Shivah.  While many other games would follow it, The Shivah shows where a lot of those later titles get their style and many of their mechanics, the ever-popular "notes and clues" system in particular.
Separate of all that though, The Shivah is a fine title in its own right.  It's a bit short to be fair, with a first-time playthrough likely clocking in at around an hour or two, but it's a solidly constructed few hours, with great voicework and a decently compelling plot.  There's also plenty of detail to the relatively small slice of virtual New York that the game inhabits.  If you're the kind of adventure game player who wants to see all the descriptions and interact with all the things you can, there's a good amount to keep you occupied.  If you're more interested in a short-but-well-done "whodunit" with a few branching paths and a fair bit of dialog to listen to, then you also will be happy.
About the only bad thing I can say about the game is that the price might seem a bit steep for something that is so relatively short, at least to people who aren't already fans of Wadjet Eye.  If you are though, then this is a fantastic version of their very first title, and well worth a play.

The game itself eventually becomes nothing more than a glorified board game.  The sheer amount of time it takes to even acheive victory in one of these games can be awful. That said, it is playable and the review that criticizes the controls must have been written before many tips were added in the starting area. The only thing I would change would be the overuse of the portrait art in the title and preview screens which, when smoothed over and increased in size ends up looking a bit ugly.
Overall It's a different approach than, say, a true remake like "Back to the Dungeon" of Dungeon Master, and a unique way to enjoy a re-imagining of the original content. And it's free! Worth checking out even if you don't know the original.

In the beginning, I thought it was very frustrating and went through some unreasonable insta-kills and some unfair level design. The game is rather hard.
But as I progressed, I got more involved with the abilities I found and the exploration of the map, a good throwback to the Metroidvania style of game
There are many referecentes to old and classic games. Initially I was too frustrated about deaths to care. Especially when the game insists on showing me how many times I've died until then.  And ESPECIALLY when I unlocked "Easy Mode" when I reached 50 deaths. Seemed like the game was taunting me. This game is harder than it looks and this may work against it. In some games like the classic Megaman, Volgarr the Viking and Dark Souls, you expect the difficulty and the deaths, so you prepare yourself. Especially when you can notice that the following moments will be hard. But when you just run into the next screen and is surprised but insta-death spikes, it's simply frustrating. Although most of it must be on purpose, since it makes so many references to classics, many of which are known to be tough.
Still, the game is enjoyable and fun once you stop caring about the deaths and accept the challenge and begin the exploration. There are many secrets and I think it's worth checking out, unless you dislike the classic style.
I Just think the developers could have put a little more time into either:
1) preparing the player psychologically for the hardships and deaths yet to come
or
2) spend more time testing and analysing player behavior for the level design and enemy placement. In one of the rooms I arrived, I instantly saw an enemy coming towards me from the left. So, I went to the right. And what I find to the right are insta-death spikes. Back to the last checkpoint, it is.
Overall, good job!

First things first, i'm not good with writing reviews, so i'll make this brief. One of my few serious reviews.
Super Dungeon Master is a FREE game that (extremely obviously) is based off Dungeon Master. With new characters and levels, and made in RPG Maker (the good part is it's not just "another rpg maker game")
Pros:
- An action-rpg despite being made on RPG Maker, which makes it way closer to the original Dungeon Master than what it would be if it were turn-based
- A wide range of characters to select from
- A nice amount of levels for a free game
- Puzzles with just the right amount of difficulty (my opinion)
- Despite having a total of 31 characters, each character has their own skills and items to use, and you can specify which the AI should favor
- Has a nice soundtrack
Neutral:
- A lot of puzzles (if you like them like i do, then you'll enjoy this game)
Cons:
- The combat part of the game is VERY EASY. I cannot explain how easy this game has been so far for me. I literally have 30 mini-altar potions which revive and fully heal every party member.
- As can been seen by the above, the regular potions are too rare while the OP potions are extremely common
- The AI is still in need of refining, my companions
- Some characters are way too overpowered, which helps making the game even easier
Overall, i recommend this game. Most of the cons are difficulty related, and if the dev fixes that, this game has a lot of potential.

I'm going to preface this review by stating that it has spoilers for some intricate game mechanics as well as light "plot" spoilers. If you're against spoiling at all, you'll more likely not want to read this, otherwise read-on. There's plenty to talk about.
I think the best way to describe my dissappointment with this game is to talk about all of my gripes with it, starting with grinding. First of all, I'm the type of person who doesn't mind grinding in games, heck I might even say I enjoy it and don't find any trouble in throwing countless hours doing the same repetitive actions when I want to. My troubles are with how the game handles it - poorly.
For starters, it makes no sense to invest anything in magic. The game has this system named "Shaping Effect", which allows you to change how the dungeon is going to be played. They have lots of effects, and some are really beneficial, like raising EXP gotten, or WP (points gained in battle to upgrade characters' skills and spells), but they all come with negative effects (unless you have an S rank Shaping Effect). These EXP and WP modifiers come with negative effects like raising SP consumption to twice as much, making you take twice as much damage or just straight up Silencing and Sealing you so you cannot make use of spells or skills - since you're going to be grinding a good deal, it makes such Shaping Effects relatively useful. Couple that with how slow it is to select spells in the menus and how many commands you'd have to input, grinding becomes considerably more efficient with just regular attacks. You can literally set up the game to "autobattle" and just pressing X to end encounters within seconds if you're building your characters with Silence and Seal in mind, which trivializes pretty much everything. If you plan on grinding for the DLC areas, you're going to be spending a lot of time battling the same monsters just to get to the DLC and then battle the same monsters reskinned in the DLC area, just considerably more difficult, which feels very lazy and isn't really worth your time or money (wasn't worth mine at the least).
And even then, this game is pretty easy even without exploiting any clearly unbalanced mechanics, and it's not really a problem in itself, especially if you're not a very big fan of grinding, Fang (the main character) is just straight up broken, all other character are exchangeable among themselves. That is... until the game 'forces' you to grind ~10+ levels to get to Lv. 40 at a specific point in the story just to get a missable party member - which doesn't even make any sense - as the game does not explain why you have to be Lv. 40 to even get him (mind you, they didn't even reference it in the game, you'd have to look this up online), which is just very frustrating. What's the point of making a game easy if you're just going to force players to grind to attain their coveted 100% completion? Sure thing, you can just wait and unlock him on New Game Plus, but hey, that's a party member, why would I have to wait him to join me if I can just make him join me now?
Speaking of skills being useless, the game gives you access to a whole load of buffs / debuffs early on for fairly cheap WP and that made me think the game would be pretty awesome, with lots of choices in playstyle and whatnot. Sure, buffs are useful if you want to make use of them, but they're completely unnecessary - now debuffs are pretty much worthless. They'll work on regular mobs, which could be pretty good since they last for quite long, but more often than not do not work on bosses - the kind of encounters you'd actually want to debuff and buff yourself for - which is a major flaw. I mean, what'd be the point of using them in random battles if they're just going to end very quickly and waste your SP that could potentially be used for healing?
The game also has a wide varity of items in it, and they're mostly pretty nice but since you can just ignore all the SP restoring ones and you'll likely be overlevelled for most of it (enemies will barely be able to touch you) you'll likely not have any use for them (Aside from: Return Wings, the 'escape dungeon' item; Dimensional Clocks, the 'respawn all enemies item'). And when it comes to collectible items, quests can be really annoying. Some of them require you to steal from countless, specific monsters to get an arbritary number of non-droppable (or low rate drop) items, whose only way to acquire otherwise is to hope for them in RNG chests (which you really should not, as stealing is a lot quicker). Not to mention the highest-chance Steal skill has been bugged since the game first released on consoles and was never fixed, which just adds to frustration. Keep in mind the rewards for these quests are often not worth it.
The story is fairly cliché, although I don't mind it much. I just feel they could have invested and fleshed out more the secondary characters, especially Ethel and Pippin. There just isn't much to connect to, so you end up not caring much about most of them. The story also feels a bit lazy, and will often make you revisit areas due to it. You'll go 'back in time' and they'll be slightly different, having some new monsters and reskins here and there, but it's pretty much the same. It also adds insult to injury that a lot of dungeon layouts might as well be the exact same. I don't mind if you're trying to save costs and reuse some of the graphics, but you know something's wrong when your Final Dungeon is a carbon-copy of another place you've already been to.
As a conclusion, this isn't the worst JRPG I've played but it's sure as hell dissappointing - I really wanted to like it.
It has a lot of things going on for it, like pretty anime graphics and a great soundtrack (which by itself was amazing, but along the game gets oversaturated by repetition), but that alone isn't enough to offset the numerous poor game design choices they've made all throughout it. The game developers really dropped the ball on this. At the end I wasn't enjoying myself and just had to rush it to put the game to a close. I'll also likely not be touching New Game Plus, as I see no point in skimming through the game to see the missable content I've already screwed myself from getting my hands on. This game does not compel you to replay it through.
Such disappointing game. I wish I could refund it.

Enjoyed the game for a good playthrough at a good price even when the game is not discounted. This review is partially written as if one plays RPGs, but may not necessarily have played comparable games such as Hyper Dimension Neptunia Re;birth. Noting some points, whether they are pluses for some, minuses for others or neutral.
* Anime-styled 3D world with mid-to-low polygon count for adventuring characters
* Detailed animating dialogue portraits and occasional cut scene art
* Mostly smooth frame rate on a moderately powered computer up to 60 FPS
* Max resolution of 1920x1080
* Can be controlled with built-in game pad support or keyboard + mouse
* Can skip dialogue, events and fast forward combat to shorten repetitious or familiar content
* Multiple ways to alter a character's performance (expounded later)
* Multiple endings and some missable content, but an option for New Game Plus to carry over much
* Optional side quest system that involves either killing X monsters, collecting Y number of materials or both for monetary rewards and frequently an item
* Optional crafting system that can provide more equipment options and recovery items when invested
* Some limited appearance customization options in-game with accessories and some costumes
* New Game Plus option if you want to try it all again
* Optional Tower and free Tower DLC to test your devotion to battle
* Up to 99 save slots in-game
Aspects I enjoyed and/or are more opinionated:
* Great English voice acting if you have an ear for it and if you don't, then there's Japanese voice with English subs
* Overall good soundtrack with some orchestrated tracks
* Great English localization
* Overall good character development of the main cast
* Game story and optional dialogue leans toward light-hearted comedy with several serious situations and dark themes
Combat:
* Takes place with up to three party members with the ability to swap inactive characters
* When your ally takes a turn, they can move around on the field, aim their attack(s) and spell(s) to hit one or more enemies
* Different enemies are vulnerable to different weapons and elements, with customizable combos allowing you to exploit these weaknesses (e.g. using a bow against flying enemies, having a sword handy for enemies vulnerable to slashing)
* The possibilities of combat were enjoyable before finding a combination of options that would clear most encounters before the enemy could act
Expounding on Character Advancement:
* Characters can improve stats through mini-achievements such as taking X amount of damage increasing max HP (health), running Y distance increases max AGI (turn order) or defeating Z amount of enemies increases STR (physical damage)
* Characters can discover and equip fairies with different foci and level them up, where one fairy may enhance your physical damage and sword skills, another fairy may improve your fire resistance and fire spells in exchange of making you vulnerable to another element
* Fairies can receive additional customization by adding traits to enhance their strengths, make up for their shortcomings or vary their play style such as improved weapon proficiency, reduced SP costs or increased elemental resistance
* Characters earn points after battle that can be used to improve stats such as strength, magic, attack range, etc. as well as be used to unlock new abilities, spells or combo attacks with different weapon styles
* Fairies can be deployed to change adventuring conditions such as increased money, but reduced defenses or increased experience, but inability to recover HP - these can be compiled for increased rewards and risk
* Gear is a mix of horizontal and vertical growth, allowing for specialized defenses, balanced defense or enhanced offensive capabilities
ESRB/Content Advisory:
* Frequent animations that bounce breasts both in low polygon combat and in high-detailed portrait dialogue
* Few instances of near nude anime women with no nipples - e.g. strategically covered by hair, shirt being removed or holy armor)
* Camera angle easily adjusted for pantie access and doesn't need to be adjusted once optional swimsuits are purchased
* Some bare chested anime men taking baths and one mostly bare-chested man fairy
* One odd elderly man warrior who joins the party while being fully nude, but has no genitalia or butt defined
* Some violence-based blood depicted on portraits and cut scene(s), as opposed to sexy nosebleeds
* Some violent NPCs who harm elderly, women, children and innocents in text depictions
* Some text depicted gore of an NPC
* Occasional language such as b*tch and sh*t

I wasn't too impressed with Dead Island; I found it quite tedious and repetitive, so even I'm suprised that I picked up Dying Light at full price. Why? No idea actually...think I was just bored.
Dying Light, however, is really, REALLY good. I am legitmately suprised. It is of similar vein to Dead Island, but they've improved upon it in almost every aspect; level design, gameplay mechanics, story, characters, missions, sound, graphics etc.
Essentially, if you liked the *idea* of Dead Island but felt it was poorly executed, you'll probably find a lot of entertainment in this. I certainly have. Of particular interest to me is the following;
- Despite a fairly simple story, most of the people in this game are characterized well...even those you meet for just a minute. Yeah, I know, it's a zombie game, but it makes a change to see a protagonist with a developing personality and moral compass.
- Some of the missions, although small in nature and few-and-far between, are really quite good. Creepy, but good. The game occasionally takes a stab at the dark in being "true horror" and I think they nail it.
- Developers have released a few decent patches already to fix flaws. One time I noticed I was using 8GB of RAM whilst playing (IE. all of the RAM I have); then a week later I noticed it was cut in half. I concluded it was an issue with my system at the time, but turns out it was a bug. Nice to see a dev fix something like this instead of saying "Actually, our game is just top of the line. You need more RAM!".
The game isn't without it's flaws. Although performance on my system is fantastic, I do notice the occasional drop in FPS (especially during heavy scenes); somewhat expected given the situation, but since it's a console part and since this is a beefy system, it would be nice to do without that. Also, the screenshots are a little misleading; I play on the highest settings and although similar, it does appear as if the screenshots are edited a bit. Not too much of an issue, but I don't really think they need to beautify their screens...the game looks gorgeous already.
TLDR; Dead Island, but significantly better.

FTL: Faster Than Light is the charming indie game you’ve never heard about. Or if you have heard about it, count your lucky stars. FTL has the feel of an instant classic and brings back everything you love about old games: humble yet lovely graphics, whimsical music, satisfying gameplay, and a dash of storytelling.
In FTL, you play a sole ship escaping to the safety of the Federation. Since the game is a space strategy game (see roguelike), you will be using your wits to survive lest you be blasted into animated space debris. If you like strategy games, or even open-ended RPGs, you cannot go wrong with FTL. As long as you can appreciate the retro graphics, the game will reward you with surprising depth and atmosphere. Space. It’s awesome.
Gameplay is where FTL delivers and micromanaging your ship is just as fluid as piloting a Nesasio Stealth Cruiser. You can open and close doors to prevent intruders or fire, send your crew to repair vital systems (or face certain death), toggle the power to your shields, and so on. A variety of ship upgrades and crew selection create choices that actually matter to the player. Outfitting your ship is complex and can be the difference between making it to the next solar system or not. Ship battles are extremely satisfying. At first, I would fire my weapons as soon as they became available. It wasn’t until my fourth run that I learned to time my lasers to break through defenses. That’s how FTL is — learning the layers of gameplay. It might seem a bit daunting at first, but the charming atmosphere will lure you in and you will be pleasantly surprised as you learn more and more.
I doubt I’m the only one to have Malcolm Reynolds pilot my ship and Tali’Zorah as my trusty engineer. It’s easy to become attached to your crew, made up of certain species with their own advantages and disadvantages. Which makes it that much harder when you accidentally send them into room with the airlock open (sorry!). The playable races range from quick-repairing Engi, vicious Mantis, to well-rounded, of course, Humans. While the actual story of the game is light, the lack never detracts from the feel of the adventure. Since the solar map is randomly generated, your crew will face different dangers each play through. Still, the scenarios will eventually be familiar and may even become monotonous. But by then, you’ve already had too much fun to care.
As for the music, it is nothing short of a retro masterpiece. The soundtrack is even sold on Steam. Bleeps and bloops bring out the charming space atmosphere and will play in your head even when you’re not playing the game. Rarely has a soundtrack fitted a game as perfectly as in FTL.
Unlockables provide substantial replay value. New ships are the main rewards and each ship has a different playstyle. The Slug Cruiser relies on taking out the enemy crew and the Zoltan Cruiser has the protection of a unique shield. A slight drawback to the game is a lack of DLC, which is weird to say since many games suffer from too much DLC.
You will die. You will die a lot. The “Normal” mode should really be called Death. Yet even when losing FTL is satisfying and not many games can pull that off. You have a sense of “maybe if I did this next time, things will go smoother” and space runs are quick enough that you won’t regret starting over. Do you have a hipster friend who tells you games are too easy these days? Yeah, right. FTL, enough said.
So like most strategy games, the most satisfying part is using a mix of brains and luck to overcome a particularly difficult situation. FTL is a master of creating those scenarios. Your ship will be on its last leg, limping just ahead of the Rebels with your crew fighting Rockmen while slowly suffocating from lack of oxygen. Oh, and your ship is on fire. What will you do? Whatever you have to do to survive.
Tip: Never fight alien spiders. Never!

To be honest, the trailer for Saints Row IV didn't do much justice to the game for me and it took a lot of thinking on my part before heading out to a local gameshop to snag it.
Obviously it was a a SR3 with a few graphical upgrades and game fixes that people wanted.
Saints Row IV puts you in the shoes of the American president. This opportunity to make change is rather short lived as an alien race pops in and kidnaps you, does some weird alien stuff to you and sends you into a virtual reality version of Steelport (the main city in Saints Row the Third). Of course this pisses you off and sets you on a quest to kill that rotten dude, much like a typical saint.
Gameplay wise, its pretty much Saints Row the Third on steroids. And that I mean you're granted superpowers to fly, jump and basically go from one end of the city to the other in less than a minutes--making cars / vehicles redundent.
Weapons feel weaker in this game as well and I found myself insta-killing my enemies with melee attacks all the time.
Old characters (and gangs) are back from previous games are back as well. So if you want some nostaligia this is probably your best bet for it. As for humour in the game, it's pretty much the same funny dialogue that one would be used to having in Saints Row the Third.
In addition, the game likes to poke fun at other games / and movies, be it from unlockable costumes (Pierce should go about shouting "Mortal Kombatttttttt!" once you've unlocked his alternate costume), quotes (and scenes) from various movies to parody missions altogether.
However, I am disappointed at the introduction of day 1 DLC. And even as I type this, there's already a few alternate costumes for $2.99 (can you believe it!) for model jobs that probably took less than a minute to make.
WHAT.
For fans of Saints Row the Third, Saints Row IV would be a decent game to grab. For anyone else that wants a story like in Saints Row 2, wait for a sale--there's none.

Half-Life 2 had all I really needed to continue on after the highly-acclaimed 1998 First-Person Shooter.
It featured a form of storytelling that was far more in your face than the original but not too in your face to drive away any fanbase.

Half-Life 2's gameplay is quite like the original in a way that includes the same puzzle-inspirations and various other things including a more intense combat experience with a few more guns.
The thing that made HL2 stand out at the time was the physics engine which for its time was revolutionary but the physics engine included in this installment is (in my opinion) better than any other physics engine to date (Portal and Garry's Mod include the same physics engine). For example if i take a look at Fallout 4, a game released this year its got nothing on HL2's physics (Gordon Freeman is a theoretical physicist so that is why they added a physics engine (totally not to make money)).
All around it was revolutionary in its day and nothing less than enjoyable today.

The art style of Mirror's Edge is minimalistic, but also appropiate and aesthetic. The supporting character of ME (no, not Mass Effect. Hey, wait a second...) is the city. Take a look at those vistas. It is amazing. However, you won't be able to enjoy those vistas peacefully, the game is so fast-paced and most of the time I was chased around from one building to the other, doding bullets, disarming guards, or simply using my momentum to parkour through the level. Some may say the city is too colourful, it doesn't look realistic, that is, dull and grey. But this is not a realistic city after all. It is a piece of art, each level and each section with its own unique hue, its own ambient sound and music. The soundtrack is awesome. Well done, Solar Fields. I think I'm going to get it for my phone right after I finish this review.
The first-person-view does its best to make me think that I am not a dot from whence a gun protrudes, but a real person with arms and legs and red shoes. There are however limits to the degree of immersion I can get from ME. It is not the game's fault that it was released many years before Occulus Rift. It would have been the perfect Occulus game. Imagine looking into the abyss, and the abyss looks back into you. And then you fall prone in your living room. The story is narrated in a very satisfactory way, but it is nothing special. The thing that makes you cling to the edge of your seat is not the story, it is the parkour. As such, I think ME is more like a proof of concept. It proves that a game about running is feasible and can also be highly entertaining at the same time.
I am definitely looking forward to Mirror's Edge 2.

- Gandhi

Okay, but seriously:

Teleglitch is a retro themed rougelike, both in visual aesthetics and gameplay. It accompanies the expected top-down perspective with the well recognizable pixel art style common for indie games in a dark atmosphere of industrial machinery and desolation. Same applies for the audio design - in-game music only consists of ambient noises found around the randomly generated levels.
The gameplay is rock solid and similar to first person DoS games where the arsenals and ammunition carried by the player defy physics, not to mention the achievable running speeds. The controls are somewhat specific, but can be learned rather quickly.
The difficulty and the challenge can be described as "tough, but fair" - risk of dying is surreal (as suggested by the name of the expansion), as enemies can drain your health in less than a second, and carelessly running into teleglitches will result in an instant death. On the flipside, starting from later levels and crafting second chance items can ease the blow of permadeath. The enemies are well balanced and are found in reasonable numbers, at which point it all boils down to the skill of making every single shot count and avoiding getting cornered.
Levels and bosses are memorable enough, however the procedural generation seems lacking and at best, as the layouts and secret placements get predictable with lots of replays. Despite it being a shooter, ammo conservation, weapon strategization on the fly, planned resource crafting and an eye for secret areas are a must if one actually expects to beat this. Additionally, the story is pretty good and doesn't get in the way of the game.
In a nutshell, it's a hard, but rewarding kind of a game.

Well it seems I have found a rather hidden gem in my expansive library of steam games (145 of em). Teleglitch: Die More Edition is a very enjoyable (albeit hard, hence the "DIE MORE") game that I got for next to nothing in a Humble Bundle, and well, I can say it was very little money very well spent, but I'd still pay full-price for this. Teleglitch is fun, and hard, and kinda scary, and potentially frustrating, but it's a roguelike so dying just means you get a new adventure every time, and I like that.
The main game is incredibly atmospheric. The story is told through abandoned computer terminals and the main character's inner soliloquies, and it's pretty messed up. Lots of illegal experimentation and mad scientists playing god with some kinda weird zombie plague they thought would save everyone, the usual stuff.
This game feels rather Resident-Evil-4-ey and Dead-Space-ey in terms of its inventory system and the gameplay elements:
-You have guns that are all very effective at killing things, but ammo is precious and can be wasted easily with a jumpy trigger finger.
-On the other hand, melee attacking never runs out, but requires enemies to be incredibly close to you and slightly to your right to successfully kill them with, therefore increasing the risk
-You also have a multitude of explosives to be found, the most common being RDX-250, a small placeable or tossable explosive that blows up a second or two after thrown/dropped, but can be dangerous to the user, so it's risky yet effective when out of ammo or when facing a crowd
-there's also a crafting system, where you can combine various objects to get better objects, such as combining healing items to get more potent ones, or combining weapon parts together to make some kind of mutant triple-barreled automatic grenade-launcher thing (it's kinda nuts) or some other crazy weapon
See? It's like top-down Resident Evil 4 or Dead Space with a little less linear-ness, roguelike elements, and a slightly more in-depth crafting system. I guess you could call it survival horror, because it's a very panicky game where you'll be fighting for your life in an abandoned space station trying to conserve ammo while also trying to kill things that are charging you.
Overall, I give this game a definite 9/10, and I'd reccommend it to anyone who likes RE4, Dead Space, or any other combat-oriented survival horrors.
TL:DR Must-have survival horror game for anyone with $15 in their steam account.

TL;DR ver: Do you like a challenge? Well then, this roguelike topdown shooter will chew you up and spit you out, Private!
Teleglitch has a very simple visual layout, akin to 8-bit gaming. However, do not be fooled by the simple appearance.
As you delve further into this sci-fi disaster, a clever crafting system, no brakes on the mutant train and a pellmell of noises that will make you jump out of your skin if you're in the right mood are there to greet you - like a hungry bear.
The learning curve is sharp, and you will die many times. Be consoled by the fact that levels are randomly generated - who needs to learn level routines anyway?
If you get too humiliated by the storyline, fear not, for there is an arcade mode where you can sharpen your skills in challenge-based arenas with a wide variety of loadouts to choose from.
Teleglitch is everything that makes roguelikes great: hard to master gameplay and brutally punishing deaths. It isn't everyone's cup of tea, for sure, but if you love roguelikes that taunt you on death then this game is a must.

This game doesn't kid around. It throws you into a dark, mysterious place full of humanoid creatures trying to annihilate you, with only a few necessary things so you're able to survive at first, with many other items scattered around the facilities and hidden rooms. Teleglitch is a real hard game, and you should experience it yourself.
There's always the same way you start, but the way you progress differs with what you find and what you craft with it. You can craft almost everything you need to stay alive, from meds, through armors to deadly weapons and bombs. The game makes you reconsider your decisions often and economical with what you own, as it tends to be scarce with ammo and other items, so you pretty much need to examine every nook and cranny and decide whether to finish off a group of zombies with a bomb or a few shotgun slugs.
The atmosphere of the game is enigmatic, and you'll often find yourself discovering data logs which uncover more and more about the game's lore. There is no music, but for me, it only makes the game darker. The graphical style is rather simple, but neat, and the glitchy effects look really good. The informations about health, ammo or items you own are short and simple, as well as the interface.
Arm yourself with a lot of patience and time, because you're going to find yourself dying over and over. This isn't the sort of game for the weak, but as earlier mentioned, you should give it a try anyways. There's even a demo so you can easily see if you're prepared for the hordes.

Fairy Fencer F is a lazy game, with a weak plot, that can be pretty fun if you catch it on sale.  I'm a little caught on whether to upvote or downvote, the flaws are SO numerous with this game, but it is still pretty enjoyable.  I'll tell you now, the game is very much average in my book (50-55% or 70-75% depending on what you consider "average").
First I'll address my "lazy" comment: why is the game lazy?  First, the battle system is just a tweaked version of what you may very well have seen five or six times before in the company's "Neptunia" series.  If it ain't broke, I'm certainly not going to tell them to fix it, though, because they might make something decidedly less inobtrusive.  As it stands, the battle system is fairly enjoyable, you're given some freedom in picking which Persona *cough* I mean, Fairy to use, which augments your stats and grants you certain bonuses and debuffs that might effect your adventure through a dungeon, like an exp bonus at the expense of having lower defense, more money but harder enemies spawn, etc.  As you earn experience, you also earn secondary exp referred to as "WP," which you can apply to the stats of your choice (if by choice, you mean adding extra attacks in battle through leveling Combo!).  Battle play out very....slowly...as characters have played out attack animations and the game requires a lot of loot farming to finish missions, luckily, this is rendered much less annoying by the fast forward button they let you use to skip animations.  Of course, a fast forward button is a bandaid solution to the greater problem that battles take very little strategy and the whole gameplay rythm relies on a lot of menial drudgery.
Side quests are lazy too.  Most of the missions in the game are shoved into a quest board with scant flavor text that is only really worth reading for the location and enemy information that it might (emphasis *might*, the times when it doesn't give you useful information are always on the rarest, most difficult-to-find items) provide.
Dungeon design is also...you get it by now.  Mostly corridors, with minimal interactibles except for the odd enemy or treasure...floating cube thing that very thoroughly fails to blend in with ANY scenery you happen to find it in.  Locales you visit have no real significance.  Go here for that MacGuffin, then go here for the next one, etc etc.  You could have flipped the order of most of the dungeons in the game and it wouldn't have really changed anything.
The plot is weak for a few reasons: the world, the characters, and the pacing.  First, the world is very shallow.  You have one hub town, and it's just a bunch of menus (Neptunia players will not be surprised by this).  There are NPC talk events that come up regularly, but most of them are either useless random comments about really nothing, like a drunk passing by or something, or vaguely silly scenes where an NPC does something weird and your character reacts to it.  World building is pretty much non-existant, except to further drive home the heavy-handed and simplistic world the main plot already sets up.  Main plot establishes really quickly: evil corporation appears good, but is really doing bad stuff!  Side NPCs occasionally: we love the evil corporation so much because they throw money at us, etc.
Second, the characters.  The characters for the most part sit very comfortably in shallow archetypes that they don't venture out of very often.  Even with fairly frequent talk topics after major plot developments, you never really see how the group becomes the True Companions that are willing to die for the main character despite his less than stellar charisma and lazy attitude for most of the game.  It doesn't help that the game resets about half way through, resetting character development for everyone except the main character in the process, and further shortening the character arcs (if you can even call them that) of the party members.
Third is the game's issue with pacing.  The fact that the timeline resets mid-game reeks as an excuse to reuse the already minimal-effort dungeons.  Indeed, after that mid-game reset, the game introduces about a handful of new dungeons, that might as well be reskins of the existing ones anyway.  This move also resets character development for most of the cast, turning the focus on the main character as he tries to convince them he isn't crazy and really IS from an alternate timeline.  If their motivations for joining the party weren't ALREADY flimsy (pervy researcher girl wants to come along so she can perv on your party's female fairies), they become seriously flimsy after the reset (hey, this crazy guy claims he's from the future, might as well tag along and perv on his fairies while I watch this play out).
Positives and Negatives Breakdown:
+Great port: Borderless windowed option, runs smooth even at high resolutions and at max detail.  No crashes, no save issues, works competently on keyboard+mouse, but best on a controller.
+Fun, if mindless dungeon crawling: the gameplay is fine.  The story can't really stand on its own, and there's little narrative or lore motivation to doing sidequests, but if you enjoy the gameplay, it's an alright treadmill to get on for a few hours.
+Good art--CGs in story events and character side-events are well done, frequently putting characters in pervy situations if that's your thing.
+/- Music--there are a few standout tracks, but it's mostly very bland and forgettable.
-Weak story
--Weak pacing
-Weak Characters
-Weak world-building
-Recycled dungeons out the wazoo

FTL is a game about managing the crew of your spaceship as you explore and fight your way through to the rebel flagship. Managing your available crew and resources such as fuel and scrap is an important gameplay element. Plan ahead so that you can make it to the next repair-station and re-stock on fuel, but at the same time taking the gamble to buy a powerful weapon or upgrading your ship might be more beneficial in the end, if you get that far that is.
The game is very difficult, and at first it will feel as if the games randomness screws you over repeatedly, but learn from your mistakes, and defating the final boss is a very rewarding experience.
There are multiple ways to bypass your enemies, some are strictly combat oriented while others are event based and you get a choice whether to attack or not. Combat is also fairly diverse with many different types of weapons systems such as lasers, drones or why not just straight up board the enemy ship, which earns you more resources and possibly crewmembers as well.
Multiple ships and crewmembers that all come with special abilities gives this game alot of replayability, though most of the ships have to be earned by finishing certain encounters that rely on alot of things happening in a certain order.
The soundtrack is diverse and it is nice how the music seamlessly switches from a calmer exploration to the more agressive combat music as you engage enemy ships.
The graphics style is also really nice, with a spirite based style of graphics that is very pleasing to look at.
All in all FTL is a nice experience, though you will probably be frustrated with it a few times as you get no repair stations and slowly die with that awesome weapon you found early.

For a Free To Play Game it is worth checking out, but the game has some crippling flaws that prevent the game from replacing whatever you go-to card game is currently.  Luckily, the devs provide a lot of free packs and easy to understand tutorials to allow you to create a competent decks without sinking hundreds of hours or real world cash.
That being said, one of the biggest flaws with the game is the excessively overpowered cards that consistently turn an otherwise unwinnable scenario into a win. There are simply far too many cards that will singlehandedly allow players to win with no way to counter. It is powercreep at its finest, but I still recommend playing Shadowverse due to the free incentives, great artwork (does suffer from accentuated anime cliches though), enjoyable solo campaign/deck building, and a slight change of pace from other CCGs.

Half-Life 2 had all I really needed to continue on after the highly-acclaimed 1998 First-Person Shooter.
It featured a form of storytelling that was far more in your face than the original but not too in your face to drive away any fanbase.
The music is centered onto events which i though were appropriate for an audial playback however I did have one point in which I felt the music wasn't right, it was close to the start when you re-acquire your suit I had the same problem with Half-Life 1 though, but 1 meh didn't deter me from the game.
Half-Life 2's gameplay is quite like the original in a way that includes the same puzzle-inspirations and various other things including a more intense combat experience with a few more guns.
The thing that made HL2 stand out at the time was the physics engine which for its time was revolutionary but the physics engine included in this installment is (in my opinion) better than any other physics engine to date (Portal and Garry's Mod include the same physics engine). For example if i take a look at Fallout 4, a game released this year its got nothing on HL2's physics (Gordon Freeman is a theoretical physicist so that is why they added a physics engine (totally not to make money)).
All around it was revolutionary in its day and nothing less than enjoyable today.

*Slight Spoilers*
The Shivah starts out very promising. Atmospherically, it perfectly captures the mundane life of the city, but mixes in heady philosophical questions and a dash of murder. Throughout the story, Rabbi Stone wrestles with what it means to be a "true Jew" while figuring out why a recently murdered acquaintaince left his failing temple a large portion of inheritance money. The game takes you to a few locations in NYC, set to slow croning music that perfectly captures the noir theme. The characters are colorful, if not just a teeny bit stereotypical.
The game is your average point and click, but the game is based less on exploration and more on discovering clues through dialogue trees. It requires a heavy amount of critical thought otherwise you will definitely reach a point where you hit a wall and cannot advance without a walkthrough or something. The difficulty is refreshing, but certain solutions to the puzzles are extremely obscured and will frustrate you. However, if not for these, the game could probably be completed in 10-30 minutes on a blind run.
However, a critical junction of the game wherein it turns into a sort of action drama is where the game falls apart. Fighting is done through a series of dialogue trees, with your choices having minimal effect outside of lose conditions and achievements. It is at this point where the game tonally shifts completely and becomes almost a self-parody. The two fights in the game center upon a sort of tongue-in-cheek reference to rabbinical procedure (answering questions with questions) and characters are punished for not adhering to this. The motivations of the characters quickly unravel as the game becomes increasingly more ridiculous.
The games abrupt ending leaves you wondering if Rabbi Stone really learned anything; and I can't help but think if this game was expanded an hour more, chose to handle the action sequences more tactfully, and actually dwelled more on the rift between Stone and the changing realities of Jewish culture it would be an effective vehicle for a compelling story. But maybe its for the better that they did not dwell too much on the religious undertones. Stone is a good example of a flawed character and one of the best aspects of the game.

- Those who are fans of Wadjet Eye, have played their newer offerings and are interested in seeing the progression in quality
- Those who are fans of Wadjet Eye and want to support them by purchasing an additional game
- Those who are interested in experiencing a very short story which captures a bit of Jewish NYC culture
It is very difficult to rate the Shivah because it hasn't aged very well in terms of game design and overall plot quality. The individual character interactions though are a delight. You can definitely see the roots of talent which the lead designer has refined over time. However, if you're new to adventure games or to Wadjet, I'd recommend one of their newer games. Antichamber is a fantastic example of what makes a puzzle game, but also a fantastic deconstruction of what makes a video game. We've become so used to certain things in modern games like dying, losing a level, how to navigate, and so on -- Antichamber takes all those expectations and turns them on their head. But it doesn't do so in a gimmicky way that makes the player feel cheated. Instead, there's a different set of physical rules that the game plays by, and the progression teaches you all of these things. Sometimes you might brute force your way through a puzzle without understanding it, but the comprehensive nature of the game means you'll probably encounter the puzzle again in a way that can't be brute forced.
The very first thing you learn in Antichamber is that there's no losing state. The game is more or less a maze that can always be escaped with the press of a button. Usually you'll find yourself doing this when you're confused about a puzzle. The non-linear nature of the game allows you to reach a dead-end in terms of what you know how to do, but continue playing elsewhere, perhaps to discover what you didn't know, or find what you needed to progress. The most famous aspect of this game is the non-Euclidian space, where returning to a previous area might not bring you to where you were before. The game also gently introduces you to these concepts, and you'll surprise yourself with how second-nature they become by the end of the game.
The art style and presentation of this game is intentionally extremely simple. You can feel it in the sound design, in the visuals, in the movement, and in pretty much every other aspect of the game. It's for that reason that I'm not at all upset about the lack of story; having an actual character would break the flow of the game. There's no explanation for who or what or where you are, and I'm fine with that because this is a game for the sole sake of it being a game.

This game doesn't kid around. It throws you into a dark, mysterious place full of humanoid creatures trying to annihilate you, with only a few necessary things so you're able to survive at first, with many other items scattered around the facilities and hidden rooms. Teleglitch is a real hard game, and you should experience it yourself.
There's always the same way you start, but the way you progress differs with what you find and what you craft with it. You can craft almost everything you need to stay alive, from meds, through armors to deadly weapons and bombs. The game makes you reconsider your decisions often and economical with what you own, as it tends to be scarce with ammo and other items, so you pretty much need to examine every nook and cranny and decide whether to finish off a group of zombies with a bomb or a few shotgun slugs.
The atmosphere of the game is enigmatic, and you'll often find yourself discovering data logs which uncover more and more about the game's lore. There is no music, but for me, it only makes the game darker. The graphical style is rather simple, but neat, and the glitchy effects look really good. The informations about health, ammo or items you own are short and simple, as well as the interface.
Arm yourself with a lot of patience and time, because you're going to find yourself dying over and over. This isn't the sort of game for the weak, but as earlier mentioned, you should give it a try anyways. There's even a demo so you can easily see if you're prepared for the hordes.

Set on a quarantined planet, Teleglitch takes you through as a lone man holed up in a facility overun by zombies, mutants and robotic combatants. Though the motif is familiar, this top-down shooter has a refreshing appeal with oldschool gameplay and modern techniques. While the game isn't really scary, the pixelated graphics and rustic noises give it serious atmosphere. Corridors that are eerily quiet can open into rooms with loud rythmic clanging and flickering lights. An enemy encounter here can seem even more intense.
The playing mechanics are simple and progressing is straightforward - BUT - the game itself is quite challenging to get through. Enemies are abundant and focused on ending your conciousness. Ammo conservation and keeping your health up are huge requirements for making it to the end, making this game a wrong choice for casual play. Dedication will be required to finish this game and until your combat skills are properly honed you can count on not making it very far. Things can go awry quickly if you aren't careful.
Scattered throughout the levels are computer terminals that give useful hints or contibute to the interesting and well-thought story that Teleglitch has. Items are also frequently found laying around and your limited inventory can fill quickly. Most Items can be combined to make new or upgraded weapons and equipment. The process is very simple and doesn't require a lot of planning like in some games.
Teleglitch isn't so much fun as it is alluring. I find myself determined to improve my skill and make it further; there is definitely satisfaction in making it to that next level for the first time. I do enjoy revealing more story elements as I progress as well.
I would recommend trying the demo first and seeing if Teleglitch speaks to you like it did to me.

Someone speedhacked this game to 1.25x speed and after two hours of trying, he got 48.33 on Hyper Hexagonest with the speedhack still active. Anyways, this is one hard game; yet it's so addictive. However, you can get that feeling of excitement when you not only beat a level, but also reach 120 seconds in the same run.
Each level has a unique color palette and a unique soundtrack to go with them, which changes every time your time reaches a multiple of 60. Sometimes, the background music will change along with the color palette! But it's turtles all the way down; eventually the screen will go black and white, the music becomes so slow that it is unrecognizable, and the colors no longer change.
When your time reaches 60, the level is beaten and a Hyper version of it is unlocked. In the level's Hyper version, the gameplay is the same, however there are new obstacles to overcome, and the overall game is at a faster pace; all but the in-game timer; it is always real-time, no matter what. You don't unlock anything for beating the Hyper levels, however beating the final Hyper level will show you a cutscene; the only one in the game, aside level beaten notifications.
There are 3 unique levels, each with a Hyper version, meaning there are 6 in total.
Anyway, the verdict? Everything is amazing about this game, except for its overmapped difficulty and the unskippable ending cutscene. I highly recommend you pick it up if you're willing to do a challenge.

Great turn-based strategy game with a few RPG elements thrown in.  This is a great game if you enjoy the strategy RPG and don't mind a bit of a challenge served up with your story.
Pros
-Good story, the plot will suck you in and you'll want to fight to save the human race
-Challenging gameplay, especially at the harder difficulties
-Lots of variety for building characters, especially if you have the expansions
-Fairly good balance when it comes to builds, there are many good ways to build characters and they all play in unique and interesting ways
-Plenty of content, lots to do, you'll be playing for a while
-Lots of cosmetic character customization
-Some basebuilding strategy
Cons
-Game can be brutal and unforgiving at times, and character death is permenant (though some might see this as a pro)
-Falling behind with upgrades/losing too many characters almost certainly spells defeat, you may have to start the game over at least once
-UI can be annoying at times and a misclick for troop placement could spell disaster
Overall this game is great and I highly recommend it as a strategy game.

Having fond memories of the original classic I can only say this remake does the original justice. I was a little dubious to begin with thinking no re-make (and a few have been attempted the "UFO trilogy") would stand up to the original. Aspects such as squad creation and progression down to tech research and engineering all are standard formats most people know, but crafted alongside a great alien invasion story and turn based tactics I would say its a must buy for anyone into strategy games with RPG elements. For those who recall the original and are wondering what is missing, main aspects are multiple base creation, allocating equipment Deus Ex style alongside more specific equipment slots. Also aspects such as squad members becoming more accurate with certain weapons the more they used them to a standard aim ability, and a limit to high ranking soldiers based on the number of soldiers you had in anyone base. But overall these are minor issues compared to new aspects of the game not in the original. I hope this review has been of some help to gamers out there!

Failed remake of a classic tabletop game...
(Short)
These are terrible representations of what was once an excellent franchise. They are single player, poorly written, 2d static worlds, where none of your dialogue choices matter, the plot is so watered down you forget why you are fighting the enemies which are all the same, and all the things that made this franchise unique to begin with have been over simplified or removed entirely.
Stay away even at 90+% off. Still not worth it. You will not play any of these titles for more than 2 hours, before wishing you had refunded it during the first hour.
(Detailed)
#1 No Multiplayer- Can you imagine how long Shadowrun would have lasted on tabletop as a single player game? Longer than this buggy mess.
#2 Hairbrained Schemes- These greedy Devs took our money on kickstarter and pre-orders then pushed back its release so many months, that they were already asking me to kick/pre-order their next title before releasing the game. Then when it finally did get released, it was filled with so many bugs and terrible save system which would cause you to lsoe your progress and force you to replay entire chapters over and over again, until we reached their set save point and hope it worked this time! What is this 1983?
#3 The writing- since this is now a single player experience, the entire game is you reading and responding to npc's. You would think that they would have at least spell checked it, or used proper punctuation. However, before you read enough of the story to see how shallow and borrowed from half a dozen movies the plot is, you see numerous spelling and language mistakes.
#4 Decking- running around in cyberspace as a super hacker, has been thrown out entriely and replaced with Deus Ex style, accessing a safe or a device. Decking was one of the FEW things that made Shadowrun unique. Had these devs even played their own game in the last decade before making this tripe? I think NOT!
So many more points of failure, but honestly not worth it me to write about it at this point...
I own all the sequels to this title as well. They managed to fix a few of the most dreadful aspects of this franchise, but not enough to warrant spending money on them.
Weak writing, boring combat, static 2d world, pointless dialogue choices when talking to NPC's whether you say nice things or mean things they answer the same way. Totally linear in every sense of the word...
No play value, let alone replay value. Overall this series of games was and still is a major let down. These Dev's greed and lack of product interest shine through in every decision they make.
Stay away from the failed GREEDY CASH GRAB MMO as well...
Such a shame, Greedy Devs kill yet another franchise...

While I like Match 3 games, and I have been enjoying other free-to-play games which have basically the same "do a puzzle to get an item" mechanic in order to complete quests across a map, this title just seems to fall short and isn't much fun.
I think the difference is that the Hidden Object and Mahjong free-to-play games require more skill and the Match 3 is heavily reliant on luck, and because the restrictions for limited play in each session means not having good luck leads to repeated failure.
In the match 3 puzzles you have a limited number of turns to either get a set score or accomplish some task (like break all the ice tiles) but unlike other Match 3 titles where half the strategy is using aiding abilities efficiently in order to do so, in this game all of those abilities are things you need to purchase with real money.  I know the free-to-play titles always have their real-money transaction stores with items designed to let you play longer or get past puzzles quicker, but this title seems to need those items in order to actually get through the game and so comes across as more of a cash grab scheme.
The game is always free to try out, so if you really enjoy Match 3 games you can always load it up and see if it is for you.  I, however, have found much more satisfyibg free-to-play games available that are less of a money-grab scheme and that I actually enjoy putting time into, so I see little reason to keep this title in my roster.

Shadowrun Returns plays like a linear detective story, taking place in a cyber-punk/magical world, based on classic isometric rpgs. You take turns using your character's established traits to find ways around conversation or scenarios, and fighting opponents in turn based combat alongside a team you construct before each mission.
There is a lot of reading, but if you’re into that sort of thing there’s plenty of world building information and atmosphere. The graphics are pretty good, plenty of detail put into the environments, but the music can get a bit repetitive.
The combat can be extensive, but that’s up to you. Want to run in with a hoard of bat and axe wielding trolls? Or, split half your team up to take on one front while another member hacks into computer system, and another member conjures spirits while buffing the team. Or you could look around for a conversation and use your knowledge of security to get you through with less violence. One-man-army it if you want.
From what I can tell, most of the negative reviews are from those who simply didn’t like the game, or didn’t take the time to explore it, not from the game being bad. It isn’t perfect, but it’s pretty decent.

Tried this game, then returned it for a refund. It's definitely a *game*, and a very arcady game at that. Definitely nothing like the good old "approachable" helo sims of the past such as Ka-52 Alligator and Enemy Engaged: Comanche vs Hokum.
The flight model is one thing. I've never flown a real helicopter so I can't really comment anything definitive, but on the most realistic "pilot" flight model setting and the joystic sensitivity at maximum I don't think it's too bad. Probably still a bit more stable and forgiving than what a real helicopter would be.
The bigger problem lies elsewhere. While the older sims were about trying to create at least semi-realistic scenarios, this game is simply all about blasting away tons of enemies with unlimited weapons in scenarios that have nothing to do with realism. If the mission is about "taking out enemy artillery positions", in practice it means that you'll take off (simply by applying full throttle), fly for something like 800 meters and engage the literally 30 guns that are scattered all around in the terrain. If you run out of ammunition, no problem. Just push a button and all your weapons are magically reloaded. There's no damage modelling, both you and the enemies just have a simple health bar (which you can hide if you want but technically it's still there). There's no avionics or targeting systems or anything on the helicopter, all the enemies are simply highlighted on the screen with red triangles. Over all it's clearly just a very simple shooter game that just happens to involve a helicopter. If you're looking for a helicopter sim with ANY degree of immersion, stay away from this one.

I've been playing since Darkness Evolved. I guess it's not for everyone, but I dramatically prefer this game to Hearthstone. The packs come easier, nerfs happen when needed, though not always in a timely manner.
Control decks are actually a thing here, and you aggro is more in check because nothing can attack on first turn without Storm. Evolve is another resource that lets you come back from behind so the game isn't too easily snowballed. We have cards with Rush which is like Storm but you can't attack face, which further keeps aggro in check.
That's not to say there aren't aggro decks. Sword an Blood are the primary aggro classes; Dragon and Haven are the primary control classes; and Shadow, Rune, and Forest are more inbetween.
Cygames is quite generous with packs, I've been able to play for free and build competitive decks each expansion. We have daily missions, log in rewards, bonus log in rewards on certain events, and free packs from time to time.
The game started out quite balanced in Darkness Evolved, but has declined slightly with more cards being added to the pool with each expansion. The most recent expansion, Wonderland Dreams, caused quite a jump in a certain class' winrate, but Cygames has since brought offending cards in line. There have been cases of Cygames creating cards I don't agree with, design-wise (I'm looking at you, Heavenly Aegis), but in general they're alright, and don't dominate the meta. They just feel bad to lose to.
If Cygames continues this trend of nerfing cards as needed, I think the game will continue to grow. If they allow it to get out of hand and leave cards unchecked for too long, it will die. Overall, the cheapness of play and balance make me believe the game is a better alternative to other digital card games for the time being.

Antichamber is a fantastic example of what makes a puzzle game, but also a fantastic deconstruction of what makes a video game. We've become so used to certain things in modern games like dying, losing a level, how to navigate, and so on -- Antichamber takes all those expectations and turns them on their head. But it doesn't do so in a gimmicky way that makes the player feel cheated. Instead, there's a different set of physical rules that the game plays by, and the progression teaches you all of these things. Sometimes you might brute force your way through a puzzle without understanding it, but the comprehensive nature of the game means you'll probably encounter the puzzle again in a way that can't be brute forced.
The very first thing you learn in Antichamber is that there's no losing state. The game is more or less a maze that can always be escaped with the press of a button. Usually you'll find yourself doing this when you're confused about a puzzle. The non-linear nature of the game allows you to reach a dead-end in terms of what you know how to do, but continue playing elsewhere, perhaps to discover what you didn't know, or find what you needed to progress. The most famous aspect of this game is the non-Euclidian space, where returning to a previous area might not bring you to where you were before. The game also gently introduces you to these concepts, and you'll surprise yourself with how second-nature they become by the end of the game.

This game has some really strong pros and cons to it.
Firstly the cons:
-Insta-death is everywhere. The levels are quite literally designed to kill someone who doesn't know the layout. This is often done with falling spikes from the ceiling. Spikes are way too common and I wish they weren't insta-kills, but they are.
-Things are fairly well hidden. Going along with the fact that the player doesn't ever have a map given to them, it is very easy to miss many things, including the optional dungeons. And missing these dungeons is a guarenteed way to fall behind the power curve and make an already difficult game even more difficult.
-Until double jump, it's effectively just going right and then going right some more.
The pros:
-Exploring and doing the optional dungeons is really fun. Even though they're completely unneeded to beat the game and get the non-100% ending, they're still really fun to go through.
-The music is fantastic. Probably my favorite track was the Sunken Temple, funnily enough, an optional area.
-Double jump makes the difference. Suddenly the game opens up wide and you can do every optional area after that. Unfortunately double jump comes two areas before the end of the main storyline.
So if I could change anything, I'd open up all of the optional areas earlier in the game. Because I felt like the first half was a slog through, but the second half was a blast. I'd like to play way more of the second half and skip the first half.
The reason why the game suddenly got better is that Castle in the Darkness is a parody of Metroidvania games. These types of games shine when you can take various paths and explore. And for about half of the game, it felt like there was no exploring. So when you could finally do so, that is when the game was really able to show you all of the cool experiences it had to offer.
I was ready to leave Castle in the Darkness a negative review, but the quality play of the second half of the game really left a positive experience with me, so I think I'd recommend this game.
