Teleglitch: Die More Edition is true to it's name as any game could be. It's a harsh rough-and-tumble roguelike that pushes the player to paranoia and makes resource management the key between success and crushing failure.
You will die. You will die a lot. You will die far more than you expect you would in a top-down pixel shooter. The worst part is you're going to like it.
The atmosphere of Teleglitch: Die More Edition is what you would expect from the survival horror genre. It's a game that throws the player into an unknown environment that is just as hostile as the terrifying denizens within it. The game takes care to only let you learn more of the story as you get further in, hooking the curious by tempting them with computer logs and various records.  With each passing death, it's surmised the player is learning more about the creatures they fight and the situation they're in.
Mechancis-wise, the game is twitchy. Very, very twitchy. Players who are slow on the draw will find themselves growing thoroughly more and more frustrated, while those with jerky reactions will find out quickly that bullets are scarce, and inaccuracy is not an option that fits well with survival. Teleglitch will, unfortunately, get more and more frustrating with each respawn, until you finally have to pull away for a bit. That doesn't make it a bad game, but it makes it a very difficult one. Mostly because it should be so easy, and the blame falls very heavily upon sheer human error.
Despite my grumblings, I'm recommending this game. It's a fun challenge, but in hindsight. So be prepared to grind your teeth as you grind through zombies and mutants, and be prepared to die more than you ever thought possible.
It will consume you.

Fairy Fencer f was beautiful. This is going to be a long review, so if you don't like reading, then the first sentence sums it up.
I've played many RPG and JRPG games through my life, and most of them were pretty spectacular. Golden Sun, Persona 3 and 4, Pokemon (if that counts), Chrono Trigger, Fire Emblem: Awakening, and Skyrim, to name a few. So I'd like so think that I've seen all the odd's and ends of what RPG/JRPG games should feel like.
Fairy Fencer f had every good thing RPG's have to offer. The story, the art, the music, the characters, the combat system, the customization, the grind (maybe not good to some people), and most importantly for me, a DYNAMIC main character. I'll be going into details, trying to avoid spoilers since I always hover over them anyways.
FF's story seems basic at first. Two deity's, the benevolent Goddess and the vile Vile God, each fighting to take over the world. They both get sealed away, and the world is left alone all normal. Your quest is to collect Furies (sealed fairies) in order to revive the Goddess and get your wish granted. Seems prety run-of-the-mill, right? But then you meet your two protagonists, the unlikeable Fang and the sarcastic Eryn, and you quickly get pulled in by Compile Heart's signature comedic dialogue. And in classic JRPG form, a TON of twists happen throughout the game that make you upset, confused or heartbroken. They come fast and strike hard, leaving you devastated or driven enough to keep playing; to solve whatever just happened. The story is far from basic. It's a wonderful tale of treachery, love, heroism, justice and cookies. Oh and Pippin I guess...
Everything in this game was gorgeous. The landscapes, the cutscences, the characters, even the menu's were well designed and easy to use. The music gave emotions to the dungeons and aligned with events in the story; mystery, excitement, regret etc. I will say that you'll be sick of hearing the word "Metamorphosize" halfway through the game, since it's the first word of the theme song that plays when you Fairize.
I figure I should also mention Voice Acting since that was pretty great too. I used the English voices because I knew Christine Marie Cabanos was in the cast. There was plenty of emotion, and none of the voices were painful to listen to like Compa from HD (Except Pippin)

I'm as much of a fan of your "Tsundere" or  "Onee-Chan" trope characters as the next guy. Heck, I played through Hyperdimension and found it enjoyable. For those of you who don't know, basically a trope is a stereotype, for example the "Rich girl with the annoying laugh". But there were only three characters I can think of that fit into a solid trope: Soji, Apollonius and (maybe) Zenke.
All the characters were so completely diverse, and their chemistry was amazing. You had the "Tsundo-masochist", "Jarl Ulfric the Baker", "Kill, Kill, Kill", and the "Japanadian". All the characters had interesting backstories, and you really felt like you were growing with them on their journey. Just not Pippin though.
The game consists of an Overworld, a single Town, Goddess Revival and Dungeons (Shukesoo's Tower included). Similar to most RPG's, the dungeons are filled with non-random enemy encounters that trigger a battle sequence. You can gain the advantage outside of battle by hitting the enemy first (akin to Paper Mario).
The combat system is almost identical to Hyperdimension; turn-based strategy. You can customize your team in many, many ways. You can change combos, armor, Fairies, stats, formation, members, partners, accessories and even fighting styles (Turning a brawler into a gunner, for example). The only thing I was disappointed with in terms of customizations is that
. Everyone gets a default costume and a bath towel/bathing suit (DLC, by the way), with the exception of Ethel, who has three.
I love grinding in RPG's. Shoot me, I'm weird. But this game was special in that it was actually fun to grind. You can upgrade each character individually using points earned from battle. Tiara can either be an all-out magic user or a Glavie wielder, or a swordsman, or an archer etc. It's very fun to play around with different strategies. I never used Pippin though, so I can't give analysis on that...

Fang get's his own section because I hated him at the beginning. If you've ever watched a Romance/ Slice of Life anime before, you've met Fang; Lazy, undecided and unworthy of the ladies he's surrounded by. But oh my word. That is all I'll say. Let him annoy you, allow him to get at you and then you will feel all the emotion I felt through this game. Amazeballs.
In conclusion!
Story: 9/10 - Draws you in. Makes you think, work and FEEL. I got the ending I didn't want, so maybe I'll edit this later.
Gameplay: 10/10 - I love the mechanics. Dungeons, shopping for armor, grinding. The whole RPG shindig.
Character's: 10/10 - Individualistic, lovable, and well defined. But Pippin...
Music: 9/10 - Electronic? Orchestra? J-pop? Rock? Yup, and it's all great. But one over repetitive song robs this of a 10.
Replay Value: 10/10 - Hard Achievements, three endings I'm dying to see, and ridiculous character customization.
Overall: 9.5/10
This game truly deserves to be among the great RPG games out there. Where Hyperdimension is niche and weird, Fairy Fencer f is a beautifully crafted masterpiece of a game that I would kill to play again for the first time. I highly recommend this game if you are a casual, hardcore or die-hard fan of RPG, JRPG or Anime games.

Risk of Rain is an incredible roguelike game featuring permanent death and a diverse item system that sets it apart from other similar games.
PROS:
-Procedurally generated worlds
-Around 10 unlockable characters
-Multiplayer, single player and local coop
- 100+ Items obtainable within games
-A Relic system, where you can unlock 'relics' that change the game in some ways
-Lots of replayability
CONS:
-There are a few bugs that need to be ironed out still
-Multiplayer requires you to host servers, meaning giving out your IP or having to portforward.
-Local co-op does not feature dynamic splitscreen, so if you move off the screen from your friends you disappear.
-Dead community
-A little thin on plot
However, the pros easily outweight the cons as the only true con is the multiplayer issues. So anyday I'd reccomend this.

I wanted to like this game. I have been a big fan of Shadowrun pen&paper and the old SR Nintendo game.
But I just can't bring myself to like it.
It has the potential to be good but just can't follow through on anything.
Character creation is ok and seems straight out of the rulebook. But it is so bare bones, it's barely being allowed to be called a RPG. The way the game actually plays, it's more of a rail shooter.
The graphics or more specifics the style of the game is very good - it almost perfectly brings to life the feeling of the retro-future of good old SR. And that's about the only good thing you can say about the whole game.
The music is bland, boring and repetitive (is there only one song or do they all sound alike)
And finally the gameplay.
This game is so linear it makes straigfht lines look like circles. You don't do any investigation for the case, nor any preparation. And once you're on a mission you pretty much just walk down a corridor.
It almost makes no difference what kind of class you choose, most missions won't change the least bit, some will be slightly (superficially) different.
And you can't really use your teammates as you would want to.
You can only use your NPC Decker to hack when your in combat, and otherwise if you don't have the decking skill as PC then your NPC Decker will only be useful half the time. (It might be that I'm missing part of the UI but then that just means the UI is so unintuitive as to not be implemented)
Dialogue is a bare minimum of what you would expect. From what I can tell most of the time it doesn't matter jack what dialogue option you choose - if there are options, anyways - there are very few.
Dialogue also is not voiced. While you may or may not see that as minor, it is something that would have filled out the atmosphere of the game. As I said, nothing major, but should be a given in todays games.
The game is short. Very short. I've logged 13 hours finishing the game and that was with me replaying some scenes, dying a couple times, and having the game paused a lot.
I bought this game on sale, so that's forgivable. But I would be livid if I had paid full price for such a short game.
There pretty much isn't anything to do except follow the one quest, Scratch that: there is nothing to do except that (well, there is one (!) super short side-mission that's just long enough to be called a side-mission).
I don't know why you have the hide-out and your stash when you will find very few things anyway. You aren't able to loot bodies - you only get the occasional keycard from the bodies.
The AI is terrible. Just an example (maybe slight spoiler):
You are fighting enemy group A. Because of the noise of the fighting enemy group B will come as well. One of your teammates will say something like "We can use that to our advantage". But Team B will run across the map, pass by all of Team A to attack you - and then probably the one teammate they shouldn't even be able to see.
I replayed that scene a couple of times and found out that ONLY if all my team is out of sight  will Enemies B not run to me but engage ENemies A ( at least most of them, a couple of them were still homing in on me)
In other fights, you can trick the AI by getting spotted, and then pulling back.
The AI will then send the enemies to you, which means because they were not all in the same place when they started, they will arrive one after the other. And since they have to come to you, they will waste all of their action points on movement leaving no AP to attack. This results in your team attacking each incoming enemy - one after the other- and most likely killing them in one round.
Doesn't work in all maps , but whenever there are corridors it most likely will.
5/10  - If you like SR and you get it on sale.

This game used to be one of the best streamlined Cardgames out there but Cygames absolutely killed their game with the last 2 expansions. They keep printing cards that completely dominate the meta to the point that at the highest ranks the meta almost exclusively consists of the two and sometimes even one best deck and the counter to it/them. It usually takes about a month until these cards get nerfed into oblivion and the next broken decks dominate the meta, then they get nerfed and the cycle repeats. Also the broken decks keep getting less and less interactive from "can't be attacked", "can't be destroyed" to just getting multiple turns in a row or forcing one specific type of deck building and playstyle to every single class they find a way to make the game less fun each expansion. It just basically seems like they are constantly trying to lower the skill level of their game as draw and going first is becoming more and more influencial to the point where the game is basically decided within the first turns. Also the game keeps getting increasingly expensive and basically impossible for a new player to find success withouth spending money on packs that also have an increasingly low chance of containing good cards as they not only contain reprints but also an absurd amount of cards that are unplayable and even a lot of prebuilt decks contain garbage tier legendaries. Also master matchmaking basically doesn't exist and people with 100 master score get matched with 10000 master score.

Cygames do not know how to playtest cards before they come out and let the meta wallow too long before responding. Bloodcraft has had a 54% playrate on ladder and is nigh uncounterable, and they left it that way for a full month. The latest expansion is the worst yet, the focus on Neutral cards, and the overwhelming power of them, has made nearly every deck open the same way. So even if you can get into a match that's not Blood, you essentially have to deal with the same opening anyway.
They're willing to announce that there will be nerfs, but they wait weeks to actually implement them; for what reason? The nerfs are coming today, but we don't know in what form they'll be or what cards they'll hit. Even if this does turn out well, this game cannot be recommended because Cygames doesn't put the effort to playtest beforehand. Their last three expansions have had overwhelmingly one-sided metagames and crafts above the 50% playrate (and in some cases, above 50% winrate). I expect more of the same in the future, and anyone getting into the game should too.

This is a sweet little game that does a lot of things right. From the start, the game works hard to build up a noir atmosphere, complete with the heavy voiceover. The jewish bits work fine with it as well, as a lot of the fun in the story comes from protagonist Russel Stone, wrestling with heavy moral issues. This he does, while balancing his role as a rabbi with his new role as a brooding noir detective, and i have to admit that i enjoyed that mix quite a lot. The semitic bits never gets in the way of the game though, and i appreciate that a little part of the game consists of learning some jiddisch for example. Also, it takes a lot of place in the dialog, and there is fun to be had seeing things from, and acting from the perspective of a rabbi, and the dilemmas they face.
This does a lot for pushing the story along, and i enjoyed interacting with the character, and slowly unravelling the thread of the investigation. The problem is that the game is over when you are just getting started.
It’s not that you don’t see the end coming, though. The game is paced very nicely. When mucking about with the investigation, you always feel like you are making progress, and you get that little AHA-feeling of discovering something new, and when you finally reach the end, there are no loose ends. But it also feels like you just got the hang of things, and now, you're all done. And that's a bit of a bummer.
The game is also pretty good looking. The visuals might get a little bit flat sometimes, but everything looks and feels nice and atmospheric, with it's glorified sierra look. It also made me miss a point system, for added replayability.
The voice acting and writing can get a bit hammy, but all that stuff is forgivable considering this is a game from a studio of just a few people. Considering that, i don’t expect Hollywood performances, but instead enjoy it for what it is.
The shivah is not an epic, but that's kind of sad, for it has potential for a far bigger and more involved story in it.

Antichamber is a game that will make you *think*. With relatively simple beginnings, the main thing that becomes clear is the developers really want to play with your mind. Levels change just by turning a corner. Doors open in the most unexpected way. Things like falling to your death actually help progress the game. Where most games like to play on the trope of "Nothing is as it seems" - in Antichamber, everything is *exactly* as it seems... it's just sometimes, you don't quite realise what it seems to be.
And if you think that review is odd, twisted, confusing and somewhat intriguing, then you'll LOVE Antichamber. Be warned though - the puzzles inside will keep you scratching your head for a surprisingly long time.

Great metroidvania. It is a rather faithful pseudo-NES game, and it's based off various early platformers from that era.
It has a solid difficulty, but even I could complete it, and almost 100% it without consulting a guide. It does get a bit spike-spammy nearing the end, but I managed to get past it. Perhaps i'm a platforming god.
However, I do have a few gripes. The boss battles, although interesting in their design, are often rather easy, with their difficulty being compensated with an insane amount of health. Those that aren't that easy just just have a very large mass that damages you while you try to to hit their weak spot. There were only a few bosses that actually satisfied me.
And building off that, some of the hitboxes are rather suspect. The ones for the spikes are very fair, which is good since they litter the stages; however some of the enemy projectiles' (or my own) hitboxes should be ashamed, as well as a few of the bosses. That's basically inexcusable.
The puzzles seem rather fair, but a the method to obtain a few items are rather obtuse. One that comes to mind is a massive floating head that appears invulnerable, and there's a clearly cut path to go around it. Turns out you have to sit there, reflect it's attacks, and kill it after 10 seconds of reflection or so... Seriously? There are absolutely 0 hints on how to get that.
The music is rather nice. Not great, but good. It's rather faithful to the aesthetic, and there are short, jaunty loops, which helps with the frustration. Perhaps if they were all a bit longer, but it's certainly passable.
All in all, the game is very good, especially with tight controls, and a broad range of weapons, items, spells, and easter eggs to find. However it's certainly not for everyone, particularly if you get frustrated easily by instant-death spikes, or if you easily resort to wikis (discovery is half the fun!)
Very addicting. The learning curve is quite nice. At first, I died a lot, but I quickly and noticably got better with each try, which was very rewarding.

Every death has so far been my own mistake - the game only being to blame for being so unforgiving as to make death permanent.
But overall this is a wonderful gem for the following reasons:
1. Tension! Permanent death means every time you play you'll be at the edge of your seat. I have yet to find any other single player experience that quite matches this game's level of stress.
2. Style! Yes, the graphics suck but the line of sight gameplay and low graphics mean that discerning and discovering foes becomes harder and adds to the game's difficulty factor.
3. Weapons. The game has an awesome item combining system and you will be very happy to make that one super powerful weapon or other lifesaving item when you'd thought all was lost. Eventually you'll memorize some item recipes and forgo combining a particular item immediately in the hopes of finding that extra ingredient for making something more useful - all the while juggling your inventory to make sure you're not leaving items on the ground behind.
4. Feedback. The developers have implemented a clever graphical trick into making all the weapons feel like they have a punch or at least a sense of personality. Firing a weapon distorts either the entire screen or at the very least distorts your character. This makes learning the intricacies of each weapon a skill and adds to the high level of skill you need to beat this game.
5. Exploration and secrets. In an environment where death is permanent, finding anything useful becomes immensely valuable. Exploring each level thoroughly to find every secret area is thus very rewarding and adds nicely to gameplay.
6. Randomization. Each level is randomized. Yes, there are some things which are key to each level that stay the same but most of the level is different each time you play. Different secrets, different enemy positions, different room locations etc. It all adds to the tension since you really never know what lies behind each door and each corner.
Cons:
- no music (some tension creating music would have been nice)
- graphics (a bit less pixelation would do the game some good)
Overall this is one of the best games I've ever played (and I've played a lot of them). You owe it to yourself to challenge yourself to beating this game. It's one of the few which makes you proud to beat each level and possibly actually gives bragging rights if you manage to complete it.

From the relatively short time that I've played this, I absolutely love it. I could go on about how the developers are some of the best in the industry, but I will focus on the game. Each perk is well designed, and I haven't found a perk that I could get behind playing. The basic premise of the game is simple: shoot the Zeds (not zombies), and don't let your entire squad get killed. Horde shooters usually get boring really quickly, but there is a certain charm that Killing Floor 2 has that keeps it from getting boring.
The actual gameplay behind Killing Floor 2 is fantastic. I could spend hours shooting zeds, and feel fulfilled. The thrill that I feel going between rooms and through narrow hallways is fantastic. The games never cease to be chaotic. There is something terrifying about being caught in a corner, constantly attacked by a Fleshpound. The guns feel incredible to fire, and every single weapon feels like like an effective weapon against the hordes of zeds. On every difficulty, targeting the head with every weapon will put down the enemies.
A minor issue that I have is with some of the perks and weapons feeling underwhelming. One of the most disappointing weapons to me is the double barreled shotgun. I absolutely love using the weapon, and by no means is it a bad weapon. In fact, it is one of my favorites. Despite my love for the weapon, I feel like it is incomplete. In fact, I feel like the entire support perk is incomplete. It is insanely fun to play as, but I can't help but feel disappointed with it. The welding is fast, and the ability to repair doors is amazing, plus all the shotguns are a hell of a lot of fun to fire, but it just feels empty. There just isn't enough to it at the moment. I love playing it so much, but I feel like it, along with every perk could go with more.
I have no doubts that the devs will address every issue that I say in this review, as they truly care for their games, and I doubt that these minute problems would be enough to cause anybody from playing the game. The game is still fairly new, and just two days ago, they added a new map and a bunch of new content for every perk.
I'd definitely recommend purchasing the game. These devs deserve support, and the game itself is phenomenal. I am more than excited to see where they take the game over the course of 2017. No doubt will I put hundreds upon hundreds of hours into the game.

This review is for Xbox controller players only. That's how I played the game. As background I loved Apache 2, Comanche, etc. some 15 years ago and had a HOTAS and rudder pedal setup back then, but no more.
TLDR this is a 7 out of 10 recommend (buy on sale) for Xbox controller gamers looking for a bit of approachable helicopter "sim-lite" nostalgia but be ready to walk away or be frustrated.
I really had high hopes for this sim. Finally an approachable helicopter combat game that can be played with an Xbox controller!
Sadly the Xbox controls don't feel good to me. Anything beside Pilot mode doesn't feel remotely helicopter-ish. In Pilot mode I've tried multiple different setups, but nothing clicks. There's too much going on and it feels like you are fighting the controls the whole time rather than feeling like the game experience was optimized for the controller. I got stuck on the Jungle Air Support mission near the end of the campaign where you have to do lots and lots of manual shooting because the auto-gunner is too slow and aims at friendly troops. Ultimately I've had some fun with the game, but not finishing sucks.
Close air support of friendly troops in particular is NOT fun. The Jungle Air Support mission is just torture.
-- The auto-gunner targets FRIENDLY troops (WHY???) and there is nothing mapped on the controller to switch targets.
-- Manual aiming is frustrating, particularly while zoomed -- the camera needs to pan to follow the manual aiming box when it hits the edge of the screen when TrackIR isn't in use. You do get this behavior in autohover & gunner camera view, but that's not always viable. The sensitivity needs to be turned way down to hit anything. Perhaps map the left stick Y-access to vertical camera pan when in autohover/manual aim?  Manually panning with the D-pad is a poor solution -- you need your hands on the sticks. Why can't tapping B switch weapons and holding B reload weapons? That frees up a shoulder button to act as a "shift or toggle key" that could remap the sticks and face buttons when held (or toggled), allowing "pilot mode" and "gunner mode" that adds more targeting functions that currently are keyboard-only and "freelook". Manual gunning outside of autohover is clearly what is intended but I have been unable to achieve the control necessary to beat Jungle Air Support mission despite many, many attempts even with all the damage settings turned off and on easier difficulty.
Most of the reviews for the Xbox One version really trash it - and I can't argue with their objections. I bought it on PC pre-release and had lower expectations for polish; but I was looking a sim-lite that I could play and have fun with a controller and it comes close but ultimately frustrates. Consider this more of a "meh" rather than an outright negative review.
I have an ambivalent relationship with isometric RPGs. I respect the hell out of the intricate and complex systems developers can implement in these games to give them the ability to create vast, sprawling worlds full of minute details. Worlds that truly seem alive and tell grand stories on a scale where the world and the characters both support the size and scope of any given narrative they want to present. However, I really get bored having to read mountains of descriptive text alongside gameplay that largely relegates the player to the backseat. Sure, there are tactical considerations you have to make concerning party composition, positioning on the battlefield and action point usage. But I just find it boring as hell clicking through all of this stuff and just relying on character skills to determine the outcome of any battle or conversation and not the skills of me as a player. Especially in cases like this, where you can stand at point-blank range, have an 85% hit chance and still miss the enemy with a mother
fuc
king shotgun.
Which is why I have put off playing Shadowrun Returns for so long. I never played the tabletop RPG it’s based on and I’m also not familiar with prior video games based on the license outside of having heard of them. But the concept behind it really intrigued me. I really like the idea of a futuristic cyberpunk setting where elves, dwarves and magic all are real too. Not the greatest or most original concept on the planet, mashing together classic fantasy tropes with William Gibson’s writing, but I’ve seen worse.
First off, I really love the look of this game. It’s not quite the picture-perfect representation of what I see before my inner eye when I envision the word “cyberpunk”, but then again, nothing has ever come close to that in my eyes, but it’s still gorgeous to behold – if you don’t zoom in to the max, since at that point you can clearly make out the seams –  and the music definitely nicely enhances the general atmosphere of this world.
The characters also managed to endear themselves to me since there’s tons of descriptive writing outside of mere conversation, since the visual style of the game and the lack of voice-acting doesn’t really permit for expressive character models to indicate their body language.
Similarly, the writing of the actual narrative is mostly serviceable, but the narrative itself is kind of a weak point for me. It’s a murder mystery filled with some fairly played out clichés, where the player ends up knowing what’s going to happen next way ahead of the characters even without being familiar with the setting.

I guess my problem with this narrative is, that it’s a) fairly predictable and b) it makes a dramatic jump in scale very suddenly, switching from the aforementioned murder mystery to some kind of corporate conspiracy, and it just doesn’t gel, since the link between these plots is basically as arbitrary as it gets. The game is also pretty damn short for an RPG with only very few locations to visit, which all in all gives me the impression that the main goal the developers had with this game was in creating a basic framework for modern game designers to use in order to create 90s-era style isometric RPGs with modern design sensibilities and player comfort in mind, given that they offer the necessary tools to create further campaigns, and they used this campaign primarily for demonstration purposes as opposed to telling a great story first.
This may also explain why my choice in race basically had no influence in the story and only marginally mattered with regards to the upgrade tree. In a universe such as Shadowrun, I’d have assumed that racial tensions would ensure that you’d have an easier or tougher time with a group based on what race you belong to, but unfortunately this isn’t the case. And it probably has to do with the fairly limited dialogue options the game offers.
Most of the time it’s just a checklist you have to go through in order to get all the information. Sometimes you get to use your skills such as charisma or strength or what the game calls an etiquette to convince someone, but it’s so rare that it really seems underutilized. Especially the etiquettes, since you can literally play the entire game and not come across instances where an etiquette would be useful, since you can end up unlocking an etiquette way after it would’ve been useful when it would’ve triggered during a conversation hours earlier in the game, and each etiquette is basically used more or less once during the game.
The gameplay also feels rather unfocused to me. It heavily borrows from X-Com in the way it handles its turn-based combat encounters. Maybe it’s because I’m unfamiliar with the tabletop game it’s based on, but as a newbie to the franchise, I have to say I found it very silly how a group of freelance spies have their infiltration missions end up consisting of tons of shoot-outs and not a lot of sneaking and hacking. I played as a decker and rarely did I get to actually use my hacking abilities. And even reducing the game back to the regular old combat, there’s hardly a lot of strategy involved to win the fights. Don’t position people closely to each other to avoid area-of-effect damage from grenades and pick off one target after the other to effectively reduce enemy firepower on a permanent basis. It’s hardly rocket science.
So in the end, Shadowrun Returns is somewhat of a mixed bag. The game already had an uphill battle against my personal preferences concerning isometric RPG gameplay, but the general somewhat lacking narrative as well as the fairly uninteractive world with not a lot of opportunities to actually use hacking all that often meant that it did little to endear itself to me beyond the beautiful visuals and interesting characters. I guess at some point I’ll end up playing Dragonfall or Hong Kong, since I already own them, but I don’t consider it a priority right now.

This is my first time playing Civ V. At first glance, Civ V is great - it has spectacular graphics, and a great audio track. The social policies system and the Science system are attention-grabbing and appear to be well thought out. But beneath the surface, Civ V doesn't quite live up to the plug. The game can be buggy mess - often times, I won't be able to click the next turn button, for example, because it says "A Unit needs Orders" when I have given all of my units orders. This is after putting in all obtainable patches, two years after the game's initial release! The combat in Civ V involves terribly very little strategy - as long as your units are not hard-countered by the enemy's (this is extremely simple to work out) all that matters is who has the biggest military. Civ V's strategy lies entirely in what order the player researches technologies, adapts policies, chooses to produce, etc. and has little to nothing to try and do with combat - reading Sun Tzu's The Art of War will not assist you here. Capturing a city takes at least 3 turns, even if your opponent has no military and you've got several sturdy units assaulting the city. Multiplayer support is horrible, with people perpetually disconnecting and bally whereas i am either in the lobby attempting to urge a game along, or already playing one. There is no thanks to change game settings once you click the "Host Game" button and open your lobby. To do so you've got to kick everybody out and begin a brand new game. This is ridiculous, strategy games from a decade ago have the ability to alter settings whereas within the lobby. Diplomacy with AIs is impossible - even a long-time ally, who I've had multiple trade deals and analysis agreements with, who is so much weaker than me, will declare war on me for no reason... twice! The only indication I had (which was quite obvious) was that the AI stationed its military units near my territory for many turns before attacking. Nothing on the diplomacy screens hinted that the AI disliked me lmao. However, the AIs have supposedly been improved in the Gods & Kings growth... I'll see if there is any truth to that.
I have to give Civilization V a 7/10 because it's fun to play, and it seems like some effort was placed into its creation. From what I've been told by longtime fans of the series going back to Civ 3 or four, Civ V is prettier, but a step backwards wherever gameplay is involved. The exclusion of key gameplay features from earlier Civ games, such as espionage and faith, was clearly a cash grab for Firaxis, now that they are charging $30 for an expansion addon to deliver more content to Civ V. I'm sick of developers churning out pretty games that have worse gameplay than their predecessors. Civ V is a prime example of this, therefore I really cannot give them a positive review.

I'll start by saying that the music is what sold me on this game through the store. It has some damn good tunes, at least for the genre. There are also a good number of areas to explore and items to collect. This has everything for the making of a truly great game... except it is quickly destroyed by the developers hubris. Games are supposed to be fun, not frustrating.
No, this is not a rant about how difficult the game is. Truth be told, its not difficult at all. The actual GAME of the game, is fairly easy, but there is so much instant death and cheap trap placements, that skill is quickly thrown out the window in favor of memory, and THAT is why I cannot reccomend this game. It is fun to enter a new area and get as far as you can before you make one mistake too many. It is downright infuriating to enter the same area for the 30th time because you keep making one mistake. This wouldn't be as bad if the boss fights were worthwhile, but they aren't. Save for one, (not the final one) they are all pretty much a joke, many of them being references to other, better games. So in a sense its a few minutes of fun for several hours of frustration getting there. Not a good formula.
Story-wise, well, some would argue a game like this dosn't need a story. The problem is, this game tries to put one in, and only goes half way. The best cinematic of the game is the introduction, then it adds cutscenes throughout the different game areas... until is just decides to give up on them and leave you guessing as to what is going on halfway through. This ends up in a narrative mess with much of the plot being unresolved (even with 100% completion). A rule of gaming when it comes to story is either go all the way, or don't go at all. Ninja Gaiden, Castlevania, Metroid, and other titles like them may not have had complex stories, but they paced the ones they did have and wrapped up all their loose ends. For a game that likes to make a lot of references, they should have actually taken a page from those games' development.
And finally, the references themselves. Why? Why so many? And why so pointless? References can be fun, but not when they are hammering you upside the head every other screen. Yes, I fought the twin Hydra in Mario Bros. 2. I don't need to fight it AGAIN here. Yes, Navi was annoying in Ocarina of Time. You know what's more annoying? Your text box blocking my veiw when she hits me in your game. Some references are good, such as the shooting sword easter egg, and some of the "mirror" scenes like the entrance to the keep in castlevania, but most are just pointless, to the point you get absolutely sick of seeing them. Even worse, they remind you that those games were better, and why.
I know I am absolutely hammering this game, which is a shame, because there were parts I like. But truth be told, without the music, it would just be another passable metroidvania game that errs on being too much like its rage game cousins.
TL/DR
A decent attempt at a metroidvania with some good music and decent early level gameplay. However late game is chock full of insta-death goodness and the tidal wave of nostalgiac refereces gets tiring quite quickly.    2/5

Antichamber is a game designed specificallly to strike terror into the hearts of players who take realistic causality and "how to play" documents in thier games for granted.
First thing you're likely to find out playing Antichamber is that there are very few reliable constants; you can generally count on the mouse to move your view and the keys to walk around. Beyond that, every other step is a chance to trip over some spacial awareness wrecking passage or infinitely looping hallway. Depending on how lost you get yourself, this might account for half your playtime before getting to the actual puzzle part of the game.
There is more to the game than just wandering lost in a building that's actively trying to get you more lost, and when you reach the point where you're intended to start solving puzzles, Antichamber does finally start to get some cohesion going on, so it's not just a "walking around lost and confused" simulation.
My biggest complaint (SPOILERS) is that there's no explanation for what's happening in the game, right up to the end. Not that there's anything wrong with making a game with no story; but Antichamber has the trappings and suggestions that there's something bigger going on, but there's nothing concrete.
Aside from all that, some of the late game puzzles can be pretty dense and difficult to figure out, and the visual motif with the outlines and primary colors can get kind of obnoxious when the game demands that you jump across giant holes in the ground.
None of these complaints are enough to keep me from issuing a reccomendation, however, since it's still a very rare example of an artsy game that doesn't feel like the video game equivilent of a coffee house art snob, scoffing at all the "normal" games for not being deep enough. Antichamber is good right at face value, on its own merits and for its own reasons. Most of which will leave you wondering how stairs work.

From the relatively short time that I've played this, I absolutely love it. I could go on about how the developers are some of the best in the industry, but I will focus on the game. Each perk is well designed, and I haven't found a perk that I could get behind playing. The basic premise of the game is simple: shoot the Zeds (not zombies), and don't let your entire squad get killed. Horde shooters usually get boring really quickly, but there is a certain charm that Killing Floor 2 has that keeps it from getting boring.
The actual gameplay behind Killing Floor 2 is fantastic. I could spend hours shooting zeds, and feel fulfilled. The thrill that I feel going between rooms and through narrow hallways is fantastic. The games never cease to be chaotic. There is something terrifying about being caught in a corner, constantly attacked by a Fleshpound. The guns feel incredible to fire, and every single weapon feels like like an effective weapon against the hordes of zeds. On every difficulty, targeting the head with every weapon will put down the enemies.
A minor issue that I have is with some of the perks and weapons feeling underwhelming. One of the most disappointing weapons to me is the double barreled shotgun. I absolutely love using the weapon, and by no means is it a bad weapon. In fact, it is one of my favorites. Despite my love for the weapon, I feel like it is incomplete. In fact, I feel like the entire support perk is incomplete. It is insanely fun to play as, but I can't help but feel disappointed with it. The welding is fast, and the ability to repair doors is amazing, plus all the shotguns are a hell of a lot of fun to fire, but it just feels empty. There just isn't enough to it at the moment. I love playing it so much, but I feel like it, along with every perk could go with more.
I have no doubts that the devs will address every issue that I say in this review, as they truly care for their games, and I doubt that these minute problems would be enough to cause anybody from playing the game. The game is still fairly new, and just two days ago, they added a new map and a bunch of new content for every perk.
I'd definitely recommend purchasing the game. These devs deserve support, and the game itself is phenomenal. I am more than excited to see where they take the game over the course of 2017. No doubt will I put hundreds upon hundreds of hours into the game.

Bought it on sale for about $10, mostly because IF and Compa were responsible for it. I played the Hyperdimension Neptunia games and loved them, and this looked similar. In terms of the bare basics, it's kind've similar, you have your overworld map, go to dungeons to beat baddies and get loot, go to town to talk to people, and buy stuff. I'm only an hour in, and it seems much more complex than Hyperdimension. First is the weapon boost system, which allows you to allocate "Weapon Points", gained through battle, to increase your combo, learn new skills, and upgrade stats. You also get "Fairies", which you can equip and level up for cool benefits that start off with little benefits such as "Ice Support +3", but they also seem to be able to give you additional skills. Your weapon also apparently changes when you equip different kinds of combos, at least that's what the game tells me. The Main Characters (Fang and Eryn) are hilarious, Fang manages to pull off being a total Jerk, while being funny at the same time, which is good, otherwise he'd be unlikable. If you like Hyperdimension Neptunia, you'll like this. If you haven't played Hyperdimension, I'd say play this if you enjoy RPGs that will suck away all your time, and then play Hyperdimension, because this is a tad more serious (and by a tad, I mean a LOT) than Hyperdimension, which throws you head first into anime and video game references, this at least so far has kept it light on the video game trope references.

This is your typical energy-driven match three.  Yes, the energy thing is a bit annoying, but playing once or twice a day is simple enough.  Cute little storyline, too.  As for those claiming it's pay to win, NO.  Everything needed to succeed is earnable in-game.  You just have to have a little bit of patience.

The ambiant music sets the tone perfectly.
Your crew support your ship.
Your ship transports your crew.
Your ship upgrades.
Your crew members rise in rank.
Your ship scrapes by... just.
You gain another crew member.
You reach a station with just enough scrap to patch the ol' girl back up again.
You venture on with a new found sense of strength.
You overextend and die in a culmination of slight mistakes and misjudgement.
I did not expect an indie game like this to put me in the seat of a spaceship and deliver such a visceral experience. It's constantly engaging, whilst allowing you to play at your own pace. It finds the perfect balance on every level it can. It is a game you don't necessarily try and beat. It's a game you sit down and play a session of. You don't save (even though you can quit and resume). You adventure through the galaxy and fight off the rebel scum for a vague victory condition yet you're still enthralled.
I realise i may have overused the word "you" in this review. But everyone deserves to play this game and enjoy it for what it is. A flexible game with classic structure. I could go on and on. I love this game, every developer should play it as a source of inspiration. I have not the linguistic capabilities to appropriately praise this game. Yet still I try.

FTL is one of the best, most holistically well-designed games I've ever played.  Occupying some nebulous, wholly unique place between RTS and space combat, FTL places you at the helm of a ship held together with duct-tape, gumption, and prayer.  Your mission: reach the other end of a galaxy hell-bent on destroying you, in the best shape you possibly can.  Behind you: a wave of rebel fighters, bringing a wall of intergalactic destruction.  In front of you: the rebel flagship; the biggest, baddest, nastiest eldritch abomination of a space ship ever to sail the stars.
Your duty: destroy it.
Your fate: to die, over and over again, as you slowly suss out the invisible wheels and levers available to you.  Though highly randomized, the game teaches you the skills and techniques necessary to overcome the vicissitudes of chance and wring victory from ridiculously overwhelming odds.  Fans of Dark Souls will feel right at home.
With the infinite replayability and emergent narrative of Dwarf Fortress, and ten times the accessibility, FTL is about as close to perfect as any game could ever conceivably get.
Just don't name your crew after people you like.

This is a frustrating game. And I don't mean that as in "it's frustrating to play" (though it is), but it's frustrating because it gets so close to being something I would recommend, yet does some things so wrong that I just have to give it a negative review.
The game looks intentionally dated, with graphics that almost look like they could belong on an NES (but not quite). There's some good spritework here, with enemies & characters that look really nice. Bosses in particular can look really nice.
But there's some issues with the colour palette. Some enemies share colour with the background, making them needlessly hard to spot. Game designers, please don't use exactly the same colour for the ground & enemies.
The soundtrack is nice and upbeat. It sounds like something that could be from an NES game, and if it was, it would probably have been remembered fondly by a lot of people. Overall, the sound design works really well, despite some intentional limitations imposed on it.
Castle in the Darkness is a metroidvania-ish game, with a large maze-like world that you have to traverse, a bit like the first Metroid or Castlevania 2. Your character moves at a really high speed, and has a relatively long attack for being a "melee" focused game. Combat is fast and lethal, most enemies can't take a lot of hits, and neither can you.
When things work, when enemy placement is good, when bosses are well designed, it's really quite fun. You constantly need to be on your toes, as only a few hits will send you back to the last save point. Even early on the game is no cakewalk.
But then there are the times when the game does not work. I guess the game designers though it would be a fun joke to have a pipe with instant death spikes at the bottom, but having such things in your game just discourages exploration (and this is trying to be a metroidvania). Then there are issues with hitboxes. Usually games will err on the side of making the hitboxes too generous to the player, because if it's the other way around the game can easily just feel cheap. This game errs on the other side, making attacks that look like they would have hit miss. There's also issues with the size of hitboxes changing. Early on there's a boss who has a sword. It has a swing animation, the problem is that it's entirely possible to be hit by the sword attack at the start of the swing animation, when the boss raises the sword above its head, because you were standing a sword length from the boss. Had the attack hit you at the end of the swing animation, then things would have been as they should have been, but it seems like the swing animation makes the hitbox extend both up and forward through the entire animation, rather than having the hitbox be where the sword is during that particular part of the animation.
Enemy placement can also be unfair. If you need to jump down, and can't see where you're landing at the start of the jump, then there should not be an enemy that can hit you on the platform you're landing on. This just results in cheap, unavoidable hits.
Castle in the Darkness is game that should have been good. All the ingredients are there for an enjoyable game, but due to issues with level design and hitboxes, it's not enjoyable. Also, the game loves references. They're just thrown in there, with little care for if they fit in or not. There's a Mario pipe, an enemy that looks like a colour swapped enemy from Ghosts 'n Goblins, a gate that just so happens to look like the one from the intro to the first Castlevania, a boss that looks like the plant from Little shop of horrors, and so on. The haphazardly thrown in references just makes the game lose any personality. It's not clever, they are just things from other things. References can be done well, but they are best used as Easter eggs, not as something that you constantly barrage the player with.

This game is essentially a love letter to the 8bit era. Tons of references and call-outs to oldschool games and even 80's pop culture if you have a keen eye (in the room where you find the ares gauntlet there's a giant painting of vigo the carpathian on the wall).
There's an area that's clearly inspired by the clocktower in Castlevania, and you fight a mini-boss that borders on infringement-territory with taito's bubble bobble.
All of this is to say that Castle in the Darkness clearly knows its audience and isn't afraid to play fan service. It has pretty solid platforming, lots of criss-crossing and back-tracking, RPG mechanics like inns and shops, and everything else you'd expect from a game that's trying to harness the power of the 80's.
So yes- thumbs up, buy this game and enjoy it if these are the types of things that you enjoy. However, there are some negative things to point out.
First, this game is pretty rough around the edges. Gamepad support is barely there, and menus are never fully navigable using only a gamepad (you always end up having to go back to the keyboard for something) which means you likely won't be enjoying this game from your couch in big picture mode.
Second, the resolution options for this game are abhorrent. It starts up in windowed mode- a
window, which almost makes sense given that it's a pixel-game. You are provided with a handful of scale-factors to choose from, which also makes sense given that you want to keep square pixels for an authentic experience. What does
make sense is the fact that everything is scaled bilinearly, which means everything gets blurry as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Why didn't they provide an option for nearest neighbor scaling to keep the pixel art nice and sharp? The developers of this game need to go play Shovel Knight and see how a retro game can be developed for modern hardware and still keep its authenticity.
Aside from those two major issues, everything else I've encountered is fairly minor.

This game should be treated as a mandatory training simulator for anyone wanting to work in education or run for public office.  Completely serious, here.
Now, I'm not saying it's a perfectly realistic simulation.  Far from it.  However, it will quickly demolish any racial and/or nationalistic delusions the player holds and forces them into the harsh reality of why societies succeed or fail - and the fact that most of it comes down to where started out on the map, a few "minor" decisions early on that snowballed into major consequences centuries later, and no small amount of plain random luck.
It also shows us how technology evolves and the iterative nature of scientific progress.  That is to say it demonstrates how everything is build on top of everything that came before it.   It also demonstrates how the world started off as mostly one big land grab until it ran out of land to grab, and how the timing of our world wars shortly thereafter was almost inevitable.  And, much like real life, how the modern "stalemate" has transformed the nature of war into a class of competing cultures and jockying for position, if only because all the players left on the board are simply too big to be taken down directly.
As for the game itself, compared to Civ4 the graphics are obviously better.  The new "one unit exclusive" hex mechanic took some getting used to, but in the long run it's still doable and does make unit rotation & survival more important than the old "stack everything to the max" method.  Most important, however, is that this is the Civ game that opened the door to modding and the Steam Workshop - and that makes a world of difference, trust me.
If Civ5 has one flaw anywhere I'd say it was in
getting Leonard Nimoy to come back & do the tech blurbs for them a second time.  I'd like to hear how that decision was rationalized in the board room.

Some games are retro in the best way, striving to be as good in reality as the games of past eras appear through rose tinted glasses. Some are labeled retro simply because they're 2D, even though their design and even visuals have nothing to do with older titles and probably wouldn't have been possible on the machines of the past.
Some ape the forms and functions of older games in total. Castle in the Darkness is one of those, and the problem with it is that most of those games were, in fact, kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥
Enemies with unclear hit boxes, bland color palette, small and undetailed sprites, deaths that can only be avoided by memorizing the locations of traps, bosses you can cheese by finding spots in their arenas they can't touch (but which are otherwise exercises in tedium, with tiny hitboxes you always have to jump to strike), no map and no sense of forward momentum. If you're devoted to the actuality of middling NES titles as well as the memory of them, you may find all of this charming. I found it, like the games it was attempting to evoke, a reminder of why we've left all this stuff behind, and why the very best titles like Mario and Mega Man generally didn’t have it to begin with.
Castle in the Darkness would have been an okay game in the 80s, but we’re decades away from that being good enough for a commercial release.

Excellent game, very fun to play.  Controls take a bit getting used to, but helicopters are hard to fly IRL as well so I find that to be okay.
Pros:
- Great graphics and effects
- Fun gameplay. I especially love the rescue missions! More of those, please?
- Excellent controls. Takes a while to get used to, but once you do you'll feel like you're actually flying a helicopter.
Cons:
- Singleplayer campaign is way too short
- You don't have to land to rearm, you can just do it in mid-air. This makes it too 'arcadey' and detracts from the experience.
I suggest adding a 'realistic' mode where you have to find a helipad (there can be a couple per map), land on it, and wait a few seconds to rearm instead.
- The hitboxes on the missiles and enemies seem to be messed up. Its incredibly hard to hit an enemy (example: tank) with regular missiles.
- Some optimization issues on certain maps, most noticable on the foggy jungle map & the arctic map.
- Some minor bugs (a few foot soldiers will still be alive even though the mission prompt says you killed everyone)
- Minor annoyances (After an instant action mission, you are taken back to the main menu instead of to the instact action screen.)
Even though there are more cons than pros, I would still recommend as this is an excellent game despite being in Early Access. I look forward to future updates from this developer & will keep an eye out for any future projects they may create.
Suggestion(s) to further expand on the game experience:
- More opportunities to land at your starting position after you complete a singleplayer mission so the mission feels more 'complete'. Perhaps this can be optional.

Having finished the game I’m updating this review but my opinion hasn’t changed. Tedious, tedious, and tedious.  I have to laugh when I read reviews about how this game doesn't hold your hand like most games.  Huh?  This is one of the most heavily scripted and linear games I've ever played.  Whether it’s through tunnels, rooms or driving down the road there's only one way to go.  It’s not open world and there's no exploring so you can't get lost, you keep going in the same direction.  Walls, buildings or something blocking your path always keeps you linearly going forward so why would you need hand holding?
As for the puzzles, there’s nothing consistent about them.  The point of puzzles or puzzling out the next step is that there has to be consistency so what you learn from the previous one can help provide a method or direction for the next one.  That doesn’t happen in this heavily scripted game.  If the script calls for you to place two boxes on top of each other to climb over something then that's the only thing you could do.  If the script doesn’t want you climbing over two boxes then you can’t, even if the scenarios is very similar to a previous one.  Meaning that the script has a different solution you have to ignore what worked before.
It’s the same with actions like jumping; if the script required you to jump 5ft from one obstacle to another obstacle to get the next point then you did it.  Try that with the next encounter and you can’t even jump 2ft because the script doesn’t want you to go in that direction.  So now you have to figure out what the lame scripted puzzle is for that scenario.  I don’t call inconsistencies in how you puzzle out the next step challenging, rather more like lazy programing.
I played Half-Life 2 and both Episodes and this inconsistency was prevalent in all of them.  In one scenario I piled a couple of boxes on top of each other to jump over a fence.  I could see that the fence ended next to small building and was clearly about a foot taller that the building.  Makes sense to move the boxes next to the building and jump on the roof, right?  Placed the boxes next to the building and jump on them and what do you know, now the building is taller than the fence.  Jumped off the boxes and stepped back and clearly the fence is taller than the building.  Jump back on the boxes and the building again is taller than the fence.  Which basically means that the script doesn’t want me to go that way.  I wasted a lot of time in this game puzzling out the next step with inconstancies like that.  Lazy, lazy programing.
Of all the games I've played this one was definitely the most tedious.  It was stretched out waaayyy too long.  Nothing but heavily scripted scenarios of endless linear hallways, tunnels, roads, waterways while gunning your way running through gauntlets of bullet sponge enemies for no particular reason.
In conclusion I can clearly see why there is no Half-Life 3.  Half-Life definitely belongs in the past when gamers weren’t so particular.

EDIT:
Well, it's been quite a while since I posted this review, and to their credit, the developers have made some solid steps in the right direction.  Not the least of which that they finally (FINALLY) broke down and started nerfing problem legendaries, which many of us feared was against some internal, unwritten policy.
The last expansion was pretty decent, aside from the wildly overtuned Prime Dragon Keeper, which has since been brought into line.  Without killing the card completely.   Which is another thing I do like: when they nerf, it's clear they at least INTEND to try and keep the card playable but fair, even if they don't always hit the mark.  Compare to Warsong Commander's 'soul of the card' nerf in Hearthstone.  Brutal.
So yeah:
Pros:
-WAY more generous than its other main competition.  Dozens of free packs just for sighning up!
-Cute Waifus.
-Overall superior class identity and interesting mechanics.
-Real attempt to support unplayable but interesting cards, and seen in the rise of Atomeme.
-Willingness to admit mistakes and address them without overnerfing.
Cons:
-Heavy push for games to end fast, often resulting in lopsided, aggro vs aggro metas.
-Every expansion seems to pretty much break the game at this point, and only a month later on their scheduled balance pass does it get better again.
-Kinda sleazy practices with the slot-machine class skins . . . though they are only cosmetic, I guess.
-Basically almost everything conceptually wrong with Hearthstone, though to a lesser degree.
I still play the game from time to time, but you really gotta make that call for yourself.  For all its faults, it's still way better than Hearthstone.  And that's something.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
One of the most shocking and saddening turnarounds I've ever seen in an online game.  How could it go so wrong, so fast?
A couple of expansions ago, I left Hearthstone for good in favor of Shadowverse, and at that time my opinion of this game was extremely high.  Now, it's only marginally better than Hearthstone was at its worst, and that's saying something.
Horrifically broken legendary win-conditions (in only a few classes, of course, to ensure nearly no diversity) have essentially power-creeped the evolution mechanic itself into irrelevancy, giving whoever goes first a massive advantage.  Games are far too close to coin flips at this point, where if the player going first has a good hand, they are nearly unbeatable.
I will continue to look in on this game, as the developers have promised frequent balance passes (unlike a certain other popular card game), and if these issues are fixed, I'll be certain to change this review to a recommendation, since the base game WAS excellent in my opinion.  And could still be again.
But as things stand now?  Stay away.  If you're really intrigued by the oodles of freebies and cute waifus, maybe make an account and gather daily login rewards on the chance that they fix this mess, but actually playing the game at this point is just too frustrating.
But that's just, like, my opinion, man.

This is my first time playing Civ V. At first glance, Civ V is great - it has spectacular graphics, and a great audio track. The social policies system and the Science system are attention-grabbing and appear to be well thought out. But beneath the surface, Civ V doesn't quite live up to the plug. The game can be buggy mess - often times, I won't be able to click the next turn button, for example, because it says "A Unit needs Orders" when I have given all of my units orders. This is after putting in all obtainable patches, two years after the game's initial release! The combat in Civ V involves terribly very little strategy - as long as your units are not hard-countered by the enemy's (this is extremely simple to work out) all that matters is who has the biggest military. Civ V's strategy lies entirely in what order the player researches technologies, adapts policies, chooses to produce, etc. and has little to nothing to try and do with combat - reading Sun Tzu's The Art of War will not assist you here. Capturing a city takes at least 3 turns, even if your opponent has no military and you've got several sturdy units assaulting the city. Multiplayer support is horrible, with people perpetually disconnecting and bally whereas i am either in the lobby attempting to urge a game along, or already playing one. There is no thanks to change game settings once you click the "Host Game" button and open your lobby. To do so you've got to kick everybody out and begin a brand new game. This is ridiculous, strategy games from a decade ago have the ability to alter settings whereas within the lobby. Diplomacy with AIs is impossible - even a long-time ally, who I've had multiple trade deals and analysis agreements with, who is so much weaker than me, will declare war on me for no reason... twice! The only indication I had (which was quite obvious) was that the AI stationed its military units near my territory for many turns before attacking. Nothing on the diplomacy screens hinted that the AI disliked me lmao. However, the AIs have supposedly been improved in the Gods & Kings growth... I'll see if there is any truth to that.
I have to give Civilization V a 7/10 because it's fun to play, and it seems like some effort was placed into its creation. From what I've been told by longtime fans of the series going back to Civ 3 or four, Civ V is prettier, but a step backwards wherever gameplay is involved. The exclusion of key gameplay features from earlier Civ games, such as espionage and faith, was clearly a cash grab for Firaxis, now that they are charging $30 for an expansion addon to deliver more content to Civ V. I'm sick of developers churning out pretty games that have worse gameplay than their predecessors. Civ V is a prime example of this, therefore I really cannot give them a positive review.

__________________________________________
'Castle in the Darkness' is a revival of oldschool action-adventure platformers full of tough bosses and hellish platformer sequences. It takes many ideas from the classics of the different genres (e.g. from the Metroid Games, Castlevania III, Ghosts 'n Goblins, Mega Man…) mixes in some interesting new elements and spices the whole dish up with some RPG elements, tons of secrets and a lot of Easter Eggs. The result is a quite tough cookie of a retro-metroidvania that is probably not the healthiest choice - neither for your controller/keyboard nor for your nerves (sometimes it will make you swear so much that even a pub full of sailors would be impressed).
__________________________________________
As the only survivor of the Royal Guard it is your duty to save the Kingdom of Alexandria from attacking monsters (and of course you need to save the princess as well). So you start running and jumping through the levels, armed with a sword, an armor and some magic while looking for treasures and secrets to make your journey easier. Which is quite necessary as the game’s difficulty curve jumps up quite fast and soon you have to face scary platforming sequences and unfriendly creatures. However as spikes kill you instantly (and the architect of the kingdom decided to put them nearly EVERYWHERE) they will probably be your toughest enemies and the stuff your nightmares are made of.
Often it‘s a wise decision to backtrack and look for different ways and areas aside from the main path that you may have missed before. (Luckily there are some Warp points which allow teleportation between several major stages.)
The amount of secrets and optional stuff is huge and if you look closely you can find lots of breakable walls, hidden entrances, fake spikes, optional areas and bosses and items to e.g. increase your health. Many of them are quite well hidden but aside from (more or less obvious) breakable blocks there are several hints to less obvious areas, secrets and abilities – keeping your eyes out in the levels is definitly recommended.
Befitting the oldschool-charm of 'Castle in the Darkness‘ the game comes with good oldschool 8-bit graphics and an (amazing!) 8-bit soundtrack that may bring out some nostalgic feels (- well, at least if you are not mad at some particular spikes and areas in the game).
__________________________________________
If you plan on finding all the secrets and getting all hidden items and stuff you will need some extra hours after finishing the game and it will bring you straight to some nightmarish jumping sections and plattforming areas where you have to start over and over and over and over… again. (At least it rewards you with a secret ending and a NG+ with additional stuff for completing the game 100%).
Always keep in mind: After dying a lot of times the amount of happiness when you finally suceed is way much sweeter:
'Great I finally got the last page from the Book of  the Dead so now I can go back to the safe poin-…
"Here lies…
Died 0000560 times.“
(…oh crap, I forgot about ceiling falling spikes.)
You and this little counter on the death screen will become pretty good friends because you will meet each other very often.
There’s an achievement for dying 500 times. If you want to finish the game at 100% you probably won’t even need suiciding to accumulate this amount of deaths. In the end it said I died 560 times – mostly to spikes I guess.
Yes it can be very frustrating and even if you're used to challenging titles and tough sequences, you will probably end in hating the game or at least some areas as much as you like other parts. Ragequitting the game after dying for the 18th time on an area, isn't that uncommon. One or two additional save points in tough sections would really have been a blessing and could have ended in letting more of my nerves survive the journey.
__________________________________________
If you expect a difficult little retro-platforming action-adventure with some RPG elements 'Castle in the Darkness‘ will entertain you a lot, providing enough content for at least ~6 hours (for the 'regular bad‘ ending) while balancing between motivation and frustration. I rate it 8 out of 10 points and can say that it’s a great little game for the common ~5 bucks in a sale. However, if you're used to difficult games and you have no problems repeating same areas a lot, the game will be funnier for you compared with those who normally tend to choose 'Easy Mode'

I cannot agree more with people whinning about the game, saying that every single expansion brings out more OP cards, some pushing people to play aggro, etc.
But I still cannot stop from RECOMMENDING this game.
I've playing TCGs, CCGs, LCGs my entire life. I played  WoW TCG and MtG for 4-5 years, then aGoT LCG and then Hearthstone for 2-3 years until I quit last year and then I started playing Shadowverse. I have to say the difference is huge.
My review for Shadowverse is(bear in mind some are compared to what Hearthstone offers):
CONS:
- Aggro is more efficient than it should be.
- If you want to get to the high ranks, you have to invest some cash, or a lot of time.
- If you are really competitive, there are only so many decks that are viable.
- Expansions bring some OP cards to make you buy packs.
PROS:
+ You get around 50, if not more, packs free when you start!
+ You get free entries in the arena if you complete the story, missions or just for logging in!
+ You get packs for free when a new expansion comes out!
+ 8 cards per pack!
+ There are very few must HAVE cards for the classes, which greatly improve diversity! Basically there is a big difference between a deck playing aggro and a control deck from the same classes!
+ If you get from one rank bracket to the next, you keep it, FOREVER!
+ You get pack rewards for hitting some score brackets, each month!
+ You get rewarded for playing good and making good decisions.
+ Not that much RNG. Really, the RNG in this game is: card draw, destroy random enemy creature, draw random creature/spell/amulet from your deck. Done. NO RANDOM CARD GENERATION!!!!!!
+ TONS OF UNIQUE MECHANICS, INTERACTIONS AND EFFECTS!
I honestly do not see how people can go back to Hearthstone and all its' RNG after playing this game.
Please give it a shot! I think you would not regret it, if you love card games.

"The Shivah" is a point & click game I have mixed feelings for.
First of all: You play  Rabbi Stone  in New York that has seen better times. Out of nowhere Stone receives the news by the police that an ex-member of his community was found dead and that he left Stone a lot of money. But why? And how did he die?
The story's not the most exciting one I've seen but it's okay. It made me curious that there's something like a Jewish crime plot created as an adventure game. But outside of that gimmick "The Shivah" is rather mediocre than good.
The game is very short. And solving the puzzles involves a lots of email reading. Not really exciting even though the mails provide you with clues like possible login data which are a pain in the *ss to figure out without consulting any walthrough guides. The rest is talking to people and going through clues a few times.
I've played a lot of adventures games and the best of them give you a variety of actions: dialogues, using and collecting objects, going to lots of places. So the gameplay in "The Shivah" feels a little dry.
One of the biggest problems is certainly a bug problem. In my case mail texts and dialogue boxes would just appear for a part of a second and then go away (so important information might get missed). If you notice the same thing, press the ESC key. But beware, it happens throughout the game, especially after leaving the Steam screen inside the game.
But what's good in the game? Well, if you love point & click adventure games, a Jewish crime plot is at least a change.
I like the music, the graphics are nice and the voice acting is a nice touch (even though it could be better sometimes).
Plus: You can consider learning a bit of Yiddish vocabulary and reading Jewish jokes as neat bonus features.
So: I neither say "Go play this game, god damnit!" nor "Avoid this!". If you're interested as I was, just give it a try but better don't pay too much for it.

I saw a short glance of this game on some video on youtube, and INSTANTLY knew that it was my kind of game. I haven't played it much yet, but I will play it to death, mark my words. It just hit my interests dead on. The story is something like they invented a teleporter, and when they turned it on, monsters came through and overtook the station. I can't get enough of that kind of stuff, like Doom, Event Horizon, and the Alien movies. This game will be a total cult hit, I'm calling it now,
Anyway, everything is randomly generated, (level layouts, loot, monster spawns) and the objective is to get through each level, and find the teleporter which will take you to the next level. In the teleporter room, you can choose between two places to go to, which determines the next level. I've only made it to the second level, so the later levels might not give you a choice.
Speaking of which....this game is insanely hard. I take pride in the fact that I still play "ancient" video games from the golden era, and I'm damn good at them. My favorite, being arcade style shooters like Strikers 1945 Plus. I'm damn good at them, so I thought I would also be damn good at this game..........I was wrong. This game is brutal....absolutely brutal.
Some people would say that the graphics are a turn off for them. To them, I say "never judge anything based on looks alone". I personally think these graphics are what makes it such a great little game. It just seems to fit the setting. Not to mention, whenever you fire a gun your character has a bit of a kickback from the kick of the gun, which makes the guns feel better than anything I've played in a long time. Also, whenever you shoot the shotgun, it looks like a roman candle went off. Very colorful.
I really don't know how to explain it. If this is your kind of game, you'll know instantly, like I did. I can't get enough of it. The only complaint that I have, is that it's hard to read some of the writing because of the 80's style computer font, but in context, you'll still be able to easily read it.
