Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Teleglitch is ♥♥♥♥ing hard. Its fast-paced nature and relentless monsters will have you rushing for tucked away secrets and dodging death around every corner; sometimes it's the actual corner that will kill you. The game blends elements from both the rouge and shooter genres perfectly, and in the most unforgiving of ways, while procedurally generated levels make for a fresh experience every play-through. Choosing the right weapon for the right moment while trying not to die from a shotgun wielding zombie is usually the last decision I have to make, but damn it if it's not worth the hour preceding. If you're looking for a challenge, like a cool and unique art style, and enjoy piecing together a legitimately interesting back-story, you've found the game.

Pros
- Simple to learn controls but delightfully complex variation in mechanics thanks to each hero having unique abilities and the truely dazzling array of monsters and items.
- Beautiful pixel art design.
- Great music and sound design.
Cons
- Difficulty can be quite punishing - even on Easy.
- Co-op is more frustrating than fun. As the game zooms out when you get further apart; splitting up or having trouble with jumpers can lead to frustrating hangs in gameplay or outright deaths in harder stretches. Additionally - the visual effects and stacking monsters means that at any zoom levels; it can be a chaotic mess even seeing which player is you among the fireworks display of abilities and monsters.
- Absolutely no narrative if you are into that sort of thing.
Overall I'd say that despite it seeming to be geared for co-op I found the game far more fun playing by myself; though ironically too difficult to beat by myself. This wouldn't be a big deal if the player classes came unlocked or were easier to unlock - but many of them require beating the game or fulfilling difficult feats for a single player run. Simply put I strongly recommend trying before you buy via sharing, refund; or some other means. The game is way too good not to recommend; but oddly unsatisfying as a co-op game.

Mirror's Edge was released in 2007 as one of the first Frostbite Engine games, as a proof-of-concept of sorts. You play as Faith, a runner (messenger) in a futuristic city that can't seem to decide whether it's in America or Asia, with signs displaying both English words and characters. The color scheme is amazing, and the way lighting and textures are handled, I probably would've guessed it was released in 2010 or 2011 based on how good it looks. Faith gets through the city using parkour moves, with the game focusing more on acrobatics than combat mechanics. Running, jumping, sliding, and the other moves feel fluid and not at all nausea-inducing, but fighting is reduced to mashing buttons and hoping you don't die. There are only 3 types of guns, which you pick up off police officers and drop when ammo is gone, but gunplay is minimal in the game. This is encouraged by not being able to do any sort of parkour while holding a gun. I found myself only using Runner Vision (slow-mo) when I really needed to, though mostly just to make long jumps look really cool. I did also find myself accidentally triggering it fairly often. Bugs are rare, having encountered only 2 or 3 in the many times I've played it.
TL;DR - Looks great, but you need a higher-end GPU. Parkour is great, combat not so much. Overall fun, and more should be expected from 2015 (?) sequel. More should be revealed E3 2014.

After almost 30 hours of play I feel this is a good point with which to step back and put down my thoughts about what is believed to be the final main Saint's Row game. I will be speaking from a point of playing Saint's Row: The Third (SRTT) to near 100% though little knowledge of the earlier two games in the series.
Gameplay
Things have improved in this iteration of the Saint's Row series, the addition of superpowers makes navigation of Steelport, formally a bit of a chore, a more pleasant experience. Collectibles scattered across the city make journeys leave you building your collection at times. Much of the handling of vehicles will be instantly recognisable to anyone who's played SRTT, though you will find yourself quickly dropping them with the introduction of your run and jump powers.
Regarding your powers, I do feel the game delivers too much too soon. I can understand that the majority of players are just dying to get their hands on what they can as soon as possible, but too much too soon is rarely good, and I feel that in this instance it spoils the pacing through the rest of the game.
Returning to Saints Row 4 are activities, some of which you will remember from SRTT, and many others which are new to the series. There is enough diversity in the activities and 'targets' (an extention of the street gang activities of SRTT) that you won't often find yourself bored with the checklist of activities your homies love to give you. The difference this time round is that you are given gold, silver and bronze rewards, allowing larger prizes from the latter. However, I found there was little challenge in most of these and the gold reward could usually be earned in under 3 attempts. Your reward for completing these events are unlocks you often can't get any other way, making them a useful thing to get as you move through the story.
Story
Unlike the Gameplay, which sometimes feels to be a clone of SRTT, the story goes far beyond the earthly constraints of its predecessor. If you're looking to throw realism out of the window then this is the game you need. There are moments of dialogue that are priceless, the majority involving your standoff with the game' main antagonist, an alien overlord with a British accent and impeccable, cultured tastes in music and literature.
My biggest gripe with the story is not in the quality of the writing, but with its' quantity. Including the aforementioned side quests, the game takes no more than 20 hours to finish and When you break it down, there's little more than 5-8 hours of actual main story. That said, though, it is a great storyline, offering fantastic insight into the background and motivation of the other characters. However, without a knowledge of the previous games, your enjoyment of the story will be diminished. Halfway through playing I felt I needed to go flick over to Wikipedia to brush up on past plot lines, though after doing so I had a renewed interest in the storyline. The game does try giving you some background before important quests, though I feel this is more to remind players what they did, rather than introduce newer players to those stories.
Beyond the main story, you can also collect sound bites from most characters as well as 'text adventure' chapters explaining the background of our main antagonist. Both of which do well to expand their thoughts and feelings and round out the Saint's journey from nobody Streetgang to the White House.
Conclusion
Aside from this game being from first appearances to be to SRTT what Blood Dragon is to Far Cry 3 (that is, a wackier, more neon-filled experience), Saint's Row 4 does a good job of doing everything its predecessor did right, again, but going beyond in almost all respects.
If you find yourself with a spare weekend with nothing to do, I would advise picking this up, especially if you've played the previous games in the series. At this point, however, I feel £40 is a little much for what is delivered to you. Wait for the Steam sale like many of us did with SRTT and you can't go wrong.

This is a legitimatley fun game that I think can appeal to a wide audience. As many are stating, if you have played C.O.D. zombies, or LFD2, there are some great similarities to this game. Personally, I have only played C.O.D. zombies, and had a great deal of hours invested back in Black Ops 2. It was a fun game that almost all my friends had at the time, and we could enjoy all the different maps, and always trying to work together. Personally, those days are over, and I mainly play games by myself since most of my friends are always too busy to ever play games with me. Killing Floor 2 now is coming through for me, and with the few hours I currently have writing this review, I can tell there will be many more to come. The game is great for any player who has lots of friends, or plays by themself like me, since there are always large open servers for all sorts of things, such as the vanilla game, and an extremely good mod community for maps.
The gameplay itself is extremely basic compared to the likes of C.O.D. zombies, but with the differnet difficulty levels make it hard to master. It mainly revolves around you choosing a class, which includes basic things, such as a dps, a healer, a support, but also fun things, like the firebug, the gunslinger, and the survivor, which causes a bit more roleplay, and a leveling system to help you get better through playing each class. This is extremely cool, as you can have people playing whatever class they like best, and not requiring specific classes, such as in Overwatch, where the current basic setup would be 2/2/2 (2 dps, 2 tanks, 2 healers). You choose your class before the game starts, and can change in the middle of rounds.
In between rounds, you visit the trader, who allows you to purchase guns, which are somewhat limited due to class choice, since you want to use the ones they suggest for your class, as they will get a boost for the gun due to class choice. You can carry 15 pounds of guns, which also makes it where you can't be Rambo and have a bajillion guns, making the game extremely unfair. It causes you to think and plan out a little, which is pretty neat.
Lastly, you have the bosses. At the moment, this is probably the only downside, as there are only 2 bosses that have a chance of spawing. Both are fun and somewhat balanced fights, but my only problem would be the lack of. More from what I can find are to be implemented soon, but if this is a major problem to you, similar to the way I see it, it can be easily overlooked, due to all the other amazing content the game offers.
There is also a PvP mode, which I'm not going to get into too much depth, as most people are not going to buy the game just for it, but I played a few rounds so far, and it is done well to where it is extremely balanced, and fun to play every now and then between rounds.
TL;DR: If you are looking here to look, this game is great, if you are on the fencepost, get it. And if the price concerns you, wait for a sale. At the current time, $20.00 (USD) is the lowest price it has gone at the current time, which I would consider a steal for all the great content and hours it can provide.

To sum up this game in a single sentence: Fairy Fencer F (FFF) is a Compile Heart RPG.
For anyone who has played Hyperdimension Neptunia (HDN) you'll know exactly what that means, and if you enjoyed those games then you will enjoy this one just as much. For those who don't like HDN there isn't anything here that will change your mind about the Compile Heart's style. The gameplay is the same, the characters are all full of tropes, the dialogue is hilarious for all the right/wrong reasons, and there's a whole lot of disjointed visual novel style scenes to go through.
Now for those who have never tried a Compile Heart game before to sum up the gameplay briefly: There's an overwold map with minor interaction where you point at the next dungeon, all dungeons are fairly short and samey, the combat system has some pretty good depth to it but due to how easy their games are any depth becomes meaningless, and most importantly you can spam jump while in dungeons.
Now speaking specifically about this game the gameplay, as mentioned above, has a serious problem in the difficulty department. There will never be a point you'll find yourself grinding for levels because the game doesn't start punishing you harshly until the enemies are basically 1.2-1.7 times your level. A cool new feature this game has is also the ability to distribute the stats into the character the way you want, AND while you perform actions with your characters they gain stats for the traits that relate (ex, jumping a bunch in the dungeon boosts agility, using magic a lot boosts SP, collecting items a lot boosts luck) unfortunately there is almost no noticeable difference because everything is just so incidental.
That may all seem negative, because it kind of is, but for some reason none of that matters once you start getting into the gameplay. The semi-strategy RPG style layout with aoe hit zones and movement zones mixed with the turn based combat is indescribably way more satisfying than it ever should be. It's hard to explain why and can only be experienced first hand.
Moving onto the story... well. It's a JRPG and Compile Heart really likes doing the classic (you're a hero now, you need to do x, and stop y from returning and save the planet) JRPG story, but they enjoy doing it with large parties of really enjoyable characters who are all quite hilarious. Also the main character in this game is quite possibly the most unlikable likable main character to come out this year.
Overall: While FFF might not be as good a game as HDN was it is certainly a fantastic addition to the library of any fan of JRPGs.

Reploished first trial of Dave Gilbert, creator of the wonderfull Blackwell series... would have been better to be left at peace. As a game, it is horrible. As a story, it is barely okay.
The bulk of the game is made up of reading e-mails after the ridiculous "hacking" of three e-mail addresses (one of which is your own, but it still requires password-guessing). According to the developer, "finding out" passwords after finding ridicolously obvious clues is a good puzzle -- not only it is not, it is tiringly repetitive here. After the e-mail reading, you have some really straightforward chitchatting and then you can come to the endgame.
The endgame is one large puzzle which can end in disasters in so many way. So most of your time playing this game will spend on re-re-re-re-re-playing the endgame and try to solve it with try-and-error. Because there is very little you can learn to help you to find out in advance how to avoid the pitfalls.
As to the story, it is schematic and largely incoherent. It is also very short. I would be willing to pay for a two-hour game if it comes up with a gripping story, but it is like the overly simplifed, bared-downed draft of a thirteenth-class film noir.
If you like this childish amateurship or you are a devouted fan of Dave Gilbert, buy this game today. If you expect the brillant, touching storytelling of the Blackwell series, stay away.

The recent Wonderland Dreams expansion has brought a lot of mixed reactions along with it (literally, check the recent reviews). Dominated by a single archetype that's fitting the name of "Spawn of the Abyss", the ladder on lower ranks turn into something of purgatory, where mirror matches are abundant and the outcome is almost very easily determined by who goes first in the said mirror match.
However, following the various desperate attempts of countering the archetype-that-must-not-be-named, the july nerfs dropped, and quite frankly, it was necessary. Overcoming their streak of not wanting to nerf any legendaries, Cygames managed to swallow their pride and nerfed not 1, not 2, but 3 legendaries in the same update.
So how is the current state of the meta? Well, it has somewhat returned to the pre-WD meta, except that the power levels of the classes are currently much more balanced, with shadow and dragon not as oppressive as it was, haven receiving new tools from the expansion, and the abundance of control decks makes combo decks like Dimension Shift, Wolf Bolt, and OTK Roach serves a purpose to counter the current meta decks in the ladder, and in tournaments.
I, and i'm sure cygames too, are aware that this game's meta is not perfect, but they are trying to balance it out by releasing an update at the end of every month now. So far, the state of the ranked ladder is much more acceptable than it was pre-nerf, and if you want to get into the game, or resume playing, now is a good time to do so.

So far in EA, Air Missions: HIND lacks some polish, needs to change some fonts and get to do some serious work on the campaign aspect. Which is really not that bad for EA - especially since the hard part, flying, is aced. HINDs feel very good to fly. The line between arcade and simulation is set so that it's easy to get into - and yet you still get to enjoy helicopter-specific maneuverability. While you can play it like a "tank in 3d space" on easiest control mode, the highest one gives you enough realism to feel just right.
As of now (v0.63) the value proposal as-is is lacking - as can be expected in NA obviously. Nevertheless the game has really good prospects - with just a few additions of more "instant-action" missions replay-ability would jump through the roof. A few more options here, a few difficulty settings there, some challenges and new missions - is all the game needs, and the framework is already there and working.
All in all, while a lot of work and love is still needed, the game shows a very good promise and - more importantly - Dev team seems to be well within the ability to provide.

It's also a reasonably pretty game. The graphics are a little cartoony, but with enough detail to let you enjoy the dystopian cyberpunk future theme.
The bad: It's extremely simple/easy, painfully linear, there's no voice acting, and while conversations give you the impression that your choices matter, the game appears largely devoid of meaningful consequences. I'd call it a "video graphic novel," except the writing isn't even all that good, and (despite some more positive reviews) there's not even that much writing to begin with. It's also short. Really short.
Bottom line: This is a simple game that would feel rewarding if it were a free mobile game instead of pretending to be a full-fledged PC RPG. If you can get it on sale for a couple of bucks, it might be worth it as a gateway to the superior Shadowrun games that follow, but as is, this is not a $15 game.
The "crime/detective" themes try to make it feel like an old point and click adventure game, except your options are so limited that it feels like a "mystery" designed for a 5 year old to solve. Despite the emphasis on "tactical combat," fights tend towards the easy. Resource management is a joke because you should always have plenty of money to buy equipment and a full high-level team, so there's no additional "should I get better armor or a new gun" type of trade-off. The result is boredom. The game spends too much time in the turn-based combat mode (even between discrete combat encounters), so simply walking from one fight to the next has to be done individual party member at a time.

I got this game when it was being offered for free, and was excited to try what I knew to be a super difficult rogue-like. I had gotten my feet wet playing Binding of Isaac, and was hungry for more brutally difficult games.
Wow, was I in for a surprise.
If you like unforgiving, brutal gameplay, dying a lot, top-down action, being mobbed over and over, and dying a lot, then you will probably rage at this game (and possibly enjoy it). Oh, did I mention you will die a lot? The game is labelled: Die More Edition because you will die more times in one hour than in most other games you have played before.
The aesthetics are rather simple and reminiscent of old-school, top-down pixel games. The different effects (weapon, item, etc) are very well done - the "stimulant" effect is really nice, making the screen look a bit erratic until the drug wears off. There is no music, but the sound assets are pretty good - especially the explosions. Much of the story is given through text, and more is available for people who choose to explore. The story is interesting enough, however, I have not advanced far enough in the game to account for more than 20% (or less) of it. The furthest I've progressed is to level 4, where I died almost immediately to an endless swarm of varying enemies. Fun times.
The controls take a bit of getting used to, especially considering that you need to be able to do things very quickly, while simultaneously dodging, running, and attacking. It is playable with a controller, but I prefer the keyboard and mouse in this case. Gameplay is very fast-paced once enemies spot you, and the learning curve is minimal to extreme - highly dependent on your experience with rogue-likes and how far you progress in the game. There is a tutorial mission that shows you everything you need to know - I highly recommend you play through this first. Teleglitch is not a pure rogue-like - the items found in each level are not randomized (only the layout of the map is) - so you will eventually be able to plan out which item combinations to use/save as you become more familiar with the game.
During gameplay, you must move through different rooms until you find a teleporter to transport you to the next stage. Sometimes, there will be a branching point (two teleporters, left and right), allowing you to select which stage to move on to. There is an insane amount of repetition here because the only thing that really changes is how each level is presented - the items stay the same. Also, the checkpoint system is very unforgiving, as you must reach stage 5 in order to start a new game at stage 3 (and so on).
Much of the game involves combining items that you find (ex: combining C4 and a can to make a one-shot RPG) to help you survive each level. Because of this, it is highly recommended that you explore as much of each stage as you can. Herein lies the double-edged sword - the more you explore, the more enemies you will encounter. Healing items and ammo are not common enough to allow you to recklessly run through the level, so finding a balance between exploring and saving items is key to success in Teleglitch.
As a top-down action game, you will have to also deal with field of view - if you are standing in front of a pillar, for example, you will not be able to see anything directly behind it. This encourages you not to run into a room guns blazing, as you may be ambushed from all sides (the enemy AI is very good at swarming tactics). A personal technique I prefer using is to quickly double-back into a narrow hallway, allowing you to funnel the enemy into your line of fire (very cost effective, considering the rarity of resources like ammo and health). Aiming is a bit tricky in the beginning, but with time, you will become more proficient. Also, you will (hopefully) learn the melee range of different opponents - it is very dangerous to try to melee more than one enemy at a time, trading HP until one of you dies.
There is an Arena mode that adds more playability (especially if you intend to achieve 100% completion). Each Arena mission requires you to perform different tasks like survive for x seconds, kill x enemies, etc. There are different equipment loadouts for you to select, and I highly recommend trying this out to help you learn which weapons/items are more suited for your playstyle. For example, the automatic pistol is a great anti-mob weapon, however, I personally prefer the slower, more accurate revolver (also has less ammo before needing to reload). As a result, I tend to keep the pistol, over upgrading it to an automatic pistol. You can drop items and equipment - dropping a weapon allows you to transfer any ammo inside it to another same-calibre weapon (ex: drop auto pistol to transfer ammo to your regular pistol). One of the first upgrades you will find in the campaign mode is the automatic pistol combo, so trying both variants will help you determine which one is a better fit. As a rule, I tend to stay away from any planted explosives, as I tend to get caught in the blast radius (and HP is your most important resource). To heal, you can use medkits and canned meat, however, canned meat and explosives (weird, I know) can be combined to give you stimulants - recommend you try it out at least one to experience the cool visual effects.
There is one environmental hazard to be aware of - parts of each level may have time distortions (you'll know what it is when you first see and hear it), and touching one will cause you to instantly die. Don't bother trying to bait enemies into it - they're not that stupid, and it's quite impossible.
Overall, Teleglitch is a great top-down (not-so-quite)rogue-like game that will challenge any and all gamers. If you are interested in the genre, you must give it a try.
Recommend!

This was a pretty pleasant little adventure down the Metroidvania hole. It's got pretty much everything you want, weapon/armor/magic upgrades, hidden paths with challenging platforming, boss fights that are, for the most part, challenging but very, very fair, and a ton of hidden goodies to go back and find. At this time I'm at 94% completion and I've finished the 'main' boss. I probably won't go back and find the last 3 or 4 things, because at least 2 of them I forgot to grab on a save and they're behind a long platforming section :^)
Sound/Graphics - 9/10: Pretty much what you'd expect from this genre. Crunchy sounds, crisp sprites that make it pretty clear that something is bad news. They do the job and don't get in the way.
Controls - 9/10: Once I took some time to get familiar with controls, I didn't have a single death that wasn't absolutely my fault. A few from impatience, but I should have stopped playing for the session before that happened. You get a jump, then you get a double jump, and there are some other mechanics involed that help you maneuver. Standard stuff executed well give the player very reliable control.
Platforming - 9/10: Platforming elements are introduced slowly and the truly difficult ones are generally either bracketed by save points OR are one way - you get the treasure and then the spikes or w/e go away. Sometimes it'll be the opposite - easy to get in, and then an unexpected wrinkle makes it hard to get out. The nice thing is that like Super Meat Boy, you're never more than a minute or two from a save point, so you don't get super frustrated if you die. Every platforming sequence is very doable, nothing is frame perfect that I've seen.
Upgrades/Findables - 8/10: All of the upgrades feel weighty and useful, and quite a few of them make the game DRAMATICALLY easier. A lot of people complaining about the game being too hard may have not put in the exploration tax. Without certain spells, or enough HP, or a certain weapon, you'll get dunked early and often. I docked two points here because the spells are just way too powerful, and unchecked. The strongest sword in the game, for which you need to defeat a fairly difficult encounter, pales in comparison to any of the top four spells. Pair that with the fact that magic is free as long as you charge it and this game can quickly turn into Megaman. It seems to be balanced around that so I can't complain, it's just that swords were a bit disappointing. I guess the best way to look at swords is as trophies, as they all come after pretty cool encounters and require some digging to get to.
Map Layout - 10/10: This game does a fantastic job of encouraging you to explore and take notes. It'll dangle doors and platforming elements out in front of you that you can't complete, and if you're thorough you'll find a key for that door or remember that a new ability will get you past an old obstacle from earlier in the game.  It's VERY easy to traverse the map given the fast travel system, and you're heavily encouraged to do so. Guides are available, but a keen eye and a will to check all available paths will get you to at least 90% complete. This game throws a lot of the classics at you: sliding platforms, nonexistent blind roof jumps, phasing platforms, nothing you haven't seen. There are some really cool exploration elements at play and if you don't go out of your way to see everything the game has to offer you'll probably miss at least half of the content. Also, the last 'level' will ♥♥♥♥ you up because you'll be super undergeared.
Enemies/Bosses - 9/10: There is not a single boss in this game that you can't beat iwthout taking more than 25% damage. If you learn the patterns you can crush everything. That said, boss art is great, attacks are fun, and with a little analysis you SHOULD be able to breeze thorugh 99% of the content. There are a few bosses that are pretty brutal, but usually there is a save point right before them so you can get reps in quick. Enemies are pretty standard and level with you as you go, but if you're gearing/exploring they should all take ~4 hits and all hit you for about 10-30% damage.
Difficulty - 10/10: I feel like this section needs to be included because of the negative reviews. This game is difficult. It's not 'brvtal' or 'savage' or 'cheap', but it's difficult. There are sections that will frustrate all but the absolute best platformers, but there's nothing that is as hard as say, the three-screen fall in VVVVVV or anything APPROACHING the high end SMB stages. It requires you to put in work to explore if you want to have a fighting chance. You will not breeze through this game with the stuff it gives you in the main quest line. The reward is that you wind up with a powerful character, some neat gear, and a great experience. I think that's a fair trade.
Overall I give this a 9.5/10. It's a recommended buy at the standard $6 and a must have at anything less.
Also, if  you're on the fence, don't hesitate to buy and try it. You will know WELL within 2 hours if this game is for you.

I hold my gun up as I approach a new door, the generators roaring in the background, I peek through the opening door. Nothing is visible. I tip over slowly to the open arena as I check over my blind spots. Still, nothing. Its frustrating to see nothing within my view. Although uncertain about the location of any Biounits, I lower my sights to look for any resources on the ground. Picking up what little provisions left in this planet. I dine on my 8th Cannedmeat, despite being sick off eating this junk, there's little room to complain when trying to survive. I open up my inventory and craft myself a Cangun from the things I've accumulated this far.
As I exit the area and onto the next, a large pipe enters my field of view. Without any methods of detection, I can only pray that nothing resides inside the complex infrastructure of the pipelines. I get ready to run away as I slowly crawl near the death trap. 10 metres is the distance between me and the pipe. 10 metres was the distance I had before sprinting away the horde of Swarmbots that started chasing me after this hell hole. Low on ammo, I didn’t want to waste any more on my chasers. As I recall a Void located near a sharp turned corner and I figured I’d use it to my advantage. I approach the emanating darkness, doing a quick turn forcing the bots to fall into oblivion. My ears cringe at the echo that rips through reality as my eyes readjust from the blurred images back to my surroundings. But I quickly collect myself to finish off the remaining bots.
I return back to the pipe room to see two Red Guards with a Twin Shotgun. I quickly retreat back behind the doors and wait to gun them as soon as they enter my sights. Reloading, I take a moment to look at the cybernetic guards that were once human. I realize that one of them was a patrol that visited my station often. He was an energetic guy that brought all kinds of restricted magazines in our isolated planet. Noticing that he was still breathing, I kneel beside, unsheathe my knife, and lay him to rest. I pick up the Twin Shotgun and head over to the next room, prepared to shoot any hostile that tries to head my way. “Goodbye, my friend.”
Clearing and searching through almost all of the available rooms in this facility, I reach a door that opens up to a large hanger. Despite not being a Robotic Engineer, I recognized that this was the hanger that produced a Grade A weaponry called the Blue Walker; a specialized Tactical Support Walker that shines in comparison to a normal War Walker. I bolt behind the pillars as the Walker awakens itself and aims its homing rockets towards me. Demolishing both walls and pillars, I carefully aim my shots between each interval of rockets as rotate towards a new pillar. The Walker destroys a wall that exposes a pipe to the hanger. And just my luck, another bunch of Swarmbots enter this confined room with little choice of maneuverability. Left with no other options, I blast my Cangun that I crafted earlier towards both the robots. After the usage of a stimulant, a RDX_500, and depleting all of my Rifle Ammo, the Walker finally deactivates.
Half my body is bruised and worn out, I’m growing weaker from fatigue and hunger, and am running out of both ammo and resources. But I must press forward. I will do my damnest to get out of this hell hole. I will get to the Master Teleporter and escaped back to my family and friends. I will-
As I opened the door to the next area, a Turret caught me right in the centre of its sights and shot a burst of rounds through me before I could get the doors to shut. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ f*ck. I can’t die here… I can’t!” But it was too late. I was already lying on the ground, my warm blood drenching the floor. The range and strength of my causality field have reduced to zero.. And just as I lost consciences, I hear an Assembly Bot dragging me away to somewhere else…
The next time I awake, I realize I’m no longer awake. I feel myself moving but am not controlling my body. I see myself shooting things, shooting humans like myself. Then I understand that I am not myself. That I have become the very entity I strived to escape from. That I became the same things that took control of my Guard friends. And as I look to the top of my vision, I see a log entry that says: ‘Game Over.’

Pros
- Simple to learn controls but delightfully complex variation in mechanics thanks to each hero having unique abilities and the truely dazzling array of monsters and items.
- Beautiful pixel art design.
- Great music and sound design.
Cons
- Difficulty can be quite punishing - even on Easy.
- Co-op is more frustrating than fun. As the game zooms out when you get further apart; splitting up or having trouble with jumpers can lead to frustrating hangs in gameplay or outright deaths in harder stretches. Additionally - the visual effects and stacking monsters means that at any zoom levels; it can be a chaotic mess even seeing which player is you among the fireworks display of abilities and monsters.
- Absolutely no narrative if you are into that sort of thing.
Overall I'd say that despite it seeming to be geared for co-op I found the game far more fun playing by myself; though ironically too difficult to beat by myself. This wouldn't be a big deal if the player classes came unlocked or were easier to unlock - but many of them require beating the game or fulfilling difficult feats for a single player run. Simply put I strongly recommend trying before you buy via sharing, refund; or some other means. The game is way too good not to recommend; but oddly unsatisfying as a co-op game.

I've spent a significant amount of hours playing this game with my two children. While the game is geared towards a younger audience, it's easily enjoyed by adults who can be proportionate with their expectations. LEGO games are generally well designed, but LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is -- at least in my opinion -- the best overall. It's easy to get into, the controls and mechanics feel intuitive, puzzles are easy enough for younger gamers (it's enjoyable to watch the trial and error as they attempt to figure out each challenge), the characters are cheesy but likeable and comical. I actually even began a play through with my ex-wife at one point and we were both entertained by it.
Overall, this game is pretty great. I'd love to see a continuation of the series that overhauls the game by taking it's foundation and expanding upon what's already layed down. Anyone with children or even those who find these games entertaining, I'd definitely recommend it.

Oh boy, what do I say? No spoilers of course.
Antichamber is a puzzle game unlike literally anything you've ever known. It's got the same 'how did I not get that, I'm so dumb' feeling as Portal/Portal 2, but also has the feel of the Stanley Parable. Like the Stanley Parable, the secret of Antichamber isn't what happens, but the underlying meaning and denseness of what's going on. It's hard to explain, but that's what it's like.
The Good:
Antichamber is something just fantastically mental. While it has the just puzzle elements of other games like Portal, the rest of it depends on your understanding of what the bloody hell is going on. The messing of perspective and non-euclidian nature of shapes and things is totally new and bonkers. Also it looks very nice too. While not particularly graphically exiting, it does have a nice colour scheme, base white with other colours painted onto it. And the exploration of the one HUGE  level (No loading screens!) and manipulation of 'stuff' with your four guns opens possibilities. Sometimes to go fowards, you have to backtrack, get something and try again.
The Bad:
The puzzles can certainly be very weak. After obtaining the guns, rather than being perspective neural nightmares, they just become block puzzles. Some can be very, very difficult, so you'll either wonder around aimlessly for while for something to do, or just google the answer. And also it doesn't support some resolutions, like 1600x900. Finally, I would say for £15, I think it's a little overpriced. Maybe £10 pounds would be more reasonable.
The Verdict:
If you just want something new and ingenious, just buy it. While you may forget it after you get stuck on one puzzle for 1000 years, the 999 years beforehand will most likely be fantastically bonkers.

Antichamber is one of the few games I ponder whether or not I really like.  It's beautiful, and surreal, and one of the most frustrating experiences I've ever encountered.  It's a little like The Stanley Parable (it's not a game it's an EXPERIMENT,) but there's no story to speak of, just a lot of puzzles and going through corridors and things of that ilk.  It looks really cool, but in terms of fun, there isn't much to be had.  It's interesting, to be sure, and I love experimental and different video games, but I like to know that I'm playing them for a set reason and will be rewarded for my time spent.  Antichamber makes no such promises.

This is a legitimatley fun game that I think can appeal to a wide audience. As many are stating, if you have played C.O.D. zombies, or LFD2, there are some great similarities to this game. Personally, I have only played C.O.D. zombies, and had a great deal of hours invested back in Black Ops 2. It was a fun game that almost all my friends had at the time, and we could enjoy all the different maps, and always trying to work together. Personally, those days are over, and I mainly play games by myself since most of my friends are always too busy to ever play games with me. Killing Floor 2 now is coming through for me, and with the few hours I currently have writing this review, I can tell there will be many more to come. The game is great for any player who has lots of friends, or plays by themself like me, since there are always large open servers for all sorts of things, such as the vanilla game, and an extremely good mod community for maps.
The gameplay itself is extremely basic compared to the likes of C.O.D. zombies, but with the differnet difficulty levels make it hard to master. It mainly revolves around you choosing a class, which includes basic things, such as a dps, a healer, a support, but also fun things, like the firebug, the gunslinger, and the survivor, which causes a bit more roleplay, and a leveling system to help you get better through playing each class. This is extremely cool, as you can have people playing whatever class they like best, and not requiring specific classes, such as in Overwatch, where the current basic setup would be 2/2/2 (2 dps, 2 tanks, 2 healers). You choose your class before the game starts, and can change in the middle of rounds.
In between rounds, you visit the trader, who allows you to purchase guns, which are somewhat limited due to class choice, since you want to use the ones they suggest for your class, as they will get a boost for the gun due to class choice. You can carry 15 pounds of guns, which also makes it where you can't be Rambo and have a bajillion guns, making the game extremely unfair. It causes you to think and plan out a little, which is pretty neat.
Lastly, you have the bosses. At the moment, this is probably the only downside, as there are only 2 bosses that have a chance of spawing. Both are fun and somewhat balanced fights, but my only problem would be the lack of. More from what I can find are to be implemented soon, but if this is a major problem to you, similar to the way I see it, it can be easily overlooked, due to all the other amazing content the game offers.
There is also a PvP mode, which I'm not going to get into too much depth, as most people are not going to buy the game just for it, but I played a few rounds so far, and it is done well to where it is extremely balanced, and fun to play every now and then between rounds.
TL;DR: If you are looking here to look, this game is great, if you are on the fencepost, get it. And if the price concerns you, wait for a sale. At the current time, $20.00 (USD) is the lowest price it has gone at the current time, which I would consider a steal for all the great content and hours it can provide.

Volition had labeled it "the climactic chapter" of the Saints Row franchise, and having played through it, I can see why. Holy crap. Think of every open-world game you've played since the first Saints Row game came out. Now think about the best elements of those all mixed into a game that I feel strangely compelled to describe with the phrase "cataclysmically ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic", as I'm not sure lesser terms will do.
Now, I'm not saying this is the game to end all games. There are quite a few repetitive side quests, it only took me about 16 hours to finish all missions (not all challenges, though) and WAY too many Mayhem missions of infinitely stale varieties (Steer a tank! Fly a UFO! Throw a ball!), but there are enough totally badass moments to make up for those. The plot is strangely engaging for the premise, really giving players a look back at the true natures of the Saints and their foes, through their nightmares and their greatest triumphs. Plus, there's a telekinesis system that actually grabs the damn thing you want it to, unlike every other game I've seen try it.
The radio selection is subpar, but the original soundtrack is bountiful, and the licensed songs that do get used are perfectly timed. The game takes all its blatant parodies in spectacular stride, while still coming across as a Saints Row story first and foremost. Those who've stuck with the series since the beginning will find a lot to love in returning content, as will PC users who had to start with SR2 (you're really going to just be confused for, like, two missions, in that case).
The powers just work well, though the game's repeated insistence on taking them away from you for missions gets a bit grating eventually. There are also some major glitches at this stage, but programmers and modders are fast at work on them. Basically, as with The Third, if you can't get past something, turn down your resolution.
All in all, this game is simply irresistible. If you haven't played the game, you probably don't get what I'm referring to. More incentive to play it.

The recent Wonderland Dreams expansion has brought a lot of mixed reactions along with it (literally, check the recent reviews). Dominated by a single archetype that's fitting the name of "Spawn of the Abyss", the ladder on lower ranks turn into something of purgatory, where mirror matches are abundant and the outcome is almost very easily determined by who goes first in the said mirror match.
However, following the various desperate attempts of countering the archetype-that-must-not-be-named, the july nerfs dropped, and quite frankly, it was necessary. Overcoming their streak of not wanting to nerf any legendaries, Cygames managed to swallow their pride and nerfed not 1, not 2, but 3 legendaries in the same update.
So how is the current state of the meta? Well, it has somewhat returned to the pre-WD meta, except that the power levels of the classes are currently much more balanced, with shadow and dragon not as oppressive as it was, haven receiving new tools from the expansion, and the abundance of control decks makes combo decks like Dimension Shift, Wolf Bolt, and OTK Roach serves a purpose to counter the current meta decks in the ladder, and in tournaments.
I, and i'm sure cygames too, are aware that this game's meta is not perfect, but they are trying to balance it out by releasing an update at the end of every month now. So far, the state of the ranked ladder is much more acceptable than it was pre-nerf, and if you want to get into the game, or resume playing, now is a good time to do so.

The game is meant to be a fast-paced reaction game with energetic music and a simplistic design, highly similar to Super Hexagon. And on a presentational front, it succeeds. Unlike Super Hexagon, however, the gameplay is conceptually flawed. (In other words, it sucks.) Where Super Hexagon almost continually presents a fair challenge, Tetradecagon  presents the player with an illusion of skill-based play without any form of a fair challenge.
The game concept seems fine at first: rotate the outer ribs of different polygonic shapes to keep a ball inside from bouncing out in an interesting combination of pong and juggling. However, the concept ends up falling flat for a few reasons.
A relatively minor problem is that the polygon spins really fast because that's the only way the game can get even remotely close to allowing you to catch the ball, which also moves extremely fast. This speed makes angling shots off of the rib pretty much impossible. That becomes a problem when the only way you can repeatedly juggle the ball is by knocking it straight to the other side ; if you knock it at too much of an angle (lets say, to the rib next to the one you hit it from), the path is so short that there is actually no way to prevent game-overing.
The more severe problem is that the rib(s) of the polygon that you're supposed to hit the ball with, change(s) with every strike at the ball, with the new rib being chosen at at random. This takes valuable time to register in your mind, time that you therefore lose to actually turn the ball in time and means that there's a high change that the new rib spawns in a location that's on the exact opposite end of the polygon from where the ball is headed. It can actually be impossible to do the 180 turn required to catch it on the other side because the pall's path through the polygon is more efficient than your speed of spinning the polygon. And even if you do manage such a clutch turn, the previous problem kicks in: it's likely that you didn't have the time to aim this shot, which means it's likely to knock the ball back at a completely indefensible angle.
Consequently, you are not guaranteed to be able to win at all. You can get a series of easy rib spawns and then get screwed by a series of two bad spawns that make you game over.
That's bad game design. And it's a real shame, because the concept seems clever; it's just not executable in any realistic way

Shadowrun Returns was one of my most hyped games the year it came out - and while I'm writing this review now that I've completed all three, I think one of the biggest things that it had going for it was nostalgia.  Of the three (SRR, Dragonfall, Hong Kong), it's the worst - but that doesn't make it a bad game in the least.  It's a fun, quick jaunt through a familiar game setting with familiar faces and it's definitely worth the play through, but (and this is a reasonably big but) even with the nostalgia factor, it pales in comparison to the other two - Dragonfall, especially.
Independent of the other two, it's an awesome intro into the universe and a lot of fun.  In context to the other two, it's like a nostalgia trip: it looks better than you remember the original, plays better, and feels better - until you actually *play* better, and then it feels good but not great.  If this all comes across as backhanded, that's not intentional; the entire Shadowrun series by Harebrained is a lot of fun and well worth checking out.

This game is very short, but worth its price tag nonetheless.  It had all the darkness-with-a-touch-of-humour that I have come to treasure in the Wadjet Eye game along with references to places and characters I was familiar with from the Blackwell series. I definitely recommend this to the people that I like and to fans of the point-and-click mystery genre.

I used to like this game but the past 2 expansions have been completely unbalanced garbage, with the most recent expansion having the game in the worst state its ever been in. This expansion focused on making neutral cards viable. That means every class you run into is running the exact same turn 1-4 plays, including the best deck in the game, which is the most oppressive deck the game has ever had. There are techs against it, but no actual counters. As far as I'm aware, no deck has a positive winrate against it. And according to Cygames, they aren't going to change any of this until the end of the month. And that's a "maybe." The game isn't fun anymore. Games end so fast they're entirely draw-dependent and going first is a huge advantage. Class identity is dead since every class optimally runs the same early-game neutral cards. The state of Ranked being nothing but a singular Tier 0 deck means Unranked is full of past metas' viable decks that don't work in today's Ranked, so you can't even play stupid meme stuff and have fun like you used to be able to. The last expansion was a mess, and this one is twice as bad. Any hope I had that Cygames would pull this game together again is dead.
11/13/17 EDIT: Hey look they actually fixed it. After that mess of an expansion, the developers basically said they'd stop being stupid by printing blatantly broken cards to push certain classes, and they've actually kept to their word. Starforged Legends is a really good set and it pulled the game back together nicely. All that needed to happen is for half of every Wonderland Dreams card to get nerfed to death, and that's okay. It's a good game now, and I think I trust Cygames to keep it that way.

Though a bit cliche, Fairy Fencer F has its plus points. If you enjoyed games like Neptunia of Mugen Souls, then you won't need to read reviews to see if it will be worth it. Just watch some gameplay and you'll know if you want to.
The game features a Fairy Link system, giving you more personality in your custimization of your character(s). If you want to have a tank, mage or maybe a strong damage per turn. The only real walking you'll be doing is in dungeons, so you don't have to sidetrack the towns in order to go everywhere before heading out. The final part that the game offers is its "Gods Revival" option. By using existing Fairies you can upgrade them once with a unique ability and World Creation stats used to powerup and powerdown your dungeon experience. These mechanics make for a unique experience, but offers only so much.
But what's
about the game?
It has some great soundtrack to accompany you through your experience. Every type of dungeon has its own unique BGM and you are welcomed with more than 1 battle track. The game is also easy to understand. The battle mechanic isn't hard to figure out, but unlike Final Fantasy X; which uses the same Turn Order for battles, there is little to take advantage of. The story is lovable and you get to enjoy many faces that develop (sort of) over the course of the game. It also takes advantage of the "cliches" of games. The side events are also very Japanese with their slapstick and airheadness and ecchi.
And what's
about the game?
Like mentioned often it suffers from cliches. If you know a bit of gaming you'll be able to foresee certain events. The game also features a cast of 6
playable characters. If you are going for completion you'll use 2 of those at any given time meaning you have 1 spare seat left. The game also suffers from the lack of difficulty. You can get behind big time, but you can train yourself back in the game, but once you get ahead by a lot you'll breeze through the game with little to no difficulty.
The game also features a huge world map that won't be used in any way
The battle music will also get on your nerves since they aren't memorable.
Lastly the biggest flaw for the game is its shortness and cryptic level. If you go for a straight playthrough you can beat it in 15 hours, no problem. If you want to go for 100% you'll have to consult a walkthrough because the game is not going to tell you anything about any unlockable or (hidden) items.
By the end if you read it you'll notice more bad things than good things, but that's because bad things stay with you better. I had a good time by the end of the game. The flaws are noticeable and could have been removed, but it's not hindering your experience. All by all I think it's still pretty fun to play. It's not New Game+ worthy though. The final verdict: It's just fun, nothing special but fun.

I picked this up from Humble Bundle on a sale along with its sequels. So, I'm only going to review "Dead Man's Switch", and the game engine here. Dragonfall will get its own, along with the Director's Cut.
FASA and Jordan Weisman; is there anything they made that wasn't awesome? Crimson Skies was one of my all-time favourite games, and the MechWarrior and MechCommander series have always remained a part of my game library. And now Shadowrun has joined them as a gaming system and setting that I really enjoyed from the get-go.
I've never played Shadowrun on the tabletop. and my only familiarity with the system is from webcomics such as Weregeek. Still, the game does capture much of the same feel, and with only text and music. I've read that they've altered the rules slightly, but it feels okay to me. The game plays out turn-based, with a fixed isometric camera (no rotation, only zoom), very similar to the XCOM games.
There's no voice-acting, and the campaign is very linear, but it makes for a good introduction to the game series. It starts out as a simple murder mystery, but it unfolds into something much more. If you're going to buy it, buy it on sale, because I've heard that the other two parts are better. However, this is still a good, fun game, and a great way to introduce yourself to the Shadowrun Universe.
Two things:
1. Customize your class. Shadowrun is classless, and the "pre-gens" are not optimized. Specialization is the way to go here, and having 1 in Strength or Intelligence will not hinder you (if that's the sort of character you're building).
2. Ranged specialization is better, because the last mission is insects, insects, insects.

I'm kind of a hard core RPG player and just like anyone who plays RPGs I always have my skepticisms about a game I pick up. Being an enthusiast about Anime didn't have anything to do with my review. I will say that this game is incredibly detailed. The developement of the characters was meticulously thought through and the interactions of the characters don't change for the sake of story developement. All characters are very different and very in personality. The idea of time and it's affect on the world when the particular sequence appears is actually quite accurate. Any change in a timeline can have the potential to change everything about the time stream that you currently travel which is why I believe it was a well thought out paradigm of the story. With the inclusion of the choice of Good or Evil makes this an interesting blend and includes several even more interesting character interations. Players don't necessarily have to grind to finish the game, but it does certainly help. The idea of overkilling enemies has always been a thing for me and with the DLC added to the game, adds the possibility of total annihilation. Getting certain materials to create new weapons, armor, items, misc. items, and other synthesis materials is difficult but if it were easy then it wouldn't be worth the effort. The synthesis items are much stronger than what you can buy and If you farm the materials then it is worth that much more. I would say to be careful about the boss battles when reviving the God or Goddess. If you have the DLC it is easier than normal, however once you reach a certain rank they will start getting though your armor so don't rely on the DLC to last you the whole game. It wont. Overall I recommend this game to any and all RPG enthusiasts out there even if you don't like Anime. It is a rich story full of spontanious and often hilarious conversations. I enjoy the game and I hope anyone who has just gotten or even just thinking about getting it will too.

After ~12 hours, I've finished the main story.. including every side mission I found.
All in all, it was mediocre experience for me. The gameplay was very slow-paced, and yet not tactical enough. Character development is very limited and bland in my opinion, you gain karma to improve your character skillset over time, like any other RPG.. but you are pretty limited in your options. I also found myself incredibly overpowered halfway through the game as a rigger. I didn't have to try very hard to finish the game.
The plot was the best part of the game, but it was very linear and was not quite good enough to make the combat sequences more enjoyable to get through. You are forced to play a character who is either greedy, ever-sarcastic, or apathetic.. there is very little depth in the conversation choices as everything is on rails here. The lack of an end combat button meant that certain sections of the story dragged on much longer than they should have as you had to move each character turn-by-turn to the next area. The decking sequences were incredibly dull, consisting of only 4 enemy types at most. The rest of the combat in the game was similar, I never really felt threatened throughout the game and didn't really feel challenged when I did the "impossible" of attacking a Corporation.
Overall, don't buy this for the gameplay or character development if that's what you enjoy. The story and setting are definitely interesting- but for the me the gameplay is just too poor to really recommend this.
There just isn't enough substance here to justify a $14.99 price tag in my opinion, thankfully I got it as part of a Shadowrun bundle.
I personally had hoped for a more tactical RPG experience in the Shadowrun universe- what I got was a decent Shadowrun story, with bland characters, not-so-great character development, very poor combat and gameplay and really a lackluster experience overall.
If you are really into the Shadowrun universe you will probably enjoy the setting and story enough to justify the less-stellar aspects of the game, but I wouldn't recommend it otherwise.
Gameplay: 4/10
You only develop your own character and none of the character tracks are very compelling, you must hire different runners before each mission who are leveled automatically as the game unfolds, the combat is very slow and monotonous, the item choices are bland.
UI/Controls: 6/10
I found moving my party around after combat to be a pain, even though all the enemies were cleared you still have to move each of your runners turn-by-turn to the next area.
Story: 7/10
It is an interesting plot and a little-visited setting, but the story is not deep enough or paced well enough to balance out the more negative aspects of the game. It also takes a very wild direction the last 1/4 of the game. I think if there was just a few more missions to flesh out the story, the pacing would be far better.
Music: 7/10
Good music, but repetitive and a limited selection. I found myself turning off the combat music halfway through the game.
Overall I would rate this game a 6/10.
As mentioned, I would only recommend this to avid Shadowrun fans ultimately.

This game has to be one of my favorite puzzlers on Steam, that is, if this maze/rhythm/simplistic whatever the heck it is can be called a puzzle game.
The game consists of three main levels: Hexagon (Hard), Hexagoner (Harder), and Hexagonest (Hardest). Each level is 60 seconds long, with the player controlling a small triangle that is bound to a hexagon in the center of the screen. Quickly lines start coming at your triangle, trying to trap it against the center hexagon (you can see this better illustrated in the trailer). Anyways, each level is randomly generated, however certain "themes" or recurring patterns are seen in the different levels. If you ever do complete one of the levels, you will unlock the "Hyper" mode, which is basically the same level but sped up to be extremely fast, and these levels warrant the difficulty rating of "Hardester".
Overall, this game is quick to figure out, but amazingly difficult to complete. It is one of those games where sometimes instead of dwelling on a level and playing it over and over again won't work as well as just trying it out the next day with a fresh start. A game that's great for passing time and great for achievement hunters, and of course with a great price!
I would highly recommend this game especially if you happen to see it on sale, or even for full price if you feel so inclined. I hope this review was helpful, understandable, and accurate. Thanks!

Risk of Rain is a survival game, with procedurally generated contents, no game is like the game before. The difficulty of the game is harder than it might appear at first - but not as hard as to call it really hardcore.
It excells in many things, like being a good game for breaks or trying to achieve some set aim... and then just some more... And it's fun, fun, fun, even though it feels like you die a thousand times... which you actually will...
Especially nasty is the mechanic that makes the game harder, the more time passes by - so loitering around on the lowest level will doubtlessy get you killed anyway. There is a lot to unlock, a lot to explore and you need to survive the ordeal that is set by the procedures.
Good news, artifacts may help to get you around, and another good news, they might stack.
The sound is rather well made, the graphics are for the game good, and actually this game is more fun than some tripple A games, because of the very straightforwardness of the gameplay... run around, shooting everything that tries to move, and shoot some more to gain the next level... go to the boss, hit em hard... and make it to the next stage. Bug off with fancy graphics, a game that runs well is more important in that matter.
And that is what you get with this game, it runs well, just till you quit it... then you get an ugly pop up... because something was not so well programmed - luckily it's after you played the game. Thus, nothing to fret about.

Let me start this review by saying I love this game. But it isn't without its faults either.
Since I'm not good at writing reviews I'll go with the classic "pros/cons" format and follow it up with suggestions how to improve on negative points. Also there are some points which can be considered pros and cons at the same time, depending on how you play games.
-Price (even at 10 bucks its worth it, at a sale even more so)
-Replayability (potentially infinite levels to go through)
-Challenging, the intensity slowly ramps up and you gives you just enough time to gather enough power ups
-Beautiful
-Almost no power up feels useless and they're all useful in their own regards
-Character diversity
-End Boss battle is actually pretty hard if you do it before getting too powerful
-Unlocking stuff can be hard to achieve but is very rewarding although some secrets like the Miner can be hard to find
-Rounds can go on for as long as you like
-I guess it's hard to play multiplayer since you need something like Hamachi for it and it can be a pain for some people to set that up
-You can actually become too powerful. If you play long enough you can't be killed at a certain point anymore because of the lifesteal/hp/armor power up and the fact that they stack.
-Some characters feel useless and by that I mean you find yourself thinking:"Why would I play this one when I can play the Archer"

I used to like this game but the past 2 expansions have been completely unbalanced garbage, with the most recent expansion having the game in the worst state its ever been in. This expansion focused on making neutral cards viable. That means every class you run into is running the exact same turn 1-4 plays, including the best deck in the game, which is the most oppressive deck the game has ever had. There are techs against it, but no actual counters. As far as I'm aware, no deck has a positive winrate against it. And according to Cygames, they aren't going to change any of this until the end of the month. And that's a "maybe." The game isn't fun anymore. Games end so fast they're entirely draw-dependent and going first is a huge advantage. Class identity is dead since every class optimally runs the same early-game neutral cards. The state of Ranked being nothing but a singular Tier 0 deck means Unranked is full of past metas' viable decks that don't work in today's Ranked, so you can't even play stupid meme stuff and have fun like you used to be able to. The last expansion was a mess, and this one is twice as bad. Any hope I had that Cygames would pull this game together again is dead.
11/13/17 EDIT: Hey look they actually fixed it. After that mess of an expansion, the developers basically said they'd stop being stupid by printing blatantly broken cards to push certain classes, and they've actually kept to their word. Starforged Legends is a really good set and it pulled the game back together nicely. All that needed to happen is for half of every Wonderland Dreams card to get nerfed to death, and that's okay. It's a good game now, and I think I trust Cygames to keep it that way.

1) Grease an 8x8 inch square baking pan. Set aside.
2)Combine sugar, cocoa and milk in a medium saucepan. Stir to blend, then bring to a boil, stirring constantly. Reduce heat and simmer. Do not stir again.
3)Place candy thermometer in pan and cook until temperature reaches 114C°. If you are not using a thermometer, then cook until a drop of this mixture in a cup of cold water forms a soft ball. 4)Remove from heat. Add butter or margarine and vanilla extract. Beat with a wooden spoon until the fudge loses its sheen. Do not under beat.
5)Pour into prepared pan and let cool. Cut into about 60 squares.

As I'm sure you've noticed from the plethora of other Steam reviews for Fairy Fencer F, Fairy Fencer F is extremely easy to compare to the other recent Compile Heart/ Idea Factory port, Hyperdimension Neptunia. This is because they are, effectively, much the same game. I didn't actually realise this untill coming to play Fairy Fencer F and only took interest in it due the aforementioned cover art.
I don't believe that Compile Heart/ Idea Factory have too much intention of copy/ pasting their old games, they've just got an engine they like and a design formula that works for them. That and they don't really like to spend effort making many new assets so they use alot of already existing enemies. Further evidence for this belief of mine is Omega Quintet on the PS4, which utilizes a higher version of the engine (or they're pushing it, at least) to make another
Compile Heart/ Idea Factory game, which again is not as good at Neptunia.
Fairy Fencer F is a fun game, certainly not the most fun I've had out of a game, but enough fun for me to play it, complete it  and leave it with happy feelings and no intention to 100% it.
That being said, I expect achieving 100% in Fairy Fencer F wouldn't be particularly difficult, as there's very little to do in it.
Extremely little, infact, to the point where the midway plot point which originally comes across as a potentially totally awesome bit of story telling starts to feel like a "We were running out of time!" cry of help from the developers, and it's quite a shame, as Fairy Fencer F is qute enjoyable to play.
With almost no post-story content aside from a tower I found completely by accident and grinding the randomised treasure chests in dungeons, there's very little backing the game. I'm not, of course, saying that a game cannot stand on it's own two legs without extra stuff to do, it's just that having extra stuff to do gives it more life, more playability and more things to keep you, as a player, interested. The tower isn't even what it sets itself up to be, it's just a menu with a list of set fights to go through. So yeah, basically, there's nothing post story unless you like luck roll grinding for hats.
Fang is, bluntly, wicked. He's great, he's brisque, a bit gruff and does what he likes, all the while making a show of being uncaring while actually being a good guy deep down. I guess that makes him a tsundere. I love me some tsunderes. Much of the first chunk of story is Fang pratting about while going on a quest to save First Girl's memories, and "gradually" warming to Second Girl. There is a Third Girl who is by far and away the best, but I'm assuming time cuts didn't give her a look in.
Fang has a mate, as well, who is basically his goofier self in large shorts. There's also another man and potentially his sister that you need to have to NG+ to feasibly get unless you grind all the nothing like a madman.
I'm making a section for this on it's own because the music is fantastic. The opening video music is awesome and much of the actual gameplay music is also fantastic. A quick bit of searching led to the discovery that the music was composed by Nobuo Uematsu, the man who did the Final Fantasy music, among many other brilliant soundtracks. Sadly, halfway through the game the cool battle music is replaced by slightly boring battle music, I can only assume this is to reflect Fang being serious, and the game being boring from this point on for a while, but never mind.
The battle system is a carbon copy of Neptunia 2, as is the dungeoneering and shopping. The only differences lie in the stat bonuses and ability unlocks being reshuffled to the Fairy Upgrade system, which allows for some mild character ability customisation and is fairly cool, and the aesthetics of the game. Visually, it's quite nice. the dungeons tend to be more detailed than that of Neptunia and alot of the tilesets are completely different, making it feel like a different world, which it is.
The story is short. Really short, but could have been brilliant, so I was quite surprised when I realised that, yes, I really was nearing the end of the game, and about to fight the Final Boss For Real, and yes, his head is hilariously tiny (I was crying laughing at him and his tiny head in this serious bit of story).
You may have noticed that I used the word "potentially" alot, that's because the mix of nothing aside from story, the story being very short at that, Fairy Fencer F comes across as a potentially brilliant game that just didn't have enough time spent on it, which is a massive shame. Furry Fencer F is still a fun game to play, it's just not as fun as it could have been. Fairy Fencer F isn't a bad game, though, it's just not what it could have been. I prepurchased the game for half price (~£11), and that's about how much the game is worth.

Personal score

The good:
Enjoyably challanging.  Character has a personality, has motive and driving action around them.  Side missions are entertaining, and not always pointless (some of the blueprints they give are very helpful).  Side missions also have a plot to each one instead of run here, grab this/kill certain number of enemies, come back hooray.  At the heart of them they may still be that but at least you feel as though you have a reason for doing it.  Parkouring is entertaining, combat is fun and more realistic than other zombie games I've played.  Also, I LOVE the no fast travel.  Makes you actually live the travelling instead of appearing there.
The bad:
Parkouring is buggy.  It occasionally has a hard time determining what you actually wanted to grab onto.  There are a few trap ziplines around the map that seem to be there to help you out, but halfway down it will kill you.  The exploding zombies are incredibly difficult to spot in a crowd/jump out of no where.  I can't count on all my phalanges how many times I've ran into a room, ran up to a van to loot, or ran out of a building to have one spontaneously appear in front of me.  First reaction:  aim for the neck for a decap or vault it (only suceeded in surviving 1 vault)....which ends badly.  I guess i could change my habits to kick first...  but it seems like they were placed in the game as a cruel joke to players.
As a side note,  I'll add that I've always had a sense of looming death (stomach in your throat, i'm about to die; not constant fear or anticipation of horror like other games) the entire time I played.  You'll never be that untouchable badass that can waltz out of every situation.  Things get seriously rough quick if you're not paying attention.  However, I enjoyed that part of it.  It's one of the few games that I've had anxiety playing it, yet enjoy it.
But seriously, ♥♥♥♥ those exploders.

First Impressions - This is GREAT!
If you liked cockpit-view semi-simulation flight games like (going way back) Gunship 2000, Commanche, Battlefield 2, etc just buy this, it's the Heli game you have been waiting for.  Even in it's current alpha state this game has all the base elements you want in a flight game:  Great Physics & Graphics, lots of controller options, a variety of views including a fully rendered cockpit (my preferred view) and gunner seat, FLIR and several external views, great Co-Op, PvP and team PvP, Single Skirmish, Campaign Mode and Free Flight.  Add to that chunky explosions, rag-doll infantry, custom loadouts, and just the right amount of simulation without being over-the-top realism.
I'm not going to dwell on the current lack of content because this is the first public early-release of the game and the missions that are included are a promising snapshot of the direction the content developers are heading.  From what I have seen so far I have complete confidence that the future content will only get better.
I bought this game along with 2 friends and we got to play all multiplayer modes together, all were extremely satisfying.  We all use Logitech 3D Extreme flight sticks that were recognized, configured, and worked almost perfectly by default.  Every feature of the Heli fits neatly on the stick so no need for mouse at all.  Even the menus can be navigated using the hat and a few buttons on the stick... very slick!  If you like to cusomize your controls, no problem, there is a full suite of custom options  including both Primary and Secondary controller recognition that has rudder and throttle-stick pilots in mind.  I also tried the keyboard-mouse controls (in Pilot mode) and found it extremely accessible to the flight-stick challenged, so don't be discouraged mouse-flyers, this game is for you too!
I'm happy to see this genre being properly resurrected and so far so good.  My friends and I are really enjoying replaying the current limited content and looking forward to what this developer will deliver in the coming months.   A sound purchase at $13 US, support these guys.

One of the best darn games I've played in a long time.
