After playing through the story of the game and trying a quick mod for it, I would say that I recommend this game.  The lore surrounds you as you play through the game, but isn't so quick to jargon or burying you in references and events non-fans of Shadowrun wouldn't know of that you get lost or overwhelmed.  I think this would serve as a nice introduction for anyone who might be curious about this fantasy world.
One aspect I appreciate most in the game are the various options available to you, depending on what race you play, though more importantly what skills you've focused on leveling.  It allows you to approach situations in different ways, giving greater flexibility.  There is a limit though, with some areas showing more versatility than others.  For instance, as I leveled up and spent my karma points (skill points essentially) I was disappointed that the pistol had so many perks and skills when levelling it up in contrast to any of the other guns.  I focused on the shotgun and I could rain death from afar, but it would have been nice picking up skills along the way instead of only doing more damage from further away.  Perhaps adding a bleeding status effect to enemies or lowering their movement as they limp off from being pumped full of lead.
I liked switching back and forth between the free exploration areas and combat, as having the two modes separated allows you to freely interact with your environment, sometimes just to nose around and other times to advance the story.  Again what is enjoyable is that you have a choice on how you progress in these areas.  Maybe you grease a palm here and there and sneak your way in or try to blow open an entrance.  Nothing huge per se, but you can play a character that way, instead of merely having to go forward in a single straight line.  The combat is pretty simple but it's certainly serviceable.  Once you familiarize yourself with the UI it makes simple sense and allows you to take cover, draw the enemy in, rush them, chuck grenades, cast spells, summon avatars, use melee weapons, or do as I did and blast away with the best guns money can buy.
I'd say my biggest complaint in the game is that there aren't more optional side missions to tackle.  With the way the programming works, with missions having options built-in I can see why it doesn't, but it would be nice to grind more money (not that you'll need it, if you're frugal), earn more karma, and have more to experience.  I kept expecting to see better armor, guns, and body mods available and was disappointed that they seemed to hint at really potent modifications you could use but never built up to.  I held off on getting any for a long time for that reason, wanting to save up my funds for when I could get the really choice items.  Having another level or two of gear would have built up a greater sense of advancement, as by the end you don't have anywhere else to go.
All in all I did enjoy the game though and am looking forward to trying other games from this series.  Plus I can try more mods in this one sometime as well.  Maybe run through it all again with a new character build and race.

I like it.  I assisted with the English translation in parts because I liked it enough to want to contribute.   Supports 2-3 players coop mission play.

It's not DCS or FSX or X-plane.  You can hook up a HOTAS, go to in-cockpit view and play it sim style, and it reminds me of Take on Helicopters at that point.  It's more game than sim, but there's enough approximation of realistic behavior that it doesn't feel like arcade nonsense.
Coop missions:  Currently you can play any of the missions with a friend or two.  Multiplayer "just works" and you host a game, your friends find it, and you take off together.  I'm "that guy" in BF4 that makes people hate helicopters, but my friends are very casual simmers.  I took them up in coop and they did very well at the same difficulty I play it at.  It's just fun, doesn't frustrate the inexperienced, and has so much potential.

After reading other reviews, I realize that this game could have been amazing if it hadn't been created in Neptunia's shadow. Personally, I didn't care for the HDN games and never got too far into them because the story/characters didn't really interest me.
As for this game, I really loved the characters (except Sherman, more on that later), the artwork is fantastic and it had a nice concept. Even the english VAs aren't too bad though some of the deliveries are poor and the fairies don't have voices in the english option without a workaround. The major downside is the game play.
There's a mechanic in the game where you pull out swords from either the vile god or the goddess using the power of fairys. The furies allow you to obtain abilities and add bonuses to dungeons.
Here's the thing though..Whether or not you pull the furies out of the beings has no impact on the story at all. So the games main mechanic and purpose is basically just pushed off to the side and when you do pull out all the furies you get a wimpy boss that's no different than the end boss.
In fact, If you want any challenge to the game, try not pulling out the furies after the first required to open new dungeons. I had actually skipped the tutorial telling me about world shaping and it didn't occur to me to put more than one fury into the ground until Zepla valley and the only reason I even bothered to at all was for achievement purposes.
That's right. The game is extremely easy if played how it was intended. My first play through was long because I read the story and I ended up playing through two more times because I missed a subevent for a fury piece required to unlock the second to last fairy. These three play through took me at most 30 hrs...So why do I have over 80 hours of play time? Freaking button mashing the last floor of Sudokoos tower while watching tv for the steam achievements.
Yeah. That's right. I did it for the achievements. If I had picked this game up on the PS I wouldn't have cared but seeing those last character achievements locked just bugged me and since I knew I wouldn't be playing this game again I made the dire mistake of saying "what the hell" and deciding to just unlock these useless grindy, boring waste of time achievements.
Now, as for my dislike of Sherman. His role in the story is useless.

If you grew up playing those games, you'll get crazy enjoyment from finding all of the hidden easter eggs in this.
There's tons of cool bosses, secrets, pretty good music, and overall a great sense of exploration. While the difficulty will rightly put a lot of people off, I also feel it adds a lot to the experience, and it wouldn't be an authentic NES game without it. I eventually completed it 100%, but it was a very punishing experience!

Shadowrun Returns is a turn based isometric strategy game based in the cyberpunk world of Shadowrun. Accompanied by dialogue and progression mechanics similar to those found in RPGs, this indie title is a very unique start to a series that seems like it can only get better with more support.
Shadowrun features a linear campaign with a highly engaging story that starts out simple and maybe just gets a little ridiculous by the end. But in a world of decking into the matrix, metahuman troll shamans summoning spirits made out of corpses, and drugs basically being entirely replaced by virtual experience chips that are eerily similar to video games? Maybe it's hard to judge when something actually becomes strange. There's plenty of dialogue to read, choices to make, and paths to explore that all come with rewards of additional money, karma, or maybe even just the opposite. The campaign lacks freedom of movement though due to its linear nature, but that's not really a con with this game. It works perfectly fine the way it is, it's just a shame the game is only about 10 hours long. Never fear if you want more content however, the game is fully equipped with modding support and plenty user-made missions and campaigns exist to lengthen your playtime. Some of them even allow you to import your character from the main campaign and continue to make him the epitome of badassedry.
Shadowrun's gameplay is similar to other games such as Avernum and XCOM, but seems to borrow far more from XCOM in terms of the fact that you can still miss a lot with a 99% chance to hit your target. Honestly though, it's a lot of fun. The strategy elements will appeal to any fans of the turn based genre and the RPG elements of how the story progresses and how you equip and upgrade your character bring it an appeal to a whole 'nother market entirely. You see the game gives you Karma instead of levels or experience, and they are essentially skill points that you earn by completing objectives, and more of by sacrificing monetary rewards to do the 'right' thing. These skill points plus purchasing gear are entirely how you shape the efficiency of your character. My only complaint with how the gameplay actually works is  the movement. When you're out of turn based movement it is very obvious that the characters are still running around in turn mode since there is a constant pause like it's processing the start of a new turn every couple of seconds of running. And when you are moving, you are incapable of quick saving your game til at least one full second after you finish moving. This makes life for save-a-holics like myself a little inconvenient, but it makes it even more evident that they didn't bother making an actual real-time freeroam mode and just reskinned the turn-based movement. It's a shame, but it's no reason to be turned away from the game.
A reason to to turned a way from Shadowrun would be that it suffers from a lot of bugs. In fact, if you have a bug and google it to get help, not only will you find plenty of persons with the same bug in the same place, but you'll find others who have a completely different bug in the same place as well! The steam version is notably the buggiest version of the game. It features extra bugs in any potential area and even features a game-breaking save-wiping bug that makes it so that if you want this game, I'd recommend NEVER buying it on steam. The GoG version being the least buggy that I've found and lacks any game-breaking bugs that I've found in 23 hours of playing it. If you're going to get this game, get it on GoG.
The graphics of this game are understandably bad for today. The game was released almost four years ago and was a difficult project that even had to be kickstarted to get off the ground, and thankfully they put most of their effort into gameplay and story rather than making it a beauty to look at. The nitty gritty feeling of the graphics however really helps to immerse you into the scary world that is Shadowrun. So long as you can ignore occasional glitches such as shooting an SMG and seeing the bullets come from the opposite corner of the map and flying off to who knows where instead of coming out of the gun like they're supposed to, the graphics really shouldn't be a con.
The soundtrack is something I'd like to describe as cyberpunk to the extreme. It definitely fits the setting and the sound effects are fine, but no standing ovation. The game however does lack any voice acting whatsoever which is good to note, because if you do not want to do a LOT of reading, then this game is not for you.
Overall, Shadowrun Returns is a charming indie title so unique in every way I really don't think you should miss it. It gets an 8/10 from me. It was reaching for 9/10, but all the problems with bugs and certain flaws stomped it down a bit, making it just barely retain an 8/10. Is it worth the full price of $15? Only yes if you plan on downloading and playing a bunch of user-created storylines. The base game is too short to justify $15 however, being barely longer than the bare-bones campaigns findable in many AAA first person shooters these days. I definitely recommend buying this if you like strategy or experiencing new and unique settings, but buy it on sale unless you definitely plan on playing every single mod you can. Just do NOT buy it on steam unless you're ok with potentially dealing with having your save games wiped or a plethora of other steam-exclusive bugs that have been reported.

This game's interesting and strange in several ways.
The story is threadbare - king becomes ill, princess is worried, and monsters suddenly attack the town of Alexandria killing the entirety of the royal guard, leaving a lone knight to defend the town. As you pass certain points of the game, you'll get little tidbits of story here and there, but for the most part the game is fine with leaving the story in the back of the car between its bigger brothers, Art Direction and Game References.
The two big forces driving Carstle in the Darkness are Gameplay with the steering wheel and Music riding shotgun and fiddling with the volume knobs. The game is very much a platforming adventure sort of thing (though I guess 'Metroidvania' is a snappier term), giving you a huge sprawling map to explore and hiding the means of expanding exploration behind boss battles. Which makes the lack of an in-game map curious, to say the least. Though it's not exactly difficult to get lost since a lot of the game is spent going down horizontal paths with far fewer vertical sections to worry about.
Fighting starts out difficult as you start with what the game calls the worst sword in the game, and a piece of armour that's worth ten coins. You'll eventually gain more weapons and armour, and even gain mastery over the forces of magic that allow you to defeat enemies in new and interesting ways.
The health bar you have is deceptive, as it never changes to show your actual HP value - it'll always show fifteen chunks regardless of your actual total HP. This can lead you to believe that enemies are doing insane amounts of damage, when in reality they're slapping a full hit-point off you. You also start with HP in single digits, which can be boosted with Boss Hearts. Every boss you kill will drop these, along with a substantial monetary payload. As for the boss fights, they're all unique - only a couple of fights are repeats, and that's because you're re-fighting old bosses that return with new tricks.
The platforming side of things can be rather punishing at times, in part due to the abundance of spikes that litters the land and the titular Castle. You might encounter some stalactites in caves that bounce harmlessly off your helmet, but pretty much every sharp object you encounter is a one-hit kill. And you'll encounter a LOT of them. I've not taken a count of them, but there's got to be at least a thousand spikes scattered around. Mistime a jump and you're gonna fall into metallic pointy death. The game even keeps count for you, just to embarrass you.
The music is chiptune goodness, reminiscient of earlier days in gaming. As are the graphics. You can even get a scanline filter to really emulate that crummy CRT look. Really, the game weaponises nostalgia - things that made sense in old games will earn you another tick on the death counter in this game. Relying on old knowledge can work against you.
However, it can help you as well - this game is stuffed to the gills with references. Some of them are subtle, others couldn't be straighter rips unless they were heterosexual Beyblades. The game does have some humour of its own, but a lot of it involves pointing at other things and saying "This is what it is!", passing them off as jokes. You might laugh at them - I was more amused by the idea that the devs can get away with this.
CitD also has a New Game+ that has some interesting changes and additions which can carry a second playthrough. What I'll say is this: if you like Symphony of the Night, you'll like this. If not, then I'd give it a miss.
(oh, and the "arsenal of over 100 weapons, armour, items and magic" is a collective number of items you can obtain; I'd be hard-pressed to even say there's a hundred items, but maybe it counts the Boss Hearts in as items to pad the numbers)

The Parkour: Really gives you that freedom of movement. The game is in first-person, and therefor there are no need for any player animations, which allows for much more diversed movement. Assassin's Creed is way too squared, as you can only jump/climb in eight different directions around you, and the parkour is very controlled by the game. You don't do much yourself, other than pushing some buttons. In Dying Light, on the other hand, you are moving freely around everywhere, so you have to watch your step. It's brutal and unforgiving, and that's what makes it so exciting. You never get bored of it!
The combat is pretty straight-forward when it comes to swinging your weapons, but you do have a lot of awesome body-attacks like jump-kicks and dodges and the like that are real fun to use, as well as effective. It does make the combat a bit tactic. You make a wrong move, you end up getting caught under a pile of zombies. The weapons are really creative, awesome and MANY. Looting is something you'll need to do constantly because you need items for repairing your worn weapons, and to create different things like molotovs and medkits. But that's okay, because the looting is pretty fast, and so is the lockpicking.
The enemies are frightening at first, but as you progress, they become easier to defeat, which gives you that awesome "I-was-afraid-of-you-before-but-now-I-kill-you"-feeling. And yet even after that, you still keep a certain level of fear for your enemies because you want to fight as little as possible so you can conserve your supplies and weapons for when you really need them. This game is, as I said already, brutal and unforgiving; the more you do, the more skillpoints you earn, but you also lose a lot of skillpoints almost every time you die. That is one thing that actually makes you afraid of dying in this game, and that is great.
The story is maybe a bit far-fetched. It's not as simple as just surviving the zombie apocalypse. Apparently this story involves trying to find the cure, and resisting the government who wants to exploit the virus to make the apocalypse even worse. Never the less, it is a very exciting story that gives you a feeling of importance. Animations and voice-actings are very good, and the characters have very strong characteristics. Especially the villain, of course.
All in all, I liked the game a lot. But like most other open-world games I've played, I don't really feel like exploring the world that much, as almost everything gets slightly repetitive. I'm mainly in it for the storyline. Despite enjoying the game, I had this really uncomfortable and scared feeling throughout the whole playtime of 19 hours that it took me to complete it. It was like "Damn, I want to just get done with this story so I can stop playing this game", and I'm not really sure. Still, a great game.
Oh, and... DON'T. GO. OUT. AT. NIGHT.

Castle in the Darkness is a wonderful challenge for those who seek it.
Our hero quests to find the missing princess and to slay the evil that has beseiged their land.  Along the way he will fight tough bosses to obtain more vitality, and through secrets and NPCs he can obtain better swords, armor, and magic.  He will also obtain relics and items that bestow various powers and abilities.
Castle in the Darkness is a challenging game that is not for the faint of heart.  The game features challenging boss fights, dangerous enemies, and instant-death spikes galore.  The checkpoint system can be punishing, but not completely unfair as long as you have patience.  In this manner, if you are a fan of games such as Dark Souls, or IWBTG, or if you are simply a fan of classic games of old, then you are the target audience of this game.  You will die a lot, in a magnitude of hundreds, but it is all part of the experience.
As for my personal opinions on the game, I had a very enjoyable experience.  I had difficulty at times, but I never felt that the game was too difficult, that there was never any hurdle too unreasonable to pass.  The game has a wonderful NG+, that is like a whole new game, and the Secret levels were a good challenge.
If I have any advice for people looking to play this game, EXPLORE!  Secrets (of which there are no end to) are always rewarding, if only in humor.  Also, experiment with your magic; I coasted through many challenging fights by exploiting magic.  Certains spells can be OP if used creatively, but every spell has a time to shine - but only if you think to try it!

Shadowrun Returns is a pretty solid RPG. You've got some interesting skill choices, a pretty damn nifty setting, and well-written story throughout. I found myself invested in what was going on, and the gameplay was interesting enough to keep me playing through the entire campaign in one go. And really, how often do you see urban fantasy elements injected into a gritty noir-SF setting? (Not very.)
I like the setting's takes on classic RPG and fantasy tropes, and there are more than a few references to classic SF books crammed in there (for instance, a lot of inspiration from
and the Sprawl trilogy, both in the world and in character names). Lastly, the music and art style were of a high quality throughout. While I don't know that I'll be listening to the OST in my free time, it did set a good tone for the game.
One neutral point worth noting is that the campaign ran me a total of 10 hours. I finished this title over the weekend and still had time for Dark Souls. If that's a downside for you, then take it under advisement. Me, I work a full-time job, and I've got a lot of hobbies. So I don't mind short games as long as they don't cost an arm and a leg. And, since I got this during a sale with the rest of the series, I have no room to complain. If you're concerned about time-to-money ratio, though, consider waiting for a discount.
This game does have its shortcomings. As with many iso-RPGs, the UI isn't perfect. Sometimes the response is slow. I often found myself wishing for the ability to rotate my frame of reference, especially in the last few levels, where enemies kept popping out of the walls. And, related to that, occasionally I'd want to move party members close together, only to find that clicking the destination just selected the schmuck I was trying to move next to. "Sorry, Jimmy, guess you'll have to die; the game won't let me stand close enough to pop a medkit." I also noted some menu glitches - I recall at least two occasions where a skill refused to execute, forcing me to waste a turn.
I felt like there wasn't enough opportunity to invest in character skills, partly due to the game's length. I went with a rifle-wielding Decker, backed up by a drone, and while my three main skills were fairly complementary, not one was maxed at the end of the game. I will also argue that the plot gets a little wacky in places, and the ending felt a trifle overdone.
So, with all that said, do I recommend the game? Conditionally, yes. If you're looking for an RPG with a neat setting, and you don't mind the traditional problems of iso-strategy-RPGs or a short-lived campaign, by all means give it a shot. But if you've got a problem with the idea of a 10-hour RPG, or you're not a fan of strategy RPG combat, then I'd recommend steering clear, or waiting for a sale. Up to you, really.

A cute metroidvania with excellent NES-style graphics and music and plenty of homages to its inspirations - some pretty obvious, and some surprisingly deep cuts (seriously, they reference 8'Eyes??). It's almost great - the game is fairly huge, the design and music keeps it fresh, and there's lots of stuff to find if you backtrack after you've upgraded your abilities; the hallmarks of a good metroidvania.
The problem with this game is that it's way too fond of instant-kill spikes. It doesn't seem to get this from its inspirations, Castlevania, Metroid, or Mega Man, but rather from Super Meat Boy and I Want To Be The Guy, and it's not a game that's designed in a way that makes getting instakilled every 30 seconds fun. The checkpoints are just far enough between each other to be infuriating. You have a lifebar - for all the good it does you - since it's rarely enemies that are the problem. The controls seem to be fine, but I wind up jumping too late or overshooting my landings a lot more than I tend to do in Symphony of the Night or Megaman. The game quickly loses the tension of trying to survive to the next checkpoint with your health dwindling from enemy attacks since you just start assuming you're going to miss a jump and die instantly with a full health bar.
It's a shame, because a lot of people are going to get frustrated with this very early into the game and will just give up, but there's a lot of love put into this game, and I think a lot of people would get a kick out of the design, the jokes, and the cute bosses in particular.

So, it took a long time for it to happen but a little while ago KF2 finally got out of early access and was fully released.  I stayed away from it for a while at first, because my experience with the game during early access was pretty disappointing.  After playing KF for a long time, I had high hopes for KF2 but at the time those hopes weren't delivered upon.  There weren't many classes and the ones that did exist weren't super fun.  I pretty much just played Medic at the time because the others were either not fun or I didn't like the guns they had.  After a while I gave KF2 another chance after the full release and I must say that I am very exceptionally pleased.  I feel like the development team has improved upon or fixed any of the gripes I had with the game before.  The game now feels a lot more fun and fresh with all the new classes and maps.  I enjoy playing this game and will definitely put as many hours into as I had the original if not more.
The gameplay is completely different.  KF had a very methodical and patient feel to it, or at least I felt like it did.  You didn't ever want to get hit or else you were either dead or severely wounded.  I always played on Hard because it felt like the best balance of difficulty.  I considered moving up to harder difficulties, but without a dedicated team it would be pretty sketchy.  I loved the sharpshooter class the most because it allowed me to be calm and slow, yet effective.  However, in KF2, things have changed drastically.  First of all, every Zed can sprint at you in some way.  As opposed to the first game, it is hard to outrun Zeds far enough to take pot shots at them.  The maps in KF2 are also a lot smaller and close quarters than the ones from the original game.  Fast Zeds + limited space = very stressful introduction.  If you come from KF expecting things to be as slow as they were before, you're going to have a bad time.  I know I did when I first started playing KF2.  Before, the strategy was "Don't get hit", but now the strategy is "Hit them before they hit you".  Running and gunning is  a lot more viable if not the best playstyle in KF2.  Learn the maps, leave yourself plenty of escape routes, and for the love of god learn to bash.
If you're new to KF in general, I don't reccomend you play the original before playing this one if you are interested in the series.  I love both the games, but they feel completely different.  If you prefer a fast paced survival game, KF2 has got you covered, but if you like to be a bit more methodical then KF is your game.
If you enjoy FPSs at all, this game is a good way to help you build some teamwork skills and good sportsmanship.  Don't join a game and be a toxic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because you'll just get kicked out.
If you like Survival games and are just ok with shooters then stick to "Normal".  It's pretty easy to get into and learn while hard enough to not just be a garunteed free win every time.
There is also a VS mode where one team can play as Zeds, but I think it is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the time of this review.  It feels super unbalanced and some of the people who play it are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.  You'll pretty much only see max level players in that mode so it is essentially late game content for a casual player.  I don't reccomend it until some tweaks are made to make it more fun.  My main issue with it is that the Zed players can sprint 100% of the time which is ♥♥♥♥ing dumb if you aren't playing a class with bonus movespeed.  If you're playing a class like demo and a player gets a Bloat, they can just sprint at you and vomit constantly making it hard to see and really hard to kill anything with any sort of accuracy while burning you alive.  I think they should have a sprint bar or something, because jesus ♥♥♥♥ sprinting is OP as a Zed.

Half-Life 2
Man of few words, aren't you?
Half-Life 2 is a first person shooter developed by Valve and released in 2004. It is the sequel to their 1998 game Half-Life and is by far the best instalment in the series.
***Warning, contains spoilers to previous games in the Half-Life series***
Gordon Freeman awakens on a train after being put in ‘stasis’ for 20 years by the G-Man. He discovers that during this time, an alien race called the Combine have taken over earth and appointed Wallace Breen, a former Black Mesa employee, as the earths administrator. The Combine treat the humans like animals, beating them with stun batons and torturing them for information if they think someone looks suspicious. Gordon Freeman must work with a team of former Black Mesa security guards and scientist to overthrow the Combine and take back earth.

This game’s storyline is incredibly good, worthy of a Hollywood movie. The character development is incredible, you become quite attached to some of the characters by the end of the game such as Alyx, Barney and even Dog. You venture to awesome locations including an old town overrun with Headcrabs and Headcrab Zombies, a prison were the Combine torture and mutilate people and the Citadel in City 17. All these aspects are notable reasons why this games storyline is amazing but the back story involving how and why the Combine took over Earth, is probably one of the most diverse and interesting backstories in videogame history save for maybe Halo.
The gameplay in Half-Life 2 is impressive, considering it was released in 2004. This was largely due to the use of Valves physics engine “source” as they were able to include the rag doll effect in death and the kick♥♥♥♥♥gravity gun. The gravity gun allows you to either fire an energy blast which allows you to clear objects out of your way or kill smaller enemies such as Headcrabs. It also allows you emit a magnetic effect where you can pick up objects just in front of or small distance away from you and launch them into the air or at enemies. This is especially enjoyable in the chapter “we don’t go to Ravenholm”, where you can pick up buzz saw blades and launch them at the Headcrab Zombies, cutting them in two. It is even more pleasant when it gets “supercharged” while you are infiltrating the Citadel, allowing you to pick up Combine soldiers and launch them at their reinforcements. Other new weapons include the Combine’s Plasma Rifle which can launch an energy ball which disintegrates everything it touches and fur pods extracted from an Antlion queen which can be used to send Antlions to attack Combine soldiers or Headcrab Zombies. The enemies in this game are largely of the Combine race such as the humanoid soldiers, the gigantic three legged Striders, gunships and other combine technology like man hacks and hunter-choppers. However there is also the return of some Xen aliens such as Barnacles, the previously mentioned Headcrabs and Zombies, and very briefly an Ichthyosaur. The Vortigaunts also make a return but because of the death of their former enslaver, the Nihilanth (final boss of Half-Life), they chose to team up with the humans to defeat the Combine. The shootouts against enemies are extremely fun and are very fluid, not having to clear out a section in order to progress. You take down Hunter-Choppers using the plasma rifle on the air boat, you shoot and run over Antlions and soldiers using the same weapon on the Scout Car, later in the game you can command a group of rebels through City 17 to help you take down Striders, and the final chapters in the citadel were you take down hundreds of combine soldiers with the gravity gun is majestic. The terrific puzzles throughout the game set new standards for the Half-Life franchise and are perfectly placed throughout the game even having both gunplay and puzzles at the same time, memorably was the crane sequence in the chapter ‘Highway 17’.
The sound tracks in Half-Life 2 really add to the enjoyment of shootouts and platforming. “CP violation” played in the chapter ‘Route Canal’ makes you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥escaping the countless Combine soldiers that have been sent to kill you. “Apprehension and Evasion” is a great number played while you are infiltrating Nova Prospect from the beach with the cover of night, it makes you feel like a ninja assassin taking out the soldiers guarding the base. There are multiple other soundtracks that add to the atmosphere throughout the game and like in Half-Life valve once again presents you with an awesome soundtrack “Tracking Device” played in the credits which goes well with knowing that you have just finished Half-Life 2.
The level design and graphics are stunning in this game. It’s hard to even describe how good the layout of each section from each chapter is. The chapter in Ravenholm has scaffolding-like structures that go incredibly well with the parkour platforming you do throughout the whole chapter. The sections where you are controlling the airboat and the dune buggy have wooden supports on bridges so you can drive through them, making them crumble to the ground. The whole rooftop battle against the Striders at the end of the game has you traversing destroyed buildings that have been brilliantly designed. Making your way underneath the bridge to the other end in the chapter ‘Highway 17’ has multiple different broken paths you can take making it fun when battling Gunships and Combine Soldiers. The graphics in Half-Life 2 contribute to the level design improving it significantly. The particle effects associated with explosions and gunfire were truly ahead of their time when it was released, the water once again looks amazing and reacts uniquely to when it is interfered with. There are also small things like when you shine your torch at Alyx’s face she will cover her eyes and if you stare at her for too long she will look away and play with her hair.
Overall this game is perfect. I’m not over stating at all here, I can’t think of a single thing wrong with it. The storyline is entertaining and is worthy of its own movie, the gameplay is incredibly fun with new weapons and enemies, the soundtracks contribute to the mood and atmosphere of each scene in the game and the graphics and level design make each chapter more exciting than the last. I would recommend this game to anyone as it is considered, by most, a masterpiece and one of the best games of all time.

An enjoyable narrative experience following a failing rabbi and his equally failing synagogue, it's fairly a bleak look into a man with a troubled past and what feels like a fundamental loss of faith that he can regrow as he investigates the death of a former member of his congregation that has left him a significant amount of money through his estate.
The story itself is actually fairly dull and pretty predictable but the game itself is heavily dialogue laden - near all conversation and text is as if it were a rabbi talking, with some "puzzles" even solved by taking the rabbinical answer to whatever situation is posed. That's really the key to the game: the dialogue and the development of Rabbi Stone as a character, they are both brilliantly written and pick up the slack in the story.
Though, it is a point and click game with a few text and combat puzzles - usually based around remembering key facts around people and placing them into the in-game equivalent of Google at your computer terminal so paying attention is actually a must. The downside to this, is the fact you normally have to travel back to your office to find the information required to progress in the story.
I would recommend this game to people that enjoy art house, narrative driven, emotionally charged indie games. It's a very niche product, but I would absolutely recommend it to those already on the fence.

Being a massive Mi-24 fan this was a must for me despite being 'arcade'. My biggest fear was that it would be like Heleborne but fortunately it's not that arcady. The controls are simplified vs a real helicopter but they still feel enough like the real thing to make you feel like you're flying.
The graphics are really nice and the maps well put together, though some of them could be bigger, and it would be nice if there was a map view so you could see your location and have some idea of when you're going to hit the edge.
The model of the Mi-24 is really nicely done though it does have some quirks. The nose landing gear retracts in a really odd manner though this is nit picking as it's hardly noticeable.
The game runs super smooth, the maps load really fast and the only drop in framerate I experiened was when firing the podded Yak-B gatling guns over the largest city. That was earlier in developement and after a year it now runs perfectly smooth in all conditions.
Usually I'm not a fan of combat in flying games, I just like flying around, however this games battles are really fun, especially the quick mission city attacks. It's actually quite challenging a lot of the time and I am really struggling to get to grips with the guided missles.
Despite the name other Soviet/Russian helicopters have been added to the game which is very appreciated. My only problem with these is that the cockpits of the Mi-28 and Ka-50 are basically unfinished with little detail and many dead guages and screens. The Mi-8 cockpit is better though it seems to be based on some weird Westernised modification to the standard Mi-8 cockpit.
Watching the game develope has been very satisfying. The developers have really listened to the community and I actually feel like i've had some input into the final product.

This game is a love letter to classic metroidvania with lots of little secrets, hidden side areas, and possible sequence breaks.
There are references to 8 and 16 bit classics sprinkled throughout, but it stands on its own as a solid entry to the genre.
It's not a perfect game -- It's possible to make it into one area without any way out again (except for a developer keycombo that can be found with google), and the design of some of the areas with respect to checkpoint placement can be frustrating. It doesn't have an in-game map, which would be very useful given the branching paths. There are also instant death spikes all over the place, including some which fall onto the character from out of view at the most assholish moments; this game has taken a page from the likes of IWBTG in that respect.
Despite these flaws, the game is very enjoyable and well worth the price if you're a fan of metroidvanias.

This game is the very definition of a lot of Japanese RPGs since 2005. Mediocre and completely soulless. It's not bad and it's hardly good either. It's average, ordinary, undistinguished, middle-of-the-road, lackluster, forgettable and other synonyms related to second-rate.
Characters are common stereotypes found in many Japanese media directed towards teenagers such as in animes and mangas. Here's some examples:
1) The "hot-blooded but borderline mentally ret-rded" MC.
2) The "cutesy but sometimes annoying" female lead.
3) The "tsundere pseudo-noble lady" rival of female lead to be the best girl.
4) The "one who exist solely as fanservice" supporting female lead.
There are a few more characters but if you're familiar with animes and mangas, then you can guess for yourself what kind of character they are. Don't bother getting attached to them either. All of them are one-dimensional. ALL OF THEM.
Story is juvenile and uninteresting as it has already been done countless times in other JRPGs. A completely average main character "accidentally" became the hero. He gains the responsibility to save the world by collecting "something" to "free the God(dess)". Main villain appear, so does other unimportant and boring side characters, hero formed a party, went travelling, stuff happens, some "plot-twist" happens, hero got defeated briefly but the power of friendships/love gave the hero strength to defeat the "real" villain and the end. In other words, been-there-done-that. No effort was put in the story at all. I personally lost interest during the middle of the story and pretty much rushed through the ending. Sorry to say it didn't get any better. In fact, it got worst. Oh, can't forget the fanservice. Think of the poor basement-dweller players if we didn't get any fanservice.
Combat system was acceptable, for the first hour at least. After that it's down hill. Despite having a number of different types of combo to execute like in Xenogears (one of my favourite JRPG of all time) and Radiata Stories, most of them became obsolete as players are forced to use only a specific amount of those combo in battles. And no, you can't change them during battles. Meaning you have to use the exact same fighting animation on every battle. Throughout the WHOLE GAME! Magics and skills are useless as normal attacks are more efficient. While you can transform into a stronger form in battle, it gets tedious doing so in every battles. Get use to the skip button 'cause you'll be using it a lot to skip the 10 seconds animation with the super cheezy song every time you transform.
Look, I could go in detail why I don't recommend this game but that would be a waste of my time. Just trust me on this, if you're expecting a masterpiece with a engaging story, memorable characters and a fun gameplay, look elsewhere. If you're really desperate in playing this mediocrity, at least buy it on sale. Don't waste money paying full price for this.
NOT RECOMMENDED

The Parkour: Really gives you that freedom of movement. The game is in first-person, and therefor there are no need for any player animations, which allows for much more diversed movement. Assassin's Creed is way too squared, as you can only jump/climb in eight different directions around you, and the parkour is very controlled by the game. You don't do much yourself, other than pushing some buttons. In Dying Light, on the other hand, you are moving freely around everywhere, so you have to watch your step. It's brutal and unforgiving, and that's what makes it so exciting. You never get bored of it!
The combat is pretty straight-forward when it comes to swinging your weapons, but you do have a lot of awesome body-attacks like jump-kicks and dodges and the like that are real fun to use, as well as effective. It does make the combat a bit tactic. You make a wrong move, you end up getting caught under a pile of zombies. The weapons are really creative, awesome and MANY. Looting is something you'll need to do constantly because you need items for repairing your worn weapons, and to create different things like molotovs and medkits. But that's okay, because the looting is pretty fast, and so is the lockpicking.
The enemies are frightening at first, but as you progress, they become easier to defeat, which gives you that awesome "I-was-afraid-of-you-before-but-now-I-kill-you"-feeling. And yet even after that, you still keep a certain level of fear for your enemies because you want to fight as little as possible so you can conserve your supplies and weapons for when you really need them. This game is, as I said already, brutal and unforgiving; the more you do, the more skillpoints you earn, but you also lose a lot of skillpoints almost every time you die. That is one thing that actually makes you afraid of dying in this game, and that is great.
The story is maybe a bit far-fetched. It's not as simple as just surviving the zombie apocalypse. Apparently this story involves trying to find the cure, and resisting the government who wants to exploit the virus to make the apocalypse even worse. Never the less, it is a very exciting story that gives you a feeling of importance. Animations and voice-actings are very good, and the characters have very strong characteristics. Especially the villain, of course.

This is part of a series of many Lego games based on licensed material, like Star Wars and DC Comics before it. However, while those are all quality games, if you have to pick just one out of the whole lot, this ought to be the one. It's not only the best based on licensed material, it's one of the best Lego-based games ever.
There are a wide variety of characters you can play as, each with their own abilities based on their actual powers, though there is a decent amount of overlap in terms of abilities. And, admittedly, once you gain certain characters, you'll generally mostly use those characters out of convenience (Super Skrull is a prime example). But the game has quite a bit of charm and personality going for it that makes playing all of these characters, and creating your own hero, worth the time to unlock and play as them all.
Otherwise, what makes this one quite a ton of fun is there is a large city-wide hub, which is basically Manhattan, which you can just mess around with in between levels. It's like playing a more family-friendly Grand Theft Auto with famous super heroes. And there are plenty of neat secrets and puzzles both in the hub and within the levels and missions you take part in, loads of knicknacks for the taking, and despite some things being easy to obtain, it's always satisfying to obtain them.
This, despite being one of the best Lego games out there, is not among the greatest games ever made, admittedly, but it is more than worth your time for being quite the fun diversion.

Arkham Knight has various side quests called Most Wanted where you hunt down some of Gotham's most notorious criminals. None of them are needed to beat the main story, but in order to experience the true ending you will have to beat them all. I have to admit Enigma was really annoying me with all of his riddles. You need to find and solve all of them which was definitely the most time consuming activity in the whole game.

It's a great feeling when you have to drive all those criminals you caught to the GCPD building yourself and they talk on the way there. It really feels so much more realistic this way. Great job! On the other hand for someone who doesn't like driving it could be a bit troublesome. There are many quests where you have to use the batmobile. Some of them require fast reactions so they can definitely be a pain in the
The combat is much more interesting and fun. But at the same time there aren't any very difficult bosses to fight this time. The game feels easier on normal difficulty than the previous ones so I would say you don't have to be worried to increase the difficulty. In Arkham Knight you get tank battles as boss fights instead, which again isn't great for people who don't like using the batmobile very much.

I was streaming it and when I tried to run it without streaming there were no issues at all.
The game has some bugs. For example I fell through the map during a difficult mission with countdown timer. It was very annoying that I had to repeat it all...
Overall, I love this game! Even after 80 hours spent in game I still feel like starting it over again. And I don't get that feeling after finishing most games. So please, guys and girls. Get this game if your PC is not a potato. You will not regret it! 100% recommended and looking forward to the next Batman game!

This game is hard.
Unforgivingly hard.
This game will punish you for breathing.
In Risk of Rain, Difficulty affects not just the enemies HP, but also affects their damage dealt, the starting cash, starting health, it even affects the number Bosses that may spawn during a wave.On Drizzle difficulty, the difficulty rises one level per every 9 or so minutes. On Rainstorm, it's around 4 minutes. I don't even want to think about what may be in store on Monsoon difficulty(Difficulty rises every 3 minutes, Blighted enemies might spawn,you start with 15 gold, and the Teleporter takes 120 seconds to spawn, compared to Rainstorm and Drizzles's 90 seconds).  Progress isn't saved on Drizzle, so think of it as more of a training difficulty.
Artifacts can either be a blessing or a curse, allowing you to only spawn one type of enemy per map(Kin, which is on the Dried Lake Map), to only spawning Elite class monsters(Honor, which is on the Desolate Forest Map). Ultimately, it's up to you to go for the artifacts or not, they're entirely optional and unnecessary to actually beating the game. Unless you're a Completionist. In that case, go for it. Have fun with the Map Variants.
Each character has their own special usages, from the beginning class Commando, who implements his gun to move quickly and shoot just as fast, to the defense-focused Enforcer, who uses his Shield to withstand powerful attacks and can shoot faster with the Shield up with his Shotgun and Concussion Grenade.
Items are vital to your survival, as you can carry any amount of items, excluding Use-Items. The Items in Risk of Rain are as numerous as they are diverse, from the simple Crowbar, which allows you to deal 50% more damage to enemies above 80% HP, to the Infusion, which gives you +1 max HP for every kill you get.
In my honest opinion, this game is fantastic. I love it, it's addictive and I can't get enough of it. But be warned. It's not easy. Providence will never be your friend. To anybody who has this game or is buying/considering buying it: Kudos to you.

Finally out of Early Access this year. I personally LOVE this game. With Payday 2, this game is another Co-Op multiplayer game, but this time you ain't a criminal gang stealing♥♥♥♥♥♥and fighting the law. Instead, you're part of a team paid to kill zeds (AKA ZOMBIIIIES). How awesome is that?! Up to a 6-man team per games, everyone have an important role in the team. Per example :
The Commando is able to show the cloaked zombies to the rest of the team when he spots them. Also able to see the zeds health bar from a certain distance (which upgrade as you level up the class)
The Medic is a MUST to have in every team, as like his name suggests, he heals your team to keep you up and alive. To continue your zombie killing business.
The Sharpshooter is, imo, the glass cannon of the team, able to put to shreds even the most durable type of zeds in a single shot with his incredible headshooting Sniper Rifles.
The Berserker is the acting tank of the team (though he's really enjoyable when you get it to Lvl 5), capable of ripping appart the zombie army at melee distance while taking a lot of beating for the rest of the team.
The Demolitionist is the explosives expert of your team, having a good selection of launchers and explosives throwables at his disposal making him a useful assets in case you're getting swarmed by the undead.
The Support is the shotgunner and official welder of the team, capable of containing large groups of zeds with his arsenal and closing entry point to the flesh-eating army with his increased welding speed abilitiy.
There is a playstyle for everyone, from the Gunslinger pistolero with akimbo, to the SWAT expert with SMGs. Though weapons aren't perks-restricted, meaning a Commando can be seen with a shotgun and the Sharpshooter can be seen with an SMG. But most perks gives boost to weapons of their own class, so it is preferable to use your perks prefered arsenal. Some weapons have selective fire mode, other don't, be sure to look it up on the weapons description before you buy it.
Gunplay mechanics is somewhat easy to adapt to, crouching while standing still makes your crosshair tighter like you'd expect, moving widens it as well, though many times it happens that even aiming at the head in point blank you can miss a shot, Trigger discipline is an important skill to own, otherwise be prepare to see your ammo counter being depleted faster than you can even comprehend and being left with only your knife for the rest of the round. Staying on the move is your main source of survival, if you crouch for too long or try to pick a shot for too long, you'll get flanked from behind and, ultimately, getting ripped by the Zeds.
there ain't much story in the game yet, the backstory is simple : Big company named Horzine wanted to created biological weapons or some s*** and f**ked up somehow. Europe is in flames and Horzine has to fix their s**t so they decide to hire people to kill their little army of clone zeds, and that is you, buddy.
I recommend this game, it just started as a full fledged game and there's a lot of potential to this game, but that's just me, guys. Happy zombie killing!

It's a picross game, so there is no excuse for how half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it is.
The interfase is clearly made for mobile, with the drag to change pages, I only noticed by accident. There is no support for the right mouse button (flagging button), instead you have to click a button to switch modes, making it as clunky as most of the UI.
There is also no restart button, you have to fail on purpose, then you can retry.
You get 4 stars for completing stages without making a mistake. It requires replaying the stages because you lack information to get through it with logic.
The stars you get are not enough to unlock all levels, so
. I have every star I can collect, and I'm at 6 stars, unlocking any of the 70 levels I can't do, requires either 10 stars, for the official ones, or 4 stars for the "community" levels. I.e. they didn't even bother to check if the game could be beaten.
Some you can cheese through by assuming that the image is symmetric, or in a particular pattern, but pretty much trial and error, particularly for the faux-minesweeper levels.
These levels are ill thought out. The number tells you if the amount of pixels to paint in the 9 pixel block that includes that numbers square. The reason minesweeper excludes the number's own square in the calculation is because that allows them to give you more information, not doing that means you can't diferentiate between neighboring squares really often.
This is compounded by the stupidest idea I've seen in a long time of making the "clues" (which numbers you can see) randomized each time you enter the stage. i.e. they only give you part of the information, most of the time, not enough to complete without having to guess your way through it, and then only letting you unlock more levels if you repeat it without mistakes.
If you want to try doing it, just bruteforce part of it, take a photo, and go on from there, and once you finish the level, repeat it following a photo of the completed puzzle.
You can get some extra stars by randomly completing "collections" of puzzles (no way to tell which levels are part of them) which build some scenes or drawings from some franchises like transformers, one piece, naruto and DBZ, but they aren't enough to unlock 10% of the levels I couldn't unlock despite having every star available.
Don't waste your time. Picross can be a "fun" turn-off my brain for a minute kind of distraction while you do something else, but this implementation shows little effort, so in my opinnion, it isn't worth supporting.

So I came into XCOM with very VERY high expectations. Bit of back sotry; when someone says TBS I am at the Kitchen Table breaking out board games before they can finish thier sentence. I am a huge TBS fan. I begrudgingly have to settle for RTS , Shoorters, MOBAs, etc because it is pretty rare for a great TBS to be put out, and competitive TBS games usually boil down to "why am i not jsut playing chess?" Back story aside you are probably thinking I am going to rip into XCOM. Well I am not. XCOM was a "good" game. Fluid storyline with streamlined controls, and competent learning curve created an enjoyable experience. But (there is always a but), XCOM is much more a story than it is a TBS. I found myself much more interested in the sotry elements then getting out there and outsmarting the AI. The macro management elements where engaging and very enjoyable, but thier depth made the micro control (Ie the Actual combat much to easy.) Even on the hardest difficulty you dont feel any sense of urgency to push back the Alien Invasion. Every problem in the game can be solved with your basic level troop and a little TBS know how: don't rush, creat kill boxes, special weapons are to be used not hoarded, there is no cover but heavy cover.  It seems simplistic but the game never forces you to think outside of that box. "GTTFP Hopper!" Xcom is a great game I loved every minute I was playing it, but like a bump of cocaine I was sad when I came down to earth and realized everything was pretty much the same and XCOM had redefined the bar for TBS.

I hate writing negative reviews, and I almost never do, but I've encountered multiple puzzles now where there is no clear solution using only logic, which negates the way this type of puzzle works, especially if you don't know what picture you are attempting beforehand. One of them turned out to be a horse, but it was a 50/50 gamble whether the "leg" should have gone up and the "tail" down or the "tail" up and the "leg" down, not knowing what you were making. It would have solved the puzzle correctly either way. I don't remember the others I encountered before it, but the most recent was an S-shaped one in the 5x5 grid. I got three horizontal lines, each 3 wide, across the center, and needed to place 4 single blocks. I had no idea where they should go, so I tried it as a "Z" shape and got it wrong, even though there was no reason it couldn't have been solved that way instead of the "S", given the clues.
It's a small nitpick, but if there are colors in a picross puzzle, usually you place them individually and they are given as separately colored clues (for example, 2 blue, 1 brown, 3 blue), and it was a small disappointment to discover that was not the case with this game and the colors are applied automatically, but that doesn't bother me nearly as much as the fact that many of the puzzles have an element of luck rather than logic, forcing you to replay the puzzle for full stars through no fault of your own.

Short summary: This game is phenomenal in so many different ways between its character design, plot progression, and even the reuse of levels (Yes, this is actually a decently done well thing in this game!). Replayability is very high (as long as you have a guide with you, preferably on the first time around so you don't miss stuff set up for the 2nd playthrough). This game is witty, hilarious, fun, and I honestly found myself addicted and wanting to get everything. And I just normally don't do that. So props to the devs.
Breaking it down...
Plot: 9/10
I wanna give it even a 9.5, but when you consider how much further they could've gone, I suppose a fantastic 9 will do. The plot isn't really predictable at all. There are few twists and turns, and the entire thing will have you laughing or crying because feels. From a story driven perspective, amazing.
Combat: 8.5
At first, combat is dull. Grinding WP to upgrade your abilities/versatility can be a bit slow BUT once you pass that hump OHMYGOD IT CAN BE WONDERFUL TO DESTROY CRAP IN THOSE B.A. FAIRIZE THINGS.
Waifu: 10/10
Just... Yes. I'm not even gonna write anything more.
Dungeon design: 6/10
This is the weakest part of the game tbh. They reuse dungeons and dungeon design for multiple places and it's dull. Despite my low score for this, nearly everything else outshines the reuse of the dungeons. I know I'm giving it a 6, but really I weight this section far lower than the others.
Character design: 10/10
And not just cause of waifus. Each character has their own unique personality and each one is lovable in their own way. Hell, even the shop keeper has a funny personality when you get new sub-events to talk with her.
Music: 10/10
Love that intro. I watch the intro video sometimes Just so I can hear it. Then again you can unlock a music gallery later <3
TL;DR: buy it if you like anime, funnies, and waifus. Also, use a guide so you don't miss stuff (cause you will otherwise).

Not a game for the faint of heart!
I will start off by saying that I am not great at platformers. However, if you would like a nice little metriodvainia with EXTREMELY punishing platforming then this is the game for you!
Time: 17 hours
Finished my first playthrough in 17 hours, but I only had a 93% completeion rate so im guessing to get that other 7% I would need to out in 20+ hours to do it.
Gameplay: Outstanding
Plays just as a Metriodvainia should. The fun of the game really comes from the megaman-esque feel to the bossfights. What I mean is that certain spells you collect are suprememly effective against certain bosses. For example, the knight in the windy ruins died in three hits to my Fire Explosion spell. As a result it really makes it valuable to experiment with certain spells against different bosses. Secrets abound in this game and are obviously pivotal to getting 100% completeion. So it makes reexploring areas that much more fun. I will say that the game dosent really open until you get doublejump but that is the case for most metroidvanias.
Music: good
8bit goodness is rampant in this game. However, as far a soundtracks go there was no track in the game that really made me stop and just listen to it. Good soundtrack,  but nothing too memorable.
Environment: Outstanding
Each area is supremely different from the last, so the areas never bleed together. They are punishing though each area abounds with spikes and traps that are instant death should you hit them, so there were points with extremely punishing jumps that took me 50+ attemps (not eaxggerating) to accomplish. It is extremely hard to rush through these areas so speed runners beware.
Great game! Even better time sink! If this company produces more metriodvanias I will be sure to buy them.

Heres my 2 cents as an avid online card player.
Shadowverse IS a well made game. First off it is a card game. Nothing I hate more than downloading a game with cards in it to find out it is a phone app energy game lol. It comes complete with a campaign, ranked, and tournament game modes. The card graphics are unique and well made while the card animations are quite smooth. In the beginning playing this game feels like a real treat and you absolutely will not regret it. There are tons of free packs and gems thrown at you like candy. You'll be getting legendaries and epics all over the place and making tons of variations to decks.
The only real issue I have and still have with this game is the extremely confined class cards. I would say about 90% of the cards are restricted to a single class and 10% are not. To top it off nearly all the classes have superior cards of the same type compared to basic cards which leaves you no reason to use them anyways except for one legendary neutral card that replenishes your evolve orbs.
Not to mention it is super easy to get a bunch of rare cards in one or two classes then a legendary in a class that you have no cards for lol.
I think something to fix this issue would be to allow someone to pick a pack for a certain class.
Overall I really enjoyed my time in this game and had some epic comebacks and losses. Also some arena decks that were so synergized I didn't lose once. It gave a lot of good feels and do not regret but I do feel the lack of customization really effects the overall replayability.

Batman™: Arkham Knight Premium Edition
==============================
Rating Score:
• ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (<=20%)
• Bad (~30%)
• Below Average (~40%)
• Average (~50%)
• Decent (~60%)
• Good (~70%)
• Amazing (~80%)
• Phenomenal (>=90%)
--------------------------
Story: Good
The story is pretty straight forward, at times there were certain points that will surprise you, and at times some things were just plain predictable. For every few high points of the story there's a low point. It's worth a mention that in order to get the true ending of the game, the game must be 100% completed
. Also, I'm very sure that you must play all the previous Arkham games in order to truly appreciate the story.
Gameplay: Good
Hand-to-hand combat: Amazing
The hand-to-hand combat has the same formula as the previous games, really addictive, really fun.
Predator: Amazing
Though at times it can be a little bit easy due to the overpowered nature of some of the gadgets, and in my opinion is the easiest predator mode compared to the other Arkham games, it's still really fun and challenging.
Tank combat: Average
The tank combat gets easier over time, and it becomes more of a chore later on.
Stealth tank combat (Cobra drone): Bad
This one makes no sense at all, how can a big♥♥♥♥♥tank move around stealthily? Either way, similarly to the tank battles, it's more of a chore than actually having fun. Fortunately, there isn't much of this in the actual gameplay.
Boss battles: Average
Say what you want about Arkham Origins, at least that one has actual boss battles. Some of the boss battles are pretty non-existent, which is extremely disappointing, while there are also some that completely make no sense.
Customization: Good
There's a lot of variety in the customization, the progression of the customizations depends on your approach in the game.
Graphics: Amazing
My potato of a GTX 770 can't play this in high-ultra settings, but I must say that it looks better in low settings compared to some other games in high.
Voice acting: Phenomenal
The voice acting in this game is stellar. Everything from the main characters to the lowlife thugs sounds great. I personally liked Two-Face's voice acting the most.
Arkham Episodes: Amazing
Each character plays differently, all of them are very enjoyable.
Harley Quinn: Phenomenal
The fact that she can't stay quite even in stealth mode makes playing as her so amusing.
Red Hood: Amazing
A Nightwing with guns, insta-kill anyone that isn't bulletproof as long as you don't mind making some noise.
Batgirl: Good
A Batman-like character with limited gadgets in her arsenal. Though the progression of her story requires a lot of gadget utilization.
Nightwing: Amazing
The gameplay itself is pretty straight forward, but Nightwing's personality will surely win you over.
Catwoman: Good
By far the hardest of the Arkham Episodes. It's fun until you die the 10000th time.
Robin: Decent
This episode has to be the weakest one. It's pretty straight forward, Robin is just a batman with limited gadgets and a shield. The overall gameplay is pretty easy, and Robin doesn't connect well with the player.
Overall: Good
It's pretty decently priced given it's content, and it's going to keep you busy for ages if you're a completionist, it's worth every penny. Though I must say that I'd rather wait for a sale since this title gets a discount very often.

Just tried out this game after the Wonderland Dreams card expansion (release on June 28, 2017) and I gotta say, this card game is really beginner friendly, despite all the negative reviews that I read before picking up this game.
Yes, there are card packs (and as of this moment pre-built decks are available too, for a really hefty price) that will cater players paying to get the best cards in the game, but every card game that offers in-game purchases or product codes from merchandises will of course put tweaks to make a combination/deck effective potentially, but not exponentially. And how does Shadowverse fare in this pay-to-win issue? Well, I for one thought that buying one would make or give you a powerful card set and decks but in this case, getting such rares will not change the game greatly, because it all plays out with your strategy, Of course, you can't win against a player who bought a 3 pre-built decks or 100 card packs with just a beginner's deck. You've gotta build it, tho it will take longer, but sure enough, you will have a great deck to duke out against those players.
And about the gameplay, well, after trying out all the classes and built some deck combinations, Fairycraft and Swordcraft decks fare out quite well with the numbers because their effects and gameplay almost rely heavily on overwhelming the board with lots of followers. As for Runecraft, well, the chances of you getting wrecked by a deck focused on this class is high, if I would concur, as this class bombards the enemies with spells with assorted effects, from drawing cards to outright dealing damage to your followers and leader, and adding to that, their followers get a spellboost every time a spell is used, which in turn makes them stronger or giving them additional effects and that would be very painful to deal with. Decks relying heavily on Dragoncraft cards deal with their enemies with early application of brute force, yes, they seem to have the most powerful low playpoint cost cards in the game, and they have many cards that add playpoint orbs, making it faster to play more powerful cards in within a few turns, and oh did I just forgot to mention that most of their cards get even more powerful as they get more playpoint orbs? That will hurt you really bad. And last but not the least, and my personal favorite among the classes, the Undead Scourge, nah just joking, of course it's none other than the Shadowcraft class. This class' game mechanic and strategy really feels unique to me compared to others, because they rely on shadows (graveyard guys, because it's the undead lol) greatly to increase the potential of most of their cards. Basically speaking, early game, it requires you to sacrifice some followers to add to the shadow count which in turn can be used in a variety of ways and effects, all of which is beneficial to wrecking your opponent. And of course, you can't call them undead if they're not raising any dead right? Annoy your opponents by thinking that he/she annihilated your board, then suddenly a pack of zombies and skeletons just appeared out of nowhere to change the tide of the battle and defeat the Alliance once and for all.
Well that's about it, I won't talk about RNGs yet, as I've yet to delve deeper through this game myself, tho I'm reading how to build great decks for starters here and on reddit.
TLDR: Try it out, as it is free and basically you've just wasted time if you found it really bad or unsatisfying.

Batman: Arkham Knight brings the series to a close with an uneven, but satisfying conclusion. Like it's predecessors before it, the game continues to cement the idea that Batman should be a master of melee combat. Unfortunately, the combat has not changed all that much from the other 3 Arkham games.
I personally believe Arkham Asylum was the peak to this series. The level design and smaller setting of a prison allowed me to appreciate the story and little side content with more focus. Arkham Knight throws you into a chaotic city with most of your gadgets already unlocked and a Batmobile. This was a little too overwhelming for the first hour, but I realize the developer made this game as a conclusion for the fans of the series.
Positives:
-The game looks incredible, and the addition of those Nvidia gameworks affects turn Gotham City into a richly textured playground where little details pop up on every corner
-The story is more serious and interesting. It's cemented from the start that this will be Batman's final journey, and they try to give a lot of the minor characters a small story segment.
-The combat stays as impactfull as ever.
Negatives:
-I love open-world games, but feel that Asylum is the right way to do a game like this instead of having an open map. There was just too much nothing in between my objectives, and it felt like I was gliding or driving for very little reason.
-The Batmobile is...not great. I mean, I know why this is in the game, but the handling just felt off and the reliance on it for most of the game detracted from the stealthy approaches in the previous games.
-The game runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥ It has the most random FPS drops I've seen in the game (especially while driving, which is another reason I dislike the Batmobile). I ran the benchmark before starting the game and was getting an average of 120 FPS. After about 1/3 of the game, I start seeing dips into the 30s for no reason.
Overall, if the game was more optimized, and did not rely so much on the Batmobile, the game would have been excellent.

This game is hard.
Unforgivingly hard.
This game will punish you for breathing.
In Risk of Rain, Difficulty affects not just the enemies HP, but also affects their damage dealt, the starting cash, starting health, it even affects the number Bosses that may spawn during a wave.On Drizzle difficulty, the difficulty rises one level per every 9 or so minutes. On Rainstorm, it's around 4 minutes. I don't even want to think about what may be in store on Monsoon difficulty(Difficulty rises every 3 minutes, Blighted enemies might spawn,you start with 15 gold, and the Teleporter takes 120 seconds to spawn, compared to Rainstorm and Drizzles's 90 seconds).  Progress isn't saved on Drizzle, so think of it as more of a training difficulty.
Artifacts can either be a blessing or a curse, allowing you to only spawn one type of enemy per map(Kin, which is on the Dried Lake Map), to only spawning Elite class monsters(Honor, which is on the Desolate Forest Map). Ultimately, it's up to you to go for the artifacts or not, they're entirely optional and unnecessary to actually beating the game. Unless you're a Completionist. In that case, go for it. Have fun with the Map Variants.
Each character has their own special usages, from the beginning class Commando, who implements his gun to move quickly and shoot just as fast, to the defense-focused Enforcer, who uses his Shield to withstand powerful attacks and can shoot faster with the Shield up with his Shotgun and Concussion Grenade.
Items are vital to your survival, as you can carry any amount of items, excluding Use-Items. The Items in Risk of Rain are as numerous as they are diverse, from the simple Crowbar, which allows you to deal 50% more damage to enemies above 80% HP, to the Infusion, which gives you +1 max HP for every kill you get.
In my honest opinion, this game is fantastic. I love it, it's addictive and I can't get enough of it. But be warned. It's not easy. Providence will never be your friend. To anybody who has this game or is buying/considering buying it: Kudos to you.

"That's XCOM"
Learn it. Love it.
A great strategy game. Best played on ironman to really get that XCOM feeling.
This game has multiple layers of playability to it. First is the main aspect of the game: combat.
Combat plays out with your squad on a field taking turns between you and the enemy forces. You engage, shoot, find cover, etc. However, what really felt different about this game than other turn based games was the fluid feeling it had. It doesn't feel like a turn based game at all sometimes.
Combat is also done in percentages rather than hard numbers. It can be amazing to get that final kill with a 7% chance shot. It can also be extremely frustrating to miss that game changing 98% shot from point blank. However, that is part of the game and you have to learn risk mitigation.
Speaking of which, if you're into numbers, you'd probably like this game. Many of the game's mechanics can be broken down into numbers.
Inbetween combat you are located at your base. The things you do at your base are just as crucially important to your success, if not more. This is where you upgrade your soldiers, fit them, build onto your base, scan for aliens, and research new technologies.
XCOM is not a forgiving game by-the-way. There is a point while playing where you are probably never going to be able to win (too many veterans permenantly dead, wrong researches, not enough satellites, people leaving the council, etc) and the game will continue letting you play until the bitter end without saying a word.
However, thats the fun part of it.
Those wanting a challenge in their games should definitely check it out.

You are an elite, multicultural fighting force whose job is to prevent ET from phoning home. Most of your time will be spent in tactical missions controlling up to a six man squad. Missions are tied together by an overall base-building meta-game where you manage resources, research, inventory and your troop roster. XCOM operates on a reverse difficulty curve, where the initial missions will be brutal. It’s unforgiving and will quickly teach you to weigh all your options before you commit to an action. Not doing so will likely see valuable soldiers (the ones you’ve spent half your time customising and developed attachments to) die painfully or nations pull funding to your cause. Permanently. As such, the campaign is pretty time consuming but is the absolute balls for turn-based strategy.
