Pros:
Shadowverse offers a great diversity of classes and cards to create many decks. There are so many decks and archetypes you can build that I've literally spent hours just playing around with cards and making as many decks as I could just for the fun of it. Many cards work well together in every class and because of this, deck building is one of the most fun aspects of Shadowverse.
The gameplay of shadowverse is very fun as well. The unique mechanic of evolution points makes the game quite interactive and creates another sense of strategy into it's gameplay. I really don't have much to say about the gameplay as it's pretty straight forward once you start playing it.
Shadowverse is probably one of the most generous games when it comes to free-to-play and/or newer players. Rewards are given daily and if you play a decent amount of time everyday you can easily gather up enough to buy card packs. However, card packs are given so often and so generously you could probably easily create any deck you want as long as you rerolled the right cards. Beginners are given 40+ packs after finishing the tutorials and more after completing things such as defeating advanced AIs which isn't too difficult of a task with a decent deck.
The art of shadowverse is simply amazing. There is much variety in the art as they are created by many different artists. They are tailored towards the Japanese/Anime community and that can be seen as a huge plus for many people. Even if you don't enjoy anime styled art, from an artist standpoint many of these cards are just beautiful to look at.
Cons:
Shadowverse is a great game. It really is. However, as the game has developed and age'd it has become less and less fun for me due to how the meta has shaped for the worse. The diversity of cards and decks in this game is amazing, yet an illusion for newer players who want to get into a card game where they want to have fun with the diversity of decks. As of now, in higher ranks you can't even climb or just enjoy the game with a fun deck you've made because the meta revolves around being quickpaced and winning by your first 4-5 turns. You want to play a deck that revolves around controling your opponent and winning with late game conditions? Yeah, good luck climbing with that. You want to play a deck you created that seem's super fun to pull off the win condition? Yeah, unless its some kind of early game aggro deck, good luck with that as you'll probably end up losing 9 out of 10 games without even getting close to your win condition.
But that's where uncompetitive play/unranked comes into the day and save us from the hell of ranked, right?
Wrong.
Even in unranked play you will find the same people playing the same decks and stomp you for even trying to have fun. It's very frustrating.
With the addition of Wonderland Dreams, every deck has been given the same access to cards that shape the current early meta of the patch. While this sounds like a great idea to give every class a fair chance at the meta, it fails to deliver any sense of fun or actual balance because different classes have different win conditions that suit the fast paced meta better. I often question the design of many cards as they are so broken the meta often revolves around every deck playing around that specific card. If you are forced to create a deck that revolves around a single card AND every deck has access to the same meta neutral cards, there is no diversity to be had.
Yes, there are exceptions because there are people who do make decks to play and have fun despite the meta. And you may run into these people as you play. It is those moments where I truly enjoy playing the game because it feels more fair and losing to a deck that isn't in the meta is like a breath of fresh air in the toxicated meta where interactive play doesn't exist. But those moments are so far and few that it will never relieve you of the stress of playing the game for fun.
However, this is a review for the game in its current state as of July 4th
TL;DR: Shadowverse is a great game. Very noob friendly and rewarding. As time goes on and you gather more cards and get higher into the rankings, it becomes less fun because of how diversity in the meta is very very limited.
Even shorter TL;DR: Great diversity in decks, Very low diversity in meta.

An absolute mindf**k. That is all that needs to be said.
I have rarely played a game so abstract, challenging, and enjoyable throughout its entire story. The puzzles are deceptively simple, with you sometimes being stuck on a single puzzle for a half hour, only to come back later and be able to figure it out in a matter of minutes.
Every single puzzle was unique and required you to completely break your standard approach and thought processes to solving puzzles and playing games. It forces you to defy all reason, and somehow, you eventually become attuned with the universe's wacked-out physics and inane logic.
You feel such a sense of joy and accomplishment at the completion of each puzzle, no matter how long it took to solve, because this game requires you to think SO FAR outside the box and so unconventionally that your brain feels like it legitimately gained from the puzzles and learned something from it. The extra life lessons connected to each puzzle also help, and there are plenty of them.
There is nothing quite like this game. The closest game I feel can compare is Fez, which also was a total mindf**k of its own, and it is hard to say which game I enjoyed more. Either way, both are must-plays. This is an experience unlike any other, and the dev deserves some SERIOUS cred, not only for thinking up these puzzles, but for successfully programming them. It has to be a programming feat because the way things loop around and behave in this game cannot abide to normal logic or reason, or even the structure of 3D spacetime.
Play this game. Blow your mind. And try not to drive yourself crazy on the puzzles that laugh at you with their utter simplicity. Everything is doable - you just gotta be clever enough.

Arkham Knight is the final chapter of the Arkham games, and a good one for that matter.
First of all, the game had a terrible release, with several glitches and performance, but almost all problems were fixed. The only problem I had was memory leaks, but I managed to reduce them by increasing my virtual memory and you can fix them by restarting the game after one or two hours of playing.
The combat is the same as every other Arkham games, although more fluid than ever. Punch, combo and counter, pretty much everything is the same, only with a few minor additions like special gadget combos, which mostly stuns everyone around you.
The story is pretty good, has some cool twists and a lot of interesting parts. Although, if you know about the Batman lore, you will know who is the titual character almost right away.
The graphics are the best in the series, and even with the settings all the way down, they are still pretty good. the only thing that bothers me is the rain, that NEVER stops through the game. It can be quite a bother because of the amount of bloom and blur that they cause, I suggest downloading a mod that removes it.
The level and upgrade system was made quite worse, on previous games you would beat up people, get a level and then you could get an upgrade. On this game, while you can level the same, you dont get experience from beating up random thugs on the streets, only from specific parts, and the upgrades cost more than one upgrade point, forcing you to play side missions and AR challenges so you can upgrade your stuff.
The innovation in this was made in the form of the Batmobile. Honestly, I found it pretty fun to drive around, but that is kinda pointless because you get a powered up grappling hook that can launch you to the stratosphere, letting you to glide across the map with ease.
That means forced Battank sections. The tank sections are fun, but happen too often. There are even Steath Tank sections to contrast the Predator/Stealth parts. You have to drive the tank around and destroy the drones or you will never be able to go around on foot. Also, if you defeat human enemies with the tank, you dont get experience.
On the gadget department, all of them are returning stuff from the previous games. One or two got new uses like the hacking device that can hack or blind enemy drones. Only one new addition, the voice synthesizer, which you use to force an enemy to get near a trap or check a trapped box.
The claw launcher, electric gloves and glue grenade from Origins dont show up. The Electric Gun can be recovered at the start of the game, but isnt used in the story until the last 2 or 3 missions and the Ice Blast is completely missable, nothing  aside some steam vents tell you about it's existance and its just sitting in a corner of a map.
There are a lot of boss fights in the game, but none of them are 1v1 battles or actually challenging. Origins actually had the best boss fights in the game.
Two are tank battles, one being Deathstroke, which is reduced to a single cutscene before he gets knocked out.
One is basically the chase levels from Crash Bandicoot, where you have to dodge obstacles with the Batmobile until the boss crashes into something.
Two-Face is a normal enemy from a Predator room and can be knocked out instantly, Penguin and Hush get knocked out in one button press, Firefly is a pursuit, Blackfire is just a bunch of enemies you have to knock out in less than 5 minutes and Pyg is an almost normal fight, you just have to knock the enemies in a specfic way.
The only thing that can be called a boss fight is against the Riddler.
Overall, I'd say the best one in the series. The tank combat might turn off some people, but is still a pretty solid game.
I'd wait for a BIG sale (preferentially outside of Steam, since every place other than Steam gives better discounts) to get the Season Pass, since the DLC is mostly skins and 30-minute long stories.

The game itself is great and while it fails to live up to previous games in the serious, it remains an enjoyable and fun batman sim with an engaging story, polished gameplay, and some of the best visuals in any game to date. However, as good as the actual game is, I still cannot reccomend buying this game on PC. Yes its been patched and greatly improved from its launch, but it still suffers crash issues as well as streaming/performance issues. For reference, I am running an RX480 8GB on the latest drivers with an i5 6500 quad core CPU and 8GB of DDR4 2133Mhz Ram. I also have the game installed on an SSD. I understand that while my system may not be the most top of the line, it is by no means underpowered for this game and it has had no trouble running almost every other game on max settings at 1080p or sometimes even 1440p while holding 60 plus fps. The real problem I have with the games performance is just how inconsistent it is. I've had long stretches where the game will hover between 70-100fps on its highest settings and it's very smooth. But as soon as you hover over a highly deatiled area of the city or drive at high speeds in the batmobile, expect performance to dip. In my case, I can see my fps go from mid 80's all the way down to 40 when driving at high speeds. The problem seems to be an optimization issue in regards to how the game streams in data as you move through the city. This problem was far worse at launch, and while it has been improved, it was never fully fixed in this port. I've actually resorted to just locking the game at 30fps and in turn playing it at 4k as at least that way the performance is more consistent and the game looks much sharper. The crashing issues have also been improved since launch, but they still exist and some areas of the city are more prone to crashes than others. The game also really loves to eat up CPU cores and you can expect some stuttering when the game hits 100% CPU usage, which seems to happen at very random times regardless of what is going on in the game. It's a shame that the game still has the problems it has, because the game itself is great, but the port is subpar even after all the updates.
TL;DR: Game is awesome, port is lackluster.

For starters this is a great game. The main and most side missions are fun to play and usually have some fun mechanics to work with. Another good thing i like about the missions and the way you progress through the game is by having to get so far in the main story to even begin some of the others. The story itself is pretty standard batman storyline which isnt a bad thing and something im not going to spoil as you really have to experience it for yourself. Although myself and alot of others who played this didnt like some certain boss fights others are fun and can be really challenging on the harder difficulties. The characters are put into places where they look like they fit most of the time apart from the few that feel as if they were shohorned in at the last second. Good voice acting which brings life to characters we otherwise wouldnt see it in such as Alfred and some of the goons roaming the street who sometimes have some pretty funny things to say. The combat is basic and easy to pick up whether you think that is a good or bad thing is up to you but i personally liked it as i didnt have to learn something completely new. Some parts of the game can feel repetitive and boring if you're going for the milestones such as 120 and 240% completion and another complaint which alot of people seem to bring up is that the batmobile is forced upon you alot of the time which i think is true. The DLC for this game is a place this game really shines in adding playable characters such as nightwing, red hood, Harley quinn, batgirl, robin and catwoman which are mostly playable in the base game but its always a win to play as those characters in their own DLC's which add a load of replayability. Even smaller things such as all the skins for a majority of the characters and the batmobile is also a nice addition, being able to choose between things like the original batman look, the 2008 batman and  tumbler batmobile or the 2016 batman v superman looks. The classic skins for the other playable characters which you can play as in either their DLC's or the AR challenges mode. Even small aspects of the game can be fun like looking for all of the firemen or solving all of the riddlers puzzles to finally confront him are incredibly fun and add quite a bit of play time. This game also runs really well only having frame drops when i'm frequently tabbing out and/or have other apps open but then even i only drop at most 5-6 frames on max settings which is barely noticeable. Overall if you just want a game to play a bit then never play again wait until the game is next on sale and pick up the base version and if you want a game you'll never put down depending on whether money is an option buy the premium edition on or off sale as it is worth it and you get so much extra content. This game is something i highly recommend with or without DLC.

If you feel even slightly interested in this game after looking at this Steam Page, don't hesitate to buy it.
An intuitive control scheme allows anyone to pick it up almost immediately (but even if you couldn't, we're on PC, so you can always change key bindings). The classes feel unique, and the ones that I've delved into are some of my favorite in gaming. The guns have weight and sound pretty great, and when you shoot an enemy, there is no doubt as to whether you hit them or not. Each impact is satisfying, and because of the way each weapon feels, what could have been incredibly repetitive never gets boring. Possibly my favorite aspect of the game is the way that you level up. Balanced perks and trait configurations mean that every time you level up (each class has unique ways to gain experience; it's not just "kill Zeds to lvl up"), the game rewards you with a satisfying perk/buff.
I was concerned when I saw that it was more enjoyable as a multiplayer experience. At the time, only one friend of mine played it, and I can't play games like these solo. I'm also no good with horror games (at all), so I thought I might give it a pass. Luckily, I didn't pass it up because not only is it not a scary game, but online matchmaking is nearly instantaneous, and most people within the community are only too happy to play with a random.
I could write several pages on my enjoyment of the game so far, but there is no need. The ratings speak for themselves.

Toukiden: Kiwami isn't your average Koei Tecmo game, it's more like Dynasty Warriors and Monster Hunter having had an illegitimate child.: A grindy as hell JRPG Musou game with a few added twists. Actually I had a lot more fun killing hundreds of gigantic Oni than killing thousands of soldiers in Dynasty Warriors, although character progression in Toukiden is a lot slower - as in even SLOWER than DW - and it is an absolute hassle to grind for equipment upgrades to get anywhere close to a legendary setup. Content wise there's half a dozen medium sized maps which are recycled all over the place by enabling and disabling different layouts. Every single room functions as a mini-sized arena, so it comes down to business as usual.
For a Musou game the story wasn't half bad, there's several hundred missions and in its best moments Toukiden actually felt atmosphereically on par with Monster Hunter.
That leaves to say that just like most Koei Tecmo games, Toukiden is a niche game, but it fills that niche extremely well. Just don't expect anything even remotely resembling a western RPG game.

Starting with the pros Killing Floor 2 is a phenomenal survival-action game.  It has a low learning curve with easy to understand mechanics which makes it very easy to pick up.  In terms of gameplay it is fairly tense, enemy spawns are too numerous to predict where enemies will come from so the player must either find a wide open place with lots of exits to train in, or kite through the map.  The maps themselves do not inherently favor one strategy over the other as each map has lots of different pathways and several open areas.
As for replayability, there are 10 classes at the moment and from how development went most likely more on the way.  I started out as a gunslinger, whipping massive pistols around the class had more of a focus on good aim and lots of headshots with small magazines and long reload times.  After leveling for a while I got bored so I switched to another class.  Whenever the game feels stale I switch classes for a new playstyle and new weapons.
The enemies are all very unique in their behavior and must be treated carefully no matter how small.  The first successful game where the player sees all the zeds and beats a boss leaves them feeling like Leon (Resident Evil) blasting through hordes of mutated chemical rejects like playing a good raccoon city.
Now the cons.  I am not one of those people who take difficulty as a con, difficulty is a choice of the developer to add flavor to the game like spice in an entrée.  However, cheating your own mechanics are.  Most of the time, the game is forgiving and allows you to travel your own path through.  Yet, sometimes, zeds coming from seamingly nowhere appear just in time to block the last escape route.  Normally I would pass this off as player error, I shouldn't have cornered myself, I could have easily gone another way, but what the problem
to be is the lack of a spawn cap on smaller pathways.  Meaning that the same number of enemies that can crop up from spawn point A as spawn point b at the one time.
There is also the fact of hidden mechanics, like reduced movement speed through carry weight, but I will leave that there.
Next is also on that replayability I love, the bosses are old.  There are
, only
, and probably for a very long time will only be
.  It's quite repetitive, fighting wave after wave with new guns and having to kill the boss in new ways is fun, but when there are a total of 20 ways.  You understand.
Regardless!  The classes are creative, the concept simple, and while there are some discrepencies with some programming it is otherwise fairly solid.  Overall it excells on what it set out to be, a cool zed killing playground albeit a mite shallow.  Because of that I give it a 8/10.

I never played Civ 4, but Civ 5 is a huge upgrade from Civ 3. Hex tiles make deciding where to build cities as easy as a point and click. Building the city, maintaining it, and making it grow are a completely different story. The units are also a huge upgrade, and their mechanics are easy to learn.
Civ 5 is very much a city builder, continuous progression game: Someone is going to win before you run out of stuff to do, unless you win first. Cities don't run out of upgrades until you reach the end of the tech tree, which is also where the Scientific Victory is. Turn based wins are a simple 'stay ahead of the other guys' concept, and the Cultural Victory is something that you can actually get on accident if you're not paying attention. Finally, there are Domination and Diplomatic Victory. Domination is taking the starting city of all the other guys, while Diplomatic is making friends with all the little AI city states that other people want to be friends with. I usually turn Time and Cultural Victories off, Time because it's a cheap win, and Cultural because I actually have gotten it on accident well before Diplomatic and Scientific victories were possible.
As for the Civs themselves, I thought only four or five were a style of play I liked. More recently, I said to myself 'This civ looks nice, but it doesn't seem as good as the others I play'. I was wrong about it, so all I can say is that I'm looking to do more then stick to my comfort zone now. That there are civs  that I likely will never play is good, becuase it gives options for people who have different playstyles.
I've also learned that keeping focused on one type of resouce at the expense of others (Food, Production, Science, Gold, Culture, Faith, or Happyness) actually gimps you early, and you can't always recover. You 'can' ignore Faith early game if you don't want to deal with it, but the others you kind of need.
The game just isn't complete without the DLC. Also, be careful when/if playing Venice, because they're a unique civ that requires a lot of precision to make work, and that Carthage actually can walk over mountains.
Also, tundra kinda sucks. Nobody really likes it, and it actually is the second worst type of terrain, Snow being the worst. Snow doesn't give you anything and only one civ even has the option of farming it, and tundra you need a river or lake to build farms.
This isn't a point and click 'this much and then you're done with this city' game. Once you build a city, you're always going to have something you can do with it.

OK, so if I have to choose Yes or No, I choose Yes, but that's a Yes with reservations. Yes because there aren't enough solid isometric turn-based-combat RPGs; reservations because the only part of that description that feels fully realized here is the isometric part. If you've never played a game like this, then first of all you're missing out on some of the absolute classics of gaming like the original Fallout games and the X-COM games, as well as some great newer titles like Dead State. But second, if you've never played a game like this, Shadowrun Returns amounts to a pretty good entry-level streamlined version of what an isometric turn-based RPG is. And that's exactly what frustrates me about it.
Isometric turn-based RPGs are kind of a perfect mixture for a certain kind of gaming experience. First and foremost, everything you do--and everything the AI does--is much more considered because of the turn-based structure. I can't remember the technical explanation exactly, but right around when Fallout 3 came out, an old-school Fallout head wrote a very long jeremiad on No Mutants Allowed, part of which explained why real-time combat AI tends to act so much more hive-mindy and stupid than turn-based combat AI. I don't know science, but that guy knew science. Anyway, point is, it creates a more thoughtful, considered, and engrossing form of combat. And the isometric view is pretty much perfect for that. Add in the RPG genre, which is in my view the most thoughtful and deliberative type of game, and you have a recipe for something great.
But everything is so stripped down here. If this is somebody's first foray into this kind of game, I want to caution you that it's the only one that is this basic. If you like how simplistic everything is, you're not going to dig Fallout 2 or X-COM: UFO Defense. But most likely, if you notice the simplicity, it's boring to you. Typically a game like this will give each character in a fight "action points," but here you just get a set number of actions, period. Running halfway across the room, swinging a baseball bat, and reloading a shotgun? All just worth one action. In a more serious turn-based RPG, each of those actions would have different action point costs--each step worth a point, reloading worth a couple points, firing or swinging a weapon worth a bigger chunk of points, etc. And speaking of reloading, you have infinite ammo. For some reason you have to go through the empty ritual of "reloading" your gun if combat lasts that long (it usually doesn't) but there's no ammo in your inventory. You just have ammo, forever.
The usual sandboxy/exploration elements of this type of game? Nowhere. Bodies disappear moments after dying. Very little in the game world can be interacted with. It seems like the only things you can even pick up are mission items, so don't bother trying to find some sort of sweet loot. (Really, that's the ultimate betrayal. No loot? What am I supposed to DO with myself? Half the fun of a game is making sure I have the baddest gear on the planet!)
The skill tree/level up system is fine. It's a fun way of doing it. Couldn't believe some reviewers here were saying it was intimidating or complicated though. It's just the Mass Effect system but with more skills to choose from. It's not even a tree. I don't want to seem like I'm trashing it, though, because it's probably the most well-executed thing in the game. It's not super-complex, but it's fine. Not everything has to be complex if it works.
Finally: the game is totally linear. Like incredibly linear. I can't emphasize enough what a disappointment that is in an isometric turn-based RPG. It just feels wrong, and it makes the game feel pointless. Linear games should be shooters. That's where linearity can make sense. A linear shooter essentially is a skill test. Generally not my cup of tea--I can enjoy House of the Dead as much as the next man, but generally I'm looking for something a little more intellectually engaging than a skill test. But at least you can understand the purpose of its existence. A linear isometric turn-based RPG? Huh? What's even the point? It basically becomes a slightly more fleshed-out version of a point-and-click adventure game, except without the puzzles. So...it's just an interactive story with some VERY mild branching in terms of how you accomplish the set-in-stone tasks which you are going to accomplish.
Here's what I will say: The writing can be very good, in places. The characters--even ones as minor as a homeless old man who's been pushed out of his alleyway by a murder investigation, or a dude who sells donuts on a street corner--feel real, in a sort of heightened stylized way, and you care about them. Granted, my heartstrings are a little easier to pluck than most, but still. It's good stuff and it works. What doesn't work so much are the attempts at setting the mood, the loading-screen text. It's an attempt at writing cyberpunk-noir, and while there are flashes of really good noir flair, it's often just very clumsily written with a lot of repeated words, similes instead of metaphors, and just plain hackneyed ideas.
I don't know. This feels a lot more like a No than a Yes in terms of whether I recommend it, now that I've written it. Still leaving it a Yes though. Lets go back to 1993 for a moment.
A ten year old boy - having never heard of pen and paper RPGs - begs his mum and dad for a SNES game called Shadowrun he's seen on all the gamer TV shows and read about in Gamesmaster... He isn't dissapointed- third favourite game of all time!
Forward to 1994/5 A twelve year old boy discovers PNP roleplaying, D&D, Call of Cthulu, Vampire/Werewolf and shortly after Shadowrun, falls in love all over again.
Forward to 2004 and we have a bitterly dissapointed 21 year old chewing his liver over the Xbox 360 remake...
So here we go, on with the actual game review:
I will state firstly that I have no familiarisation with the original Shadowrun ruleset barring a twenty year gap and a pathetically unskilled DM.
But I love this game, I will try and keep it neutral and objective.
What we are given here is somewhere between a major studio and an indie development team production, it has the feel of indie with the look and polish of AAA.
What is it? It's a cyberpunk RPG adventure with a fantastic amount of love poured into it and when it filled up they carried on pouring and now its all over your hands and trousers.
The game is flash, very flash, it looks and feels like Shadowrun, dark, trashy streets, interesting characters and a storyline as fleshed out as you choose it to be.
What I really liked is that although the game has a fairly linear story(nothing wrong with that, not everything has to be open-world) you do get a few options, pay attention and you can find a few secrets to earn extra cash or a few secret hallways.
What I really like however is the balls on this game! It just feels great, every time I load it up I am immediately immersed up to my eyeballs in it, from the sountrack to the art style it is just a wonderful rendition.
There are a few niggles, my 99% to hit attacks seem to miss a lot more than 1% of the time, sometimes it takes four or five clicks to wake up the NPCs to talk to them  and some people have accused the soundtrack of being deliberate nostagia pandering but you know what? That's fine with me... It all works.
I really reccomend this game, it is the sort of game I wish Steam would add an extra two buttons for; Avoid, Do not reccomend, Reccomend and Must play. Because this game sits squarely in the "Must play" category.
Now please excuse me whilst I install Dragonfall.

Another entry from BN games that I tried. I've previously played their Lost Lands Hidden Object/Mahjong game(s) and if you compare this to them, well...
They're very similar in their build, yet they have very different art styles, and obviously the main game is played differently as well. I haven't come a long ways yet, but here's what I've gathered so far:
- Unlike in Lost Lands, buildings aren't present here. Which is both a good and a bad thing, as buildings provided some useful bonuses in the form of equipment and keys, yet were a pain to find materials for. With them out of the way, you'll be playing the game a little longer to find what you're looking for, but at least the inventory won't be cluttered with useless materials once you're done building.
- I've yet to find any chests, but I'll be sorely disappointed if don't, seeing as they were a welcome distraction from the main game in Lost Lands with their own little mini-games and plentiful rewards. I hope to see some new mini-games when and if I find them.
If you look aside from these things I've mentioned so far, Lost Lands and Clover Tale are very similar in how they're built. It's a step up from blatantly copying the story and art of your other game and just replacing the main gameplay, but it's still a bit cheap. But then again, it's a FtP-game, so you shouldn't have too high standards. Don't go in playing Clicker Heroes expecting Doom 4.
Anyway, that's all I have to say about that. Again, it's a free game, so try it out if you're curious. And if you don't like it, no loss. But if you do like it, remember this: Finish in as few moves as possible to reap greater scores than you otherwise could. That is all.

The game itself is great and while it fails to live up to previous games in the serious, it remains an enjoyable and fun batman sim with an engaging story, polished gameplay, and some of the best visuals in any game to date. However, as good as the actual game is, I still cannot reccomend buying this game on PC. Yes its been patched and greatly improved from its launch, but it still suffers crash issues as well as streaming/performance issues. For reference, I am running an RX480 8GB on the latest drivers with an i5 6500 quad core CPU and 8GB of DDR4 2133Mhz Ram. I also have the game installed on an SSD. I understand that while my system may not be the most top of the line, it is by no means underpowered for this game and it has had no trouble running almost every other game on max settings at 1080p or sometimes even 1440p while holding 60 plus fps. The real problem I have with the games performance is just how inconsistent it is. I've had long stretches where the game will hover between 70-100fps on its highest settings and it's very smooth. But as soon as you hover over a highly deatiled area of the city or drive at high speeds in the batmobile, expect performance to dip. In my case, I can see my fps go from mid 80's all the way down to 40 when driving at high speeds. The problem seems to be an optimization issue in regards to how the game streams in data as you move through the city. This problem was far worse at launch, and while it has been improved, it was never fully fixed in this port. I've actually resorted to just locking the game at 30fps and in turn playing it at 4k as at least that way the performance is more consistent and the game looks much sharper. The crashing issues have also been improved since launch, but they still exist and some areas of the city are more prone to crashes than others. The game also really loves to eat up CPU cores and you can expect some stuttering when the game hits 100% CPU usage, which seems to happen at very random times regardless of what is going on in the game. It's a shame that the game still has the problems it has, because the game itself is great, but the port is subpar even after all the updates.
TL;DR: Game is awesome, port is lackluster.

The characters are put into places where they look like they fit most of the time apart from the few that feel as if they were shohorned in at the last second. The DLC for this game is a place this game really shines in adding playable characters such as nightwing, red hood, Harley quinn, batgirl, robin and catwoman which are mostly playable in the base game but its always a win to play as those characters in their own DLC's which add a load of replayability. Even smaller things such as all the skins for a majority of the characters and the batmobile is also a nice addition, being able to choose between things like the original batman look, the 2008 batman and  tumbler batmobile or the 2016 batman v superman looks. The classic skins for the other playable characters which you can play as in either their DLC's or the AR challenges mode. Even small aspects of the game can be fun like looking for all of the firemen or solving all of the riddlers puzzles to finally confront him are incredibly fun and add quite a bit of play time. This game also runs really well only having frame drops when i'm frequently tabbing out and/or have other apps open but then even i only drop at most 5-6 frames on max settings which is barely noticeable. Overall if you just want a game to play a bit then never play again wait until the game is next on sale and pick up the base version and if you want a game you'll never put down depending on whether money is an option buy the premium edition on or off sale as it is worth it and you get so much extra content. This game is amazing. A must play for any fan of LEGO games or just Marvel in general.
On the LEGO side of things, this is by far the best LEGO game I have ever played. The fundamental gameplay mechanics are generally the same across LEGO titles, but this game expands on that by giving you an open world to play around in when you're not actively in missions (in contrast to the smaller hub-style areas from other games). This alone gives the game so much more replayability as you don't feel necessarily confined to repeating the same thing over and over again.
On the Marvel side of things, they nailed it. I've never played a game that so perfectly captures the greatness of Marvel's universe. There are so many characters to choose from, and it's been quite fun seeing who they decided to include in the game. There are a couple major characters that I think are missing (Quicksilver, for example), but there's loads that I was pleasantly surprised to see playable (Squirrel Girl, Moon Knight, Rescue, etc.). The game as a whole is very respectful to the source material, but does the typical LEGO thing where it pokes fun at the silliness of everything. It's tastefully done. If you like Marvel but don't like LEGO gameplay, you may still enjoy this for the fanservice alone.

I truly do love this game. It's difficult, it has a great storyline, and it has a lot of character customization and battle-varieties. It's got a LOT of gameplay material, in that if you're looking to go from beginning to end in the storyline it'll take you quite a bit of time to complete it. It certainly warmed me to the idea of monster hunters, seeing that I haven't had a whole lot of experience with them in the past so take this with a grain of salt. But objectively I'd say this is a great game - maybe not $60.00 worth, but if you buy it during a generous Steam sale I'd say that's fair.
The only real complaint I have is the HUGE lack of information on the game online. It may be since it's a somewhat obscure game that really isn't advertised very well, but if you're looking to find guides or even a decent wiki on the game you certainly aren't going to find it. I remember specifically looking online to find out where to farm a specific material for armor crafting (which, by the way, there's a whole lot of armor and weapons to choose from in the game), and there was zero - literally, zero - results that popped up for a certain item in the game that without a doubt existed. When you want to find out how to do something or where to find it in the game, it really is a guessing game. Even if you decide to start a thread on the Steam discussions page, no-one will respond. I'm pretty sure I've had a question up there for a month or so at this point and no-one has responded.
All of that aside, when it comes to content, this is a great game. I think the developers could have done a little better in terms of variety, as this game can get very repetetive what with fighting the same monsters over and over again. Not to mention the scenery being very limited. But the story is great, the combat mechanics aren't bad at all, and I certainly recommend it to anyone who has the slightest bit of interest in monster hunters.

After finishing the story and most of the extra objectives in the game, all I can say about this game is one word, amazing.
First off, the game runs great. I had no problem maintaining a nice smooth 60 fps on ultra settings with vsync enabled. I'd say as long as you've got a nice recent card, you should be fine when it comes to running the game.

A LOT of people have been dissing the game because of the fact that you have superpowers, and they think that just because of this fact that everything will be too easy to finish. There are some points in the game that using superpowers makes it easy, but there are also some points in the game where your powers are completely stripped from you and you are forced to play without them.
Finally, the mission layout. Everything is laid out very nicely in your menu. You can do things from upgrading your power and abilities, to selecting other missions, calling in homies ect. There wont be a point in this game when you get lost or dont know what to do because everything is basicly explained how it should be. There are tons of different ways to customize things from what your player wears, to the weapons you use, the cars youll drive and more. And once you beat the game, there is always much more to do in saints row.
Bottom line, if you're looking for a great game with tons of playing time, I completely recommend Saints Row IV. It is a must buy.

I wanted to like this game so much.
And I did, too, for about three hours. Castle in the Darkness is an unapologetic love-letter to the 8-bit era of gaming, both in aesthetic and challenge. You play a peppy little knight who is the sole survivor of a curse that took hold of your castle. It's up to you to explore every corner of the kingdom to find all the gear and doodads you need to save the princess, and there is a LOT to find. The game is most like Simon's Quest if you ever played that. It's a side-scroller where the stages are stitched together into a continuous world, full of side paths and secrets. There's no map, but the level design is mostly direct enough that you should have no trouble navigating.
It's important to note that Castle holds nothing back in its fanatical adoration for the NES era. Enemies are pulled right from Metroid, Castlevania, Gargoyle's Quest, and even stuff like 8 Eyes and Magic of Scheherazade. Also in line with the bygone days of gaming is the challenge. The difficulty ramps up quickly, with enemies doing huge chunks of damage to you and more and more insta-kill spikes making appearances. Finding better weapons, armor, and spells can mitigate the former, but the latter will quickly become the bane of your existence.
There's no getting around it, sadly. Unless you're the kind of person who got Impossible Boy in Super Meat Boy, you're going to reach a point where the difficulty becomes too much. Mine was right at the end of the game, when I discovered that the final boss would take almost five minutes to kill and could kill me in maybe five hits. I started looking for more secrets that could help mitigate this, and got through an insane gauntlet of spikes and collapsing floors to find an even harder boss. As much as I (mostly) enjoyed the journey there, reaching that point of frustration and defeat soured me on the entire game. I really want to be able to recommend Castle in the Darkness, but I wouldn't want anyone else to suffer that same heartbreak.

I finished the game.
This game was developed for tablets and it hinders the game massively, many reviews seem to leave this part out.
+ The story is great and very well fleshed out
+ The NPCs you will interact with are interesting, unique and fun to read
+ The graphical presentation suits the game's style very well, although key items and interactable objects blend in with static scenery
+ The pacing is good
+- The ending was satisfactory but nothing great
- Short game, for an RPG, definitely not worth full price
- A watered down XCOM combat system, boring, dull and clunky. Percentages seem to be broken, movement is annoying, cover is scarce and in illogical places. You can't peak around walls or anything like that.
- The UI is barebones at best, you wont spend much time in menus, and as far as I could tell, there's no way to customise your character's gear and inventory unless you purchase something first.
- There is little to no explanation of key features of the game, the UI, or the combat. I had to trial and error pretty much everything in the game.
- No permanent party members, this means no customisation other than your character, no relationships to develop, no party member backstories to uncover.
- The game locks you in combat between encounters, making exploration and navigating and absolute chore. Killing any semblence of enjoyment in exploring the detailed environments.

Free To Play is not as impressive if you're not into Dota but I do admit that I was eager to give it one more try (even if it's not entirely my cup of tea) just because of this documentary and its beautiful CGI battles. It also explains why this game isn't always newbie friendly. People are truly competitive when playing Dota, and you need a good team and a lot of spare team to make it your own. Something this documentary shows very well.
I was a bit frustrated by the people/gamers in it, however. Being a little bit older than most of them I thought some of them came across as being extremely naive. Yes, there's money to be made, but there are millions of gamers who would like to do the same. Not everyone can do this. It requires dedication. There are lots of people with social lives or other, more important things. People grow older and wiser and realize that they can't always do what they want, even if it's playing games your entire life. Heck, if I could play games my whole life I would absolutely love it. But, there's money to be made and I know deep down in my heart that I can't do this by playing games. Competitive gaming also relies on luck and other random things you don't have a grip on. You can train for it but you also can't, if you know what I mean. No game is ever the same.
Competitive gaming is a future of sports, I believe it, just not
future. If you honestly believe you can play the same game your entire life and make money while doing this then the best of luck to you. I will respect you for your dreams and dedication but I will also think you're being extremely naive. Playing games is just not a job for life (unless you're a professional reviewer, maybe). You might not understand now, but someday you will.
Now, as a documentary it was pretty good, but I just can't help but feel disappointed.

Shadowverse, Shadowverse ... so, where do I start?
- The game is very, very reliable. There is nearly no rng involved (well, there are rng-based cards, but only a few and most of them arent really worth the risk), besides the obvious variance through carddraw and the "who goes first"-gamble which, in return, has a relatively high impact on the outcome of a match - but thats a coinflip and it balances out the more you play. For me the lack of rng-based cards is a good thing, since I prefer less rng-decided clown-fiestas after losing years of my potential lifespan in Hearthstone ... The evolve system also allows players to produce some good tempo-swings in their favor if used at the right time.
- As a result of this, the quality of your deck has, lets say compared to other ccgs, an even higher impact on your winrate. This leads to some kind of inflationary state where 40 % of the decks played are based on one decklist, since this specific decklist is the one "most efficient" available right now - it is kind of boring to face the same faction over and over again, with the exact same cards, knowing, that your opponent just googled "best deck shadowverse 2017" and netdecked like a madman ;) (*saltyoff) - this may be fine for ranked-mode, its still competitive, but its a pain in unranked. Its not impossible to survive with fun meme-decks though ;)
- The 20 HP each player starts with are quickly gone. Aggro decks tend to be a bit stronger in Shadowverse compared to some other ccgs, even though its not like a "tyranny of aggro decks" like some people tend to describe it. Its also possible to create some OTk-combo decks, so if youre not a fan of that, maybe reconsider playing this game ;)
- The free to play model of Shadowverse is great. Youll receive an incredible amount of freepacks just for starting to play, followed by daily login rewards (20+ gold every day and 1freepack every 4-5 days), 3 daily missions which can be rerolled, and even more event-based freepacks every now and then. Whoever cries about this game being pay2win or not free2play-friendly is objectively wrong - its the, by far, most generous ccg ive ever encountered. The only thing you wont be able to enjoy as a free2play-player is a huge diversity in "competitive" decks or maybe the most expensive 2391932934 legendaries rampdragon-timmy-deck. Based on your freepacks and 1-2 weeks of doing all the singleplayer content and farming dailys, you will be able to craft at least 1 competitive deck, thats for sure. Im still using the deck I crafted right after starting to play (midrange-sword) and it works just fine even in master. Whenever a new expansion hits, youll receive 10 freepacks of said expansion - combine that with cautious/tacitcal disenchanting and the gold you (hopefully) accumulated and everyone should be able to get at least one of the new "meta"-decks.
- The whole anime-style of Waifuver- eeehhh Shadowverse isnt everybodys thing. If youre into that kind of stuff, youll enjoy the cards artwork most of the time - even though some of them are irritatingly ugly - the rest of the game (menues, battlegrounds, etc.) fullfills its puropse without being overwhelmingly jaw-dropping, its still a tablet-port.
tldr
Its a pretty good game if youre into animestyle, reliable ccgs and able to endure a lot of filthy netdeckers in unranked ;)

I've always romanticized space travel.  There's something about that endless unknown that is enlessly alluring.  My greatest dream is to step beyond the confines of this pale, blue dot and find the countless wonders waiting in that great unknown.
FTL ruins that dream.  FTL turns that unknown into a frantic, frightening, and stressful experience, and I absolutely love it.  You never know what waits at the end of the next jump.  You never know if you're prepared.  You never know if your choices are the right one.  Usually, it's something nasty.  Usually, you're not.  Usually, they weren't.  And usually, you die.
Still, there's joy in staving off death, in fighting to the bitter end.  There's joy in finding all the secrets that await in this universe.  And when you die, there's joy in starting from scratch and seeing just where this new journey leads you.
It's fantastic.  It's addictive.  It's an absolute must-play.

Do you remember Lost Lands: An Hidden Object Adventure and Lost Lands: Mahjong? Well, if yes, Clover Tales is belonging to the same kind: only the gameplay and the graphics were redone.
Indeed, this free-to-play is similar to the two games: ypu have an energy bar, like a Facebook game, a experience bar, because you can level up, a ingame shop where you can buy with cristals or money items needed to defeat... eeer sorry, feed animals or energizers or anything else, the real shop where you can buy money and crystals...
To summarize, I'll copy past some parts of my previous reviews apart for the main core of the game: the match-3 gameplay.
The gameplay itself is to reach an objective given: score, destroy specific tiles, etc.. For that, you have to swap two gems to make a line of 3-4-5 of the same kind. If you're doing a chain with more than 3, a bonus can be unlocked. However, you have a real problem there: you have a limited amount of swaps. If you have to reach the objective under 15 swaps, unless you have tools that can grant you a continue, you'll be forced to retry if you reached 0. I wished that players were free as anyway, you have an energy bar. Besides, in both Lost Lands, you have a timer, which is the most used limit in match-3.
The story is divided in a series of quests that, while needing explorations for anything (food, tools, ressources, etc..), can also involve cute animals to feed or anything, instead of fantasy creatures to defeat with weapons. Also, the more you're earning experience, the more you're leveling up and the more you're unlocking. There are also chests you can open though I didn't see any mini-game.
Exploring a location costs energy and that's bothering me - I didn't change my position about it -, the energy regenerating slowly unless you buy some potions with the crystals you're earning. Crystals are pretty rare but there is the easy way: spent real money to acquire them (or to acquire more golds). Gold is mainly used for weapons for example. Here's an idea for the cost: 10 crystals = 0.88 euros - I've checked the next price and it's already nearing 10 euros).
I don't mind having quests to do and I don't mind the level up system to access new locations. Even the shop isn't really bothering, as far as you can use the gold you're earning. However, preventing me to play a game because of a decreased energy on Steam, that's something I can't imagine. For me, that kind of gameplay is reminding me of my Facebook games time. Weirdly enough, it would have been on Facebook, I would have find it normal. Here, on Steam, I'm not at ease with the concept. Ubisoft released games about CSI and Assassin's Creed on Facebook, yet, the main series were totally different.
You'll probably find it weird that I'm bothered by the Facebook-like when the game is a free-to-play and that the concept of the energy is also there to push you to buy some (the game is also released on Android and iOS devices). But that's my feeling. Many people will feel that they're trapped and will want to advance. However, I tend to use a simple thought to avoid spending money: there is no rush. You're there for fun (I'm not reading the story though).
But here, I have the impression that it's a game a kid can play: the graphics are cute, colorful, the way everything seems to be easier (achievements, no minigames, cute animals to feed)... I don't mind the graphics, it's suiting the game and the quests. However, if you let a kid play the game, have money on your steam wallet destined to something else than an ingame purchase and don't look at what's happening, they can easily empty your wallet if they want to buy more crystals or more gold. I know that it's a scenario that will not happen in a majority of cases, but this push to buy to advance quickly is not needed in a game that seems to be also destined to kids.
Anyway, the soundtrack isn't extraordinary: many tracks existed in both Lost Lands.
Is Clover Tale a nice game? I largerly prefer the Lost Lands free-to-plays. Not because Clover Tales is more child-oriented but more because Clover Tales miss some features like mini-games, buildings to repair AND a safeguard to avoid kids emptying your wallet. However, as it's a free-to-play too, you can play it if you like match-3, not bothered by the energy system and cute graphics.
And remember: DON'T FALL INTO THE "NEED ENERGY" TRAP. If there are indeed micro-transactions, don't fall in that pit of addiction. You don't need to go forward immediately. Just quit the game and come back later. It's the best way to play these kind of games, because after all, you're not going to be attacked by another player, your quests aren't timed and besides, why would you rush?

Been playing this game since the release of Rage of Bahamut (December 2016) and I've seen the meta go from "not too bad" to "all the same". With the newest expansion of Wonderland Dreams, I decided to make a review for this game. Here's my list of pros and cons as a casual player in rank A0 (ranked goes from D0-3->C0-3->B0-3->A0-3->AA0-3->Masters->Grandmaster)
Pros:
-Great artwork (many waifus and husbandos for everyone)
-Very stylish card animations
-Decent ratio of amount of playtime to cards gained
-Evolve system is interesting and helps with tempo swings
-Distinct play styles for each of the seven classes
-Fast games?
Cons:
-Fast games = lose faster if you don't have a meta deck
-Very meta heavy with almost no room for fun decks
-Unranked and ranked are the same meta decks
-Wonderland Dreams made every class implement Neutrals
-Balance patches every couple months
See where most of my cons are? As a casual player, I dislike playing the meta decks, and would rather be creative and make my own. At this point, it's a cycle of: new expansion -> people buy lots of packs -> new meta -> people buy packs to play the meta -> nerf old meta -> release new expansion. There are so many interesting cards that are ignored because this game is so heavily dominated by the tier 1 decks.
TL;DR: Play the meta or don't play at all

BATMAN.EXE HAS STOPPED WORKING

You have a lot of build variety, the weapons have a moveset that is sufficiently varied to give you a new experience if you want to try another role : The spear can lock you in place to empale ennemies that charges you, wich is not what you're gonna do as a DPS, but as a tank or a support it's a very good tool to resist a hit AND stun the oni. The club can have slow combos that get more and more powerful, or a counter-attack if you want to stun the oni. The gun can deal a lot of precision damage, or you can load a shotgun ammo to get close and personnal, or some kind of vortex ammo to lock the oni in place while your buddies do their things.
Alongside the build variety the game offer, you actually have a very decent storyline, the characters you meet are all developped one by one, and have their quirks and flaws.
The onis are pretty diverse in gameplay and design, and you actually have incentives to dismember them for loot, instead of running through them.
The game also has some very cool shintoism references, and a very cool concept for customisation.
You gain the soul of japanese personnalities or gods, and each of them actually talk to you during the fight, has a biography, links to other souls, and grant specific bonuses (Sister Zenshin is a support that can also be used to reinforce your tank build)
The fights are a bit tedious (5-15m against a large oni, depending on many factors) and it's boring to face many times the same oni before being able to do something new, but that's a given in this type of game -sadly-.

If you've ever played any of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games, you already know what to expect. You can skip reading this and pick it up as you will fit right into Fairy Fencer F.
Fairy Fencer F ditches the futuristic feel of the Hyperdimension games and returns to the more traditional scene. Countryside with shopkeeps and all kinds of taverns. It feels very Atelier-esque. Basically, Hyperdimension Neptunia, but set in the scenery of Atelier Rorona/Atelier Totori.
You play as Fang, a
main character and meet
Eryn, a fairy that inhabits a weapon. Together you must find 100 other fairies to revive the Goddess and stop the Vile God from destroying the world
...you know, standard JRPG stuff.
While I joke about Fairy Fencer F being Hyperdimension Neptunia in a different setting, FFF actually does a good job in separating itself from HN. Sure there are Nep references here and there (Pudding!) but on the whole, FFF really does feel like it's own universe.
If anything, the game sort of feels too short. It's about half of Hyperdimension Neptunia. Half the party members, half the dungeons, half the items and half the length to beat a playthrough.
One thing FFF beats Neptunia over though, is a fully fleshed out combo system for attacks. While Special Attacks are rather limited (Each Character has around ~5 of these) the standard attacks can be combo'd with an insane amount of styles. Your weapon will automatically shift from a sword, to a gun, to a scythe or arrow depending on how you set up your chain attacks. Also, the EXE gauge returns in the form of "Fairize". Build up the gauge and Fairize to do double the damage.
Another thing that FFF does uniquely, is the Fairies themselves. I really liked this. You can assign any fairy you have to any of your party members, and each Fairy has different stats to boost the character with. Equip a Fairy that gives you bonus Fire damage to a member who specializes in Fire attacks to do insane damage.
I wish there were more fairies though -- the game says you have to find 100 fairies to revive the goddess, yet I believe there are only around ~45 fairies you can actually obtain. They all range from badass dragons and monsters to cutesy fox girls and buff tough-talking dudes. They each have their own charm (they are all fully voiced too!) and I just loved collecting all of these different kinds of fairies.
I would have liked to of had an option to take fairies from defeated foes. Several enemies and baddies had some very fantastic and cute looking fairies that I would of liked to add to my roster instead of them just dying. Yeah sure the dude is dead, but I can take his cute fairy and make her my companion can't I? ;_;
I hope Fairy Fencer F gets a sequel. I'd love to play another one. It has it's own unique charm that's different from Hyperdimension Neptunia.  Heck, you know what would be even greater? A Hyperdimension Neptunia x Fairy Fencer F crossover. YES PLEASE.

XCOM has proven to be one of the freshest, and most challenging games I've played in recent memory. Being a huge fan of grid-based tactical combat games, this particular title oozes with a classic feel, while still offering new gameplay mechanics and a modern graphical facelift. While the game isn't necessarily the most original (mankind must stop oncoming alien threat to save the Earth from certain destruction), it handles its subject matter with a pretty large level of depth, pages upon pages of information on each successful research project embarked upon, or every alien autopsy completed. The permadeath factor is unnerving and really keeps you on edge, where a single mistake can mean the life or death of one of your best soldiers. This constant threat keeps you from ever feeling like you're unstoppable on the battlefield, a prize I feel that far too many games give out freely. You earn your success in this game, and you'll find yourself patting yourself on the back after every successful operation. Fans of games like Fire Emblem and Advance Wars, be sure to pick this up for one hell of a great time. It's time to show those aliens who's boss, like Will Smith in Independence Day: Welcome ta Erff.

This is the first experience that I've had with the Shadowrun game and its associated universe and I have to say that I highly enjoyed it. I liked how fleshed out the world around me seemed and even though I only got to roam around a small subset of what is supposed to be Seattle in the mid 21st century, it felt lived in, and expansive if that makes sense. The dialogue was fresh, realistic as much as it could be with the premise, and besides a few typos that I found, was well written.
I enjoyed the graphics and the isometric viewpoint throughout, reminding me of many hours spent playing Diablo and Diablo 2 back in the day as well as Starcraft among others.
I have to state though that there were a few bugs that I encountered including one that didn't allow me to continue on with the story until my characters had all roamed around to certain areas of the map in order to "trigger" events. I found this to be frustrating but not too much to the point of disavowing the game entirely. At this moment, I am actually downloading Dragonfall and Hong Kong and intend to finish those as well before playing modded campaigns in order to get the whole experience.
Overall, if you are a fan of the cyberpunk genre, then I would recommend this as I feel like it is a good representation of it, especially for beginners who are just stepping into the genre. It has a good mix of Blade Runner and Ghost in the Shell in terms of inspiration which adds to the experience.
For my first run through this game, I would give it an 8 out of 10. Very solid gameplay but a few bugs keep it from being perfect in my opinion.

This game is fantastic. It has minor flaws, but those didn't stop me from 100%-ing it over the course of three days, and now I'm very much looking forward to playing the bonus stuff and NG+.
But anyway, let me detail why this game is great.
First of all, the graphics are not just pixely, they are actually stylized very well after a real 8-bit game, which many "retro" game authors don't do. Technically I suppose there are things that a NES couldn't do in this game (some bosses are huge, sometimes there's many sprites at once, etc), but it sets the tone perfectly in my opinion. Doesn't hurt that it all looks nice by itself.
The music is great, too, not simple generic chiptune stuff, it's actually very memorable, gets stuck in your head, but doesn't detract from the gameplay, instead enhancing it by adding a lot to the atmosphere. My favorite tunes are the last area's and the cave's. And the boss music is awesome too!
The atmosphere is top notch. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, but it pretends to. It has a lot of easter eggs and references, but they are somehow done very unobtrusively and I never thought that they distracted from the immersion as they often do when done hamfistedly. If you like the mood of those old castle-featuring NES games, you're gonna get that and more.
The controls are damn near flawless. Your character is pretty mobile, perfectly responsive and everything bad that happens to you is usually your fault.
The gameplay is addicting. It gets hard, very challenging in fact, but 99% of the time it's fair.
There's some exploits for the bosses making them pretty easy if you know the right spell to use (there's one that kills pretty much every boss insanely fast...), but they're still mostly pretty fun. The platforming will keep you on your toes but none of it is obloxiously hard. It's very refreshing and keeps you engaged even when you have to retrace large sections of the game with shiny new items or abilities - the enemies are much easier when you return, making it fun to slash them all apart with ease, but the platforming is still respectably dangerous but not overly specific or complex. This makes it fun to backtrack.
The layout is sort of linear, unlike a typical metroidvania: this game is sturctured more linearly, with a single linear path from start to finish and diverging dead ends with goodies (many of which you won't be able to access on your first run through the world). And there's several quick travel waypoints. This makes backtracking very manageable. I tend to dread having to comb a world of a metroidvania after getting a bunch of abilities, because it's often a chore. However, in this game you won't easily forget some random corner somewhere and forever forget to check it. It's really easy, for example, to get through almost the entire game again after you get the double jump and find all the places that were just too high. There's some unique stuff you should memorize the location of, but that's easy too. In conclusion, the exploration aspect is very light but very fun.
There's a whole bunch of secrets and all of them are really fun to discover, too. Some make you feel clever even when it's simple stuff.
Overall, pretty much everything about this game is done well and it's definitely worth a playthrough or several. If I were to pick it apart and mention some flaws, I would only be able to find minor things: a few magic spells seem to be entirely useless, some equipment parts as well (over the course of the game I found like three swords while already having better ones). Some pre-boss cutscenes are unskippable. That's pretty much it.

I am a huge Metroidvania fan, so when I saw this game on a Livestream, I was eager to get it. It was definitely worth picking up. While I got it on sale, the full cost of $6 is a more than reasonable price for it. It is not flawless, but it is a lot of fun.
The storyline is nothing special. The kingdom is overrun by monsters, you are the only guard left to save them. The end. Oh and I guess there's a frog knight or something. It's enough of a tale to tell you what your goals are and why you are adventuring, and that is really all it needs.
The gameplay is what the focus is on. Let me clarify that the controls are fair, but the level design is not always going to be fair. During your first playthrough, unless you are being very careful the entire time, it is inevitable that you will have spikes fall out of nowhere to kill you. Spikes in general will be your worst enemy. Monsters will very rarely kill you, given that save points restore your health, as do warp points. But spikes are instant death, and they are everywhere. Get used to that death jingle; odds are that you will be hearing it a lot. On the bright side, there is an achievement for it, so embrace being killed many times!
It is likely that a lot of people have already expressed this problem, but I'm going to beat the dead horse and say it anyway. The biggest issue is that the save points are spread out horribly. At the beginning, you will find a save point every few screens. This is nice for beginning players. However, as you get further into the game, they become more and more scarce. Yet even then, you are unlikely to die to monsters. So the lack of healing points is not making the game much more difficult. The huge, glaring flaw with this is that it provides difficulty through frustration.
Here is a prime example. As I write this review, I am on the final level of the game. There are at least seven screens between one save point and another, probably more. Yet I am stuck on that seventh screen. The other six are easy, and then I keep falling to my death due to an irritatingly-placed broken block. Now, if the save point was a screen away, or a few screens away, I would be happy to keep trying until I got through. But having to keep walking through the seven areas, some of which are a bit lengthy, gets extremely tedious. This is not legitimate difficulty. The only thing it makes me want to do is play something else so I don't smash my head into a wall from the same boring six screens.
But otherwise? It's a great game. There are a lot of fun little references to other games, some of which I got and some that I didn't. The controls are good, even on a keyboard, which is what I have been playing with. I enjoyed most of the boss fights, and there is a lot to collect, which suits me just fine. It has a handful of achievements and some trading cards. It also has music that I personally like quite a bit. I also have never had the game crash on me, or any kind of terrible glitches, so that's always a plus.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who likes the genre. Just be prepared for some frustration later on.

Something about this game. I cursed it initially. My attempts, feeble. Then you have an amazing run, and you realize it's actually possible to proceed. The mood, the environments, the story (if you're paying attention) are all quite macabre. Bird's eye view with an in your face sound. The crafting system is nothing short of genius with its ease and simplicity. The graphics are pixelated, and they add nicely to the overall creep factor going on here.
At its heart, this game is a brutal shooter with rogue/survival horror like elements. Not everyone will like this game due to its ridiculous difficulty. The onslaught is generally relentless and you're damn lucky if you have a moment to catch your breath and re-align yourself. Ammo and health and crafting supplies are few and far between and the further you go, the less you'll find.
But there is so much to this game. 40+ hours in and I'm discovering new items, enemies and weapons still. Every gameplay is a critical and unforgiving surprise. Every choice and shot counts. The tensions at times are cruel. Wasted ammo and supplies will happen, and you'll mess up and die. Again and again. And you'll get mad, And you'll have learned. And your failures will taunt you to do better. And you will. And the game knows that.
Simply brilliant. An easy favorite.

I was extremely surprised at how much I ended up liking this game. For the price I bought it for (about $2), I expected something playable, if not great. Well.
Rather than simply being another "retro for the sake of retro" title, CitD feels as though it was made by someone who genuinely loves 8-bit games and isn't just trying to cash in on a trend. The graphics are detailed and crisp, the music is catchy, and the game plays super fast and smooth. The sheer amount of references to other games (and even movies) constantly had me smiling as I discovered more and more of them. It was all of these things that made this stand out for me and they're what kept it from being just another "retro game."
This game is hard, though. Really hard. Super hard. But due to its Metrovania style gameplay, being able to discover new weapons, spells, accessories, and health increases is always possible thus making the difficulty fair. While it is hard for the sake of being hard at times, with the instant death literally lining the floors, walls, and ceilings at times, CitD never made me want to stop playing because of its difficulty. I always felt that if I just continued to explore, I could find something new that would help if I came back to a tough spot.
This game is great. It's a blend of fast-paced action, pixel-perfect platforming, and RPG exploration. It's as if Faxanadu, Metroid, and Little Samson were all rolled into one.

Light-hearted and funny, Lego Marvel Super Heroes rests on a solid foundation of fan-based humor, inside jokes and ironic references to keep the player involved.
An easy plot, lots of secondary missions, a whole ton of characters to get and quite a number of available achievements will do for hours of playing. It was a bit disconcerting to end the main story with a mere 21,4% of the game done, but it was very nice to have quite a way still to go to reach the completion.
There're a few sore points, so, let's go with the PROs and the CONs.
PROs:
The lenght. It's a very long game. It's actually the longest game I've ever played on Steam, wow. There're a billion of secondary quests and lots of things to obtain all around the game. You'll have to play each level at least twice, if you want to complete it, and a few ot those levels have hidden secrets difficult to uncover without help.
The variety. Lots of characters, lots of available vehicles, lots of different quests and a whole lots of tricks to get on your way towards the end.
The humor. It's a bit childish - like, a few of those lines sounded like something that a ten-years-old would have enjoyed, but having Iron Man flirting with Captain America never gets old. And Hulk's sandwich! I loved that and I really needed a game like this after an handful of days spent on Transistor's melancholic atmosphere. It would actually be a nice game to play with children.
CONs:
- Controls and commands. Like, no. I'm obviously talking about PC controls - do you want to know what is really frustrating? To try and change Hulk with some other character and to get instead Bruce Banner... because I didn't press U for long enough. Or without truly believing in myself, I don't know, there had to be a special magic combination of pressure and timing, but I didn't get it right up to the very end. Or when I needed to put the game on double player to get an Achievement and me and my brother spent twenty minutes trying to understand how to do it. No, no, no.
- Badly Functioning Menus. They're like the contrary of self-explanatory and intuitive. And, by the way, the same command won't necessarily work the same way on each page of the same menu. I'm not kidding about it.
- Annoying Bugs. There're quite a few of them - even if they're less then you'd expect in such a long game - and some of them are really frustrating. An example? There's a secondary mission in New York where you need to reach an object under a grill. I changed into Ant-Man to try and slip through the bars and it worked - but, once there, I couldn't touch the object. I couldn't leave. I couldn't do anything. I was stuck. Being stuck somewhere in New York was actually a more common occurrence than I would have liked; but, at the same time, the story level were mostly bugs-free.
It wasn't a very original or a particularly beautiful game, but it was well-built, with a bright, light atmosphere and more than a few interesting moments. At first I was quite disappointed with my purchase - my problems with the controls gave me a bad feeling about it - but I've since decided I've spent well my money.

Things to keep in mind before you play or buy this game:-
1. You will die.  A lot.
2. It is not fair and doesn't pretend to be.
3. It's a gamble whether or not you'll get to the last sector - let alone be equipped enough to deal with the Big Bad Boss at the end (it's entirely possible to only have starting weapons).
Anyone familiar with the Rogue concept (who has actually played Rogue?) will know that a lot is based on random chance and what skill there is? Is minimal.  For example: targeting specific systems is all very well, until you meet an enemy that is vastly overpowered to you and you have no hope of winning.
But, despite this, FTL is a fun distraction.  In fact, whilst people (including myself above) have compared this to Rogue, it might be better compare and contrast FTL with Ludo (or other simple board game).
Going to each sector is a dice roll in of itself, you might knock someone else off or they might knock you off, in your desperate attempt to get home (or in this case, the Federation fleet and beat the boss) and sometimes in your travels? Nothing of any import will happen.
Some improvements might have been to have short-range sensors so you can have information on the immediate surrounding sectors you can get to, shields and weapons rooms to be combined or be manned by multiple crew members, a securtiy detachment to protect your crew from invaders, the ability to sell missiles and/or drone parts for the universal currency that is "scrap" (which you may spend on your ship and have nothing left for equipment)...still, even with all that said? FTL is a decent enough game but is it worth £6.99? Well, I've gotten 10 hours out of it and I bought it as part of an Indie Humble Bundle...would I have bought it at £6.99 and thought it a decent enough buy? Possibly.
At the time of typing, FTL is currently in a sale and at it's current price (£3.49) is more than worth it for a quick-jaunt kind of deal that you can easily go back to.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes é um jogo de ação e aventura desenvolvido pela TT Games e publicado pela Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. Inicialmente lançado para as plataformas Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 e Wii U. Este jogo contem jogabilidade similar a outros jogos LEGO, alternando entre várias sequencias de ação/aventura e a, boa e velha solução de quebra-cabeças.
O jogo foi lançado como Lego Marvel Super Heroes: Universe in Peril para os portáteis Nintendo DS, Nintendo 3DS e PlayStation Vita.
Umas das surpresas do jogo foi ter Clark Gregg representando seu papel no universo de cinema da Marvel como o Agente Coulson e Stan Lee tendo o seu próprio personagem que inclusive é dublado por ele mesmo.
A principal inovação deste jogo é uma versão LEGO de Nova Iorque com todas as construções já conhecidas do universo Marvel, além disso foi criada um versão LEGO de Asgard.
Como disse, o game mantém todas carecteriscas lego com bastante variação de personagens com mais de 150 sendo eles:
Personagens para desbloquear com moedas LEGO, ou nas missões secundárias encontradas no Jogo Livre:
entre outros, além de versões alternativas, como o Capitão América clássico, as armaduras do Homem de Ferro, e a forma Fênix de Jean Grey, por exemplo.
