BATMAN.EXE HAS STOPPED WORKING
I was using msi afterburner to record stats, and my gpu sat at mostly 99% usage while my cpu sat at 60-70% usage. My ram though? 6 gbs of it at all times. I have windows 10 with 8gb of ddr4 ram. So I figured out my problem.
This game is so broken, so messed, so utterly ♥♥♥♥ed, that on windows 10, IT REQUIRES AT LEAST 12 GBS OF RAM TO STAY AT A STABLE 60 FPS. WHAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAT?! I'm so confused as to how someone can ♥♥♥♥ up a port this badly!

After finishing the story and most of the extra objectives in the game, all I can say about this game is one word, amazing.
First off, the game runs great. I had no problem maintaining a nice smooth 60 fps on ultra settings with vsync enabled. I'd say as long as you've got a nice recent card, you should be fine when it comes to running the game.
Now, about the gameplay. A LOT of people have been dissing the game because of the fact that you have superpowers, and they think that just because of this fact that everything will be too easy to finish. Well this completely wrong. The enemies you fight while in the simulation also have the ability to have thier own different powers, so everything balances out. There are some points in the game that using superpowers makes it easy, but there are also some points in the game where your powers are completely stripped from you and you are forced to play without them.
Finally, the mission layout. Everything is laid out very nicely in your menu. You can do things from upgrading your power and abilities, to selecting other missions, calling in homies ect. There wont be a point in this game when you get lost or dont know what to do because everything is basicly explained how it should be. There are tons of different ways to customize things from what your player wears, to the weapons you use, the cars youll drive and more. And once you beat the game, there is always much more to do in saints row.
Bottom line, if you're looking for a great game with tons of playing time, I completely recommend Saints Row IV. It is a must buy.

The Stick of Truth, at its core, is a Paper Mario-esque RPG that can be enjoyed even if you've never seen the show. A lot of combat abilities boil down to "mash the button as fast as you can" or "hit the button with the right timing", but it works fine for an RPG. These QTE's have some quirks that are explained pretty poorly at times, but are extremely satisfying when pulled off correctly.
South Park's artstyle works great for an RPG, as does the score and the writing. This comparison has been made often, but it really feels like you're just watching an episode. Some of the humor is referential, but most of it is accessable to those of you who have somehow never seen South Park.
Despite all of this, the game clocks in at about 8 hours and change with all of the sidequests completed (not all of the collectables, however). I really wish the story was longer, or there was NG+ content, or even some kind of post-story. As a positive from this, the game doesn't even come close to staying past its welcome.

Mirror's Edge is a game I would recommend anybody looking for something different should try. On your first try it can last about 5 to 6 hours, but once you get better you find more paths through levels, and can bring that down to 1 1/2 to 2 hours. This is one of the main joys of the game, is the replayability as you explore to find quicker ways through the levels. The story is not very strong, but it is easily ignored and only really needs to give a vague setting as to why you are in a certain area. The running feels very solid and responsive, and the game runs very smoothly.
The only real issue I have with the game is that there are a few parts in which you need to partake in the difficult combat system. Most are avoidable, but there are some forced fights which can get rather tedious, as this is a game where you are supposed to run and flow smoothly from wall to wall, floor to floor, so stopping in order to fight takes away from the real strong point of the game.
All in all, if you want something different, then I highly recommend Mirror's Edge, if you enjoy platforming, especially in the first person perspective, and for £10, its worth every penny.

Everyone knows this game was a huge mess for much of the first year it was on Steam. Warner Bros has essentially thrown in the towel on the PC platform, or so they say. They had such a difficult time getting this thing to run well that we may not see any more big budget PC releases from them, although we did get the Arkham VR game recently. There were so many technical issues that this was the game that warranted the refund option on Steam to finally be automated without needing to argue your case on a support ticket and hope for a miracle.
So is it technically sound these days? For the most part, yes. I didn't suffer any crashes and performance isn't totally consistent, but if you have an SSD and current gen graphics card, you should be good. You could also look up the Steam Guide for the Arkham Knight Config Tool. Follow the suggested settings and you should see improvements. This is still one of the best looking games ever, so expecting perfect frame rate might not be fair.
As for the game itself, it's worst enemy is franchise fatigue. This really is the ultimate Batman experience, but if you've played through the previous 3 games thoroughly, you'll likely feel a bit burnt out here. Very few new gadgets or new gameplay systems to be found. The big addition is the batmobile. With some practice, it's not as bad as they said. The combat does get stale late in the game and it's a very sloppy way to get around but it works.
The story was about as epic as Arkham City's was, albeit with more proper sendoffs for the villains this time. The Arkham Knight's identity is unfortunately a gigantic let down you'll see coming a mile away. The devs claimed this was going to be a whole new original character, but that was a flat out lie. The rage from the fans was on point here. The whole time you're waiting for a twist, thinking "there's no way they just reskinned and renamed ______, right?" Oh, but they did.
The amount of content is absolutely unrivaled here. The main quest is lengthy. The side quests are mostly creative, but can get tedious near the end if you're going for 100%. There are 4 DLC sidequest chains that are all very welcome. Like always, there are hundreds of Riddler trophies and puzzles to gather if you care about that. There are 6 standalone side stories, 5 of which are about 20 minutes, while Batgirl's is a proper expansion with a small carnival to explore and collect some things if you wish. All of these 6 stories showcase new locations.
Then you have your challenge mode. Not a mode I ever invested much time in as it's just leaderboard focused and often regurgitated material from the campaigns, however it does have some unique locations not found in the game otherwise. The best stuff was the racing stages inspired by Adam West's, Michael Keaton's, and Christian Bale's Batman roles. Nice fanservice here as you drive their classic machines complete with their show/movie scores.
Finally you got a ridiculous amount of optional costumes for everyone to try on. Also, an art gallery, stories, and 3D models to unlock.
This was a great sendoff for the Bat. Whatever Rocksteady is doing next, however....it needs to be either a dramatically different kind of game, perhaps with the Batman Beyond universe, or they need to try a different universe altogether.
All told I spent about $17 for the complete package. Great deal.

The bad reviews are mostly because
- This game had a rough launch.

- People hate reading subs (There is no English dub)
Now that that is out of the way, lets get to the good stuff.
This isn the most shameless recreation of a monster hunter game ever made (moreso than Freedom Wars, Soul Sacrifice, Godeater, etc...) and I mean that in the best way possible. Lets face it, MH fans had nothing on PC. Sony just took the opportunity since Capcom has been holding the MH series over the burning building that is Nintendo for the past few years. For the record I think both Nintendo and Sony are horrible companies, so I have no bias there. I'm here to enjoy myself, not pick sides between companies that give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about me and only care about my wallet. I can care less who came up with the ideas first if someone starts doing it smarter, And that is capitalism (at least what it's SUPPOSED to be)
I'd recommend this if:
- You like Monster Hunter games, or others like it.
- You like the combat mechanics in Dark Souls, Dragons Dogma,
- You don't mind grinding boss fights for badass armor/weapon rewards.
- You have a few mates to co-op with.
- You're into Jrpg's and want to try something similar.
And that's kinda it. Unfortunately, this genre isn't one with a very large audience, and thats what makes this such a treat. There aren't enough games like this because it's a risky investment, especially when Capcom sits on the MH throne dominating it. I agree this game had a lot of problems, and it still does. But, I'm also really glad Sony decided to port this (If you can call this halfa** job a port) because it means not only that PC gamers can have more of this genre, but I think it's very likely that Toukiden coming to PC will cause MH to come to PC as well, especially if it does well.
If you're into this sorta game, definitely get it. It's one of the better ones.
If you're on the fence, wait for Toukiden 2 (March 21 2017 for PC release) It will be more fleshed out, and has open world and all those goodies. Hopefully they'll put some f***ing effort into porting it next time.
Anyway I'm definitely gonna support the hell out of this, even if it has its flaws. I've been a huge MH fan since the original, but I won't shame a good game for copying a good thing. Plus, IM TIRED OF MONSTER HUNTING ON A LITTLE 3DS! Come on Capcom...

I recommend the Xbox One controller simply because it works on PC without any special software.    Most of the bad reviews I've seen were because the person didn't have a controller. That's not to say this is going to appeal to everyone.  But I can't imagine anyone without a controller liking this game.
I'm recommending this game.  Why?
Simply put, this is as close to Monster Hunter you're going to get from a PC game.  There are a lot of similarties.  Mostly the game works pretty well in the same way Monster Hunter works.
Difficulty:
It's not as difficult because the controller scheme is much more simple.  You don't use the analog sticks to swing your weapons like in the original Monster Hunter.  It's also easier because the monsters (I've played the first 3 chapters) are just not as deadly - at least in offline solo play.  But you get to a point with the large monsters that it's challenging enough that you'll bring other group members.
Grouping:
You can group with NPCs in offline mode, or you can group with real players in online mode.
Max group size is 4.
In solo mode, the NPCs will run the mission while you just stand there, until you find a large/boss monster.
Weapons & Armour:
All the gear is from Japanese history/lore.  It's Japanese themed.  If that's ok, you'll like the game.  If not, go find another game.
Upgrading:
Like in Monster Hunter you have to carve off (or in the case of this game do a purification ritual to pick up) pieces of monsters in order to get gear crafted.  You don't craft it yourself.  You take it to the village blacksmith and he crafts and upgrades it for you.  To get the better gear, you have to fight the harder monsters.
Weapon 'sockets':
Weapons have sockets.  You put souls of fallen heroes that you find inside those sockets.  That's how you get access to special abilities.  You get a lot of these souls and they all have a specific style and specific bonuses.  For example, if you want to be 'a tank' then you go with a defender soul and  you can then put it in any weapon.  The weapon does not determine your role.  But there are definite advantages to different types of weapons based on what style you choose.
Story:
It's not completely baffling like a lot of Japanese games I try to play.  It took me a while to get into the story.  But once I did, it got to be engaging.
Cons:
The one thing I don't love about the game is that the boss fights aren't (yet) deadly enough.  They can take a long time but that's mostly because the bosses have a ton of hit points. But it's not tedious and boring like Dragon's Dogma.  I feel like the bosses should be able to punish mistakes a lot more readily.  They should be able to wipe a stupid party (i'm thinking of Land and Sky from Monster Hunter.)  But this is a minor con.  I am a huge Dark Souls fan, and enjoy punishing games.  This game is just not like that.  At least not in solo mode.
Overall, I recommend this game because it's fun.  It's not perfect.  It's 3.5 or 4 out of 5.  But I haven't stopped playing it for a couple of days.

I never played Civ 4, but Civ 5 is a huge upgrade from Civ 3. Hex tiles make deciding where to build cities as easy as a point and click. Building the city, maintaining it, and making it grow are a completely different story. The units are also a huge upgrade, and their mechanics are easy to learn.
Civ 5 is very much a city builder, continuous progression game: Someone is going to win before you run out of stuff to do, unless you win first. Cities don't run out of upgrades until you reach the end of the tech tree, which is also where the Scientific Victory is. Turn based wins are a simple 'stay ahead of the other guys' concept, and the Cultural Victory is something that you can actually get on accident if you're not paying attention. Finally, there are Domination and Diplomatic Victory. Domination is taking the starting city of all the other guys, while Diplomatic is making friends with all the little AI city states that other people want to be friends with. I usually turn Time and Cultural Victories off, Time because it's a cheap win, and Cultural because I actually have gotten it on accident well before Diplomatic and Scientific victories were possible.
As for the Civs themselves, I thought only four or five were a style of play I liked. More recently, I said to myself 'This civ looks nice, but it doesn't seem as good as the others I play'. I was wrong about it, so all I can say is that I'm looking to do more then stick to my comfort zone now. That there are civs  that I likely will never play is good, becuase it gives options for people who have different playstyles.
I've also learned that keeping focused on one type of resouce at the expense of others (Food, Production, Science, Gold, Culture, Faith, or Happyness) actually gimps you early, and you can't always recover. You 'can' ignore Faith early game if you don't want to deal with it, but the others you kind of need.
The game just isn't complete without the DLC. Also, be careful when/if playing Venice, because they're a unique civ that requires a lot of precision to make work, and that Carthage actually can walk over mountains.
Also, tundra kinda sucks. Nobody really likes it, and it actually is the second worst type of terrain, Snow being the worst. Snow doesn't give you anything and only one civ even has the option of farming it, and tundra you need a river or lake to build farms.
This isn't a point and click 'this much and then you're done with this city' game. Once you build a city, you're always going to have something you can do with it.

Just finished the game, and as an avid roleplayer who grew up with the pnp rpgs of the 90s I had long been aware of Shadowrun being one of the more popular settings, but had yet to make any foray into that world in any form. This being my first experience with the setting I was quite pleased that it met my expectations both in terms of gameplay and of such a widely acclaimed roleplaying setting.
TL:DR;
-setting: successful fusion of Dungeons and Dragons and the film Bladerunner (game setting was developed on the tail of that era, obviously derived)
-stylish read-along in a detail-rich setting, not much "choices matter" here
-easy to learn, fun turn-based isometric rpg
-best suited for: anyone looking for a short, lite rpg or anyone curious about the Shadowrun setting
The game was what precisely what I expected: short and sweet, stylish, with simple, yet effective, and fun game turn-based rpg mechanics. This is not, however, much of a "choices matter" style rpg, as the story is quite linear, with whatever you say or do having virtually no impact on the sequence of events to follow. Therefore, I cannot suggest this to any of the "true rpg" fans that heckle games like Fallout 4 for their streamlined dialogue choices of "yes I accept the quest" or "no, I don't want a quest, get rekt please" (<3 Fallout 4, it's an "exploration shooter with rpg elements" people, get over it!...).
Then again, "true RPG" and "choices matter" are topics each worthy of reviews of their own.
That said, I didn't expect it to be much more than what it was, and looked at the game as more of a read-along with some character customization and turn-based strategy thrown in, therefore enjoying the game as an appetizer for the acclaimed Shadowrun setting, wetting my appetite for more. In my eyes, the game succeeded at plunging a newcomer into the role of a Shadowrunner in a very stylistic and detail-rich futuristic fantasy/cyberpunk setting. It succeeded to the extent that it makes me want to go pick up some of the current Shadowrun rpg books to live out even more runs and delve deeper into the world of Shadowrunners.
I can assure you, with this last keystroke, that I am immediately off to play the sequels, grinning from ear to ear in anticipation of more Shadowrun goodness. I can't believe I was missing out on this setting all these years. Great work Harebrained Schemes! Keep 'em comin'!

If you're a gamer that is into the JRPG genre, turn-based battling, visual novels, beautifully drawn anime and background art and hours on end of quests, leveling, skill customization and fairies then Fairy Fencer F is for you. Word of advice to completionists not wanting to miss anything on their first playthrough, upon entering a new dungeon and viewing the cutscene, leave immediately and go back to town and accept Lola's quests as they are time sensitive. Try to fight every enemy you see at least once, inspect the maps throroughly to look out for diamonds containing possibly missable loot and obtain the Item Sonar ability as soon as you can.
Overall I recommend this game highly to any JRPG fan that is into a good story filled with likeable characters with a great balance of drama, action and comedy.

Honestly, I do recommend this game, but only if you buy it on a good sale (glad I did). I was expecting a bit more from a Nicalis title, considering the tightness of their prior games like Cave Story.
The Pros:
-Fun and nostalgic, with genuine NES-era graphics and lots of funny references.
-Simple, minimalistic controls (again, like an NES title) that are easy to pick up.
-Save points are plentiful, making it so that dying (which you will do a lot of) is minimally punishing.
-Fun, challenging bosses.
The Cons:
-Character movement is incredibly squirrely, which is a bad combination with all the heavy platforming and insta-kill spike traps throughout.
-This game still employs bloxk-screen scrolling (think original Legend of Zelda), but it is very rapid, with many screens having instant death traps like spikes only a single tile away from the scroll point.
-On top of the point above, there are several kill-bait moments like a Mario-Bros.-style pipe that says "do not enter" but fails to mention that unlike the game itreferences, even *standing* on the pipe will cause you to fall in to your death. I suppose this is slightly amusing in the same dickish way that the many unforeseeable death tricks in Dark Souls are, but I'm not quite as keen on it.
-Despite the many, many cheap ways in which you can die, there is also a death counter. Once again, it's a number that you should just ignore, but nevertheless annoys the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me.

I can't say this is one of the better JRPGs on Steam, given that most JRPG players demand a certain level of depth and character development in their games, but nonetheless I would still recommend it.
It's a very well designed game, in that all the art, animations, menus, and customizations are well polished. Most people that catch me playing it think it looks really cool, and you get that feeling while playing it too. The dialogue is often funny and the characters will even surprise you, but it's still as a whole a kind've hollow experience.
It's easy to become overpowered, the monsters and environments aren't very diverse, the story is pretty generic with no real revelations or challenges, and sometimes the characters seem bored and flippant about everything that going around, not to mention the bad guys aren't very interesting or intimidating. Depth is certainly not the games forte, but I didn't end up minding it too much.
It's actually kind of nice to have nothing invested sometimes, the characters almost seem aware that they're in a silly JRPG and the developers put in plenty of missables/grinding/extras for people hoping for more of a challenge. There's so much fun small stuff packed in, like all 39 of the furies you can collect having something to say about current events, or buffing/debuffing areas to grind more efficiently. Lots of cool ideas with the battle system, even though it mostly doesn't matter since you can blow away anything in the main game after level 40. Even though the characters aren't going to have any complex problems or feelings, they are all colorful and enjoyable, I ended up liking everyone and having a hard time choosing my party.
If you really dig playing RPGs and don't mind a bit of repetivieness and grasping plot points, it's a really fun game. I feel like I've been negative, but I really loved it quite a bit (obviously... my hours)! I stopped playing just to write a positive review, and now I'm getting back to it...

I was a complete neophyte to the Shadowrun series when I first played Shadowrun Returns. I was looking for a strategy oriented RPG with a scenario that would keep me interested in playing the game, the futuristic setting was a bonus.
The character's customization offers many "carreer" possibilities, whether you want to be a Street Samurai, blading and gunning through the streets of Neo-Seattle, a hacker or "Decker" and turn the situation to your advantage by jumping in the matrix and hacking your way through the top, or someone in touch with his inner self and the old spirits of nature, such as a shaman. Or maybe you would rather unleash your fury on the local gangs and punch whoever is stepping in your way. You could also combine any of the different skill trees to make your own and unique gameplay, but remember that a jack of all trades is a master of none...
However, this is not why I am recommending this game. Because even if the gameplay and the overall aesthetic of the game are worth the price, the scenario and roleplaying aspect of Shadowrun Returns is, in my humgle opinion, what makes it an amazing game. It all starts off simple, and then escalates to a breathtaking scenario carried by well-written dialogues and a very peculiar ambiance (at least for a newcomer like me).
In conclusion, if you're looking for a neofantasy roleplaying oriented strategy RPG, this is your game.

This reveiew is based on one playthrough of the game.  Considering the achievements (of which many are rediculous), the game is expected to be played through multiple times (NG+).
FYI : TLDR at the bottom.
Actually has a clearly explained plot line.  Some plot twists and variation of character. Very comedic.
The intereactions b/t characters is fun, energetic, and sometimes realistic.  Very few of the character's personalities evolve.
The bar for the difficulty lvl is set way to low.  It's not in the least bit hard.  I expected at least some challenge.  I'm not counting the lvl req'd DLC dungeons(which aren't plot related and aren't req'd to be completed or even played at all), that's a cop-out.
At least fairies could be used to modify the stats of any given dungeon.  So if you just wanted things to be hard, you could make it so no spells/ablilties can be used, chars take dbl dmg, have reduced resistances, can't cure debuffs, etc.  On the flipside, +% exp/gold/WP/stats/droprate.  Most faires gave both a (+) & a (-).  Still didn't improve overall game difficulty.
Battles are easy to learn, manage, and fun to watch. Quickly becomes repetitive.
Equipment was too easy to come by to bother making it with mats. Level growth was automatic boosts to all stats, and the only variation is via equipped Fairy and Weapon Points (WP).  Don't get me started on the player specific abilities, that is a sordid story rife with complaints.
On the plus side WP had a good deal of variation, but alot of the magic/weapon attacks seemed either useless or overtly interchangeable with 2-3 others.  Why would I want to use magic to cure a debuff if there is an item for it?   Nothing in the game denies the use of items.  Granted AoE dispell of all debuffs was nice, but characters were only ever afflicted with one at any given time.  Not mentioning most were temporary or lacked any sort impact on the battle.
It was fun to make a bunch of items I'd never need or use, though. (Max Elixirs, the AoE HP pots, etc)
Some people complain about the AoE targeting sensitivity being too high, but these people are just lazy. This is easily remedied by rotating the camera.
Game has low hardware requirements but remains nice to look at.  Art style and quality gel together well.  Objects in the world look like they belong and doesn't have any obvious/jarring visual errors.
Loses a point for poor dungeon initialization programming.  Major FPS drops everytime a new dungeon is loaded, due to all the mobs being spawned simultaneously.  Major programming bug that should have been fixed prior to port.
To my surprise, the english voice acting was superb.  I'll probably play through the game again with the original voices to see how it compares, but not anytime soon.
Music was enjoyable for the first 10hrs or so. By then you've heard almost 80% of the music you'll hear all game and they're just on repeat.  Was nice that one of the battle specific songs was swapped out halfway through.  It was seriously grinding on my nerves, by then.
Overall, I enjoyed the game.  The characters were entertaing to watch and the plot held together.   NOT worth $30.  I'd consider it to be worth $20.
I still recommend it for the story and characters.  It was fun to play through and I will prolly play NG+ one time through just to see what it's like and what changes.

'Jesus Object Christ, this game is amazing.
I'm sorry. I can play this game hours, and hours, and hours on end. Teleglitch refines the "careful planning" of a roguelike with the intense fast-paced adrenaline rush that Hotline Miami delivered. It also provided me with a couple jump scares and the overall atmosphere is very intensified.

Unlike some other walls in the game they feel like things completely not supposed to be there. There was a difference between a corridor that ended with a cave-in and a corridor that ended with a teleglitch blocking the way.
The difficulty curve is ridiculous and unpredictable in the right direction. The game slowly eases from mutants to zombies, then introduces guards at the same time. Suddenly, if not prepared, the few bosses encountered can catch you off guard and force you to use your powerful weapons you planned to save for further on.

Ammo is very, very scarce early on, and forces the player to use every weapon even when they believe it's the wrong time to do so. I've used rocket launchers on tiny mutants and been forced to use my last 9mm bullets to take down the Big Bad coming my way.
This game needs more attention on all fronts.'

Quick note: The downvote button doesn't make me wrong. It makes you a fanboy who accepts low tier garbage ports.
I make no commentary on the gameplay. I stopped playing after less than ten minutes.
This was originally a mobile game. It looks like a mobile game. It plays like a mobile game. The game runs in windowed mode natively, and when I started playing, it completely skipped over a main menu to immediately force me into a tutorial. I hit the 'maximize button' and instead of stretching to fill my screen, it merely expanded "a bit" and filled up 75% of my 1080p monitor, and hard-jammed itself to the left side of the screen, leaving an ugly space on the right where I could see my wallpaper.
When you click anything ingame, massive sparkles erupt everywhere. Why? Because this was designed for mobile and thus it needs to visually show where your finger pressed. The sparkles are INCREDIBLY distracting, they're easily the size of three facebook 'like' buttons stacked on top of each other and last for at least half a second. With all the clicking you'll be doing, you'll quickly feel like they designed the game for people with short attention spans so they can have something flashy to look at.
Except this is a PC game. This port is lazy. In the year 2017, some basic, rudimentary graphics options, like being able to disable touch screen swiping and tap indicators, along with resolutions and such are a requirement in every 'top quality' PC game.
I thought the voice dialogue was a bit cringy, and the japanese voices from the very little I saw were terribly linked to the action onscreen, but the 'weeb' nature of the game didn't put me off. Hell, it drew me in.
Again, the gameplay may literally be ten times better than Hearthstone. I don't doubt it is, but this is the PC version. Crappy ports are inexcusable.

Let me just say that I'm also tired of zombie games. But I'm also tired of zombie games that are made by poor and bad developers. Dying Light however, is a good game. Though made by the creators of Dead Island which might turn off most of you guys.
If you're worried that this game will be not worth your time because it's made by the same creators of Dead Island, drop your worries right now. This is a good game for real this time. To be honest, I also like Dead Island a bit despite it's unfinished quality.
Now before I continue, let me put a spoiler warning because, I'm going to be explaining the story right now. Skip this if you don't want the story spoiled.
**SPOILER ALERT**
You play as Kyle Crane. Working for the GRE which, I think is a secret government agency. Your mission being you have to receive private information from your target and kill him. As you arrive in town, things go to hell and you get infected. After looking for a shipment containing crates of antizen which surpresses the symptoms of the infection, GRE contacts you saying that you have to burn some the crates. Kyle didn't want to, but was forced to. Hours of doing favours for the survivors that saved him, he's now in a constant battle between the trust of the survivors that saved him and his boss on the radio.
*END*
Let's talk about the gameplay now. To be expected, it plays a lot like Dead Island with new features. There's the epic parkour system. If you've played Assassin's Creed before, it's kind of like that except in 1st person. The game starts out a little slow as you're really vulnerable to the zombies when you first start out. Especially when it turns dark and super zombies start patrolling the streets.
If one super zombie spots you while you're out at night, you better get out of there right now. There's no sense in running since they run faster than you. They can also parkour like you can. Fortunately, there are ways of dealing with them to prevent them from chasing you.
As you survive, you get different experience points depending on what you've been doing. If you run, jump and climb a lot, you'll get Agility XP. This allows you to perform better tricks at getting around the environment. If you hit and kill zombies, you'll get Combat XP. Which allows you to perform better and deadlier attacks. Yes you do get Combat XP just by hitting them so, there's no need to finish the zombie off. Though you get extra Combat XP for doing so.
Finally, there's Survival XP. This is achieved through helping out your survivors. Which include completing quests, bringing them supplies from airdrops or helping other survivors that are in trouble. You'll also get Survival XP based on how long you survived through the night without dying. Oh and there's one good reason about being out at night. If you can stay out of the way of the super zombies, the XP you gain will be doubled for Agility and Combat. Like if you get 15 Agility XP for climbing over a fence at day, you'll get 30 instead if you do it at night. But remember, night is very difficult.
Now the combat is just like Dead Island. Smack at the zombies face until it stops moving or its head explodes in to a gooey red paste. Though don't swing too much or else you'll tire out. Now here's another good thing. There's regular stamina and combat stamina. Regular stamina is only used when you sprint and run around while combat stamina is only used whenever you swing your weapon. This is good because, there will be times where you'll have to dodge out of the way whenever you run out of combat stamina. No dodging doesn't use combat stamina thankfully. Also like Dead Island, you can add elemental upgrades to your weapons and as well as modifications that add bonus stats to your weapons. Though weapons only have a few slots of modding and weapons will degrade until they break if used too much. Not to mention they only have a few number of repairs before repairing does absolutely nothing. Once you used all the repair slots on the weapon, it's time to get a replacement. Not everything lasts forever and this is especially true to items in real life.
The graphics is amazing. The sun glares beautifully at your face and the destroyed and dark urban scenery really makes you feel sad for it. The sound is great too and it can even make you scared and really make you get goosebumps. Which I think is cool because, it adds a good horror element to it. The characters of the game also make you want to care for them. They have a good purpose for staying alive and even the main villain on the game makes you wish the guy was dead. He does a fantastic job at being a villain.
The co-op is also good. Running around the environment, completing quests and killing zombies together is really fun indeed. Also, there's a new mode called "Be the Zombie" mode. This allows players to play a super zombie that also gets stronger just like when you play the campaign. These player controlled zombies are tough if you're very sneaky. You have to be a predator. Stalking your prey and waiting for the exact moment to strike. Not to mention this allows players to invade other player's games. It's just like in Dark Souls whenever you get invaded by a red spirit. Though you do have the choice of turning off invasion like a pansy if you want.
Also the special zombies from Dead Island are also back. The slow walking biters, the fast running infected, the big zombie that wields a big stone rebar, the acid spitting spitter and the exploding bomber. These add more to the difficulty and tension to the game as you need to be careful when facing these special infected.
Now you guys might be wondering what are the bad things to this game? You make it sound like it's one of the best games ever. Well, that may be true but, you do have a solid point. It's time to get down to the nit picky and discuss the bad parts.
As I've said, the game starts out slow and it's a bit difficult. The game only gets more interesting the further you get through the story. You also can't do co-op unless you complete the prolouge chapter first as well.
The game also has a few frames per second issues so you'll have to tone down the graphics just a bit to get a stable FPS.
The controls on the keyboard can take a while to get used to but, fortunately you can also use a 360 controller if you want.
The other bad factor is that this game borrows a lot of mechanics from other games. The obvious one being Assassin's Creed with it's parkour system. You can also perform a leap of faith if you see a pile of blue trashbags. It also has a mission where you have to climb up an antenna tower and turn the power on once you reach the top. Which is very similar to Far Cry 3 when you climb up a tower to reveal part of the world map. Thankfully, this only happens once after completing the quest for it.
You'll be grinding for XP a lot if you want to have any advantage at surviving this game. Even more if you do things during the day time. So this might turn off some players that don't want to spend hours trying to get stronger.
The co-op is really hit and miss. Since there's a lot of players that have already gotten very far into the story and are a lot stronger than you are. Which means, the co-op is not really balanced to fit newer players. Also, if these kinds of players give you overpowered weapons, it could really ruin the experience and fun of your game. So try not to accept weapons from them.
There's also no fast traveling system except when you're in co-op. One player can teleport to another player that's waiting to advance a quest but, that's just about it. There's also no vehicles so, you'll be running from point a to point b for countless minutes. But thankfully, there's a craftable drink that allows you to run faster and jump farther. It also gives you unlimited running stamina too.
Should you play it? YES! It will suck a lot of hours out of you. Trust me.

I'm going to start a small pro vs. con for this game. This is based on my time playing. I've played through the whole story and many of the achievements.
Pros:

Cons:

- Bugs and getting stuck in random places
- No controller button customization

OMG the references. The references, OMG.
Horray for a South Park game that doesn't feel like some crap clone-reskin of some other bland game. The Stick of Truth is like your own little interactive South Park episode; traversing most of the the town's locales, with the rich lore of 17 seasons. The story feels like an episode too, not surprising, since creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker were heavily involved in the production, Graphics are near-indistinguishable from the TV show, adding to the immersion. Sadly, the gameplay is nothing more than a simple turned-based affair, lacking any depth. Quickly, killing trash mobs in a single turn becomes the norm. Most bosses don't last over 5 turns. Many times I mis-timed my attack just to extend the fight to see the variety of unique boss-specific attacks. I felt I missed out, Zerging them all on my first playthrough. I also spent a good half-hour reading all the captions on the trash items, something else I missed the first time through. There's plenty of nostalgia to be had here.
Overall, I recommend South Park: The Stick of Truth to any moderate to hardcore fanboy. The references alone are worth the cost of admission.  Anyone else should avoid it, finding only a mediocre turned-based RPG with potty humor.

A strong finish to the Arkham Trilogy.
I enjoyed this game - it felt like a natural evolution from Arkham Asylum > Arkham City > Arkham Knight.  The overall game mechanics are polished, and nothing felt like it was tacked on as a gimmick, though the Batmobile came close.  Having all of the Riddler tasks that required the use of the Batmobile reminded me of Half Life 2 right after you get the gravity gun - the developer wants to show off how cool they think their ideas are by having you use it in random ways as a thinly veiled tutorial.  Honestly, unless I needed it for a mission, I preferred to glide and grapnel boost over the roofs of Gotham.  The side missions, much like Arkham City, really made the game.  Tracking down Firefly, Penguin, Two-Face, etc kept the Batman experience strong.
As with the other games in the series, the augmented reality challenges allow you to both practice your skills, but also earn Waynetech upgrades if you can 3-star the objectives.  By the end of the game, you could in theory have everything maxed out.  This makes New Game+ a lot easier.
Graphically, the game is obviously the best of the series, though unless you have a high end CPU/GPU you'll often struggle when there's rain, explosions, or driving the batmobile.  I basically maxed out the graphic settings for my GPU (EVGA 960) using the VRAM calculator on the screen, but even then I'd get some serious stuttering from time to time...I'm talking single-digit FPS.  Periodically restarting the game helped as it seemed like they didn't do a very good job of memory recycling.  If I played for too long, often the game would keep running even though I had exited to desktop from the menu.  I'd have to kill it in taskmanager to get it to stop.
I'm hoping that the next game(s) in the series further expand the roles of the other characters - I'd love to have more Batgirl, Catwoman, Nightwing, Harley, and Robin missions as part of a fully fleshed out game.

For someone who is completely incapable of finding fantasy and magical settings interesting or enjoyable, this game series is surprisingly good.
Oldschool isometric games are a dying breed from a bygone, better era when players were expected to be able to use their own brain. What was lacking in graphics was more than made up in gameplay, writing and location art.
Shadowrun series hails back to that bygone era.
While lot of the micromanaging and details such as having to worry about ammo or weapon customization has been filed down and out of the game, the game still retains that feel that appeals to us RPG veterans.
Characters are distinct, unique and well-written with plenty of dialogue options which range of variety depends on character's skills and chosen "etiquette". Players who prefer pacifist runs are going to be disappointed, because as the plot(s) progress, there'll be inevitable and unavoitable encounters that you can't get through without re-enacting a calm day in Detroit.
The weapons themselfs are generic and clearly not the focus of the game, instead the effort has been put in to making a compelling, believable storytelling with high-quality dialogue. While the game doesn't allow you to deviate much from the plot(s), you can still have many ways to deal with the final fight. From talking the big guy into giving up, to shooting him or even joining him, all these combined with the previous acts you've carried out during the progression of the storyline affect the ending.
With so well detailed options for less violent runs, the game also gives no penalties for players who want to do their part in imposing an anarchist solution to anarchist problem.

Saints bless the universe!  Finally, it's here!  The game I've been waiting for ever since I didn't like
!  Saints Row IV takes you on an epic journey from President to alien slave to superhero!
Saints Row IV is a violent good time.  While I have not played coop mode, single-player mode is awesome.  I like the super powers a lot.  The first two are exactly like the movement powers you may have seen in the Prototype games, super speed and high jumps.  Later powers get more combat oriented, and most of the upgrades are useful.
There are a lot of hilarious antics going on around you, and the music is sometimes enough to make you laugh.  Think South Park style humor then Matrix style fight-the-man resistance (starring you, the former "The Man") with a bunch of other crazy little aspects.
There are some glitches.  You can get stuck very easily early in the game if you jump on some simple boxes.  It upset me a lot because it meant I had to replay the most boring part of the game: the intro.  That said, if you try not to jump around too much there, the later levels let you jump as much as you like.  Also, I experienced some friendly AI characters going crazy and trying to kill me... no real explanation.  I guess that's alright. Just more cannon fodder for my plasma pistol.
Overall, I give this game a solid 5/5.  It's as fun as a game could be.  It doesn't take things seriously, but it gives you enough story to care about what you're trying to accomplish.  It had great visuals, that SR3 art style we all love, and tons of video game cliches.

So. My first review on any game on steam. Why this game? TL;DR, it sucks. so. much. "but whyyy". Many things, I'll try to keep it short. There is no map, why. You run around and of course the path branches off. You take one, branching again, and again. Suddenly, boss. You die miserably. Let's go back, but where to!? There is no sense of direction, you just backtrack to find some item that makes the boss beatable, speaking of which: You need the right item, always. This game has this illusion of choice, enemies simply become unbeatable with the wrong item "choices". You die, often. Every minute, why? because you're bad? No. Because the game's "traps" are either invisible or if not yet killed by impossible to dodge. You simply get killed for no reason, BUT NOW YOU KNOW, that at that exact spot is a trap. The game doesn't really teach you much any other way. There are apparently mechanics that never get used, like reflecting projectiles. (srsly, why implent it if you can't literally reflect any afterwards, you try anyways and die ofcourse.) Safe points are sometimes 3 screens apart, sometimes 50. (wtf). You collect money, fooor...? There are sometimes mechants selling exactly 1 item. Wow. Much choice, so grind. I forgot about dodging things, enemies can turn immidiately, while you merely "swing" back. Your sword has the basically the range of male genetalia, so yeah, you cannt dodge simple enemy movement, which is just unfair. You get magic to help you out range-wise. You use it. You ONLY use magic. You run around waiting for it to charge, because you suck at melee. But again, the game forces you to change strategies by simply making enemies immune, wow. Btw most of the bosses are immune to every sort of magic, makes sense, right? I have now roughly played 3-4 hours, still playing right now. There are teleporters all over the place that are inactive (why). Ah, and after you beat your goddamn boss ( I forgot to mention that bosses always have exactly one strategy to beat, the mechanics are so simple my little brother could programm those.) you can ask yourself: Where is the next safe point, which heals me. (thats the only way to heal). You can backtrack, but can you make it with your low health? All the way back? Well, you can try advancing into the unknown, where any reasonable dev would place a safe point near, not this one. After every boss I ALWAYS go back and safe. had to repeat many bosses because afterwards no safe point for 20 screens, and lots of fun traps.
TO SUM IT UP: This game lacks about everything and it's "difficulty" comes from all the unfair things happening to you. You run around and remember things, you don't solve any problems, you learn to avoid them. Without a sense of direction and the really cheap story you feel lost all the time. Equipping different items to suit your style is also not feasible, cause enemies need hard counters. I bought this for 2,50 and more would be overpriced, honestly. It copies castlevania and stuff (probably for fun) but even those old games had better graphic, better music, better gameplay, better exploration and just about everything. Castle in the darkness sucks.

A strong finish to the Arkham Trilogy.
I enjoyed this game - it felt like a natural evolution from Arkham Asylum > Arkham City > Arkham Knight.  The overall game mechanics are polished, and nothing felt like it was tacked on as a gimmick, though the Batmobile came close.  Having all of the Riddler tasks that required the use of the Batmobile reminded me of Half Life 2 right after you get the gravity gun - the developer wants to show off how cool they think their ideas are by having you use it in random ways as a thinly veiled tutorial.  Honestly, unless I needed it for a mission, I preferred to glide and grapnel boost over the roofs of Gotham.  The side missions, much like Arkham City, really made the game.  Tracking down Firefly, Penguin, Two-Face, etc kept the Batman experience strong.
As with the other games in the series, the augmented reality challenges allow you to both practice your skills, but also earn Waynetech upgrades if you can 3-star the objectives.  By the end of the game, you could in theory have everything maxed out.  This makes New Game+ a lot easier.
Graphically, the game is obviously the best of the series, though unless you have a high end CPU/GPU you'll often struggle when there's rain, explosions, or driving the batmobile.  I basically maxed out the graphic settings for my GPU (EVGA 960) using the VRAM calculator on the screen, but even then I'd get some serious stuttering from time to time...I'm talking single-digit FPS.  Periodically restarting the game helped as it seemed like they didn't do a very good job of memory recycling.  If I played for too long, often the game would keep running even though I had exited to desktop from the menu.  I'd have to kill it in taskmanager to get it to stop.
I'm hoping that the next game(s) in the series further expand the roles of the other characters - I'd love to have more Batgirl, Catwoman, Nightwing, Harley, and Robin missions as part of a fully fleshed out game.

A friend once described this game to me as "learning to walk backwards." After playing it myself, I have to say this game feels more like "learning to *think* backwards."
Antichamber is a first-person puzzle game that plays with the idea of non-newtonian space. This means that if you walk down a hallway and turn around, what's behind you isn't necessarily the same as what you just walked through. There are a couple of points in the game where the only way to progress is to walk right back where you came from, which turns out not to be the same place at all.
The process of learning to deal with non-newtonian space is confusing for some, although I have to admit that I am not one of those people. If you approach each room as a puzzle and ignore your ideas of what is in front of you or behind you, (as well as some real-world ideas like 'common sense,') the game itself is not actually very difficult.
What nailed this game for me was the atmosphere. Set in what many have described as an Escher-esque world, the game's stark minimalism and use of visual space meant that even though the entire complex is built out of white walls, there was always something interesting to look at or think about. In some ways, I found this atmosphere to better than that of Portal - while GlaDos made the Portal series fun to listen to, with an ever-present and witty dialogue that provided much of the tone and narrative depth for the game, Antichamber removes the narrator entirely and forces the player to decide how much - or how little - narrative is present in the game at all. The lack of a Narrator Voice lets the game's own tone settle in the player's thoughts more closely, a tone that I can only describe at varying times as 'child-like discovery' and 'calm confusion', as oxymoronic as that last statement might seem.
Antichamber is the kind of game that is best played without a guide, not knowing where to go next, with as much or as little confusion as that might bring you. This is one of those few interesting games that can intrigue storytellers and non-story gamers alike with a dialogue and narrative that barely exist, in a setting that does not conform to the vast majority of popular videogames.

- The closest thing you'll get to playing Monster Hunter on PC outside of China, while still being its own thing. Does not have the overall polish of a Monster Hunter game but it is still a very enjoyable romp for any fan of the franchise.
- It even puts it's own spin on the old MH fight formula: monsters in Toukiden do not take damage until you've broken their parts and revealed their true ethereal form. The classic rage mode of Toukiden's monsters is also much more dramatic in than in MH, often resulting in them fighting you in a vastly different way.
- The weapons are a mixed bag of melee and ranged; any MH fan will immediately feel at home here, and like with the monsters Toukiden puts it's own spin on them too by having a system in place with Spirits you can collect and socket into your weapon for various bonuses.
- Tons of content, like you would expect from a Monster Hunter-like game. Of course most of it is just basically fighting bosses over and over and over, but if you're a MH fan that is what you're looking for, right? I'm at a little over 100 hours played at the time of this review and I'm nowhere near "done" with the game.
- It is an OK port. You know, tolerable. Locked to 30 FPS and forget about keyboard and mouse and use your gamepad of choice and you'll be fine.
All-in-all, I'd say that if you are a fan of the Monster Hunter style of gameplay and like me desperately hunger for it on PC, at the very least put Toukiden on your "Wait-for-a-sale"-wishlist. I'd be hard pressed to recommend it fully at 60 euro/dollars due to the port being what it is.

Including bosses, and you always act first. This is even more annoying when the game tells you via cutscenes that the upcoming boss is supposed to be super powerful and all, and then you almost one-shot them on the first turn, at which point the fight is interrupted by another cutscene that shows your characters inexplicably getting the crap beaten out of them. Followed by some
they throw you back into the fight and you now proplerly one-shot the boss. It's really stupid and happens many times throughout the story.
Enemies do so little damage that it's virtually impossible to lose. I was surprised to see that there was no achievement for getting a game over. which I was only able to get after stacking various damage increasing effects on a dungeon (quadruple damage - for your party and enemies alike) and randomly missing my first attack against a boss.
And if it wasn't clear by now, there is no difficulty slider or anything. At. All.
The dungeon design is acceptable, but eventually reaches the pinnacle of laziness when they send you back in time halfway through the "story" and make you go though all the previous dungeons again, with the same enemies and the exact same bosses.
Fairy Fencer F is one of those generic low budget JRPGs that usually get scores around the 55-65% mark.
If you've really already burned yourself out on every other JRPG out there, you could probably grab this. but if you're playing your games for the story or the battles you're going to be disappointed.

Medal of Honor: Allied Assault is primarily a novel about growing up under extraordinary circumstances in the 1930s in the Southern United States. The story covers a span of three years, during which the main characters undergo significant changes. Scout Finch lives with her brother Jem and their father Atticus in the fictitious town of Maycomb, Alabama. Maycomb is a small, close-knit town, and every family has its social station depending on where they live, who their parents are, and how long their ancestors have lived in Maycomb.
A widower, Atticus raises his children by himself, with the help of kindly neighbors and a black housekeeper named Calpurnia. Scout and Jem almost instinctively understand the complexities and machinations of their neighborhood and town. The only neighbor who puzzles them is the mysterious Arthur Radley, nicknamed Boo, who never comes outside. When Dill, another neighbor's nephew, starts spending summers in Maycomb, the three children begin an obsessive — and sometimes perilous — quest to lure Boo outside.
Scout is a tomboy who prefers the company of boys and generally solves her differences with her fists. She tries to make sense of a world that demands that she act like a lady, a brother who criticizes her for acting like a girl, and a father who accepts her just as she is. Scout hates school, gaining her most valuable education on her own street and from her father.
Not quite midway through the story, Scout and Jem discover that their father is going to represent a black man named Tom Robinson, who is accused of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and beating a white woman. Suddenly, Scout and Jem have to tolerate a barrage of racial slurs and insults because of Atticus' role in the trial. During this time, Scout has a very difficult time restraining from physically fighting with other children, a tendency that gets her in trouble with her Aunt Alexandra and Uncle Jack. Even Jem, the older and more levelheaded of the two, loses his temper a time or two. After responding to a neighbor's (Mrs. Dubose) verbal attack by destroying her plants, Jem is sentenced to read to her every day after school for one month. Ultimately, Scout and Jem learn a powerful lesson about bravery from this woman. As the trial draws nearer, Aunt Alexandra comes to live with them under the guise of providing a feminine influence for Scout.
During the novel's last summer, Tom is tried and convicted even though Atticus proves that Tom could not have possibly committed the crime of which he is accused. In the process of presenting Tom's case, Atticus inadvertently insults and offends Bob Ewell, a nasty, lazy drunkard whose daughter is Tom's accuser. In spite of Tom's conviction, Ewell vows revenge on Atticus and the judge for besmirching his already tarnished name. All three children are bewildered by the jury's decision to convict; Atticus tries to explain why the jury's decision was in many ways a foregone conclusion.
Shortly after the trial, Scout attends one of her aunt's Missionary Society meetings. Atticus interrupts the meeting to report that Tom Robinson had been killed in an escape attempt. Scout learns valuable lessons about achieving the ideal of womanhood and carrying on in the face of adversity that day.
Things slowly return to normal in Maycomb, and Scout and Jem realize that Boo Radley is no longer an all-consuming curiosity. The story appears to be winding down, but then Bob Ewell starts making good on his threats of revenge. Scout is in the Halloween pageant at school, playing the part of a ham. With Atticus and Aunt Alexandra both too tired to attend, Jem agrees to take Scout to the school. After embarrassing herself on-stage, Scout elects to leave her ham costume on for the walk home with Jem.
On the way home, the children hear odd noises, but convince themselves that the noises are coming from another friend who scared them on their way to school that evening. Suddenly, a scuffle occurs. Scout really can't see outside of her costume, but she hears Jem being pushed away, and she feels powerful arms squeezing her costume's chicken wire against her skin. During this attack, Jem badly breaks his arm. Scout gets just enough of a glimpse out of her costume to see a stranger carrying Jem back to their house.
The sheriff arrives at the Finch house to announce that Bob Ewell has been found dead under the tree where the children were attacked, having fallen on his own knife. By this time, Scout realizes that the stranger is none other than Boo Radley, and that Boo is actually responsible for killing Ewell, thus saving her and Jem's lives. In spite of Atticus' insistence to the contrary, the sheriff refuses to press charges against Boo. Scout agrees with this decision and explains her understanding to her father. Boo sees Jem one more time and then asks Scout to take him home, but rather than escort him home as though he were a child, she has Boo escort her to his house as a gentleman would.
With Boo safely home, Scout returns to Jem's room where Atticus is waiting. He reads her to sleep and then waits by Jem's bedside for his son to wake up.

Alright. Review time. After quite a few hours with this game, I can safely go into detail about whether you should buy it or not, keeping it spoiler free.
If you are TL:DR then here's the nutshell version: I love it.
STORY: Again not going to spoil anything in the story and rather experience it yourself. However, in terms of how good it is...It can be slow to repetitive at times, and i think I skipped a scene at one point because I felt it was irrelevant. The story itself is okay with quite a few twists to keep things refreshing. Though I feel that the story may be the weakest element in the game, AGAIN not that it's bad, it's enjoyable, but it ain't exactly perfect. If it's worth something, I did tear up a bit at times from certain heavy moments. SADLY: You don't get to make any real choices, it's rather straight forward with only three endings. One you get from ignoring all subevents involving your party. And two for...just google it.
Characters: Most if not all of them are brimming with personality and are unique in their own way, including the Fairies in which our main characters possess. The protagonist thankfully is not the cliche brave and goody-to-shoes hero, rather far from it as you will see if you start the game. Each character is lovable and I remember their names well, and I'm bad at remembering names, so that's quite the accomplishment.
Gameplay: Turn based as one might expect. Nothing much to say. You can use basic attacks, magic, or special animated skills to attack your opponents. You may also customize combos in which to attack your enemies with. Each character also has a special ability with special effects for each individual. There are other elements as well which are quite refreshing, but I don't feel like going into detail since it would be explained in the game later.
Soundtrack: Fairly nice, especially when you use you VERY VERY powerful ability or 'FAIRIZE' as well. Though it can get a bit bland, but overall there are some tracks that stick out.
Voice Acting: FOCUS FOCUS FOCUS FOCUS!!! This is important! In my opinion i highly recommend you play this game with the japanese voice over in the options tab. The english dub is...there for those who really hate japanese, but I don't...find them believable like I do with the japanese Dub. The characters feel more alive without the english voice over, and the experience with the game fell a bit when I tried the english version for a while. Japanese is my recommended voice over.
Overall rating: I would at least give this game a 8/10. Still places to improve on, but I've played a solid 24 hours with it, and even if you beat the game, you can restart the story without losing all your progress and restarting. There is replay value depending how you do on the first run.
WARNING: I do not think there is an autosave for this game so before you leave and murderize your computer when you come back, always save. ALWAYS. I didn't lose any progress because i was paranoid as hell since the game leaves save points to help you do it manually. But you can also do it on the world map.
Hope this was helpful.

What is Castle in the Darkness?
A fast-paced action platformer with metroidvania elements. I do think enough to call it a metroidvania, but its areas are relatively linear with a few side-paths and the whole game is basically a left-to-right quest with extra dungeons tucked away.
And really, it's pretty great. The character speed is fast and the combat is fast, leading to a very high-energy playing experience. Only in later/harder parts of the game does dying really feel that consequential, before then checkpoints are frequent and reloading is simple and easy if you die. It's fun to die, it really is.
The game pulls some traps and a few puzzles but for the most part it's straightforward platforming and poking enemies with your sword or using one of the variety of spells. You gain more HP for each boss you kill and gain better weapons and armor as the game progresses, plus you can find some really strong gear hidden away in one of the many bonus dungeons. Until you get your double jump there are a lot of inaccessible goodies, leading to some backtracking to find them all, but you can warp between areas and there's never a huge massive distance between warps given the fast-pace of the game.
At times there are a few spots where checkpoints seem a little far apart, primarily in the last main area and in some of the hidden dungeons, but it's never really too far. There are however a few pretty rude traps that feel a little unfair. Not too many, though. The platforming is tight and the combat is designed such that you can avoid hits almost all the time if you play well, and you'll need to as even at max HP and defense your character is pretty squishy, to say nothing of how easy it is to die with the basic gear.
There's a lot of game here too, for only $6; it took me 10 hours to 100% the game, and beyond that there's a NG+ with some extra items and a no-damage challenge (that I did not do). For the price, it's definitely a good amount of content. The art looks fine enough and the music is pretty good, as well. The bosses are pretty varied and each area tends to have some unique platforming to it as well. Overall? Definitely a good experience for anyone interested in metroidvanias or action platformers in general, I really enjoyed this little game.

Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is the most fun I've had playing a game in the series since the fourth one. It has an interesting premise with precise controls fitted for mouse and keyboard with competent level design and good pacing. Frankly the differences were jarring coming right off of Resident Evil 6.
Any fan of the series will have a blast with this game. There are several humorous callbacks to the early installments involving sandwiches, masters of unlocking and Samurai Edges. The monster designs are very creative in the sense that different types of enemies force you to consider different types of strategies. Just shooting at anything that moves isn't as effective. I especially liked one particular type of monster where you have to use one character to spot it and then switch back to the other one to shoot it. This may sound overly complicated but it's actually quite fun to do, even in single player.
Unlike Revelations 1 this game actually had a revelation about something in one of the main character's past. Though it's not lore-shattering the game at least tries to live up to its own title this time. That always bothered me while playing the first one. Barry and his daughter Moira's story is engaging and heartfelt and leagues beyond any narrative plot in the first game. I thoroughly enjoyed their arcs from start to finish. I also found it humorous that in Barry's story he becomes a surrogate father to Natalia in the same vein of Resident Evil Gaiden. And even though Gaiden isn't canon it's still interesting to see how many similarities its plot and ending shares with Barry and Natalie's story in this game.
The game is goofy but grounded in reality in the same way that Resident Evil 1 was. Especially towards the end when the plots starts getting cartoonishly campy with you having to infiltrate the most evil-looking tower ever. It all screams classic Resident Evil and it plays like it knows all the ridiculous things in the previous games really happened and then running with it.

I think is the most authentic modern-retro game that I own.  Sadly, the term "retro" is thrown around much too often in the Steam store.  The term is sometimes used as a cover for bad graphics and simple gameplay.  Sometimes you have games that try to be "retro" but without understanding retro gaming and what made it great.  Take some sprite graphics, throw it into a half-decent platform engine, throw in some tough enemies, and whammo you have yourself a "retro" game – or do you?  Such games fail to grasp what made retro gaming great.  Difficulty was never the goal, it's more of a side effect that sometimes happens when you get the recipe right.  It takes some good level design, some unique and interesting enemies, good boss fights, and excellent controls.  Castle In The Darkness has all of these in spades.
Clearly the biggest influence here has been Castlevania, visually inspired by the 8bit games, controls inspired by the more fluid movements of SotN and the handheld games that succeeded it.  Even the name of the game is a nod to Castlevania.  The game is hard, yes, but fair.  The enemies are strong but consistent and predictable, you need to use reflexes but also strategy to survive.  The mood and tone of the game hits a balance somewhere between 8bit Castlevania and 8bit Link/Zelda.  The NPCs are spot-on and run the full gamut from helpful to cryptic, hilarious, or useless.  The controls are tight, the combat is fast but not frantic, the platforming skill needed is moderate for most of the game, though a few sections do require extreme precision.  You put all of this together and you have one of the most authentic retro gaming experiences on Steam right now.  You will die, you will die a lot, but you'll never get stuck for long in the same place, and when you beat that boss or hit that save point, you will feel a true sense of accomplishment that's often lacking from modern games.
I think this game would have fit right in on NES or SMS and I think it would have been well received at the time by critics and gamers alike.  Back in the NES days, I would have spent $6 just to rent a game like this for two nights, so to be able to buy it for that price, I think that's a great deal.

All of these Freddi Fush and other Humongous Entertainment are fantastic. All of their point and click adventures have great animation and large creative worlds to explore. You are Freddi Fish and your pal is Luther; your goal is to figure out why a sea monster is terrorizing coral cove park. You do this by pointing and clicking objects to solve puzzles and interact with characters until you gather enough information to solve the mystery.
I find there's a lot more visual humor than verbal in this Freddi Fish game; a lot of the jokes are told through pictures and character actions than said outloud. The puzzles themselves in this game seem simpler than in previous Humongous Entertainment games, a lot more straigthforward A to B puzzles where you have a very obvious keyhole and your goal is to find a key. While for me this made the game slightly less engaging, i found it made this freddi fish to be the best to introduce the series with. While the puzzles are simple, the world is still quite complicated. There's a lot of fun and quirky characters to meet, all well voice acted and offer some sort of interaction towards helping you save the day.
If you ever want to show a friend a great old school point and click, this is a good starting point.

Unless you liked Dark Souls, The Binding of Isaac, or Dead Space, do not buy this game (unless it is on sale).
Teleglitch is one-part Binding of Isaac, one part Dead Space. It is a top-down roguelike twin-stick shooter with a heavy emphasis on survival horror. The game prioritizes good aim, conserving resources, and as a consequence, knowing when to run. Its sound design is extremely minimalistic, but efficient; every enemy growl and the whine of background machinery instills fear and tension. The level design is not quite as solid: although each room and the enemies/resources within it are randomized every run, you will go through the same labeled rooms (like the Plankton Farm) and general environments every time. And you will go through them a lot; each death is permanent, meaning you will have to restart with 0 resources from the very beginning each time you bite the dust, which is frequent considering the enemies you must face.
The enemies are terrifying. Even though they have less resolution than a Nokia flipphone camera photo, the sound design coupled with their relentless assault patterns will have you looking over your 2D shoulder. The weapons are also extremely sound. Anything that isn't the default knife is a godsend, and the stopping power each weapon packs (even the pistol) is intensely satisfying. The crafting system is simple but effective. Whenever you have craftable items in your inventory, simply select one and press C to see what you can combine. Then select your desired combinations and craft. It sounds simple enough, but the sheer variety of craftable objects lends the game an extra strategic element.
Overall, the game is not for the faint of heart nor those uninterested in roguelikes, twin-stick shooters, or survival horror. But if you have a solid constitution and/or like at least one of those genres, Teleglitch is a thrilling, intense, terrifying, and rewarding twin-stick shooter.

For those whom are sick of Hearthstone's stagnant metagames, this is a refreshing change of pace. Sure, there's going to be waifus and anime galore in terms of artstyle and general feel for those whom aren't a fan of the artstyle, but fundamentally this plays fairly similar to Hearthstone save for some critical differences that add a bit more of a pleasant touch to this game.
While you have your typical keywords like Ward (Taunt), Last Rites (Deathrattle), Fanfare (Battlecry), and Storm (Hearthstone Charge), along with Rush (Charge but only against enemy creatures instead of face), there's a few key differences in mechanics. The first and biggest change is the Evolution system. Starting at turn 4 for second player (Turn 5 for first) you can Evolve a creature on the board to give it a stats boost as well as Rush along with playing something out from hand, and a number of creatures have special attributes or functionalities to accompany it. It feels really good to be able to make a good board swing to come back from behind, but keep in mind that the enemy can do something similar as well. Board control is the name of the game for most archetypes, and Evolution certainly helps sell that point save for a few class specifics. You also have a 40-card deck for the majority of play (Take-Two/Arena works off 30 cards), and you can have up to 3 of any card including legendaries compared to 2-pieced like Hearthstone.
Classes in this game are quite specialized in contrast to a game like Hearthstone. For example, Forestcraft is reliant on a Combo system for cards played and generating 1/1 tokens to use as buffers. Swordcraft is somewhat zoo-oriented with several tokens on the board and two tribes that buff one another called Officer and Commander. Runecraft is spell-heavy and involves boosting other spells or creatures by casting more (For example, the card Wind Boost deals one damage more to enemy creatures per spell that's been cast while it's in hand). Bloodcraft is all about dealing damage both to your enemy and yourself, with several boosts to class cards when you are at half-life or lower to play out that razor's edge of mortality. Dragoncraft is both a ramp class or a discard class depending on if you seek heavy stat value or a killer finisher. Havencraft revolves around hard control and countdown-cards that have you pay via time rather than mana costs (For example, Tribunal of Good and Evil destroys a creature when it first comes down, ticks for two turns while still on the board, then destroys a creature again before disappearing for just one mana payment). Shadowcraft revolves around Last Rites, forcing a Morton's Fork-typed scenario where killing their creatures can make the situation even worse for the enemy unless they can deal with the tricks.
The developers are actually quite generous, surprisingly so considering how most card games operate. You immediately can start with 5 packs of 10 cards apiece from every expansion, as well as a campaign mode that lets you earn exclusive cards as well as crafting materials (Liquid). Pair that with daily bonuses that ramp up over time, and you can quickly amass plenty of cards and ingame funding for more without paying anything at all.
However, while this all sounds good, there are some key things to mention. First of all, it's rare to have a game of Shadowverse go on longer than about 10-15 minutes or turns each. This is in part to a combination of mobile-game design for being played on the go, as well as powerful finishers in cards. Life totals are lower than what you would expect from Hearthstone, and the endgame finishers can be very surprising with their burst amounts or other trickery (Think Quest Mage, but imagine getting multiple of the quest reward and Arcane Giants). While second player gets one more Evolution point than the first player, as well as being able to use it first on turn 4 instead of 5, it's difficult to deal with an early curve if the first player has a 1-drop followed by a 2-drop and so on since there is no Coin equivelant here. There's also a little bit of power creep as well (Shadowcraft's Eachtar is a good example of this), but the metagame does shift every three months or so with expansions causing several lineup changes.
Still, if you enjoy online card games, this is quite a pleasant surprise. I felt I constantly had more control over my wins and losses than in Hearthstone thanks in part to Evolution helping with the comeback swings to keep things fairly close, and it's easy for a free-to-play player to get off to a brisk jog. Keep in mind that with less classes to play comes more focus on deck archetypes rather than pure class variety. Honestly, give it a try for about an hour or two, see if it sticks after playing through the Solo Campaign. While I can't say I'm a fan of the story elements or whatever, it does a wonderful job of introducing mechanics and it's very easy to get adjusted to save for the keyword changes.
Overall, I'd say this game is an 8/10. There are some design choices I don't exactly approve entirely of (Eachtar, Dimensional Shift, Vagabond Frog are the three big ones off the top of my head), it's still quite an enjoyable experience and I will be certain to keep playing this for a while to come. Give it a try. Just beware the waifus.
