I love this game so much I decided to do my first review about it.
While there are many games out there that are difficult for the sake of being difficult, few of them find the balance of also being fun at the same time.  I've white-knuckled my way through many many sessions on this game, but I've never rage-quit on behalf of the insanity that eventually brought my demise.  Instead, Risk of Rain achieves that "just one more time" feeling and I've been coming back to it for years.
In the vein of some other modern roguelikes, this game maintains the "one and done" approach, but there are items and unlockables that carry over to your next playthrough.  Items are gathered throughout the game and (at least initially) are randomly generated.  This puts the emphasis on plowing forward instead of staring at menus and preparing your loadout.  Some may not like the lack of control this gives them, but as someone who spends way too much time in other RPGs trying to find that "perfect" build only to get crushed in the next dungeon, it is refreshing to just let the chips fall and roll with what the lords of RNG provide.
The action is non-stop and the difficulty ramp-up is steep, although once you get rolling 40 minutes can pass by in a fever-dream like state of flow.  The graphics are "pixel-art", yes, but unlike the trendy "indie scene" games that explicitly and shamelessly rip-off a style from a 8 or 16-bit game, Risk of Rain has its own unique aesthetic that heightens the atmosphere of the dank and dire storyline.
About the story, the game allows the narritave to develop through devices tied to gameplay instead of bashing you over the head with dialog or exposition.  For example, every item you unlock has a corresponding journal entry, and instead of just saying "this increases the jump height" it is written out as the main character would describe it in a research report.  There are also "monster logs" that you can collect that share this style of curious observation about the things encountered in the alien worlds.  This lets the story unravel in sync with the gameplay and provides a compelling reason to progress and solve the mysteries laid out before you.
In a time where "roguelike", "pixel-art", and "indie" have become tired buzzwords, Risk of Rain awakens the sense of excitement and wonder that these types of games should evoke.

I would classify this as a walking simulator designed for crafting game fans.
It has light skill-based RPG elements, using upgradeable skill trees to build everything from your stats (Tailoring) to occupation, and everything in between. Heck there's even upgradeable skills to allow stacking of resources.
Basically you're walking long trails that are broken up in camp locations through various environments gathering resources to craft with.
Each camp offers a quest to complete before reaching the next camp in order to earn skill points to apply to the character building skill trees.
You gather resources, hunt animals, chop trees along the trail to craft items to sell in the next camp or equip on your character. Items degrade pretty rapidly, so you're always replacing clothing and gear, while also gathering/crafting in order to sell items at the next camp.
There's also a large town to live in and well as player created towns that a player can live in, build a house and run a business out of.
The play style is very relaxed. Every camp being a save point, with walking from camp to camp or town only taking a few minutes, so it's very relaxed and casual.
It can be kind of grindy since items do degrade pretty fast and you may have fast travel back to a previous area in order to gather certain resources to craft with.
All in all, if you're a fan of relaxed, casual crafting games and like to have a wide variety of how they're played, this walking/crafting game would probably be something you'd want for your collection.
If you're easily bored of repetitive actions or need a lot of action and eye candy then I'd definitely watch a few Let's Plays to judge your interest in this.
Personally I'm enjoying the heck out of it.

Let's be honest, you've got no reason to listen to me. I'm not a big name or famous in any capacity, but I do hope you'll heed the message that this game is very special and can be very fun for a certain kind of player.
Castle in the Darkness is good. It has more references than you can shake a stick at that span from various iterations of Castlevania to the original Zelda for the NES, and many others that I won't get into just so you'll be pleasantly surprised when you stumble across them. That comes as the sugar coating to let you know it is also difficult, but not in the bad, frustrating kind of way that feels utterly unfair.
I, personally, am not very good at games, and especially not anything of Kaizo-level proportions, but Castle in the Darkness takes a step back from some of the other kind of trial and error, die until you win situations by making the game control very well even on a keyboard (My preferred method of gaming), and the mistakes that are made never feel as if they were caused by bad design. In fact, the game is designed extremely well in order to actually make things difficult without making them too punishing.
Save points start off separating every half dozen or so screens, give or take, but as the game advances they become more and more scarce and increase the level of punishment for mistakes made, which can be a bit of a drag, but again I feel the design of the game even allows the less-than-adequate among us, like myself, to come across victorious after a few tries, and completing game is definitely rewarding when you finally lean back and breathe a sigh of relief.
I'm not going to be giving any kind of arbitrary scoring system, but I will say that this game is full of homages to games of the past, it is designed extremely well in a simplistic package that can be deceiving to some, and offers a great kind of sidescrolling, metroidvania experience that, for six dollars at full price, is definitely something I'm glad I picked up when I saw it.
Buy, download, die repeatedly, and enjoy every second of it.

Not sure where to start with this review so let's start with the basics. Do I think Batman Arkham Knight is a good game? Yes. Did I enjoy playing through it? No, not really.
So now the explanation:
I loved Arkham Asylum and City (haven't played Origins) so I thought this would follow suit with a deep interesting story matching it's intuitive, simple but rewarding controls. Matching great cut scenes with fun and varied gameplay mechanics. Binding moments of humour with...... well you get my point.
Control wise it hits the nail on the head. Fast fluid movement from one thug to another, countering multiple attacks at the same time and that slow motion last hit signifying the end of the battle. The ability to use gadgets throughout the fight means you can play with enemies for your own amusement. There is also a reasonable spread of enemy types meaning you have to consciously switch up tactics or die trying. It feels like a batman game regarding combat, and to me that's a good thing.
The Batmobile also offers some fun to be had, with the ability to change instantly into the errmm, Battank? You can tell Rocksteady liked their new toy as it is used very often, sometimes maybe a bit too often??? The handling is, as expected, very arcade like but it does the job.
Now we get to the part I was disappointed with, the story. I will try and stay away from spoilers as best I can. The story brings in a lot of the different characters Batman has faced over the years. This means there is a lot of story paths to go through and complete. I wonder how long it will be when we will be able to have another pixel-perfect, tough-as-nails platformer that isn't just a homage-fest. This game isn't it. I want to let it be known that before I wrote this review, I did in fact 100% everything in the game as far as percentage and achievements go. So this isn't a case of a salty review. I wish to inform people what this game IS and what this game ISN'T:
What this game IS:
-More of the same. It has more in similarity with I wanna be the Guy then a game like Meat Boy for example. Right down to all the other video game references and ideas it shamelessly borrows from.  Even down to the trial and error methods of tackling levels.
What this game ISN'T:
-It is NOT a metroid vania. Not even loosely. Just because a game has powerups and backtracking does not make it a metroid-vania. It doesn't even have a MAP.
Most of the game, and I do mean the vast majority is backtracking. If you take nothing else from this review, understand my hatred of backtracking is absolutely immense. To add insult to injury, in a game where maneuvarability is paramount, your double jump ability is kept from you until around the first third of the game has passed. You will encounter a ton of areas that will require that double jump to uncover the secrets. That is probably the most laziest way to hinder progression. It shows not a lot of thought or care was put into actually creating a world worth exploring but instead wanted to pad the game as much as possible with backtracking. To make matters worse, the warp zones are put in the absolute worst positions, you will become lost for a good majority of the game, and al lthis does is add time to the clock but nothing is getting done. That is inexcusable for a game that came out in 2015.
and I know what you are going to say, "but Starman! Super Metroid is one of the best games ever with a similar grab the powerups to open new areas game, it had a lot of backtracking too!" Ok first off, Super Metroid was THE game that "metroid-vania" was based off and for good reason. You wanna know why it holds up to this day? It created interesting powerups. It created interesting beam combinations. It created an environment you wanted to explore. It had so many powerups and collectibles for it's time that it offered a much more fulfilling sense of accomplishment. It also didn't rely on cheap trial and error segments to pad the game for length.
"But, But castlevania! Symphony of the night! It was the -vania part of metroid! it did similar things!" Not even comparable. Castlevania: SOTN was more like Metroid, but built upon the idea with a huge array of secrets, weapons, spells, and other things. Also, NG+ allowed you to play as other characters and the like.
To even COMPARE this game to a metroid-vania is an absolute lie. Don't even. First third of game is playing crippled, the last 2/3's is backtracking and getting lost, and dying at segments where there are 4-5 screens before your next save point.
So, why did I play this game to completion? I clearly HATED the game right? No. I didn't hate the game.  The fact is, the game's core gameplay has proven itself to be rewarding, as most of these platformers tend to do. My issue is that the game took the lazy, cheap way out of dealing with things. It has no identity for itself. It's just some frankenstein monster of other game's great ideas hindered by lazy development and shoddy "HAY GAIZ, REMEMBER THIS FROM [this game]?"
I want new, unique titles. You can have your trial and error pixel perfect jumps. But stop trying to be every other game.
and if you really want to create a metroid-vania, CREATE, a genuine metroid-vania experience. Not this.

Before people start giving me crap for the negative review, I would like to say that these are opinions based solely on my own experience with the game.
, I'm just very disappointed in my experience with it. If anything, I want to like this game more than I actually do. With that said, onto the review.
TL;DR version: A pretty bland game with bland characters, a bland story and bland combat. It's not worth nearly 30€ for this. If you plan to get it, get it while it's at least 50% off.
I came into this game from Idea Factory's Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 and 2, expecting it to be a somewhat more serious but still a lighthearted JRPG. For the most part, I got that. However, as I dug deeper into the game, there were so many different things that got to me that didn't really make my experience any more enjoyable.
My first problem is with the characters. They're not all that interesting, good character development happens mostly for 3 characters only (out of a possible 14) and I found none of the characters to be anything special. For example, Fang is a selfish guy who just wants to live his life the way he wants but eventually has to mature up to be a hero-type, Tiara is a noble-like character who seems to have a fetish for being verbally degenerated (I'm not kidding, she seems to get these moments of euphoria every time she's called the b-word), Pippin is a walking talking cat pillow that's supposed to resemble something of a veteran noble or something... Then there's Harley...
. In short, none of the characters have anything that makes them especially interesting (other than a few small quirks), which makes them kind of bland in my eyes.
Without spoiling the game, the plot doesn't really hold water for me either. The objective is stated at the very start of the game: "Collect furies, revive the Goddess, you win". Pretty much towards the end of the game the objective stays the same, until some small changes happen here or there. The story itself isn't so bad that it's hateable, but when you're finished with the game you'll be left with several plot holes that you don't really get an answer to. In addition, not many moments really stuck with me as I progressed through the game. I guess the word that describes the plot is bland. In addition, there are some plot related things that left me with more questions than answers. Those would fall under spoilers, however, so I won't talk about them.
How about character levelling and combat? Well, coming from the HDN games, they're definitely different. The game uses a system called "Weapon Boost" to make your character better. Through combat you gain WP, which you will use to level up character stats as well as to learn skills, magic, abilities and new combo techniques. It's a rather simple system, but it might require the player to grind a bit to unlock some of the stuff he or she wants but overall, I like it. The combat still seems to come short of being interesting though. Comparing it to the HDN combat system, I feel it's easier to navigate menus and harder to make silly mistakes like cancelling your own turn because you accidentally pressed the cancel button twice when trying to leave the item menu. That's definitely improved, but at the same time the fighting itself is made slightly more boring than in the HDN games. Bosses and enemies no longer seem to heal themselves or their allies, which gives you less of a reason to prioritize different targets or strategize using more hard-hitting skills. Just gather enough adrenaline, put on your serious face, activate Fairize and whack the crap out of the boss and hope he doesn't deactivate your Fairize before you kill him. In the end, the experience left me with a rather bland taste in my mouth.
You might be noticing a pattern in my review. I keep using the word "bland" a lot, but that's about all I can say about this game. It's bland. Really bland. Coming in from HDN, I expected funny, quirky characters; I got boring, uninspired people I didn't much care for. I expected an enjoyable plot: I was left with more questions than answers. I expected a bland combat system to be remastered into something better; I got the same one with a few differences here and there. I want to like this game, but having experienced all of this just makes it very hard for me to call it a sufficiently enjoyable experience. Toward the end I just wanted the game to be over so I can move on to other games that I've wanted to play for a while now. Now that I've finished the game once already, I'll do just that. I'm definitely coming back to this later to play NewGame+ and hopefully get a different ending. And when that time comes, I hope I'll see the game in a new light and I might be able to rewrite this review and be more positive about the game itself.
But until that day, I'll stand by these words and say the game is, at the very least, not worth full price. If you have to get it, get it while it's on sale for at least 50%.

Killing Floor 1, was extremely well put together but each map had a 'spot' where you could force the game to balance in your favor. The 'spot' would have one point of entry, a beserker and a support specialist could win any match up to 'Hell on earth' without moving from the 'spot'(aside for ammo and armor).
What i like the most about this game is that there are no decernable 'spots' to exploit. I feel the map creaters took a lot of time to create openings for every class to rack up kills.
Classes:
They bought back all the classes and added more. The new classes are much more flexible than the older classes. The game needed this because many of the other classes are easily over run if certain zeds show up in mass. This brings a nice burst firepower while the other classes are reloading/recovering
Teamwork:
With the removal of 'spots' it now forces two general play styles.
1) divide and conquer: team breaks up into two groups, a group of 4 generally and a group of 2. they go to two defensable spots and reak havoc only coming together when hopelessly overwhelmed.
2) area denial: More popular but requires alot more coordination for success. find a more wide open area with 3-4 points of entry.
The bosses:
The Patriark is easier than Haans...
To beat the patriark you simply need to use your bodies to block his exit(when he runs to heal) and mag drop into him. if he does not get away he is easy to kill.
Haans...so annoying to kill, you just need to stay away from him and mag drop into him. but he runs faster than you, the gas slows you, and explosives rip through your armor. It just sucks.
Therefore, I recommend a Nerf of Haans and maybe a "teleport to run away" ability for the Patriark.

UPDATE: The latest patch reduced the enemy spawn rate by 40% in solo Hell on Earth games. While this makes the game easier, it doesn't fix the problems related to the spawn volumes. It seems that Tripwire hopes to reduce the chances of the RNG putting the player in unfair situations, but those situations still occur, and they still occur almost as frequently -- they're just easier to deal with now (one might argue too easy).
Hell on Earth didn't need to be easier. It needed to be made more logical and fair.
These issues break the flow of the game and cause confusion because they're illogical. Zeds are supposed to slowly and menacingly close in on the player. But rather than do this, it feels like they're defying physics and beaming down from spaceships. It ruins immersion and it can punish the player for mistakes they never made.
Lastly, Hans is still a tedious DPS race when in solo Hell on Earth. His shield health is still too high, and killing him requires abusing his AI. It's just not fun.
----
Killing Floor 1 was a flawed gem with many arbitrary and poorly implemented mechanics. Some of its problems included, but were not limited to: Infamously buggy medic darts, a weight system that slowed the player down depending on how much gear they were carrying (more on why this was, and still is, a bad idea later), headzones that would occasionally disappear and render headshots impossible, and bizarrely placed spawn volumes that would result in zeds appearing out of thin air behind the player.
But hoo boy, the guns were great! Recoil was high, the sound design was superb, and weapons felt used and rickety, like they could fall apart at any moment. This gave the guns personality and a feeling of authenticity, and every bullet felt meaty and satisfying.
Killing Floor 2 should have taken the excellent-feeling weapons, done away with the meaningless mechanics, and fixed the bugs. Add a fresh coat of paint, and it could have been one of the best shooters available. But sadly, Tripwire has recreated many of the first game's flaws and introduced a few new ones out of what seems like blind and misguided mimicry.
To the game's credit, the guns are still satisfying to use, with excellent sound design and game-feel. And some improvements have been made, like headshots and medic darts working perfectly now. But that's where the pros end.
Killing Floor 1's level design was spearheaded by Alex Quick, and some of the maps he created (such as West London) were wide open, with plenty of room to dodge clots and groups of enemies. This helped balance the game by making it easier for the player to avoid being grabbed -- if the player was grabbed, it was their own fault. That's good level design.
But Killing Floor 2's maps are narrow, and spawn volumes are placed at chokepoints so that zeds can easily clog up doors and block a kiting player, killing them unfairly with sheer numbers or HP. It feels like the level designers don't understand Alex Quick's original intentions or the flaws of the system that they inherited. This problem is made worse by the fact that spawns are more random and unpredictable than they were in Killing Floor 1; sometimes two clots appear, other times two sirens and a bloat, and other times four husks. It's frustrating to be kiting down a hallway, only to have two sirens and a scrake spawn and block the only exit. It's RNG, plain and simple, and that's lazy programming. It's also poor enemy placement. And that's arrogance.
When it comes to camping, enemies like albino crawlers, sirens, husks, scrakes, and fleshpounds can zone players by design and can spawn in unusually high numbers, forcing players to kite through no fault of their own. On top of this, players often have to camp on top of a spawn volume, not by choice, but because spawn volumes are everywhere. This creates an additional risk -- if the spawn volume is within view of the player, or the player is standing on top of it, zeds won't spawn. But if the player is pushed a little too far away from the spawn volume, and they have to turn away from it to shoot a zed, more zeds can spawn close behind them, and they can quickly be overrun. This makes solo games too stressful to be fun. Killing Floor 2 manages to discourage both camping and kiting because of poor level design and spawn volumes that are too numerous and too random.
Lastly, the weight system feels like a lame attempt at increasing the game's difficulty. The more weapons the player carries, the slower their run speed. But the effect is so subtle that the player is unlikely to notice it or consider its impact on the game, especially since it makes no difference on the lower difficulties. And when the player finally enters Hell on Earth, they die -- a lot -- and are left wondering why the zeds are so fast and why it seems impossible to kite them. The solution to this isn't to shoot better or even find a better kite path -- it's to carry fewer weapons when kiting. If the player does this, they can reliably outrun the zeds and reduce the difficulty of Hell on Earth substantially. There's a lack of conveyance that makes it all too deceptive; it feels like the game is trying to hide this mechanic from the player so that they die.
Killing Floor should be a game that challenges the player to shoot better, not a game that forces them to use gimmicks or pull up the maps in the SDK to figure out where the spawn volumes are and how to manage them. That's not the correct kind of learning curve. It's not fun. It's not challenging. It's just unintelligently designed, gimmicky, and random.

Tasty Planet is a simple, silly game where you play as an itty-bitty blob with eyes just as big as your ever-growing stomach.  You roam around varying eras of history eating anything smaller than you, growing a bit whenever you do.  Then you eat things a little bigger, and grow a little bigger, and eat things a little bigger, and grow a little bigger, and....well, you get the idea.
There are quite a few environments across the many stages, plus additional 'challenge' levels and gold/silver/bronze medals to obtain depending on how quickly you can grow your blob - so there is a decent amount of content and replayability to keep you going.  Additionally, short comic book 'cutscenes' tell the story of your blob as you progress through the game, which is a nice extra tidbit to break from the eat-eat-eat action, and provides a little incentive to keep playing through the story mode.
The graphics certainly won't astonish you, but are perfectly suitable for the casual action of the game.   The audio is much the same - there isn't a huge amount of variety, but the bouncy beats, gulping sounds, and agonized screams of poor widdle creatures as you finally grow large enough to eat them all fit remarkably well into the simple, mindless gameplay.
The only real negative to this game is a slightly awkward control scheme; You move your mouse to move the blob, which adds a unique challenge to the game, but can lead to some edge-of-mousepad annoyances.  Unfortunately, there is currently no gamepad support to make this easier.
All in all, everything about Tasty Plane fits perfectly into it's niche - a casual way to blow some time with uncomplicated, mindless fun.  It may not be a genre-defining game that will be remembered through the ages, but it definitely succeeds as a simple game with plenty of levels and extra challenges for (re)playability, providing quite a bit of fun for a rather small investment.

Castle in the Darkness is a throwback to "Nintendo hard" games from the NES/SNES era.  It's a basic action platformer where your basic goal is to defeat bosses, collect hidden gear and treasure, and eventually save the king.  It's not a one-of-a-kind game, but what it does it does very well.  You'll be faced with a handful of enemies that are basically a cakewalk, a couple instant death spiketraps, various other obstacles, and eventually an area boss.  The only catch is that if you die, you lose everything since the last time you activated a checkpoint.  Just got some treasure?  Run back to the checkpoint or risk moving forward and hoping for a new one.  Just found an item?  Better go to the checkpoint.  And the most beautiful situation of all:  Did you just beat a boss?  That's right, many bosses don't have checkpoints near them, and the level design is actually clever enough to function in a harder fashion on the way back to the checkpoint.  Nothing about the areas change, spawns are the same, layouts are the same, crumbling blocks respawn, but because of the way the areas are laid out, going backwards is often harder than the original progression towards treasure, gear, or bosses, and holding onto the spoils of victory makes the trek back even more nerve-wracking.  If you like hardcore NES titles, you'll love this game.  It has a NG+ if you really enjoyed the experience, and by the end of that, if you started really getting the hang of things, you can always go for the super secret item, which is acquired via the most intense of feats.
Oh, and if you don't like NES hard games, and you don't like being punished or carrying the weight of consequence, skip out on this one.

...

Power Creep: the devs have stated they want this card game to be very high-powered, but balance is still important. I feel they still have a few lessons to learn in regards to card design and balance, and I'm very curious to see what the game will look like in a few years.

Revelations 2 copies a copious amount of elements from other games, ending up with a predictable and linear, yet enjoyable third-person horror shooter, where the replay value comes from the grinding requirements in both the campaign and the looter side game.
Resident Evil: Revelations 2 tells a new side story to expand upon the franchise’s universe, this time bringing back two old-time protagonists, Claire Redfield and Barry Burton. They share a unique setting, where all four separately purchased episodes divide into a Claire chapter and a Barry chapter, with different enemy compositions, but often sharing stages.
Old-time RE gamers will probably recognise that both stories are copy-pasted: Claire’s is from Code Veronica (she ends up with a sassy teenage sidekick on a prison island run by a crazy Umbrella employee), and Barry’s is from Gaiden (he escorts a little girl with psychic powers that allow her to sense enemies).
Luckily, the game mechanics show more innovation. The campaign uses co-op mechanics, where only one player gets guns, whereas the other can stun enemies, open locks, and find consumables. This all falls apart in single-player though, since the non-controlled character usually just stands idly, turning fights into frantic character switches for sheer survival.
Grinding is an integral part of RER2, even in the campaign, where unlocking every possible skill and medal requires at least six full runs (although replaying the entire campaign takes less than 90 minutes).
It is even more prevalent in Raid mode, the looter side game returning from RER1, since all skills and all characters level separately, and weapon parts act more like consumables. It is a matter of taste if players prefer this or the more streamlined approach of RER1 Raid—especially if we consider that RER2 Raid levels are mostly tiny reused RE6 stages—but it is undeniable that this game mode feels rewarding and fun, even in the long run.

The game is set into 4 main chapters, in 2 story lines running 6 months between eachother. Barry is in the future, and the girls are in the past. Gameplay plays pretty well, and doesn't seem to have any issues with how it functions. The problem I had the most with the game, was the fact that is had lots of dark atmostpere, but never changed much. UPDATE (8/14/2017): I actually beat this game a while back, and I forgot to update my review upon completing the game, and now that I've beaten the game I can guarantee that I don't recommend it. I just recently started playing the game again, and I've been able to notice all sorts of silly design choices (mistakes in my opinion) that completely ruin the game for me.
1.) TRICKY JUMP ARCS
The jump arcs seem fast and parabolic. Yes, this models real life, but if you look at any good platformer the jump arc is usually either somewhat slow for the ascent or somewhat slow for the descent. This is to allow the player better precision in controlling jump height and landing point, respectively. This game doesn't have that, so any occurrence of the insta-kill spikes becomes a chore and a heavy risk because the mechanics have been designed against the player, and due the the nature of the game's save points, it ends up becoming extremely punishing for no reason whatsoever. He could've done both and that would've suited the game well. The jumps may have felt floaty, but that's not necessarily a bad thing for game design. Super Mario had pretty floaty jumps, and that was so the play could maneuver the game without having an aneurism. Imagine Mario if you could only jump as high as Mario and you only had half a second until Mario returns to the ground -- that's what the jumping mechanics feel like for this game.
2.) UNFORGIVINGLY POOR LEVEL DESIGN
The later levels of the game are more designed for forward progression than back-tracking. This is fine -- the original Castlevania games made some of the same design choices -- but the problem is that it's a Metroidvania game, and so it's expected to be sensibly traversible in both directions rather than just one. This game has many places where the insta-kill spikes were place decently for forward progression for a nice challenge, but coming back they just become an extra annoyance that can have pretty grand punishments as described above ( I had many occasions where they would kill me after a boss and I'd have to fight the boss all over again ).
3.) POOR BOSS DESIGN
The boss fights felt more focused on "How well can you not get hit?" Now don't get me wrong, avoidance of attacks is part of designing a boss fight, but two hits shouldn't be all it takes for a boss to kill you in my opinion. To me, that begins to limit the creativity of most of the boss fights because you can basically figure out upon entering the room how to kill the boss. The reason being is that the designer needs to convey to you how the boss takes damage so you don't die 20 times just figuring out what you need to do to damage the boss.
My point is that it leads to pretty uninteresting boss fights that are only difficult because they were designed to be able to figure out within seconds so you only have to spend one life trying to figure out how to kill a boss. This is probably what led to my problem with the fish boss on which I had to use the thunder orb thing. Because I was so used to the previous bosses being as simple as "Here's an obviousing hitting spot. Avoid all the other stuff," I tried using that tactic on the boss, only to figure out it's completely infeasible. My problem is that the bosses should've have felt so bland and uninteresting in design that I felt like it was sensible to assume they could all be defeated in the same basic way.
4.) TRITE NARRATIVE
The narrative was pretty generic and it's pretty easy to tell it wasn't the focus of the game, but nevertheless I'm a fan of games at least having an engaging narrative if not a meaningful one. That would especially let me feel more motivated to play through the game if I actually felt compelled by the narrative. For example, in this game I barely care about the princess or her dad because there's nothing for me to care about either or them as characters other than the fact that they're royalty and the princess is trying to save her dad because she loves him. It didn't compell me to put up with the rest of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of the game and emerge the hero, which I thought would be the aim of what it was trying to do. Instead, I was just bombarded with bits and pieces of dialogue that I barely cared about throughout the game (granted, they're pretty short and far between).
PROS:
On the other hand, there were some good aspects about the game that I enjoyed somewhat.
1.) AESTHETICS:
The game had some excellent pixel artwork throughout most of the game, and it had a nice cartoony style throughout a lot of the game, and much in the style of an NES game you can tell the designer limited himself to a pretty selective palette for most parts of the game, but without the restrictions of an 8-bit processor. So he does well it incorporate a vivid set of few colors to make levels that feel like they have a cohesive atmosphere. For example, Alexandria had a lot of blue, brown, white, and black, which I felt was a nice palette for an introductory level in a nighttime city. The lighter shades of color kind of gave a feeling a optimism and gallantry, but oh boy was the hope about to fade -- especially when you hit the jump and attack buttons for the first time.
2.) AUDIO:
The sound effects and music were quite good -- especially the music. I didn't much care for the music in Alexandria, though. It sounded extremely repetitive in my opinion -- like an "8-bit" version of the intrumentals for the pre-chorus and chorus for a generic power-metal song. A lot of the other songs I very much liked, though. The sound effects also all fit their respective usages pretty well, so I think that was another decent design choice.
FINAL OUTCOME:
If I were to give this game a rating like a jackass, I'd give it a 3/10. It's certainly not the worst I've played, but I think it sucks. It feels more like a chore to play at this point than a genuinely fun experience -- and for me that's the mark of a bad game.

Revelations 1 was my first game in the Resident Evil series, and after completing Resident Evil 1, 4, 5 and 6 I finally decided to go back and finish Revelations 2 - and I was not disappointed.
The first half of the story revolves around Claire Redfield and Moira Burton who are kidnapped and sent to an island full of crazy people (and monsters) as part of a fear experiment, with a woman who calls herself The Overseer monitoring their every move.
In the second half Barry Burton arrives at the island six months later in search of his daughter Moira, teaming up with the mysterious, young girl Natalia who seems to have some sort of connection to the island and the monsters on it.
When playing as Claire or Barry the game plays out fairly similarly to the first game. You use your knife, guns and bombs (crafted using bottles and various supplies) to get to where you're going while fighting off the bad guys. In some parts you can choose to take a more stealthy approach, which lets you save your ammunition and herbs. As in most Resident Evil games managing your resources is very important, especially on the harder difficulties.
Unlike the first game the "partner characters" have their own role in this game. Moira is in charge of the flashlight and the crowbar, while Natalia has her "enemy detection" and brick. Yes, she uses a brick, and it's actually quite effective. They use their flashlight/senses to find hidden items all over the map, which can come in handy when you're running low on resources.
In addition to the standard story mode you have a countdown mode, invisible mode, DLC bonus stories and raid mode:
-
: In countdown mode you are on a timer, and have to finish the levels as fast as possible. You get extra time for breaking hourglasses across the map as well as killing enemies. For someone like me who usually kills everything and examines everything from top to bottom, having to rush through the levels as fast as I could was a nice change.
-
: All enemies are invisible. This mode was included in some of the other Resident Evil games as well, however in this game you can actually see the enemies briefly using Moira and Natalia, which makes it a bit easier to kill them when switching over to Claire or Barry.
-
/
: The DLC bonus stories were nothing special, however they do give you more information on Moira and Natalia, so it's worth playing through them at least once.
-
: After having gotten sick of raid mode in Revelations 1 I did not think I would enjoy raid mode in Revelations 2. I was wrong. The enemies keep coming, and you have to kill them all to gain gold/xp, upgrading your characters and weapons between stages. Many of the enemies and areas from the previous games such as Revelations 1, Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6 also pop up, which was great.
My expectations for Revelations 2 were very high, and although I did enjoy the game a lot, there were some things that I felt could have been improved. The story, characters and atmosphere were not as good as in Revelations 1, and the game also felt a bit shorter. That said, Revelations 2 is still a great game, and raid mode as well as countdown mode and invisible mode were all great. As someone who cares about achievements, the game was far less grindy than some of the other Resident Evil games, which was also a plus.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game.

Dying Light is an incredible game. Although extremely similar to Dead Island, it’s a more perfected version of the zombie slashing series. I feel that the added parkour and dynamic day/night cycle is what gives Dying Light a unique edge not only from Dead Island, but from all games out there.
Debuting the new Chrome Engine 6, I was seriously impressed with the graphical fidelity of the game. The various weather patterns, lighting, and the overall quality of effects (explosions, decapitation etc), made me feel like I was finally playing a next gen game. You can tell that the game was built around the fluid parkour movement system, but at the same time they managed to create a believable world with realistic design.
One of the most impressive aspects of Dying Light is how relevant I found the upgrade system. Every skill felt like it had meaning and wasn’t just there as an option. I found myself using almost all the skills in normal combat throughout the 50 hour or so campaign. Techland advertised a 50 hour campaign and I can safely agree with them. It took me 50 hours to complete every quest solo, and complete several random encounters, and challenges (not all of them though).
As great as I found this game, there were some balance issues for me. The night sequences are supposed to challenge you against faster zombies, but I found myself either avoiding or escaping them all too easily. Towards the end of the game I was straight up hunting them down. Repairing weapons uses metal parts which are ridiculously common. The grappling hook made free-running obsolete and made the night sequences even more trivial. Be The Zombie mode is just a glorified version of Left 4 Dead’s asymmetrical multiplayer. In other words, nothing special with little reason to play it over the standard co-op. This will appeal to some people, but it really didn’t seem special to me. The Old Town level should have been the modern metropolis setting we get to see in the distance from the Slums level. It felt like an entirely different country instead of being consistent with the Slums level.
Overall, you are definitely getting your money’s worth with Dying Light. Despite those few issues, there is plenty to do and plenty to keep you playing for days to come.

Had fun playing it, was long but didn't drag out, story missions were a little weak, but everything else makes up for it.
Game play is good, parkour can be alittle hard to get used to at first, but once you do, you'll notice it missing in other games. Melee combat is good, doesn't get out of hand like in Dead Rising, and even when your at full power(max levels) you can still be overwhelmed by the zombies if not careful.
Had a nice variety of melee weapons, but didn't like escalation of melee weapon damage, making some of your favorite weapons obsolete, and alot of the weapon craft recipes obsolete also. Probably could of done it another way, but it's not a deal breaker. The variety of grenades would of been nice if at least half of them were effective, but the ones that work, really work, while the others were just wasted resources. Another thing about melee combat: why can't you parry like the human NPC's can?
Gun combat was probably the weakest part of the game, variety of firearms sucks, and the ones you do get generally don't get used much because of the noise they generate. No Suppressors for firearms. Minor spoiler, later in the game you run into someone who should be able to make them, but nope. You can craft all kinds of weird stuff, but no suppressors. There were a few times your pretty much forced to use firearms, and when you do, they just don't "feel" right. They do work though, you just won't be using them much.
Day/night cycle was great. During the day, you scavenge, get stuff done. There is danger, but for the most part you can get into and out of trouble without dying(going to want to concentrate on building up agility at first, mobility is the key to survival). Night, well, it's been awhile since a game has made me nervous. Nighttime in this game is deadly. Other types of zombies come out to play, and even at the later levels its pretty easy to get killed. Unless you play with the gamma up, it's DARK. You eventually do get some night vision, but when you do venture out at night, you need a plan. It helps greatly to get familiar with your surroundings, the closest safe house, and the path there.
Variety of enemies is mixed. Human enemies come in the have guns and don't have guns variety. They can be a pain to fight, though you will figure out a few tactics that make them easy to kill. Nice variety of zombies, most are the slow kind, but even that can be deceptive because some of them are as quiet as the grave and can sneak up on you if your not paying attention. There are some fast ones, some tough ones, and then there are the ones at night who are fast, tough, and generally unkillable until later in the game. Even then, they like to call for help, so again, night combat is hit and run.
There are a small variety of activities that can give you something to do, and alot of them will at least help you level up, if not give you weapon upgrades and recipes. Don't let the story rush you, far as I can tell there is no time limit. The story  missions...meh. Some were good, but I really hated how they forced you into situations. They will take control of the clock, so even if you started in the morning, you could wind up out at night. Or gear is taken away from you(they at least give you the option of getting it back, but it only made sense once). And the end fight is anticlimatic at best. Still, not deal breaker,
The game world itself is nice. Graphics look good, and the world itself shows that they put effort into this. Nice variety of locations, and even traveling from one end of the map to the other didn't feel like a chore most times. Exploring would yield rewards much of the time, and there are all kinds of out of the way or almost hidden places. You can jump or climb to almost any place, though some places did take alittle thinking to get to. Another thing, heights. I hate heights. I actually got a bit of vertigo climbing some of the towers.
All in all, I loved playing this game. Room for improvement, sure. But this is one of the best games I've played in a long while.

One of the most original games of recent years. I would never have guessed that a developer company would some day release an FPS game where the emphasis would be on running, sliding, jumping, vaulting, rolling, crouching and all this done on the rooftops of skyscrapers. These are the movements your protagonist, Faith, uses whenever she is faced with an obstacle.
The game is an unstoppable roller coaster ride. All the movements you do you do while running. And to make it more exciting the game does not want you to stop - your "vision" enables you to see certain objects, ramps, ledges and pipes highlighted in red so you know you can interact with these objects and you do not need to stop to look for clues. Later on as the game gets gradually more difficult this assistance is reduced and you can even turn it off completely so that the game can offer you the ultimate challenge.
Enemies can be taken down with melee combat but most of the time you need to run. Those that have weapons can easily eliminate you. Interestingly, you can knock out some of these police officers and pick up their weapons. Bear in mind that the ammo is limited so once your magazine is empty you should get rid of your firearm. But with weapons you want to aim like in a true FPS game, right? So, using a firearm will break the pace here, therefore, it's best to just skip this opportunity and run all the way till the game ends.
And pretty much that is the only problem with Mirror's Edge. You run fast and you reach the end fast. They could have included some extra chapters to make the game longer. You have time trial challenges so that you can keep playing stages over and over again improving your total time for completion.  I really wish, however, if there was a sequel to this game as it was such an exciting ride. It would be really nice to be a courier again in the new era of next-gen games.

For those of you familliar with rebinding keys in the days of PPSSPP/PCSX2 and/or playing ports like DMC3SE on PC with just a keyboard, rest assured - you'll feel right at home with this game.
For those unwilling to re-map their brains to memorize that left shift is L1 and spacebar is R1 and so on, for your own sanity, stay away. Stay FAR away from ANY game that was ported from a non-PC platform to PC. Also, stay away the ported game's guides/walkthroughs/tutorials, because they're all gonna probably be referencing the controller keys instead of the keyboard keys too.
CAPCOM did it this way with DMC3SE LONG ago and nobody complained - in fact, back in those days many of the crazy-fast combo maniacs that you often see in youtube dmc3 videos used keyboards and not controllers of any sort, simply because it was relatively easier to jump cancel in quick succession with a keyboard than with a controller.
Seriously, I don't see what the big deal is that could come from just taking 10 minutes to learn to set-up keyboard controls to mimic a controller, and THEN learning to memorize your own keyboard setup. All this 'controls learning' is a moot point if you already own an xbox/ps controller though.
All that being said, I do NOT recommend you start playing WITHOUT first rebinding the keys to something that feels natural for you relative to a controller layout (I rebound only 4 keys in total to feel like old dmc3 controls, and also having Q,E,F,R as default camera controls is just a bonus in my opinion, because in DMC3 I don't recall being able to rebind camera controls away from the arrow keys).
Oh and before I forget, those of you complaining about the lack of mouse controls - where would you put the 4 attack/dodge functions tied to the keys for your right hand onto the mouse?
Sure, you could put dodge somewhere on the left hand (say.. Z key) and then you're left with the 3 attack functions - just nice for 3 mouse keys/clicks right? Wrong.
As a naginata/gauntlet user you end up having to spam your middle mouse button for your Special Attacks(circle key on PS4) - I'd instantly switch back to the keyboard just because of this.
Yes, games like Vindictus did it, but they didn't have a 3rd attack key. There were only L and R combos (left click and right click).
Indie game devs like the Japanese folks at Zenith Blue had the right idea - look at their Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae game.
In summary, lack of mouse functionality is less a technical 'problem' and more of a game design constraint:
Would you rather have 2 attack buttons (with combo variations limited by 2 keys) and precise camera controls with a mouse? (i.e. like Vindictus)
OR would you rather have 3 (or more) attack buttons (with a LOT more combo variations/combat scenarios) on the keyboard and 4 keys controlling camera movement (with adjustable speed)?
If you prefer stuff like Vindictus, then play Vindictus.. or wait for games like Black Desert Online.
Please note that Toukiden Kiwami on PC has a hard framerate cap of 30 frames per second; hardcoded framerate == if you were to increase it, you end up hastening the game's physics cycles (i.e. time itself goes faster).
My opinion on the framerate cap is this - I can see it, I know it's bad/ugly, but I don't care; the game still responds quickly to my input regardless of the FPS cap and I'm able to time my dodges and parries with the same accuracy as what games like DMC4SE and DMC3SE has allowed me (look up DMC royal guard just guards and just releases, this is what you will do with the naginata and hammer counter-attack in Toukiden Kiwami - hint: that's your square+x attack).
In short, the game is framerate capped, but still responds instantly to your input regardless. If it doesn't your PC probably isn't beast enough to play this stuff.
I personally didn't get a single problem from the start of playing this game. Mind you I'm on Win7x64 running an i7 4790K along with a GTX 760 card running on 350.12 drivers (these drivers were released for GTA V), so your mileage may vary.
Now, with all that technical jazz aside, I can start talking about how much I love this game compared to the standard Monster Hunter games that came before this.
*Note: If you like the last 4 points, then good for you - stick with Monster Hunter.
Since I take no issue with the controls or the 30FPS cap 'port problems', I'd have to recommend this game, but ONLY if you're filthy rich (or single) and can afford a 50 USD hit to your wallet.
Otherwise, wait for summer/christmas sales or some random weekend or Koei Tecmo sale (good luck with that - it took quite awhile for Dynasty Warriors 8 Xtreme Legends to go on sale that's more than -33%, lol).
Happy hunting!

FTL was one of the early Kickstarter successes, and I couldn't be happier that it was. In the simplest of terms, FTL is a roguelike in space, where you control a whole ship and it's crew, rather than a single character. There is some loot in the form of upgrades and new crew members, and some leveling to be done. If that sounds minimal, it's because on paper it is. The real strength of FTL is how fantastically fun it is to play. Every mistake and death won't draw rage, but rather motivate you to jump right back in, swearing you've learned and can do better. Even if you "beat" the game, all the possible situations you can run into (randomly) will keep you playing time and time again. FTL's parts may be modest, but their sum truly is a treat.

This one of the best first person shooter games I've ever played, plain and simple.
Half Life 2 begins 20 years after the original Half Life. As Gordon Freeman awakens from stasis he finds himself on a train heading to City 17 which is overrun by the combine. You find yourself as the leader of the resistance and you must take down the Combine.
Half Life 2 is at this point one of the best received games and I'm sure pretty much everyone has played it. If not well what the hell are you doing reading this review ? You need to go buy this game straight away and play it right now.
The game is a simple first person shooter, but it does plenty things different than the regular first person shooters. You have a health bar and you have to do platforming to solve some of the puzzles.  Not to mention the source engine physics are absolutely insane.
For a game that came out back in 2004 it still looks amazing. Now while it does have so low res textures it's still looks breath taking, like in the final chapters.
The game for the most part is pretty easy. I played through the game without a problem, even though some segments were tough due to the fast movement you have to pull off to avoid gunfire. Not to mention the Strider battles are incredibly intense and quite difficult.
The game took me 10 hours to finish. I felt this was the perfect amount of time for the price I paid for it and this was worth every single penny.
Apart from the single playthrough there's not much replay value. The only reason to replay it twice is to look for the G-Man Easter eggs.
In the end Half Life 2 is a fantastic game. It's a must own for everyone who is a gamer. This game is a piece of history and without a doubt one of the best games I have ever played in my entire life.
I experienced zero problems while playing the game. I ran the game on ultra settings 60 FPS the entire time of playing. This game runs really well and should run on pretty much all systems.
Final Rating:
9.5/10 -  A Must own and must play

I really enjoyed LMSH. This was my first Lego game, but apparently they all share similar core gameplay concepts featuring button mashing combat (a la Double Dragon) where your characters can never die and very simple puzzles that require you to use your characters' special abilities to progress through levels (e.g., use the Hulk to smash through a brick wall). The combat does get repetitive, but the game looks great, the cutscenes and level composition are fantastic, and the heroes are fun to play around with.  I particularly liked flying around as iron Man and swinging around as Spider Man.
The game includes a large, open-world version of New York that you can explore between missions (the main missions take place in closed areas like a prison and Asgard, and when you complete one you can choose to go on to the next mission right away, or to spend some time in the open world for a while). The open world contains small quests and puzzles that give you collectible items and character and vehicle unlocks. Jetting or swinging around NYC is great. Smashing through it as the Hulk is also fun. And trying out the various lego cars, cycles, planes, helicopters and boats is fun.
Although the game advertises that it has 150 unlockable heroes and villains, there are only 10-20 core abilities shared between all those characters (flying, levitating, web-swinging, ranged attacks, invisibility, etc). So a lot of the unlockable characters are just reskins or remixes of characters you already have. I didn't really mind this for unlocks that had their own animations, like Sandman (when he runs it looks like he's surfing on sand, when he hits people he grows huge sand fists). But it was disappointing to spend lots of hard-earned, in-game money just to unlock someone who offered nothing new. Eventually I got bored of working to earn money to unlock new characters.

As someone who does not write reviews. This is worth reviewing.
Map design:
Killing Floor 1, was extremely well put together but each map had a 'spot' where you could force the game to balance in your favor. The 'spot' would have one point of entry, a beserker and a support specialist could win any match up to 'Hell on earth' without moving from the 'spot'(aside for ammo and armor).
What i like the most about this game is that there are no decernable 'spots' to exploit. I feel the map creaters took a lot of time to create openings for every class to rack up kills.
Classes:
They bought back all the classes and added more. The new classes are much more flexible than the older classes. The game needed this because many of the other classes are easily over run if certain zeds show up in mass. This brings a nice burst firepower while the other classes are reloading/recovering
Teamwork:
With the removal of 'spots' it now forces two general play styles.
1) divide and conquer: team breaks up into two groups, a group of 4 generally and a group of 2. they go to two defensable spots and reak havoc only coming together when hopelessly overwhelmed.
2) area denial: More popular but requires alot more coordination for success. find a more wide open area with 3-4 points of entry.
The bosses:
The Patriark is easier than Haans...
To beat the patriark you simply need to use your bodies to block his exit(when he runs to heal) and mag drop into him. if he does not get away he is easy to kill.
Haans...so annoying to kill, you just need to stay away from him and mag drop into him. but he runs faster than you, the gas slows you, and explosives rip through your armor. It just sucks.
Therefore, I recommend a Nerf of Haans and maybe a "teleport to run away" ability for the Patriark.

It took me two hours in two sittings to finish this game. It has a story which can easily be skipped, even though clues can be found in the pieces we get throughout the game. The book helps keep track of the current mission but never shows where you should go. I had to use the hint-gem too often to not have to click around and not being able to find that one room where I am supposed to find one small item to be able to move forward.
There were a lot of small puzzles, many which I truly enjoyed. Some felt original (no idea if they were) and some were classics like Memory. Sometimes I needed to combine items to create one item needed to move forward and it felt like it was just to drag out the gameplay. I stood at one end of the map and needed to go all the way back to the beginning. I managed to get through by stopping in every room before going back to where I was. This happened a lot towards the end.
During the small minigames of searching for objects it was fairly easy to just click around the screen. This made the minigames too fast and smooth which eventually was all I wanted since I came back over and over to the same scenes to pick up the same objects. Some objects on the list stood out and did not melt into the background properly which made it too easy to find. Many of these searching games were only to find an item needed to put together a bigger item which could then be used to move forward in the story. It felt forced and I sighed a lot when I discovered I needed to do another one of those. Even though the game is basically all about the searching minigames I think it could have been fewer of those in the same area with the same objects.
The hand-drawn backgrounds were gorgeous. I spent some time just looking at them when entering them for the first time. Really skilled work and it looked great on the screen. Impressed! The soundtrack was also relaxing and never felt repetitive.
The story was not very interesting. It had potential but was not executed to its fullest. It was simple and straight forward, but nothing surprised me and the ending was unsatisfying. I do not recommend this to impatient players, but if you are looking for something slow and easy this might be for you.

This is a top down rogue-like (sort of, explain later ) "DOOM" game.
As a employee of a military space operation, you are trapped with no chance of rescue in sight.  From the start of the game, players will guide this character out guns blazing since dying of hunger is the last thing that he wants to do.
The general consesus is to scavenge for materials, crafting ammo, modding weapons and make due by either running or killing everything. Choice is yours.
...
Although I would recommend this game, there are reasons why. For one, be aware that it's not as "rogue-like" as it appears.  Yes, the environments change but after doing some digging around the files. There's a CSV file that presets all of the items and monster amounts that are there.
It's makes me kind of sad because players are going to have a great chance of making the same decision with a potential set of outcomes -- whether it be saving to craft for better weapons or dealing with different monsters.
Another point of contention is running. Running is NOT a viable option.  Once monsters have found you, they will chase you through countless doors even after line of sight has been broken a long time ago.  There's very little ammo in comparison to the monsters that you do face that you pretty much have to knife ALL of the lesser threats to conserve for the more dangerous threats.
But all in all, because of the files that you can configure, you can mod it to your liking.
There are some recommendations on how to modify the amounts that make it more interesting and plethora of more monsters to keep you on your toes.
I simply don't recommend to play it vanilla.

All right, so I've been playing this game for quite a bit and I think it's time to write my review on it.
Shadowverse is similar to hearthstone in many ways, but there's some significant differences too.
- the art style is japanese and therefore like anime and manga
- you can evolve cards during a match, which makes that evolved card more powerful and/or activates an effect which can affect the course of the game.
- in Hearthstone your leader has 30 health, in Shadowverse 20
- There's a story mode which you should play before starting to play online, because it teaches you how to play and other useful stuff, and you also gain in-game money and take two tickets by playing it
- Shadowverse gives you free packs of cards pretty often (sometimes after maintance breaks and when new update is released)
My opinion of this game is positive, firstly because I really like watching anime and reading manga, and secondly because Shadowverse isn't so pay to win like Hearthstone is. In Shadowverse you have 3 missions and when you complete those missions, they update after 24h AND you get a prize every day you login, so that's nice.
The only negative things I've found in this game are bugs, like when the enemy disconnects, but you stay in the match and you have to log out and the game says that you lost the game because of disconnecting, but that has happened only a few times, so I don't find that as a big problem.
I recommend this game if you like Hearthstone but think that it's too pay to win. Also english isn't my first language so forgive me if I messed up something.

Shadowrun Returns is a science fantasy turn based tactical role-playing game developed and self-published by Harebrained Schemes. It takes place in the Shadowrun campaign setting from the science fantasy tabletop role-playing game. This is the first in the line of games that Harebrained Schemes done for Shadowrun.
If you liked the Pencil and Paper RPGs  (Shadowrun, Cyberpunk 2020, Gurps Cyberpunk), cyberpunk themed games and playing turn-based single player campaign games, you might love this game.
It has a game editor for making new missions that the community been using to improve it with and to extend the life of the game. Go through the Workshop and subscribe to the large selection of community made campaigns. It comes with the HBS campaign called The Dead Man's Switch.
You play a character that can hire others to his team and do a mission.  You control the actions of each member of the team. While gameplay is mostly linear, some small amount of exploration is possible while completing objectives. The player can enter into dialogue with various characters, with different statistics and skills giving new dialogue options.

I played this game up to a certain map where you infiltrate a certain group next to a concert that's being set up (being vague to avoid spoilers), then I quit because it kept freezing up when I entered the aforementioned group's building, and I would have to backtrack a save from like 5 minutes prior, but I chose not to, because I was bored with the game and not having fun.
Then I played Shadowrun: Dragonfall, loved it, and was determined to play through this game to its completion from the very beginning, because Dragonfall was so endearing. What I actually highly recommend is Googling how to play Shadowrun Returns -from- Shadowrun Dragonfall, because you get some nice upgrades to the user interface. Shadowrun Returns has a user interface that was a bit confusing and unattractive in my opinion, while Dragonfall's is quite sleek. Making Returns look like Dragonfall was quite nice! I noticed no glitches or problems from doing this, whatsoever.
How does this game compare to Dragonfall? And how is it as a game in general? Well, it's pretty decent, but not great. I generally dislike this entire genre, but this developer has made a series of games I'm liking thus far (just starting the Hong Kong one now). I am awful at tactical squad combat games; simply horrible at them. However, this one is outrageously easy. Unless I just do something insanely dumb, like leaving all of my characters out of cover at the wrong ranges to hit with their weapons, this game is a -breeze.- I only had two tough spots in the game: one, at the very beginning, which I actually liked, because unlike Dragonfall, this game has you take hits in the very first battle that let you know that a Body score of 3 or higher is practically mandatory, even for a decker/rigger hybrid such as my character, and the second time, was when I took on a "boss" about half-way through and didn't take a single companion to the mission because I'm the biggest cheapskate in video games with limited cash, so I got wrecked. The part that made me angry at myself was that I didn't notice there's a FREE shaman you can hire. =p
So yeah, this is a very, very easy tactical squad game. I was playing on normal, and i'm sure I would get obliterated if I raised the difficulty, but I guess what I'm saying is that "normal" should not be tough, but a moderate challenge you can overcome when you learn the systems. Since I'd played Dragonfall and everything here is identical, for the most part, with weak enemies who seemed to have derpier AI, though, I steamrolled normal. The story and setting are the biggest draw for these Shadowrun games, at least for me, though.
In regard to the story, though, Shadowrun Returns' story isn't "bad," per se, but it's a bit weak. There aren't a lot of persistent characters to the same extent that there are in Dragonfall, especially when it comes to your party. There's one female runner (runners are fellow criminals you can hire to go on missions, but they cost money and there is a set amount of money in the game!) who uses a shotgun that is available on most of the game's runs, either for free, or for very cheap (and she's quite good!), while three other runners are available for a brief time for free.
Unfortunately, I feel this detracted from the game's team dynamic. On the one hand, I got the random team member experience that can make the Shadowrun experience interesting...but on the other hand, the characters I could hire that weren't part of the plot (which is most of them) have nothing to say and don't feel like characters at all, whereas in Dragonfall, within -minutes- of reading through each of the initially introduced characters' dialog on the first mission, I was really interested in learning more about them and even liked certain characters!
Speaking of characters, the interpersonal contact in the game is rather poor. You can take Charisma to help with dialog options throughout the game, kinda like in Vampire - The Masquerade: Bloodlines, Deus Ex HR, Deus Ex MD, Mass Effect 1,  2, 3, etc. However, while Dragonfall's charisma expenditures paled in comparison to most of the aforementioned games, it was at least okay, with a few places to score extra karma (i.e. skill points), occasional additional money, and interesting facts you might otherwise miss. In Shadowrun Returns, though, I didn't find the new information you get from having higher charisma very interesting, it didn't really change much of anything or give a sense of power in conversation, and the extra money is just kinda nice, without any real karma rewards for the cost of the charima. If not for how much karma this game throws at you, I would completely skip Charisma in Shadowrun Returns if I ever played through it again.
That brings me to karma rewards. This is another kinda pro and kinda con situation. While Dragonfall is very anal about how much karma you're awarded, Shadowrun Returns gives you a ridiculously high amount of karma. Whereas Dragonfall gives you chunks of karma spaced out quite a bit, Shadowrun Returns will having you getting karma rewards every couple of minutes in the first half of the game. I kinda like it, because being awarded experience/skill points is fun, but it was so extreme that it actually came off as patronizing when I talked to one NPC, got some karma, then ran like 300 feet over to another NPC the game pointed me directly to, with no combat or thinking required, and dumped more karma in my lap. This went on and on like this. I would prefer a happier medium of frequent rewards and enough karma, but which feel earned.
Lastly, I know I touched on the story, but the writing in general (the narration rather than the plot) felt much weaker than Dragonfall. There were exceptions I loved, such as a character named Cherry Bomb being described as she "...had a hard face, armored with lipstick and low expectations. On another occasion, a location was described as being at the corner of "illegal" and "opportunity." These lines, and several others, had a real noire vibe to them, and they were fantastic. If I didn't know the same company made Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall's campaigns, I would have suspected otherwise. I think it stands as a testament that so much about Dragonfall was a massive improvement over Shadowrun Returns.
Why do I recommend Shadowrun Returns? Well, it's just good enough to merit playing, even if the story wasn't that great and the team members who travel with you rarely have any dialog or story permanence/relevance. The setting is cool and they represent it nicely in this game. If you haven't played Dragonfall and aren't that good at tactical squad games, this is a good starter game since it's much easier than Dragonfall. If you complete it, you'll have some knowledge to help you do better in Dragonfall, and you could build the same type of character but spend your karma smarter the next time around.

Shadowrun returns is the first step in a series that just keeps on getting better and it is already pretty good.
The unique setting paves the way for a plot that isnt chewed out and interesting to follow. It all feels very cyberpunky and having played the actual pen and paper I am fully satisfied with the translation of systems to a videogame. The characters in game are all unique but dont get explored a whole lot. Unlike later parts you dont really have a crew of people to run with that you get to know better throughout time, just some reccuring allies.
Gameplaywise you spend the largest part of the game with turn based combat akin to the XCOM series. Another thing they have in common is a hyperunrealistic amount of 90% hit chance misses. If I hadnt done it all on normal difficulty that would have probably led to quite a few frustrated reloads. You have a very decently large amount of fighting styles to choose from, unlike in later parts you cant put a low priority on fighting and talk your way through things though.
The soundtrack is the best in the series so far, though probably not worth buying a 10 dollar DLC for. Give it a listen on its own on youtube or something though, it is pretty cool.

All in all if you like the pen and paper or like cyberpunk with fantasy or simply a turn based combat game with decent story I would reccomend it even at full price. Dont expect to get more than 16 hours at the most out of it without modding though.

The only AAA game to come out and actually live up to its hype and not be a buggy pile of trash. For that alone it's worth the purchase, but all in all it's a really fun time. Parkour is fun and actually takes a little more than just holding a button to climb whatever.
The game defnitely makes it's statement in beginning, and you really do feel helpless and overpowered by the hoards of zombies. I'm a big horror game buff and I was sceptical this game would have an impact on me, but I've got to admit that it got to me in the beginning. With little to no skills, and dealing barely any damage, mobs of zombies are a legitmate threat and their moans are truly disturbing. On that note the sound design is spot on. The screams the zombies make when you produce a loud sound and the ambient sounds in the background of boards breaking, metal rattling, etc, reqally made it disturbing and added to the feeling of helplessness/isolation. Oh right, then there's night... The game doesn't throw night at you until you complete a few missions, but when it finally happens and you're left in the dark, your heart will race and it is terrifying. The volatiles will give you a run for your money in the beginning and yes, they are better, faster and stronger than you. All in all, the night makes for a great way to mix up the unmistakably Dead Island gameplay.
Now all this talk about the beginning being so great and terrifying. While the game holds up throughout (I enjoyed the story, but can see why people don't think its the strongest and your character is an arrogant idiot), it definitely runs into the problem that so many horror games run into, which I refer to as Dead Space syndrome (it's existed in games before Dead Space, but hear me out). Simply put, as you go on you become unstoppable and everything I mentioned before that makes the game so disturbing and terrifying in the beginning vanishes. You'll go from hiding and cowering, to just blasting and slashing away without any care of making sound, using ammo, or damaging weapons. It's not all that bad though, but it goes from "oh god a mob of 100 zombies, better climb this roof and go around" to "hell yes a mob of 100 zombies! I'm going to jump in the middle of them and spin around in circles with my fireman's axe!" Even the night, which before I contemplated avoiding at all costs by sleeping, becomes a slaughter fest and even a group of volatiles stand no chance against a sword that does almost 2000 damage.
Anyways, that shouldn't be a problem for most people. I had countless laughs drop kicking zombies off roofs and watching their heads pop as they hit the pavement or hood of a car, and yes it's a riot to run into a group that fills your whole screen and just slicing heads off with ease. But I was a little bummed when I became less disturbed and terrified. For a long time the game made me think of Max Brook's World War Z (the book for god's sake), then it turned into Grindhouse Planet Terror. Again, not a bad thing, just two completely different spectrums and I prefer the former.
