Dead Island 2..I mean Dying Light....has arrived!
For those who cried about Dead Island or avoided it, well, here you go. Basically Dying Light is a better version of Dead Island Riptide (which itself was vastly improved over Dead Island) with parkour, a more serious story, true open world, and much better game mechanics. Not to mention the graphics are great.
Going along with the switch from Deep Silver to Warner Brothers, this game has a better story (in a sense) and more sincerity than that of Dead Island, where it was just "We got to get out of heaah!". That doesn't mean the story is great or well written, as it is not. It embraces every zombie genre cliche remotely possible - from the guys who declare themselves lords of the wasteland to the journalists, movie producers, politicians and everything else turned psychopaths and leaders in Harran. Kyle Crane is dispatched to the city with a mission and things go very wrong very quickly, and thus begins the absolute predictability.
Thus also begins the "Do all this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; questing for every jerkoff in the city. Although, at least the quests feel slightly more organic this time around. There also aren't too many of them so while a lot of it is mundane - find a guys binoculars, spare glasses, etc., you won't be doing them for long. Many of the quest chains also have a noticeable effect on the world. Many times when you do a quest or quest chain, it ends up clearing out a base for a group of people to move into, who will then give you more quests. In addition, NPCs will talk of your deeds ad nauseam, repeating the same lines literally every time you come anywhere near them.
DL has a day/night cycle, which dictates the gameplay during the day and night hours. At night, zombies are crazy fast and powerful and if you end up getting chased, you better evade or kill them all and hide really quickly before the entire city is after you. So as many have said, during the day the game is more or less Dead Island with parkour, but during the night it is flat out survival horror and stealth. Make no mistake, even at lvl. 25 all three trees, you WILL be paying attention or else you will be dying at night.
As for the parkour and free running, it's about as solid as Assassin's Creed, Mirror's Edge, or Shadow of Mordor. So what this means is it works well and its very fun to do, but occasionally you're going to jump the wrong way and fall hundreds of feet to your death. In addition to the climbing and improving upon it through the agility tree, you get a grappling hook whichessentially lets you run around like Ada Wong or Batman. Jokes aside, it's pretty damn sweet.
Really the only thing to complain about is that like any game, there are some glitches. I fell through the map for the first time after 30 hours of play with no significant glitches, and I died. I don't mind dying, even though dying makes you lose Survivor XP, but it happened. There are also a lot of texture problems but it's not a big deal. The one thing though is, the two-hander zombies will often hit you with their ground strike attack despite being way out of range.

Neat little game that, while not entirely faithful to its predecessors, manages to stand on its own two feet. The premise and setting are hardly original, and even the story itself manages to take a page out of at least a dozen other books, but the gameplay manages to keep you hooked until the anti-climactic, generic ending.
First and foremost; you can't play it vanilla, not unless you like raging and shutting the game down every time the enemy takes a turn. The probability rating is utterly broken; you'll miss shots at a 100% chance while enemies will get critical headshots with pistols from halfway across the map, even while you're behind cover. There are a ton of invisible factors that the game does NOTHING to inform you of or even make light of in the slightest. Find a mod that fixes the probabilities, or you're going to be leaving with a sour experience involving an RNG more broken than even the Fire Emblem series has to offer.
With that out of the way, the good parts of the game shine that much brighter. There isn't much class variation, but each class gets its own unique set of upgrades, and they all function differently enough to warrant at least one of each class being present in your team at any given time. There are some balance issues, such as high-ranked snipers being able to clear 6 enemies in a single turn, but there isn't anything that overbearing. Naturally, being built on the Unreal engine, it's a little unoptimized in areas and you WILL see stuttering no matter how insane of a build you're playing on, but once again, it's nothing that glaring.
The macromanagement is pretty much the high point of this game. Managing resources, units, research, and production are all things you have the option and obligation to do, and these elements never get stale because the game is always adding more to do. It's a little frustrating starting out since it'll take pretty much all of your money just to get some satellites functional, and you WILL lose at least two or three countries, but it forces legitimate decision-making beyond those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue wheels, which is a treat in and of itself in modern games. I found myself wishing that UFO deterrence had been a bigger part of the game, seeing as how there's only two ships and one of them is a direct upgrade, although half the time the standard interceptor can take on pretty much any threat once you get plasma cannons fitted on everything.
Ultimately, my only real beef with this game is that it can get very tedious, and that the probabilities, when unchecked, can pretty much ruin anything even remotely resembling a good experience. The story is bland, flavorless, and predictable, but it serves its purpose in pushing the gameplay forward, which is also a rare treat in an industry where every other game has to be a cinematic storytelling experience.

XCom is basically Independence Day (ID4) as a strategy sim, where you are the commander of the humans' secret Area 51-style Earth defense force during an alien invasion. You spend about 10% of your time managing the headquarters for research, production, expanding facilities, and searching for new missions. The individual missions are like Final Fantasy Tactics, small-squad turn-based isometric strategy. Combat resolution feels a lot like Fallout 1\2 where skills, range, and cover affect damage taken. This game is too effing good. It's slow-paced due to its turn-based nature but creates a lot of edgy excitement with the music and sound effects which are a tense garnish to the high-consequences, life-and-death gameplay situations you encounter and the anticipation that's built up while you're waiting to see attacks resolve at critical moments. It is rogue-like in that your soldiers can perma-die but this is all part of the depth and charm of this game; there is technology and strategy designed to preserve your soldiers but the game is great about rewarding ballsy risk. The difficulty adjustment does what it's meant to - you can enjoy the game and have it feel basically the same regardless of which difficulty you pick, but Classic and Impossible will require advanced thought or you may not even finish. Ironman mode prevents backing up your save so all failures are final. However, you may want to play through on Normal without Ironman Mode as it's forgiving enough to beat but still lets you taste the pain when you get cocky. Expansion is a must, it improves the incredible game even more.

This game is super good. The beginning is definitely the least interesting part and goes on pretty long, so tough it out until you get to the forest at least before you give up from going nuts over listening to that one music track over and over and over again. Once you get into it, this is probably one of the best "retro" platformers that have been made in a while and possibly in the entire craze of retro style indie games.
The platforming is actually very difficult and the game has a great difficulty scaling in terms of both difficulty of platforming, difficulty of enemies and frequency of checkpoints. The game actually lets you go for a large chunk of the game without having a double jump and once you get it, the game has very good platform challenges taking advantage of the arc and the games deadly spikes. Bosses are frequent and generally very good. They are almost all very simple but have patterns you figure out and manage which happens quickly due to their simplicity. They are also (mostly) not crazy damage sponges which I feel ruins a lot of retro style games I've played though this is mostly a problem with the new roguelike/lite games. When you get to a boss, they do enough damage that you have to not just soak damage, but they typically die fast enough that the primarly enemy isn't boredom.
The game hits a pretty much perfect balance in map complexity. The map is very large and complex and has no map. This actually works pretty well given that you typically can move through earlier areas pretty quickly by having more armor and the relatively late game double jump. I'm generally for maps in games regardless of the "retro" design of a game, but this works well since the map is pretty much as complex as you can get without feeling you "need" a map. If you are the sort to actually make your own map though, you will feel rewarded for it in this case.
There are some old game references in this. A decent amount but most are secrets and the game stands up well enough on its own that I don't find myself being irritated as I am when this is a thing in lesser games. I figure it's mentioning for anyone who just can't stand that sort of thing.
All in all, this game is great and well worth its full asking price which is something I rarely say since I'm cheap as hell and indie games are literally a dime a dozen with the various bundles available. This game transcends that though and is worth a purchase on its own if it sounds like your sort of thing.

I feel like I've played enough of the game to make a proper review of it, although I will say in advance that I haven't bought it, a good friend gifted me a copy. As usual, I'm gonna start with the negative parts first:
First and foremost, the music. I know some people will instantly bash on me for this, but I will clarify: The music isn't bad. Most of the soundtrack is good, infact. However, does it fit the game? That's debatable. Killing Floor 1 had custom themes for each map, something that helped a lot in setting a cool atmosphere for each map. This game instead plays a random Death Metal theme on your ears for each round, which just seems dumb. If instead they made two sick Death Metal themes that fitted each map (one for the survival part and another for the minute you'll spend running to the trader), then it would help A LOT. The game does have an option to add lyrics to the themes if you feel like, although it seems barely anyone likes them.
Something that also seems weird is the new trader. Remember the old one? Sure she had average dialogue and wasn't really that important, but she would grew on you, you'll get used to her dumb quotes. Now instead you have a french-AI robot that's unable to shut up. It will be constantly treating you like a child, throwing you notes on how to play and what to do, it gets a bit irritating. I have 100 health, why do I have to hear a french robot tell me that "You need medical attention"? Specially since the trader bot's audio clips will mute any chatter coming from the characters, which is dumb. I'm also not the biggest fan of switching the makeshift shops for weird looking pods, but that does help the gameplay as there's more of them out there and reminds everyone that moving around is better than camping.
Third is something that's becoming a pest lately. Companies kinda need the money to stay in business, thus adding micro-transactions in games is pretty popular. Does Killing Floor handle them well? No. Copying the business model of another game and thrusting it in your game does not always work; it backfired horribly in Payday 2 when it was added, and here it's not much better. From game to game you have the chance of getting USB's that you can unlock for the price of 2$ and a half. And what do you get? A lousy paint job on your gun or a cosmetic item. The cosmetic items are okay, but the gun skins? What the f#ck is this? Most of them look like f#cking Nerf toys! Why not having something like the original game? New characters and maybe some weapons and crossovers? It's way more interesting than making your silver-looking deagle be f#cking orange.
Lastly, while I like that this game has more variety in perks, I think they're alienating for anyone that's not familiar with the franchise. In the perk menu you'll see around 10 perks and the game doesn't really bother much to tell you what each perk does. It just tells you that you'll get a bit more resistance on this, more damage on that, maybe a starter weapon and that's it, you figure the rest. It's quite dumb when you gotta look online what's the best advantage and weak points of each perk because the game asumes you'll figure it out instantly. And the game has a tutorial, why didn't the perk system get explained a bit there?
That being said, the game is surprisingly fun, and has quite the amount of good points going for itself.
First is that the maps, even though there's not that many official ones yet, are good and offer a decent variety. I'm not a big fan of how some of them just feel like an over-sized labyrinth (specially the Catacombs one), but they're okay. They also have hidden collectables to look forward for during the trading stages, although I'm not yet sure what they do.
The shop has recieved quite the overhaul, and I'm glad it did. Between each wave you can spend the weird money you get in new gear or reparing the gear you already own, and it both looks and feels way better than it did on the original title. If anything, I'd just say that some perks need more weapons (or ANY weapon at all, as the Survivalist perk has nothing to call it's own).
The characters themselves are also cool and worth a mention. Sure the original game had tons of them, but they all shared the same voice and felt completely the same. Here though, they all got different voices, different specific cosmetic items and you can customize them a bit. And the voices aren't terrible as I expected, though some characters like the japanese one feel overly clichéd and boring as hell, and the new voice acting doesn't even compare with the purely hilarious voice-acting of the first game. The original one had quite the dark sense of humor, and it was fun. This one seems like it tries too hard to be edgy as f#ck most of the times, with the exception of some characters such as the Knight. I mean come on, I haven't heard A SINGLE CHARACTER say "Dosh" a single time, that's serious.
The guns and perks themselves feel mostly balanced. Back on the original game you could see tons of people always going as the same class, here it still happens with classes such as SWAT, but to a lesser extent. Though I will say, I've tried a handful of perks when I was starting on the game, and I found the Gunslinger to be far stronger than most.
The vs. mode is also cool. Played it a few times so far and it feels like L4D's vs mode done right. Tons of fun to be had there, and if you do buy it, I totally suggest you gather some friends someday and play it all together.
Lastly, I'm surprised by the performance. I got an outdated PC and the game still runs quite well. It only seems to struggle when someone uses the Firebug and shoots flames all over the place, but it seems noone likes it on this game either.
Do I recommend the game? Yeah. However it's current price-tag for the content in the game might be too much for some, specially if you look at the Deluxe edition, which I don't really recommend at all. The game costs 27€, and I would wait for a sale that drops it, at least, to half of it. The game is way better when played with friends, so I suggest you buy it on a sale if you have friends to share it with, it will be tons of fun. Alone or with random people you might not enjoy it as much, but you won't regret it if you have a decent computer, a liking Metal, you enjoy FPS games and spraying a map on blood seems like fun to you.
TL;DR Edition: Fun FPS-Gorefest, improves much of the stuff the previous game had, though it fails flat in some areas. With friends is fun as d#cks, though you should wait for a sale, not everyone can throw 27€ at Steam just like that.

Based on the similarly retro aesthetic you may feel tempted to assume Castle in the Darkness is in the vein of Shovel Knight, another throwback platformer of recent times. That would be a mistake, because the two games have fundamentally different design philosophies. Shovel Knight aimed to emulate the games of old, but not copy them blindly; it included many modern touches that made it a stronger game overall. Unfortunately, the same cannot be said of Castle in the Darkness.
Speaking plainly, I am not certain the developers understand why some trends in gaming have died. In seeking to emulate older platformers, this game simply adopts old design ideas without much apparent thought as to what works or doesn't. It is, fundamentally, a game of trial and error. Instant death spikes run rampant, there are no health pickups whatsoever, and your character has the endurance of wet toilet paper.
On their own, none of those things are inherently negative, but combined they make for an experience that simply is not enjoyable. Frequent save points in another game would be an act of mercy. In Castle in the Darkness, they reek of lazy design: of the developers knowing exactly what is wrong with what makes their game difficult and not caring to fix those problems, instead using the many save points as a two-inch bandage over a gaping wound.
To be clear, this review isn't me going "Waah, game too hard!"... I have no issue with games choosing to be difficult. The Souls games are among my favorite in existence for a variety of reasons, difficulty curve included. I don't care about games being hard, I care about WHY they are. A well-designed difficulty curve is a fantastic thing, worth notice precisely because it is not easy to make a game that is difficult for the right reasons.
Unfortunately, this game is one of many that don't understand what those reasons are. If, knowing that, you want to give it a try more power to you.

Castle in the Darkness which is published by Nicalis who you may have heard of from Cave Story+ and Night Sky. Matt Kap developed the game, and it is a fairly challenging platforming game. You can pick the game up on Steam for $5.99 but if you do so before Feb 12, 2015 it is on sale for $4.97!
The game just gives me a Ghosts and Goblins feel. Swords and zombies probably is the reason behind that. As you progress deeper into the game, the sword you use grows bigger and bigger. Coins and all sorts of equipment litter the games many levels. Locked doors require keys to open, some take just a normal key, while others take keys that are specific to that door that must be found in different areas of the game.
Keyboard controls by default are just odd, and I used my controller after a few mins using a keyboard. As you can see in my stream it took a few tries to get the game running properly after switching to a controller set up. Hopefully that gets fixed (or I figure out what I did, so I don't cause that bug again) soon. Once I switched to a controller I had a much easier time with the game, but at least the game comes with a keybinder, so you can still use a keyboard with better controls (I'd imagine running WASD instead of arrows with space for jump and shift or tab for attack (if you can set either of those, if not c or v may work for me as well).
The game is very challenging, I could see what I needed to do very easily but lots of room for stupid mistakes. Reminds me a lot of basic math tests back in school. In the lets say 30 minutes that I played I probably died 25 times. Mind you I'm in no way an expert on this style of game, so if you enjoy these games, you shouldn't die every minute the way I did. Despite my numerous deaths, I enjoyed the game, but can't imagine doing a marathon session of the game for hours on end due to my lack of skill in this style of game. Short bursts however would be great for me.
There were numerous areas to explore, each adding something slightly different than the last, and many leading to areas that were inaccessible until gaining a key. Sadly I would go to the blocked off areas before heading towards the unlocked areas. This lead to numerous deaths for no reason. And since the game tracks your deaths (even if you delete a file you keep your deaths!!!) I got annoyed with myself for going that direction (not a complaint against the game, just against my RPG nature of explore everything, the out of the way stuff before the easy stuff).
The game was fun, and worth the $6 price tag, even better if you can catch it on one of Steam's sales. For me a session of an hour or less is ideal, but I could see someone sitting in front of it for hours on end trying to finish something harder than what I've seen so far. The game rotates between a 7 and a Negative 1523563676 when I'm dying in the same spot over and over (the game cheated! /rollseyes), so in fairness I'll give it the 7.

I don't usually like indie games, nor am I a fan of strategy for the most part. This is an exception. It's strangely charming. The soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful--enough so to warrant me downloading it from the Humble Bundle a while back. The visuals are serviceable, and absolutely do not detract from the experience at all; in fact, it adds to the feel of the game. This game is such an exception to what I normally like: amazing visuals and a mind-blowing experience. Faster Than Light is a different breed, and it's so good it's hard to dislike.
The gameplay is actually easy to pick up. People everywhere have always said that this is a hard game. It is and that's not a lie. However, the learning curve is quick. Just do the tutorial and you'll have it down. I'm not a particularly good player either. Really, if you're worried about the difficulty--don't. It'll make you miss out on the rest of the game.
It's primarily about light RPG elements and micromanaging your crew and ship while fleeing the Rebel fleet and finding, and fighting, friends and foes along the way. As far as I can tell, each game is randomly generated. This makes for a new experience every time. Loot is an important factor, as is upgrading and maintaining your ship. It's a very simple system, but full of difficult choices. It manages not to be overwhelming but still have some depth.
Overall, this is easily one of my favorite games. I have a very busy schedule, so I have to pick up and play for a little bit at a time, but it does have the depth to play for a long time straight.

I loved the way the graphics expanded to reveal the larger world and new larger meals that awaited,  This is a game for the time constrained, those in need of a small pick me up and those who love to over run a buffet and eat every thing in sight. It’s easy to learn and tough to master as the further you delve into the game the harder the challenges become. Everything works as intended and the game has been Steamified with achievements and trading cards for the collectors.
Overall, a very enjoyable game that is easily recommendable.

I just finished the main campaign on this and I don't see what everyone is enjoying. This is a simple short story found in the back of a sci-fi magazine that wants badly to be a role playing game. The entire story is on rails; nothing you do influences anything except maybe pick up a loot item or combat option along the way. The "loot" itself is a medic pack or grenade. No combat enhancers, no cool clothes, no fun +5 underpants of incontinence protection or anything like that. I realize this is a TBS tactical combat game but if you're going to look and feel like an RPG, you may want to have better RPG elements or divorce your game from it altogether. The combat is a sterile turn-based fare. The "hacker" aspect runs on the same combat system as the magic powers, just with the graphics suddenly turning to wire frame as you navigate "the matrix" (seriously?). Even then, hackers are rarely needed yet they seem like they should be a primary function in this cyberpunk game. There's a skill leveling system that lets you focus on all or one combat aspect but what you lack in your character you can make up for by hiring mercs to help you out. I went straight ballistic the whole way through and can't think of any aspect of the game I may have missed thanks to hirelings. There are no real side missions except for one run-n-gun to pick up extra cash, and no true dialogue trees you'll miss out on except maybe at the end to pick up one extra sentence. Even the main story is sorely lacking. It captured a good noire feel and tried to copy Blade Runner but the anti-climax sort of killed anything it was trying to build. The game itself is beautiful with an oil painting feel but it's quickly dismissed when I realized there are a multitude of repeated textures and items. I'm glad I picked this up on sale because I would have been disappointed if I paid more than a few dollars for it. I hope Harebrained Schemes continues to develop story games as they certainly have a knack for it. I appreciate the fan base they have and I'm thrilled to see this type of game becoming popular again, but I just can't recommend Shadowrun Returns.

Note: This is a mixed review, I'm explaining below, but I've decided to give thumb down rather than thumb up. Steam didn't properly count that I've played most of the game in offline mode, I should have over 6 hours of gameplay.
It was a pleasant surprise to find out that a game which I've remember playing such a long time ago (and one of the few digital games I've ever purchased) is now on steam. However, there was more than one Tasty Planet game and sadly, this isn't the best one in my opinion.
As you can tell, you control a blob which consumes anything of a smaller size which helps it grow to eat bigger things, until it consumes the whole universe. The game is a decent casual fun, it's relaxing, all you need is your right hand (I'm not going there) and you're set, but if you want a challenge, going for gold medals or playing the bonus levels is a way to go too. Eating things is fairly enjoyable when levels are nicely composed, and it's always satisfying to get a revenge on a previously larger predators that were threatening you.
Some of the levels are nicely paced and varied, but ultimately, most of the are the same, and the game can get stale really quickly. There just isn't enough varienty in terms of levels, sometimes you encounter something more than just level where you continuously eat things around you to get bigger, something that requires a little bit more effort, but those levels are few and far between. Which is where we're getting straight into a value, because everything else regarding presentation is sufficient enough.
Despite having a decent time with it, I can't wholeheartedly recommend it - the problem lies within the fact that this game is a remake/sequel of original Tasty Planet, and not a very good one at that. I'm not recommending it simply because there is a better game that has not been ported to steam.
While my memory is a little hazy, since it has been years, original utilized the plot better into each level - the "story" isn't really important, the original did much better job putting you on a journey to eat the whole planet, while in Back for Seconds you often feel like you're just jumping around doing random stuff like eating cats and dogs. I also don't rememeber too much copy-pasted levels from original, which this game often does - after each episode, it has a tendency to throw all the levels you just went through into one final, which usually doesn't offer anything else other than let's say 5 levels placed into one gigantic level. Last level of this game is everything you've encountered from the very beginning until the end, and the level lasts over 20 minutes, while regular time of a single level is usually around 5 minutes. It's actually fairly annoying for a last level.
There are plenty of bonus levels, but they feel even cheaper and sub par to some of the more uninspired ones from the campaign, and they've obviously not placed into any kind of theme, just random stuff that's without a doubt more challenging, but that's not really what I'm looking for in a casual game.
Back to the original. It looked better - it had more hand-drawn look to it, which this one doesn't, and some of the things/enemies look downright appaling, or lazy. As for the pacing and gameplay value, the original had more shorter levels with far more varienty, and also one thing that helped out with a challenge a bit more, you could die from one hit from some of the enemies. Here, when levels can sometimes take 10 minutes, it's obviously not possible, the variety is questionable (there is one level where for most of the time you eat red stars, that's it, they don't even change colors).
In the end, you have a game that looks OK, the music is kind-of elevator music kind, which is fine (and I think all the tracks are taken from the original game), level varienty is lacking, they get repetitive and sometimes literally get repeated, and they aren't that many. And unlike the first game, the only challenge here is to get medals - if you play the game, you can't really lose, unless you will purposely try. You will never repeat a level because you've failed and you want to overcome the challenge it poses, that will only come to play if you're trying to beat it in a certain time - that's it, there are no levels that would be even remotely challenging on their own.
So I'm not recommending this game not because it's bad, but because it's not as good as the other one. The original is currently only available from Dingo Games homepage for the same price (although it says 20 dollars, in the actual order form the price is 6 dollars just like on steam), and I would suggest buing Back for seconds only if you've played the original and want more.

Okay, I liked Spore. I liked the ConSumo minigame in Bully. A game where you have to gather 'food' in order to 'grow' to advance can be fun, especially if there's some skill needed and you have additional benefits/hazards on advancing like evolving and encountering harder enemies.
And then there is Tasty Planet. Yes, the devs have taken the time to fit a comic-book style of storytelling inbetween levels, one mark in their favor, but that does not make a game. Let alone a good one. Essentially, every level has your blob of grey goo (nanomachine colony) either following the mouse, or going to a clicked-on spot. Anything smaller than you is absorbed (randomly accompanied by 'yum'-sounds and the like, eerily reminiscent of the old recorded voice-works in fairytale themepark De Efteling. Anything larger might be harmful to you. The more you absorb, the larger the objects you can consume.
Sounds fun? Trust me, it isn't. Every level your size is reset randomly. Grow to over a meter? Reset to a milimeter. Resources are scattered randomly and the locator arrow is mostly useless, making it nigh impossible to meet the time-limits for the bronze, silver and golden medals. Not that it matters, you just have to absorb enough things to fill the growthgauge in order to unlock the next level. By all means, look at my playtime. I've played through a third of all standard levels in that and was bored to tears by then.
Not even the resources make up for it. Let's face it, aside from the M&M's clones the sheer volume of them is implausible and variety is simply lacking. Yes, each set of levels has a theme of sorts: labs, dino's, egypt... blah blah blah. Thing is, you have to gulp down a ton of stuff too small for you on average before you can absorb something your size or marginally larger. Perspective jumps are also quite random. The worst though is that the devs did not bother with much historical or paleontological accuracy, nor with creativity in displaying actual differences between consumables.
So, is this game worth €5,99? Ahaha, NOPE. This time-waster doesn't register as a game with me, nor should it with you. Get a proper game and send this unabashed piece of garbage back to NewGrounds.

Harebrained Schemes made a nice but not too spectacular attempt at adapting the rules of the original Shadowrun game books in a video game format. The end product is a bit simple but still enjoyable, medium-length turn-based tactical combat RPG in a great cyberpunk setting.
Whenever pen-and-paper RPG rules are adapted in video game format, the results are always unpredictable. In the case of Shadowrun Returns though, there was no risk involved: one of the original creators of the Shadowrun universe leads Harebrained Schemes, the studio behind this game.
On the flipside, the developers pretty much assumed that those who will play this game are already familiar enough with the setting. While this lack of handholding can be refreshing, it may scare away a few people who won’t have the patience to delve into the depths of the game mechanics.
And learning is an important part, since Shadowrun Returns is an almost purely tactical combat RPG. There are plenty of dialogues and datalogs to read, but they have very little influence on the events; the bulk of the game is spent on the turn-based combat levels.
Said levels try to offer many different layouts, settings, and even enemy types, but they lack in variety when it comes to approach. Out of all the possible classes, deckers (hackers) have incredibly limited roles on a handful of runs, and magic or hand-to-hand feel underpowered compared to a simple-as-a-stick assault rifle wielding warrior. (Not to mention that one mission will force the player to use a specific weapon type, even if they have zero points in that skill.)
Some of these unbalances can be corrected with a good party, but by limiting the player in choices, one still cannot help but feel as if this game is only good as a first attempt, nothing more—which would be correct, as the later entries will open up a much wider world…

First off, I love LEGO games. Seriously. Lego Star Wars: The Video Game was my very first video game, and it still holds a fond place in my heart.
That being said... I don't know if I'd necessarily recommend this game or not. Here are my opinions, and you can decide:
PROS:
-Free-roaming is one of the best aspects of gameplay in LMSH.
-The sheer amount of characters included in the game (including people you never see in a Marvel game, like Psylocke or the Guardians of the Galaxy, or Phil Coulson, or Stan Lee himself!).
-The team pair-ups in the levels themselves are very pleasantly unorthodox, such as Captain America, the Thing, and Storm teaming up.
-The story in LMSH, while drawing elements from the Marvel films, is totally original and manages to connect to the comics fairly well.
-The character creator allows you to make some very fun combinations (for example, I gave Thor's hammer to Mary Jane Watson).
-There is a huge amount of attention to detail in the design of the levels, the overworld, and the characters in particular.
-Every car you see is more than willing to let you just jump in and "borrow" it for "official superhero business."
-Everyone (and I mean EVERYONE) makes bad jokes or puns throughout the game.
CONS:
-You NEED to play this with a controller. There's not really a good way not to.
-There are a lot of small bugs and glitches in the game, such as characters taking too long to switch between, or someone's arms disappearing.
-Some of the hitboxes or ranges on the different powers/abilities are not very clear or consistent (i.e., activating a power from right beside an NPC or several feet away from them sometimes doesn't work).
-The character creator, while it has A LOT of combinations, is sometimes very goofy in the way that some of the combinations work together. For example, I paired Wolverine with the Human Torch, and the character got all of the shared powers except flight.
-If you are not playing with two people, the second player's AI is garbage. Often times they will get stuck in a location, or go off somewhere else just when you need their help.
-The levels themselves...just aren't very fun. Numerous times throughout my playthrough I found myself completely confused about what I was supposed to do, particularly during the boss fights. The hint system for the Minikits and overworld locations is sometimes just as bad.
-For me, there was not a lot of replayability in LMSH. By the time you unlock all of the characters, you've essentially done everything the game has to do several times over, so even though I had gotten some characters I love playing as, there was nothing left for them to do...besides run around and "borrow" taxicabs.
While this game is fun, it feels a bit hollow. 7/10

Techland offered us a great game with Dying Light. This is not a sequel to the Dead Island serie but it shares a lot of similarities; the weapon crafting, the quests system, the loot and of course the setting. However, Dying light improves most of the mechanics found in Dead Island and also add some new fun stuff.
The Parkour is what make this game shine. Navigating through the city of  Harran is fast paced and after a while you get to know the best route to get from point A to point B very quickly while dodging, beheading and crushing zombies on the way. And once night time comes the difficulty increase a lot and new kinds of crazy zombies gets out to hunt you.
Like Dead island you can play co-op and there is also a game mode call Be the Zombie that lets you play the infected and invade other player's games.
The story is nothing special and most characters you encounters are very sterotypical of any Zombie story. Most of the important plot of the story were easy to foresee making the moment less intense or exciting. This is a fantastic set of puzzles in the guise of a first-person shooter.  Puzzles are hard to really do right -- they can be too easy, or too hard, to too dependent on some easily-missed detail -- but this game does them *so right.*  So, stay away from walkthroughs -- if you're stuck, just try a working on a different puzzle and/or take a break and return later. The ambient soundtrack and mostly black-and-white line-drawn environments make for a great aesthetic. For example: ***very minimal spoiler alert for the first 15 seconds of the game***
That being said, I think there's unofficial Oculus Rift support, so that's something to look into if you have one, and really want to sink into the alternate reality of Antichamber.
No characters or traditional narrative --- which is completely approprite for what this strives to be (and achieves impeccably!), but that might bore you if you play games for the story.  Gameplay mostly depends on having an effective strategy, and only minimally/infrequently requires high-level "twitch" skills for unforgivingly precise and rapid action.  According to the FAQ, folks average reaching the end in 5-10 hours (although reaching the end doesn't mean you've necessarily seen everything in the game).  So the harshest criticisim I can lay here is that you may not get as many hours of gameplay per dollar compared to some other games, and replay value is limited.  But that's inherent to the puzzle-solving genre, and the hours of gameplay you get are unique and interesting.

This is not your typical zombie game.  Sure you explore, gather supplies, run missions to make friends, etc.  However, you are much better off avoiding combat because these infected corpses don't take no crap from mere mortals.  Thats right, you are not the super strong macho guy with ninja-like reflexes. At least at the start you arn't. You are just a normal person who tires easy when swinging that baseball bat or running short distances from that zombie hoard.
On the positive side, the story line was good as were the graphics.  Also, there was a bit of a sense of immersion. For example, I'll never forget running from the nighttime baddies that first night in the WRONG DIRECTION because the terrifying noises they made caused me to panic.  After that, however, it was rather easy to avoid them on subsequent night time trips.
On the negative side, the interface that allows access to your inventory can be a bit tricky. I managed to waste precious moltovs accidently a frew times; and at key combat moments found I could not access key items like throwing stars.  That's a minor and temporary annoyance, though.  The big let down was that many of the missions made me feel like I was training to be an acrobat.  I appreciate the option of avoiding combat with zombies and the like by jumping on roof tops etc, but after a while it seemed as if I was just a circus monkey performing tricks for the Devs.  Again, the acrobatic stuff was great idea, just poorly implemented IMHO.
As a semi open world, it's fun to just explore and gather supplies; however, I kept having to come back and do those stupid 'monkey has to do it THIS way' tricks on the main quest to keep going.  For me, the fun just quickly died out.  Overall, I was rather disappointed.  As a result, I cannot recommend it.

To sum up this game, all you need to do is play through the finale. No real spoilers here, just going to list off non-story related things (even though the end of the story is pretty unimpressive as well): you are forced to run back across the maps to get to the finale (because there is no fast-travel and going anywhere takes forever, ESPECIALLY this ridiculous run that they only make more difficult), once you get there you basically get entered into a giant platforming mini-game without the use of your grappling hook that you leveled for and have equipped, get introduced to a zombie that sprints at you and kills you on impact (which is the only one in the game and is positioned right around a corner that you have to die to discover and potentially die more to get past), more platforming that you just trial-and-error through by dying over and over, then once you get to the actual finale it's a quicktime-event cut scene (THE ONLY ONE IN THE GAME) with about 7 buttons that you just have to die over and over to memorize unless you have the reaction time of a 17 year old on crack. The only redeeming qaulity is running around in co-op and being absolute idiots with other people online. I would actually be 100000% down if that was all this game was, but with the weapon damage and the tiny trickle of money you get in the game, that's not really possible.

In this review I'll cover some common aspects like the gameplay, graphics, performance and other noteworthy things about this game. This is all from my personal point of view and experience.
Killing Floor 2 is a sequel to the very popular game Killing Floor (which is being played to this very day still): a wave-based FPS set in a variety of locations. You have to survive and exterminate the outbreak of military experiment subjects called Zeds by using various weapons as various classes called perks.
The gameplay is pretty intense: lots to shoot, lots of weapons to use, lots of different takedown methods. Shoot, hack, slash, decapitate, burn and blow up hundreds of Zeds of varying sizes and varying attacks.
A noteworthy thing about the difficulties is that the first two (Normal and Hard) and second two (Suicidal and Hell on Earth) are quite different in the sense of that Zeds will develop new attacks on Suicidal and Hell on Earth difficulty they would not portray in the lower difficulties. This makes progressing through difficulties interesting and keeps the gameplay fresh.
It's surprising that you don't need to have a high-end PC. Medium-end PCs can run this game just fine. Maybe not on maxed graphics but it will definitely have a good framerate.
For high-end PCs though, everything maxed out makes the game look really pretty.
Just like in KF1, KF2 has metal music by various artists like Zynthetic, Demon Hunter, Living Sacrifice and Rocky Gray. While I personally don't find it as brutal as in KF1, it still gives the game a nice touch.
There's an option in the main menu to turn all tracks which have vocals into instrumental tracks. Useful if you don't like the screaming and grunting.
This is the one thing of KF2 that I truly dislike: the players. The problem I have with many many players is that a lot play on difficulties they clearly cannot handle and add insult to injury by not taking any grain of advice from experienced players and even go out of their way to insult and ridicule far better players for saying it to them. They throw all advice in the wind or pretend they didn't hear it, get themselves (and the team) killed, then just leave like they don't give a fȕck. It's truly a nuisance and happens all the bloody time. This is a game where every head in the team counts and when you have an annoyingly underexperienced player who refuses to leave, it's going to be a burden to stay alive up to the point where the team can't and will die. This is one of those games you wouldn't do an injustice to get yourself your own server with admin controls.
This is a bigger issue than I describe it as. Especially when a sale or update brings in more players/content into the game, the problem grows worse. For reasons like "leveling up", "I'm good enough" (no way) and "just because I can" people will just continue to join the two hardest difficulties, Suicidal and Hell on Earth and cause distruptions to otherwise proper teams.
KF2 is a pretty new game and the devs of it keep working on new content, performance improvements and squashing bugs. They're a very active team and treat their game and userbase pretty fairly. Every now and then free updates with more maps, weapons and cosmetics arrive.
All and all a pretty fantastic game with a much less fantastic playerbase. I recommend entering the
group, friend some people here and have fun with a premade team. Otherwise you'll just have to live with the possibility that some Ídiot is going to join your team sometime.

It's a very funny and entertaining game despite moments of glitchiness.
South Park fans such as myself will enjoy it the most since the story is chocked full of references and plot elements from numerous episodes, though the game manages to integrate these in fresh way.  Like most South Park episodes, the game's story becomes more and more offensive and insane as your character progresses, so just when I thought it couldn't get any funnier it kept surprising me until the very end.
As for gameplay, it's a turn-based RPG with quick-time events. I generally dislike QTEs but it's hard not to enjoy them when you are mashing down buttons to prevent Princess Kenny from being impaled by his unicorn or to scorch Nazi zombies with Cartman's flaming farts.  While some of these events are overlong (the fart magic tutorials in particular), most of them are fun to perform.
The game has a few flaws, however, in that you will encounter some annoying glitches and bugs.  Sometimes my character would flicker or parts of his costume would become transparent, but that usually fixed itself when I moved to a new screen.  Also, the loading screens became tiresome in certain areas.  In addition, some players have said that there is a gamebreaking bug near the end that made it impossible for them to complete the game, but I never encountered it so it could have been patched by now.
It's also a little too easy.  I played on Hardcore mode and I didn't have too much trouble.  Certain special abilities are far too powerful and make the endgame trivial, and some status effects cause massive damage to most enemies.  While I doubt that many people want this game for the challenge, it would have been nice to have an additional difficulty level.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game, especially since I can't remember playing a good one based on licensed cartoon characters since Beavis and Butt-head in Virtual Stupidity.

Overall, Castle in the Darkness is a great throw back to 8-bit, action platformers. The controls are tight and easy to get the hang of, and the gear differs well and gives the player a feeling of freedom. The frustrating back tracking, and insta-deaths, are the hardest part of the game to come to terms with, and are further compounded by the merciless death counter on the game over screen. But even with its frustrating elements, I still had a great time testing my metal in Castle in the Darkness.
Developed by indie game designer Matt Kap, and published by Nicalis, Castle in the Darkness is an action, adventure, platformer with some RPG elements. The kingdom of Alexandria, is attacked one night by an evil sorcerer. The royal guard do their best to defend their king but are  overrun by monsters. The last remaining member of the royal guard awakens to find the kingdom under siege, and the king and princess missing.
The story while basic fits in perfectly with Castle's nostalgic 8-bit theme. Players are thrown straight into the action, and taught the basics of the controls as they traverse the first few levels. The controls are simple in their design, players jump through levels, attack enemies, and can use charged magic spells to decimate their opponents.
Each level follows the same formula, platform through a series of spike filled screens, while fighting progressively harder enemies before facing off against a boss. This formula is straight out of the 8-bit play book, but where Castle in the Darkness changes things up, is in gearing up and stage secrets. Each enemy drops coins on death, which can be used to purchase new armour, spells and weapons. Also each level has a host of secret rooms and alternate paths to follow, which often lead to new gear for your character.
This gear can be changed out at each save point, and many boss battles can be near on impossible unless you have the right gear for the job. This gear system is simultaneously my favourite and most frustrating part of Castle in the Darkness. The gear is great, as it offers a feeling of progression and lets the player choose how they approach battles. Sadly however, if you decide to take the most direct path through this game, you will miss much of the equipment on offer and eventually find yourself up against bosses you can't beat.
I should note, the game includes warp points to allow the player to backtrack through the game to get the gear you missed, but sadly these are few and far between. For me there is nothing more frustrating than dying repeatedly while back-tracking for gear, that you need to progress. Another little issue for me, is the rinse repeat play style it uses. Many deaths you suffer will be as you enter a new screen and have no time to react, or from enemies or level hazards that you haven't seen before. While this is a hallmark of the 8-bit era, I think it would have been more prudent to leave that play style in the past.

12 Labours of Hercules IV: Mother Nature is the fourth game in the franchise. The game is not much of a difference from its predecessors. The gameplay remains similar to those in most of the builder games out there; this involves building and upgrading facilities, fixing roads, getting resources and at times, summoning the "useful" Hercules to clear the heavy boulders and Megara to grow trees on deserted lands. In Mother Nature, queuing worker’s tasks are easier than ever – there are numbered flags that indicate the order in which the tasks will be completed.
Special power-ups also are back. They are really useful, especially as the levels get more complicated. Moreover, there are hidden puzzle pieces to collect in each level – every 10 levels, they can be put together to form a mosaic picture. Get that 100% while you can.
On the presentation side, 12 Labours of Hercules IV offers an ok experience, although nothing spectacular. The artwork is cartoonish with bright colors and a simple visual style; still, the animations are surprisingly nice and smooth.
The soundtrack, playing from game to game in the series, gets repetitive. It's sort of new for every game, but it just gets too repetitive and not memorable.
There are three difficulty settings available to select in Mother Nature; Relaxed, Casual and Expert. No matter which mode you decide to play on, 12 Labours of Hercules IV is a very challenging game. The difficulty of the game progresses nicely from the first level to the last, the latter levels really require some careful strategic planning as well as management skills.
Overall, this game is just like the others. The Collector’s Edition is not exactly heavy on the extras. It featured 10 bonus levels, a strategy guide, wallpapers, achievements and collectibles. Still, you get it when you purchase the game. Enjoy it, and hopefully you won't get too bored of it.

Killing Floor was (is) one of the most popular FPS games on Steam, and I am really excited that its finally spawned a sequel.
Graphics has definitely improved greatly compared to its predecessor, with support for alot of lighting effects and bells and whistles. In-game characters are now more customizable with cosmetic items such as Hats, Glasses, Scarves etc which can be earned thru gameplay instead of static character models in the first game.
Microtransactions for now doesn't feel too intrusive, and is definitely not pay to win. Most items are cosmetic. There is however 1 melee weapon that can only be unlocked when you purchase another game "Chivalry Medival Warfare" but even if you don't have it, it is available if you have any team member that has it. Even so, it isn't even a very good weapon to use. (Nerfed recently I understand)
Sound design remains relatively unchanged from KF1 with similar roars, screeches, satisfying gun sounds together with a rocking metal soundtrack. Gone however are the provocative female trader who peppers her speech with sexual innuendos. In game banter among characters also seems to have tone down alot and lost quite a bit of the british feel. (No more jokes about Wayne Rooney i'm afraid lol)
Gameplay remains the same being a horde mode with increasing difficulties in each upcoming waves culminating in a showdown with a boss.
There are a few new perks added to satisfy more styles of play. In essence, this is what makes the Killing Floor franchise shine I suppose. Anyone with any kind of style can feel comfortable picking whichever class they like to play and adapting it to work well with any combination of team members. This time round, there are alot more options of guns and this game even made melee combat more fun as I never played much melee in KF1 so much kudos to that.
Downsides, I miss the old maps in KF1 such as West London and the Classic Biotics Lab and wished the developers did an official remake of them and add them to the map rotation instead of relying on modders for this. That said, the new maps are still fun, but just can't quite compare to the old ones.
While KF1 obviously has older graphics compared to KF2, strangely, I feel KF1 evokes a stronger sense of horror and fear compared to the crisp clear (almost too clean) graphics of KF2. In KF1 especially the Farmhouse map, the general feel of darkness in the wilderness can feel very overwhelming and gives this extra layer of dread which I find lacking in KF2's version of Farmhouse.
On a Nvidia 970m, this game can be quite taxing as I had to turn most options to lowest to avoid graphic lag spikes. Still there will be times where the game can hang for a few seconds unexpectedly and can be quite frustrating when you're in a middle of a fierce firefight. Never came across this issue when it was early access though.
That said, comparing KF1 to KF2 is a tad unfair as the former has had years of updates and refinement to it. KF2 is a very good game itself and improves on lots of things that KF1 falls short on. With time, I am very sure it will surpass and exceed KF1.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
A very capable sequel and mostly gets the Killing Floor formula just right which was what made it a successful franchise in the first place. For newcomers to the franchise, KF2 is a very good introduction. If you do not mind the older graphics and lesser populated KF1, I recommend giving that a go too if you enjoyed KF2.

I'm going to make no comparisons and just focus on what I found worked and did not work in this game.
What worked,
Combat: feels fluid and the weapon types range simple (longswords) to exotic (sickle and chain). AI teammates help out a lot in combat with breaking parts, purifying them, and healing you if you fall. However, combat is quite easy and once you know a good combo, that's what you will use in every battle essentially. However, skills are a changable way to add flavor to the slashing and hacking.
Gathering: there is not a lot of grinding required to get certain materials and once you attain a certain helper, it becomes extremely easy to get non monster materials, and there do not seem to be extreely rare monster materials so it only ends up taking a 1 or 2 kills to get what you want.
Upgrading: Upgrading equipment happens after a boss kill and you will really only have to re-kill that boss abut 5 times to get a full set of equipment, and then there is fortifying which you can do after using certain equipment for a certain amount of time, for no material or monetary cost.
What doesn't work
Missions: While I personally prefer it, the missions are sort of arena style. There are different maps but only a few areas of said map available in each mission and monsters can't move areas. I understand this might be boring for many people, but I think it keeps the game action focused.
Story: The story is fairly run-of-the-mill save the world from impending doom. I am only in chapter 3 of 13 or something like that, and it is hinting at something more intricate, but I'm not sure if it will end up that way.
Finally, some comparisons (sorry). It is essentially an action alll the time monster hunter (no mining, gathering herbs, combining, no changing health bar or stamina bar size, no hunger) with the setting of something close to the manga/anime Bleach (sould devouring oni, souls in weapons, purifying souls) and I think this marriage goes exteremely well and that the way the game progresses lack a lot of the false difficulty that plagues the Monster hunter series (enemies run away, parts are super rare, slow animations, mining and pickaxe breaks randomly etc.). I strongly recommend this if you think you're system is compatible. I personally have windows7 and a nvidia 750ti and everything is butter smooth, and I can't seem to mind the 30fps lock.

After two years of tense waiting, I have finally gotten my sweaty paws on
.  Does it live up to the lofty expectations we neoretro-lovers had placed on it after playing Matt Kap's surprising 2013 demo?  Most will say yes.  And *
* will say that the full version has exploded my own predictions into smoking confetti with how awesome it is!
takes place in a sprawling 2D kingdom, every corner of which is stuffed with secret bosses, optional weapons and nostalgic cameos, all rendered in some of the most authentically gorgeous 8-bit art I've seen.  The nameless little knight at your command rips joyously across this pixelated wonderland with the the speed of NES
's Ryu, vaulting instakill spikes and stabbing his comically huge blade into the game's sizable menagerie of beasties as quickly as you can hammer the X button.
Some people call it a "metroidvania," but I don't think that's the right word;
feels far too open, too rollicking and venturesome for that (rather stodgy) designation.  It's precisely the kind of game I hoped
was before discovering it to be the impossibly esoteric rite of some bizarre cult:  fast-paced and challenging with a million things to look at and secrets that are not too obscure and
required for progress.
's secrets are so compelling, though, that you'll be driven to seek them all out (I 100-percented the game without feeling one iota of weariness)!
Watch the trailer.  If this looks like your type of game, then it definitely IS your kind of game -- and at this immorally low price, you have no excuse not to buy, save dirt-caked poverty.  If incredible games like
are still being made when I am 80 years old, then I will sure as hell still be playing them!

Unfortunately, the further you get into the game, the less it becomes a punishing 2d platform RPG and the more it becomes a Super Meat Boy-esque precision platformer with every room filled by instakill spikes, and checkpoints few and far between.  By the time I realized that I was going to be in spike jumping hell until the end of the game, I was already far enough in that I didn't want to give up, and forced myself to suffer through the last half of the game, with much screaming of curse words and throwing of controllers along the way.  Ultimately the game left me feeling very bait-and-switched, as the game set me up to expect a 2d action RPG and eventually forced me to spend hours playing through something entirely different.

Fairy Fencer F is a strange game.
On one hand, some top-tier talents were involved in it's production (Yoshitaka Amano and Nobuo Uematsu of Final Fantasy fame, and Tsunako, the illustrator of the Neptunia games), and it shows in some ways, like it having some very catchy musical themes and appealing character designs.
On the other hand, despite all the promise the names give, this is still a very generic JRPG, with party members, turn-based battles, cliche'd characters, tons of grinding, and overly long visual novel-esque character banters. These don't make this game bad by themselves, but because they are not implemented in any stand-out way, the game overall feels only mediocre.
The first 20 hours of the game are decent, as you constantly obtain new party members and dungeons to grab your interest. However, after those initial 20 hours, you reach a point where the battles and dungeons start to constantly repeat themselves, and even though the story is far from over, with so few unique things to hook you to the game, it eventually becomes a boring grindfest.
I really wanted to like this game, but I just can't as it doesn't bring anything new and exciting to the table, just recycles familiar genre traditions, with nothing but a bit of polish and very little charm.
I won't recommend it to you unless you crave for about 20 hours of decent content (about a half of the game), and find it at a very steep discount.

I have really mixed feelings about this game, and wish Steam had a 'maybe' or 'neutral' option for the recommendation. Without that, I have to err on the side of not recommending it.
The Good
The actual combat is fun enough. It's turn-based strategy style. There are a good number of decisions to make without being overwhelming. The biggest of these are which of two guns to use, which special skills to use and in what order, and where to position yourself (mostly about accuracy vs defense). Whether using guns or magic or fighting through a summoned creature or drone, skills include: wide range or spread shot, stun, damage over time, armor breaking, and various buffs. Choosing which to use in which order (they have cool-down times so you can't just spam 'the best skill') is probably the most fun aspect.
The stories are complex and multilayered. The plots are amazing. And the political and philosophical aspects are deep (though easily ignored if you're just into it for the steam-punk-ish fantasy).
The Bad
The stories are almost entirely told through walls of text. There's no animation, no voice acting, minimal cut scenes, etc, to tell the story for you. And even when story could be told through gameplay itself, it's done through more pop-ups to read. (For an idea of what I mean, think of games like Dragon Age or Skyrim, where you find books that explore the lore and history of the worlds. In this game, the whole story is kind of presented that way, not just the lore and history).
The cash and shop system is pretty lame. You only purchase things for your main character, so the vast majority of shops and goods just get in the way (eg. if you're a spell-caster you have no interest in the summoning totems, guns, drones, spirit magic, implants, hacking tools, etc). It'd be great if you could purchase gear for your team as well. On top of that, it mostly feels like you're just buying upgrades, rather than choosing different gear for different strategies. There's a little bit of the strategy thing (like stun grenades vs direct damage grenades), but it's really minimal, and the upgrades are too essential to waste what tight money you have on optional things anyway.
The decking/hacking/matrix aspect seems like it should be the most unique aspect to the game... but it's just simplified version of the usual combat. Same effects, same strategies, but only one character, fewer abilities, and simple graphics. It really should be some unique kind of minigame; or at least involve a very different style of combat.
There is little or no point to exploring. All that happens if you explore is: you wait a minute for your character to run to where you want; you see a white magnifying glass icon; you click on it and get a useless amount of money or low level healing pack. That is, you don't uncover interesting enemies, side plots, unique items, secret areas, mini-games, etc.
All in all, I enjoyed the game while I was playing it, but when I wasn't playing it I had no drive to hurry up and start again.

Took me 36 hours to finish, I completed all main quests, all side quests and unlocked 32 out of 50 achievements.
Dying Light is a great game, simple as that. It's the perfect mix of parkour/zombie killing. Techland has improved on the formula they created with their previous game Dead Island, in almost every way, and added features that will surely be a mainstay in open world zombie games in the future.
I will start off talking about the parkour and combat. The parkour is a more streamlined version of free running seen in games like Mirror's Edge and Assassin's Creed. The amount of verticality and player control this gives you is essential in a game like this, were fast movement and even faster enemies are needed and prevelant. Ocasionally there are moments were the parkour doesn't work as it's intended (mostly due to the late game unlock of a grappling hook, which hooks onto anything regardless of if you can actually climb it) but overall it's a great system that really feels like it's the next natural step in the zombie survival genre.
The combat, while simpler than Dead Island's analog swing system, is still a visceral, engaging, and tactile combat system that almost gives you the feeling of overpowering your enemies but the balance of power can change at any minute due to the games stamina system, were swinging too much or running too hard will gas you and let the zombies get the upper hand. The gunplay, is the weakest side of the games combat system, the guns don't feel as good as they should, comparitive to the excellent melee system. and there are no upgrades or custom blueprints for them, unlike the melee system which has really interesting and often over the top upgrades for weapons. The guns feel like a bullet point on the box that were added to satisfy a small portion of people who need guns in their zombie games, they absolutely could be better, and more time could have been spent making them a more viable and fun option.
The story is nothing to write home about, it's typical bad guy/bad organization doing bad things while good guy has to stop them, the cast is sort of interesting, with some stand out characters, but most are typical character types seen in many games before. The side quests have some of the better story interactions and characters in the game, they sometimes go in a goofy or outlandish direction which is fun compared to the serious, sometimes overly so, story quests.
On closing, Dying Light deserves praise for how well it's gameplay systems work together to take the genre in the direction it was naturally going, by adding an excellent combat system with a neccessary parkour system. I look forward to playing whatever Techland does next with the series and I hope other games borrow the features of this game and use them in theirs.
Pros
- Very nice visuals, the slums and city look real and gritty, and the gore is top notch
- Parkour is well done and feels right
- Combat feels more streamlined but still incredibly satisfying
- Some fun side quests make up for lack luster main questline
Cons
- Main questline isn't great, it feels very generic and predictable
- Gunplay isn't as deep or as fun as it could be
- Minor technical problems occur (most have been fixed but a few remain, like a bugged achievement remains, while performance and a couple stuck quests have been mostly fixed).
9 out of 10

In final words: it is a bare-bones yet soild title with a nice amount of content for $5, however it is drastically out shined by CW3.

Castle in the Darkness is one of the hardest games I've taken on in a long time, and I mean DIFFICULT. However, that's not a bad thing in the slightest.
CitD is a pixel-styled 2D platformer/beat 'em up, but in no way does that make it unoriginal. The world is surprisingly open, and the textures are top notch. Around every corner, in every area, there's secrets to be found. Some of these secrets are actually quite massive (namely, the hidden areas-Ex, Torture Chamber). Reminiscent of Castlevania, this game will slap you in the face for even attempting it, and require you to slap it back to progress. Its the kind of game that forces you to analyze bosses, and enemies before you can even come close to beating them. It may be contraversial to come out with this, but I think it does the whole "NES-gen gameplay replication" thing many times better than even Shovel Knight.
A solid 9/10, but definitely not a game for people with fragile controllers, or short tempers. So far, the best game of 2015.

I'll start this by saying that it's a simple game, for people who don't want super flashy systems, and just want that old-school action platformer feel again. It has amazingly simplistic controls of 6 buttons (4 movement keys, attack, jump) and feels totally natural to play on a controller.
This game will kill you. A lot. Not all these deaths will be fair, and some will be more than frustrating. Many will also be amazingly pathetic, and you'll wonder why you just did that (like walking into a room, and then walking straight into spikes for no particular reason)
The game has an almost non-existant fast travel system (about 5 points throughout the game that you can only warp to, from one of the other points) and saving is limited to only set points, with no version of auto-save on boss kill. This means if you die after killing a boss, but before saving, you have to kill the boss again. Sometimes the lack of fast-travel access bugs me, but overall you live with it.
This may be sounding a bit of a negative review overall, but honestly, it's not. Nothing takes too long to do again if you die (To the extent that I've died, respawned, and died to that same thing within seconds because I was playing stupidly) so you're never sitting there thinking "There goes 4 hours of my time."
The developer also has a wonderful response time to issues, and isn't afraid to let people play their way. A Bug was found allowing access to an area much earlier than intended, but would prevent anyone who did so from getting back out. When the dev fixed this, they fixed it by letting players get back out, not by preventing them from getting in early. Which means for the most part, if you see something you can only do with that pixel perfect jump timing, while it may not be intended, it likely won't be patched out just because "it's not how you're supposed to play."

I don't usually like indie games, nor am I a fan of strategy for the most part. This is an exception. It's strangely charming. The soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful--enough so to warrant me downloading it from the Humble Bundle a while back. The visuals are serviceable, and absolutely do not detract from the experience at all; in fact, it adds to the feel of the game. This game is such an exception to what I normally like: amazing visuals and a mind-blowing experience. Faster Than Light is a different breed, and it's so good it's hard to dislike.
The gameplay is actually easy to pick up. People everywhere have always said that this is a hard game. It is and that's not a lie. However, the learning curve is quick. Just do the tutorial and you'll have it down. I'm not a particularly good player either. Really, if you're worried about the difficulty--don't. It'll make you miss out on the rest of the game.
It's primarily about light RPG elements and micromanaging your crew and ship while fleeing the Rebel fleet and finding, and fighting, friends and foes along the way. As far as I can tell, each game is randomly generated. This makes for a new experience every time. Loot is an important factor, as is upgrading and maintaining your ship. It's a very simple system, but full of difficult choices. It manages not to be overwhelming but still have some depth.
Overall, this is easily one of my favorite games. I have a very busy schedule, so I have to pick up and play for a little bit at a time, but it does have the depth to play for a long time straight.

Be forewarned this game is difficult and desires a place with the NES platformer classics of yore. It has earned its place in my opinion based on its design and control. However it does have certain limitations and design quirks which may bring down the experience for some.
- Graphically wonderful, if you can stomach 8/16 bit pixel style.
- Audibly wonderful, if you can stomach chip tunes.
- Controls wonderful, not as tight as I'd like.
- Serviceable to decent level design.
- Levels littered with little secret nuggets.
-
- Full screen option doesn't work, at all. It worked once and never again, be prepared to stare at game surrounded with thick black bars.
- Can only open inventory at save screens. It's extremely annoying and limits your ability to check your items and magic.
- Framerate decides to kill itself for no reason at times.
- Insta-death spikes everywhere, these will wear you out very quickly.
- Jumping sometimes feels off and unresponsive to the button presses especially when about to jump off the last pixel of a block.
- Visual inconsistency, some blocks that can't be broken looks like those than can.
- Bosses are damage sponges.
- Would've loved to see a bit more originality character and enemy designs instead of rips from other games.
- No map (Can often get confused when looking for secrets but not a turn-off without one)
- No quick select for choosing weapons or magic at least, not a big deal.
The game is frustrating in the latter half however it is fun and enjoyable oddly enough. The frustrating is a result of a plethora of insta-death spikes especially in the final area before the true final boss fight and some trolly bits.
