This game has been receiving some bad reviews calling it a horrible port. I am writing my first ever steam review to say it is fact a great, very fun game.  Also TLDR version at very bottom.
Negatives (Not really)
I only truly see two “issues” with this game really. The lack of mouse/keyboard, and the 30 FPS lock. The 30 FPS lock is not an issue to me as this game runs VERY smooth for me. I have had no stutters, glitches, or crashes in my 15 hours of play. Granted I have a EVGA Windforce GTX 770 4gb card, but I am playing with every setting maxed, and I feel lesser hardware should run this fine. The mouse/keyboard may been a huge problem for some people. This game is designed for a controller, and ported with one in mind, plain and simple. There are no keyboard buttons on screen, and even using a keyboard and mouse everything on screen still refers to X,Y,A,B keys. Koei has a problem with doing this on their latest ports as Dynasty Warriors 8: Empire did the same, but in reverse as it only showed keyboard commands in game. As I only use controllers for these types of game, that game did bother the HELL out of me, so I can see the keyboard/mouse community's issues here.
Positives
This is a Monster Hunter style game on pc, plain and simple if you are into that sort of thing. There a quite a few different maps to run around, varied monsters, and crafting to make bigger better weapons to slay with. The game is faster paced than Monster Hunter, but is still slower than Dynasty Warriors. Add to this a pseudo spell system and different weapon types and styles; you end up with a surprisingly deep game once you start trying out different weapons and skill builds.
The story is pretty good. Nothing super deep or profound, but it does give you a reason to kill all those demons, and I genuinely find myself liking many of the characters as you get to interact with them and learn their back stories.
Online – There is up to 4 player co-op through the games missions, and I can say it is hella fun (if you can find other people to play with). Some folks say their game had horrible online syncing, well as far as I can tell there is no server based gameplay. If the host has crap internet then you will experience lag. I hosted my own online matches, and had no issues with the other players syncing. If you want to minimize the potential for lag go into the settings and tell it to only connect to other English players. I have never seen a Japan hosted game ever run smoothly.
TLDR
If you want a fun Monster Hunter style game on pc, this game is great; as long as you don’t mind using a controller. It wont ever receive the glorious pc master race seal of approval for its port job, but as long as you aren’t “trying to run it on a potato” (a quote from my best friend) you should have a great experience with many hours of play ahead of you.

Faster Than Light is a game that has grown on me fast.  One really gets the feel of commanding a Starship on a desperate mission across vast sectors of space.  The task is to relay sensitive information to the remaining Federation Command located eight sectors away before you are apprehended by the recently victorious Rebel Fleet.
The majority of the dialogue is well written and at times compelling.  It's easy to become attached to the multi-species crew as they toil away repairing the oxygen system, sealing breaches, putting out fires, or simply manning their stations.  Management of system resources; engines, shields, weapons, teleporter, cloaking, etc; is key as you do not get control over what will be available during a particular playthrough.  Furthermore, one must plot their course knowing that The Rebel Fleet is ever advancing all the time and limiting flight options.
The completion of game events in certain ways or finishing certain game tasks will unlock new ships for the player to use totaling nine.  Each ship also comes with a second layout featuring a different systems setup as well as a varied crew compliment.  A few of the ships are designed as a challenge for replayability.

Adding futher to FTL's replay value are the "blue" options that sometimes appear during a game event.  These options are available when you have the proper system upgrades aboard the ship or have a crewmember of the proper species.  Many of the game's tasks are full of risk.  With foresight and a bit of luck the player can use these advantages to achieve a more favorable outcome from otherwise risky scenarios.

As a rogue-like this game can be frustrating for many (think %10 win rate by design) but is equally rewarding as there are many surprises built within the events and  a secret placed within this great Indie title.
Update -
Advanced Edition breathes new life into FTL with the addition of a new sector type, species, weapons, systems, and new events throughout the beacons.  All ships have been given a new Type C layout.  The new species available, known as the Lanius, offer a unique challenge as well as their own playable ship.  Advanced Edition very much helps round out and complete the choose your own adventure style story arcs that appear with each playthrough.

In this review I'll cover some common aspects like the gameplay, graphics, performance and other noteworthy things about this game. This is all from my personal point of view and experience.
Killing Floor 2 is a sequel to the very popular game Killing Floor (which is being played to this very day still): a wave-based FPS set in a variety of locations. You have to survive and exterminate the outbreak of military experiment subjects called Zeds by using various weapons as various classes called perks.
The gameplay is pretty intense: lots to shoot, lots of weapons to use, lots of different takedown methods. Shoot, hack, slash, decapitate, burn and blow up hundreds of Zeds of varying sizes and varying attacks.
A noteworthy thing about the difficulties is that the first two (Normal and Hard) and second two (Suicidal and Hell on Earth) are quite different in the sense of that Zeds will develop new attacks on Suicidal and Hell on Earth difficulty they would not portray in the lower difficulties. This makes progressing through difficulties interesting and keeps the gameplay fresh.
It's surprising that you don't need to have a high-end PC. Medium-end PCs can run this game just fine. Maybe not on maxed graphics but it will definitely have a good framerate.
For high-end PCs though, everything maxed out makes the game look really pretty.
Just like in KF1, KF2 has metal music by various artists like Zynthetic, Demon Hunter, Living Sacrifice and Rocky Gray. While I personally don't find it as brutal as in KF1, it still gives the game a nice touch.
There's an option in the main menu to turn all tracks which have vocals into instrumental tracks. Useful if you don't like the screaming and grunting.
This is the one thing of KF2 that I truly dislike: the players. The problem I have with many many players is that a lot play on difficulties they clearly cannot handle and add insult to injury by not taking any grain of advice from experienced players and even go out of their way to insult and ridicule far better players for saying it to them. They throw all advice in the wind or pretend they didn't hear it, get themselves (and the team) killed, then just leave like they don't give a fȕck. It's truly a nuisance and happens all the bloody time. This is a game where every head in the team counts and when you have an annoyingly underexperienced player who refuses to leave, it's going to be a burden to stay alive up to the point where the team can't and will die. This is one of those games you wouldn't do an injustice to get yourself your own server with admin controls.
This is a bigger issue than I describe it as. Especially when a sale or update brings in more players/content into the game, the problem grows worse. For reasons like "leveling up", "I'm good enough" (no way) and "just because I can" people will just continue to join the two hardest difficulties, Suicidal and Hell on Earth and cause distruptions to otherwise proper teams.
KF2 is a pretty new game and the devs of it keep working on new content, performance improvements and squashing bugs. They're a very active team and treat their game and userbase pretty fairly. Every now and then free updates with more maps, weapons and cosmetics arrive.
All and all a pretty fantastic game with a much less fantastic playerbase. I recommend entering the
group, friend some people here and have fun with a premade team. Otherwise you'll just have to live with the possibility that some Ídiot is going to join your team sometime.

In terms of graphics and retro gameplay, Castle in the Darkness sets a high standard of quality that any developers attempting this type of game should strive to achieve. However, I've noticed a lot of people complaining that the one-hit kill spikes are a detriment to the game. I'm here to set the record straight and offer a new opinion. The one-hit kill spikes are integral to keeping Castle in the Darkness engaging and consistently enjoyable. Explanation commence.
There are spikes in Super Metroid that don't kill you in one hit should you fall into them from time to time. Therefore, avoiding these spikes offers little sense of acomplishment as they were only a minor obstacle. The same goes for Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. While the spikes in SotN may cause a hefty amount of damage, they still do not kill in one hit. Thus the sense of acomplishment is only marginally greater.
In Castle in the Darkness, there are spikes littered throughout every level in sporadic patterns that often challenge you to alter your normal jumping strategy. Every time you jump over a spike, you just traversed something that has such a serious ramification as killing you, and that gives you a sense of acomplishment. If spikes merely chipped away a bit of health, then their weight as a threat would be completely dissipated. Not to mention the challenge of many of the game's rooms would be invalidated.
One-hit kill spikes keep you on your toes. They keep you from getting complacent and bored. Thus they keep you engaged and having fun. Dying ten times on a particularly difficult spike room only makes it all the more invigorating when you finally traverse the obstacle that you have been struggling with and claim your reward.
If you would like to know all the other reasons this game is amazing and should be purchased at the very low asking price, check out any of the other splendid reviews from fans. I just wanted to take a moment to explain how what many believe is a fault of the game is actually a strength in my opinion.

I see a lot of people comparing this game to Monster Hunter. While that's a good comparison for the core of the game, the combat is really a lot closer to that of Vindictus. Faster paced and kind of more forgiving. It is a fun game, though, and that is all that matters to me.
Visually it's a lot better than MH, but you can still tell it is a port from a Vita to the PS4 to the PC. I'm hoping someday we can really have a PC worth hunting game - MHO come to America please!
I'm loving the soundtrack. Well composed instrumentals that would fit into any other JRPG like the Final Fantasy series. I really can't decide if I like MH or T:K's soundtrack more. They're both really lovely.
I have not run into any glaring issues. 30 FPS isn't an issue as the game looks fluid, but I am using a GSYNC monitor, so that may be why I'm okay with it that low. I still don't think it's an issue, though. Also, there is no noticable input lag.
EDIT: To force 30 FPS and fix the speed-up caused by an unlocked framerate, I used Nvidia Inspector to create a profile for the game and limit the framerate to cap at 30 FPS.
You will need a controller to play. I can't imagine trying to juggle this game around on a keyboard. Buy a wired Xbox 360 controller or Xbox One controller - its great for other games you might want to play, such as racing games when you have no wheel, or any other 3rd person game like GTAV.
If you are budget consious, I can't recommend this game at $60, but if you are looking for a good cross between MH and Vindictus, have a decent PC and have the money to blow, go for it. I'm happy with my purchase and imagine I will be playing for some time to come.

Just finished Shadowrun Returns, took just under 18 hours, excellent game. The story was better than the gameplay, there are just so many character options, it can be a bit overwhelming. Multiple races and multiple classes. Each race is built for one or two classes, otherwise you'll have a cap on how much you can invest into certain skills. For example you don't want to use a Troll for a charisma build, because they have a level cap on charisma early on, that would be better suited for an Elf, but the Troll would be good for a strength build. I played as an Elf and went charisma, it went well. I think it's probably the best choice I could have made, but I didn't use my Shaman class at all hardly, the magic in the game can be kind of pointless, but useful at times, but I found it generally easier to just shoot people in the face with a shotgun.
You work with a team, which you pick every mission, they upgrade themselves overtime, you don't get to upgrade them, so the only customizable character is your own. However I found myself frustrated on multiple occasions when I would bring a Decker (tech person) and not be able to interact with tech objects as my personal skill was too low, despite having a qualified Decker attempting to interact with the object. So I missed some opportunities by not playing as a Decker. As a Shaman your base stat is charisma, meaning if you want to improve your skills you need to first boost charisma. This means youre dumping skill points here instead of intelligence for a Decker build for instance. Despite missing some opportunities, I feel like charisma was the best possible outcome. You are constantly interacting with other characters, having high charisma means easier time manipulating people, also you unlock ettiquites along the way. These ettiquites essentially allow you to know what to say to a certain type of people to get your way. For example, if you've unlocked the security ettiquite, your dialogs with security will go swimmingly compared to not having them.
All things considered, I feel like there wasn't enough emphasis on the magic system, as I played through the game and pretty much overlooked it entirely, the gameplay was ok, a pretty generic turn based game, but the story was solid. I kept coming back for the story. You get multiple dialog options when interacting with other characters, I went for the snarky asshat approach to most situations.
TL;DR: Gameplay is par, Some mechanics are easily overlooked, Story is on point. Buy it for the story, if you're on a budget but curious, look up the story or watch a playthrough. I recommend this game, for sure if it's on sale.

I must say, I wasn’t expecting much from this game. All I knew about the franchise was that it had an old♥♥♥♥♥game on an old♥♥♥♥♥console, it got a seriously horrible FPS game on the Xbox era, and this was a much needed reboot. As usual, I will explain first what the game does wrong, so to warn you on what to expect:
The biggest problem this game has is the cover and shooting system, and how it works. Have you played XCOM; Enemy Unknown? It’s like that, but harder to understand. For example, there you could lean on objects that give you protection and shoot by leaning out of it. That doesn’t work here, as your character seems to get glued into whatever place you tell him to go. Now granted, most areas are really open on this game instead of closed up like in the sequel, but you’ll also find that cover doesn’t seem to do sh#t, and that’s something that the sequel did fix. Here it seems that bullets do either half or double the damage in complete random ways, and cover just BARELY raises the chances of that bullet hitting something else entirely.
The other negative part of the game is the story itself. Now, don’t get me wrong here, the setting and the writing is great. However, it feels rushed at times, not giving nearly any other side-story or missions to go along with the main story. At times you’ll get an optional mission you can do for profit, but there’s around 3 of them in the entire game, and for a game that has the “Gun for hire” thing so burned on itself, that’s really disappointing. The worst part is that the sequel tried to fix it... And well, it pretty much just gave three more missions to the game.
Lastly, a minor problem is that you can’t rotate the camera. Now granted, that’s because the maps are more 2D than the 3D maps you’d see in games like XCOM, but that makes it at times difficult to select an area for your characters to move, and even at times it makes the characters do things you didn’t want to because there’s sh#t in the way and you can’t click it.
However, ignoring that, what do we have left? A really fun strategy/RPG game, with a weird setting that actually works quite well.
The story, even if rushed at times as I’ve said, is good, and gets you hooked up for more. Furthermore, the characters are well written and developed. Maybe I would’ve liked to know more about Sam or other secondary characters, for example, but all can’t be perfect.
Another thing you’ll love about this game is the progression. The level up system is nearly perfect, and the stats you pick can have an impact on conversations as well, since you can get special options based on your character. Seriously, I love leveling Charisma in games like these, it’s so worth it just for the laughs you get.
The game also has an interesting system when going into a mission: hiring people to help you out. At times you get a free character to go along your main character, but most of the time, 4 man crews are needed as sh#t can get pretty tough. So, you hire other guns for hire and sh#t, something that’s quite unique and works quite well with the game.
Lastly, the game is easy to mod and has Steam Workshop support, allowing you to install extra stuff if you feel like it.
In the end, do I recommend picking Shadowrun Returns, though? Sort of. If you like this kind of games or are a big fan of the series, go ahead. If not however, I suggest you ignore this game and buy the sequel, Dragonfall instead. Why? Well, it improves in most of the stuff this game misses on, has a better story, and better workshop support. Overall, Dragonfall is way superior, although that doesn’t mean this game is crap. Pick it on a sale or so, just play that one first.
TL;DR Edition: A good mix between the gameplay from XCOM and the dialogue from Knights of the Old Republic. A good game, although the sequel is way better. Good purchase in a sale.

If I had to choose a game that could be held as a perfect model of game making, I would choose Super Hexagon.
- The rules and controls are obvious from the get-go and do not change on you.
- The game is simple to play but seemingly very difficult to master.
- The game tests the player's ability in the conception of space and time, not merely on muscle-memory of certain inputs. Because of this, the player always has to be alert. (It tests fluid intelligence instead of crystallised intelligence.)
- It is immediately and lastingly fun to play.
- It is one of those rare games which is both good and absent of violence.
- It is a unique design. If it is not original (as far as I know, it is), then it is nevertheless unique in the current market.
- The program loads practically instantly.
- To start the game is obvious and quick.
- It has a sense of fun: it throws you ridiculous and unexpected challenges and all of them are fair and within the rules.
- The core design is sufficient; the game does not rely on flashy extras.
Overall, Super Hexagon hits the mark on every level of its being. It is a quality game worth trying.

I don't have many hours in yet, but, I intend to have quite a bit.
Let's start with a basic disclaimer: Yes, the game has its problems. However, claims that the game is unplayable and "bad" are just... Really big exaggerations. If you demand 60 FPS? Yeah, you might be disappointed. However, my experience while playing was buttery smooth with no hitches or lag in graphics. So, if the game IS only running at 30 FPS? Big whoop. I don't notice the difference between this or any other game I've played. Runs fine.
As a second note, I also see a lot of complaints about there being no mouse support. While this is a fair issue, you're WAY better off playing this game with a controller anyways. These types of games were designed for it.
As for me, my only real issues came with initially starting the game. Whoever coded the game for the US/EU release made the odd choice to have the graphics menu when first booting the game start in japanese rather than English (or another language). It's an easily remedied problem, as the option for English is IN English, but, it scared me at first before I looked at it.
MInor sound problems in the form of volume for the movies not being linked to ANY of the sound options means you'll need to lower the volume of the overall game in the mixer, then adjust your music, SFX and voice volumes to match it so your ear drums aren't blown when a cinematic plays.
Now, for the good stuff. Like Monster Hunter? Like Dynasty Warriors? This game has the best of both worlds. Intense fights with big monsters and the sort of grace and over-the-top athletics of Dynasty Warriors will have you dancing around the monsters (or Oni) with all the awesomeness of your favorite action anime. Controls are smooth (once you learn them. Definitely hit up Yamato once you've gotten to chapter 1 and learn the basic controls, as there is no way to view what button does what in your controller scheme except through that) and I had little trouble in learning small nuances that make the combo system so much fun.
All in all, it's not a bad port as many claim. Game runs fine, it's fun. Maybe a little expensive, but, if you're a Monster Hunter fan, you know the amount of hours you can sink into a game like this.

Killing Floor was (is) one of the most popular FPS games on Steam, and I am really excited that its finally spawned a sequel.
Graphics has definitely improved greatly compared to its predecessor, with support for alot of lighting effects and bells and whistles. In-game characters are now more customizable with cosmetic items such as Hats, Glasses, Scarves etc which can be earned thru gameplay instead of static character models in the first game.
Microtransactions for now doesn't feel too intrusive, and is definitely not pay to win. Most items are cosmetic. There is however 1 melee weapon that can only be unlocked when you purchase another game "Chivalry Medival Warfare" but even if you don't have it, it is available if you have any team member that has it. Even so, it isn't even a very good weapon to use. (Nerfed recently I understand)
Sound design remains relatively unchanged from KF1 with similar roars, screeches, satisfying gun sounds together with a rocking metal soundtrack. Gone however are the provocative female trader who peppers her speech with sexual innuendos. In game banter among characters also seems to have tone down alot and lost quite a bit of the british feel. (No more jokes about Wayne Rooney i'm afraid lol)
Gameplay remains the same being a horde mode with increasing difficulties in each upcoming waves culminating in a showdown with a boss.
There are a few new perks added to satisfy more styles of play. In essence, this is what makes the Killing Floor franchise shine I suppose. Anyone with any kind of style can feel comfortable picking whichever class they like to play and adapting it to work well with any combination of team members. This time round, there are alot more options of guns and this game even made melee combat more fun as I never played much melee in KF1 so much kudos to that.
Downsides, I miss the old maps in KF1 such as West London and the Classic Biotics Lab and wished the developers did an official remake of them and add them to the map rotation instead of relying on modders for this. That said, the new maps are still fun, but just can't quite compare to the old ones.
While KF1 obviously has older graphics compared to KF2, strangely, I feel KF1 evokes a stronger sense of horror and fear compared to the crisp clear (almost too clean) graphics of KF2. In KF1 especially the Farmhouse map, the general feel of darkness in the wilderness can feel very overwhelming and gives this extra layer of dread which I find lacking in KF2's version of Farmhouse.
On a Nvidia 970m, this game can be quite taxing as I had to turn most options to lowest to avoid graphic lag spikes. Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
A very capable sequel and mostly gets the Killing Floor formula just right which was what made it a successful franchise in the first place. tl;dr version: A good game unfortunately marred by shoddy work in the porting. Locked at 30fps, if you care about that sort of thing, and very hit and miss at the moment. Some will be able to run this no problem, and some may have problems running it with certain Nvidia cards, and some may not even be able to run it at all.
The game itself plays like a Monster Hunter type, with several weapon types with their own movesets and gimmicks, and passive skills attained not from armor, but from souls one can equip and level to unlock more passive skills. Each soul are categorized into different types, such as Attack, Speed, Defense and the likes, with each of those types having three active skills unique to the type.
The combat are fast paced, though early on in the chapters the enemies are sluggish, weak and tend to stand around doing their idle animation. Then in the later chapters, it slaps you in the gonads, kick your dog, and burns your pancakes, as monsters get faster and gain new attacks.
The AI companions you can choose to bring along to both offlne and online are thankfully intelligent, as far as I could see from my own games, so they rarely need to be babysitted, and very often able to take care of themselves.
The Graphics are good, though locked at 30 fps, if youre the type to care about those. For me, 30 fps still looks smooth on my computer, so I didn't mind.
All in all, it plays like Monster hunter, with much less emphasis of the preparation and gathering, and more into the combat and action. Gathering is still important though.

This game sucked me in extremely fast. I didn't buy it until a friend started playing it, and after watching him, I had to try it myself. The game has a very high replay value, but that might be due to the game's quite short playthrough.
To start, the game is brutal and unforgiving. Making mistakes will quickly lead to a game over, and sometimes the RNG plays dirty by giving you time and time again the negative side of every random event. The enemies scale quickly, so you'll need to find a way to keep the pace. The first 10, maybe even 20 times you're going to lose. On easy.
However, once you've got an understanding of how the game works, it's not as random and luck based as people make it out to be. Being tactical about your movements and not taking needless risks will take you consistently to the end of the game. Using resource management for your ship can save you tons of cash that you can use to upgrade other things or purchase more weapons at stores. Playing smart will almost always win, except for the very worst generated maps.
No matter what type of gamer you are, I highly recommend this game. For $10, it's well worth the money.

It's unfortunate that the game didn't get as much user-generated content as the developers expected it would, but the game is still worth its salt.
The game stays true to its strategy-RPG roots, and it pays off. The main game is about your character's rise from a has-been Shadowrunner to the hero of Seattle. The characters are complex individuals with connections (and chains) to various factions that have serious beef with each other. Magic is back, and with it comes the horrors of witchcraft that the old world feared and persecuted. But that hasn't stopped the megacorporations from mastering the art and making a bloody profit off it.
Your character can play one of five different roles, each with their own unique abilities and playsets. Street Samurai use swords and guns, and must rely on precision and speed stun and disable their opponents before they bring the hurt. Deckers tag their prey and can hack into the virtual reality of cyberspace to convert enemy synthetics to their cause (mostly turret systems). Riggers use their brains and cyberlink themselves to killer robots that are tough to kill and tougher to survive against. Mages buff and heal their teammates with surgeon-like effectiveness. Physical Adepts can buff themselves until their fists become living chainsaws. Shamans can convince powerful, nigh-unkillable spirits to lend a hand.
The plot is quite harrowing, the setting is dark and gritty, the gameplay is your everyday strategy shooter, and the choices you make can become the difference between life and death for a few pitiful souls.
And as for user-created content? I HIGHLY recommend Nightmare Harvest, it's a standalone game of its own.

When I started this game it was so awesome. But unfortunetly this changed when Wonderland Dreams was released and Cygames's design philosophy for the future becomes clear after some expansions. Well with Starforged Legends they released again a fun expansion. Now the selling point are more or less valid again :D
What were the selling points of the game:
- Generous developer: you get many packs to start competetively and you are able to get a really good collection as a F2P player
- Interesting mechanics
- All classes have a great and unique identity that feels different from each other which lead to class diversity with interesting mechanics. (Beware that this point is written in past tense, because the newest expansion killed it and according to their recent nerfs Cygames is happy about that and doesn't want to restore the class identity)
- Win Conditions, it is nice to have finishers that could end games by turn 10+, so that control decks don't need to grind your opponent to death. But you could also tech against it, and even after played you had options to counter it which lead to a tactical depth.
-Tactical apects where your decisions matter where not many effects rely on RNG.
After some nerfs the following points on why the game isn't good are not true anymore.
Now to the turnoffs which also invalidates many of those earlier mentioned pros:
- Powercreep: The amount of powercreep is immense and grows from expansion to expansion. Do you hate a broken legendary and wish it to be nerfed? Fear not it will be nerfed by the next expansion when a much more powerful legendary appears which makes the earlier one look like utter trash. Each expansion gives also always one of the following: more and better boardclears to powercreep the old ones. To handle this amount of removal new cards are printed that can flood the board really hard or buff your followers so good that they can withstand that removal. At the moment it's just clear the enemy board, and flood it again.
- With the newest expansion they decided to push neutralcraft, which happened one of the offender of powercreep where your followers buffs are steamrolling. Due to their strength everyone plays them. You have 7 classes where all of them play literally the SAME deck. T1 Goblin, T2 Lyrial, T3 Wise merman + Actress Feria T4 Alice. This leads to dead class identity where everyone plays neutral.
- Win Conditions: They got powercreeped and win conditions that triggered at around turn 10 are now way to slow (read trash and you can lqiuefy them.) You need to win by turn 8, because at turn 9 there exists a card called Aegis. It doesn't have any counter, nothing works. (Well it can be countered by stat manipualtion, but good thing that cygames never printed cards to manipulate stats in a negative way.) So everything that triggers later than that is too slow. The current win conditions are setting off at turn 7 with eachter, whose head cannot be nerfed.
Over 400 hours invested into that game. Seeing how this all turns out to be wasted since Cygames destroys their own game is quite frustrating. #RIPShadowverse. It got resurrected :D

I started with Creeper World 3 here on Steam, and liked it a lot. So when the Anniversary Editions of the older games showed up, I decided to check them out too. And on first impression... I was going to give this game a thumbs down. Not because it's bad, but because to almost every introduced thing I would think "Oh, like in 3, but simpler or cruder." Since 3 has a bajillion stages, why not just play more of that?
But then I kept playing, enough to finish all the standard stages and get all the achievements, and it's still just too much fun to give a thumbs down. And having every single stage be exactly one full square screen of size is more different than bad, really. Fairly fun game, especially if you played Creeper World 3 and 2 and wanted to see where it started. But if you're interested in these games I actually recommend playing the third one first, as it's the best, and if you liked it, then checking out the first two. Compared to the latter two, the first one's quite primitive in story and gameplay. The characters have no names, for instance (except for one, near the end). No portrait art either.
I mainly played the game to get some background story info on the masterpiece of the third game, but was somewhat disappointed to find it didn't even have that much background info; the story was very bare-bones. Obviously this game was made much earlier, when the developer was still learning to program games, so some roughness is to be expected. If you don't expect a lot, it's worth the price (even if you can play it for free elsewhere, with some minor differences).
The one interesting thing about this game that the others don't have is its upgrade system. Unlike the others, you can't just upgrade whatever you want based on tech points or whatever, instead, you have only 6 possible upgrades, and you need to collect, on each level/map, upgrade tokens to use. Often maps don't have 6 tokens, so you need to prioritize which to spend them on. This can lead to some interesting gameplay, although in practise it's so simplistic that you almost always will just spend them on increased tower range and firing rate (those advantages are just too good to pass), and then spend the other tokens (if any) on the less attractive four options. But overall this system of upgrading is interesting and I hope it returns in Creeper World 4 or perhaps in other games by other developers.

For those who love turn-based tactical games, XCOM is an excellent choice. A friend described it to me as "It's like Fire Emblem but with guns." In each mission, you command a squad of up to six members. There is, in fact, perma-death, so if there are casualties in combat, then they're lost forever. In between each mission, you go back to the base where you can assign research projects, assign construction projects, upgrade equipment, and manage satellite coverage around the world. So you, as The Commander, have control over the tactical combat side and the managerial side, making the learning curve a bit steep, but the tutorial does a good job of explaining things.
Pros:
+ You can fully customize your squad. You can change your squad members' names, hair colors, hairstyles, faces, and skin colors.
+ Everything looks cool. A few animations are a little choppy or awkward, but overall it's well done.
+ The soundtrack sounds like it could be from an awesome action movie. (I've recently discovered that it's the same composer for Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which is another great game.)
+ The voice acting is well done.
+ There are lots of options after completing the game to make future playthroughs more challenging.
Cons:
- The interface is a little glitchy.
- The Random Number Generator can be infuriating at times (or maybe I just have crappy luck). I've experienced several instances where one of my units would miss a shot that had a > 70% chance of hitting. At mid range. While flanking.
- Online multiplayer is a little disappointing. Network lag makes the interface behave worse than usual, and being limited to preset soldiers, as opposed to full customization of each soldier's abillities, takes away a significant part of the XCOM experience.

Let's get the good stuff out of the way first: the graphics are awesome, the music is wonderful and the boss battles are great. That being said, this game has one enormous flaw: it's punishing rather than challenging.
The first few levels are extremely deceptive in that the jumping puzzles are short, easy and require minimal retries to complete. Later levels are so difficult that some of them require SURGICAL PRECISION in order to beat them. The difficulty curve is so steep that at one point I got stuck on a level and revisited every area before it five times because I thought I was missing an item that I needed in order to continue.
Later levels also take away save points before the level's boss. So for some levels you actually have to run a gauntlet of enemies, spikes and jumping puzzles just to get to the boss and you'd better hope you have enough health to beat it or it's right back to the beginning of the gauntlet. Eventually, the level design becomes so incredibly difficult that beating them becomes a matter of luck. And, frankly, that should be enough for me to hate this game with every fiber of my being so intensely that it reverberates throughout the universe and destroys many small planets.
So why am I recommending this game given how much I despise the level design? Well, because everything else is really, really good. I loved the early levels. I loved the references (even the ones that killed me.)  I loved the boss battles and the graphics and the music and everything else. Every area that didn't suffer from the bad level design felt awesome and fun. If the game gave you the option of skipping the difficult precision based jumping puzzles it would be perfect, but as is it's a pretty good game that suffers due to a few extremely bad levels.
Buy it if you want, but be warned that you will grow to hate it.
Update: Having played further, it turns out I was missing items (once again) at the places where I was having trouble advancing. Not ability enhancing items, but armor. Having done some experimenting, it seems like wearing different armor affects your speed and, possibly, double jump height. Certain jumps are impossible in some sets of armor, but are possible in others. This is never adressed in game and it isn't very apparent, but the results speak for themselves.
Do I still think the level design is bad? A little less so now, but yeah. Some of the sections I encountered after further exploration were just ridiculous. And yes, some of them do still rely on luck (for most people.) So I get the feeling a lot of people (the people who actually stick with it to the end,  that is) are going to be stuck with the "bad ending", because some of the levels are simply too frustrating to complete.
But again, it is still good and I do still recommend it.

Now kick back as I write my own wiki page for the game.
What makes this game so unique? The combat and gunplay is some of the best you will ever have in a first-person shooter. This isn't just some game where you simply shoot enemies with guns that are bland and only vary in fire rate/damage. Killing Floor 2 goes in depth with each of its weapons and has advanced enemy AI mechanics that allow them to react to your weapons, and how you play.
It turns out that I used up all my space, so I will use this review jus to talk about the playstyles in the game and how they affect the gameplay:
There are 10 perks in the game that vary in gun types and play styles.
Beserk is the melee tank that works on the front line to absorb damage and dish out a ton as well. Berserk has weapons varying from a bladed shovel to a sawblade launcher that also has a chainsaw. Beserk is meant to be a very powerful perk that can survive a lot of close combat, but shouldn't try to shine mainly over others because other perks can do certain roles way better than another could.
Commando is the assualt-rifle wielding soldier that is able to call out invisible enemies to teammates, state how much health an enemy has for prioritization, and remove smaller-medium sized threats for other perks to take out larger enemies. Commando performs a large team role which should be recognized. Commando also extends the feature known as zed time, which is a period of time that occurs randomly after a headshot or explosion goes off, making the game go into slow motion and allowing players to line up shots better. Commando gives players more time to utilize this for aiming and taking down enemies, since at max level, each perk gains an ability in zed time that can improve their effectiveness. For example, a beserk can move in real-time speed while everything moves in slow-motion, and a commando can extend how long the beserk can do this by earning zed-time after each kill the commando gets while it is activated.
Support is all about heavy damaging and close quarters through shotgun and supplying the team. Support can be at the back of the team and be used as a fallback to take out numerous enemies while the team recoups. Support can also work itself to be shining on the team through its powerful arsenal and assortment of shotguns, with the AA12 being the major player in its loadout. Support is used to fill in all the extra damage a team needs to take out large enemies, as well as having a unique ability to shoot through multiple enemies to take out multiple enemies with one shot. This makes support one of the best perks to play when holding a choke point. Not only that, support grants the team with a very useful ability: the ammo backpack. Any player that looks at another player who is support can press E on them to receive ammo, which can be used to save money on buying ammo or to make a desperate refill in the middle of a wave.
Field Medic is the next perk, and is the savior of the team, for obvious reasons. Medic has a varying arsenal of a pistol, smg, shotgun, and assault rifle, all with the function to shoot a healing dart at teammates to heal them. The healing dart has autoaim, so that frustration of trying to have your teammates stand still is gone, but, it might things get kinda easy. Nevertheless, the medic is supposed to do this and correct the mistakes of the team by restoring health and applying buffs to everybody. Buffs include increase speed, damage, and damage resistance for a shoot amount of time. Medic is the best for recharging healing supplies and keeping the team healthy.
Demolitionist is the perk dedicated to high power explosives and gadgets. The demo is used to take out both groups of small enemies and the most dangerous mini boss, the fleshpound. Demo is a perk that takes a certain degree of skill and patience to use. Most of the demo's arsenal is single fire explosives, which require timing and distance to avoid splash damage. Demo can save a team from a dangerous scenario and make quick work of the fleshpound, a hulking monster that can make quick work of your team without careful attention. The demo's weapons very in area of effect (AOE), reload speed, and utility. The demo has a diverse loadout that can be used for many scenarios. Some to mention would be C4, which can be stuck anywhere (even on enemies) and detonated at anytime. The demo has two types of grenade launchers, one being the m79 with the largest AOE, and the other being an underbarrel attachment to an m16, which has smaller AOE but more versatility because of the m16, allowing demo to be more effective in close quarters. The demo also has an RPG, which just destroys the target you aim at unless it's a tougher enemy.
Firebug is the madman's perk that allows you to just set everything on fire. The perk is so mad that the devs have trouble finding balance for it. Firebug is the BEST perk for holding choke points AND keeping the zeds (the threat of the game) away from the team. Firebug however requires a good understanding of enemy mechanics in the game, since the amount of fire a firebug can spew out can also cause large enemies to become enraged and bum rush your team, which can really screw everybody over. However, firebug can also save the team from being surrounded. Firebug has two flamethrowers, a fire trenchgun with a lot of power to it, and a microwave energy weapon that does significant damage to enemies with metal on them, and has an alt fire which can send enemies flying a few feet backwards.
Gunslinger is every cowboy's dream. Gunslinger is devoted to dual wielding powerful pistols and being fast at running. Gunslinger is definitely the HARDEST perk in the game to play, as the pistols require good aim and control with the amount of recoil they have. Gunslingers make use of revolvers, M1911 pistols, Desert Eagles, and .500 Magnums. A skilled gunslinger can decimate groups of smaller enemies with heashots and annihilate a large zed with a good amount of well placed shots to the head. The gunslinger is evasive, but not strong on health, so know when to back up and run back in for more damage.
Sharpshoooter is my personal favorite perk, and an alteration to gunslinger's playstyle. The sharpshooter is the sniper of the team, and is geared to take on all large enemies, including the fleshpound which demo is the most effective against. The sharpshooter is skilled in taking out large zeds through the use of a lever action rifle, a high powered modern crossbow, the amazing m14, and the almighty powerful railgun (An extremely strong sniper rifle). However, sharpshooter lacks strength in close quarters when using bigger guns, and needs help from teammates. When the team backs up the sharpshooter, the sharpshooter can make quick work of large enemies at a distance before they even reach the team. Lining up these shots can be tricky, and making them requires patience, as expected.
Survivalist is the "Jack of All Trades, Master of None Perk". The perk is designed to fill in multiple roles on a team and be decent enough to help the team with whatever scenario. The survivalist doesn't perform a specific role well, but performs multiple roles ok. The survivalist can use weapons from all the other perks and be decent with them, as well has get skills to help the team and resist some amount of damage.
SWAT is an alteration of commando that focuses more on tactical gameplay. SWAT uses SMG weapons and can tank enemies through the use of strong armor, or move fast while aiming and crouching. SWAT is highly efficient in dispatching smaller enemies for other perks, and can get them out of sticky situations thanks to having a flash grenade that stuns enemies.

If you liked Dead Island but hated how "co-op" it felt because your character had little input in the story and it was just "the group", you might enjoy this more. Crane is a lot more engaged than the protagonists of Dead Island, which is pretty nice. However, his personality is lacking and all over. Oddly enough, he starts getting interesting during a story mission half way through the game, but the following mission has him making wise-cracks the entire time.
Even though the story is better than Dead Island, it is still very predictable, incredibly cliched, and hilarious most of the time. I mean, the game craps its self in the most glorious ways for no reason. If you think something is going to happen, you probably already know what is going to happen. Also, Rais is a good villain in the sense you hate him and just want to kill him so you can make him shut up. But he's really a terrible villain with no real logic behind his motives and he's probably Russian just so we could have that Cold War grudge against him as well. There's a side quest where you have to track down a serial killer in the Old Town that has a more interesting antagonist than Rais because you can believe he's actually crazy.
The urban exploration is really the highlight of this game; getting around can be very fun when you start upgrading your agility and especially after you get the grappling hook. Many of the towers you can climb really are fun to scale and even feel like you are there with both how good the game looks and how well it handles ambient noise. For instance, while climbing a radio tower, you can hear the steel beams creak and sway in the wind. Also how Crane constantly adjusts himself while on thin ledges really add to the feel that you are a human doing these things, unlike most games where you feel like you are playing as a box. I say this game would have been perfect if it had no zombies or story and focused purely on the parkour.
However, the parkour is not without fault. Sometimes, Crane refuses to grab onto ledges while scaling and that can result into accidentally falling to your death (which also is your number one cause of death). Also Crane is just so slow when you start the game. Yeah, he's just a guy; but he is also a special agent and he doesn't really feel like he has had any physical training besides "Above Average Strength and Stamina". I suggest not sleeping at night and just let the Volatiles chase you around while you get double XP and get to a safe zone for the agility bonus until you get the first intermediate upgrade. Even then, just play at night anyway because the game becomes more fun.
The combat is simultaniously one of the worst but best part of the game. It's either frustrating because the big enemies have incredibly big AoE attacks that you have to dodge 2-3 times in one direction to maybe dodge (even though you may still get hit), or too easy because the same big guys can be killed in two or three well placed hits with an upgraded mid-game weapon or a vanilla late game weapon. For how realistic the game looks, it's crazy how cartoony the fighting is. You should be disgusted that you just kicked the hipbones out of a zombie's body, but
. The combat skills you get are hilarious and are very effective; you can dropkick a zombie and send him flying like he got shot out of a cannon, or you can kill a zombie by grabbing his head and gently turning him to the right, or you can kill a zombie by jumping off a roof and slamming an axe through its body with enough force to create a shockwave that sends every zombie in a 3m radius flying.
Even then, the game put a lot of focus on the melee combat but forces you into firefights frequently in the main story. There are only five guns to pick from (two handguns, two rifles, and one shotgun), and they never scale in stats. That rifle you found at level 11 is the exact same at level 25 although it now costs more because it is orange. Also you'd imagine that since you can find the same guns all game, you can find the same melee weapons too, but apparently there's weapon extinction. I have a blueprint I never used because it needs a baseball bat and I never found a baseball bat all game and now I can't ever find one because they are "Low Level" weapons. I can fill all 18 inventory slots with Katanas and Khopeshes though!
I feel like the game blows its load on "Visually Interesting" very early then doesn't pick its self back up again until much later for how muddy and brown almost the entire game is, and then Old Town just feels like Italy which felt out of nowhere, because apparently the Harran World Games were to put it "on the map", but Harran was a global trade center for hundreds of years and a huge oil export with a rich cultural history.
This is the most well off apocalypse I have ever seen. You will get an abundance of cash and supplies only a few hours into the game. Just by playing as a kleptomaniac, you will never run out of anything you need besides String (at least in my experience, I only found about 20 pieces my entire time playing the main story, but started finding it all over after I beat the game). I'll even go so far to say that if you need ANY supplies right now, you could just add me and I could throw 20 of something at you and still have too much crap. You can even cross the bridge to get to a medical outpost and get about 25 medkits and gauze (as well as several police vans and ambulances to lockpick) inbetween missions and always have enough supplies.
I do find it very funny that the game tries to set up that the supply drops are a massive point of the game and the focus of survival, even though they stopped after two hours of playtime for me. Then they become far too common in the Old Town district (I found enough supply drops to get over 205,000 survival experience just by running around for an hour-- Not counting the XP you get from liberating the drops as well).
I also find it hilarious how often Crane gets his cover blown for how he is supposed to blend in and be a secret agent.
I will say the impression I got from early videos of the game was that you were just in the quarantine zone already and had to fight other survivors to get to the supply drops to survive, which I thought would be very interesting; seeing how people would act when supplies are low and there are zombies everywhere. But we barely get that and the game is just littered with random neutral survivors you have to save from time to time. I won't go so far to say that Techland again didn't deliver what they promised, but...
.

To start out, I'm a massive Monster Hunter fan and even though I hate to compare games I can't help myself sometimes so I'm going to weigh the pros and cons of this game here for you all. As a preface, most of the negative reviews under 30 minutes of gameplay are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I've played 15 hours in the game and haven't had a single crash or gameplay glitch, the 30 FPS lock is unnoticable and the game runs extremely smooth and looks beautiful, with that out of the way, here are my opinions.
Fast, fluid combat.
Easy to access multiplayer.
Skills are easy to use and the Mitama system makes changing armor sets easy (especially compared to MH)
The Tenko companion is adorable and not annoying compared to the Palicoes in MH4U.
Graphically impressive.
Forced to use a controller (I'm okay with it personally since all Koei Tecmo games on Steam pretty much require a controller)
Fights are easy to hack and slash (This one is mainly due to the Mitama I use, I'm able to get soak a free hit, and at the current stage I'm at, getting hit really doesn't do too much damage, that will most likely change in the future, till then it's a con)
Multiplayer lobby is one room only and lacking access to crafting, Tenko, and other village options. You're able to fortify your weapons/armor (which is a small stat boost to them) in the Lobby, but you can't see what you need to craft the next set, check what you Tenko brought you, or anything else village related without leaving the lobby entirely. This is okay if you have a dedicated friend to play with, but don't be surprised if you find it hard to keep playing with the same people as you keep leaving to check on your Tenko or see what that last boss's parts can be crafted into.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone with a Controller and who's a fan of Monster Hunter style games. It's far more action based than Monster Hunter, there is no weapon sharpness, gather quests, potion maintenance or anything of the sort. It's purely hunting, and that's enjoyable to me. The cons are mainly my personal opinion of the game mechanics, and nothing actually game breaking.

Castle in the darkness is a really good platformer that you can sink your teeth into.
it is inspired by the good old school platformers we played as kids and enjoyed, and this game brings them all to life with references and easter eggs.
I can say without any doubt there isn't one thing wrong with the music and the enemy/character design and backgrounds and everything but there are some things that just turns this game OFF completely for some players will get to it in a bit just stay with me here.
The Controls do not feel clunky or anything, Movement, Jump, And attack button thats basically it
Know that if you are using a controller like I do, You will need to use the keyboard to pause the game or close it.
The music in the game are just some old school awesomeness, The story is lovely and the gameplay is great, A lot of secrets that would take you time to get 100% of them, (And as far as i know good and bad endings)
Great Boss battles, Each having its own weakness and unique fighting style.
All seems well right ? Well thats a no no because unlike old platformers this is not a platform metroidvania game, Its more like a
.
You will die A LOT, the death counter is set for even 7 digits that's never a good thing, You will get frustrated by all the spikes that will kill you and even more angry at the trolling spikes on the roof that will fall on you once you get right under them, you'd think you can see and dodge that but sometimes they dont even show because the roof is too far to show in the screen and you simply die while trying to figure out where to jump to next.
I am sure a lot will vote this review down after reading this but I will never hide anything in a game and show the positive stuff so here  goes.
There are some flaws in the level design, In some places its literally impossible to go back through a place, There are other ways around if you want to go back to a warp point but still seeing that gives me an uncomfortable feeling that they didn't do it right, And not only that .. In most places while going back the focus on where enemies are and spikes makes it harder so you can expect to die a lot more when going back than you do going forward.
This is why i called this game Trial-And-Error, You will keep dying from spikes and platforms that shatters when you stand on them, And places that you will just have to die at least 5 times to know what you are doing wrong.
If you are thinking you would get some challenge from monsters or bosses I can tell you now if you are a "Hardcore" gamer you will get disappointed because.
- Enemies look tough at first but after getting a certain sword you can pretty much kill them without sweating.
- Boss battles are fun they are but I don't know if its me always finding their weakness by equipping the right skill by luck or just them not being that hard, Hardest boss killed me about 3 times before figuring out what I was doing wrong or figuring out how to kill it.
So yeah your main enemy are those spikes ... Spikes SPIKES SPIKES everywhere enjoy dying a lot.
So gonna get to the pros and cons to get to my point.
PROS :
1 - Old school magic revived in a beautiful game, Music and sounds its all bringing memories.
2 - A lot of time to spend to grind for all the hidden items and what not.
3 - A lot of secrets to find and secret levels you'd need to play.
4 - Very reasonable price for this great game ( and a lot more pros )
CONS :
1 - At the first 3 days of launch it advertised Full Controller Support and I can assure you thats fake because you cant close the game or even pause it using a controller ( at least they edited it back to partial controller support ), Still not a reason Not to buy this game.
2 - A Few flaws in level design that might throw the game for some as you probably saw in some negative reviews, Yes the game is ridiculously hard at some points, you will die and die and die.
3 - The game has "fullscreen" but it doesnt cover my entire screen, In my 15.6 inch laptop with 1366x768 resolution, The game is 960 x 640 Although it doesn't even show in the screenshots I uploaded but its the truth, And the rest of the screen is just annoying black boarders, And the 1-2-3 windowed scaling's at number 3 the game goes out of my screen boarders ( Cant see hp and money .. etc )
4 - a few bugs here and there and this is what i found so far.
A - When the screen transition happens going from a screen to a screen sometimes it feels glitchy.
B - When dying or opening menu ( You can only open menu at save points ) it freezes for a few seconds and considering you will die a lot in the game thats bad, BUT the freezing is soo short but thought I should bring it up.
C - Most of the time when I kill monsters the gold they drop gets inside a rock and gets stuck there, Although I have an item that gives me the ability to act like a magnet to it, Still they get stuck and most of the time I cant pick them up.
D - When killing a boss and taking the Heart ( the victory music starts and character jumps ) SOME times after it ends the character will either do an extra jump or will walk a few steps to the direction I'm facing, Nothing wrong with it right ? wrong .. some bosses have spikes on the floor and after killing a Certain Crab boss I automatically walked left and fell to spikes and had to do the fight all over again.
E - After killing a boss if you touch it while its dying you will get damaged, And it killed me once and had to do the fight again, This might not be a bug might be how they wanted it for you to stay away after killing it so just be careful here :).
F - Theres also some serious FPS drop issue at the Final boss Spoiler >
it stayed around 36-38 the entire battle was all in slow motion, in both my pc and laptop ( and my pc is pretty tough )
and also some usual fps drops every now and then.

or to think that I just think its reasonable to have stuff like that fixed

Very good game. Overall good port from console, even if you want to play with mouse/keyboard (needs a little remapping, but not that much).
Story-wise, this game is a typical J-RPG : the main part of the narration are the relations between the main characters, which have various personnalities. The story/universe is original enough to keep us interested, but not used to its full potential. Instead, it's used to bring more dialogs and character-development. Like most J-RPG. You like it or you don't, it's just a matter of taste. But if you like J-RPG, you'll probably like it.
Like usual : you play western RPG for the world, eastern RPG for the characters.
Now the graphics : pretty good. Full 3D anime-style with VN-like dialogs. The FPS are steady everywhere, the loadings are fast. You never really wait while playing this game.
Gameplay-wise, it's a mix between action-RPG and turn-based RPG. Mostly turn-based. But it's complex enough to allow strategy during the battles. Not that much as a full T-RPG. If you like T-RPG, but don't want to think to much or like the visuals of action-RPG, then this battle system is for you.
However, battles can become a bit boring when you travel across a dungeon filled with weak enemies. But since we can avoid most battles, it's not that bad.
Balancing : I haven't reached the end-game yet, but I can already see it coming. The main character is just a beast. Unlock the right skill (I don't remember which, but it's fairly fast to unlock), and spam it against medium-strong enemies. Money is not a problem after like 2-3 hours, so you can buy lots of TP potions and spam your skills. So, the strategy is : buff your main character, use him to focus on the DPS (don't waste damage on near-dead enemies unless you really need to lower their number), and finish the crumbs with the other characters. The support character can deal some damage, but not enough to really match the dps of the main character. I find this kinda sad : all other strategies make the battles a lot longer, and thus bring boringness.
Last words : worth buying, worth playng, if you like J-RPG. You probably won't play it for 10 hours straight (it's not the kind of game that makes forget the flow of time), but you'll have no problem playing it like 2-3 hours a day everyday until you finish the game once or twice, since it's very enjoyable.

After dying over and over and over again in this permadeath game that is extremely hard for the wrong reasons, I gave up and am done with it. I just died on level 4 because I went into a room and two big zombies and three little ones were right against the door and two shooters were in the room and I had 75 health and no kits and died in about 2 seconds. And that is considering that it takes a incredible amount of luck to get to level 5 so you can permanently unlock the ability to start the game from level 3. Which is a bad idea anyway because when you start from a higher level at a later date, you keep none of your supplies. So basically, you absolutely have to do this game in one run. What makes the game so bad are a few things. First is that they expect you to navigate a list of ten or more items in the game while backpedaling from enemy swarms. It is very difficult because of the unnecessarily large variety of guns and bombs and food. It could have been somewhat easier had there simply been a few less different items to navigate. You can drop nailbombs and what not to blow up a pack of zombies while you run away, but you have to be extremely careful or it kills you too. Normally this all would be great, but the real game killer in my opinion are two things. One is hitboxes. They are very tiny. To shoot an enemy with your pistol you have to hit it directly in the head twice to kill. A body shot and your bullets pass through it without damaging it. I frequently find myself taking more than 2 shots to kill something and wasting my ultra scarce ammo because of the biggest flaw in the game which is the only real reason that it is so extremely difficult: enemy sliding and circle-stepping around you. I have seen it in many other games in my lifetime and I am not sure why developers do it. It is when an enemy gets close to you and melee attacks you but you can't land any shots or melee hits of your own because it magically circle floats around you while hitting you, draining tons of your life. This one is doubly upsetting because enemies also walk towards you in a slightly wobbly pattern, which combined with their very small one millimeter hitboxes, make it unbelievably frustrating.
The only thing I liked about this game were the graphics. They are vomit inducing blurry Atari 2600 graphics to most, but I found that it works alright for this particular game. Considering that it is a cheap game, I am perfectly happy just forgetting about it and playing one of the other 140+ great games that I have installed right now. I do not have to have anything else to do with this game to prove my gaming skills. I have beat some of the hardest games of all-time because they did not have poor hitboxing and float circling from enemies, two hallmarks of a poorly made game.
This game is a rare example of one that does not deserve the high praise that it got from some reviewers, but amazingly somehow ppl like it. I don't get it because I have had an easier time beating harder but much better programmed games.

So, I just beat Antichamber. I think. The fact that I'm uncertain about that already tells you a whole lot about this game. In technical terms, one would describe it best as a first-person Metroidvania puzzler; but most conventional genre descriptors are far too generic for this convention-defier. If you love puzzles that are so headache-inducingly ingenious that the preposterous becomes intuitive, or if you just like to have your gray matter tickled, I'd definitely recommend this game.
One downside I'd note, though, is that - for some people, such as myself - the game is not only figuratively, but also literally headache-inducing. I'm not sure whether it's the brightness of the visuals, the ambient sound design, or what, but I found it difficult to play this game for extended stretches of time, which is a shame because the game is quite addicting!
Oh, I should also add, the game was very kindly gifted to me; I would not say it's worth its current price tag, though how long you'll be playing it will strongly depend on your wits and your willpower to resist looking up strategy guides.

Keep to the high ground, and best of luck!

For those who love turn-based tactical games, XCOM is an excellent choice. A friend described it to me as "It's like Fire Emblem but with guns." In each mission, you command a squad of up to six members. There is, in fact, perma-death, so if there are casualties in combat, then they're lost forever. In between each mission, you go back to the base where you can assign research projects, assign construction projects, upgrade equipment, and manage satellite coverage around the world. So you, as The Commander, have control over the tactical combat side and the managerial side, making the learning curve a bit steep, but the tutorial does a good job of explaining things.
Pros:
+ You can fully customize your squad. You can change your squad members' names, hair colors, hairstyles, faces, and skin colors.
+ Everything looks cool. A few animations are a little choppy or awkward, but overall it's well done.
+ The soundtrack sounds like it could be from an awesome action movie. (I've recently discovered that it's the same composer for Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which is another great game.)
+ The voice acting is well done.
+ There are lots of options after completing the game to make future playthroughs more challenging.
Cons:
- The interface is a little glitchy.
- The Random Number Generator can be infuriating at times (or maybe I just have crappy luck). I've experienced several instances where one of my units would miss a shot that had a > 70% chance of hitting. At mid range. While flanking.
- Online multiplayer is a little disappointing. Network lag makes the interface behave worse than usual, and being limited to preset soldiers, as opposed to full customization of each soldier's abillities, takes away a significant part of the XCOM experience.

If you liked Dead Island but hated how "co-op" it felt because your character had little input in the story and it was just "the group", you might enjoy this more. Crane is a lot more engaged than the protagonists of Dead Island, which is pretty nice. However, his personality is lacking and all over. Oddly enough, he starts getting interesting during a story mission half way through the game, but the following mission has him making wise-cracks the entire time.
Even though the story is better than Dead Island, it is still very predictable, incredibly cliched, and hilarious most of the time. I mean, the game craps its self in the most glorious ways for no reason. If you think something is going to happen, you probably already know what is going to happen. Also, Rais is a good villain in the sense you hate him and just want to kill him so you can make him shut up. But he's really a terrible villain with no real logic behind his motives and he's probably Russian just so we could have that Cold War grudge against him as well. There's a side quest where you have to track down a serial killer in the Old Town that has a more interesting antagonist than Rais because you can believe he's actually crazy.
The urban exploration is really the highlight of this game; getting around can be very fun when you start upgrading your agility and especially after you get the grappling hook. Many of the towers you can climb really are fun to scale and even feel like you are there with both how good the game looks and how well it handles ambient noise. For instance, while climbing a radio tower, you can hear the steel beams creak and sway in the wind. Also how Crane constantly adjusts himself while on thin ledges really add to the feel that you are a human doing these things, unlike most games where you feel like you are playing as a box. I say this game would have been perfect if it had no zombies or story and focused purely on the parkour.
However, the parkour is not without fault. Sometimes, Crane refuses to grab onto ledges while scaling and that can result into accidentally falling to your death (which also is your number one cause of death). Also Crane is just so slow when you start the game. Yeah, he's just a guy; but he is also a special agent and he doesn't really feel like he has had any physical training besides "Above Average Strength and Stamina". I suggest not sleeping at night and just let the Volatiles chase you around while you get double XP and get to a safe zone for the agility bonus until you get the first intermediate upgrade. Even then, just play at night anyway because the game becomes more fun.
The combat is simultaniously one of the worst but best part of the game. It's either frustrating because the big enemies have incredibly big AoE attacks that you have to dodge 2-3 times in one direction to maybe dodge (even though you may still get hit), or too easy because the same big guys can be killed in two or three well placed hits with an upgraded mid-game weapon or a vanilla late game weapon. For how realistic the game looks, it's crazy how cartoony the fighting is. You should be disgusted that you just kicked the hipbones out of a zombie's body, but
. The combat skills you get are hilarious and are very effective; you can dropkick a zombie and send him flying like he got shot out of a cannon, or you can kill a zombie by grabbing his head and gently turning him to the right, or you can kill a zombie by jumping off a roof and slamming an axe through its body with enough force to create a shockwave that sends every zombie in a 3m radius flying.
Even then, the game put a lot of focus on the melee combat but forces you into firefights frequently in the main story. There are only five guns to pick from (two handguns, two rifles, and one shotgun), and they never scale in stats. That rifle you found at level 11 is the exact same at level 25 although it now costs more because it is orange. Also you'd imagine that since you can find the same guns all game, you can find the same melee weapons too, but apparently there's weapon extinction. I have a blueprint I never used because it needs a baseball bat and I never found a baseball bat all game and now I can't ever find one because they are "Low Level" weapons. I can fill all 18 inventory slots with Katanas and Khopeshes though!
I feel like the game blows its load on "Visually Interesting" very early then doesn't pick its self back up again until much later for how muddy and brown almost the entire game is, and then Old Town just feels like Italy which felt out of nowhere, because apparently the Harran World Games were to put it "on the map", but Harran was a global trade center for hundreds of years and a huge oil export with a rich cultural history.
This is the most well off apocalypse I have ever seen. You will get an abundance of cash and supplies only a few hours into the game. Just by playing as a kleptomaniac, you will never run out of anything you need besides String (at least in my experience, I only found about 20 pieces my entire time playing the main story, but started finding it all over after I beat the game). I'll even go so far to say that if you need ANY supplies right now, you could just add me and I could throw 20 of something at you and still have too much crap. You can even cross the bridge to get to a medical outpost and get about 25 medkits and gauze (as well as several police vans and ambulances to lockpick) inbetween missions and always have enough supplies.
I do find it very funny that the game tries to set up that the supply drops are a massive point of the game and the focus of survival, even though they stopped after two hours of playtime for me. Then they become far too common in the Old Town district (I found enough supply drops to get over 205,000 survival experience just by running around for an hour-- Not counting the XP you get from liberating the drops as well).
I also find it hilarious how often Crane gets his cover blown for how he is supposed to blend in and be a secret agent.
I will say the impression I got from early videos of the game was that you were just in the quarantine zone already and had to fight other survivors to get to the supply drops to survive, which I thought would be very interesting; seeing how people would act when supplies are low and there are zombies everywhere. But we barely get that and the game is just littered with random neutral survivors you have to save from time to time. I won't go so far to say that Techland again didn't deliver what they promised, but...

Castle in the Darkness is, as is evident from the screenshots, a retro love letter very similar to last year's Shovel Knight. An apparently one-man affair, Castle is full of references to old games, controls like old games, and has similarly frustrating design elements that old games have - remember all the instant-death spike pits in old games, like the NES Mega Man games? Remember how fun those were? No!? That's because they weren't fun, and they are ALL OVER this game.
The save points are frequent, but spaced out unevenly. Several times, I would beat a boss only to go to the next screen, die due to insta-death spikes, and have to rekill the boss. Also, the first time I launched the game, the sound didn't work at all - sad considering the soundtrack seems pretty good. Furthermore, it didn't detect my PS4 controller, so I had to play with a mouse and keyboard. A lack of display options is also frustrating, locking the game to an "old school" resolution. For a one-man effort, it's pretty impressive, and overall I'd recommend it. But for the love of god, STOP putting instant death spike pits into your retro platformers. Oh, and stop putting references to memes... it's so terrible and has never, ever, ever, EVER been funny in a video game.
