WARNING: Game requires a little effort on the players side to play the game... This game is not spoon fed to you. This game requires skill, timing, and hand eye coordination....
Sorry to break it to you guys but this game is heavily skill based... sure no mouse support... so what? keyboard controls are intuitive and relatively easy to use. They are in clusters that do not feel out of the way from one of the other keys you are using. That being said I'm using qwerty.
Pro's:
-Smooth playing experience
-Graphics feel like the old monster hunter games (I like them but I guess it is preference)
-Unique enemies with different move sets that FEEL exciting when fighting a new archtype.
-AI allies are GREAT sometimes too good actually, often find myself only selecting two or three versus the four.
-Tons of item trees and enough elemental strengths / weaknesses for you to really put thought into what you'll face.
-Town buff system(s) keep you going back for the extra boost that may make or break your next run!
-A bunch of different weapon archtypes that allow for you to find a playstyle that fits you!
Cons:
-A little unusual setup required with some hardware
-Fiddling with settings often required for a good experience
-Leaves you wishing the team that ported this simply added the keyboard keys for the animation and button listings in game as you have to think for the first hour or so what x,y,a,b or start for instance translates to on the keyboard.
Now with that out of the way, after the initial setup my experience has been AMAZING with this game. I love this type of game so my opinion might be biased but I highly recommend this for anyone who loves monster hunter games. Yes this game is locked at 30 FPS, and? it runs and plays better than some AAA games have on launch. No there is no mouse support, would honestly make the game too easy. The complaints on the controls are unjustified, if you can't be bothered to learn the controls how do you think you'll do with the more advanced mechanics of the game? Controller support is there but for brand name controllers which I think is understandable but a bit lacking for a broader audience. All in all I don't see what most of the quips are about, I paid ~50$ for the game and would pay it again.

I haven't played much yet but if you take games seriously you can already feel the multiple flaws that ruins the experience before you're even an hour in. I've played a lot of sidescroll/platformers over the years and I can say that this is not recommended until they patch the gameplay. From my perspective this feels like an easy money grab from the devs because I don't see how they would even dare release this game if they actually play tested it internally. Again, this game has potential if they fix it but in it's  current state it is a disaster.
Where to even start with this mess. The movement (jumping, moving and combat) is unacceptable quality for a game that isn't more than 50 megabytes. The acceleration is unnintuitive and the response time is poor. I have died way too many times because it's unnecessarily clunky/difficult to jump over gaps/pits when you stand still near the edge. Jumping is too fast relative to the game mechanics. I don't even know how they muck up the combat considering you can only press ONE button to attack enemies (no down/up attacks). Combat is clunky in the sense that your melee range is tiny and you can't make ANY contact with enemies after hitting them or you lose a third of your HP. You maybe have 10 pixels of safety when you got to melee enemies. Hitboxes vs bosses (I only played one mini-boss but again if they can't even get that right then the rest of the game can't be much better) are a joke. The visual animation of the sword attack doesn't reflect the hitbox either.
I was pretty excited for the death traps in the game but it's not what I expected. I was expecting that I would have to be aware at all times for any signs of traps but there is simply no way to know without dying or checking a playthrough. It makes the game unnecessarily repetitve because you get punished for things that are beyond your control which is not the "frustration" i look for when playing challenging platformers. One of the big flaws that essentially killed the game for me is the forced animation you get for picking items. You are forced to jump on the spot for about 30 seconds after getting a new item and imagine having to do that every time you die (which is very often). On top of it, the devs have joke based achievements related to death count when most of your deaths are from traps that you cannot fortell or because of terrible combat.
If you liked Super Mario games, Sonic, Donkey Kong Country or Shovel Knight I would highly recommend that you don't get the game in it's current state. If the devs fix the movement and the combat I think it would be worth the 5 euros either way.

In Mirror's Edge, you can choose to either play aggressively or passively. The whole fun of the game (and the obvious core) is running around and doing parkour in possibly one of the most beautiful cities you could ever parkour in (and clean).
For a game released in 2009, it's more than what you could ask for (visually/aesthetically talking).
The clean, peaceful and safe feeling that the environment around you provides is simply amazing (which is funny seeing how sometimes you might be running for your life).
Even though the overall game is visually stunning, some of the levels (again, visually speaking) will just keep you speechless (causing my deaths several times in several levels, but..."IT WAS TOTALLY WORTH IT."
The game itself, well. Some levels you will find incredibly frustrating and nearly impossible at times, but that's actually a good thing, or a pro about the game. The reason behind this is, because once you manage to accomplish the level, the satisfaction and the sense of accomplishment (and lets admit, cleverness) is beyond satisfying.
Cons? Well, my top recommendation is to disable physx. That is basically the killer of the game. It can cause severe (and I mean SEVERE) frame issues and lag, even going as far as crashing your game.
I'd also recommend avoiding confrontation when faced against many cops or snipers (oh how I despise those snipers).
Oh and, you'll find out what I mean when I say that you should probably RUN FOR YOUR LIFE when you're being chased by your shadows (or runner's shadows, not quite a spoiler. As you probably don't have a clue of what I'm taking about).
If you're having problems in deciding if the game is worth it or not, I guarantee it, if you love parkour and stunning visuals, go for it. I'd also recommend it so you get to know the origin of Mirror's Edge (as the second one will be coming out eventually).
What are you waiting for, buy the game!

It's a fun game.  But I find that it challenges your suspension of disbelief.  As you continue playing it, you start to realize that the story can dissociate drastically from the gameplay.
For instance...on the first playthrough, I one-shot a boss.  Cue the upcoming visual novel cutscene where the characters are wincing in pain and groaning about how strong the boss is.  I reaaally didn't get that impression.
So my suggestion is that if you get the game...play the game and follow the story.  But don't play the game AND follow the story.  Treat the two separately, and I think you'll find that it's entertaining as a game and tells a fairly interesting story.  But if you treat the two as one unit, expect to lose some brain cells when the gameplay and story start hand-waving.
This game is a bit weird.  In an era of RPGs where you're able to allocate your stats as you see fit, this game sort of falls back to the traditional method of level-up = auto-allocate stats.  Granted, there is a way to boost your attack stats, but I dearly wish I could up my characters speed / accuracy.  Speed because I'd like to give a certain character in the party the ability to attack first.  Accuracy because there are certain attacks in the game that give 300% damage, but they miss really often.
It turns out that it's not so much that they miss often but that the enemy has an easy time dodging them.  I figured this out when I used these techniques on low level enemies...whereas I would have a 20% hit rate on equivalent level opponents, At level 55, I had a 100% hit rate on level 30 mobs.
The only way to boost the speed and hit rate is to complete a set of challenges.  These require you to do weird things like jump around as the leader of the party or send the enemy flying so you can use interception attacks.  They wouldn't be so bad ordinarily, but I do have complaints about jumping 5000 times per character just to max out the challenge.
Personally, I liked playing this game a lot.  I just wish that I managed to get the Eryn ending first try.  I don't know what I did wrong to get the Tiara ending.
Oh yeah, I suggest turning on Japanese voices occasionally.  You'll find that all sorts of things are voiced that aren't in the English Dub.  For instance, the Fury Fairies.

12 Labours of Hercules IV: Mother Nature is a casual resource/time management strategy game. This time around, Hercules and Megara are trying to restore the land. Hercules still does the heavy work if there's a boulder in the way and Megara still brings the fruit bushes to life and also restores life to the dead trees. At the start of each level, you have 1 or 2 workers who you direct to do various things ranging from collecting resourses to constructing and upgrading buildings or gold mines. You also have to contend with bandits trying to steal your resourses. There are the familiar characters of Medusa, Cerberus, Cyclops, and Pegasus who help get rid of the minotaurs, ghosts, rescue sheep and move rocks to aid in the journey. If you find all the puzzle pieces in levels .1-.10 you can put the puzzle together and unlock a bonus level. Nice forth entry of the series and overall it's a very enjoyable time management and if you're a fan of the genre you should pick it up.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 / Biohazard Revelations 2 Review – Raymond KT
Summary: The beginning of the Resident Evil Revelations 2 tale sees fan favorite Claire Redfield make a dramatic return. Survivor of the Raccoon City incident depicted in previous Resident Evil games, Claire now works for the anti-bioterrorism organization Terra Save. Moira Burton, is attending her welcome party for Terra Save when unknown armed forces storm the office. Claire and Moira are knocked unconscious and awaken later to find themselves in a dark and abandoned detention facility. Working together, they must find out who took them and to what sinister end. Will Claire and Moira make it out alive and discover what’s led to them being taken to this remote island? A story of twists and turns will have players guessing the next step at every turn.
Overall, these “new” Resident Evil games I’m overall disappointed with, I personally wish the series returns to it core, which I’m happy they did btw.
Recent releases in the series vary sharply in quality. For example, Resident Evil 6 is a much messier game than the first Revelations. But they share one important trait: an uncertainty about what Resident Evil is and a willingness to throw everything at the wall. Revelations 2, it seems, has it figured out. By sticking to the tense action first brought to the series in Resident Evil 4, Revelations 2 finds a focus that recent entries have sorely lacked. It has its own strange experiment as a series of episodic releases, but that's just a distraction from the exceedingly strong game at the core here. The dueling storylines set up a predictable rhythm to each episode of the game: You explore an area as Claire and Moira, reach a cliffhanger ending, switch over to Barry and Natalia, the mysterious little girl he teams up with, and retread the same areas but from a different angle. The repetition can get a little numbing by episode three or so, especially because these aren't terribly unique or beautiful settings. Aside from a few outdoor areas on the scenic island where Claire and Moira have been dumped, Revelations 2's locations read like a checklist of generic video game levels: abandoned prison, sewer system, rundown apartment building, etc. The graphics — a minor upgrade over the first game — weren't impressive enough to make those spaces much more interesting. I always pushed through, but that was completely thanks to the solid essentials of the gameplay. The main essential is, of course, combat. Resident Evil Revelation 2's gunplay just feels really good. Even with my earliest, weakest weapons, the shambling hordes of the undead actually reacted to being shot, so I knew I was causing damage. Headshots and hitting other weak points brought enemies down faster; I felt rewarded for thinking my actions through and playing strategically. You can also expand your options through skills that you purchase with gems scattered throughout each area. New finisher moves for Barry and Claire were essential unlocks, while I struggled to get a handle on other upgrades, such as one that caused my shots to do more damage if I fired while crouching. In a single playthrough, I unlocked less than half of all the skills available, so there are almost certainly other cool strategies I completely missed. With all of this emphasis on shooting, old-school Resident Evil fans may be wondering where the horror is and, well ... it's not really here at all. Ammo can be sparse at points, especially given the huge number of enemies you're put against, so resource management is a concern. But this mostly just serves to raise tension. Beyond a few early jump scares, there weren't many moments of pure terror in Revelations 2.

XCOM: Enemy Within is mostly a turn based strategy game with a small hint of RPG. You are the commander of a revived faction known as XCOM. Your mission: Protect planet earth from the incoming invasion of an enemy we know little about. Sixteen nations fund this project and will continue to do so if they feel you are helping them against this intrusion but if eight nations withdraw from the project it is game over. Starting from scratch you must decided what to build onto your base, hire and train a small army of soldiers, manage fighter aircraft to control and montitor the skies, assign research projects to develope new weapons and tools, and use your engineers to build the technology developed.
This game will keep you glued to your seat as you either hopeless try to survive each month or you get the upper hand and begin taking the fight to the aliens. Your decisions directly effect the outcome of the planets future and failure is always just one wrong move away. The only downside to this game right now is a number of bugs that make it frustrating to play, but these bugs don't happen that often.
The multiplayer is addictive. Using a point system assigned to each type of unit each commander in the duel can build a loadout compose of six 'slots'. The loudout has  a certain point limit that each player must stay within and then the duel commences, it is always a different game when you play XCOM whether it be in SP or MP.
Overall I give this game a 9 out of 10. (10 being the best)

If you own any Monster Hunter game at all, and you are after an experience that will match a true Monster Hunter game I would not personally look here. I was personally unable to run it without it causing my Nvidia 780Ti driver's to crash after about 10 minutes or so of gameplay. However, I did study available footage of the PS4 version to see if struggling to fix the game was worthwhile, and if I hadn't I would not be wasting my time with this review with such little time played.
On every account the game seemed to be the Hack-and-Slash gameplay of a Dynasty/Samurai warriors game. Which I can and do enjoy on their respective series. However, I do have trouble imagining that this formula which works well for tearing through entire armies would work equally well for lengthy fights on single creatures. Sadly it looks like the majority of fights in this game are also considerably underwhelming and uninventive; amounting to little more than perhaps an uninteresting MMO boss with a big HP bar. In contrast Monster Hunter's monsters have significantly more interaction, varying states, are faster paced and have interaction with their environments (climbing, hunting, eating, sleeping, hanging from ceilings and more). While both games do boil down to "dodge the attack on the tell", Monster Hunter gives you a significantly larger pool of options to combat your adversary.
The contrast between these two game's weapon and item systems is evidently told through discussions and guides in each weapon found online. Both games fundamentally have a three button weapon style in addition to a dodge button. While both games have weapon combos, the combos and rate of attack are what set most melee weapons apart in Toukiden: Kiwami. In a Monster Hunter game, despite having a significantly larger pool of weapons each plays significantly differently. Despite the Greatsword, Longsword and Sword and Shield all having swords in their name, none of those weapons truly play in any similar fashion, and not all enemies can be approached the same way with the same weapon; with many monsters moving in different ways and their individual parts all taking different varying damage to different types and elements. In the case of Toukiden however the the largest significant difference of any weapon is that ranged weapons can hit high targets consistently.
Customisation in items and gear are significantly different. Toukiden: Kiwami’s armour only significantly varies on its defence and resistance values. Weapons differ only on damage values, elemental bonuses and slots. These “slots” are for the Mitama system, which is a much more pick up and play, simple variant of Monster Hunter’s decoration system. By using the Mitama which are basically the spirits of fallen Toukiden heroes of the past, you can level up and receive bonus skills that improve attack, HP etc. It is more simple than the Monster Hunter system, which that game was never good at explaining (after all it isn’t uncommon to see new people with mixed gear sets with less than +10 in skills online - rendering it useless). However one of the fan favourite aspects of any Monster Hunter entry is delving into the gear progression it offers. This isn’t even counting the fact MH has a significant pool of consumable items that make preparing for any individual fight a take in itself.
Other issues I will run off quickly. The female walking animation was significantly bad, like some kind of demon warding washing machine dance of the wrists. The hub town was bland, unintuitive and the game’s pacing rushes you right back out of the town before you can become acquainted on your first visit. Lastly despite the fact the game advertised that it would auto-save, it never onced saved after the first tutorial fight, forcing me to face that Oni five times due to crashes.
I wanted nothing less than this game to be good. I do believe there is room for a Monster Hunter clone on the PC, especially one capable of bringing some decent competition to Capcom's dominating franchise. Port issues aside, I do not believe I could have reccomended this game due to its lack of complexity and the uninspired adaptation of Dynasty Warriors gameplay to the MH genre. Keep playing Monster Hunter if you have the choice. In case you still want to go forward and purchase this game, make sure you have a controller and I hope for the best you don't run into significant port issues.

Edit 3.5: Short conclusion: I personally enjoy the game content itself, but list several shortcomings below.  If you still want to buy the game after reading this, there's a really good chance you'll enjoy it.
You may enjoy this game if:
* you like co-op action/RPGs or games similar to Monster Hunter or Phantasy Star Online (PSO)
* looking for a feudal / ancient Japanese themed setting
* have a game pad or don't mind playing with keyboard without a mouse
* have an existing group of friends playing this game for multiplayer co-op
* do not mind playing in full-screen
* do not mind playing with capped frame rate of 30 FPS
* appreciate a well-rounded soundtrack
* don't mind payng full game cost (at the time of this review)
Do NOT get this game if:
* (Partial Addressed as of 7/6) if you have any of the "problematic" hardware or software (may want to check the discussion boards here to see what those have been) as you may be troubleshooting or reconfiguring your hardware just to play this one game
* you're hoping for an seamless multiplayer interface as it is a lobby-based interface that requires a player to be idle in a lobby for you to join (cannot play a mission, cannot select a mission, cannot be crafting.)
* no automatic refresh or join on the lobby system, either create a lobby and wait around or manual refresh to find a compatible game
* you use keyboard and mouse, because the game cannot reassign actions to the mouse (if the reverse happened, where a PC port to console required you to use a keyboard/mouse to enjoy the game, I suspect many console gamers would not be pleased that their primary interaction method is not supported)
* you like to play in windowed mode and have a decent framerate -- the game speed is literally tied to frame rate, so a steady frame rate of 20 FPS means 66% gameplay speed
* you like to play games at 60 FPS and run at normal gameplay speed (Omega Force had the DW6 port for PC capable of running at 60 FPS in 2008)
* would like to use the keyboard to chat with people you meet, input names or notes -- you have to use the game's UI to select one letter at a time
* would like to look up the Steam name of someone you meet to chat with them there, because there doesn't seem to be a way yet -- use the preprogrammed messages in the game instead
* you would like an English dub or even English subtitles for the "battle cries," -- neither exist and I don't think they will
* do not like a UI that does not move if you move too fast through it
* if you would like to customize your face by eye style, eye color, nose style, mouth style, chin style, or facial hair -- you have 1 of 20 pre-configured faces per gender to choose from and possibly only two with facial hair that does not reflect your hair color
* if you want other body types per gender -- as you cannot be a slim ninja, a short rifleman, or a hulking hammer wielding warrior, you all have the same body size
Minor things I personally don't like on top of the above:
* animation locks and slow animations can make combat feel not as fluid as Dynasty Warriors 8 (a Tecmo Koei game)
* segmented maps with multiple loading screens during a mission
* (7/6 update) frame rate dips in full screen have been rare these days
Things I do like:
* the music
* the Japanese era-like setting
* story character portraits
* used to like forcing V-Sync on the GPU and running at 60 FPS even if the game speed is doubled ~ actually feels more fluid (accidentally ran with V-Sync off and the game was running 200+ FPS ~ could not even select Continue) (7/6 Update) this is no longer a possibility with the current executable and is far more stable across my three machines
* variety of bosses to fight
* variety of combat styles and configurations
* the ability to hide helmet on most armor styles
* hoping senpai will notice me in the hot springs
* no crashes on primary machine yet
The store page game summary reflects single-player gameplay elements and story well enough.
Conclusion as of July 2, 2015):
I saw the negative reviews in the most helpful section and could not find a positive review for many pages so I looked at the positive reviews only.  I was cautiously optimistic for what looked like a "samurai" themed co-op action RPG.  Some may wonder, "You have a lot of hours clocked in and it works for you, why don't you recommend it?  I don't understand."  In terms of the game working for me, I feel like I happen to be lucky.  I typically don't feel lucky with these pre-2012 machines, but it's like this game was made for it (and that's bad in 2015.)  At first I tried to give the game at least three hours to give my review some weight and then once I was past the reasonable refund point, I felt obligated to get my money's worth.  I'm also starved for this niche atmosphere with RPG elements.  The gameplay is a 3 out of 5 stars for me with co-op tipping it upward.
I probably dialed my expectations back to 2007, because when I think about things we've seen in other games these past fews years: separation of character face options, the ability to dye clothing, drop-in and drop-out co-op, responsive controls, KB/M support (look at almost any 3rd person action game for working examples), the list goes on.  And then I realized how much potential the game doesn't tap into, but even before that, some basic PC features aren't addressed properly.  Even the "console expectation," that the game will work right out of the box is not an unreasonable expectation.  Even still, there's a few things that would nudge this game into the recommended / thumbs up side:
* Keyboard and Mouse support
* Improved PC optimization
* Support for 60 FPS
In general, if Koei addressed those three points above on top of not cutting out features found in console versions, I believe that TK could prevent most of the negative reviews (and probably get a lot more sales out of not just this game, but their other products as well.)  Please consider this for the future TK.

================THE REVIEW================
You've probably heard two things about Teleglitch: it's a rogue-like, and it's hard.
This is an exaggeration and underestimation, respectively.  Teleglitch is a rogue-like only insofar as the rooms are arranged differently each playthrough, and it's hard like a diamond ball bat to the groin.  Let's examine these points in more depth, because there are some things you need to know.
Once the awe of
(sarcastic "ooooh! aaaaah!") wears off, you'll quickly start to notice that every game of Teleglitch is essentially the same.  The items you receive on any given level are the same items you'll ALWAYS recieve on that level.  The question is whether or not you'll find them BEFORE or AFTER that room where you always get mobbed by that one enemy type that's always in there.  End result: each game of Teleglitch is unique in only the most superficial way.  And because you will die SO MUCH, the whole thing quickly becomes tiresome and repetitive.  This repetition wouldn't be a bad thing if, like many other rogue-likes, there was some incremental GAIN or REWARD at the end of each game.  But there isn't.  The recipe for success in Teleglitch is 5% experience, 10% luck, 25% resource conservation, and 70% ninja master reflexes.  Yes, that adds up to 110%, because if you give less, you will FAIL.  That brings us to the second topic.
I know what you're thinking: "Oh, but I'm the exception.  I have superior gaming skills.  I'm sure Teleglitch will be easy enough for me that I won't want to BRAIN A KITTEN in frustration."
NO.  You are NOT special.  Well, maybe to your mom.  Lemme hit you with some cold, hard statistics.  Literally NINETY NINE POINT ONE PERCENT of players never beat the game.  But that's setting our sights too high.  What are the odds that you'll give up before even beating level THREE?  of TEN!?
91.3%
That's right.  You have less than a ten percent chance of making it less than a third of the way through Teleglitch before refusing to ever play it again.  Some games manage to find the recipe for making brutal difficulty enjoyable.  Teleglitch's brand of hard is more like a basketball game between an NBA team going all-out and a team of middle school girls with Down Syndrome.  Sure, it sounds amusing at first, but only the truly sick fail to quickly realize it's just in very poor taste.
Oh, and it also has bugs that can cause you to die, just in case you were legitimately doing well.
Honestly, I really want to like Teleglitch.  Instead I just friggin' hate it.  Yet for some reason I'll probably play it another 20 hours.
================END OF ORIGINAL REVIEW================
Do I still hate Teleglitch?  Yes.  But it is a hate tempered with respect.  And... I... kinda like it.
Will I change my recommendation to "Yes"?  No.  You should still be afraid of Teleglitch.

I love this game! I adore it! Besides classic roguelikes this is the indie game where I sunk the biggest amount of time.
The gameplay (and the most thourough): The gameplay is teeeeense! Thanks to permadeath. The gunplay is great. I really enjoy the (lack of) accuracy in some weapons, forcing us to close in. I really enjoy the weapon variation in this game. The only completely useless weapon is the nailgun but I guess it isn't that useless to a newbie that preferes to avoiding taking matters in their hands.
I am talking about the knife of course. Lots of players think that the first levels are tedious because we have to knife pretty much everything the fodder mutants. And maybe the reactivated zombie.
The variety of enemies is also amazing because they feel very different from each other with different patterns. I really love the bosses (wish there were even more bosses) and I liked that "surprise" in level 6. You know the one. As if I didn't need another reason to be tense.
The crafting is also a very important aspect of the game. I really don't feel the need to install mods that lets me dissessemble things because I already have pretty everything I need during the game. I need to try a mod sometime. But the thing is, the decisions that needs to be made regarding "Do I use this now or later? Should I drop something to take a mg-3600 with me to get highter chances of getting that minigun in the future? I won't really need this nailbomb do I?" Just wish there were more yellow items.
The Arena is also mad fun for someone that wants to kill mutants, reactivated units, bots without the concern of dying and running out of ammo. So very satisfying.
The randomness in this game gives me very fresh feeling runs one after another. You have no idea how much I would've played Metal Gear Solid or the Souls series if they randomly changed the enemy placements, this is the essential for a game with infinate replayability. Of course you went with the other roguelikes formula and you also randomly placed the map rooms and corridors. Simple but imensely effective. Which leads too...
Graphics/Sound: Hell, it is not even simple, because then the devs went "Ok, so these are kinda static rooms so I guess we need to go ahead and give it some detail.". I wouldn't say that the graphics are bad. They just leave a huge amount to the players imagination. Hell, I know I spend some time imagine some of the sectos in the game. 12 Labours of Hercules: Mother Nature is the fourth installment of its' series developed by JetDogs Studios and Zoomout Games. Previous installment: 12 Labours of Hercules, Cretan Bull, Girl Power.
There is a storyline for the game but it isn't much to it nor its' rememberable. The gamplay formula is pretty much the same as its' predecessors.
Unlike its' predecessors. This is the first game from the series to have a platinum edition.
This is a time management game, where careful planning is required, limited amount of resources that are available throughout the game; hence the word management.
This game has the total of five episodes with eleven levels each; totaling out fifty-five levels altogether. The five bonus levels can be unlocked when the jigsaw puzzle is completed. The fifth episode is a bonus episode.
There are three modes, relaxed; casual and expert, the difference between them is the timer speed and scoring. In relaxed mode, no timer and no scoring. In casual mode, the timer drain a slowly and the scoring is moderately low. In expert mode, the timer drain much quicker and the scoring is much higher.
The stars that are earned from completing the level depends upon on how much time is left on the timer. This only applies to the causal and expert modes
Three Gold star is when the time has not gone pass the arrow. Two Silver star is when the time has gone pass the arrow. One Bronze star is when the timer is empty.
Replaying any of the levels will improve the game score and the amount star.
The Palace is build after each levels that has been completed in gold record time.
There are few special bonuses: Freeze Time, Worker Movement/Work Speed, Additional Worker and Increases Resources. All of these special bonuses has a certain time limit but they can be used again once the bar fills-up. These special bonuses are very useful when the game is being played on expert mode.
There are twenty-two different achievements to earned from playing the game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements in order to unlock them.
There are nine different wallpapers. They can be accessed through the game's main menu screen.
There are seven different trading cards to collect. Only three cards are dropped from the game. The remaining cards:  Purchase from the Steam Market; Steam Booster Pack Creator and or Drop; Trade with friends. The cards are then used to craft the game's badge and upgrade it.
I don't think that this game much of replay value to it. If you're into time management games then you might find this game somewhat enjoyable to certain extent.

Pros;
- was actually quite scary to begin with (the first night was awesomely pant staining)
- the free running is pretty fluid and they don't make a big thing of it, its just a good game mechanic.
- some of the climbs you have to do are truly vertigo inducing and very fun.
- weapon modding is ok (although you can't mod firearms), it requires a fair bit of scavenging and it enables you to make some pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥weapons.
- the map, the detail! omg this game is stunning. I frequently found myself being like a tourist and stopping to take pictures. Especially at sunset or dawn, it really is a work of art.
- combat with the z's is enjoyable at all stages of the game. to start with they're quite a problem, later you can cut your way through whole crowds of them. But it lulls you into thinking you're unstoppable and then they over power you!
- the "volatiles" (which come out at night) are really hard to deal with (and in the beginning pretty scary). For at least half way through the game you don't really stand a chance trying to fight them (1 maybe, any more and your doomed), so RUN! Later on when you've made some powerful weps you can deal with groups of them, but you don't have much room for error otherwise they will overpower you. So I found that a fun aspect.
Cons
- lock picking. I can see what they're going for, making you sit in a potentially dangerous area while trying to pick the lock, but the process gets really tedious.
- DEATH - WORSE ASPECT OF THE GAME. when you are on a mission and not just roaming, dying really sucks. It makes the game FAR too easy because the world does not get reset. So you spawn back in having dealt with half the Z's but now you're at full health and its just way way too easy. You also lose out of some nice scripted sections because having spawned back in the script has already run and doesn't get reset. So try not to die!
- SPOILER ALERT
End boss fight.  Lame lame lame lame lame. Maybe its cos I'm of the generation who grew up on games like System Shock 2 and HL1. But boss fights where all you do is mash certain keys are just so boring and unsatisfying. I want to actually fight, maybe get creative (and perhaps a bit sadistic) in how I deal with the boss.  Not to just hit a key when it flashes up. Breaks immersion and its so darn easy, it's just a pre-rendered sequence (amusing your inner chimp manages to mash the right key on time).
The game does make you feel pretty vengeful towards the boss and you really want to slice him up limb by limb, but all you get is press A press D press W, then masturbate the F key a bit and your done.

is an action horror game that plays like a FPS. Fans of the old-school RE games will find the harder difficulties more to their liking, where the game is more about dodging and running and conserving ammo than about shooting everything that moves.
The campaign has 5 difficulty modes. First, you have your casual, normal and survival modes (= easy through hard). While playing those, you'll unlock 'countdown mode' and 'invisible mode'. The former means you're on a timer and the latter means all the monsters are invisible. Yes, really.
Raid mode has 4 difficulties. You start with the normal difficulty levels and play through these to unlock the hard, very hard and 'code red' varieties of the missions.
When you increase the difficulty, monsters have more health and deal more damage, but they also move faster. Especially that last part makes the increase in difficulty very noticeable, requiring you to adapt your tactics.
Just like in the first
game, you'll be going through the campaign with a partner. However, the role of these companions is greatly improved in this sequel. There is a lot more interaction between them and you can control either of the characters, and switch between them as needed. Generally speaking, you have a gun-wielding character and a support character who can find hidden items (this replaces the 'Genesis' from the first game) and can stun monsters. The game does a good job of explaining the dynamics between the characters and the tactics you can derive from their synergy.
Companion AI is pretty bad, though. Even after purchasing a skill that allows characters to shoot guns while AI controlled, they will mostly still use melee attacks. Or do absolutely nothing. They get stuck everywhere, even at the edge of an open door. They always insist on moving away from the spot where you left them when switching to the other character, confusing you when you switch back.
The theme of bioterrorism is again present in this sequel but it's only grazed, really.  The story is pretty much stand alone, although some of the main characters are recurring from earlier RE games and sometimes refer to events that took place in those games.
Claire Redfield and her friend and co-worker Moira Burton are kidnapped and put in a creepy detention facility that's inhabited by zombielike creatures. A woman who calls herself 'the overseer' talks to them through a strange bracelet they find on their wrists, but she mostly speaks in riddles.
In each episode, there's a second storyline that sees Barry Burton tracking his daughter, trying to find her. He teams up with a young girl called Natalia, another of the overseer's kidnap victims who appears to have a sixth sense for spotting hidden monsters and items.
At the end of the fourth episode, the whole story doesn't make a lot of sense when you think about it, but the story does keep you interested and entertained enough while it unfolds.
At the end of each campaign mission, you're awarded BP ('bonus points') that you can spend in two ways:
The difficulty modes, medals, skills and rewards add a huge amount of replayability. As does the fact that you can select any campaign mission to replay, and all of your items carry over. So you can farm ammo and other items in an easy mission to have an advantage in a difficult mission. Lastly, Barry's campaign takes places 6 months after Claire's. This means that while playing as Claire, you can take certain actions that influence how Barry's campaign plays out when he arrives at the same place.
Raid mode is back but it's vastly expanded and improved upon compared to the first game: more missions (53), more weapon types (6), more weapon upgrades (41), more playable characters (15) and more elite monster skills (15).
You start raid mode in a vestibule where you select the character you want to play, your weapons, the upgrades for those weapons and your character's active and passive skills. You also have access to a store where you can buy weapons, weapon upgrades and ammo.
You then select a mission to play. By completing missions, you earn gold, XP, weapons or weapon upgrades and you unlock more missions and more playable characters. The maps for the raid mode missions are mainly taken from
. One or two are from the first Revelations game and you'll recognize the rest from Revelations 2's campaign.
Your character gains levels from 1 to 100, allowing you to tackle increasingly more difficult missions. Each time you level up, you get some skill points to spend. Weapons also have a level from 1 to 100, reflecting their power.
Graphics have a higher resolution than the first
game, which means they're sharper but everything's a bit smaller. The graphics are also darker and less colourful this time, but that adds to the grim atmosphere of the game.
The music is great. Not in the way that you'd want to listen to the soundtrack when you're not playing
, but in the way that it fits the game's atmosphere perfectly. The music is usually subtle and quietly in the background, adding to the creepy atmosphere, and it gets symphonic and bombastic when you're in an epic fight against a boss or running for your life against the clock. The sound effects are very good, too.
The voice acting is top notch and all the voice actors deserve the highest praise for adding a lot of personality to their characters and for delivering their lines with the right amount of emotions.

The game moves fast. So you have to be faster. You’re in a ship within a space IN space. (Space-ception? O.O) And your limited range of movement makes it that much more difficult to time your attacks and maneuver your way around and away from enemies.
Timing is very important as it’s the key to get the highest score and staying alive. Using your Pulse Cannon let’s you destroy a bunch of enemies in a small radius around you. This is absolutely vital because if you find yourself cornered, a perfectly timed Pulse Cannon can stand between sweet, sweet victory or utter death and dishonor on your family and your cow.
I admit, at first, I really did NOT like this game simply because I got frustrated very easily because I was dying all the time. But after I revisited the tutorial and fiddled around with the Pulse Cannon, it became progressively easier if a bit more challenging, but in a ‘I’m not dying every 2 minutes’ kind of way. And that’s good.
There are a variety of levels with various enemies that come at you in patterns or sporadically. You need to be alert as sometimes they mix. What may start as a pattern could quickly end up a smorgasbord of death coming straight for you if you don’t pay attention. Also, don’t go willy nilly with the Pulse Cannon as the ring your ship is inside of indicates how much juice you have left to use it. Killing enemies refills it and there are tricks to use the Pulse Cannon indefinitely if you can kill as many enemies as you can and time its use. Killing enemies also changes your single shooter and upgrades it to a triple stream of death.
You can play with a keyboard/mouse or controller. I
recommend playing with a controller. It just feels a much more natural. Left thumbstick moves your ship while the right fires. Left and right bumper activate your Pulse Cannons.
Low-poly make for lovely visuals as the colors are vibrant and the particle effects are great. The music is outstanding and I found myself moving and bobbing left and right to the music. It definitely fits the genre well and changes with and during each level, so it’s never the same.
If you’re a fan of twin sticks with a twist and swarms of enemies trying to kill you all at once, then Son of Sc♥♥♥♥♥♥ is deininitely one you shouldn’t pass up. Coupled with challenging gameplay, sick beats, and pleasing visuals, SoS is a pretty good time if you don’t mind dying a whole lot before coming up with the perfect strategy. You will die A LOT in the beginning, but once you master your Pulse Cannon timing, picking off packs of enemies becomes easier. I believe in you, Young Padawans!

Many people told me to play South Park: Stick of Truth. I stopped watching around Season 12 and after playing through this masterpiece I am going to revisit the cartoon series.
Story: 9.5 / 10 - A satirical and enjoyable RPG with all the flavour of Trey Parker and Matt Stone.
Sound: 10/10 - Be prepared for tonnes of great voice acting, sounds and nostalgic South Park music packaged nicely in this game as well as some gratuitous flatulence and more.
Gameplay: 9/10 - An open-world map but I rarely felt challenged in combat. There were enough puzzles and abilities to keep the game rolling. I would compare combat to Paper Mario or perhaps Super Mario RPG. There are also many side quests and fun to be had aside from the main story. Four classes to choose from I would say it's replayable on a higher level of difficulty.
Graphics: 8.5/10 - Perfection in design. It was like watching an episode of South Park except you control a character.
Controls 9/10 - The controls were intuitive and easy to learn. I used Keyboard/Mouse because I could not figure out how to fart with my controller.
Overall 9/10 - I can definetely tell Trey Parker and Matt Stone were very involved with this South Park game and it is scripted perfectly by Obsidian. Don't miss this one if you are currently or ever have been a fan of the series!
Completion time: Approx 15-20 hours for Main quest + Side stuff playing on Normal

Son of Scoregasm (SoS) is an excellent but difficult twin-stick shooter, where you manouver through 28 unique levels. Every level has it's own special challenge. In one level you are faced with hordes of enemies, the next one you have to keep two rollers at bay.
Most interesting is the score-system. It is perfectly possible to finish a level, kill all enemies, and have zero points. This is due to the face that you have two attacks, one with regular bullets, and one that acts like a proximity EMP. In order to score points, you have to first kill enemies using your EMP attack, which increases your multiplier, after which you can score points with your bullets, This leads to very interesting gameplay: while trying to survive, you also have to balance killing enemies with your two attack-types. How far will you raise your multiplier before going for the bullet-kill? It's the difference between simply survival and the top-score on the leaderboard!
SoS is a fun, but difficult game. But of course you don't shy away from a challenge, do you?

Where to start..
First of all: Toukiden is a one-of-a-kind hunting experience on the PC, in a unique mix between the button-mashing, spectacle fighting experience of Dynasty Warriors and Monster Hunter.
Sounds quite hard to manage, doesn't it? However Toukiden manages!
Hundreds of Armor und Weapon Sets each coming with it's own Stat-Boni and absolute gorgeous and unique design with each and every single Set. You have every possible customization option avaiable, up until the higher ranks.
What makes Toukiden different however is first and foremost it's Mitama System. Every few bosses/quests, you will loot a Mitama - some sort of Spirit Essence of Ancient Personalities (= that actually existed. It's really interesting to read up on those)
These Mitama can be inserted in your Weapons to give not only Stat Boni, but also alter your Skill Set. This highly influences the Dinamic of High-Ranked fights, when in a party of up to 4 players. It's way more engaging than Monster Hunter and communicating with your fellow Slayers is not only a necessity, but through a 5-Pages Message Menu not only easy but it can wholly substitute a voice chat, making Matchmaking with Strangers more pleasant than other Games of a similar genre.
Another huge difference is the much more developed story of Toukiden in contrast to Monster Hunter, a Story which albeit lacks depth, can be engaging in certain key moments and had me on the edge of my chair in certain situations, like the finale of Ch. 2. It manages your tension and keeps you interested, even if you may or may not be a fan of the hunting genre.
Lastly the Boss-Fights. They are exactly what you'd expect. It's Monster Hunter, but with giant, greatly designed Demons, based on Japanese Mythology. It has it's own charme, but I do find some of the Bosses lacking in personality in contrast to the Monster Hunter Franchise.
To conclude:
Toukiden is a gorgeous mix between Dynasty Warriors and Monster Hunter, which exceeds the Customization Options of the latter with the Mitama System. It tries to get you interested in the History surrounding this very over-the-top hunting game through the Mitama-History Section as well as reading up on what the Oni for example are actually based on.
The combat is fluent and keeps you hooked for hours on end, as well as being less grindy than Monster Hunter. Especially if you're shooting for a 100% Completion. Multiplayer got much more love and interaction between players is highly supported, which makes the random-matchmaking an absolute bliss.
Additionally (even if I lack some experience in that field) - the Game seems to have a very good Netcode, so that I was able despite my very bad Internet-Connection to even Host entire Lobbys without Lag or similar issues.
All in all, if you can be interested in the Style of Toukiden and you're looking for a more fast-paced Monster Hunter: This game is definitly woth every cent!

Having never played the originals I cannot comment on the nostalgia feel, or improvements that were made or not implimented.
However, the game itself is a pure tacticians dream.  The game immerses you as the officer in command who must tell his troops where to go and what to do.  In the beginning you control up to 4 soldiers on a field of battle that is turn-based.  You must first order your soldiers where to move, and if possible what to do after moving.  Such as attacking an enemy, or setting up cover fire, throwing a grenade, etc.
You are also in command of the main base where your soldiers are housed and all the technology and weapons come from.  As you progress in the game you are given currency to spend on makeing facilities, building armor or weapons, and also building aircrafts to protect the skies with as well.  Depending on how well you do in the missions you can also gain access to various research options which will allow you to make better upgrades for your soldiers or aircrafts you make.
This game can become highly addictive, and if you play each mission very cautiously like I did you will end up finding yourself watching the hours go by as you become immersed within the game.  There is too much to do and far little time from my experience.  Finding the right balance is key, and if you are a perfectionist expect to start the game over a few times until you get the hang of it.
Have yet to play the expansion, but I've heard its even better and offers more of a challenge but also even better upgrade options.  Well worth the price.

When I first purchased "Castle in the Darkness", I wasn't expecting much more than a simple: "Stage-To-Stage" platformer. Good God was I wrong! This game went above and beyond my expectations, at any opportunity it got!
From the moment the game started, I was graced with a beautifully colored cinematic, in the fashion of older games, such as "Phantasy Star". And then, seamlessly, the cinematic transferred me into a full-on "Metroid"-style open world, with vibrant colors that reminded me of the old "Megaman" and "Castlevania" titles.
From here, I took my first steps into the kingdom of Alexandria. Where I was greeted by a child being chased by a ghoul. Upon saving the kid, I was granted some copper coins. Which were added to a coin-count at the top of the screen. This automatically registered into my brain, that there were going to be some RPG elements involved. So, I made sure to gather most every coin I could, as I walked through the kingdom, slaying minions along the way. At one point, I ran across a villager, whom told me: "Some attacks can be knocked back at enemies". Truly helpful information as, two screens later, I found myself against my first boss. A floating eyeball demon, which launched laser "O"s at me, that I had to knock back at said boss, to injure it. After the boss was defeated, I was given a "Boss Heart" heart container. Which raised my maximum HP.
Four hours later, I found myself still playing, and looking forward to new areas, and amazing throwbacks to retro games from the NES & SNES era of gaming (trust me, there were a LOT of them!).
Now, onto the scoring:
[Graphics: 10/10]
- Pleasing to the eye, this game is filled with smooth-flowing, colorful pixel graphics. That capture the NES era of gaming perfectly.
[Sound: 9/10]
- The music in this game is crisp and clear, not to mention: "Well composed". This game's music rivals that of "Megaman 2"'s: "Wiley's Castle".
[Controls: 8/10]
- Nearing perfection, the controls to this game are precise, yet fluid enough to keep it from feeling too stiff. Though, there are times where the jumping feels a little floaty.
[Story: 9/10]
- Being a retro-style game, there isn't too much depth to the story: "You are a Knight of the kingdom, in charge of defending the ill king, when monsters attack." Why Bad?
Cost:
This game is ridiculously pricey for a port with subpar standards at release. Valkyria Chronicles came out as a fantastic port at a very reasonable price tag. This is way overpriced. Don't buy it outside of sales unless you have disposable cash on hand.
Framerate:
I have yet to encounter any framerate dropping issues in-game, at max settings. But the main issue at hand is that the framerate is locked at 30fps. This is unacceptable for a PC game in 2015, port or not. Although playable, movements and animations can feel jerky and unresponsive. Forcing it to run at 60fps using G-sync or V-sync makes a hilarious "Everybody's on their 10th cup of coffee" playthrough.
Controller:
This game did a terrible port job for the keyboard controls (DOES IT EVEN WORK?). It requires a controller to play comfortably. Good luck playing it with a mouse and keyboard, because I don't even know how to proceed beyond the start menu without the controller. Like Monster Hunter and God Eater, this game is built with controllers in mind.
Graphics:
I'm not sure if the port is using the Vita or PS4 version, but it does feel dated. Even at highest setting, the graphics are underwhelming.
Why Good?
Breasts:
Yes, the females in this game has them. And they are very nice. You get to see a nice selection of them during the bathing scenes too. Unfortunately, I played as a male character, so I didn't get to see much before getting kicked out of the bathing pool.
Storyline:
Generic "Hero comes from somewhere and feels the need to defend this village" storyline. The interesting parts aren't the villages, but each individual character's background story.
Armour/Weapon Design:
Not as in-depth as Monster Hunter's style of armour skills and Math involved. Instead, you get skills from your Mitamas (hero spirits) that are equipped on your weapon. This makes it a lot easier for players to change into different types of weapons without having to stress over incompatible armour skills on the new bling armour you just painfully crafted. Just swap your Mitamas while wearing your favourite stylish armour set. The weapon and armour designs are flashy and impressive looking.

The fourth time management game in the long run series produced by

I must admit coming into this game I wasn't really expecting much as the previous 3 are pretty much the same thing. However this is by FAR is the best champagne corker and need of a toast that the developers can come up with new ideas if i have ever seen one. In fact if they finish the series off on this one I would understand as it would be difficult for them to top as they have really set the bar high for themselves now.
The biggest difference to me is that your time management actions and mangament of resources actually changes the backgrounds of each level as you create rivers and forests and beautify the surroundings. On the downside this doesn't last long as you will have to do it again each time you replay the level. Like in Hercules 3 though you do get to decorate a palace which stays that way for good.
There are many new characters, obtscales and decors that have not been in any of the previous versions. Some which at first created a 'what the hell' moment as I scratched my head how to defeat this new enemy. Also worthy to mention is that the level layout itself seems to be improved and some of them made me stop and think what i actually needed to do to get over there. I also like how they have changed the expert level so that it represents one big star and boy are they challenging. No longer is it about just the quickest way through the level but also what else can i click on in the level to raise my score up. Try and beat the developers record on 1.1 and you will soon see what i mean.
The fact that Hercules eventually travels to an alien God Like land and traverses the portals and landscape to subdue his enemy was also well done. The story seemed some what more interesting than previous versions and was slightly disappointed that we did not get to see more of him and 'yoshi' eating megara's fruit afterwards.
I would be seriously surprised if Jetdog trumps this version any more without ruining it, but just in case they are up for the challenge here are a couple of things that i would like to see them maybe implement...
1) More unusual achievements for us to try and get than the old ones you constantly rehash.
2) Instead of a palace which gets better and better, how about a garden like the 'hanging gardens of babylon'.
3) While your 12 desktops are welcoming thought they could have been better placed as an unlockable reward for those who go the extra mile to unlock all the achievements.
4) It would be nice if there was a super reward for those who are truly daring to beat the developers records on all the levels.
5) Maybe some other unlockable cards, music, facts or even a developers photo gallery at the end.
In final i guess this made the biggest impact on me only because i played the previous three and they didn't reach further than a mediocre experience. This one really showed that Jetdogs has the ability to think both out of the square, puch the boundaries and deliver. Thankyou.

Its good, a traditional JRPG with a few gimmicks such as a heavy visual novel approach (Tears to Tiara 3, Hyperdimension for example) and  extremely flashy encounters that you'de normally see on consoles.  Some of the best parts of this game, despite the combat being simplistic is how pretty it looks.  All of the spells, and abilities have their own little cutscene and  all actions happen snappily and quickly. The audio is good, the English dub is liveable but the Japanese dub is better (especially if you understand things that don't translate well).
The story is anime influenced and is more on the silly/moe side of that.  It is a fun story, nothing too serious and  slightly cliche at points.  The story is self aware of just how cliche it can feel, and sometimes makes fun of itself.  There is a deeper undertone but I doubt it'll matter.  Now get the boy his damn /FOOD/!  It is more cohesive then most straight up Visual Novels, but there isn't much choice as it only has 3 possible endings without much deviation in your activities.
As a PC port, it works perfectly.  And really that is the #1 criteria for any game that exists. The game only has resolution settings, including borderless mode.  That is pretty much all there is for PC related enhancements, everything looks crisper and cleaner then the console version so I can't really find anything to complain about this.   Its a fast game, the FPS feels smooth, the action is smooth.
Overall it is a fun game to play, especially at its current price of $15.  Its a competent port, and is pretty to look at.  Its a bit easy, so you won't enjoy this game if you want a challenge.  Nor will you want this game if you're looking for a deep engaging story that will make your brain think on all cylinders.  But if you want something light hearted and easy to digest then this games story will pass for you.  Thumbs up~!

The game starts as a hard boiled cyberpunk murder mystery and ends as
That's Shadowrun! The game itself is fine. The graphics are fantastic, the music is fantastic, the setting is fully realized, the characters are cool, the character customization is ok, the writing is ok, the choices aren't very noticeable, and the game is short, 9 hours for me, and nearly 100% linear. When making your character, min/max a little. Make sure to make a custom class and hyperspecialize in one stat with one combat ability, Body (if you die, it's Game Over), and secondary skills as an afterthought. Pregen character classes have wasted attributes! They seem to be going for a more "well rounded" approach but honestly won't need Strength ever on a Mage, etc. I beat it in three days. All in all it was more satisfying than I expected considering that Dragonfall and Hong Kong exist and are regarded as much better games. If that's the case, I'm looking forward to them.
However, here's the issue: I ran into gamebreaking bugs.
First of all, I was no longer able to get it to run with the Steam overlay. As you can see, I've logged in some hours already from previous half finished playthroughs, so it worked at one point, but for whatever reason, I got a black screen with 1/10th of the menu showing and the cursor loaded unable to do anything. I linked my Steam account to my GOG account and got a free copy there, and finished it DRM free. So you'll probably want to get the GOG copy of the game over the Steam copy. This is totally bogus. More info here:
Next, in the first Brotherhood battle, it would lock up once a certain dialog initiated and the villain monologues and reveals their plan. No matter what I did, the game would not proceed. I think this is somehow due to a new character being added to my roster mid-fight. What I did to fix it was to right before the dialog make sure all three of my characters used up all their AP and my main character went last. This allowed me to go first at the top of the next round with the NPC integrated into the group, because otherwise I'd see another character's moves and loadout, while on my main character, but unable to select anything.
The next bug was in the same scenario, where right before the new character was leaving cyberspace. When she'd leave, she'd be unable to move. Save right before she exits. I'm not sure why this worked for me, but it did.
Truth be told, if you're interested in Shadowrun in video game format, there are better and worse games out there. This one falls in the middle. Nothing will beat the warm fuzzy feelings of Shadowrun on Super NES, but it was really cool to see Jake Armitage back for a little while. The lack of continued support by the devs is kind of disheartening, but whatever, it was fun and I beat it.

Shadow Man is a sadly forgotten Action-Adventure/Horror game which got released on PC, Dreamcast, N64 & Playstation 1 in 1999.
Recently it has been buried even further by YouTubers who reviewed the game on the basis of the worst port they could find (Playstation 1 Version), but don't be fooled.
The PC Version is the best port of this game along with the Dreamcast Version and while it takes some tweaking to get to work properly on modern machines it is definately not hard to do, it even has a very good HD Texture Mod on Moddb which I recommend to use, it not only refines the textures but adds some additional tweaks & options.
The soundtrack by Tim Haywood is fantastic, the challenge good and never unfair. The controls haven't aged all that well but they are easy to get the hang of. The voice acting is terrific for it's time & the writing while edgy at times also pretty good.
Exploration is key to beating Shadow Man because you need to find certain amount of Dark Souls to reach the next power level, which in return lets you access more areas.
It features many levels with varying styles, boss fights & a diverse cast of enemies.
Some soundscapes might be disturbing to some players but this just adds to the darkness of the world Shadow Man plays in.
Strong recommend especially if you dig the mixture of PS1-era 3D-Action-Adventure with a good pinch of Horror.

X-Com: Enemy Unknown is not quite the easiest game to get into and not as self-explanatory as it could be, but the four things it is should be more than enough to warrant a recommendation. It's unique, it's intuitive, it's absorbing and it's a hell of a lot of fun. The game is essentially a strategy RPG where you have to plan every move you make meticulously and with attention to military squad and cover tactics, but you have to manage the back end as well. Engaging in a bit of building and management simulation akin to a 4x game to make sure that your troops are able to keep up with the enemy's technology levels. It's incredibly engaging to pull off a perfect mission, or have to make difficult decisions where one side of the game has to make sacrifices for the other. The game can be very unfair or even luck-based at times, but it's easy to get back into and it can make hopeless battles if not fun then still engaging and rewarding on a more personal level (in an emergent storytelling sort of way). Consider this one a strong general recommendation, walking a perfect line between accessibility and compexity.

This game is one of the pioneers of the parkour genre.  That's about it.  I remember playing the demo for this game when it first came out on the peasant box and I was really interested in playing it.  Several years later, I finally picked it up.
The free running aspects and art style are indeed very amusing.  However, the combat system and story can prove to be what makes this game unsatisfying going into it with high expectations. Sadly, like many modern games, the length of the game also leaves one wanting.
I found myself being constantly frustrated by not being able to progress a level due to unavoidable confrontations with the armed antagonists.  Some are avoidable, some just aren't, and can prove to be very frustrating if you are looking for a zen-like free running game.  Also at times, the mechanics itself can be frustrating.  I recall attempting at least a dozen times to grab on to a pipe due to the precision required to land some stunts.
The story itself lacks depth, and some characters are very shallow and feel very generic.
Graphics-wise, the game still holds its own and is quite pleasant, although the constant white-washing and high brightness can be annoying.
I'd recommend this game, but I would not recommend paying full price.

If you want one word to describe Shadowverse, that word is this:
.
I am a former legend ranked Hearthstone player, and I forced myself to power through to rank "AA0" (the second highest tier in the ranking system) in order to consider myself qualified to write this review. I would have hit master easily, but it would have been redundant, for reasons explained below. However, I will be making many comparisons to Hearthstone.
Shadowverse is a game that offers a couple genuinely unique, creative and healthy mechanics that could have lasting repercussions in the world of childrens' card games. The "evolve" mechanic for example adds a whole layer of potential card mechanics and doubles the amount of voice lines and artwork while also significantly combatting the disease of goingseconditis. The "take two" system in arena, which forces you to pick cards in pairs, forces you to think creatively about which pair is better rather than simply taking the best card. The story mode is mildly interesting and the PvE AI is great. However, this is where the positives end.
Shadowverse's selling point is ostensibly "consistency". The game for people who are tired of games randomly being decided by rng. However, whereas Hearthstone succumbs to that problem, Shadowverse succumbs to the exact opposite problem: it's
consistent. You're allowed to have 3 copies of a card in your 40 card deck, representing 7.5% of the
deck, up from 6.66% in Hearthstone and Magic. You're also allowed to have 3 copies of a legendary card in your deck. This means that you can never,
play under the assumption that your opponent doesn't have a given card in their hand, because they simply
have it, every time. As a result, ironically, the going first problem becomes worse than in any other card game. Entire matchups are decided by a coin flip. If you're in a haven mirror and going second, you might as well just insta concede, because their Heavenly Aegis will hit the board before yours and there's nothing you can do about it so you lose. And even the ones that aren't decided by a coin flip just autoplay themselves. You play your cards, they play theirs, and if you draw better you win. That's it.There's no rng opportunities for disadvantaged players to make comebacks.
Despite the evolve mechanic, all of the cards are incredibly boring. So many things just
mechanics in Shadowverse:
Weapons are not a mechanic
Silence is not a mechanic
Mill is not a mechanic
Buffing your opponent is not a mechanic
The "damaged" status on minions is not a mechanic
Tie games are not a mechanic
Secrets are not a mechanic (glad about this one tbh)
Interacting with your deck is not a mechanic
Stealing your opponent's cards is not a mechanic
Minion positioning on the board is not a mechanic
This means that every single card that makes it into a ladder deck has the words "storm", "ward", "fanfare: heal" or "fanfare: damage" on it. You either play hyper aggro and rush your opponent down before they play their instawin legendaries, or you play a ton of wards/heals/instawin legendaries. That's as deep as it gets. It's also why I call the game
uninteractive, and why I say it's redundant to hit master rank. Because if you're good enough to play your overly consistent deck with a 51% winrate, there's no skill involved beyond that. No creative thinking. It's just a matter of how long you're willing to grind the same mindless, automatic games. And people will lie and say that it only became like
this after the latest expansion, but the truth is its always fundamentally functioned this way. Now it's Ouroboros and Heavenly Aegis and Grimnir, War Cyclone and Demonlord Eachtar, before that it was Rhinoceroach and Albert, Levin Saber and Dimension Shift and Dark Dragoon Forte and Cerberus.
In summary, this isn't a "game". How can you call it a "game" if you can't change anything? It's a job. Here's the deck I used to steamroll to AAO, I call it Compton Blood since it doesn't have a single card above silver (could craft the entire deck from scratch for less than the price of 1 copy of 1 legendary) and beats peoples heads in while they're physically incapable of playing the 17 antifun autowin legendaries in their 2 card hand.
And here's proof of work.

Well, having recently replayed the game in its updated version after a pretty long time of not doing so (it's been like 4 years since I last fully played through it), I can safely revalidate my opinion that this game is alright!....Yea..
Honestly I can’t really praise the hell out of this game. It’s fun to play through every once in a while but really, I can’t call this one of the greatest games ever made. There are a few things holding it back from being that.
First off, the pacing. It’s probably my biggest gripe with the game and it’s what has held me from fully replaying it for such a long time. There are so many sequences that just bring the gameplay to a full halt. It’s not that big of a deal the first time through since the story is interesting, but once you’ve experienced it all, you’re basically just stuck waiting for the game to finally move on. This sort of storytelling is something I have a gripe with in many modern games as well.
One side note is the amount of loading screens in the game. There's tons of them and they get annoying pretty quick since they constantly break up the action and atmosphere.
Then there’s the gunplay which really doesn’t feel satisfying at all. The only weapons that are kinda fun to use are the Gravity gun and on occasion, the shotgun. The rest just feel and also look kinda boring, which is a shame, since Half-Life 1 and its expansions had a bunch of pretty cool and interesting weapons.
It doesn’t help that the enemy variety is kept pretty minimal. The Combine forces pretty much all feel the same, the only difference being the weapons they carry. Their AI is also pretty dull, so gun fights really aren’t all that interesting. There’s a couple of intense fights where you have to fight Combines and huge forces like gunships or striders at the same time but other than that, most firefights are pretty dull.
Thankfully, the headcrabs are a bit more interesting, since there’s multiple versions of them. But what about all the other cool aliens from Half-Life 1? This sort of ties in with the weapon selection as well. The HL1-Games had a bunch of really cool alien weapons. Half-Life 2 has pretty much 1 (the Combine rifle) and honestly, it doesn’t really handle that much differently from the SMG you get earlier in the game.
One thing that is still top notch is the atmosphere of the game. It still sucked me in just like it did back when I last played it. I’m a big fan of these sorts of dystopian settings.
However one thing I will mention is that it feels entirely different from Half-Life 1. I didn’t mind, personally, but it’s still something that should be mentioned since it’s rare that a sequel feels so radically different from its predecessor. Half the time I forgot that I was supposed to be playing a sequel to Half-Life. That is, when people aren’t constantly shouting Gordon’s name around.
The graphics are still pretty good, although they do show their age, but that doesn't bother me. The physics engine is still probably one of the best ones around, though it's implementation in this game seems a bit gimmicky. By the third time they recycled the "Use gravity gun to build bridges over hazardous ground"-part, I was like "Alright, I get it".
The level design's alright as well. What I like is that there's a lot of variation. There's straight up shooting bits, mixed with some fast-paced vehicle sections and slower paced, atmospheric bits here and there.
Overall, I encourage everyone to play this game on their own with a neutral mindset to get their own opinion. I think it’s important for everyone to see for themselves whether or not this game is worth all the praise or not. It is a fun game after all, just not “one of the greatest games of all time”, in my personal opinion.

The creators of the 12 Labours of Hercules series are releasing the games faster than I can complete them :) Less than 1 year passed since the first game, and now I'm trying to finish the 4th and the 5th is already in sight. This rapid pace makes you suspicious that we have a "more of the same" situation here - and yes, while there are slight changes between the episodes, we basically have four near-identical games with almost 200 levels altogether. More of the same is not a sin, of course - if the quality remains stable and the pricing is right, it can be quite attractive. Fortunately, this is the case with 12LoH.
At this point, the game shouldn't need much introduction - if you're unfamiliar with the series, start with the first one, there's a demo and everyting. As a short summary, it's a time management game with appealing audiovisuals, good level design and a decent challenge on the hardest difficulty.
Compared to the first game, there are a few new elements, the most notable being Megara (Hercules' wife) playing an active part (starting from ep3, actually) - since she doesn't introduce strategic variety (ie. you're always best off doing all her tasks early), I don't find much value here. Thieves were also new in ep2 or ep3 (you can guess what they do), and in ep4, sometimes an evil version of Herules appears to scare your servants. Managing thieves does add an additional dimension to the gameplay, while evil H is just an annoyance.
The level design quality remains more or less constant. On most levels you need to make sure you balance your resources well, but there are some levels where you can find different solutions - these tend to be the more enjoyable.
Difficulty is an interesting question. I do feel that the games get easier as the series progresses, but it's quite possible that I'm so used to the gameplay that I automatically make better choices than in the first game. To counter this a bit, there's a developer record for each level beyond the gold time, but to be honest, I can't believe it's really what it's called - many times, I do better than that on the first try. So in the next installment, some extra difficulty would be nice.
All in all, it's easy to recommend the 12 Labours of Hercules series - buy one, play it through, if not bored yet, buy next, repeat. If bored, stop for a couple of months, and try again. When I think of the term "quality casual game", 12LoH is definitely one of the first game that springs to mind.

Definitely a good intro to shadowrun, though veteran players of it and other party-based RPGs may find it a bit lacking. If games can be "short and sweet" it would certainly fit that description.
The story isn't bad, and the dialogue can be interesting and faithful to shadowrun's mythos. Although there's a variety of things to say, choosing different options won't effect gameplay or results much. There is enough dialogue with meat on it to keep players interested however.
The gameplay is diverse enough to make strategy matter, but Shadowrun Returns eases you into difficult situations enough for room to experiment. The game is so short though that this means you'll only need to strategize combat for about half of the ~20 hour campaign. Still, it's fun for anyone wanting to get into shadowrun and could maybe be seen as a cute little 'expansion' for those who already are.
