My playtime: 3 hours (based on steam).
Crystals of Time is a Hidden Object game which mostly focuses on the said part. The story was made very simple and straightforward, making explorations to be the most thing you'll do in this game. Because of it, don't be surprised because there will be no cutscenes in this game. The intro and ending are all using text conversation.
Although there are some puzzle in this game, the numbers are scarce compared to the Hidden Object games in this game, making the genre "Hidden Object" to be very accurate. However, i have to admit that most of the Hidden Object games are unlocked at unpredictable times and places, which makes me not knowing that it's already been unlocked. Because of that, i either have to exploring all places or clicking the hint button whenever i'm stuck.
Note that because there are a lot of Hidden Object games in this game, you might get tired doing it so you might want to take a break when you are playing it.
As i said before, the story in this game is very straight forward. The story was made as minimal as possible, although it's still retaining the most important part. The story progression flows smoothly, although the ending is quite dissapointing because of the minimalism. The ending is somehow like telling you "Hey, this game is ending. Bye.", and it just.. send you back to the main screen.
The graphics in this game are on par with similar games (ex: Artifex Mundi titles), and i don't really have any complaints with that. The walkable paths are clear enough, and the hidden objects are blending perfectly with the background.
To be honest, the sound doesn't bad nor great. The bgms are relaxing. However, it can be quickly forgotten.
There are a lot of Hidden Object mini games in this game. One scene can be used for like 3 hidden object games. If you don't really like Hidden Object games that much, you'll mostly just random clicking everything, hoping that you'll find something listed there, or clicking the skip button, as there is no achievements both in game and in steam to 100% with.
Most of the items are hidden well; some items even have almost the same color with the background. Some are placed in the foreground, and some in the background. You'll probably have been thinking to click that hint button even once, and clicked it.
Pros:
- Tons of Hidden Object games
Cons:
- Crappy ending
It's a Hidden Object heaven. There are tons of Hidden Objects to spend your time with.

Awesome game, i was engrossed in the whole story very quickly.
So Fairy Fencer F is a game where you are on a journey to collect fairies from furies, i will get to those in a second. So the game starts off with introducing the main character, Fang, who is one of the laziest protagonists ive ever seen, his first priority in any situation is food, and next is sleep. Having heard that pulling a fury out of teh ground will let him make any wish, and with a wish for food, he pulls the fury out and in turn becomes a Fencer, who wield a fury, and the fairy Eryn is introduced. She is really funny, and is the stragiht man to his antics, like food and sleep. They go on a journey and you meet another fencer in the first dungeon, but i wont go into detail as the story is one to experience for oneself. Just one quick word, ive only played a small amount of the story but its so gripping i cant stop, and have already played near 5 hours in the story mode (The ingame menu will tell you the total play time and this sessions play time)
The tutorial level comes quite quickly in this game and i for one love the combat system. Its turn based but each turn a character can move around a field in the map that has their starteing position as teh center of teh field.
When your characters turn is in play, they can choose a variety of options, those being attack, skills/magic, items, wait and fairize. Ill get to attack a bit later.
The skills/magic menu when opened has two submenus for skills and magic, skills being physical attacks. Many different magics and skills have different radii and fields where you need to line up the attacking area, which is in red, with the enemies you want to fight.
Huh? Whats Fairize you ask? Its sounds wierd but its where a fencer resonates with their fairy and thus their attack increases and special fairize skills are unlocked, oh and you get an anime-esque transformation sequence. And then theres also wait, Increases attack in teh next turn and makes you guard. A queue of who goes next is displayed on teh left side of teh screen.
Now we'll get to attack. which when pressed can start a combo, this cant be done at the start, but as you go thorugh the game youll learn how to execute long combos.
As you go through the game collecting furies, they will have fairies which you can equip to your characters, which increase stuff like strength of sword/glaive/knuckle/etc attack or increase attack of one element of magic, you know earth air fire water. There is a way to make fairies stronger, but its part of teh story and i dont want to spoil anything.
All thats left to talk about is options, in which you can increase bgm voice and sound volumes seperatley and there a japanese to english voice switch, which is english default, which is a nice addition that i like seeing in these sorts of games.
I highly recommend this to beginners of teh jrpg genre, veterans of rpgs in general, and anyone who wants a nice singleplayer campaign rpg expereince.

I thought this game was interesting, but, it doesn't do a good job at keeping me hooked.  The game being so open is both a good and a bad thing:  It's good, because it feels less linear and as gives a good sense of exploration.  It's also good in case you get stuck.  However, the bad part is you're often found trapped at several doorways and you don't know how to get past them because you're not aware there are more tools to your disposal.  I've wasted at least 1.5 hours total trying to solve puzzles that could not be solved because I needed some gun upgrade.  Then, you need to spend the time figuring out which of the several pathways leads to that gun you need.
All this being said, if you don't know what to expect, you're going to waste a lot of time wandering or trying to solve something you can't solve yet, without knowing why you can't.  But part of the "magic" of this game is the unknown, so the layout of the game is somewhat counter-intuitive.
On a side note, some of the puzzles felt a little "sloppy", where you have to make a lot of rough estimates to accomplish your goal.  Again, not a big deal, but there are a handful of puzzles where I'm sitting there thinking "am I doing this right...?"
Still a fun game and worth playing, but you need a lot of patience.

I started playing Shadowverse like 2 weeks ago, because I got bored with HS aggro meta. From the very first moment, I just couldn't stop playing. The game provided me with tons of free packs and content. After 100 hours in the game, I spent 50$, bought some prebuilt decks and perfected my Sword and Forest collection. It took me approximately 10 days to get from Beginner 0 to AA0. I honestly had a lot of fun.
However, at rank AA0, I learned the other, frustrating side of SV. I am currently facing Dragon Ramp and Aggro Shadow in 70% of games. In 20% I face Albertcraft and Aegis Haven. The remaining 10% consists of Blood Aggro, Roach Forest and D-Shift Rune. The missing balance in deck usage and performance slowly kills the fun I have with the game.
Dragon can ramp up without taking any risks, because he heals himself, draws cards, clears the board and generates threats at the same time while ramping. Then he easily stomps/outvalues opponents with big legends, storm followers and unmatched AOE removal.
Shadow swarms the board and gets boosted when you actually clear their board. If you manage to somehow completely remove his followers while barely staying alive, there's still Phantom Howl and Cerberus combo which makes for a nice 9 or more dmg out of hand. There are endless possibilities for balancing, for example making Reapers pay for Ambush with shadows, forcing other abilities from evolves (Orthrus comes to mind) and so on.
From what I read I found out that Cygames intentionally boosted these classes, because they were bad before. Okay, I take it, this is also a way of rotating the meta. But God, there is a difference between making a class viable and making it unmatched... Since Dragon pretty much destroys every conrol and Shadow outplays every aggro, there is very limited selection of viable decks for current meta. Both leading decks are also very different, which makes teching against one break the deck consistency.
The worst thing is that the situation in unranked play is completely same, so you cannot just take it casually and expect to avoid FOTM decks in unranked games.
Despite all that I said, I recommend the game. The quantity of free content is undeniable and the game is very entertaining when you don't take it too seriously. As for me, I will probably just farm rupies and wait for a better meta situation. After all, Un'Goro made HS enjoyable again, so I can as well return for some time.

For reference, i've played Resident evils 1, 4, 5, 6, O.R.C, and revelations 1. I believe they are all fun titles (save for ORC), even if they may have a flaw or two.
This has got to be the absolute worst resident evil i've ever played in terms of campaign. I would honestly rather replay ORC's campaign over this one, because it's just as mediocre and unfun but at least it ends quicker.
The campaign drags on for so damn long and you can't co-op it with a friend to make it suck less.
You will be investigating boring enclosed corridors for the entirety of the game and doing 10 very easy puzzles that take 5 minutes each to complete because they're designed to be slow to complete for the sake of padding gameplay hours, and you'll get at least 7 puzzles per half of an episode. You will spend, on average, an hour completing each half of an episode, except for the first half of episode 4 which took 10 minutes because there was really nothing to it.
Whichever of the two endings you get is determined solely by one simple choice you won't even know you have in a QTE. If you're like me and play QTE's as "Quick Time Events" or even "Press X to not die" instead of "take your time and bumble♥♥♥♥ around waiting for something else to happen" events, then you will be locked into the very bad ending where absolutely nothing good happens. Cool videogame.
The story of the campaign is monotonous, boring, and uninspired. Gameplay is taken back to it's survival horror roots, but I guess they forgot to put the horror in the game because it wasn't scary save for two very cheap jumpscares. Speaking of gameplay, it's not very good in the campaign. You are forced to have an AI-controlled partner at all times, and you can use the Call or Wait shouts to tell them to do things. This would be fine if they actually listened, but they absolutely do not, and if the main character of the episode goes down, even if you are or aren't controlling them, you are not given a chance to revive them as you would if the side-character went down. It's game over. You will die many, MANY times because claire just had to knife fight the hulking man with a greataxe, no matter how many times you scream for her to come to you. On top of this, there are invisible instant death monsters that will spawn in areas you've previously cleared and are attempting to backtrack through, even in the parts of the campaign where you do not have the means to know they even exist. This can result in your death for simply wanting to hurry the process up, which will just put you back further because you died.
So yeah, the campaign is absolutely terribly thought-out and I didn't enjoy a second of it. So, why did I suffer through it instead of immediately refunding?
To unlock characters in Raid Mode, the good part of the game. How RER2 works is, you have to suffer through the travesty of a story mode to unlock some of the content in the ACTUAL, FUN part of the game. If you have a friend who can play Raid with you, then this could be a worthy time sink, and therefore worthy of your money. It's just fast-paced co-op action shooting with upgradeable guns, skills, levels, and characters. Good stuff.
If you don't have anyone to play Raid with, this game has no redeeming qualities and is a 5/10 at best. It tries many things and does none of them well. I've had more fun with RPG Maker Games, hell i've had more fun MAKING RPG maker games. RER2 is a title that will be largely forgotten, and for very good reason.
TL;DR Just order a pizza instead. You don't have to suffer any to enjoy a pizza.

Considering the numerous adjustments and fixes put in since launch, i'm changing my review to recommended.
Good Stuff :
+ Great Music (except the first area)
+ Good Sprites (except the large ones, which vary wildly in quality)
+ Quite a few secrets and silly asides to find
+Good feeling, fairly balanced gameplay (After about 50% through the game)
+20-Something Bosses to fight
+NGplus adds replayability to it (slight map changes, new hidden items, some silly jokes), if you decide you like it enough to bother
+Tons of fixes to serious design issues the game launched with. Continued Support.
Bad Stuff :
-combat is attack-button-mash-heavy until you find strong spells very late in the game, at which point you'll basically stop using your sword all together.
-Drowning in references to classic games
-tons of instant death traps placed in kind of mean locations
-Questionable level design related to said traps
-tons of breakaway blocks that you must be carefully looking for your first time through (major improvement from launch)
-mostly boring enemies
-early game gameplay balanced horribly. 3 hits to death, and one attack that has your character's width for range. Touching enemies kills you, and you have a very short melee attack.
-odd camera issues related to how the screen system works (jumping up from one screen into another screen that it multiple screens long results in a very nauseating few moments of camera flipping out.
-many important items/abilities/weapons are kept in totally difficult or hard to find locations. The game expects you to have them for specific bosses later in the game, and doing them without the right gear is nightmarish.
-lackluster player progression
Would I recommend it? Yes, considering the fixes the dev has put in. It's not for everyone, but it's definitely enjoyable now.
The beginning of the game is has an unfortunately high difficulty requirement, related to the player's health and attack range.  The starting weapon has measly range, and because you must get close to enemies to deal damage early on you get hit more often at the start. Considering for the first lahf of the game it only takes about 3 hits to kill you, that's a steep requirement for newbies.
As you press on you get more HP, better armor, and weapons that do more damage and have multiple times the range of the initial sword. You also get spells that range from useless to kills-most-enemies-in-one-hit, over a large radius. You just have to find them.  Until you get the better gear, it's a slow, cautious, sort of punishing game with a player that feels a little too quick and jumps a little strangely.
The enemies are all unfortunately 'whatever'. Some of them are cool to look at, but none of them are any fun to fight. Most of them just walk back and forth and face you, throwing a projectile or slashing with their weapon on a timer. Enemies that charge at you are obnoxious depending on the strength, and range of your weapon.
Bosses are the best parts of the game, but fighting most of them boils down to throwing spells at them. Jump height is dependent on holding the jump button, and you are expected to mash the attack button on the way up, during, then performing a double jump, and continuing to mash. Not only is this uncomfortable, but it feels spastic and poorly thought out.  Beyond that, the bosses and enemies all seem to have different i-frame windows after taking damage, so some respond more to mashing than others.Combat's a mixed bag in this game. Good that most enemies can be jumped past, i suppose.. You mash a lot until you find spells, then you just charge the spell up and dodge stuff until you have a moment to throw it at them. Rinse repeat.
The game is also full of instant death traps. Most of the time it's spikes on the ground, and falling spikes from the roof. Most falling spikes are instant death, and ALL of the ground spikes are. Some areas have an issue where the spikes are the same color as the walkable surfaces, and thus don't stand out like they ought to.
Speaking about the numerous  spikes sticking out of the ceiling; they fall when you pass under them, and fall very quickly (at a constant velocity, no accel). The spikes are usually very dark, as are the backgrounds. You seldom see them coming and are often placed in spots the dev felt you'd stop to attack something, or stand thinking you were safe. This is just unfair design for the most part. If they stood out a little more clearly against all backgrounds, you could plan accordingly and dying to them would be on you. However, they're very hard to spot and often you find yourself dying mysteriously.  It's punishing, and doesn't feel like a fair challenge.
Another prominent, frustrating part of the game are Breakaway Blocks. Breakaway Blocks can either fracture when you step on them, and then disappear maybe half a second later (with a noise and visual cue, so you know what's about to happen and can jump away) OR, they immediately crumble and send you into what's effectively the game's double jump. You must hold jump before you land on these blocks to get the extra vertical boost required in almost areas with them, and you never know until you land on a block what kind of block it's going to be.
When the game launched (when i first played through it) these blocks looked identical to the surrounding blocks. You never knew when a block was going to kill you. This has been remedied, and all breakaway blocks are fairly marked (visibly broken compared to their stable surroundings). What kind of breakable block it is is still a mystery, but at least you know now. The trap for the completely ignorant is there, and you can plan around it. Much improved from launch, and it wipes out this entire chunk of former complaints.
In the game's favor, there are a few areas based almost purely around platforming challenges and i found these to be the most fun in the entire game. It did away with most of the combat and just focused on a relatively fair, somewhat complex physical navigation challenge and felt great. I wish there was more of that in the game. Any deather there feel very fair.
The last thing i have to go on and on about is the player progression. As i mentioned, you start out with a miserable attack that gets you damaged, and what amounts to 3 hits before you die (unless it's spikes). When you defeat a boss, you get a Boss Heart which adds 1HP to your maximum. The game has 50HP max. The way the damage that the enemies does, however, doesn't scale in a similar fashion. Even after the first 5 or 10 HP ups, you still only take 3 or so hits before dying. And enemies later on, obviously do more damage to you on contact than early ones, so for about half of the game you have a small weak weapon and die in very few hits. After about halfway through the game, you'll have had the opportunity to find some additional armor that raises your defense (i don't even know how that works), and you have around 30hp. Now you don't have to worry about enemies at all and can just run through them, and the only things that will kill you are traps, bad jumps, forgetting about a breakaway block or some bosses with absurd damage output.
Basically, it doesn't feel good to get stuff in this game. None of the boss hearts feel like they matter, when 1HP is like 1/6 of an enemy attack, and the (at time of writing) unskippable victory sequence that lasts for 10 seconds every time you pick one up feels lame, rather than an actual victory.
I say all this to say that this game has some good ideas, some great assets, and some ho-hum level design with a few shining moments here and there. Some of the boss fights are great. It's mostly pretty. It launched sort of awful, but the game is now definitley worth playing if you enjoyed Symphony of the Night, Zelda 2, or (loosely!) I Wanna Be The Guy.

A really fun experience.
Dying Light could be described as "Yet another zombie game, with improved elements..." in a short sentence. Yes it is a zombie game with a simple story line and simple objectives through the game. The main story is very simple, the company that created the game will use the well known elements of other zombie apocaliptic games and recycle them in the main story. As a matter of fact the side quests are also running from point A to point B.
The graphics and the animations are great, and although you may experience some random lag now and then when playing on ultra settings it is a gorgeous trip through slums and a detailed city areas. The map is about 3 times bigger than that of the original Dead Island.
One of the new elements introduced in Dying Light is the addition of free running. You will hop through roofs and obstacles while gaining ability points to level up your character in the 3 different skill trees. The leveling of your character depends on: mission objectives getting complete, slauthering the infected (or human enemies), or free running. There are again many different weapons you can combine and craft through the game and yet again the weapons will break relativly fast so the game forces you to change them or repair ofthen.
Then there is the night gameplay, which makes the game hard and you will need to sneak around to prevent being chased by mutated infected cratures that will kill you in about four hits. The night is very dangerous and totaly different from the day cicle. Yes there is a constant day/night cicle in the game, which changes every houer.
In conclusion Dying Light is an upgreated version of Dead Island with some fresh elements and dull mission objectives, however if you like sandbox games this is a fun game to mess around and an addition of night survival elements.
The game is also very long with tons of sidequests and challanges to do!
Good:
- Graphics and overall presentation of the menus.
- Many fun ways to slauther the enemies
- Day/night cicles change the gameplay
- Tons of quests and challanges to do
Bad:
- Human AI can be aweful and gets stuck in corners
- Mission objectives are dull (but the stories of survivals are cool to hear)
- Some performance issues and some strange animations (fixed in patch ----)
83/100

And look, you can be a hulk here!
HULK SMASH!
CLUBBERING TIME!

Shadowrun Returns is a cRPG that was successfully kickstarted and has made its way to steam. The game is set in a cyberpunk world where risk takers, known as shadowrunners, undertake dangerous jobs for whoever pays the most. The game has no multiplayer but instead focuses on its strong singleplayer story and even has steam workshop support so that people can create their own stories and share them with others. Shadowrun Returns is a reboot of an old franchise on SNES going by the same name. This reboot truly sets a new standard for cRPG's with its phenomenal storytelling and graphics that really immerse you in the world of cyberpunk Seattle.
-
Shadowruns combat is turn based and, as is usual in the genre, in order to perform any action you require AP. You start the game with 2 points of AP and about halfway through the main story you upgrade to 3 AP. The combat in Shadowrun is pretty usual and there really isn't much special about it. You play as one of 6 classes but really they only affect how you start off early on in the game. Something pretty cool about Shadowrun is that you can build your character however you want regardless of class and your build will still be viable. There are a handful of main skills you can upgrade, such as charisma and strength, and then under those you have at least four or five sub stats such as melee weapons or rifles. The problem here is, at least in the main story, that there are so many stats to upgrade that you can only get about halfway through the skill tree before the game is over. I did almost every side objective there was and I still only got about 3/4 of the way through some of the trees. The game is incredibly linear too so that there is very little you can do in the way of exploration or side objectives. Sometimes you can pass stat checks so that you can avoid combat or haggle price when selling an item but overall the stats really don't feel like they matter in most cases. In some cases, like upgrading rifles or submachine guns you can unlock new abilities to use in combat on those weapons but overall the upgrades from the skill trees are pretty boring. Some of the classes feel really unique and different but others are just typical RPG classes. The rigger, for example, is a class completely focused on controlling your own robots that can do things like sneak through ducts and ambush enemies. Other classes are just basic mages or soldiers and I feel that, while the unique classes are certainly cool, they're overshadowed by the more basic ones. The most interesting part of the game was when you get to hire mercenaries to go on runs with you. You put together a team of runners who come with you on missions and, for the most part you get to pick who you want to come with you, but in some cases you are forced to take main characters. Generally the gameplay is average for a game like this, but I feel they managed to pull it off in a way that, while getting stale after a while, still is respectable for the genre.
Now lets talk story. Shadowrun is quite short for a game in the same genre as Fallout 2 and Wasteland but I feel the story is compelling enough to make up for the poor length. You play as one of the aforementioned shadowrunners and you're in your apartment when you get a recording from your friend, Sam Watts. He tells you that if you are hearing this then he's dead.However, he has set up 100,000 nuyen (The games currency) wired on a dead-mans switch to be transferred to you if you can find his killer. You accept the job, be it for loyalty, money, or a mixture of the two and set out to look for the man that murdered one of the few you called friend. You journey through this gorgeous cyberpunk Seattle and as you do the game starts pulling you in and immersing you into this dog-eat-dog world. The environments are so incredibly detailed that you can't help but to want to know more about them. The game, however, doesn't really give you much backstory on the world and tries to keep you focused on the main storyline. The first half of the story you're looking for the cyberpunk equivalent of Jack the Ripper and for the latter half you have to stop an invasion by a horde of monstrous spirit bugs that cannot die. Every character you meet will make you care about keeping them alive and doing right by them or, at the very least, get you to want to learn more about them. Even though it's incredibly linear the story itself is very unique and fits in perfectly with the settings and characters in Shadowrun.
Shadowrun Returns shows that combat isn't everything and an intriguing story and artwork to match can be just as important

Definitely provides a look into e-sports, and adds some drama in the form of player's lives, but I think it fell flat of What It Could Be
. There is so much more to the scene than what they show, the sheer amount of personality in some of the players, the competitiveness, the amazing stories of comebacks and strategy that come with sports. As someone who watches gameplay streamed from tournaments, I kept on waiting for the bread and butter, the scenes you would expect to see from a movie about a tournament, but was instead served a limp dish of what boiled down to pre-rendered scenes that looked like the quality you'd see in a trailer (read; commercial). The storylines from the players looked like they just grabbed whatever they could and ran with it. Lack of actual interesting events lead to obviously pre-scripted scenes, like cringeworthy moments such as having a shot of one of the players at the pond that their dead father and them used to fish on, for no particular reason.
The title Free to Play inspires tales of freedom from the stigma of the title "gamer", and how these athletes followed their passion and achieved their goals of playing professionally, but unfortunately I feel this movie skirted around this topic without addressing the main meat.
Overall, well constructed, has a passable storyline to follow, but falls flat of what is expected of the inspiring and inovating documentary genre. Would recommend, but it's far from perfect.

On January 14th, I bought LEGO® Marvel™ Super Heroes on pc. I was a big fan of Lego video games, most of which I bought for console, and I originally thought that it would be exactly like LEGO® Batman 2 DC Super Heroes™ just with different characters and a different free roam world; however, LEGO® Marvel™ Super Heroes proved to be an even more interactive game than I had originally anticipated.
LEGO® Marvel™ Super Heroes is one of the most entertaining Lego games released. The free-roam aspect of the game not only let you complete certain tasks like time trial runs and mini-boss battles; instead, it introduces racing with friendly NPCs, better/bigger boss battles with villains such as red hulk (that are completed through a certain combination of keys that the game instructs the player to use), and saving civilians from fires and other catastrophes. The story line and bonus levels offer player(s) opportunities to think outside the box when faced with the puzzles and challenges of each level which gives some variety to the game. There is one big issue with the game: once it is completed, there are no updates or DLCs that give new content to the game save new characters only. Also, co-op gameplay is limited to one device such as a laptop or “local co-op” which may prove difficult since gamers have to share one screen and one keyboard. This problem can be fixed though if the players have external keyboards and a big monitor that hooks up to their computer.  Despite this, the game is still enjoyable for kids and adults alike who crave for games with action, nostalgia (due to the many classic characters in the game), and problem solving.
Over all, the game is quite successful in introducing new exiting concepts to a Lego game and making it a memorable experience. Adding new free roam activities within an amazing city landscape is a marvelous feature. Also, being able to adjust screen resolution, vibration settings, and brightness settings can help players reduce lag spikes as much as possible. From a scale of 1-10, I would rate the game 9/10 due to the wonderful experiences that the game can provide.

I suppose, when you get right down to it, this documentary is trying to tell us that so called "e-sports" (somehow the term bothers me) are on the verge of becoming a very big international business, with large prizes involved. This one team certainly made a lot of money.
But what it ultimately comes down to is that for most people this is not a "career" that's going to get them anywhere. Can you really measure your success in life by how good you are at Dota, Counter-Strike, Star Craft, or WOW? And never mind success, what about happiness? What about experiencing the world around you, when all you do is eat, sleep, and spend the other 15 hours you are awake playing one.single.game over, and over again?
In a way, these guys can be proud to have gotten as far as they did. However, the impact on their lives (except for the winning team) has been mostly negative. A few years from now, when Dota 3, or some new game becomes popular, and a young kid runs circles around these "veteran" players, what skill sets will they be left with? What possible contribution to their families, communities, or the world?
That's the biggest problem with gaming as approached by these "professionals". That it eclipses everything in their lives, but leaves them with nothing in the end. Eerily similar to an addiction if you think about it.

Also, when hiring mercenaries, you'd think they would be able to hack computers/open locks for you -- they cannot.  It all relies on your character's skill set.
Being able to hire said mercenaries also allows you to get a taste for the different classes/races/weapons/tools and removes any sort of replayability.  The storyline is very linear.
The in/out of combat system is finicky as well, and I had to reload more than a few times to fix.

The best tactical strategy game I've played in a very long while. A pretty exahustive, progressive and customizable campaign, extremely challenging AI, solid storytelling (for a game like this) and enough diversity to ensure that you won't play two similar campaigns.

Enemy Within DLC is the icing on the cake, it gives you far more options for your campaigns and ensures that the games are more dynamic and challenging (Exalt attacks and Meld harvesting are tough objectives on harder dificulties). Treat it as an old-fashined expansion pack more than a mere DLC; it's completely worth it.
The only downside to this game is the disappointment that you won't be able to find similar games with such a good quality as this one.

I think Castle in the Darkness (herein referred to as just "Castle") is proof of a few things:
-You shouldn't judge a book by its cover (or a game by its trailer in this case)
-There are certain gaming staples that needed to die long ago
-You get what you pay for
-A "Neutral" option for reviews would be really nice
I'll get this one out of the way first. Yes, Castle IS fun. But it's the kind of fun that needs to come with a few asterisks (more on that later). The game has a very simple charm to it that transcends words. Movement and attacking are quick and fluid. Enemies are nicely varied, if a little arbitrary at times, and fighting them is engaging enough. Bosses are equally varied (and there's quite a few of them!), virtually no boss (from what I've played so far) is remotely like any other, and it's fun trying to figure out their patterns and how to take them down, though I would argue that perhaps they aren't spaced out very well. Sometimes it seems like you're fighting a boss every 5 rooms, other times you're wondering if the area has a boss at all.
You start with basic equipment (short sword, basic armor) and gain more as you explore the world. These include various weaponry (of course), better armor, various magic (used by holding Attack to charge), relics which offer passive benefits (break certain blocks, keep traction on ice, etc), and Life increases (dropped by bosses). Some equipment you must buy from various NPC's, requiring you to keep on top of collecting all the coins that enemies drop.
It is cool to explore the world and gain an arsenal of equipment, but I can't help but feel that it's also a bit superfluous at the same time. The game seems to be designed so that enemies' strength is pretty much always on par with your own, so why even put in all the stat and weapon upgrades if they never add to your power relative to the enemies'? There are a few exceptions; entering Ruth's Hall at the first possible moment is essentially suicide, but then, why even bother letting me enter at all until I'm further along in the game?
The story is relatively vague, or perhaps a better word would be loose. What's there isn't bad. But at the same time, it's not really what you're there for. Playing Castle for the story is somewhat akin to playing Mario Bros. or Dota 2 for the story.
Now for what I didn't like. While the action is fun, the platforming is not. It's flat out frustrating. Well, the platforming itself isn't strictly bad, it's platforming around all the stuff that instantly kills you that's maddening. There's something about the way the Protagonist jumps that just feels off. It's so close to perfect that it's maddening, but it's not quite there. As I hinted above, the developer seems to have an insatiable crush on spikes that instantly kill you, and traps that instantly kill you. I'm going to reckon the vast majority of any players deaths will be to some form of instant-kill environmental hazard. Actually, there were times I forgot I had a life meter at all. In one room, there's a rugged series of steps with a single spike on one of them, and the spike blends into the background really well. In fact, the first time I passed through that room, being somewhat focused on the enemies, I missed it by chance, and had no idea it was even there. The second time through that room, it killed me (I hadn't even seen it until it did so), and I seriously considered uninstalling the game and never playing it again.
But the absolute worst thing about this game are the blocks that break when you step on them. You can (and in most cases MUST) hold Jump to gain extra height as you jump on these blocks to reach whatever destination you're striving for, generally this is "ground that doesn't have instant-kill spikes coming out of it". Which is fine and all. Except for one tiny detail: these blocks look the exact same as every other block. If a block serves a different function from a standard block, it should look different. I'm no game designer, but that seems like a basic. What we have here results in a very I Wanna Be The Guy-esque trial-and-error experience. And it's not like IWBTG, where it's so absurd it's actually funny, it's straight-up frustrating, unfair, and terribly designed. The game is withholding information from you.
The final thing about Castle that bugs the hell out of me is its sense of humor. Before I go any further on that, I have to kinda explain what I mean. See, there's a difference between making a subtle, clever nod or shout-out to something, and just pointing at something, saying it exists, and that by merely confirming its existence branding yourself as a comedic genius. And what Castle seems to love to point at is none other than Zelda 2 (and to a lesser extent Zelda in general, and a few other games), but it's not pointing at it, it's just quoting it verbatim, and at the same time portraying Link as (just to avoid having to ask everyone to pardon my French) a sadistic jerk, and even then it was a one-time joke that added nothing to the game. There comes a point where I'd rather a developer just not make any nods to other video games at all, and Castle has crossed that point and then some.
At the end of the day, yes, Castle is fun, but this is coming from someone who had the patience to finish Demon's Souls. My recommendation must come with the caveat that if you're not okay with dying a ton, or just dying unfairly in general, then you probably won't like this game. My recommendation must also come with the caveat that I have not beaten it yet. Perhaps I'll have a more definite stance on the game once I do, but even though there's a simple charm in Castle that keeps pulling me in, there's also the game's unrefined platforming pushing me away.

A game about running. It cleverly juggles action and puzzle elements. When exposed, the player has to run away to the music of firing guns and shouting policemen. During calmer moments the player has platforming puzzles to solve, much like in Portal, but with wall jumps and climbing instead of a portal gun.
It is set in a postcyberpunk future, in a beautiful and unique city. Its emptiness serves the feeling of isolation, but the story suffers from it. There are no people to talk to, no context to put the protagonist’s actions into. You’re a freedom fighter in a city with no civilians. It’s so painful that those amazing vast spaces are not inhabited. The city is breathtaking on the outside, but lacks substance.
We never learn how constant invigilation affects normal people or why and how the resistance movement works. It’s not even clear what messages the runners actually carry or who do they serve: only the resistance or anyone who pays the money. It’s even less clear why runners are so important for the police to form a specialized unit for hunting them down. We never see any (political or personal) consequence to a runner delivering a package. There are so many interesting questions here that never get explored or answered.
Instead the game focuses on right now and personal. Our charming protagonist, aptly named Faith, breaks into offices and runs around the city trying to figure out conspiracy around a murder that her sister gets unjustly accused of.
Even though this is a game about free running, the progression around the city is pretty linear. Mechanically the city acts as a space to traverse, providing platforms and ledges to climb and jump over. Sadly there is no gameplay support for the backstory, e.g. there are a lot of cameras around the city, but they don’t affect the game in any way: you cannot get spotted or hide from them, they’re just decoration.
In spite of those limitations the core of the game is executed perfectly. You feel each step, each jump and fall. Running around the city is a pleasure: the clear visuals, a fitting soundtrack and the immediacy of movement gives a true feeling of freedom. It’s hard not to feel compassion for Faith. She is a very human protagonist, stubborn yet caring. She hugs her sister before running away again - a sympathetic gesture seldom seen in video games so dominated with violence and power fantasies.
Its innovative mechanics are still blended with a lot of existing game tropes. There are valves to turn, vents to crawl and exploding barrels. Elevators act as an intermission, we have a mission control guy, there are secret packages to find, there is even a bit of shooting. The Icarus Project sounds like a direct reference to the original Deus Ex.
Mirror’s Edge is a great game, but it could have been much more. Time will tell if Mirror’s Edge 2 will turn out to be a worthy successor.

Hidden object games are so formulaic that you'd think they'd be hard to screw up, but Crystals of Time has found a way.
Most hidden object games offer some leniency in where you can click on an object, but in Crystals of Time the clickboxes are very narrow. Sometimes clicks failed to register, so I kept searching for that object even though I had already spotted and clicked it. Unnecessary confusion.
The game often has you revisit hidden object scenes and resets them each time, so you'll be looking for the same objects over and over. This makes for a repetitive and tedious experience. Not helping matters is the fact that much of your time is spent looking for X number of copies of a given macguffin before you can proceed, which just pads the game out further.
Crystals of Time has made looking for hidden objects, the core element of its genre, into annoying busywork. Go dig through junk heaps somewhere else.

One of the most frustrating HOGs I've played. Frustrating because it could have been so much better. The graphics and music are both fitting and immersive and the story is interesting.
Then the annoyances kick in.
For large parts of the game, there is no direction. You find objects but have no idea what they interact with without using the hint button.
There is no indication as to how many parts/pieces you need to complete objectives. Leaving you running around the map with pieces, only to be told you need more, or running around the map looking for pieces when you already have enough.
Some interactive areas give no hint they are interactive unless you click on them.
If you are stuck ... don't worry, you just have to re-visit "every" location in case a HO scene has appeared since you last visited. Missing a piece? explore the entire map for a HO scene .... and that leads to the next problem.
There are a lot of HO scenes ... and that wouldn't normally be a problem, but this game repeats the scenes. You might have to revisit the same HO scene 4 times during gameplay, and not only does it use the same scenes over and over, it uses the same objects! So 80-90% of the objects you are required to find, are the same objects, in the same places, as the previous 2 or 3 or 4 times you did it!
Some objects have poor click detection. You see the fishing rod, you click the fishing rod, nothing happens. You have to re-click in different areas on the object before it is found.
Some of descriptions are un-clear, and the most annoying feature is that sometimes objects with same description are in the scene, but it will only accept one of them. i.e. Find the "peppers". Is it the large red pepper in the middle? no, it's the jar of peppers on the shelf. Find the "nuts". Is it the large bowl of hazelnuts? no, it's the walnuts in the corner.
What's a sac? .... hint .... oh, you mean "sack"
This game could have been so much better, and that's what's annoying about it. Playing through it was an exercise in patience more than enjoyment, and the ending!?!?!? seriously?!?!? .... the payoff at the end was disappointing to say the least.
If you like HOGs, try something else, and if you must, try to pick this one up in a bundle or on sale.

Gameplay-wise, the combat feels solid and fluid, connecting hits feel like they have impact, and the weapons feel solid. The abilities you obtain as you level up are mostly useful, though grapple is a little difficult to pull off because you need to break your fingers to use it unless you rebind it.
The story is a little generic, but it gets the job done and it keeps moving throughout. My one gripe with the story-quests though is that
QTE and breaks all the immersion and just left me feeling disapointed and the story feeling anticlimactic.

They weren't well 'advertised' either - we happened across the one we actually played by accident, thinking it was a safe house.

I do understand why - you have to be Kyle to get the information, to take the calls, etc. I just would have preferred a different character to co-op with -  e.g. perhaps adding a couple of other characters from the Tower. I've never been much into superheroes, puzzle games or platformers, but this game sucked me in quick nontheless. Even with my somewhat limited grasp on who all the characters are, the humor and narrative just works perfectly. The story is thoroughly enjoyable, and there are vast amount of side challenges out in the open world of Manhattan. It's quite cool to pick your favorite superhero/villain - or one you've never heard of - and fly, run or drive between the skyscrapers, determined to save the world's best cameo actor from all his perilous adventures.
With only keyboard controls, flight can be a bit iffy, though; it's very easy to fire up the overdrive and end up far away from wherever you wanted to go. Not really an issue in the missions, but can make some of the challenges around Manhattan quite tough.
Also, whomever designed the awning bouncing minigame deserves a solid bonk on the head. I'll never hit 100% completion of this game because of that one element. If only a mind-controlled character could take command of a helicopter to skip the wallclimbing... :-p
As any three-year-old knows, it is quite satisfying to smash Lego things to bits, and you can do that aplenty in this game. One of the side missions is even entirely dedicated to this pursuit, and the open world of Manhattan also lends itself well for a quick aggression dump between the harder puzzles.
All in all, a game well worth the money.

First thing's first: this game is awesome. There's really no other way about it, especially if you play on iron man mode (which is the most frustratingly fun thing you'll do in a game for a while, I'd imagine).
In short, there are two parts to the game: base management and combat missions. The base management starts you with some money, some undeveloped caves, and some options.  From there, it's up to you. What structures you build, when, and where, is pretty much mostly up to you, and all of those decions are important, especially in the early game, when you'll be hurting for funds. It requires some forethought and some tough decisions.  It's where you build new weapons, research new technologies, perform alien autopsies, and manage your satellite coverage of Earth.
You play as the commander of the X-COM project, which is Earth's military defense against aliens. Over time, UFOs will attack various countries, and if you don't have the ability to stop the attack, their panic will rise. Once the panic levels reach a certain point, that country will drop out of the X-COM project, and you'll lose their funding and such. Once a certain number of countries (four, I believe) leave, you lose.  There are also always more than one attack at once, and you can only stop one, so choosing which country to help and when can have a huge impact on the game, and is yet another interesting choice for you to make.
The combat missions are what really make this game so awesome, though.  You start with a squad of four soldiers that you can completely customize pretty much however you like.  It might sound weird, but you will develop an attachment to your soldiers, and death in this game is permanent.  Once a soldier dies, they're gone for good.  This can be an emotional rollercoaster later on in the game, when losing a soldier not only means losing a character you've grown fond of, but also losing all the time, experience, and resources you poured into training them.  Thus, do you keep a large host of soldiers that you swap out every mission in order to keep them all roughly the same rank, but level up quite slowly, or do you keep using the same ones to get a super powerful squad that, if it falls, you have no way of replacing?
The combat is turn based, and every character gets two actions per turn.  There are also several different classes, such as support (medics), snipers, heavies, and assaults.  They all do pretty much what their name says. You basically have to move your characters around the map (staying in cover!!) and eliminate the alien threat. There are also hostage rescue missions and the very occasional escort mission (which aren't as bad as they are in other games, to be honest).  Because each action has a certain chance of success, balancing positioning, aggression, and your own patience are what keep the game tense and fun.  There are also a bunch of different maps, so you shouldn't see the same ones too often, which is nice.
There is also a story, but it's pretty much what you'd expect from an alien invasion game. That isn't to say it's bad, but it's not what you'll remember this game for.  I found that the stories you developed around your individual characters to be much more exciting (and though it might sound stupid, you will develop these stories as you get attached to them).
The issues that I encountered with this game were minor. Occasionally there will be weird things that happen with the camera during combat animations, and sometimes odd things will happen such as shooting through a wall or boulder, but these are minor, and don't affect the actual gameplay in anyway.
So, if you like strategy games, turn-based games, or really just fun in general, you should try this game.

It's hard to pick between going with a "yes" or a "no" for HL2, as it is an extremely impressive piece of work with mostly excellent gameplay that can at times be very tedious. As someone that comes from the Doom 1 and 2 school of FPS gameplay (tank through levels and frag everything that moves with the biggest gun you have), I must say that I was not a fan of the slower portions of the game, such as Water Hazard, Highway 17, and the first portion of Sand Trap. This was mostly due to the vehicle mechanic presenting a frustrating obstacle more often than not, especially due to various irritating "idiosynchracies" of the physics engine in relation to vehicles. This, more often than not, left me stuck on guard rails if I was not careful. I must say that the airboat portion felt much more orthagonal and navigable than the "scout" (dune) buggy, as I feel that too much time was spent trying to locate the exit from an area whilst being assaulted by fast-moving melee enemies in addition to ranged enimies (civil protection). Although the Tau Cannon is mounted to the buggy, it is more of a hinderance than a help should you try to use it, and I may have gotten four kills with it at most.
That being said, once you finally make it through the blasted "grand theft half-life" portion of the game, things become much more manageable, with standard combat mechanics becoming the norm once again, in addition to the fact that you are now able to dispatch a squad of very sharp, large, alien insects to do your bidding. This is very amusing, and well worth the time spent to get the bug hunt achievment should you want to.
In summary, this is a good title, should you be willing to spend the time to get through the very tedious beginning, with lots of gameplay, amusing humour (should you pay attention to what various NPC's are saying, both to you and to others).
I would also like to note that the soundtrack for HL2 versus the original Half-Life, and Episode One (I have yet to start E2) is rather lacking if you should want an action soundtrack.

One of the most frustrating HOGs I've played. Frustrating because it could have been so much better. The graphics and music are both fitting and immersive and the story is interesting.
Then the annoyances kick in.
For large parts of the game, there is no direction. You find objects but have no idea what they interact with without using the hint button.
There is no indication as to how many parts/pieces you need to complete objectives. Leaving you running around the map with pieces, only to be told you need more, or running around the map looking for pieces when you already have enough.
Some interactive areas give no hint they are interactive unless you click on them.
If you are stuck ... don't worry, you just have to re-visit "every" location in case a HO scene has appeared since you last visited. Missing a piece? explore the entire map for a HO scene .... and that leads to the next problem.
There are a lot of HO scenes ... and that wouldn't normally be a problem, but this game repeats the scenes. You might have to revisit the same HO scene 4 times during gameplay, and not only does it use the same scenes over and over, it uses the same objects! So 80-90% of the objects you are required to find, are the same objects, in the same places, as the previous 2 or 3 or 4 times you did it!
Some objects have poor click detection. You see the fishing rod, you click the fishing rod, nothing happens. You have to re-click in different areas on the object before it is found.
Some of descriptions are un-clear, and the most annoying feature is that sometimes objects with same description are in the scene, but it will only accept one of them. i.e. Find the "peppers". Is it the large red pepper in the middle? no, it's the jar of peppers on the shelf. Find the "nuts". Is it the large bowl of hazelnuts? no, it's the walnuts in the corner.
What's a sac? .... hint .... oh, you mean "sack"
This game could have been so much better, and that's what's annoying about it. Playing through it was an exercise in patience more than enjoyment, and the ending!?!?!? seriously?!?!? .... the payoff at the end was disappointing to say the least.
If you like HOGs, try something else, and if you must, try to pick this one up in a bundle or on sale.

Short Review:
A very solid class based fps focused mostly on "PvE" rather than the usual pvp, with lots of classes to try (10 as of this review) and enough variety in the maps to make you play long enough...until you see that this game's fatal flaw is repetition.
Give it a shot if you loved the first and just want some basic zombie shooter that isn't an asset flip
Avoid it if you never liked the first or just don't want to move on.
Long Review:
Killing Floor is quite a game for me: it was literally my first game purchased on steam (my very first game was actually the orange box as a retail) and thanks to my clan I actually spent countless hours in it, despite being having the flaws of being grindy (reaching level 6, the max, was a chore beyond belief) and also incredibly repetitive. On top of that certain classes weren't as great for higher difficulties, like the Berserker being shred apart or requiring a sniper to kill out Fleshpounds or you'd wipe, so in the end it was very "meta".
KF2 on this regard, feels incredibly polished and despite some flaws, I'm honestly baffled by the amount of cure and detail in it.
First things first, the core game remains the same: various waves (from 4 to 10 + boss) will send you various kind of Zeds that you must kill in order to continue, and while most of them are fodder for your guns you'll eventually get to fight beefy ones (Scrakes, Fleshpounds, husks and eventually the boss) which require some focus to take them down. One of the most interesting features is the perk system which allows you to choose 2 different passives every 5 levels, which is quite useful and gives some variation to the old formula. LEvelling is also straightforward: you must kill with your designated weapon (aka, a sniper must kill with the Winchester) or do something specific (heal with medic, headshots with sniper, etc). On top of that you can also level up other classes thanks to this system by simply using a weapon of another class, although I don't see why you would do that unless you need to support damage.
At any rate, it's simple yet very important upgrades: the grind is still there but each level gives you boost to your stats and every 5 levels will unlock a perk, and each class are pretty useful and give enough variation to the gameplay that I'm genuinely looking forward to try every class
My issue however is...well the game itself: it's repetitive. VERY....VERY repetitive, and this is unfortunately an issue that also the first game had. Sure it's more varied, you can download maps, skins and other things, but the game will remain the same and nothing really changes. I know there's also Survival VS, which should be team deathmatch or something, but I haven't found many groups for it, since that KF2 is essentially a PvE game.
Another issue I found is the stability: I don't have an extremely strong pc but the game tends to crash or stop working quite often, especially right at the beginning. I can play most fps at a reasonable setting, but this game feels very unstable sometimes and right a moment ago, while doing solo for fun, the map started to glitch out and made me nearly have an headache. I hope it's just an occasional bug.
And for last, but not the least, microtransactions: it uses the TF2 system where you either get random drops OR boxes you must unlock for loot, as well as a shop for additioanl stuff to get. I don't like this system personally but I don't like DLCs either, but at least it's entirely cosmetic stuff so that's at least something...for now.
So, do I recommend? Yes! I thought it was great and it's a fun game to play in short bursts: after 1 or 2 matches you'll most likely take a break and stop, but I think that's the way to play: just play a little bit, enjoy, then take a break for a couple of hours and whatnot for then return fresh and ready for more.
...although I can see room for improvement on this.

This is a must have if you're into hardcore, permadeath rogue-like genre like me.
The price is a bit high for what the game is, if you're not sure if you want it then wait for a sale/bundle but no matter the price - I think it's definitely worth it.
It's fast paced, it is brutal as hell, it's unforgiving... but most importantly, It's fair in my opinion. If you screw up - it's your fault because the game gives you everything you need to beat it, it's just hard not to screw up at times. One second you're fully stocked on ammo, guns, have a lot of food and medicine... you open the door and an army of hungry and rogue biounits and reactivated organics along with War Walkers and All-Terrain Heavy laser Squidbots charge your position and - if you're lucky - you made it out alive, you find all you have is a few bullets in your heavy rifle - THAT'S when the game begins, and the game is great at doing that.
You have to scavenge, conserve every bullet (I mean it, once you've played it you'll understand after a few dozens of stupid deaths) and constantly be on your guard. Doesn't matter if you're armed to the teeth, you can get screwed by a single encounter.
- Hard difficulty but it's fair and the game teaches you everything you need to know in the tutorial and during the gameplay itself.
- Simple yet effective graphic design. Some people might say it looks like crap but I think it looks good, especially when considering the dynamic shadows and the way game renders the walls and light sources.
- Good sound design, it's nothing outstanding but considering it's indie and so and that some of the sounds were sourced from different websites I think it works well, and the sound IS important in this game so keep that in mind.
- Cool level design, it reminds me of games like DOOM or Quake but in 2D, heh.
- Enemies. There's nothing wrong about them, really... It's just that you're basically fighting zombies all the way through the game, wish the enemies were a bit more creative. They still have different ranged attacks so at least there's that.
- No way to save middle of the game, no matter what. You unlock save points by beating levels, so let's say you get to level 5 and the game unlocks the start from level 3 for you. Sadly, if you leave middle of the game - tough♥♥♥♥♥♥- you have to start all over again if you want to play again or use one of the unlockable save points. This really, really sucks in this game because it's God damn hard, so let's say you play for 5 hours, have to leave and close the game - boom, gone. No way to continue from that point :(
- Stupid DLC which doesn't even include the soundtrack into the game, you have to play it in a music player. I'd advise not to buy it, unless you want the soundtrack for whatever reason (Again, it's not in game if you don't buy it so you have no idea what the soundtrack actually is, lol)
All in all, I recommend this game.
Have fun!

Do not mistake this game for a Portal remake. It's less about learning the rules and how to apply them... but more about discovering how the creators can well and truly bend the rules to screw with you. In fact, where Portal sometimes suffered with 'puzzles' coming down to how quickly you could react / move - 99% of Anti-Chamber comes down to purely trying to out-think it. The puzzles are divine and the steady inclusion of increasingly-versatile matter guns keep the challenges and dynamics fresh
For the most part, the balance is struck just right: That frustrating mind-ache as you get completely stumped, followed by that invigorating moment when you finally crack it. There's no tutorial, which creates a nice quirk where you're forced to explore, look around and touch things - doing God-knows-what to try to make sense of what is and isn't possible. You can't help but smile weakly as it feels like the puzzles are mocking you in the background... revenge for all those times you laughed as your less-gamer siblings tried to play your games and hopelessly failed. It's surreal but so enjoyable
There's no 'plot' per se... but you are guided around by some very simple, yet beautiful, chalk drawings. They're charming, sometimes quite funny and really add a warm touch to an otherwise sterile environment

I've picked up Teleglitch: Die More Edition during Humble Bundle 13 and I have not regretted it and I'll explain why. Teleglitch builds upon the already well-known rogue-like genre and it does so very well. This of course means permadeath is apparent but the game features an arsenal of weapons and items for you to craft and use against the dangers you might encounter throughout your adventure.
The story revolves around you trying to escape an abandoned military facility on the planet Medusa-1C which now is mostly overrun by the mutants and zombies that the experiments and tests have achieved there. I won't spoil the story for you so I'll stop there but I have to mention the fact that it is quite an interesting story.
Although the game graphically might look dated the atmosphere is certainly there and the world (even though it is abandoned) feels alive. The sound design adds another level to the immersion of the game since it has an incredible ambience to it and most rooms and places have different audio queues to warn or inform the player about the possible threats and dangers.
If you're familiar with the rogue-like genre you know that these types of games mostly consist of "runs". Now Teleglitch provides a great way of randomizing room orders so that the game feels somewhat different on every run. As I said the game randomizes room orders but the room layout stays the same so it is important to known what each room does or what enemies they might have in them. If you've played enough you'll most likely develop a strategy which is essential since certain items are quite rare and you will need them to upgrade weapons or craft (or "combine") useful items.
Don't get fooled by the look of the game because it is quite hard and you often will end up with no bullets and only a simple combat knife to fight your way through the facility. Ammo is scarce and resource management is important. You will soon realize that every missed hit on a target is a huge waste of resources and that you will have to be precise and most of all, completely calm!
Teleglitch is immensely fun and it has a great amount of replay value. It is challenging enough to keep veterans playing but also forgiving enough for new players to get comfortable with the genre. The story is interesting and actually well-thought-out and the sound effects and ambiance is immersive. Only downside I could find about the game would have to be that it is quite short even with the added Arena. That said, I would recommend this game to anyone who would enjoy all the above mentioned points, pick it up as soon as possible!

Resident Evil Revelations 2 was another step in the right direction for Capcom in bringing back horror to the franchise. Revelations 1 helped begin that with Chris, Jill, Jessica, Parker and various other colorful characters, exploring caves, creepy abandoned ships and more.
Revelations 2 takes that up a notch and conitnues to bring the horror.
PROS
-Atmosphere is on point in this game. Pretty much whatever area you are exploring in Rev 2, you are feeling the fear and shadows looming around you and constantly feel like you are being stalked.
-Ammo is rare. And thats a great thing for old school RE fans like myself. Much like the original Revelations, Rev 2 makes you feel like the island you are on is VERY dangerous due to the lack of enemies not dropping ammo and finding ammo being tough at times. Its spread out just enough to make it fair but also makes you save ammo the best.
-Co-op is fantastic, its unlike RE5 and RE6 where you and a friend just gun down swarms of infected, no no! This time, one person is the gunner the other provides follow up assists and skills. There's a strong team work system here that is fantastic.
-Replay Value is VERY high in this game, there's tons of medals to unlock by doing certain requests during the main game, hidden coins to shoot, and various other things to keep the campaign going for max replay value. (The harder setting really puts you through the ringer)
-Raid Mode is 10x better than it originally was. You still have to grind to level up, but honestly, not like how you did in the original Rev1 Raid Mode. Its more fun and relaxing, until you get to the harder levels, then its all business. Plus there's various skills, weapons, characters and ammo to unlock, it'll keep you busy, ESPECIALLY if you got a friend to play it with!
-Barry ♥♥♥♥ING Burton is back! What else do I gotta say!?
CONS
-Dark, yeah the games pretty dark, even if you pump up the brightness, in some areas its just really hard to see, and not how it should be.
-Budget title. The problem with this game is its clearly a budget title. Graphic wise it should look better than it does, and cutscene wise, they dont look as polished as they should be.
-Short in play. Sadly the game isnt that long, even with its side stories you can play, its still not too long of a game. Thankfully the replay value and Raid mode make up for that.
-Janky controls. The run option in this and dodging left or right or even turning while running seems rough and a bit tight, more than it needs to be, its caused a lot of my deaths.
-Grainy effect. I couldnt stand this. I felt like I was playing the game through a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ security camera feed. There is no reason for a game to have grainy effects like that, especially in the era of HD and 720p and higher resolution.
All in all, this game is worth a buy. When I originally bought it on PS3 I was disapointed at how bad it looked but still enjoyed it. Now playing it on the PC, its incredible, beautiful, and runs a lot better and is just as fun as it was when it first came out. Buy it on sale or buy it at full price, this is one RE title you can pay any price for and be happy with.

I purchased Batman™: Arkham Knight at release and I wasn't impressed by it's performance. Had quite some issues and so I waited for a few weeks and when nothing happened except for the removal of the game and the final patch kept being delayed, I did finally uninstall it and forgot about the game. I loved the two predecessors, but Arkham Knight was such a mess, that I lost interest in it. If it wasn't for a Youtube channel that mentioned the game as one of it's must-have games for Playstation 4 it would have been lost in my library forever.
Thanks to this lucky incident it didn't. The game is really great and the story-telling is on point - it even manages to surprise you with some really well done jump-scares. Batmobile is actually fantastic, though it's handling is a bit slippery at first. Arkham is huge and there is so much stuff to explore and do. It was fun sending Batman into retirement. Seeing Batman as the hero of this game series (which fell flat in Origins) I will remember him like Geralt of Rivia, Kerrigan & Raynor and so many others. Batman in the Rocksteady-installment is one of the greatest game protagonists I have ever controlled. The series introduced me to the Freeflow Combat system, something that I have seen in so many games that came after Asylum and I am thankful for that.
I am not thankful for the amount of Batmobile/Tank-battles in the game, but they are not really hard and I did all of them.
I do highly recommend to play the game and finish the triology, especially if you played Asylum and City. And I do highly advise that you leave an "Most-Wanted" mission open for after the last fight if you are not intending to 100% the game that is not the Riddler. This game has a
which will prohibit you from seeing the games ending if you go into the final mission with 13/14 "Most-Wanted" fullfilments. To see the true ending (a slightly longer cutscene) you will have to 100% the game anyways, but being unable to initiate the non-100% ending because the only open one is the case of the Riddler is really horrible. There is something like 250 (!) challenges awaiting and while most of them are not really hard, I think it is an horrible thing to force upon a player because you aren't able to get your bugged game together.
Bugged game? Yes. Sadly. On the technical side it's still horrible, fps drops in the Batmobile are massive when going fast and the final patch, which Rocksteady released after trying to fix the mess that PC developer Iron Galaxy left behind, is actually a sign of sheer incompetence. I lost my trust in Rocksteady. After the first two games you had me, I was yours. That's why I purchased this game on release. Shadow Man is an action adventure game similar in gameplay aspects, dense atmosphere and, dare I say, overall quality, to the Legacy of Kain series. The difference between the two is that this one focuses on ranged combat to the point where even when Shadow Man finds a weapon that kinda looks like a sword, he ends up shooting fireballs out of it. So, instead of hacking and slashing enemies with the Soul Reaver, you will be shooting them with your "Soul Revolver".
Your goal in the game is to go through different areas, while collecting dark souls which are needed to open certain gates, so you can progress further and eventually kill some serial killers (like Jack the Ripper) and the main bad guy, who calls himself Legion ("for we are many") and prevent the apocalypse from happening. Some of those dark souls will be unreachable at first, but throughout the game you will be gaining different abilities like walking/swimming in lava, climbing waterfalls of blood, grabbing to fiery edges, etc., so later you will be able to backtrack and get them. Taking notes while encountering areas you can't reach might not be a bad idea, becuse I can guarantee that there will be moments when you will be confused and have no clue where to go next.
The game has a fantastic atmosphere. While the blurry textures might be a bit of an eye sore nowadays, the music and various unsettling environmental sound effect are great. You will be hearing a lot of moaning, screaming, squeaky noises and even something that sounds like a dentist's drill (the horror). Blood and gore elements are present in the game also, if you're a fan of those type of things.
I haven't encountered any issues when it comes to performance. The game was running flawlessly in high resolution on Windows 7 and crashed only once, but since there is a quick save option, it wasn't a big deal. So, make sure to save often and you should be fine.
The only real problem I have with Shadow Man is the awful final boss fight. The design of the fight is terrible and it is really hard to get a lock on the boss, to be able to shoot him, at least when playing with the keyboard (I have no idea how the gamepad support looks in this game), which resulted in me getting destroyed over and over again. Eventually I got frustrated to the point where I decided to give up. Maybe you will be more lucky and actually beat the game, if you decide to play it. I would highly recommend doing so, because, in conclusion, the game is very good (maybe even one of the best in it's genre?) and I like it a lot.
