My inventory is nearly empty. It always is, I don't know why I thought this time would be any different. My health is low and I haven't seen a can of rejuvenating meat in what seems like hours. Everything is completely silent. In front of me I see a pair of doors leading to the only area I have yet to explore. I take a breath and slowly walk forward.
As the doors open, I hear the screams. A pack of things rush me and I only have a few shells left in my shotgun, not nearly enough to take down this frenzied mass. As I wait for them to get closer, I say my prayers and ready my last explosive. I place it at my feet and, at the last second, run back through the doors. The explosion echoes faintly and, with my gun raised, I wait to see what's going to come rushing through.
This is Teleglitch: Die More Edition.
Teleglitch is a top-down roguelike with omni-directional shooting that launched late last year on PC. The Die More Edition institutes enemy AI tweaks and adds new levels, weaponry and lore information. It tells the story of a hapless researcher stuck in a military complex after a teleporter experiment goes awry and something comes through from the other side. It's a typical sci-fi trope to be sure, but it makes for a quick and easy vehicle to explain fighting monsters, zombies, robots and other genetically enhanced nightmares.
After emerging from his hiding place and pushing aside a clumsily arranged barricade, the silent protagonist must progress from zone to zone, always in search of the next teleporter that will bring him one step closer to freedom. That pursuit is a silent one: Without a backing score and only the faintest inclusion of sound effects (gunfire, monsters screaming and explosions) the silence only amplifies the tension accompanying each step forward. It's an interesting choice to forego any sort of musical accompaniment, one that serves the atmosphere's overall sense of terror in a palpable way.
In Teleglitch: Die More Edition, you can choose to start with only your 9mm pistol (as in the original game) or to spawn with random items - fitting given how integral randomization is to the experience – but it's never enough. You're never truly equipped to handle the situation at hand.
No two sessions of Teleglitch: Die More Edition are the same. The levels are randomly generated, as are the enemy sets, item drops and layouts of each particular wing of the massive facility. And every single level is a haunting endeavor, full of enemies silently milling about, waiting to pounce as soon as they sense your presence. You never know what might alert them – it could be a stray bullet or something as simple as opening a door.
Part of what makes the experience so harrowing is just how strong and unpredictable enemies can be. Low-level enemies tend to employ patterns, behaviors you can monitor and learn and adapt to. Later on, you have to deal with groups of mixed enemy types, and certain baddies start packing guns. One high-level enemy shooting at you is tough enough – surround him with a horde of zombies and panic sets in. And you will panic. Mistakes will be made. Death will be inevitable.
Every enemy in Teleglitch is dangerous, which adds weight to every encounter. Learning and understanding enemy patterns is challenging, but the real payoff comes from exploiting them at a moment's notice during tense, sudden skirmishes – the intrinsic value of Teleglitch: Die More Edition's combat model. When you desperately lead a line of running madmen into a carefully placed bomb and watch seven of them go down at once, it's utterly empowering. And Teleglitch: Die More Edition offers no aid whatsoever. There's no tutorial to guide you by the hand. You're all alone, and you'll have to discover the game's essential strategies organically.
That's a rewarding experience, but it's also a brutally difficult one. Teleglitch is demanding and hostile towards its players, and that's bound to turn some people off. There's incredible satisfaction to be drawn from success, but some may not find it a worthy trade-off for all the frustration.
Outside of discovering random items, a rudimentary crafting system is in place to create your tools of survival. Combining a can with a high-powered explosive and a box of nails can turn it into a devastating nail bomb or a vicious can gun, a single-use weapon invaluable for dispatching crowds at close range. You can create stimulants that boost your performance, modify guns to be even stronger or even build detectors that help warn you of nearby enemies.
The crafting system works well, though sometimes it's impeded by the game's art style, which is full of chunky pixels and basic sprites that can make it hard to see items within the level. It's crucial that you uncover and acquire everything you can, because the game so seldom tosses you a bone. It's a shame, because the art style is unique and beautiful, but it's frustrating to occasionally backtrack through a room and discover you missed a vital pickup the first time around – not to mention however many items you may have overlooked entirely.
Progress in Teleglitch comes at a snail's pace. Every death earns you more knowledge and (hopefully) you get just a little further along each session. Thankfully, you won't always have to restart from the very beginning, as reaching certain levels allows you to start from later in the game. If you reach level five, for example, you can start a new game from level three.
That adds to your sense of accomplishment, obviously, although completing any level in Teleglitch already feels like a triumph. Even the first level is tough, and once you reach the first teleporter it's a satisfying and formative moment, one where eventual victory seems possible – until the next level kicks your teeth in, of course.
Teleglitch's greatest strength isn't the constant tension and the ever-present fear of what lies around the next corner, it's the empowerment you feel from besting the seemingly impossible odds. It's the sense of development, learning from each death and relishing in the sweet moment of triumph when you deftly react to a sudden problem. Teleglitch is a harsh mistress, but the cruelest lessons are often the ones that truly stick with us.
I give Teleglitch: Die More Edition a 4.5/5

Finished in about 13 hours, so I will talk very consciously about it. I didn't know it was an indie kickstarted project developed for smartphones and tablets in mind and this explains a lot of cons.
First, I would like to talk about the gameplay. Having experience with a lot of RPGs and turn-based games I have been disappointed: percentages to hit seem to be flawed, covering system is ridiculous, inventory is caotic, some combo are overpowered (you'll instakill with rifles and relative stats at 8+), experience points are given not by killing enemies, your party doesn't upgrade, AI always attacks first (resolved in S:HK) and it' also dumb (you can wait for them at corners and instakill with overwatch), you are not given so many possibilities of attacking, you can't use your items outside of combat, you are not given the option of using your teamates abilities in the quests, you have a limited choice of weapons and upgrades, etc.
Then, the story: the first hours were nice (I felt like in sci-fi crime scene) but when things started to became interesting... game ended. This is not the only con: 1) Dialogues are scripted, the choices you'll make DO NOT alter the game 2) Skills are useless for dialogues: even when you are given the choice to use them, they just provide a couple of more rows of text to read or just a 20% more money 3) *someone die, so we have to find the culprit* bla bla *turns out all the city is in danger* bla bla  *gear up and go final attack*.
Graphics: from the screenshots it seems to be very powerful... it's not. Just colourful.
The matrix puzzles are few and could be passed easily. Same as the envinroment puzzles: you just have to search a little around. There isn't enough attention to the gameplay.
I enjoyed it? Yes and no. Yes because I like these type of games, no because X-Com, Civilizations, Fallout still stand on a higher level. I would call it a nice time waster. If you are looking for a solid game, you should look elsewhere. Dragonfall is better, but I hope they'll get even better in the next chapters.

Even being a decade or so old, this game still stands the test of time and I can see why gamers loved it so much.
Even by today's standards, the graphics are still brilliant to look at yet run very well on lower-end PCs. And what really makes this game stand out is just how well it gives you a sense of immersion into the plot and setting; it does a great job at making you feel like you're really there and care about what happens.
The game's combat and mechanics are quite good and slick and using the unique weapons such as the gravity gun is quite a blast.
If there's any con to this game, it's that it occasionally feels a little empty, as the player will travel through vast expanses of cityscapes, caves, plains, and deserts and only occasionally run into a hostile encounter. There are also no "bosses" to speak of, and the final encounter isn't particularily challenging. (The additonal chapters however ramp up the action aspect of the game quite a bit compared to the original)
The game can also take quite awhile to complete, and you'll be so immersed in the plot and seeing it through that it'll be hard to put it down.
If you have about 20-30 hours to invest in a game, I recommend giving this one a shot, and seriously doubt you'll regret it (save the fact that the final chapter ends on a cliffhanger, and the sequel promised over 10 years ago has still yet to be released).

I've always been a fan of card games, but I kind of suck at them. After trying for a while to find an online TCG that I could get behind, I settled on this.
It's like a faster, more competitive, less grindey version of Hearthstone. If that sounds appealing to you, give it a try. Game gives you a ton of rewards when you get started and gives away free stuff frequently.
It has the same netdecking/meta problems all online TCGs have, but at least this game's pretty accessible to players who prefer not to spend money on card packs. Currently Shadowverse seems to be adding new cards sets at an acceptable rate, and even gives away free packs when a new set launches.
If this game has one issue looming in it's future, it might be card rotation. The meta's constantly changing, but as of now the sets don't rotate out so problem decks/cards tend to stick around. If you're serious about ranking then you'll probably appreciate that there is far less RNG in this game than some other TCGs, but you'll probably have a hate list of cards once you wrap your head around current decklists. I suppose that's just an aspect of TCGs in general though so I won't hold it against this game.
The only bad thing I can think to say is that the majority of daily missions aren't completable in practice games against the AI or in story missions. Kind of sucks for people like me who like to build up a card collection before they start playing other people, but the daily rewards, mission completion bonuses, and card pack give aways help ease the pain a bit and give you a respectable card base to work with when you finally decide to dive into online matches.

Really fun game with a story that's a pretty even mixture of hype and cheese.
- Runs really well, now.
- The batmobile is way more fun than reviewers led me to believe. Speedy and handles well in drive mode. Easy to control and pretty thrilling in tank mode. The few puzzles that require it are pretty clever.
- Predator and Vigilante combat are both as excellent as they were in previous games. Not all gadgets make it into this game, though (the remote bat claw is one that doesn't make the cut).
- Characters are voiced convincingly.
- The Arkham Knight is a cool villain. The desperate, angry youth vibe he gives off is executed really well by the voice actor and the script.
- The side quests have pretty fun payoffs, even though the journey to reach those payoffs is still a chore. Do this one thing 8 times, then super do it a 9th time with the supercriminal involved.
- Beautiful game is beautiful.
- Gotham feels different than usual. We hang around Wayne Tower, which is usually in an area that's inaccessible in other games. We don't see Amusement Mile, the Bowery, or many of the other memorable locations of City and Origins, though.
- Arkham Knight's closure is pretty cool (his identity and implications for his future).
- The Joker is extremely back in this game. He's way too back for my tastes.
- There are many moments during which a character really needs to stop talking, but they don't stop talking. I'm looking at you, Joker. You too, Scarecrow.
- The chief villain exposition dumping and taunting through a loud speaker is super overplayed and trite, these days.
- The Scarecrow is not a cool villain. He's played like Dr. Strange with a creepy mask. Monotonous tone that's meant to sound menacing. He says the word "fear" approximately 1,000 times per sentence. He overdoes the "verbally describe the hero's psych profile so the audience knows how threatening the villain is" trope.
- Riddler puzzles are still a chore.
- Huge, gigantic, ostentacious narrative conceits for the sake of videogames. For example, Gordon calls some kind of national agency for help in the beginning, after Scarecrow threatens to gas Gotham, everyone evacuates, and the Arkham Knight's private military occupies the city. Gordon hangs up the phone, angry, mutters "bureaucrats," and then tells Batman that they're on their own. That's not even close to the way real life would work.
- Bare minimum boss fights. Outside of the main villains, they're all normal brawls with one tougher enemy (the super criminal). I miss Asylum's boss fights. A lot.
- Arkham Knight's closure is visible almost an entire game's length away. Batman is stumped the whole time. But you know who it is. Feelsweirdman.

Shadow Man is a 1999 action-adventure game in the vein of the old-school Tomb Raider games, brought to us from the long-defunct Acclaim Entertainment.
I'm a stern believer in the idea that a game does not have a shelf-life. It was either always good, or it was never particularly good to begin with and you were simply making do. What flaws Shadow Man does have, and it does have flaws, don't stem from age but from some timeless design.
Shadow Man has a Metroidvania approach to level design. Maze-like levels, with long winding tunnels and massive, multiple-pathed layouts, some of which require abilities to access that you won't acquire for hours yet, Sprawling complexes and perpetually grey wastelands with walls so high and paths so twisty so you can end up in a circle before you realise it.
This is where Shadow Man's biggest flaw comes into play: it doesn't have a map. With level design traditionally designed to confound you and with levels a hell of a lot bigger than you'd expect, getting lost, missing a required entrance or just some small but required detail is a constant threat and hindrance to progress. This can easily become headache inducing as you're combing levels for the umpteenth time searching for a clue to progress, in a game with so many reused texture assets that every go-over just exacerbates the problem.
This lack of a map slam dunks Shadow Man from "cult classic" to "hard sell".
Fortunately that is the biggest of the game's problems and if you can look past that the rest easy to glaze past. It does suffer from some very underwhelming boss fights, an aspect that Acclaim Entertainment was easily infamous for, and the combat itself never evolves from "lock on and strafe/kite while firing charged Shadowgun shots".
Writing - both dialogue and plot - is easily one of the game's stronger features. You play as Micheal LeRoi, an English Lit. college drop-out whose desperation resulted in the death of his family and a stint as an amnesiac hitman, who now serves as the Shadow Man for Mama Nettie, an immortal voodoo warrior for an immortal voodoo priestess haunted by his past and his own bloodied hands. Even on paper it sounds fantastic, and it's almost fully realized ingame.
Micheal LeRoi suffers from some inconsistent writing. At the drop of a hat he'll switch from your usual braindead action-adventure protagonist to narrating dark scenes in prose so purple it's practically ultraviolet, belying his English Lit. education. Micheal LeRoi as an action hero is not nearly as compelling as Micheal LeRoi as a narrator, and it's a shame that Acclaim Studios Teesside didn't manage to fully incorporate the latter into the gameplay.
Antagonists don't far much better. Despite dealing with some hideously and respectably dark themes - sexual assault, suicide, mental retardation - "The Five" come across ingame as a bunch of giggling bufoonish comic book villains. Which while understandable given the source material, completely undermines the themes and ideas behind them. "Legion" especially is straight-up camp.
Art direction is fantastic - the dark and oppressive Deadside atmosphere never lets up for a moment, helped by both that and some truly excellent sound design (as anyone who has played through the infamous Playrooms can attest to) and the locales go wild towards the end with the completely different Liveside areas introduced.
An utter lack of handholding - while resulting in that map problem mentioned earlier - also means that exploring is its own reward. It really captures the spirit of exploration, where every area feels like a surprise and the effort put into finding it feels worth it. The game expecting you to explore in order to earn its secrets even helps it along.
As an aside, there is partial controller support, but emphasis on the "partial". Half the buttons on the gamepad I was using, the game didn't recognize. But given the relatively simple control scheme, rebindind the stupid defaults and using the gamepad anyway was easy enough. There was also a Windows 8 glitch that required running a 3rd party program to force the game to run fullscreen.
Shadow Man is a hard sell. It has undeniable, headache-inducing problems. But despite its shortcomings it remains an incredibly interesting game, definitely worth checking out with those with either a good sense of direction, or those who don't mind getting lost.

There is a grain of truth in calling this game "Hearthstone but it's anime now" but it's so much more than that, and honestly I think it's one of the best card games on the market right now. I'll try not to make too many comparisons of this to other card games on the market, but it's difficult to not do so and still make a compelling argument on why this specific one is worth your time during a time when everyone has their own card game.
Whenever I look into a new card game I'm always a little intimidated because I'm worried it will take a long time for me to make a fun or meta relivant deck in a reasonable amount of time without spending money. This is pretty much a non-issue in Shadowverse which has a dendency to just absolutely bury you in both pack and gold awards. Single player story rewards, ranked play rewards that reset every month, three simple quests per day AND a login bonus is just the half of it. You'll be catching up in no time without spending a cent.
My favorite thing about Shadowverse (which is definitely my biggest problem with Hearthstone while I'm using that comparison) is their willingness to make rebalances to the game in a reasonable amount of time. Anyone who even knows a little bit about current Hearthstone should be fully aware of the dreaded Pirate meta, which went largely unchanged for months despite how oppressive it is. These are digital card games and I think it's important for developers to keep their game fun and competitive. Cygames has shown it's not afraid to to make minor adjustments when things get out of whack and are fairly transperent with win rates and why they make the decisions they do... although you'll have to dig for it, given that this is a Japanese company that often has this information in places more accessable for the Japanese speaking audience.
From there it's simply being a solid and fun game overall. The music is great and the anime art style is extremely high quality. You can link the same account to both iOS and Android, play with friends, and best of all it's free! If you're not keen on games with that anime look and pass up trying this game for that reason alone, you're really missing out on something excellent.
Whether it be with friends, or just by yourself, Civilization V is a masterpeice of a game that brings strategy and great laughs together. 10/10 Would recommend

I think the most advance would probably be the World Shaping. So far, I only used it to get more WP at the cost of double SP usage, but I didn't need to use SP anyway. This is definitely a recommend for JRPG fanatics that love deeper mechanics.

I've heard a lot of bad things about KF2, specifically during its early access stage of the game. How valid the complaints were I don't know, but I went into the game after it's full release expecting something bad. However, what I got was, in my opinion, a very good sequel to a very good game.
Nearly everything has been improved, from the UI, graphics, gore, AI, weapons, music,  map design, and also the perks, as well as a few gameplay changes. The most notable changes are the blocking and parrying mechanics. initially I was put off by the parrying and blocking abilities but after playing a bit more I find that they're not necessary to use in order to win; they're a nice little utility for a player to choose to use if they need to.
Now there's a total of 10 perks, each with 10 skills. You can have 5 skills at max level, every 5th level granting you 1 of 2 skills to pick from as well as every level giving you minor perk bonuses.
This is probably the best change since it allows players to adjust their perks to better suit their playstyle. It's definitely given this berserker player a breathe of fresh air.
The gore is also top-notch, the blood is persistent throughout the match so whatever room you hole-up in will be completely covered in blood and guts the entire game. The enemies also take visible damage when shooting or hitting them with a melee weapon, it's a very neat feature.
Overall, this game took what made the original killing floor so great, and made it even better, it's what a proper sequel should do and this game does it well.

For a game whose name is based on a disgusting meme, I didn't expect much. That's why I was pleasantly surprised that
was actually a decent game.
A game such named needs a story full of toilet humor. Well, you're welcome. It's a shame it's not very fun humor, even with the low standards of toilet humor.
In the story some bad guy has stolen the
, some mythically important artefact, and they send a purple ninja with questionable tendencies to get it back. Every completed level is rewarded with a short, baffling cutscene that makes you ask the ultimate questions:
or even more importantly,
Indeed! Platforming is actually quite well executed.
You can run, jump and throw shurikens. I used Xbox controller to play but keyboard was the default, and as a small inconvenience you have to choose the input device in the options.
The ninja slides a bit after falling on platforms, which can be rather tiny. This sometimes results in some awkward and annoying deaths.
Otherwise, the basic platforming elements are there: bottomless pits, moving platforms, breaking platforms, spikes and sawblades, cannons... Even effing lasers. I found the variety sufficient and platforming sequences adequately challenging.
Weirdly enough, one of the most annoying spots in the whole game was right at the beginning, when you have to jump towards a spiky wall and fall onto the floor beneath it without touching the spikes. I tried it unconfortably many times before succeeding.
Check points are reasonably often, usually just few tens of seconds apart, and respawning is smooth and immediate - there's no annoying waiting for "you died" messages or similar that some games employ.
Of course ninjas have enemies! Some are enemy ninjas that stand there and shoot at you. Some periodically running and chasing creatures are there, as well as the ever popular giant bees.
The two boss fights are not too easy (read: I managed to die a few times), and are pretty well designed as a challenge. It was cool that both fights have their gimmicks that have to realized before they can be beaten.
Shurikens can be thrown in horizontal, vertical and diagonal directions, but since the direction is derived from where you are pointing with the stick (in case of controller), especially shooting diagonally is a bit awkward and may stress your fingers at certain targetting-heavy sequences.
Play it for the platforming and sneer at the stupid story. I consider myself a decent platformer-player and beat it in a bit over 2 hours, even luckily finding all the collectibles in one run (they are cleverly but not unfairly hidden around the levels).
I probably won't play it again, but that's what you get for $1 (or cheap bundle like myself).
My final verdict:
was a surprisingly cool platformer.

There's a stereotype that games make you turn OFF your brain, and are a mindless slug through mundane, disengaging setpieces, This game is a living, breathing, tangible contradiction to that claim. In this part turn-based startegy part base management game, you protect Earth from an invading alien force. Sound familiar? Just another alien game? Rest assured, this game is much more than it appears to be, and is a rare treat for tose looking for a game that pushes you cognitive abilities.

I have never felt my brain go into strategic-overdrive as it did when I played this game. Fair-warning, this game does NOT hold your hand, and to avoid losing (that's right, you can LOSE a 20 hour game) you'll have to be both quick-witted and an effective  base manager. Only those who conduct the proper research, manage resources and money efficiently, smartly equip their soldiers, and maintain their relationships with the countries in the XCOM council will succeed in their turn-based skirmishes, where players control up to six marines to eliminate the alien threat.
The duality of this game is one of its strengths, as the ground battles and the base management go hand-in-hand. Didn't invest in the titan armor research? Well I guess your soldiers are going to perish an unnatural death down on the ground. Failed to protect a member of the council on an important mission? Well I guess Nigeria is pulling out of the XCOM project and thus cutting its funding.
Speaking of failure, that is also another one of the game's strengths, and something you'll be deeply terrified of. You can name and customize your soldiers, and eventually you become attached to them (think pokemon), arming your favorite guy to the teeth and giving him a badass nickname. And these soldiers will go through Hell, facing a mulitude of different alien classes, each with completely distinct looks and effective strategies to use againts. However, your precious characters can die permenantly in these missions if you don't do everything with clockwork effiency. That same urgency extends to the diplomatic side of the game. If you screw up to many times, enough nations will leave the council and you LOSE. This sort of challenge is rare in modern games and is a welcome revival.
All in all, if you're looking for a exhilerating game that engages your brain, tis one's for you.

Over the course of South Park: The Stick of Truth's 12-plus hour running time it throws probably a thousand (or more) jokes at you. Big jokes. Small jokes. Short jokes. Sight gags. Elaborate jokes. Dumb jokes. Offensive jokes. Political satires. Sociological commentaries. Video game commentaries. Commentary commentaries.
In other words, everything you'd expect from a South Park game. And therein lies both its biggest strength—and biggest problem.
The South Park half
The game is an open-world RPG, with the entire town of South Park—and part of Canada—for you to explore. You control the New Kid, a.k.a. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, on a quest to make friends. This quest sucks you into a war between Cartman's human and Kyle's drow elf kingdoms. They're fighting for the titular Stick of Truth—your average, garden-variety stick, except this one has the power to control the universe, ostensibly.
South Park
And then around hour six everything goes off the rails and it all gets way weirder, though I'll leave you to find out how.
Stick of Truth is, in many ways, similar to a two-hour episode of the show stretched over too many hours of game. It looks like South Park and thanks to Trey Parker and Matt Stone's involvement, it sounds like South Park too. Kudos to everyone involved—this is a South Park game that does its lineage proud, at least aesthetically.
South Park: The Stick of Truth had the promise of an unfettered Trey Parker and Matt Stone experience. Freed from the confines of television's oh-heavens-think-of-the-children morality, Stick of Truth could do all the things Parker and Stone couldn't get away with normally.
South Park
And in some ways it did. There are no bleeps here. No blurs either. Just pure, uncensored (sorry Europe) swearing and nudity and fetuses and anuses and farts. As always, South Park is not for those easily offended. Like, seriously. I cannot stress enough how much you should not play this game if you are easily offended or triggered by subjects like, oh I don't know,♥♥♥♥♥♥
Yet despite some so-absurdly-horrific-I-can't-really-decide-whether-I'm-offended occurrences in the latter half, Stick of Truth feels predictable. Like Celine Dion trotting out on stage to sing "My Heart Will Go On" just one more time, I can't shake the feeling that Stick of Truth does what's expected of it and nothing more.
South Park the TV show has made its mark lampooning pop culture, and Stick of Truth is at its best when it's cracking meta-jokes about video games—like lampooning me for spending so much time on side quests and urging me to get back to the main story.
South Park
But South Park's best feature is the rapidity with which Parker and Stone put together an episode. (Watch the fantastic documentary 6 Days to Air if you get a chance.) It bestows upon South Park a wonderful responsiveness no other show matches—a sense of being there, of understanding pop culture and reacting to it on the fly.
Game development is clearly a different beast. Stick of Truth went through one round of delays after another, and while the story is remarkably current for such a troubled game, it mostly relies on your nostalgia for the show.
South Park
Set up the ol' favorites and fart 'em down. Al Gore. Chinpokomon. Jesus. Mister Hankey, the Christmas Poo. At one point you'll battle the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Mouse. There's no joke, per se. Just a pleading, "Remember the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Mouse? Remember how funny that episode was?" Sure I do, South Park. Sure I do. But just showing me something that was funny previously doesn't make it funny again.
As I said, Stick of Truth does what's expected of it, and what's expected of it is fan service. I can't fault them for it, but I also don't think the game is that funny as a result. It's a parade of old South Park jokes you've no doubt seen before or assimilated through the cultural hivemind, and only in rare moments will it really surprise you.
The Obsidian half
That being said, I really enjoyed playing the game. The aforementioned aesthetics are part of it—this is undeniably South Park, construction paper and all. But Obsidian did its job well.
Outside of a criminally limited Options menu on the PC (you can change resolution and gamma and...that's it) and some obnoxious screen tearing (no way to enable Vsync) the game even managed to avoid that legendary Obsidian bugginess during my playthrough—though it sounds like the console versions may not be so lucky.
Character customization is endless here. I ran most of the game as a fourth grade David Bowie, with glam makeup and red mullet, but you could just as easily play as a Goth kid or a bearded hobo with mud on his face.
Combat is active turn-based—similar to the Mario & Luigi games, if you've played them. Your attack can be bolstered or hindered by the way you respond to quick-time events in the midst of combat. For instance, during a standard melee attack if you right click at the correct time you'll do a power attack and inflict more damage.
South Park
You can also use your "magic"—farts—against enemies. You unlock new farts over the course of the game (through some of the worst tutorial segments I've seen in recent history) and each has its own uses in combat. Nagasaki, for instance, can blow enemies out of the combat arena if used properly.
But any sense of tactical depth is largely unnecessary. Combat is fun, but poorly balanced. You'll always fight alongside one companion, and the two of you combined will easily walk through most fights. By the end I was one-hitting most enemies, and thanks to a handy helmet that let me attack again after KOing an opponent I'd then kill every single enemy in my first turn.
Even the harder fights are rendered silly by the sheer number of potions the game gives you. It's hard to feel threatened when you're sitting on a stockpile of fifty or sixty health potions by the end of the game.
South Park
Stick of Truth also falls into the Final Fantasy hole—some of the most powerful attacks are tied to a fifteen or twenty second animation that's funny once, a bit lengthy the second time, and tedious by the third. You end up brute-forcing many battles with the simplest moves just to avoid watching those scenes again, which is a shame.
All that said, the combat is engaging—at least more so than straight turn-based systems. And the team really outdid itself coming up with character-specific abilities; unlocking new companions for use was always exciting.
The real joy, however, comes from exploration. Because it's in exploration that Stick of Truth's fan service feels least obtrusive—just wandering around South Park opening drawers and learning more about the town's denizens. Finding new abilities, Metroidvania style, to open previously unaccessible areas. Reaching that treasure chest you were confused by earlier, and finding a sweet wig inside. It's actually funny the game nags you about returning to the main storyline while exploring, because I found the latter far more interesting.
South Park
Bottom line
If you're not a South Park fan, well, there's not much to recommend. Stick of Truth is the same brand of humor, only distilled. The game is so reference-based, it's hard to know how much you'd understand if you don't watch the show regularly.
But the game's a lot of fun, though less in a laugh-out-loud funny way than a this-is-satisfying way. As I said, Stick of Truth throws a thousand jokes at you and most of those jokes don't stick. There's enough here, however, that South Park fans will want to check it out. This is a respectful and faithful adaptation—something other tie-in games could learn from.
South Park: The Stick of Truth
3.5/5

This is a puzzle game set on confusing the hell out of you in various entertaining ways. It takes about 10 hours to beat, but instead of story and graphics, the game is packed with content instead.
There are, as always, a few hickups:
First of all, if you don't install nVidias PhysX engine, this game will crash upon loading.
Second of all, the game only looks 95% finished. For instance, there is a puzzle that doesn't have a solution, and two dead ends at the end of fairly complicated puzzles. Would this have been a new game, I'd happily sit around and wait for more content, but at this point I can conclude that the author just abandoned any ideas of expanding the game.
There's also the odd viewport bleed glitch, and that platforms with high enough velocity will glitch through obstacles.
Some of the more advanced mechanics can be frustrating to execute, but unless you want to 100% the game, they're optional.
That said, this was a fun puzzler, that set the bar for last year.
I rate it 7/10.

Resident Evil Revelations 2 continues the survival horror series shooty spin off. Revelations was a shooty spin off, but considering RE5 and RE6 one might say the spin off is now closer to the survival horror roots than the main series. It's still a zombie shooter more than survival horror. Somehwt surprisingly, it's also a very good RE game.
I liked the previous Revelations, grinding the raid mode was fun even if the story was a bit forgettable. I think the sequel has a better story overall and equally engrossing raid mode. I'm not a fan of the episodic structure, but as long as you buy the full experience it kinda works ok.
I was a bit reluctant to delve into RE:Rev 2 due to mediocre reviews, but when I finally did it turned to be the best Resident Evil game since a while. Yes, there is quite a lot of shooting, but nothing compared to RE6. Maybe due to the 6th Resi this one feels more survival horrony than usual. Even if it really isn't. It is a lot of fun tho. Story is interesting, doesn't overstay it's welcome at around 12hrs of gameplay and is perfectly complemented by grindy (in a good way) raid mode that can take forever (at more than 50hrs I have only Claire on max lvl). And it's fun!
I liked:
* the story
* feels more resident'y than RE6
* zombies
* shooting zombies
* great raid mode with lots of characters
I disliked:
* invisible mode (and invisible enemies in general)
Get this if:
* you like the Resident series
* you liked RE Revelations
* you'd like to know in another RE story
Don't get this if:
* you like more survival in your horror
* you liked the way RE6 went (ie. you like more shooting and less horror)

While technically a first-person puzzle game (portal, not tetris), the rules of antichamber are not as concrete as in most puzzle games.  Without spoiling anything about this compelling experience, I will iterate that this game's style of puzzles are not something I've seen accomplished in a video game.  Most "puzzles" in this game are not traditional logic puzzles found predominantly in Portal, nor do they require the same cryptic detective work necessary for the Myst series.  Instead what we have here are more like spacial brainteasers manifested into a 3d exploration game.  The world plays around with what we expect to happen in a normal 3D environment, but it does not stick to the now popular perspective swap trickery like echochrome or fez.  Every corner you turn you must learn something new about the world you exist in, and almost none of that applies to the next room.  It somehow does this without ever contridicting itself.  This is not a game for the man looking for a set of logic puzzles like soduko, which increase in difficulty but with static mechanics.  It also does not contain any real narrative, instead preffering the abstract over explicit.  But having a traditional story or characters would dilute the potent head trip offered up here.

There's a stereotype that games make you turn OFF your brain, and are a mindless slug through mundane, disengaging setpieces, This game is a living, breathing, tangible contradiction to that claim. In this part turn-based startegy part base management game, you protect Earth from an invading alien force. Sound familiar? Just another alien game? Rest assured, this game is much more than it appears to be, and is a rare treat for tose looking for a game that pushes you cognitive abilities.

I have never felt my brain go into strategic-overdrive as it did when I played this game. Fair-warning, this game does NOT hold your hand, and to avoid losing (that's right, you can LOSE a 20 hour game) you'll have to be both quick-witted and an effective  base manager. Only those who conduct the proper research, manage resources and money efficiently, smartly equip their soldiers, and maintain their relationships with the countries in the XCOM council will succeed in their turn-based skirmishes, where players control up to six marines to eliminate the alien threat.
The duality of this game is one of its strengths, as the ground battles and the base management go hand-in-hand. Didn't invest in the titan armor research? Well I guess your soldiers are going to perish an unnatural death down on the ground. Failed to protect a member of the council on an important mission? Well I guess Nigeria is pulling out of the XCOM project and thus cutting its funding.
Speaking of failure, that is also another one of the game's strengths, and something you'll be deeply terrified of. You can name and customize your soldiers, and eventually you become attached to them (think pokemon), arming your favorite guy to the teeth and giving him a badass nickname. And these soldiers will go through Hell, facing a mulitude of different alien classes, each with completely distinct looks and effective strategies to use againts. However, your precious characters can die permenantly in these missions if you don't do everything with clockwork effiency. That same urgency extends to the diplomatic side of the game. If you screw up to many times, enough nations will leave the council and you LOSE. This sort of challenge is rare in modern games and is a welcome revival.
All in all, if you're looking for a exhilerating game that engages your brain, tis one's for you.

There is no doubt - "Mirror's Edge" is a masterpiece.
It was released in 2009, but even now it's a pretty good game. In fact, I think "Mirror's Edge" was one of those pattern-makers in game industry, which highly increased awesomeness of first-person-games-gameplay.
This game kinda reminds me "Portal", because the point of the game is finding a way out. That's it.
You can distinguish two parts in "Mirror's Edge".
First one. I'd call it "Flying part", because in these moments you can truelly relax and go with the stream. Just fast running, jumping, finding new directions to go. This part makes an impression of this game, cause it takes the most time of the game.
The second one is a "Puzzle part". Like in "Portal", you can go through the game with insane speed and then BOOM. You got stuck. There was a couple of places where I really got stuck for a long time, but this makes this game more interesting. Sometimes you gotta stop and realise that this game is not about button-mashing. There is some intellectual work here, you know.
So both of these parts are perfectly combined in one game, mixed and interfered from time to time by a simple combat with enemies. And when you play it, it goes really well.
I can't say that there are some deep thoughts in a story-line, jokes in a dialoges or some really unexcpected plot-twists, BUT this game is amazing. It's all about gameplay, I guess, and about this freedom that you feel in a mid-air.
And having good gameplay only doesn't spoil anything. Very unique game. Totally a "must-have".
So go buy it, cause I'm out of words.
